<p><a name="page_15"><font size="1" color="green">p. 15</font></A></p>  <h1 align="center">RECORDS OF ANCIENT MATTERS</h1>  <h3 align="center" align="center">[SECT. I.&#8212;THE BEGINNING OF HEAVEN AND EARTH.]</h3>  
<p>The names of the Deities&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_125"></A><A HREF="#fn_125"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> that were born&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_126"></A><A HREF="#fn_126"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in the Plain of High Heaven&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_127"></A><A HREF="#fn_127"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> when the Heaven and Earth began were the Deity Master-of-the-August-Centre-of-Heaven,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_128"></A><A HREF="#fn_128"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> next the High-August-Producing-Wondrous Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_129"></A><A HREF="#fn_129"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next the Divine-Producing-Wondrous-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_130"></A><A HREF="#fn_130"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> These three Deities were all Deities born alone, and hid their persons.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_131"></A><A HREF="#fn_131"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> The names of the Deities that were born next from a thing that sprouted up like unto a reed-shoot when the earth,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_132"></A><A HREF="#fn_132"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> young and like unto floating oil, drifted about medusa-like, were the Pleasant-Reed-Shoot-Prince-Elder Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_133"></A><A HREF="#fn_133"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> next the Heavenly-Eternally-Standing-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_134"></A><A HREF="#fn_134"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> [16] These two Deities were likewise born alone, and hid their persons.</p>  
<p>The five Deities in the above list are separate Heavenly Deities.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_135"></A><A HREF="#fn_135"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<p>

<p><a name="page_16"><font size="1" color="green">p. 16</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_125"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_125">15:1</A> <a name="page_15"><font size="1" color="green">p. 15</font></A> For this rendering of the Japanese word <i>kami</i> see Introduction, pp. <A HREF="kj003.htm#page_xvii">xvii</A>-xviii.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_126"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_126">15:2</A> Literally, "that became" (<A NAME="img_01500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/01500.jpg">). Such "becoming" is concisely defined by Motowori as "the birth of that which did not exist before."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_127"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_127">15:3</A> In Japanese <i>Takama-no-hara</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_128"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_128">15:4</A> <i>Ame-no-mi-naka-nushi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_129"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_129">15:5</A> <i>Taka-mi-musu-bi-no-kami</i>. It is open to doubt whether the syllable <i>bi</i>, instead of signifying "wondrous," may not simply be a verbal termination, in which case the three syllables <i>musubi</i> would mean, not "wondrous producing," but simple "producing," <i>i.e.</i>, if we adopt the interpretation of the Verb <i>musubu</i> as "to produce" in the Active sense of the word, an interpretation as to whose propriety there is some room for doubt. In the absence of certainty the translator has followed the view expressed by Motowori and adopted by Hirata. The same remark applies to the following and other similar names.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_130"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_130">15:6</A> <a name="page_16"><font size="1" color="green">p. 16</font></A> <i>Kami-musu-bi-no-kami</i>. This name reappears in later Sections under the lengthened form of <i>ami-musu-bi-mi-oya-no-mikoto</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, His Augustness the Deity-Producing-Wondrous-August-Ancestor, and also in abbreviated forms.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_131"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_131">15:7</A> <i>I.e.</i> they all came into existence without being procreated. in the manner usual with both gods and men, and afterwards disappeared, <i>i.e.</i>, died.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_132"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_132">15:8</A> Here and elsewhere the character <A NAME="img_01600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/01600.jpg">, properly "country" (<i>regio</i>), is used where "earth" (<i>tellus</i>) better suits the sense. Apparently in the old language the word <i>kuni</i> (written <A NAME="img_01601"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/01601.jpg">), which is now restricted to the former meaning, was used ambiguously somewhat like our word "land."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_133"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_133">15:9</A> <i>Umashi-ashi-kabi-hiko-ji-no-kami.</i> For <i>hiko</i> here and elsewhere rendered "prince" see Introduction <A HREF="kj002.htm#page_xvi">p. xvi</A>; <i>ji</i> is rendered "elder" in accordance with the opinion expressed by Motowori and Hirata, who say that it is "an Honorific designation of males identical with the <i>ji</i> meaning old man."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_134"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_134">15:10</A> Or, the Deity-Standing-Eternally-in-Heaven, <i>Ame-no-toko-tachi-no-kami</i>. The translation of the name here given follows the natural meaning of the characters composing it, and has the sanction of Tanigaha Shisai. Motowori and Hirata take <i>toko</i> to stand for <i>soko</i>, "bottom," and interpret accordingly; but this is probably but one of the many instances in which the Japanese philologists allow themselves to be led by the boldness of their etymological speculations into identifying words radically distinct.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_135"></A><A HREF="kj008.htm#fr_135">15:11</A> This is a note in the original, where such notes are indented, as has also been clone In the translation. The author's obscure phrase is explained by Motowori to mean that these Heavenly Deities were separate from those who came into existence afterwards, and especially from the Earthly-Eternally-Standing-Deity (<i>Kuni-no-toko-tachi-no-kami</i>) who in the "Chronicles" is the first divine being of whom mention is made. These five were, he says, "separate" and had nothing to do with the creation of the world. It should be stated that the sentence will also bear the interpretation "The five Deities in the above list are Deities who divided Heaven" (presumably from Earth;) but this rendering has against it the authority of all the native editors. As the expressions "Heavenly Deity" and "Earthly Deity" (lit., "Country Deity" are of frequent occurrence in these "Records," it may be as well to state that. according to Motowori, the "Heavenly Deities" were such as either dwelt in Heaven or had originally descended to Earth from Heaven, whereas the Earthly Deities were those born and dwelling in Japan.</P>
<p><HR>

<p><a name="page_17"><font size="1" color="green">p. 17</font></A></p>  <h3 align="center" align="center">[SECT. II.&#8212;THE SEVEN DIVINE GENERATIONS.]</h3>  
<p>The names of the Deities that were born next were the Earthly-Eternally-Standing-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_136"></A><A HREF="#fn_136"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> next the Luxuriant-Integrating-Master-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_137"></A><A HREF="#fn_137"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> These two Deities were likewise [17] Deities born alone, and hid their persons. The names of the Deities that were born next were the Deity Mud-Earth-Lord next his younger sister the Deity Mud-Earth-Lady;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_138"></A><A HREF="#fn_138"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> next the Germ-Integrating-Deity, next his younger sister the Life-Integrating-Deity;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_139"></A><A HREF="#fn_139"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> next the Deity Elder-of-the-Great-Place, next his younger sister the Deity Elder-Lady-of-the-Great-Place;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_140"></A><A HREF="#fn_140"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next the Deity Perfect-Exterior,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_141"></A><A HREF="#fn_141"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> [18] next his younger sister the Deity Oh-Awful-Lady;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_142"></A><A HREF="#fn_142"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> next the Deity the Male-Who-Invites, next his younger sister the Deity the Female-Who-Invites.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_143"></A><A HREF="#fn_143"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">From the Earthly-Eternally-Standing Deity down to the Deity the Female-Who-Invites in the previous list are what are termed the Seven Divine Generations.</p>  
<p>(<small>The two solitary Deities above [-mentioned] are each called one generation. Of the succeeding ten Deities each pair of deities is called a generation.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_144"></A><A HREF="#fn_144"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_18"><font size="1" color="green">p. 18</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_136"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_136">17:1</A> <a name="page_17"><font size="1" color="green">p. 17</font></A> Or, the Deity-Standing-Eternally-on-Earth, <i>Kuni-no-toko-tachi-no-kami</i>, <i>Conf</i>. Note 10 to Sect. I.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_137"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_137">17:2</A> <i>Toyo-kumo-nu-no-kami</i>. There is much doubt as to the proper interpretation of this name. The characters <A NAME="img_01700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/01700.jpg"> ("cloud-moor"), with which the syllables read <i>kumo-nu</i> are written, are almost certainly phonetic, and the translator has followed Motowori's view as corrected by Hirata, according to which <i>kumo</i> is taken to stand for <i>kumu</i>, "integrating," and <i>nu</i> is considered to be an apocopated form of <i>nushi</i>, "master" (or more vaguely "the person who presides at or does a thing"). Mabuchi in his "Dictionary of Pillow-words," Article <i>Sasutake</i>, argues that the syllables in question should be interpreted in the sense of "coagulated mud"; out this is less satisfactory.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_138"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_138">17:3</A> <a name="page_18"><font size="1" color="green">p. 18</font></A> <i>U-hiji-no-kami</i> and <i>Su-hiji-ni-no-kami</i>. The names of this pair tend themselves to a variety of interpretations. Motowori's view of the meaning of the first three syllables in each seems best, if it is founded on the Chinese characters with which they are written in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles," and it has therefore been adopted here. Hirata interprets the names thus: First-Mud-Lord and First-Sand-Lady, and takes <i>ni</i> to be an alternative form of the Honorific <i>ne</i> found in so many proper names. This view of the meaning of <i>ni</i> has been followed by the translator. On the other hand Mabuchi explains the names to mean respectively Floating-Mud-Earth and Sinking-Mud-Earth. The only thing therefore that is granted by all is that the names in question refer to the mud or slime out of which the world was afterwards made. The reader will bear in mind that "younger-sister" and "wife" are convertible names in Archaic Japanese. (See Introduction p. XXXVIII.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_139"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_139">17:4</A> <i>Tsunu-guhi-no-kami</i> and <i>Iku-guhi-no-kami</i>. The interpretation given is one in which the commentators agree, and which has some probability in its favour. It must however only be accepted with reservation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_140"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_140">17:5</A> <i>Oho-to-no ji-no-kami</i> and <i>Oho-to-no-be-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_141"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_141">17:6</A> <i>Omo-daru-no-kami</i>. We might also render <i>omo-daru</i> by "perfect-face," <i>i.e.</i>, perfectly beautiful."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_142"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_142">17:7</A> <i>Aya-kashiko-ne-no-kami</i>. For "awful" we might substitute "venerable." Hirata, commentating on this name and the seven which precede it, says: <i>U-hiji-ui</i> and <i>Su-hiji-ni</i> are so named from their having contained the germs of what was to become the earth. <i>Oho-to-no-ji</i> and <i>Oho-to-no-be</i> are so called from the appearance of the incipient earth. <i>Tsunu-guhi</i> and <i>Iku-guhi</i> are so called from the united appearance of the earth and the Deities as they came into existence. <i>Omo-daru</i> and <i>Kashiko-ne</i> are so called from the completion of the august persons of the Deities. Thus their names were given to them from the gradual progress [of creation]."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_143"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_143">17:8</A> <i>Izana-gi-no-kami</i> and <i>Izana-mi-no-kami</i>. There is some slight diversity of opinion as to the literal signification of the component parts of the names of these the best-known of the Deities hitherto mentioned, though the gist of the meaning remains unchanged. Motowori would prefer to read <i>Iza-na-gi</i> and <i>Iza-a-mi</i>, taking the syllable <i>na</i> as the Second Personal Pronoun "thou," and understanding the names thus: "the Prince-Who-Invites-Thee" and the "Princess-Who-Invites-Thee." It seems however more natural to look on <i>izana</i> as forming but one word, viz., the Root of the Verb <i>Izanafu</i>, "to invite." The older native commentators <a name="page_19"><font size="1" color="green">p. 19</font></A> mean the same thing when they tell us that <i>na</i> is an Expletive. The syllables <i>gi</i> and <i>mi</i> are of uncertain etymology, but occur in other Archaic words to denote the female and male of a pair. The appropriateness of the names of these deities will be seen by referring to Sect. IV.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_144"></A><A HREF="kj009.htm#fr_144">17:9</A> For explanatory notes which are printed in small type in the original, small type is likewise used in this translation.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_19"><font size="1" color="green">p. 19</font></A></p>  <h3 align="center" align="center">[SECT. III.&#8212;THE ISLAND OF ONOGORO]</h3>  
<p>Hereupon all the Heavenly Deities commanded the two Deities His Augustness the Male-Who-Invites and Her Augustness&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_145"></A><A HREF="#fn_145"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> the Female-Who-Invites, ordering them to "make, consolidate, and give birth to this drifting land." Granting to them an heavenly jewelled spear,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_146"></A><A HREF="#fn_146"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> they [thus] deigned to charge them. So the two Deities, standing upon the Floating Bridge of Heaven,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_147"></A><A HREF="#fn_147"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> pushed [19] down the jewelled spear and stirred with it, whereupon, when they had stiffed the brine till it went curdle-curdle,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_148"></A><A HREF="#fn_148"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and drew [the spear] up, the brine that dripped down from the end of the spear was piled up and became an island. This is the Island of Onogoro.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_149"></A><A HREF="#fn_149"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_145"></A><A HREF="kj010.htm#fr_145">19:1</A> <a name="page_19"><font size="1" color="green">p. 19</font></A> For this rendering of the Japanese title <i>Mikoto</i> see Introduction, p. xvi, last paragraph.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_146"></A><A HREF="kj010.htm#fr_146">19:2</A> The characters translated "jewelled spear" are <A NAME="img_01900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/01900.jpg">, whose proper Chinese signification would be quite different. But the first of the two almost certainly stands phonetically for <A NAME="img_01901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/01901.jpg"> or <A NAME="img_01902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/01902.jpg">,&#8212;the syllable <i>nu</i>, which is its sound, having apparently been an ancient word for "jewel" or "head," the better-known Japanese term being <i>tama</i>. In many places the word "jewel" (or "jewelled") seems to be used simply as an adjective expressive of beauty. But Motowori and Hirata credit it in this instance with its proper signification, and the translator always renders it literally, leaving the reader to consider it to be used metaphorically if and where he pleases.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_147"></A><A HREF="kj010.htm#fr_147">19:3</A> <a name="page_20"><font size="1" color="green">p. 20</font></A> <i>Ama-no-uki-hashi or Ame-no-uki-hashi</i>. The best authorities are at variance as to the nature of this bridge uniting Heaven with Earth. Hirata identifies it with the Heavenly-Rock-Boat (<i>Ame-no-iha-fune</i>) mentioned in some ancient writings, whereas Motowori takes it to have been a real bridge, and finds traces of it and of similar bridges in the so-called "Heavenly Stairs" (<i>Ama-no-hashi-date</i>) which are found on several points of the coast, forming a kind of natural breakwater just above water-level.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_148"></A><A HREF="kj010.htm#fr_148">19:4</A> <i>I.e.,</i> "till it became thick and glutinous." It is not easy to find in English a word which will aptly render the original Japanese onomatopoeia <i>koworokoworo</i>. The meaning may also be "till it made a curdling sound." But though the character <A NAME="img_02000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02000.jpg">, "to make a noise," sanctions this view, it is not the view approved by the commentators, and <A NAME="img_02001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02001.jpg"> is probably only written phonetically for a homonymous word signifying "to become," which we find in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_149"></A><A HREF="kj010.htm#fr_149">19:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Self-Curdling," "Self-Condensed." It is supposed to have been one of the islets off the coast of the larger island of Ahaji.</P>

<p><a name="page_20"><font size="1" color="green">p. 20</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. IV.&#8212;COURTSHIP OF THE DEITIES THE MALE-WHO-INVITES AND THE FEMALE WHO-INVITES.]</h2>  
<p>Having descended from Heaven onto this island, they saw to the erection&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_150"></A><A HREF="#fn_150"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> of an heavenly august pillar, they saw to the erection of an hall of eight fathoms.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_151"></A><A HREF="#fn_151"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Tunc [20] qu&aelig;sivit [Augustus Mas-Qui-Invitat] a minore sorore August&acirc; Femin&acirc;-Qui-Invitat: "Tuum corpus quo in modo factum est?" Respondit dicens: "Meum corpus crescens crevit, sed est una pars qu&aelig; non crevit continua." Tunc dixit Augustus Mas-Qui-Invitat: "Meum corpus crescens crevit, sed est una pars qu&aelig; crevit superflua. Ergo an bonum erit ut hanc corporis mei partem qu&aelig; crevit, superflua in tui corporis partem qu&aelig; non crevit continua inseram, et regiones procreem?" Augusta Femina-Qu&aelig;-Invitat respondit dicens: "Bonum erit." Tunc dixit Augustus Mas-Qui-Invitat: "Quod</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_21"><font size="1" color="green">p. 21</font></A></p>  
<p>quum ita sit, ego et tu hanc c&#339;lestem augustam, columnam circumeuntes mutuoque occurrentes, augustarum [<i>i.e.</i> privatarum] partium augustam coitionem faciemus."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_152"></A><A HREF="#fn_152"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> H&acirc;c pactione fact&acirc;, dixit [Augustus Mas-Qui-Invitat]: "Tu a dexter&acirc; circumeuns occurre; ego a sinistr&acirc; occurram." Absolut&acirc; pactione ubi circumierunt, Augusta Femina-Qui-Invitat primum inquit: "O venuste et amabilis adolescens!" Deinde Augustus Mas-Qui-Invitat inquit: "O venusta et amabilis virgo!" Postquam singuli orationi finem fecerunt, [Augustus Mas-Qui-Invitat] locutus est sorori, dicens: "Non decet feminam primum verba facere." Nihilominus in thalamo [opus procreationis] inceperunt, et filium [nomine] Hirudinem&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_153"></A><A HREF="#fn_153"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> [vel Hirudini similem] pepererunt. This child they placed in a boat of reeds, and let it float away. Next they gave birth to the Island of Aha.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_154"></A><A HREF="#fn_154"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> This likewise is not reckoned among their children.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_155"></A><A HREF="#fn_155"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_150"></A><A HREF="kj011.htm#fr_150">20:1</A> <a name="page_21"><font size="1" color="green">p. 21</font></A> The original of this quasi-causative phrase, of which there is no other example in Japanese literature so far as the translator's reading goes, is interpreted by Motowori in the sense of the English locution to which it literally corresponds, and it has here been rendered accordingly, though with considerable hesitation. Hirata does not approve of Motowori's view; but then the different text which he here adopts imposes on him the necessity of another interpretation. (See his "Exposition of the Ancient Histories," Vol. II, pp. 39-40).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_151"></A><A HREF="kj011.htm#fr_151">20:2</A> The original word <i>hiro</i> (written <A NAME="img_02100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02100.jpg">) is defined as the distance between the hands when the arms are outstretched. The word rendered "hall" may also be translated "palace."&#8212;The text of the parallel passage of the "Chronicles" is "they made the Island of Onogoro the central Pillar of the land,"&#8212;a statement which seems more rational and more in accordance with general tradition than that of these "Records."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_152"></A><A HREF="kj011.htm#fr_152">21:3</A> This is Hirata's view of the import of the somewhat obscure original (see his "Exposition of the Ancient Histories," Vol. II, pp. 61-64). Motowori's interpretation is: "auguste in thalamo coibimus."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_153"></A><A HREF="kj011.htm#fr_153">21:4</A> <a name="page_22"><font size="1" color="green">p. 22</font></A> The name in the original is Hiru-go, an instance of the fortuitous verbal resemblances occasionally found between unrelated languages.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_154"></A><A HREF="kj011.htm#fr_154">21:5</A> Literary "foam." It is supposed to have been an islet near the island of Ahaji in the province of Sanuki.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_155"></A><A HREF="kj011.htm#fr_155">21:6</A> Hiru-go was not so reckoned, because he was a failure.</P>

<p><a name="page_22"><font size="1" color="green">p. 22</font></A></p>  <h3 align="center" align="center">[SECT. V.&#8212;BIRTH OF THE EIGHT ISLANDS.]</h3>  
<p>Hereupon the two Deities took counsel, saying: "The children to whom we have now given birth are not good. It will be best to announce this in the august [21] place&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_156"></A><A HREF="#fn_156"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> of the Heavenly Deities." They ascended forthwith to Heaven and enquired of Their Augustnesses the Heavenly Deities. Then the Heavenly Deities commanded and found out by grand divination,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_157"></A><A HREF="#fn_157"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and ordered them, saying: "They were not good because the woman spoke first. Descend back again and amend your words." So thereupon descending back, they again went round the heavenly august pillar as before. Thereupon his Augustness the Male-Who-Invites spoke first: "Ah! what a fair and lovely maiden! Afterwards his younger sister Her Augustness the Female-Who-Invites spoke: "Ah! what a fair and lovely youth!" Tali modo quun orationi finem fecerant, auguste coierunt et pepererunt a child the Island of Ahaji, Ho-no-sa-wake.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_158"></A><A HREF="#fn_158"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Next they gave birth to the Island of Futa-no in Iyo.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_159"></A><A HREF="#fn_159"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> This island has one body and four faces, and each face has a name. So the Land of Iyo is called Lovely-Princess;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_160"></A><A HREF="#fn_160"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> the Land of Sanuki&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_161"></A><A HREF="#fn_161"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> is called Prince-Good-Boiled-Rice;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_162"></A><A HREF="#fn_162"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> the Land of Aha is called the Princess-of-Great-Food;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_163"></A><A HREF="#fn_163"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> the Land of Tosa&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_164"></A><A HREF="#fn_164"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> is called Brave-Good-Youth.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_165"></A><A HREF="#fn_165"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> Next they gave birth to the Islands of Mitsu-go&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_166"></A><A HREF="#fn_166"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> near Oki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_167"></A><A HREF="#fn_167"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> another name for which [islands] is Heavenly-Great-Heart-Youth.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_168"></A><A HREF="#fn_168"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A>&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_169"></A><A HREF="#fn_169"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A></p>  
<p>

<p><a name="page_23"><font size="1" color="green">p. 23</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> This island likewise has one body and four faces&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_170"></A><A HREF="#fn_171"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> and each face has a name. So the land of Tsukushi is called White-Sun-Youth;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_171"></A><A HREF="#fn_172"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> the Land of Toyo&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_172"></A><A HREF="#fn_173"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> is called Luxuriant-Sun-Youth;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_173"></A><A HREF="#fn_174"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> the Land of Hi is called Brave Sun-Confronting-Luxuriant-Wondrous-Lord-Youth;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_174"></A><A HREF="#fn_175"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> the Land of Kumaso is called Brave-Sun-Youth.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_175"></A><A HREF="#fn_176"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> Next they gave birth to the Island of Iki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_176"></A><A HREF="#fn_177"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> another name for which is Heaven's One-Pillar.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_177"></A><A HREF="#fn_178"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> Next they gave birth to the Island of Tsu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_178"></A><A HREF="#fn_179"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> another name for which is Heavenly-Hand-net-Good-Princess.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_179"></A><A HREF="#fn_180"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> Next they gave birth to the Island of Sado.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_180"></A><A HREF="#fn_181"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> Next they gave birth to Great-Yamato-the-Luxuriant-Island-of-the-Dragon-Fly,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_181"></A><A HREF="#fn_182"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> another name for which is Heavenly-August-Sky-Luxuriant-Dragon-fly-Lord-Youth. [24] The name of "Land-of -the- Eight-Great-Islands"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_182"></A><A HREF="#fn_183"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> therefore originated in these eight islands having been born first. After that, when they had returned,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_183"></A><A HREF="#fn_184"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> they gave birth to the Island of Ko[-shima]&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_184"></A><A HREF="#fn_185"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> in Kibi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_185"></A><A HREF="#fn_186"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> another name for which [island] is Brave-Sun&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_186"></A><A HREF="#fn_170"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Direction-Youth. Next they gave birth to the Island of Adzuki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_187"></A><A HREF="#fn_187"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> another name for which is Oho-Nu-De-Hime. Next they gave birth to the Island of Oho [-shima],&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_188"></A><A HREF="#fn_188"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A> another name for which is Oho-Tamaru-Wake. Next they gave birth to the Island of Hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_189"></A><A HREF="#fn_189"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> another name for which is Heaven's-One-Root. Next they gave birth to the Island of Chika,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_190"></A><A HREF="#fn_190"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> another name for which is Heavenly-Great-Male. Next they gave birth to the Island[s] of Futa-go,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_191"></A><A HREF="#fn_191"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A> another name for which is Heaven's-Two-Houses, (Six islands in all from the Island of Ko, in Kibi to the Island of Heaven's-Two-Houses).</p>

<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_156"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_156">22:1</A> <a name="page_23"><font size="1" color="green">p. 23</font></A> The characters <A NAME="img_02300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02300.jpg"> here translated "august place" (the proper Chinese signification is "imperial place") are those still in common use to denote the Mikado's palace.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_157"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_157">22:2</A> <a name="page_24"><font size="1" color="green">p. 24</font></A> For an elaborate account of the various methods of divination practised by the Ancient Japanese see Note 5 to Mr. Satow's translation of the "Service of the Gods of Wind at Tatsuta" in the "Transactions of the Asiatic Society of Japan," Vol. VII, Pt. IV, p. 425 <i>et seq.</i> "The most important mode of divination practised by the primitive Japanese was that of scorching the shoulder-blade of a deer over a clear fire, and finding, omens in the cracks produced by the heat."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_158"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_158">22:3</A> <i>Aha-ji</i> signifies "foam-way," <i>i.e.</i>, "the way to Foam (Aha)-Island," on account, it is said, of its intermediate position between the mainland and the province of Aha in what is in modern parlance the Island of Shikoku. The author of the "Chronicles of Old Affairs" fancifully derives the name from <i>a hoji</i> "my shame." The etymology of Ho-no-sa-wake is disputed; but Hirata, who in the body of Vol. III of his "Exposition of the Ancient Histories" had already expended much ingenuity in discussing it, gives the most satisfactory interpretation that has yet been proposed in a postscript to that volume, where he explains it to signify "Rice-ear-True-Youth." <i>Wake</i> (sometimes <i>wake</i> or <i>waku</i>) is a word of frequent occurrence in the names of gods and heroes. Whether it really signifies "youth," as Hirata believes and as it is most natural to suppose, or whether Motowori's guess that it is an Honorific title corrupted from <i>waga kimi ye</i> (lit. "my prince elder brother," more freely "lord") remains undecided. When it is used as a "gentile name," the translator renders it by "lord," as that in such cases is its import apart from the question of derivation. <i>Sa</i>, rendered "true," may almost be considered to have dwindled down to a simple Honorific.&#8212;It is this little island which is said by the author of the "Chronicles" to have been the caul with which the great island of Yamato was born. Ahaji and Ho-no-sa-wake must be understood to be alternative names, the latter being what in other cases is prefaced by the phrase "another name for whom."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_159"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_159">22:4</A> <i>Futa-na</i> is written with characters signifying "two names," and Motowori's derivation from <i>futa-narabi</i>, "two abreast," does not carry conviction. The etymology of Iyo is quite uncertain. It is here taken as the name of the whole island called in modern times Shikoku; but immediately below we find it in its usual modern acceptation of one of the four provinces into which that island is divided. A similar remark applies to Tsukushi a little further on.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_160"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_160">22:5</A> <i>Ye-hime</i>. For the rendering of <i>hiko</i> and <i>hime</i> as "prince" and "princess" see introduction, p. xvi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_161"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_161">22:6</A> Probably derived, as Hirata shows, from <i>saho-ki</i>, "pole-trees," a <a name="page_25"><font size="1" color="green">p. 25</font></A> tribute of poles having anciently been paid by that province. Motowori adopts the unusual reading of the name given in the "Japanese Words Classified and Explained," viz. Sanugi, with the last syllable <i>nigori&#8217;ed</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_162"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_162">22:7</A> <i>Ihi-yori-hiko</i>. The translator, though with some hesitation, follows Motowori in looking on <i>yori</i> as a contraction of <i>yorishi</i>, "good." The character used for it in the original is <A NAME="img_02500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02500.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_163"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_163">22:8</A> <i>Oho-ge-tsu-hime</i>. Remember that <i>aha</i> signifies not only "foam" but "millet" so that we need not be astonished to find that the alternative designation of the island so designated is that of a food-goddess.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_164"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_164">22:9</A> Etymology uncertain, only fanciful derivations being proposed by the native philologists.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_165"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_165">22:10</A> <i>Take-yori-wake</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_166"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_166">22:11</A> <i>Mitsu-go</i> signifies "triplets," lit., "three children." The three islets intended are <i>Ama-ma-shima</i>, <i>Mukafu-no-shima</i> and <i>Chiburi-no-shima</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_167"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_167">22:12</A> <i>Oki</i> probably here signifies "offing," which is its usual acceptation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_168"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_168">22:13</A> <i>Ame-no-oshi-koro-wake</i>. The syllables <i>oshi</i>, which recur in the names of many gods and heroes, are rendered "great" in accordance with Motowori's plausible conjecture that they are an abbreviation of <i>ohoshi </i>("great," not "many" as in the later language). The translation of <i>koro</i> by "heart" follows a conjecture of Hirata's (Motowori acknowledged that he could make nothing of the word), according to which it is taken to be an abbreviated form of <i>kokoro</i>, "heart."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_169"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_169">22:14</A> None but fanciful derivations of this word are suggested by the native philologists.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_170"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_186">23:9</A> Etymology uncertain, only fanciful derivations being proposed by the native philologists.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_171"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_170">23:15</A> A note to the edition of 1687 says: "Should the word 'four' be changed to 'five?'" For most texts enumerate five countries in this passage with slight variations in the names, Himuka, (Hiuga), which it certainly seems strange to omit, being the fourth on the list with the alternative name of Toyokuzhi-hine-wake, while the alternative name of Hi is Haya-hi-wake, Motowori argues that an enumeration of four agrees better with the context, while Moribe in his Critique on Motowori's Commentary decides in favour of the five. There are thus texts and authorities in favour of both views.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_172"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_171">23:16</A> <i>Shira-bi-wake</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_173"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_172">23:17</A> <i>Toyo</i> means "luxuriant" or "fertile." <i>Hi</i> appears to signify "fire" or "sun." <i>Kumaso</i> is properly a compound, <i>Kuma-so</i>, as the district is often mentioned by the simple name of <i>So</i>. <i>Kuma</i> signifies "bear," and Motowori suggests that the use of the name of this the fiercest of <a name="page_26"><font size="1" color="green">p. 26</font></A> beasts as a prefix may be traced to the evil reputation of that part of the country for robbers and outlaws. He quotes similar compounds with <i>kuma</i> in support of this view.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_174"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_173">23:18</A> <i>Toyo-bi-wake</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_175"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_174">23:19</A> <i>Take-hi-mukahi-toyo-kuzhi-hine-wake</i>. The interpretation of this name follows Motowori.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_176"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_175">23:20</A> <i>Take-bi-wake</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_177"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_176">23:21</A> Etymology uncertain, but there seems reason to suppose that the name was originally pronounced Yiki or Yuki.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_178"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_177">23:22</A> <i>Ame-hito-tsu-bashira</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_179"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_178">23:23</A> <i>Tsu</i> (Tsu-shima) means "port," "anchorage," a name probably given to this island on account of its being the midway halting-place for junks plying between Japan and Korea.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_180"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_179">23:24</A> <i>Ame-no-sade-yori-hime</i>. The interpretation of <i>sade</i> (rendered "hand-net") is uncertain. The translator has followed that sanctioned by an ode in Vol. I of the "Collection of a Myriad Leaves" and by a passage in the "Japanese Words Classified and Explained." Hirata takes <i>sa</i> to be an Honorific and <i>te</i> to be the usual word for "hand," while Motowori gives up the name in despair.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_181"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_180">23:25</A> Etymology uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_182"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_181">23:26</A> <i>Oho-yamato-toyo-aki-dzu-shima</i> (the original of the alternative personal name is <i>Ame-no-mi-sora-toyo-aki-dzu-ne-wake</i>). The etymology of Yamato is much disputed. Mabuchi, in his "Addenda to the <A HREF="errata.htm#7">Commentary</A> on the Collection of a Myriad Leaves," derives the name from <i>yama-to</i>, "mountain-gate." Motowori, in a learned discussion to be found in his "Examination of the Synonyms of Japan," pp. 24-27, proposes three other possible derivations, viz. <i>yama-to</i>, "mountain-place," <i>yama-to</i> (supposed to stand for <i>yama-tsubo</i> and to mean "mountain-secluded"), and <i>yama-utsu</i> (<i>utsu</i> being a supposititious Archaic form of <i>uchi</i>,) "within the mountains." Other derivations are <i>yama-to</i> (<A NAME="img_02600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02600.jpg">), "without the mountains," <i>yama-ato</i>, "mountain-traces" and <i>yama-todomi</i>, "mountains stopping," <i>i.e.</i> (as Moribe, who proposes it, explains), "far as the mountains can be seen." Another disputed point is whether the name of Yamato which here designates the Main Island of the Archipelago, but which in the common parlance of both ancient and modern times is the denomination on the one hand of the single province of Yamato and on the other of the whole Empire of Japan, originally had the wider application or the more restricted one. Motowori and the author of the "Exposition of the Foreign Notices of Japan" seem to the present writer to make <a name="page_27"><font size="1" color="green">p. 27</font></A> out the case in favour of the latter view. Motowori supposes the name to have denoted first a village and then a district, before being applied to a large province and finally to the entire country. The "Island of the Dragon-fly" is a favourite name for Japan in the language of the Japanese poets. It is traced to a remark of the Emperor Jim-mu, who is said to have compared the shape of the country round Mountain Hohoma to "a dragon-fly drinking with its tail." <i>Conf</i>. also the tradition forming the subject of Sec. CLVI of the present translation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_183"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_182">23:27</A> <i>Oho-ya-shima-huni</i>. A perhaps still more literal English rendering of this name would be "Land of the Grand Eight Islands" or "Grand Land of the Eight Islands," for the word <i>oho</i> must be regarded rather as an Honorific than as actually meant to convey an idea of size.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_184"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_183">23:28</A> "To the Island of Onogoro," says Motowori; but we are not told that the god and goddess had ever left it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_185"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_184">23:29</A><i> Ko </i>means "infant" or "small." The original of the alternative personal name is <i>Take-hi-gata-wake</i>. <i>Gata</i> (or, without the <i>nigori</i>, <i>Kata</i>) here and in other names offers some difficulty. The translator renders it by the equivalent of the usual Japanese signification of the character <A NAME="img_02700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02700.jpg">, "direction," with which it is written.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_186"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_185">23:30</A> Etymology uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_187"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_187">23:31</A> <i>Adzuki</i> is written with the characters <A NAME="img_02701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02701.jpg">, which signify a kind of bean (the <i>Phaseolus radiatus</i>); but it is possible that they represent the sound, and not the sense, of the name. In the alternative personal name <i>oho</i> signifies "great," and <i>hime</i> "princess," while the syllables <i>nu-de</i> are of altogether uncertain interpretation. Motowori suggests that <i>mu</i> may mean "moor" and <i>de</i> (for te) "clapper-bell."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_188"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_188">23:32</A> <i>I.e.,</i> Great Island. The word <i>tamaru</i> in the alternative personal name is so obscure that not even any plausible conjecture concerning it has been ventured and the name is therefore of necessity left untranslated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_189"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_189">23:33</A> <i>Hime</i> signifies "princess" or "maiden." The original of the alternative personal name is <i>Ame-hito-tsu-ne</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_190"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_190">23:34</A> Etymology uncertain. Motowori would take the name in a plural sense as standing for the modern islands of Hirado and Go-t&#333; (Goto). The original of the alternative personal name is <i>Ame-no-oshi-wo</i>; in which as usual, <i>oshi</i> is supposed to represent <i>ohoshi</i> (<A NAME="img_02702"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02702.jpg">), "great."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_191"></A><A HREF="kj012.htm#fr_191">23:35</A> <i>Futa-go</i> means "twins." The original of the alternative personal name is <i>Ame-futa-ya</i>.</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_28"><font size="1" color="green">p. 28</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. VI.&#8212;BIRTH OF THE VARIOUS DEITIES.]</h2>  
<p>When they had finished giving birth to countries, they began afresh giving birth to Deities. So the name of the Deity they gave birth to was the Deity Great-Male-of-the-Great-Thing;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_192"></A><A HREF="#fn_192"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> next they gave birth to the Deity Rock-Earth-Prince;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_193"></A><A HREF="#fn_193"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> next they gave birth to the Deity Rock-Nest-Princess;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_194"></A><A HREF="#fn_194"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> [26] next they gave birth to the Deity Great-Door-Sun-Youth;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_195"></A><A HREF="#fn_195"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> next they gave birth to the Deity Heavenly-Blowing-Male;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_196"></A><A HREF="#fn_196"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next they gave birth to the Deity Great-House-Prince;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_197"></A><A HREF="#fn_197"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next they gave birth to the Deity Youth-of-the-Wind-Breath-the-Great-Male;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_198"></A><A HREF="#fn_198"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> next they gave birth to the Sea-Deity, whose name is the Deity Great-Ocean-Possessor;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_199"></A><A HREF="#fn_199"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> next they gave birth to the Deity of the Water-Gates,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_200"></A><A HREF="#fn_200"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> whose name is the Deity Prince-of-Swift-Autumn;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_201"></A><A HREF="#fn_201"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> next they gave birth to his younger sister the Deity Princess-of-Swift-Autumn. (<small>Ten Deities in all from the Deity-Great-Male-of-the-Great-Thing to the Deity Princess-of-Autumn.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_202"></A><A HREF="#fn_202"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> The names of the Deities given birth to by these two Deities Prince-of-Swift-Autumn and [27] Princess-of-Swift-Autumn from their separate dominions of river and sea were: the Deity Foam-Calm; &nbsp;<A NAME="fr_203"></A><A HREF="#fn_203"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> next the Deity Foam-Waves; next the Deity Bubble-Calm; next the Deity Bubble-Waves; next the Deity Heavenly-Water-Divider;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_204"></A><A HREF="#fn_204"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> next the Deity Earthly-Water-Divider; next the Deity Heavenly-Water-Drawing-Gourd-Possessor;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_205"></A><A HREF="#fn_205"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> next the Deity Earthly-Water-Drawing-Gourd-Possessor. (<small>Eight Deities in all from the Deity Foam-Prince to the Deity Earthly-Water-Drawing-Gourd-Possessor.</small>) Next they gave birth to the Deity of Wind, whose name is the Deity Prince-of-Long-Wind.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_206"></A><A HREF="#fn_206"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> Next they gave birth to the Deity of Trees, whose name is Deity Stem-Elder,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_207"></A><A HREF="#fn_207"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> next</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

</p>  
<p><a name="page_29"><font size="1" color="green">p. 29</font></A></p>  
<p>they gave birth to the Deity of Mountains, whose name is the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_208"></A><A HREF="#fn_208"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> Next they gave birth to the Deity of Moors, whose name is the Deity Thatch-Moor-Princess,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_209"></A><A HREF="#fn_209"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> another name for whom is the Deity Moor-Elder. (<small>Four Deities in all from the Deity Prince-of Long-Wind to Moor-Elder.</small>) The names of the Deities given [28] birth to by these two Deities, the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor and the Deity Moor-Elder from their separate dominions of mountain and moor were: the Deity Heavenly-Elder-of-the-Passes; next the Deity Earthly-Elder-of-the-Passes;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_210"></A><A HREF="#fn_210"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> next the Deity Heavenly-Pass-Boundary, next the Deity Earthly-Pass-Boundary;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_211"></A><A HREF="#fn_211"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> next the Deity Heavenly-Dark-Door; next the Deity Earthly Dark-Door;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_212"></A><A HREF="#fn_212"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> next the Deity Great-Vale-Prince; next the Deity Great-Vale-Princess. &nbsp;<A NAME="fr_213"></A><A HREF="#fn_213"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> (<small>Eight Deities in all from the Deity Heavenly-Elder-of-the-Passes to the Deity Great-Vale-Princess.</small>) The name of the Deity they&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_214"></A><A HREF="#fn_214"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> next gave birth to was the Deity Bird's-Rock-Camphor-tree-Boat,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_215"></A><A HREF="#fn_215"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> another name for whom is the Heavenly-Bird-Boat. Next they gave birth to the Deity Princess-of-Great-Food.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_216"></A><A HREF="#fn_216"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> Next they gave [29] birth to the Fire-Burning-Swift-Male-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_217"></A><A HREF="#fn_217"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> another name for whom is the Deity Fire-Shining-Prince, and another name is the Deity Fire-Shining-Elder.</p>  
<p>

<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_192"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_192">28:1</A> <a name="page_29"><font size="1" color="green">p. 29</font></A> <i>Oho-koto-oshi-wo-no-kami</i>. "The Male-Enduring-Great-Things" would be a possible, but less good rendering. This god is identified by Motowori with <i>Koto-toke-no-wo</i> mentioned in "One account" of the "Chronicles of Japan."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_193"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_193">28:2</A> The original <i>Ika-tsuchi-biko-no-kami</i> (<A NAME="img_02900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02900.jpg">) is identified by Motowori with <i>Uha-zutsu-no-wo</i>, (<A NAME="img_02901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/02901.jpg">) mentioned in Sect. X (Note 18). He would interpret the first <i>tsu</i> (<i>dzu</i>) as the Genitive particle and the second as identical with the "Honorific appellation <i>ji</i> of males," such as <i>Hikoji</i>, <i>Oho-to-no-ji</i>, etc. If this surmise were correct, the entire name would signify Upper-Lord-Prince; but it is safer to be guided by the characters in the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_194"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_194">28:3</A> <a name="page_30"><font size="1" color="green">p. 30</font></A> <i>Iha-zu-bime-no-kami</i>. Here too Motowori takes the syllable <i>zu-</i> to be "connected with" the syllables <i>tsu-tsu</i> interpreted as above, forgetting apparently that the second <i>tsu</i> (<i>ji</i>) is said to occur only in the names of males.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_195"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_195">28:4</A> <i>Oho-to-bi-wake-na-kami</i>, a name which Motowori, by supposing corruptions of the text and by making a plentiful use of the pliant and powerful system of derivation with which the Japanese etymologists lay siege to the difficulties of their language, identifies with <i>Oho-naho-bi-no-kami</i>, "the Great-Rectifying-Wondrous-Deity," mentioned in Sect. X (Note 16).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_196"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_196">28:5</A> <i>Ame-no-fuki-wo-no-kami,</i> identified by Motowori with <i>I-buki-do-nushi</i> mentioned in the "Ritual of the General Purification." (See his Commentary on this Ritual, Vol. II, pp. 29-32.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_197"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_197">28:6</A> <i>Ohoyabikonokami</i>, identified by Motowori with <i>Oho-aya-tsui-bi</i> mentioned in "One account" of the "Chronicles."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_198"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_198">28:7</A> <i>Kaza-ge-tsu-wake-no-oshi-wo-no-kami</i>. Motowori's conjectural interpretation has been followed; but both the reading and the meaning of the original are encompassed with difficulties. Motowori identifies this deity with <i>Soko-sasura-hime</i> mentioned in the "Ritual of the General Purification."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_199"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_199">28:8</A> <i>Oho-wata-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>. The interpretation of <i>mochi</i>, "possessor," though not absolutely sure, has for it the weight both of authority and of likelihood.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_200"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_200">28:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, river-mouths, estuaries, or ports. In the original <i>Minato-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_201"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_201">28:10</A> <i>Haya-aki-dzu-hiko</i>. <i>Aki</i>, whose proper signification is "autumn," might also by metonymy be interpreted to mean "dragon-fly" or "Japan." Motowori, <i>&agrave;propos</i> of this name, launches forth on very bold derivations and identifications with the names of other gods. The original of the sister-deity is <i>Haya-aki-dzu-hime-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_202"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_202">28:11</A> The text here omits the word "Swift" from this name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_203"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_203">28:12</A> The original names of this deity and the three that follow are <i>Awa-nagi-no-kami</i>, <i>Awa-nami-no-kami</i>, <i>Tsura-nagi-no-kami</i>, and <i>Tsura-nami</i>, <i>no-kami</i>. The interpretation of the component parts is open to doubt but that here adopted has the authority of Motowori and Hirata.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_204"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_204">28:13</A> <i>Ame-no-mi-kumari-no-kami</i>. The following deity is <i>Kuni-nomi-kumari-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_205"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_205">28:14</A> <a name="page_31"><font size="1" color="green">p. 31</font></A> This Deity and the next are in the original <i>Ame-no-ku-hiza-mochi-no-kami</i> and <i>Kuni-ito-ku-hiza-mochi-no-kami</i>. The etymology is obtained by comparison with a passage in the "Ritual for Averting Fire" (<A NAME="img_03100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03100.jpg">).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_206"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_206">28:15</A> <i>Shina-tsu-hiko-no-kami</i>. The original of this name is explained by Motowori, who founds his view on two passages in the "Collection of a Myriad Leaves," to signify Prince-of-Long-<i>Breath</i>. But the translator feels confident that <i>shi-na</i> by him interpreted in the sense of "long breath" (or rather "long of breath") should he connected with <i>shi</i>, an old word for wind which we see in <i>ara-shi</i> ("storm-wind"), <i>ni-shi</i> ("west-wind"), <i>hi-gashi</i> ("east wind"), and perhaps under a slightly altered form in <i>kaze</i>, "wind," whereas shi nowhere occurs in the sense of "breath." Hirata notices approvingly this etymology of <i>shi</i> ("Exposition of the Ancient Histories," Vol. III. p. 63), though without venturing flatly to contradict his <A HREF="errata.htm#8">predecessor's</A> decision as to the import of the name in question. The difference in the meaning is after all slight. <i>Na</i> is to be taken as an apocopated form of <i>nagaki</i>, "long." In later times <i>Shinato</i> has been used as a name for the north-west wind.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_207"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_207">28:16</A> Such seems to be the meaning of the original <i>Kuku-no-chi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_208"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_208">29:17</A> <i>Oho-yama-tsuna-ka-mi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_209"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_209">29:18</A> <i>Kaya-nu-kimi-no-kami</i>. The etymology of the alternative personal name (in the original <A HREF="errata.htm#9"><i>Nu-dzu-chi-no-kami</i></A> is not quite certain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_210"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_210">29:19</A> The original of these two names is <i>Ame-no-sa-dzu-chi-no-kami</i> and <i>Kuni-no-sa-dzu-chi-no-kami</i>. Their signification is obscure, but the translator has, after some hesitation, followed Motowori's interpretation. The words "heavenly" and "earthly" should probably be considered as qualifying "passes." This word "pass," used here and elsewhere to render the Japanese term <i>saka</i> (<i>sa</i>), must be understood to include lesser ascents than those very arduous ones which are alone denoted by the word "pass" in ordinary English parlance. In the later language of Japan the word <i>tauge</i> (<i>t&#333;ge</i>) generally denotes "passes" properly so called, while <i>saka</i> is restricted to the meaning of small ascents or hills. But this distinction is by no means strictly observed.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_211"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_211">29:20</A> <i>Ame-no-sa-giri-no-kami</i> and <i>Kuni-no-sagiri-no-kami</i>. <i>Sa</i> seems to be rightly considered, as in the two preceding names, to be an archaic form of <i>saka</i> (properly <i>sa-ka</i>, "hill-place"), and <i>giri</i> as an apocopated form of <i>kagiri</i>, (properly <i>ka-giri</i>, "place-cutting") "limit" or "boundary". Hirata however, following the Chinese character with which <i>kiri</i> is written, interprets it in the sense of "mist."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_212"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_212">29:21</A> <a name="page_32"><font size="1" color="green">p. 32</font></A> <i>Ame-no-kura-do-no-kami</i> and <i>Kuni-no-kura-do-no-kami</i>. Motowori explains <i>kura</i> (<A NAME="img_03200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03200.jpg">, "dark") by <i>tani</i> (<A NAME="img_03201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03201.jpg">, "valley"), and <i>to</i> "door" by <i>tokoro</i> (<A NAME="img_03202"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03202.jpg">, "place").</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_213"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_213">29:22</A> Such appears to be the proper interpretation of the original of these two names, <i>Oko-tomato-hiko-no-kami</i> and <i>Oho-tomato-hime-no-kami</i>, <i>tomato</i> being plausibly referred to <i>towomaru</i> and <i>tawamu</i>. It is difficult to find an English word to represent exactly the idea, which is rather that of a gentle <i>fold</i> in the mountains than of the narrower and steeper hollow which we call a "valley."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_214"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_214">29:23</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Prince-Who-Invites and the Princess-Who-Invites (<i>Izanagi</i> and <i>Iza-nami</i>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_215"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_215">29:24</A> <i>Tori-no-iha-kusa-bune-no-kami</i>. The alternative name is <i>Ame-no-tori-bune</i>, from which the title of Deity is omitted. Motowori's Commentary, Vol. V, pp. 52-53 should be consulted on the subject of this deity.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_216"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_216">29:25</A> Homonymous with the alternative personal name of the Island of Aha. (See Sect. V, Note 8).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_217"></A><A HREF="kj013.htm#fr_217">29:26</A> <i>Hi-no-haya-yagi-wo-no-kami</i>. If, as seems likely, <i>yagi</i>, is an incorrect reading for <i>kagi</i>, we should have to translate by "shining" the word here rendered "burning." The alternative names are <i>Hino-kaga-biko-no-kami</i> and <i>Hino-kaga-tsuchi-no-kami</i>. In "One account" of the "Chronicles" and elsewhere in the "Rituals" this fire-god is called <i>Ho-musubi</i> <i>i.e.</i> the Fire-Producer."</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_32"><font size="1" color="green">p. 32</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. VII.&#8212;RETIREMENT OF HER AUGUSTNESS THE PRINCESS-WHO-INVITES.]</h2>  
<p>Through giving birth to this child her august private parts were burnt, and she sickened and lay down.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_218"></A><A HREF="#fn_218"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> The names of the Deities born from her vomit were the Deity Metal-Mountain-Prince and next the Deity Metal-Mountain-Princess.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_219"></A><A HREF="#fn_219"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> The names of the Deities that were born from her faeces were the Deity Clay-Viscid-Prince and next the Deity Clay-Viscid-Princess.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_220"></A><A HREF="#fn_220"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> The names of the Deities that were next born from her urine were the Deity Mitsuhanome&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_221"></A><A HREF="#fn_221"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and next the Young-Wondrous-Producing-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_222"></A><A HREF="#fn_222"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> The child of this Deity was called</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_33"><font size="1" color="green">p. 33</font></A></p>  
<p>the Deity Luxuriant-Food-Princess.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_223"></A><A HREF="#fn_223"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> So the Deity [30] the Female-Who-Invites, through giving birth to the Deity-of-Fire, at length divinely retired.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_224"></A><A HREF="#fn_224"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> (<small>Eight Deities in all from the Heavenly-Bird-Boat to the Deity Luxuriant-Food-Princess.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_225"></A><A HREF="#fn_225"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></small>)</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">The total number of islands given birth to jointly by the two Deities the Male-Who-Invites and the Female-Who-Invites was fourteen, and of Deities thirty-five. (<small>These are such as were given birth to before the Deity Princess-Who-Invites divinely retired. Only the Island of Onogoro, was not given birth to.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_226"></A><A HREF="#fn_226"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and moreover the Leech-Child&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_227"></A><A HREF="#fn_227"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and the Island of Aha are not reckoned among the children</small>).</div></p>  
<p>So then His Augustness the Male-Who-Invites said: Oh! Thine Augustness my lovely younger sister! Oh that I should have exchanged thee for this single child!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_228"></A><A HREF="#fn_228"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> And as he crept round her august pillow, and [31] as he crept round her august feet and wept, there was born from his august tears the Deity that dwells at Konomoto near Unewo on Mount Kagu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_229"></A><A HREF="#fn_229"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and whose name is the Crying-Weeping-Female-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_230"></A><A HREF="#fn_230"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> So he buried the divinely retired&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_231"></A><A HREF="#fn_231"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> Deity the Female-Who-Invites on Mount Hiba&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_232"></A><A HREF="#fn_232"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> at the boundary of the Land of Idzumo&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_233"></A><A HREF="#fn_233"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> and the Land of Hahaki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_234"></A><A HREF="#fn_234"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_218"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_218">32:1</A> <a name="page_33"><font size="1" color="green">p. 33</font></A> "Lying down" (<i>koyasu</i>) is a term often used in the Archaic language in the sense of "dying." But here it must be taken literally, the death ("divine retirement") of the goddess being narrated a few fines further on.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_219"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_219">32:2</A> <i>Kana-yama-biko-no-kami</i> and <i>Kana-yama-bime-no-kami</i>. The translation of this pair of names follows the plain sense of the characters <A NAME="img_03300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03300.jpg"> with which they are written, and which seems appropriate enough, coming as they do between the deity of fire and deities of clay. Motowori however, declaring both characters to be merely phonetic, derives <i>kana-yama</i> from <i>korena-yamasu</i>, "to cause to wither and suffer." And interprets the names accordingly. This is at any rate ingenious.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_220"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_220">32:3</A> <i>Hani-yasu-biko-no-kami</i> and <i>Hani-yasu-bime-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_221"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_221">32:4</A> <a name="page_34"><font size="1" color="green">p. 34</font></A> The signification of this name is not to be ascertained. In the text it is written phonetically <A NAME="img_03400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03400.jpg">, and two passages in the "Chronicles," where this deity is mentioned as <A NAME="img_03401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03401.jpg"> and <A NAME="img_03402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03402.jpg"> with directions in each case to read the name with the sounds here given to it, do not help us much, except in so far as they show that Mitsuhanome was conceived of as the deity of water and as a female.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_222"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_222">32:5</A> <i>Waku-musu-bi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_223"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_223">33:6</A> <i>Toyo-uke-bime-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_224"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_224">33:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "died."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_225"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_225">33:8</A> There is here an error in the computation, as <i>nine</i> deities are mentioned. The total of thirty-five deities given immediately below is still more erroneous, as no less than <i>forty</i> are named in the preceding passage. Motowori makes an ingenious effort to reconcile arithmetic and revelation by supposing the five pairs of brothers and sisters with parallel names to have been considered as each forming but one day.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_226"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_226">33:9</A> See Sect. III. This island was not <i>born</i>, but arose, spontaneously from drops of brine.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_227"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_227">33:10</A> <i>Hiru-go</i>. See the latter part of Sect. IV for these two names, Hiru-go was not counted among the children of these Deities for the reason that the latter abandoned him as soon as he was born, he being a failure. The reason for omitting Aha from the computation is not so clear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_228"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_228">33:11</A> The text here is very peculiar, the characters <A NAME="img_03403"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03403.jpg"> rendered "single child" being where we should expect <A NAME="img_03404"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03404.jpg"> or <A NAME="img_03405"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03405.jpg">. Hirata proposes to consider <A NAME="img_03406"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03406.jpg">, "tree," while most scholars agree in reading <i>ke</i> instead of <i>ki</i> in this place, as phonetic for <i>ke</i> (<A NAME="img_03407"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03407.jpg">) "hair," and to interpret the god's words to signify that he values the child no more than a single hair in comparison with the wife whom that child's birth has lost for him. Moribe, in his "Examination of Difficult Words." s.v. <i>Ko no hito-tsu ki</i> (Vol. I. p. 8 <i>et seq.</i>), ingeniously argues that <i>ki </i>was an old native Japanese "Auxiliary Numeral" for animals, afterwards driven out by the somewhat like-sounding Chinese word <i>hiki</i> (<A NAME="img_03408"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03408.jpg">) which is now in common use, and that the god employs this degrading Auxiliary Numeral in speaking of his child on account of the resentment which he feels against him. On the other hand we gather from the "Chronicles of Japan Explained" that <A NAME="img_03409"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03409.jpg"> was used in its natural sense as an "Auxiliary Numeral" for gods and for men of exalted rank. This seems to the translator the better view to follow, and it is supported by the use of <a name="page_35"><font size="1" color="green">p. 35</font></A> <A NAME="img_03500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03500.jpg"> <i>hashira</i>, as the regular "Auxiliary Numeral" for divine personages. The parallel passage in the "Chronicles" has simply <A NAME="img_03501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03501.jpg"> "one infant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_229"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_229">33:12</A> This rendering is but tentative; for it is not certain that Hirata, whose view has been adopted, is right in regarding Konomoto and Unewo as names of places. If we followed the older authorities, we should have to translate thus: "The Deity that dwells at the foot of the trees on the slope of the spur of Mount Kagu." The etymology of the name of this celebrated mountain (known also as <i>Ame-no-kagu-yama</i> or <i>Ama-no-kagu-yama</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "Heavenly Mount Kagu") is disputed. But Hirata's view, according to which it should be connected with <i>kago</i>, "deer," is the most plausible. If it were established, we should be tempted to follow him in rendering by "deer-possessor" the name of the deity <i>Kagu-tsu-chi</i>, of whom were born the eight gods of mountains, and whose slaying forms the title of the next section. That the fire-deity should be connected with the mountain-deities, and thereby with the deer who roam about the mountains and furnish the hunter with a motive for penetrating into their recesses, is of course but natural. The character <A NAME="img_03502"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03502.jpg"> with which Kagu is written signifies "fragrant"; but it has been suggested that the Japanese word may be connected with an <A HREF="errata.htm#10">expression</A> signifying "heaven-descended," in allusion to the supposed origin of the mountain as related in an old geographical work (now lost) treating of the Province of Iyo.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_230"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_230">33:13</A> <i>Naki-saha-me-no-kami</i>. The sense of the second word of the compound is "marsh" or "stream but Motowori seems right in considering the character <A NAME="img_03503"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03503.jpg"> to be here used phonetically as an abbreviation of <i>isaha</i> from <i>isatsu</i>, "to weep."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_231"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_231">33:14</A> <i>I.e.</i>, dead.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_232"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_232">33:15</A> Etymology uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_233"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_233">33:16</A> For this name see Sect. XIX, Note 6.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_234"></A><A HREF="kj014.htm#fr_234">33:17</A> Etymology uncertain.</P>

<p><a name="page_35"><font size="1" color="green">p. 35</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. VIII.&#8212;THE SLAYING OF THE FIRE-DEITY.]</h2>  
<p>Then His Augustness the Male-Who-invites, drawing the ten-grasp sabre&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_235"></A><A HREF="#fn_235"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> that was augustly girded on him, [32] cut off the head of his child the Deity Shining-Elder. Hereupon the names of the Deities that were born from the blood that stuck to the point of the august sword</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_36"><font size="1" color="green">p. 36</font></A></p>  
<p>and bespattered the multitudinous rock-misses were: the Deity Rock-Splitter,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_236"></A><A HREF="#fn_236"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> next the Deity Root-Splitter, next the Rock-Possessing-Male-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_237"></A><A HREF="#fn_237"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> The names of the Deities that were next born from the blood that stuck to the upper part&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_238"></A><A HREF="#fn_238"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> of the august sword and again bespattered the multitudinous rock-masses were: the Awfully-Swift-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_239"></A><A HREF="#fn_239"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next the Fire-Swift-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_240"></A><A HREF="#fn_240"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_241"></A><A HREF="#fn_241"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> another name for whom is the Brave-Snapping-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_242"></A><A HREF="#fn_242"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and another name is the Luxuriant-Snapping Deity. The names of the Deities that were next born from the blood that collected [33] on the hilt of the august sword and leaked out between his fingers were: the Deity <i>Kura-okami</i> and next the Deity <i>Kura-mitsuha</i>.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_243"></A><A HREF="#fn_243"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">All the eight Deities in the above list, from the Deity Rock-Splitter to the Deity <i>Kura-mitsuha</i>, are Deities that were born from the august sword.</div></p>  
<p>The name of the Deity that was born from the head of the Deity Shining-Elder, who had been slain was the Deity Possessor-of-the-True-Pass-Mountains.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_244"></A><A HREF="#fn_244"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that <A HREF="errata.htm#11">was</A> next born from his chest was the Deity Possessor-of-Descent-Mountains.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_245"></A><A HREF="#fn_245"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that was next born from his belly was the Deity Possessor-of-the-Innermost-Mountains.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_246"></A><A HREF="#fn_246"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that was next born from his private parts was the Deity Possessor-of-the-Dark-Mountains. The name of the Deity that was next born from his left hand&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_247"></A><A HREF="#fn_247"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> was the Deity Possessor-of-the-Dense[ly-Wooded]-Mountains. The name of the Deity that was next born from his right hand&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_248"></A><A HREF="#fn_247"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> was the Deity Possessor-of-the-Outlying, Mountains. The name of the Deity that was next born from his left foot&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_249"></A><A HREF="#fn_248"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> was the Deity Possessor-of-the-Moorland-Mountains.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

</p>

</p>

</p>  
<p>

<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_37"><font size="1" color="green">p. 37</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> The name of the Deity that was next born from his right foot&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_250"></A><A HREF="#fn_249"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> was the Deity Possessor-of-the-Outer-Mountains. (<small>Eight Deities in all from the Deity Possessor-of-the-True-Pass-Mountains to the Deity Possessor-of-the-Outer-Mountains</small>). So the name of the sword with which [the Male-Who-Invites] cut off [his son's head] was Heavenly-Point-Blade-Extended, and another name was Majestic Point-Blade-Extended.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_251"></A><A HREF="#fn_250"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A></p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_235"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_235">35:1</A> <a name="page_37"><font size="1" color="green">p. 37</font></A> One "grasp" is defined as "the breadth of four fingers when the hand is clenched," so that the meaning intended to be conveyed is of a big sabre ten hand-breadths long. The length of sabres and of beards was measured by such "grasps" or "hand-breadths."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_236"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_236">36:2</A> The original names of this deity and the next are <i>Iha-saku-no-kami</i> and <i>Ne-saki-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_237"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_237">36:3</A> Or the Rock-Elder, <i>i.e.</i>, the Male Deity the Elder of the Rocks, if with Motowori we regard the second <i>tsu</i> of the original name <i>Iha-tsutsu-no-wo-no-kami</i> as being equivalent to <i>chi</i> or <i>ji</i>, supposed to be "the honorific appellation of males" elsewhere rendered "elder." The translation in the text proceeds on the assumption that this <i>tsu</i> represents <i>mochi</i>: The purport of the name remains much the same whichever of these two views be adopted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_238"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_238">36:4</A> Explained by reference to the parallel passage of the "Chronicles" through a character signifying "the knob at the end of the guard of the sword.'&#8212;(Williams' "Syllabic Dictionary.")</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_239"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_239">36:5</A> <i>Mika-haya-bi-no-kami</i>. Motowori seems to be right in regarding <i>mika</i> as equivalent to <i>ika</i>, the root of <i>ikameshiki</i>, "stern," "awful," and <i>bi</i> as the root of <i>buru</i>, a verbalising suffix.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_240"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_240">36:6</A> <i>Hi-haya-bi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_241"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_241">36:7</A> <i>Take-mika-dzu-chi-no-wo-no-kami</i>, written with the characters <A NAME="img_03700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03700.jpg">. The translator has without much hesitation followed Motowori's interpretation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_242"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_242">36:8</A> <i>Take-futsu-no-kami</i>. The text name is <i>Toyo-futsu-no-kami</i>. <i>Futsu</i> is interpreted in the sense of "the sound of snapping" by reference to a Passage in the "Chronicles" where it occurs written both ideographically and phonetically in the name of the deity <i>Futsu-no-mi-tama</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_243"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_243">36:9</A> The etymology of both these name is obscure. <i>Kura</i>, the first element of each compound, signifies "dark."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_244"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_244">36:10</A> <a name="page_38"><font size="1" color="green">p. 38</font></A> This is the explanation of the original name <i>Ma-saka-yama-tsu-mi-no-kami</i> which is given in the "Secret of the Chronicles of Japan," and is approved by the later commentators.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_245"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_245">36:11</A> <i>Odo-yama-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>. The English rendering is uncertain, as it rests only on a conjecture of Motowori's, deriving <i>odo</i> from <i>ori do</i> (<A NAME="img_03800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/03800.jpg">), "descending place," "way down."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_246"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_246">36:12</A> The original names of this and the following five deities are: <i>Oku-yama-tsumi-no-kami</i>, <i>Kura-yama-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>, <i>Shigi-yama-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>, <i>Ha-yama-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>, <i>Hayama-tsu-mi-no-kami</i> and <i>To-yama-tsumi-no-kami</i>. <i>Shigi</i>, here translated "dense," seems to be almost certainly a contraction of <i>Shigeki</i>, which has that signification. <i>Ha-yama</i> is a term for which it is hard to find an exact English equivalent. It denotes the lesser hills or first visibly rising ground forming the approach to an actual mountain-range. The signification of <i>to</i> in the last name of the set is disputed. Mabuchi takes it in the sense of "gate." The translator prefers Motowori's view: but after all, the difference in meaning does not amount to much. A third derivation proposed by Motowori is <i>tawa-yama</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "mountains with folds."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_247"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_248">36:13</A> Or "arm."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_248"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_249">36:14</A> Or "leg."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_249"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_250">37:14</A> Or "leg."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_250"></A><A HREF="kj015.htm#fr_251">37:15</A> These two names are in the original <i>Ame-no-wo-ha-bori</i> and <i>Itsu-no-wo-ha-bori</i>. Their import is not absolutely clear, but they seem to designate a weapon broad towards the point, such as is represented in the illustrations given in Vol. I, pp. 19-20 and Vol. II, pp. 4-5 of the "<i>Tokiha-Gusa</i>."</P>
