<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_38"><font size="1" color="green">p. 38</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. IX.&#8212;THE LAND OF HADES.]</h2>  
<p>Thereupon [His Augustness the Male Who-Invites], wishing to meet and see his younger sister Her Augustness the Female-Who-Invites, followed after her to the Land of Hades.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_252"></A><A HREF="#fn_251"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> So when from the palace she raised the [35] door and came out to meet him,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_253"></A><A HREF="#fn_252"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> His Augustness the Male-Who-Invites spoke, saying: "Thine Augustness my lovely younger sister! the lands that I and thou made are not yet finished making; so come back!" Then Her Augustness the Female-Who-Invites answered, saying:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_39"><font size="1" color="green">p. 39</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> "Lamentable indeed that thou earnest not sooner! I have eaten of the furnace of Hades.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_254"></A><A HREF="#fn_253"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Nevertheless, as I reverence&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_255"></A><A HREF="#fn_254"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> the entry here of Thine Augustness my lovely elder brother, I wish to return.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_256"></A><A HREF="#fn_255"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Moreover&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_257"></A><A HREF="#fn_256"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> I will discuss it particularly with the Deities of Hades.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_258"></A><A HREF="#fn_257"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Look not at me!" Having thus spoken, she went back inside the palace; and as she tarried there very long, he could not wait. So having taken and broken off one of the end-teeth&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_259"></A><A HREF="#fn_258"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> of the multitudinous and close-toothed comb stuck in the august left bunch [of his hair], he lit one light&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_260"></A><A HREF="#fn_259"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and went in and looked. Maggots were swarming. and [she was] rotting, and in her head dwelt the Great-Thunder, [36] in her breast dwelt the Fire-Thunder, in her left hand&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_261"></A><A HREF="#fn_260"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> dwelt the Young-Thunder, in her right hand&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_262"></A><A HREF="#fn_260"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> dwelt the Earth-Thunder, in her left foot&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_263"></A><A HREF="#fn_261"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> dwelt the Rumbling-Thunder, in her right foot&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_264"></A><A HREF="#fn_261"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> dwelt the Couchant-Thunder:&#8212;altogether eight Thunder-Deities had been born and dwelt there.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_265"></A><A HREF="#fn_262"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> Hereupon His Augustness the Male-Who-Invites, overawed at the sight, fled back, whereupon his younger sister Her Augustness the Female-Who-Invites said: "Thou hast put me to shame," and at once sent the Ugly-Female-of-Hades&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_266"></A><A HREF="#fn_263"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> to pursue him. So His Augustness the Male-Who-Invites took his black august head-dress&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_267"></A><A HREF="#fn_264"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> and cast it down, and it instantly turned into grapes. While she picked them up and ate them, he fled on; but as she still pursued him, he took and broke the multitudinous and close-toothed comb in the right bunch [of his hair] and cast it down, and it instantly turned into bamboo-sprouts. While she pulled them up and ate them, he fled on. Again later [his Younger sister] sent the eight Thunder-Deities with a thousand and five hundred warriors of Hades to pursue [37]</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_40"><font size="1" color="green">p. 40</font></A></p>  
<p>him. So he, drawing the ten-grasp sabre that was augustly girded on him, fled forward brandishing it in his back hand;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_268"></A><A HREF="#fn_265"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> and as they still pursued, he took, on reaching the base of the Even Pass of Hades,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_269"></A><A HREF="#fn_266"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> three peaches that were growing at its base, and waited and smote [his pursuers therewith], so that they all fled back. Then His Augustness the Male-Who-Invites announced to the peaches: "Like as ye have helped me, so must ye help all living people&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_270"></A><A HREF="#fn_267"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> in the Central Land of Reed-Plains&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_271"></A><A HREF="#fn_268"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> when they shall fall into troublous circumstances and be harassed!"&#8212;and he gave [to the peaches] the designation of Their Augustnesses Great-Divine-Fruit.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_272"></A><A HREF="#fn_269"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> Last of all his younger sister Her Augustness the Princess-Who-Invites came out herself in pursuit. So he drew a thousand-draught rock,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_273"></A><A HREF="#fn_270"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> and [with it] blocked up the Even Pass of Hades, and placed the rock in the middle; and they stood opposite to one another and exchanged leave-takings;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_274"></A><A HREF="#fn_271"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> and Her Augustness the Female-Who-Invites said: "My lovely elder brother, thine Augustness! If thou do like this, I will in one day strangle to death a thousand of the folks of thy land." Then His Augustness the Male-Who-Invites replied: "My lovely younger sister, Thine Augustness! If <i>thou</i> do this, <i>I</i> will in one day set up a thousand and five hundred parturition-houses.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_275"></A><A HREF="#fn_272"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> In this manner each day a thousand people would surely be born." So Her Augustness the Female-Who-Invites is called the Great-Deity-of-Hades.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_276"></A><A HREF="#fn_273"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> Again it is said that, owing to her having pursued and reached [her elder brother], she is called the Road-Reaching-Great-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_277"></A><A HREF="#fn_274"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> Again the rock with which he blocked up the Pass of Hades is called the Great-Deity-of-the-Road-Turning-back,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_278"></A><A HREF="#fn_275"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_41"><font size="1" color="green">p. 41</font></A></p>  
<p>and again it is called the Blocking-Great-Deity-of-the-Door-of-Hades.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_279"></A><A HREF="#fn_276"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> So what was called the Even-Pass-of-Hades is now called the Ifuya-Pass&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_280"></A><A HREF="#fn_277"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> in the Land of Idzumo.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_42"><font size="1" color="green">p. 42</font></A> <a name="page_43"><font size="1" color="green">p. 43</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_251"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_252">38:1</A> <a name="page_41"><font size="1" color="green">p. 41</font></A> The characters in the original which are here rendered Hades are <A NAME="img_04100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04100.jpg">, lit. "Yellow Stream," a Chinese name for the Underworld to which a remark of Mencius and a story in the "<i>Tso Chuan</i>" appear to have given rise. They here represent the Japanese word <i>Yomo</i> or <i>Yomi</i>, which we find phonetically written with the characters <A NAME="img_04101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04101.jpg"> in the name of <i>Yomo-tsu-shiko-me</i> a little further on, and which is defined by Motowori as "an underworld,.... the habitation of the dead,.... the land whither, when they die, go all men, whether noble or mean, virtuous or wicked." The orthodox Japanese derivation of <i>Yomi</i> is from <i>Yoru</i>, "night," which would give us for <i>Yomo-tsu-kuni</i> some such rendering as "the Land of Gloom." A suggestion quoted by Arawi Hakuseki ("<i>T&#333;ga</i>," art. <i>Idzumi</i>) that the word may really be but a mispronunciation of <i>Yama</i>, the Sanscrit name of the Buddhist god of hell, is however worthy of consideration; but it seems best on the whole to translate <i>Yomi</i> or <i>Yomo</i> by "Hades," a term which is itself of uncertain derivation, and the signification attached to which closely resembles the Japanese <i>Shint&#333;</i> notion of the world beyond, or rather beneath, the grave.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_252"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_253">38:2</A> The original text <A NAME="img_04102"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04102.jpg"> seems to be corrupt, and Motowori, unable to make anything of <A NAME="img_04103"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04103.jpg"> leaves <A NAME="img_04104"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04104.jpg"> without any Japanese reading (see the remarks in his Commentary, Vol. VI. pp. 5-6). Mr. Aston, in the version of this passage given in the Chrestomathy appended to his "Grammar of the Japanese Written Language," follows Motowori in not translating <A NAME="img_04105"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04105.jpg">, but does not allude to the difficulty.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_253"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_254">39:3</A> <i>I.e.</i> "of the food of Hades." It would be more obvious (following the text) to translate "I have eaten in the doors [<i>i.e.</i> in the house] of Hades;&#8212;but the character <A NAME="img_04106"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04106.jpg"> in this place stands almost certainly for <A NAME="img_04107"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04107.jpg">, "a place for cooking," "a furnace."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_254"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_255">39:4</A> The word <i>kashikoshi</i> (<A NAME="img_04108"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04108.jpg">), here translated "reverence," exactly corresponds to the modern polite idiom <i>osore-iri-mashita</i>, for which there is no precise equivalent in English, but which conveys some such sentiment as "I am overpowered by the honour you do me," "I am sorry you should have taken the trouble."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_255"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_256">39:5</A> <i>Q.d.</i> "with thee to the land of the living."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_256"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_257">39:6</A> <a name="page_42"><font size="1" color="green">p. 42</font></A>The original here has the character <A NAME="img_04200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04200.jpg"> which signifies "moreover" as in this translation, and Motowori's proposed emendation to <A NAME="img_04201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04201.jpg"> has for it the authority of no manuscript or earlier printed edition. In his "Records of Ancient Matters with the Ancient Reading" he actually substitutes this very new reading, accompanying it in <i>kana</i> with the Japanese words <i>ashita ni</i>, "in the morning." But what is to become of the text if we are at liberty to alter it to suit our convenience,&#8212;for there is more than one other passage where <A NAME="img_04202"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04202.jpg"> is similarly used?</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_257"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_258">39:7</A> Yomo-tsu-kami. Both Motowori and Hirata take the word "Deities" in the Plural, and the translator therefore renders it in that number, though the Singular would be at least equally suitable to the text as it stands. Of the Deities of Hades little or nothing is known. Conf. Note 23 to this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_258"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_259">39:8</A> Literally "the male pillar," <i>i.e.</i> the large tooth of which there is one at each end of the comb.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_259"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_260">39:9</A> The use of the expression "lit <i>one</i> light," where it would have been more natural to say simply "lit [a] light," is explained by a gloss in the "Chronicles," which informs us that "at the present day" the lighting of a single light is considered unlucky, as is also the throwing away of a comb at night-time. It is allowed that the gloss is a late addition, and its statement might perhaps be considered a mere invention made to account for the peculiar expression in the text. Motowori tells us however that "it is said by the natives" that these actions are still (latter part of 18th century) considered unlucky in the province of Ihami, and the same superstition also survives, as the translator is assured, in Yedo itself. It is to be understood that it was the large tooth broken off from the comb which the god lighted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_260"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_262">39:10</A> Or "arm."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_261"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_264">39:11</A> Or "leg."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_262"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_265">39:12</A> The Japanese names of the eight Thunder-Deities are: <i>Oho-ikadzuchi</i>, <i>Ho-no-ikadzuchi</i>, <i>Kuro-ikadzuchi</i>, <i>Saka-ikadzuchi</i>, <i>Waki-ikadzuchi</i>, <i>Tsuchi-ikadzuchi</i>, <i>Naru-ikadzuchi</i>, and <i>Fushi-ikadzuchi</i>. Moribe in his Critique on Motowori's Commentary, has some observation on the appropriateness of each of these names which the student will do well to consult if the work should be published.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_263"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_266">39:13</A> <i>Yomo-tsu-shiko-me</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_264"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_267">39:14</A> We might perhaps with equal propriety render by "wreath" the word here translated head- dress,&#8212;leaves and flowers having been the earliest ornaments for the hair. In later time, however, it has been used <a name="page_43"><font size="1" color="green">p. 43</font></A> to designate any sort of head-dress, and that is also the dictionary meaning of the Chinese character with which it is written. The Japanese words for "head-dress" and "creeper" are homonymous, and indeed the former is probably but a specialised acceptation of the latter.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_265"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_268">40:15</A> <i>I.e.</i>, brandishing it behind him.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_266"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_269">40:16</A> Or Flat Hill of Hades, <i>Yomo-tsu-hira-saka</i>, said by Motowori to form the frontier-line between Hades and the World of the Living. See also Note 27 to this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_267"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_270">40:17</A> The three characters <A NAME="img_04300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04300.jpg"> here rendered "people" are evidently (Motowori notwithstanding) meant to be equivalent to the common Chinese expression <A NAME="img_04301"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04301.jpg">, which has that signification. The word translated "living" means literally "present," "visible."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_268"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_271">40:18</A> <i>Ashi-hara-no-naka-tsu-kuni</i>, a common periphrastic designation of Japan. It is better to translate the name thus than to render it by "the Land in the Middle of the Reed-Plains," a forced interpretation which Motowori and Hirata would only seem to adopt in order to veil the fact that one of the most ancient and revered names of their native land was imitated from that of China.&#8212;everything Chinese being an abomination in the sight of these ardent Shintoists. Yamazaki Suiga, as quoted by. Tanigaha Shisei, is more sensible when he remarks that each country naturally considers itself central and foreign countries barbarous and that Japan is not peculiar in being looked on by its inhabitants as the centre of the universe. This is also the view taken by the other earlier scholars.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_269"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_272">40:19</A> <i>Oho-kamu-dzumi-no-mikoto</i>. The difference between Singular and Plural is not often present to the Japanese mind, and though there were three peaches, we might just as well render their name by the words "His Augustness, etc.," considering the three as forming together but one divinity. The interpretation of the name here adopted is the simple and natural one which Motowori borrowed from Tanigaha Shisei.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_270"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_273">40:20</A> <i>I.e.</i>, a rock which it would take a thousand men to lift.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_271"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_274">40:21</A> That some kind of leave-taking and separation is intended seems certain; but the precise import of the characters <A NAME="img_04302"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04302.jpg"> in the text is not to be ascertained. Motowori's "Commentary, Vol. VI, pp. 29-30 and Vol. X, pp. 52-55, should be consulted for an elaborate discussion of the various interpretations which they may be made to bear. Moribe, in his Critique on this Commentary, argues that "divorced each other" is the proper signification of the words, and supports his opinion by the Parallel passage of the "Chronicles."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_272"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_275">40:22</A> <a name="page_44"><font size="1" color="green">p. 44</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, "I will cause fifteen hundred women to bear children." For the custom of erecting a separate hut for a woman about to be delivered see Introduction, <A HREF="kj004.htm#page_xxviii">p. xxviii</A>.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_273"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_276">40:23</A> <i>Yomo-tsu-oho-kami</i>. On this rather embarrassing statement Motowori is silent, and Hirata simply says: "It must be supposed that the 'Deities of Hades' previously mentioned had been its 'Great Deities' up to this time, a position which was henceforward assumed by Her Augustness Izana-mi (the Female-Who-Invites"). Conf. Note 7 to this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_274"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_277">40:24</A> <i>Chi-shiki-no-oho-kami</i>. [This is Motowori's reading. We might also read <i>Michi-shiki-no-oho-kami</i>]. Motowori conclusively proves that "reaching" is the signification of the word <i>shiki</i> which is here so translated. That it was already obscure at the time of the compilation of these "Records" is however shown by the fact that it is written syllabically in the first instance, and with a "borrowed character" (<i>i.e.</i>, a homonymous word) in the second.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_275"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_278">40:25</A> Because the goddess was turned back by it on the road where she was pursuing her brother-husband. The original is <i>Chi-gaheshi</i> [or <i>Michi-gaheshi</i>]<i>-no-oho-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_276"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_279">41:26</A> <i>Sayari-masu-yomi-do-no-oho-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_277"></A><A HREF="kj016.htm#fr_280">41:27</A> <i>Ifuya-zaka</i>. Moribe in his "<i>Idzu-no-chi-waki</i>" conjectures that Ifuya may be derived from <i>Yufu-yami</i>, "evening darkness," an etymology which has at least the merit of suiting the legend.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_44"><font size="1" color="green">p. 44</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. X.&#8212;THE PURIFICATION OF THE AUGUST PERSON.]</h2>  
<p>Therefore the Great Deity the Male-Who-Invites said: "Nay! hideous! I have come to a hideous and polluted land,&#8212;I have!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_281"></A><A HREF="#fn_278"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> So I will perform the purification of my august person." So he went out to a plain [covered with] <i>ahagi</i>&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_282"></A><A HREF="#fn_279"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> at a small river-mouth near Tachibana&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_283"></A><A HREF="#fn_280"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in Himuka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_284"></A><A HREF="#fn_281"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> in [the island of] Tsukushi, and purified and cleansed himself. So the name of the Deity that was born from the august staff which he threw down was the Deity Thrust-Erect-Come-Not-Place.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_285"></A><A HREF="#fn_282"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> The name of [40] the Deity that was born from the august girdle which he next threw down was the Deity Road-Long-Space.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_286"></A><A HREF="#fn_283"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_45"><font size="1" color="green">p. 45</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> The name of the Deity that was born from the august skirt which he next threw down was the Deity Loosen-Put.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_287"></A><A HREF="#fn_284"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that was born from the august upper garment which he next threw down was the Deity Master-of-Trouble.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_288"></A><A HREF="#fn_285"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that was born from the august trousers which he next threw down was the Road-Fork-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_289"></A><A HREF="#fn_286"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that was born from the august hat which he next threw down was the Deity Master-of-the-Open-Mouth.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_290"></A><A HREF="#fn_287"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> The names of the Deities that were born from the bracelet of his august left hand&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_291"></A><A HREF="#fn_288"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> which he next threw down were the Deities Offing-Distant,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_292"></A><A HREF="#fn_289"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> next the Deity Wash-Prince-of-the-Offing, next the Deity Intermediate-Direction-of-the-Offing. The names of the Deities that were born from the bracelet of his august right hand [41] which he next threw down were: the Deity Shore-Distant, next the Deity Wash-Prince-of-the-Shore, next the Deity Intermediate-Direction-of-the-Shore.</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">The twelve Deities mentioned in the foregoing&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_293"></A><A HREF="#fn_290"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> list from the Deity Come-Not-Place down to the Deity Intermediate-Direction-of-the-Shore are Deities that were born from his taking off the things that were on his person.</div></p>  
<p>Thereupon saying: "The water in the upper reach is [too] rapid; the water in the lower reach is [too] sluggish," he went down and plunged in the middle reach; and, as he washed, there was first born the Wondrous-Deity-of-Eighty-Evils, and next the Wondrous-Deity-of-Great-Evils.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_294"></A><A HREF="#fn_291"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> These two Deities are the Deities that were born from the filth [he contracted] when he went to that polluted, hideous land.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_295"></A><A HREF="#fn_292"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> The names of the Deities that were next born to rectify those evils were:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_46"><font size="1" color="green">p. 46</font></A></p>  
<p>the Divine-Rectifying-Wondrous Deity, next the Great-Rectifying-Wondrous-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_296"></A><A HREF="#fn_293"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> next the Female-Deity-Idzu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_297"></A><A HREF="#fn_294"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> The names of the Deities that were next born, as he bathed at the bottom of the water, were: the Deity Possessor-of-the-Ocean-Bottom,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_298"></A><A HREF="#fn_295"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> and next His Augustness Elder-Male-of-the-Bottom. The names of the Deities that were born as he bathed in the middle [of the water] were: the Deity Possessor-of-the-Ocean-Middle, and next His Augustness Elder-Male-of-the-Middle. The names of the Deities that were born as he bathed at the top of the water were the Deity Possessor-of-the-Ocean-Surface, and next His Augustness Elder-Male-of-the-Surface. These three Ocean-Possessing Deities are the Deities held in reverence as their ancestral Deities by the Chiefs of Adzumi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_299"></A><A HREF="#fn_296"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> So the Chiefs of Adzumi are the descendants of His Augustness <i>Utsushi-hi-gana-saku</i>,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_300"></A><A HREF="#fn_297"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> a child of these Ocean-Possessing Deities.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_301"></A><A HREF="#fn_298"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> These three Deities His Augustness Elder-Male-of-the-Bottom, His Augustness Elder-Male-of-the-Middle, and His Augustness Elder-Male-of-the-Surface are the three Great Deities of the Inlet of Sumi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_302"></A><A HREF="#fn_299"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that was born as he thereupon washed his left august eye was the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_303"></A><A HREF="#fn_300"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that was next born as he washed his right august eye was His Augustness, Moon-Night Possessor.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_304"></A><A HREF="#fn_301"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> The name of the Deity that was next born as he washed his august nose was His Brave-Swift-impetuous-Male-Augustness.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_305"></A><A HREF="#fn_302"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">The fourteen Deities in the foregoing list from the Wondrous-Deity-of-Eighty-Evils down to His Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness are Deities born from the bathing of his august person.</div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<p><a name="page_47"><font size="1" color="green">p. 47</font></A> <a name="page_48"><font size="1" color="green">p. 48</font></A> <a name="page_49"><font size="1" color="green">p. 49</font></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_278"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_281">44:1</A> <a name="page_47"><font size="1" color="green">p. 47</font></A> The words "I have" thus repeated are an attempt to render the concluding words <i>ari keri</i> of the sentence in the original, by which, though they have no particular sense, the author evidently set great store, as he writes them syllabically. They may be considered to emphasize what goes before and, says Motowori, "convey the idea of lamentation." The idiom occurs some half-dozen times in the course of the present work.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_279"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_282">44:2</A> This botanical name is identified by Arawi Hakuseki and Hirata with the modern <i>hagi</i>, or "bushclover" (<i>lespdeza</i> of various species). The received opinion used to be that the <i>awoki</i> (<i>Aucuba Japonica</i>) was here intended.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_280"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_283">44:3</A> Tachibana is understood to be the general designation of trees of the orange tribe. (See however Sect. LXXIV, Note 7). Here it is used as a proper name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_281"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_284">44:4</A> This name, which signifies "sun-confronting," was not unnaturally bestowed on a province in the eastern part of the westernmost of the larger Japanese islands, as it might well be conceived as lying "opposite the sun." It has, however, been <A HREF="errata.htm#12">supposed</A> to have originally denoted the whole of the island in question. In any case the name is not inappropriate, as the island has a long eastern sea-board.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_282"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_285">44:5</A> In our text <i>Tsuki-tatsu-funa-do</i>. But <i>funa</i> should almost certainly be <i>ku-na</i>, and the name (which has here been translated accordingly) is then illustrated by the more extended version of this myth which is given in the "Chronicles," where we read that the god (probably addressing his sister) threw down his staff with the words: "Come no further." "Stand" must be understood in a Transitive sense: the god <i>stood</i> his staff up by thrusting it into the sand.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_283"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_286">44:6</A> This is Moribe's explanation ("<i>Idzu-no-Chi-waki</i>." Vol. IV, p. 44) of the meaning of the original name <i>Michi-no-naga-chiha-no-kami</i>, the syllable <i>ha</i> of which is considered by him to be an alternative form of <i>ma</i> (<A NAME="img_04700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04700.jpg">, "space"). It is however a great crux, and Motowori confesses his inability to explain it satisfactorily. Other views as to the import of the syllable in question will be found in the "<i>Jin-dai no maki Mo-shiho-gusa</i>." Vol. II. p. 29.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_284"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_287">45:7</A> This seems to be the meaning of the original name, if we retain the reading <i>Toki-okashi-no-kami</i>. See however Motowori's remarks <i>in loco</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_285"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_288">45:8</A> <i>Wadzurahi-no-ushi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_286"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_289">45:9</A> <i>Chi-mata-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_287"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_290">45:10</A> <a name="page_48"><font size="1" color="green">p. 48</font></A> <i>Aki-guhi-no-ushi-no-kami</i>. The English rendering of this obscure name proceeds on the assumption that Motowori is correct when he proposes to consider <i>kuhi</i> as equivalent in this place to <i>kuchi</i>, "mouth." The gaping trousers no longer filled by the deity's legs would perhaps suggest the idea of an open mouth, though it is true that this is not the deity said to have been actually born from that portion of the attire.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_288"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_291">45:11</A> or "arm."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_289"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_292">45:12</A> The names of this deity and the five who follow are in the original <i>Oki-zakaru-no-kami</i>, <i>Oki-tsu-nagisa-biko-no-kami</i>, <i>Oki-tsu-kahi-bera-no-kami</i>, <i>He-zakaru-no-kami</i>, <i>He-tsu-nagisa-biko-no-kami</i> and <i>He-tsu-kahi-bera-no-kami</i>. The word "wash," by which for want of a better one the Substantive <i>nagisa</i> has been rendered, must be understood to signify the part nearest to the strand o the sea or of a river,&#8212;the boundary of the waves. The third and sixth of this set of names, in which the syllables <i>kahi-bera</i> (here represented by "Intermediate Direction") offer a good deal of difficulty, have been translated in accordance with Motowori's explanation of their probable meaning.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_290"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_293">45:13</A> Lit. "right." In Chinese and Japanese compositions the lines follow each other from right to left instead of from top to bottom as with us. "Right" therefore signifies "foregoing," and "left," "following."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_291"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_294">45:14</A> The names of these two deities in the original are <i>Ya-so-maga-tsu-bi-no-kami</i> and <i>Oho-maga-tsu-bi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_292"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_295">45:15</A> Viv. to Hades.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_293"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_296">46:16</A> The names of these two deities in the original are <i>Kamu-naho-bi-no-kami</i> and <i>Oho-na-ho-bi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_294"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_297">46:17</A> <i>Idzu-no-me-no-kami</i>. The word <i>Idzu</i> is incomprehensible, unless indeed, following Motowori, we identify this goddess with the god and goddess <i>Haya-aki-dzu-hiko</i> and <i>Haya-aki-dsu-hime</i> mentioned in Sect. VI, Note 10, and consider <i>idzu</i> as standing by apheresis for <i>aki-dsu</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_295"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_298">46:18</A> The original names of this deity and the five who follow are <i>Soko-tsu-wata-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>, <i>Soko-dzutsu-no-wo-no-mi-koto</i>, <i>Naka-tsu-wata-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>, <i>Naka-dzutsu-no-wo-mikoto</i>, <i>Uha-tsu-wata-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>, and <i>Uha-dzutsu-no-wo-no-mikoto</i>. There is the usual doubt as to the signification to be assigned to the syllable <i>tsu</i> in the second, fourth and last of these names. If it really means, not "elder" but "possessor," we should be obliged to translate by "the Bottom-<A HREF="errata.htm#13"><i>Possessing</i></A>-Male." etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_296"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_299">46:19</A> <i>Adumi-no-murazhi</i>. This name is said by Motowori to be taken from that of a place in the province of Shinano. But Moribe shows that <a name="page_49"><font size="1" color="green">p. 49</font></A> at any rate the etymology of the word may be traced to <i>ama-tsu-mochi</i>, "Possessors of fishermen."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_297"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_300">46:20</A> It is impossible to translate this name which, according to Motowori, is derived from those of two districts in Shinano to which the word <i>utsushi</i> (for <i>utsutsu</i>, "present" or "living") is prefixed.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_298"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_301">46:21</A> Attention must again be drawn to the vagueness of the Japanese perception of the distinction between Singular and Plural. As three deities are particularly and repeatedly mentioned in the foregoing text, we are forced to translate this passage in the Plural; and yet how could one child have three fathers?</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_299"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_302">46:22</A> <i>Sumi-no-ye</i>, also called <i>Sumi-yoshi</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, by a play upon words, "pleasant to dwell in." The real etymology of <i>sumi</i> is not certain.&#8212;Instead of "the three Great Deities," we might translate by "the Great Deities of the Three Shrines."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_300"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_303">46:23</A> <i>Ama-terasu-oho-mi-kami</i> (<A NAME="img_04900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04900.jpg">). The reading <i>terasu</i>, which is established by the authority of the "Collection of a Myriad Leaves" and by almost universal usage, must not mislead the student into imagining that the Verb, because it is Causative in form, has a Causative meaning which would require some such English translation as "Heaven-Illuminating." The Causative form is simply Honorific, and the two words <i>ama terasu</i> signify, as Motowori explains, "shining in heaven."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_301"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_304">46:24</A> <i>Tsuki-yomi-no-kami</i>. There is no doubt as to a moon-god being intended, but the precise import of the name is disputed. The translator has followed Mabuchi's view as quoted by Motowori, and which is supported by the fact that, from classical times down to the present day, <i>tsuku-yo</i> or <i>tsuki-yo</i> has been a word in common use to denote a fine moonlight night. If we were to take <i>yomi</i> as one word, we should have to render it either by "Moon-Hades" or by "Moon-Darkness," which seem less appropriate designations, though still of plain enough intent. The characters <A NAME="img_04901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04901.jpg">, <A NAME="img_04902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04902.jpg"> and <A NAME="img_04903"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/04903.jpg">, with which the name is variously written, seem all phonetic unless we might take the second set to mean the crescent (lit. "moon-bow).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_302"></A><A HREF="kj017.htm#fr_305">46:25</A> <i>Take-haya-susa-no-wo-no-mikoto</i>. <i>Susa</i>, which is sometimes read <i>Sosa</i>, is rendered by the word "impetuous" in accordance with Mabuchi's View as quoted by Motowori. The first member of this compound name is frequently omitted.</P>

<p><a name="page_50"><font size="1" color="green">p. 50</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XI.&#8212;INVESTITURE OF THE THREE DEITIES; THE ILLUSTRIOUS AUGUST CHILDREN.]</h2>  
<p>At this time His Augustness the Male-Who-Invites greatly rejoiced, saying; "I, begetting child after child, have at my final begetting gotten. three illustrious children," [with which words,] at once jinglingly taking off and shaking the jewel-string&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_306"></A><A HREF="#fn_303"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> forming his august necklace, he bestowed it on the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, saying: "Do Thine Augustness rule the Plain-of-High-Heaven." With this charge he bestowed it on her. Now the name of this august necklace was the August-Store-house-Shelf-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_307"></A><A HREF="#fn_304"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Next he said of His Augustness Moon-Night-Possessor: "Do Thine Augustness rule the Dominion of the "Night."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_308"></A><A HREF="#fn_305"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Thus he charged him. Next he said to His-Brave-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness: "Do Thine Augustness rule the Sea-Plain."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_309"></A><A HREF="#fn_306"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>

<P><A NAME="fn_304"></A><A HREF="kj018.htm#fr_307">50:2</A> <i>Mi-kura-tana-no-kami</i>. Motowori comments on this name by saying that the necklace was doubtless so precious, that it was carefully kept by the goddess on a shelf in her store-house.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_305"></A><A HREF="kj018.htm#fr_308">50:3</A> <i>Yoru-no-wosu-kuni</i>.</P>

<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XII.&#8212;THE CRYING AND WEEPING OF HIS IMPETUOUS-MALE-AUGUSTNESS.]</h2>  
<p>So while [the other two Deities] each [assumed his and her] rule according to the command with which [their father] had deigned to charge them, His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness did not [assume the] rule</p>  
<p><a name="page_51"><font size="1" color="green">p. 51</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> [of] the dominion with which he had been charged, but cried and wept till his eight-grasp beard&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_310"></A><A HREF="#fn_307"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> reached to the pit of his stomach.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_311"></A><A HREF="#fn_308"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> The fashion of his weeping was such as by his weeping to wither the green mountains into withered mountains, and by his weeping to dry up all the rivers and seas.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_312"></A><A HREF="#fn_309"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> For this reason the sound of bad Deities was like unto the flies in the fifth moon&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_313"></A><A HREF="#fn_310"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> as they all swarmed,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_314"></A><A HREF="#fn_311"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and in all things&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_315"></A><A HREF="#fn_312"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> every portent of woe arose. So the Great August Deity the Male-Who-Invites said to His Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness: "How is it that, instead of ruling the land with which I charged thee, thou dost wail and weep?" He replied, saying: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_316"></A><A HREF="#fn_313"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> wail because I wish to depart to my [45] deceased mother's&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_317"></A><A HREF="#fn_314"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> land, to the Nether Distant Land."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_318"></A><A HREF="#fn_315"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Then the Great August Deity the Male-Who-Invites was very angry and said: "If that be so, thou shall not dwell in this land,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_319"></A><A HREF="#fn_316"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and forthwith expelled him with a divine expulsion. So the Great Deity the Male-Who-Invites dwells at Taga&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_320"></A><A HREF="#fn_317"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> in Afumi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_321"></A><A HREF="#fn_318"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_307"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_310">51:1</A> See Sect. VIII, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_308"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_311">51:2</A> Lit, "in front of his heart,"</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_309"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_312">51:3</A> <i>Sic</i> in the original, to the perplexity of commentators.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_310"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_313">51:4</A> "Flies in the fifth moon" is the received interpretation of the original term <i>sa-bahe</i>. <i>Conf</i>. <i>sa-tsuki</i>, the old native name for the fifth moon.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_311"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_314">51:5</A> The text has here the character <A NAME="img_05100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05100.jpg">, "to be full," for which Motowori somewhat arbitrarily reads <A NAME="img_05101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05101.jpg">, "to bubble up," taking this word in the sense of swarming. The translator has endeavoured to preserve the vagueness of the original Japanese, which leaves it doubtful at first sight whether the flies or the deities should be regarded as the logical subject of the Verb. There is an almost identical passage near the beginning of Sect. XVI.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_312"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_315">51:6</A> Lit. "a myriad things," a Chinese phrase for totality.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_313"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_316">51:7</A> The Chinese character for the First-Personal Pronoun used here <a name="page_52"><font size="1" color="green">p. 52</font></A> and below by this deity is the humble one <A NAME="img_05200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05200.jpg"> signifying literally "servant" The commentators read it simply "I."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_314"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_317">51:8</A> The Japanese authorities simply read "mother." But the character <A NAME="img_05201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05201.jpg">, which is used in this place, specially designates a mother who is deceased.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_315"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_318">51:9</A> <i>I.e.,</i> Hades. The translation follows Motowori's explanation of the original term <i>Ne-no-kata-su-kuni</i>, which is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_316"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_319">51:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, say the commentators, "in this realm of ocean which I granted to thee as thy domain." Probably, however, this is reading into the text more than it was meant to contain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_317"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_320">51:11</A> Derivation unknown.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_318"></A><A HREF="kj019.htm#fr_321">51:12</A> From <i>aha-umi</i>, "fresh sea," <i>i.e.</i>, "lake." The province of Afumi was doubtless so called from Lake Biha which occupies a great portion of its surface. It is also known as <i>Chiku-tsu-Afumi</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the Nearer Afumi," in contradistinction to <i>Toho-tsu-fumi</i> (in modern pronunciations <i>T&#333;t&#333;mi</i>), <i>i.e.</i>, "Distant Afumi," a province further to the East. The modern pronunciation of <i>Afumi</i> is <i>Omi</i>.</P>

<p><a name="page_52"><font size="1" color="green">p. 52</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XIII.&#8212;THE AUGUST OATH]</h2>  
<p>So thereupon His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness said: "If that be so, I will take leave&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_322"></A><A HREF="#fn_319"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> of the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, and depart." [With these words] he forthwith went up to Heaven, whereupon all the mountains and rivers shook, and every land and country quaked. So the Heaven-Shining-Great-August Deity, alarmed at the noise, said: 'The reason of the ascent hither of His Augustness my elder brother&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_323"></A><A HREF="#fn_320"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> is surely no good intent.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_324"></A><A HREF="#fn_321"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> It is only that he wishes to wrest my land from me." And she forthwith, unbinding her august hair, twisted it into august bunches; and both into the left and into the right august bunch, as likewise into her august head-dress and likewise on to [46] her left and her right august arm,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_325"></A><A HREF="#fn_322"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> she twisted an augustly complete [string] of curved jewels eight feet</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_53"><font size="1" color="green">p. 53</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> [long],&#8212;of five hundred jewels,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_326"></A><A HREF="#fn_323"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and slinging on her back a quiver holding a thousand [arrows], and adding [thereto]&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_327"></A><A HREF="#fn_324"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> a quiver holding five hundred [arrows], she likewise took and slung at her side a mighty and high [-sounding] elbow-pad,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_328"></A><A HREF="#fn_325"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and brandished and stuck her bow upright so that the top&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_329"></A><A HREF="#fn_326"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> shook, and she stamped her feet into the hard ground up to her opposing thighs,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_330"></A><A HREF="#fn_327"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> kicking away [the earth] like rotten snow,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_331"></A><A HREF="#fn_328"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and stood valiantly like unto a mighty man, and waiting, asked: "Wherefore ascendest thou hither?" Then His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness replied, saying: "I have no evil intent. It is only that when the Great-August-Deity [our father] spoke, deigning to enquire the cause [47] of my wailing and weeping, I said 'I wail because I wish to go to my deceased mother's land,'&#8212;whereupon the Great-August-Deity said: 'Thou shalt not dwell in this land,' and deigned to expel me with a divine expulsion. It is therefore solely with the thought of taking leave of thee and departing, that I have ascended hither. I have no strange intentions." Then the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity said: "If that be so, whereby shall I know the sincerity of thine intentions?' Thereupon His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness replied, saying: "Let each of us swear,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_332"></A><A HREF="#fn_329"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> and produce children." So as they then swore to each other from the opposite banks of the Tranquil River of Heaven.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_333"></A><A HREF="#fn_330"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> the august names of the Deities that were born from the mist [of her breath] when, having first begged His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness to hand her the ten-grasp sabre which was girded on him and broken it into three fragments, and with the jewels making a jingling sound&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_334"></A><A HREF="#fn_331"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> having brandished and washed them in the True-Pool-Well of</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_54"><font size="1" color="green">p. 54</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Heaven,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_335"></A><A HREF="#fn_332"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> and having crunchingly crunched them, the [48] Heaven-Shining-Great-Deity blew them away, were Her Augustness Torrent-Mist-Princess,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_336"></A><A HREF="#fn_333"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> another august name for whom is Her Augustness Princess-of-the-Island-of-the Offing; next Her Augustness Lovely-Island-Princess,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_337"></A><A HREF="#fn_334"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> another august name for whom is Her Augustness Good-Princess; next Her Augustness, Princess-of-the-Torrent.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_338"></A><A HREF="#fn_335"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> The august name of the Deity that was born from the mist [of his breath] when, having begged the Heaven-Shining. Great-August-Deity to hand him the augustly complete [string] of curved jewels eight feet [long],&#8212;of five hundred jewels,&#8212;that was twisted in the left august bunch [of her hair], and with the jewels making a jingling sound having brandished and washed them in the True-Pool. Well of Heaven, and having crunchingly crunched them, His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness blew them away, was His Augustness Truly-Conquer-I-Conqueror-Conquering-Swift-Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_339"></A><A HREF="#fn_336"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> The august name of the Deity that was born from the mist [of his breath] when again, having begged her to hand him the [49] jewels that were twisted in the right august bunch [of her hair], and having crunchingly crunched them, he blew them away, was His Augustness Ame-no-hohi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_340"></A><A HREF="#fn_337"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> The august name of the Deity that was born from the mist [of his breath] when again, having begged her to hand him the jewels that were twisted in her august head-dress, and having crunchingly crunched them, he blew them away, was His Augustness Prince-Lord-of-Heaven.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_341"></A><A HREF="#fn_338"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> The august name of the Deity that was born from the mist [of his breath] when again, having begged her to hand him the jewels that were twisted on her left august arm,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_342"></A><A HREF="#fn_339"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> and having crunchingly crunched them,</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_55"><font size="1" color="green">p. 55</font></A></p>  
<p>he blew them away, was His Augustness Prince-Lord-of-Life.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_343"></A><A HREF="#fn_340"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> The august name of the Deity that was born from the mist [of his breath] when again, having begged her to hand him the jewels that were twisted on her right august arm,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_344"></A><A HREF="#fn_341"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> and having crunchingly crunched them, he blew them away, was His-Wondrous-Augustness-of-Kumanu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_345"></A><A HREF="#fn_342"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> (<small>Five Deities in all</small>).</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_56"><font size="1" color="green">p. 56</font></A> <a name="page_57"><font size="1" color="green">p. 57</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_319"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_322">52:1</A> <a name="page_55"><font size="1" color="green">p. 55</font></A> The English locution "to take leave" exactly represents the Chinese character here used which, from having the sense of "asking permission," has come to mean "bidding adieu."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_320"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_323">52:2</A> He was her younger brother. But see what is said on the subject of names expressive of relationship on <A HREF="kj005.htm#page_xxxvii">p. xxxvii</A> of Introduction. The phonetic characters <A NAME="img_05500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05500.jpg"> are here used to represent <A NAME="img_05501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05501.jpg">, "elder brother."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_321"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_324">52:3</A> Literally "heart," here and elsewhere.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_322"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_325">52:4</A> Or "hand."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_323"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_326">53:5</A> The original is here obscure, but the translator has, as usual. followed the Chinese characters as far as possible, and has been chiefly guided by Moribe's interpretation. According to this, the "eight feet" (which Moribe takes to mean simply "several feet") must be supposed to refer to the length of the necklace which, he says, probably resembled a Buddhist rosary, only that the beads were somewhat larger. For a discussion of the various interpretations to which this phrase descriptive of the Sun-Goddess's ornaments may be subjected, see Note 4 to Mr. Satow's third paper on the "Rituals" in Vol. IX Pt. II, p. 198 of these "Transactions," and Moribe's "Examination of Difficult Words," Vol. II. pp. 4-5, <i>s.v.</i> <i>Ya-saka-ni no iho-tsu no mi sumaru no tama</i>. Mr. Satow, adopting some of the bolder etymologies of the Japanese commentators, translates thus: "the ever-bright curved (or glittering) jewels, the many assembled jewels," and concludes that "a long string of, perhaps, claw-shaped stone beads" was what the author meant to describe.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_324"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_327">53:6</A> Hirata supposes this additional quiver to have been slung in front.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_325"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_328">53:7</A> Motowori's long note on the expression <i>taka-tomo</i>, to be found in Vol. VII, pp. 39-40 of his "Commentary" seems to prove that "high-low-sounding elbow-pad" (<A NAME="img_05502"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05502.jpg"> being written phonetically for <A NAME="img_05503"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05503.jpg">) is the most likely meaning,&#8212;these pads, of which one was worn on the left elbow, having been made of skin. Arawi Hakuseki however takes <A NAME="img_05504"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05504.jpg"> in its <a name="page_56"><font size="1" color="green">p. 56</font></A> literal sense of "bamboo" and Moribe suggests the (<A NAME="img_05600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05600.jpg">) which occurs so often in proper names with the signification of "bold," "brave," or "stout."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_326"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_329">53:8</A> The reading <i>yu-hara</i>, here rendered "top [of the bow]" is doubtful, and <i>yu-hadsu</i>, "bow-notch," has been proposed as an emendation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_327"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_330">53:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "both legs penetrated into the ground up to the thigh," a proof of the vigour with which she used her limbs in stamping.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_328"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_331">53:10</A> Lit. "bubble-snow."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_329"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_332">53:11</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "pledge our faith," "bind ourselves," in order to show forth the sincerity of our intentions.&#8212;Hirata has a long note on the word <i>ukehi</i>, here rendered "swear" (elsewhere as a Substantive, "oath,") which the student will do well to consult. It is contained in his "Exposition of the Ancient Histories," Vol. VII, pp. 61-63.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_330"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_333">53:12</A> <i>Ame-no-yasu-kaha</i> (according to Motowori's reading <i>Ame-no-yasu-no-kaha</i>), our Milky Way. The "Chronicles of Old Matters of Former Ages" perhaps preserve the true etymology of the word by writing it <i>Ama-no-ya-se-kaha</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the Heavenly River of eight currents (or reaches)." This would mean simply "a broad river." The text literally says: "having placed the Tranquil River of Heaven in the middle," etc.; but the sense of the clause is that given in the translation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_331"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_334">53:13</A> These words seem, as Motowori says. to have been erroneously brought in here from the next sentence, where they come in appropriately.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_332"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_335">54:14</A> <i>Ame-no-ma-na-wi</i>. The interpretation adopted is that which has the authority of Motowori and Hirata. Perhaps only "Heavenly Well" is intended. The above authorities warn us that the word <i>wi</i>, "well," was not in ancient days restricted to its modern sense, but was used to designate any place at which water could be drawn, and Motowori thinks that Heaven contained several such. That mentioned in the text seems to have been a pool in the bed of the Tranquil River of Heaven.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_333"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_336">54:15</A> This is the interpretation of the original name <i>Ta-kiri-bime-no-mikoto</i> which is proposed by Moribe. It is less far-fetched, and agrees better with the name of the sister deity Princess-of-the-Torrent, than do the other explanations that have been attempted. The alternative name is <i>Oki-tsu-shima-no-mikoto</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_334"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_337">54:16</A> <i>Ichiki-shima-hime-no-mikoto</i>, <i>ichiki</i> being an unusual form of <i>itsuki</i>. The island, which is in the Inland Sea, is still celebrated, but bears in common parlance the name of <i>Miya-shima</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "Temple Island." <a name="page_57"><font size="1" color="green">p. 57</font></A> The alternative name is <i>Sa-yori-bime-no-mikato</i>, in which <i>sa</i> is an Ornamental Prefix not calling for translation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_335"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_338">54:17</A> <i>Tagi-tsu-hime-no-mikoto</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_336"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_339">54:18</A> <i>Masa-ka-a-katsu-kachi-hayabi-ame-no-oshi-ho-mimi-no-mikoto</i>. The word <i>mimi</i> (<A NAME="img_05700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05700.jpg"> "ears") forms part of a large number of Ancient Japanese proper names. Motowori, who of course passes over in silence the fact that large ears are considered lucky, not only in Japan, <i>but also in China and Korea</i>, suggests the etymology <i>hi&nbsp;hi</i> or <i>bi&nbsp;bi</i> (<A NAME="img_05701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05701.jpg">), <i>i.e.</i>, the word "wondrous" or "miraculous" repeated. But there are examples of such names in which the interpretation of <i>mimi</i> as "ears" is unavoidable. Thus Prince Umayado (commonly called <i>Sh&#333;-to-ku Tai-shi</i>) had also the name of <i>Yatsu-mimi no Tai-shi</i> <A NAME="img_05702"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05702.jpg"> bestowed upon him on account of his extraordinary intelligence. Is it not therefore simpler in all cases to allow to the word this its natural meaning? The proper names in mi do however undoubtedly offer some difficulty, and Motowori scarcely seems content with his own derivation of the troublesome syllable. <i>Oshi</i>, as in other cases, is taken to represent <i>ohoshi</i>, "great"; and after much hesitation the translator has followed Motowori in regarding ho likewise as an abbreviated form of that word.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_337"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_340">54:19</A> <i>Ame-no</i> signifies "of Heaven" or "heavenly." The syllables hohi are incomprehensible.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_338"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_341">54:20</A> <i>Amatsu-hiko-ne-no-mikoto</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_339"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_342">54:21</A> Or "hand."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_340"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_343">55:22</A> <i>Iku-tsu-hiko-ne-no-mikoto</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_341"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_344">55:23</A> This god does not seem to be known by any other name: but is conjectured by Hirata to be identical with <i>Ame-no-hohi</i>, the second of these divine brothers. <i>Kumanu</i>, or less archaically <i>Kumano</i>, is said to be, not the well-known Kumano in the province of Kishiu, but a place in Idzumo near Suga (see Sect. XIX, Notes 1 and 2). The name is written with the characters, <A NAME="img_05703"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05703.jpg">, "bear moor." The native commentators however interpret it as a corruption of <i>Komori-nu</i>, <A NAME="img_05704"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05704.jpg">, "the moor of retirement," on account of a tradition preserved in the "Chronicles" of Izanami (the Female-Who-invites) having been interred at the Kishiu Kumano.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_342"></A><A HREF="kj020.htm#fr_345">55:24</A> There is no footnote 24&#8212;<i>JBH</i>.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_58"><font size="1" color="green">p. 58</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XIV.&#8212;THE AUGUST DECLARATION OF THE DIVISION OF THE AUGUST MALE CHILDREN AND THE AUGUST FEMALE CHILDREN.]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon the Heavenly Shining-Great-August-Deity said to His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness: "As for the seed&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_346"></A><A HREF="#fn_343"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> of the five male Deities born last, their birth was from things of mine; so undoubtedly they are my children. As for the seed of the three female Deities [50] born first, their birth was from a thing of thine; so doubtless they are thy children." Thus did she declare the division. So Her Augustness Torrent-Mist-Princess, the Deity born first, dwells in the Inner temple of Munakata.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_347"></A><A HREF="#fn_344"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> The next, Her Augustness Lovely-Island-Princess, dwells in the middle temple of Munakata. The next, Her Augustness Princess-of-the-Torrent, dwells in the outer temple&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_348"></A><A HREF="#fn_345"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> of Munakata. These three Deities are the three Great Deities&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_349"></A><A HREF="#fn_346"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> held in reverence by the Dukes of Munakata.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_350"></A><A HREF="#fn_347"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> So His Augustness Brave-Rustic-Illuminator, child of His Augustness Ame-no-hohi, one of the five children born afterwards (<small>&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_351"></A><A HREF="#fn_348"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> this is the ancestor of the Rulers of the Land of Idzumo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_352"></A><A HREF="#fn_349"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Land of Musashi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_353"></A><A HREF="#fn_350"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Upper Land of Unakami,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_354"></A><A HREF="#fn_351"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Lower Land of Unakami,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_355"></A><A HREF="#fn_352"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Land of Izhimu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_356"></A><A HREF="#fn_353"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> of the Departmental Suzerains of the Island of Tsu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_357"></A><A HREF="#fn_354"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and of the Rulers of the Land of Tohotsu-Afumi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_358"></A><A HREF="#fn_355"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A></small>). The next, His Augustness Prince-Lord-of-Heaven (<small>is the Ancestor of the Rulers of the Land of Ofushi-kafuchi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_359"></A><A HREF="#fn_356"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> of the Chiefs of Nukatabe-no-yuwe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_360"></A><A HREF="#fn_357"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Land of Ki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_361"></A><A HREF="#fn_358"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> of the Suzerains of Tanaka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_362"></A><A HREF="#fn_359"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> in Yamato, of the Rulers of the Land of Yamashiro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_363"></A><A HREF="#fn_360"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Land of Umaguta,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_364"></A><A HREF="#fn_361"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Land of Kine&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_365"></A><A HREF="#fn_362"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> in Michi-no-Shiri,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_366"></A><A HREF="#fn_363"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Land of Suhau,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_367"></A><A HREF="#fn_364"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> of the Rulers of Amuchi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_368"></A><A HREF="#fn_365"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> in Yamato, of the Departmental Suzerains of Takechi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_369"></A><A HREF="#fn_366"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> of the Territorial Lords of Kamafu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_370"></A><A HREF="#fn_367"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> and of the Rulers of Sakikusabe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_371"></A><A HREF="#fn_368"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A></small>).</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_343"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_346">58:1</A> <a name="page_59"><font size="1" color="green">p. 59</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, the origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_344"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_347">58:2</A> A place in the province of Chikuzen. The name signifies either "breast-shape" or "body-shape."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_345"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_348">58:3</A> Or "sea-shore temple."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_346"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_349">58:4</A> Or "'the Great Deities of the three shrines."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_347"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_350">58:5</A> <i>Munakata-no-kimi</i>. Remember that all the names in this and similar lists are hereditary "gentile names" (see Introduction, <A HREF="kj002.htm#page_xvi">p. xvi</A>), and that "Duke" and the other tides used in this translation to designate them must only be regarded as approximations towards giving the force of the Japanese originals, which are themselves by no means always clear, either etymologically or historically. Indeed Motowori in a chapter entitled "<i>Kuni no Miyatsuko</i>" (<A NAME="img_05900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/05900.jpg">) in his "<i>Tama-Katsuma</i>," Vol. VI, p. 25, remarks that the distinctions obtaining between the various titles of <i>Kimi</i>, <i>Wake</i>, <i>Murazhi</i>, etc., are no longer to be ascertained, if indeed they were ever sharply drawn, and that Kuni no Miyatsuko (here rendered "Rulers of the Land") seems to have been a general term including all the rest, and roughly corresponding to the modern title of <i>Daimyo</i>.&#8212;It must be well understood that all these names, though properly and originally denoting an office, were inherited as tides, and ended (after the custom of conferring new ones had died out) by being little more than an extra surname appended to the surname proper (<i>uji</i>). This kind of quasi-official quasi-titular surname is what is called by the Japanese a <i>kabane</i>, which the translator, for want of a better equivalent, renders, by "gentile name." Motowori's learned note in Vol. XXXIX, pp. 14-15 of his Commentary, should be consulted for a full exposition of this somewhat intricate subject, on which there has been much misapprehension, chiefly owing to the want of a fitting Chinese character to denote the word <i>kabane</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_348"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_351">58:6</A> Here and throughout the work passages of this nature containing genealogies are in all the editions printed small, and might therefore be supposed to be either intended as foot-notes, or to be later glosses. Motowori however rightly rejects such an inference. To an English reader the word "this" may seem, by disturbing the grammar of the sentence, to support that inference; but in Japanese construction little importance need he attached to the presence of this double Nominative.&#8212;The name in the original of the ancestral deity whose children are here enumerated is <i>Taka-Hira-Tori-no-mikoto</i>, and the interpretation thereof in the sense given in the translation is Motowori's <i>Hira-tori</i> being supposed by him to stand for <i>Hina-teri</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_349"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_352">58:7</A> <i>Idzumo-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_350"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_353">58:8</A> <a name="page_60"><font size="1" color="green">p. 60</font></A> <i>Muzashi-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>. In classical and modern usage <i>Musashi</i> does not take the <i>nigori</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_351"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_354">58:9</A> <i>Kami-tsu-Unakami-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>. Unakami was a part of what forms the modern province of Kadzusa. The name probably signifies "on the sea."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_352"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_355">58:10</A> <i>Shimo-tsu-Unakami-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_353"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_356">58:11</A> <i>Izhimu-no-kuni-miyatsuko</i>. Izhimu (given in the "Japanese Words Classified and Explained" as <i>Izhimi</i>) was a portion of the modern province of Kadzusa. The etymology of the name is unknown.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_354"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_357">58:12</A> <i>Tsushima-no-agata-no-atahe</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_355"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_358">58:13</A> <i>Toho-tsu-afumi-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>. In modern times <i>Toho-tsu-afumi</i> has been contracted to <i>Tohotafumi</i> and is pronounced <i>T&#333;t&#333;mi</i>. The name signifies "distant fresh sea" (<i>i.e.</i> "distant lake") the province which bears it being thus designated in reference to a large lagoon which it contains, and in contradistinction to <i>Chika-tsu-afumi</i>, "near fresh sea," the name of the province in which lies Lake Biha. In modern times the latter has come to be known simply as Afumi (pronounced Omi), and the original connection of ideas between its name and that of T&#333;t&#333;mi is lost sight of.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_356"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_359">58:14</A> <i>Ohoshi-kafuchi-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>. <i>Ohoshi-kafuchi</i> (in modern times pronounced <i>Ochikochi</i>) signifies "within the great rivers."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_357"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_360">58:15</A> <i>Nukatabe-no-yuwe-no-murazhi</i>. The meaning of this name is not certain, but <i>yuwe</i> seems to be the word for "bathing woman" mentioned in Sect. LXXI (Note 11). See Motowori's remarks in Vol. XXIV, p. 56 of his "Commentary" and the story of the origin of the name given in the "Catalogue of Family Names," Vol. II, pp. 8-9, edit. of 1834).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_358"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_361">58:16</A> <i>Kino-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>. <i>Ki</i> signifies "tree," and the province doubtless received this name from its forests. Motowori supposes the character <A NAME="img_06000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06000.jpg"> to have been lost in this place, and reads <i>Ubaraki</i> (the modern <i>Ibaraki</i>), a portion of the province of Hitachi. See Vol. VII, pp. 75-76 of his "Commentary."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_359"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_362">58:17</A> <i>Tanaka-no-atahe</i>. The word <i>tana-ka</i> signifies "in the middle of rice-fields."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_360"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_363">58:18</A> <i>Yamashiro-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>. <i>Yama-shiro</i> signifies "behind the mountains," though it is now, by a play upon words, written with characters signifying "mountain-castle."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_361"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_364">58:19</A> <i>Umaguta-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>, Umaguta is a portion of the modern province of Kadzusa. The etymology of the name is not known.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_362"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_365">58:20</A> <a name="page_61"><font size="1" color="green">p. 61</font></A> <i>Kiuhe-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>. The etymology of the name and the position of the place are equally obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_363"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_366">58:21</A> The modern province of Echigo, or perhaps any not well defined district in the north of Main Island. (See Section LX, Note 20.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_364"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_367">58:22</A> <i>Suhau-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko</i>. The etymology of Suhau is not known; but the name sounds Chinese.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_365"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_368">58:23</A> <i>Amuchi-no-miyatsubo</i>. The derivation of Amuchi is unknown.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_366"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_369">58:24</A> <i>Takechi-no-agata-nushi</i>. Takechi means "high market" or "high town."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_367"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_370">58:25</A> <i>Kamafu-no-inaki</i>. Kamafu was a portion of Afumi. Motowori's suggestion that the name may be derived from <i>kama</i> (<i>gama</i>), "a bullfrog," does not seem a happy one.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_368"></A><A HREF="kj021.htm#fr_371">58:26</A> <i>Sakikusabe-no-miyatsuko</i>. <i>Sakikusa-be</i> means literally "lily clan," <i>saki-kusa</i>, the old name for the lily (or one species of lily) being literally "the luck-plant." The story of the origin of this cognomen is to be found in the "Catalogue of Family Names," Vol. II, p. 9.</P>

<p><a name="page_61"><font size="1" color="green">p. 61</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT XV.&#8212;THE AUGUST RAVAGES OF HIS IMPETUOUS-MALE-AUGUSTNESS]</h2>  
<p>Then His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness said to the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity: "Owing to the sincerity of my intentions I have, in begetting children, gotten delicate females. judging from this,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_372"></A><A HREF="#fn_369"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> I have undoubtedly gained the victory! With these words, and impetuous with victory, he broke down the divisions of the ricefields&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_373"></A><A HREF="#fn_370"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> laid out by the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, filled up the ditches, and moreover strewed [53] excrements&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_374"></A><A HREF="#fn_371"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in the palace where she partook of the great food.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_375"></A><A HREF="#fn_372"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So, though he did thus, the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity upbraided him not,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_376"></A><A HREF="#fn_373"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> but said: "What looks like excrements must be something that His Augustness mine elder brother has vomited through drunkenness. Again, as to his breaking down the divisions of the rice</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_62"><font size="1" color="green">p. 62</font></A></p>  
<p>fields and filling up the ditches, it must be because he grudges the land [they occupy&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_377"></A><A HREF="#fn_374"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A>] that His Augustness mine elder brother acts thus." But notwithstanding these apologetic words, he still continued his evil acts, and was more and more [violent]. As the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity sat in her awful&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_378"></A><A HREF="#fn_375"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> weaving-hall&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_379"></A><A HREF="#fn_376"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> seeing to the weaving of, the august garments of the Deities, he broke a hole in the top&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_380"></A><A HREF="#fn_377"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> of the weaving-hall, and through it let fall a heavenly piebald horse [54] which he had flayed with a backward flaying,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_381"></A><A HREF="#fn_378"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> at whose sight the women weaving the heavenly garments were so much alarmed that impegerunt privatas partes adversis radiis et obierunt.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_382"></A><A HREF="#fn_379"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_369"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_372">61:1</A> <a name="page_62"><font size="1" color="green">p. 62</font></A> Literally "if one speak from this."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_370"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_373">61:2</A> The character used is <A NAME="img_06200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06200.jpg">, which in Chinese does not necessarily signify a <i>rice</i>-field. But in Japanese it seems to have been always limited to this narrower meaning, to which likewise the context here clearly points.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_371"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_374">61:3</A> In the original written <A NAME="img_06201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06201.jpg"> which is partly ideographic and partly phonetic for <i>kuso-mari</i>. Motowori interprets it to signify "excrements and urine"; but the parallel passage of the "Chronicles" which he himself quotes goes to prove that <i>mari</i> had not the latter meaning, as does also another well-known passage in the "Tale of a Bamboo-Cutter."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_372"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_375">61:4</A> <A NAME="img_06202"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06202.jpg"> read <i>oh-nihe</i>. The word <i>nihe</i> now denotes "a sacrifice," and <i>oh-nihe no matsuri</i> is the religious festival of the tasting of the first new rice of the season.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_373"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_376">61:5</A> We might, following classical usage, translate the Verb <i>togamezu</i>, which is written phonetically, by the words "took no heed" or "made no observation"; but in this passage it certainly seems to have the stronger and more specialized signification of "upbraiding," "scolding," which attaches to it in the colloquial dialect.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_374"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_377">62:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, he thinks that none of the land should be wasted in ditches and embankments, but should all be devoted to the production of food.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_375"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_378">62:7</A> The character used is <A NAME="img_06203"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06203.jpg"> "to shun," which in Japanese has approximately the meaning of "sacred." Thus a certain family of priests <a name="page_63"><font size="1" color="green">p. 63</font></A> was called by the name of <i>Imibe</i>, lit. "the shunning clan," on account of the uncleanness from which they were bound to abstain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_376"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_379">62:8</A> Written with characters signifying literally "garment-house," but the meaning, as understood by the native commentators is that given in the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_377"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_380">62:9</A> <A NAME="img_06300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06300.jpg">. This character is taken by the native commentators in the sense of <A NAME="img_06301"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06301.jpg">, <i>mune</i>, "ridge-pole."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_378"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_381">62:10</A> <i>I.e.,</i> it is supposed, beginning at the tail. That this was considered criminal may be seen by comparing Sect. XCVII. Note 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_379"></A><A HREF="kj022.htm#fr_382">62:11</A> In the parallel passage of the "Chronicles" it is the goddess who injures herself with her shuttle, but without dying of the effects of the accident.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_63"><font size="1" color="green">p. 63</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XVI.&#8212;THE DOOR OF THE HEAVENLY ROCK-DWELLING.]</h2>  
<p>So thereupon the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, terrified at the sight, closed [behind her] the door of the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_383"></A><A HREF="#fn_380"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> made it fast,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_384"></A><A HREF="#fn_381"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and retired. Then the whole Plain of High Heaven was obscured and all the Central Land of Reed-Plains darkened. Owing to this, eternal&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_385"></A><A HREF="#fn_382"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> night prevailed. Hereupon the voices of the myriad&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_386"></A><A HREF="#fn_383"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Deities were like unto the flies in the fifth moon as they swarmed, and a myriad portents of woe all arose. Therefore did the eight hundred myriad&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_387"></A><A HREF="#fn_384"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Deities assemble in a divine assembly in the bed&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_388"></A><A HREF="#fn_385"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> of the Tranquil River of Heaven, and bid the Deity Thought-Includer,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_389"></A><A HREF="#fn_386"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> child of the High-August-Producing-Wondrous-Deity think of a plan, assembling the long-singing birds of eternal night&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_390"></A><A HREF="#fn_387"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and making them sing, taking the hard rocks of Heaven from the river-bed of the Tranquil River of Heaven, and taking the iron&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_391"></A><A HREF="#fn_388"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> from [55] the Heavenly Metal-Mountains,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_392"></A><A HREF="#fn_389"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> calling in the smith Ama-tsu-ma-ra,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_393"></A><A HREF="#fn_390"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> charging Her Augustness I-shi-ko-ri-do-me&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_394"></A><A HREF="#fn_391"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>
