<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_64"><font size="1" color="green">p. 64</font></A></p>  
<p>to make a mirror, and charging His Augustness jewel-Ancestor&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_395"></A><A HREF="#fn_392"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> to make an augustly complete [string] of curved jewels eight feet [long],&#8212;of five hundred jewels,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_396"></A><A HREF="#fn_393"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A>&#8212;and summoning His Augustness Heavenly-Beckoning-Ancestor-Lord&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_397"></A><A HREF="#fn_394"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> [56] and His Augustness Great-Jewel,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_398"></A><A HREF="#fn_395"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> and causing them to pull out with a complete pulling the shoulder [-blade] of a true&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_399"></A><A HREF="#fn_396"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> stag from the Heavenly Mount Kagu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_400"></A><A HREF="#fn_397"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> and take cherrybark&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_401"></A><A HREF="#fn_398"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> from the Heavenly Mount Kagu, and perform divination,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_402"></A><A HREF="#fn_399"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> and pulling up by pulling its roots a true <i>cleyera japonica</i>&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_403"></A><A HREF="#fn_400"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> with five hundred [branches] from the Heavenly Mount Kagu, and taking and putting upon its upper branches the augustly complete [string] of curved jewels eight feet [57] [long],&#8212;of five hundred jewels,&#8212;and taking and tying to the middle branches&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_404"></A><A HREF="#fn_401"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> the mirror eight feet [long],&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_405"></A><A HREF="#fn_402"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> and taking and hanging upon its lower branches the white pacificatory offerings&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_406"></A><A HREF="#fn_403"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> and the blue pacificatory offerings, His Augustness Grand-jewel taking these divers things and holding them together with the grand august Offerings,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_407"></A><A HREF="#fn_404"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> and His Augustness Heavenly-Beckoning-Ancestor-Lord prayerfully reciting grand liturgies,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_408"></A><A HREF="#fn_405"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> and the Heavenly Hand-Strength-Male-Deity&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_409"></A><A HREF="#fn_406"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> standing hidden beside the door, and Her Augustness Heavenly-Alarming Female&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_410"></A><A HREF="#fn_407"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> hanging [round her] the heavenly clubmoss of the Heavenly Mount Kagu as a sash,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_411"></A><A HREF="#fn_408"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> and making the heavenly spindle-tree her head-dress,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_412"></A><A HREF="#fn_409"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> and binding the [58] leaves of the bamboo-grass of the Heavenly Mount Kagu in a posy for her hands, and laying a soundingboard&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_413"></A><A HREF="#fn_410"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> before the door of the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling, and stamping till she made it resound and doing as if possessed by a Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_414"></A><A HREF="#fn_411"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A> and pulling out the nipples of her breasts, pushing down her skirt-string usque ad privates</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

</p>  
<p><a name="page_65"><font size="1" color="green">p. 65</font></A></p>  
<p>partes.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_415"></A><A HREF="#fn_412"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> Then the Plain of High Heaven shook, and the eight hundred myriad Deities laughed together. Hereupon the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity was amazed, and, slightly opening the door of the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling, spoke thus from the inside: "Methought that owing to my retirement the Plain of Heaven would be dark, and likewise the Central Land of Reed-Plains would all be dark: how then is it that the Heavenly-Alarming-Female makes merry, and that likewise the eight hundred myriad Deities all laugh?" Then the Heavenly-Alarming-Female spoke saying: "We rejoice and are glad because there is a Deity more illustrious than Thine Augustness." While she was thus speaking, His Augustness Heavenly-Beckoning-Ancestor-Lord and His Augustness Grand-jewel pushed forward the mirror and respectfully showed it to the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, whereupon the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity, more and more astonished, gradually came forth from the door and gazed upon it, whereupon the Heavenly-Hand-Strength-Male-Deity, who was standing hidden, took her august hand and drew her out, and then His Augustness Grand-jewel drew the bottom-tied rope&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_416"></A><A HREF="#fn_413"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> [59] along at her august back, and spoke, saying: "Thou must not go back further in than this!" So when the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity had come forth, both the Plain of High Heaven and the Central-Land-of-Reed-Plains of course again became light.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_417"></A><A HREF="#fn_414"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_380"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_383">63:1</A> <a name="page_65"><font size="1" color="green">p. 65</font></A> Motowori says that the word "rock" need not here be taken literally. But it is always (and the translator thinks rightly) so understood, and the compound considered to mean a cave in the rocks, which is also the expression found in the "Chronicles" (<A NAME="img_06500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06500.jpg">).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_381"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_384">63:2</A> The word <i>sasu</i>, which is here used, implies that the goddess <a name="page_66"><font size="1" color="green">p. 66</font></A> made the door fast either by sticking something against it or by bolting it,&#8212;perhaps with one of the metal hooks of which mentioned is made in Sect. LXV (Note 7).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_382"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_385">63:3</A> <i>Toko-yo</i>, here properly written <A NAME="img_06600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06600.jpg">, and a few lines lower down semi-phonetically <A NAME="img_06601"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06601.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_383"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_386">63:4</A> Motowori supposes "myriad" to be a copyist's error for "evil." This clause is a repetition of one in Sect. XII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_384"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_387">63:5</A> The parallel passage in the "Chronicles" has "eighty myriads."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_385"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_388">63:6</A> The Japanese word <i>kohara</i>, translated "bed," is thus defined in Dr, Hepburn's Dictionary, 2nd Edit. <i>s v.</i> <i>Kawara</i>: "That part of the stony bed of a river which is dry except in high water."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_386"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_389">63:7</A> <i>Omohi-kane-no-kami</i>, "He <i>included</i> in his single mind the thoughts and contrivances of many," says Motowori.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_387"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_390">63:8</A> <i>I.e.,</i> as is generally believed, the barndoor fowl.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_388"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_391">63:9</A> The text has the character <A NAME="img_06602"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06602.jpg">, "iron," which Hirata. reads <i>ma-gane</i>, lit. "true metal," the common Japanese term being <i>kuro-gane</i>, lit, "black metal," Motowori prefers to read simply <i>kane</i>, "metal" in general, The main text of the parallel passage in the "Chronicles" omits to mention the metal of which the mirror was made; but "One account" has the character <A NAME="img_06603"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06603.jpg">, "metal" in general, often in Chinese, but rarely if ever in old Japanese, with the specific sense of "gold." The "Chronicles of Old Matters" alone, which are of very doubtful authenticity, say that the mirror was made of copper. (Copper was not discovered in Japan till the eighth century of the Christian era, a few years before the discovery of gold). The best and most obvious course is to adhere to the character in the text, which is, as above stated, "iron."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_389"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_392">63:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the mines. The original expression is <i>Ame no kana-yama</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_390"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_393">63:11</A> <i>Ama-tsu</i> signifies "of Heaven," but the rest of this name is not to be explained. Motowori adopts from the "Chronicles" the reading, <i>Ama-tsu-ma-ura</i>, where the character used for <i>ma</i> signifies "true," and that for <i>ura</i> signifies "sea-shore." (It should be remarked that the forging of a spear by this personage is referred by the author of the "Chronicles," not to the "Divine Age" but to the reign of the Emperor Sui-zei.) Motowori also proposes to supplement after the name the words "to make a spear." Hirata identifies this god with <i>Ama-no-ma-hito-tsu-no-mikoto</i>, His Augustness Heavenly-One-Eye, who is however not mentioned. in the "Records." Obvius hujus nominis sensus foret "Coelestis Penis," sed nullius commentatoris auctoritate commendatur.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_391"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_394">63:12</A> This name is written in the "Chronicles" with characters signifying Stone-Coagulating-Old-Woman, which however seem to be as <a name="page_67"><font size="1" color="green">p. 67</font></A> merely phonetic as those in the present text (<A NAME="img_06700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06700.jpg">). Motowori proposes the interpretation of "Again-Forging-Old-Woman" (<A NAME="img_06701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06701.jpg">, <i>I-shikiri-tome</i>) which is supported by a tradition preserved in the "Gleanings of the Ancient Story," where it is related that the mirror, not having given satisfaction at first, was forged a second time. There is a long note on the subjects of this name in Hirata's "Exposition of the Ancient Histories," Vol. IX, p. 56, where that author propounds the novel opinion that I-shi-ko-ri-do-me was not a goddess at all, but a god.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_392"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_395">64:13</A> <i>Tama-noya-no-mikoto</i>. The "Chronicles" write this name with characters signifying "Jewel-House," but such a reading seems less good.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_393"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_396">64:14</A> See Sect. XIII, Note 5.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_394"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_397">64:15</A> <i>Ame-no-ko-ya-ne-no-mikoto</i>, also reads <i>Ame-no</i> etc. and <i>Ama tsu</i> etc. The signification of the syllables <i>ko-ya</i>, rendered "beckoning ancestor" in accordance with Motowori's view connecting the name with the share taken by the god who bore it in the legend here narrated, is obscure. Mr. Satow thinks that Koya may be the name of a place (see these "Transactions" Vol. VII, Pt. IV. p. 400).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_395"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_398">64:16</A> <i>Futo-tama-no-mikoto</i>. The name is here rendered in accordance with the import of the Chinese characters with which it is written. Motowori, however, emits a plausible opinion when he proposes to consider <i>tama</i> as an abbreviation of <i>tamuke</i>, "holding in the hands as an offering," in connection with what we are told below about this deity and <i>Ame-no-ko-ya-ne</i> holding the symbolic offerings.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_396"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_399">64:17</A> The word "true" (<i>ma</i>) here and below is not much more than an Honorific.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_397"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_400">64:18</A> We might also, though less well, translate by "Mount Kagu in Heaven." This would suit the view of Motowori, who is naturally averse to the identification of this Mount Kagu with the well-known mountain of that name in Yamato (see Sect. VII, Note 12). But of course an European scholar cannot allow of such a distinction being drawn.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_398"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_401">64:19</A> Or perhaps the bark of the common birch is intended. The word in the original is <i>haha-ka</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_399"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_402">64:20</A> See Mr. Satow's already quoted note in Vol. VII, Pt. II, p. 425 <i>et seq</i>, and more especially pp. 430-432, of these "Transactions."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_400"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_403">64:21</A> In Japanese <i>saka-ki</i>. It is commonly planted in the precincts of Shint&#333; temples.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_401"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_404">64:22</A> We might also translate in the Singular "to a middle branch," in order to conform to the rigid distinction which our language draws between Singular and Plural.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_402"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_405">64:23</A> <a name="page_68"><font size="1" color="green">p. 68</font></A> A note to the edition of 1687 proposes to substitute the characters <A NAME="img_06800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06800.jpg"> for <A NAME="img_06801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06801.jpg"> and a note in the original tells us to read them not <i>ya-ta</i>, but <i>ya-ata</i>. Hereupon Motowori founds his derivation of <i>ya-ta</i>, from <i>ya-atama</i>, "eight heads," and supposes the mirror to have been, not eight feet in length, but octangular, while Moribe, who in the case of the jewels accepts the obvious interpretation "eight feet [long]," thinks that the mirror had "an eightfold flowery pattern" (<i>yaha-na-gata</i>) round its border. But both these etymologies are unsupported by the other cases in which the word <i>ya-ta</i> occurs, and are rendered specially untenable by the fact of the mirror and curved beads being spoken of together further on as the <A NAME="img_06802"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06802.jpg"> (Sect. XXXIII, Note 20).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_403"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_406">64:24</A> In rendering the original word <i>nigi-te</i> (here written phonetically, but elsewhere with the characters <A NAME="img_06803"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06803.jpg">), the explanation given by Tanigaha Shisei, and indeed suggested by the characters, has been followed. Motowori's view does not materially differ, but he considers "pacificatory" or "softening" to be equivalent to "soft" applied to the offerings themselves, which consisted of soft cloth, the syllable <i>te</i> of <i>nigi-te</i> being believed to be a contraction of <i>tahe</i> which signifies cloth. The white cloth in ancient times was made of the paper mulberry (<i>Broussonetia papyrifera</i>), and the blue of hemp.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_404"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_407">64:25</A> The original word is written with the same character as the <i>te</i> of <i>nigi-te</i> translated "offerings" above.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_405"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_408">64:26</A> Or in the Singular "a grand liturgy," or "ritual."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_406"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_409">64:27</A> <i>Ame-no-ta-jikara-wo-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_407"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_410">64:28</A> <i>Ame-no-uzume-no-mikoto</i>. The translator has followed the best authorities in rendering the obscure syllable <i>uzu</i> by the word "alarming." Another interpretation quoted in Tanigaha Shisei's "Perpetual Commentary on the Chronicles of Japan" and adopted by Moribe in his "<i>Idzu no Chi-waki</i>," is that <i>uzu</i> means head-dress, and that the goddess took her name from the head-dress of spindle-tree leaves which she wore. The character <A NAME="img_06804"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06804.jpg">, with which the syllables in question (here written phonetically) are rendered ideographically in the "Chronicles," signifies "metal head-gear," "flowers of gold or silver."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_408"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_411">64:29</A> <i>Tasuki</i>, "a cord or sash passed over the shoulders, round the back of the neck, and attached to the wrists, to strengthen the hands for the support of weights, whence the name, which means 'hand-helper.' It was thus different both in form and use from the modern <i>tasuki</i>, a cord with its two ends joined which is worn behind the neck, under the <a name="page_69"><font size="1" color="green">p. 69</font></A> arms and round the back, to keep the modern loose sleeves out of the way when household duties are being performed." (E. Satow).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_409"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_412">64:30</A> <i>I.e.</i>, making for herself a head-dress of spindle-tree leaves.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_410"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_413">64:31</A> The original of these words, <i>uke fusete</i>, is written phonetically, and the exact meaning of <i>uke</i>, here rendered "sounding-board," is open to doubt. The parallel passage in the "Chronicles" has the character, <A NAME="img_06900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06900.jpg">, which signifies a "trough," "manger" or "tub," and the commentators seem therefore right in supposing that the meaning intended to be conveyed in both histories is that of some kind of improvised wooden structure used for the purpose of amplifying sound.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_411"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_414">64:32</A> Neither the text nor Motowori's Commentary (which Hirata adopts word for word) is absolutely explicit, but the imitation and not the reality of divine possession appears to be here intended. In the parallel passage of the "Chronicles," on the other hand, we seem to be reading of genuine possession.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_412"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_415">65:33</A> The subject of the Verb is not clear in many of the clauses of this immensely long sentence, which does not properly hang together. Some clauses read as if the different deities who take a part in the action did so of their own free will; but the intention of the author must have been to let a Causative sense be understood throughout, as he begins by telling us that a plan was devised by the deity Thought-Includer, which plan must have influenced all the subsequent details.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_413"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_416">65:34</A> <i>Shiri-kume-naha</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, rope made of straw drawn up by the roots, which stick out from the end of the rope. Straw-ropes thus manufactured are still used in certain ceremonies and are called <i>shime-naha</i>, a corruption of the Archaic term, Motowori's explanation shows that this is more likely to be the proper signification of the word than "back-limiting-rope" (<i>shiri-ho-kagiri-me-naha</i>), which had been previously suggested by Mabuchi with reference to its supposed origin at the time of the event narrated in this legend.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_414"></A><A HREF="kj023.htm#fr_417">65:35</A> Motowori plausibly conjectures the character <A NAME="img_06901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06901.jpg"> in the concluding words of this passage to be a copyist's error for <A NAME="img_06902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06902.jpg">, and the translator has accordingly rendered it by the English word "again." As it stands, the clause <A NAME="img_06903"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/06903.jpg">, though making sense, does not read like the composition of a Japanese.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_70"><font size="1" color="green">p. 70</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XVII.&#8212;THE AUGUST EXPULSION OF HIS-IMPETUOUS-MALE-AUGUSTNESS.]</h2>  
<p>Thereupon the eight hundred myriad Deities took counsel together, and imposed on High-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness a fine of a thousand tables,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_418"></A><A HREF="#fn_415"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and likewise cut his beard, and even caused the nails of his fingers and toes to be pulled out, and expelled him with a divine expulsion. Again he begged food of the Deity Princess-of-Great-Food.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_419"></A><A HREF="#fn_416"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Then the Princess-of-Great-Food took out all sorts of dainty things from her nose, her mouth, and her fundament, and made them up into all sorts [of dishes], which she offered to him. But His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness watched her proceedings, considered that she was offering up to him filth, and at once killed the Deity Princess-of-Great-Food. So the things that were born in the body of the Deity who had been killed were [60] [as follows]: in her head were born silkworms, in her two eyes were born rice-seeds, in her two ears was born millet,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_420"></A><A HREF="#fn_417"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in her nose were born small beans,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_421"></A><A HREF="#fn_418"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> in her private parts was born barley,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_422"></A><A HREF="#fn_419"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> in her fundament were born large beans.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_423"></A><A HREF="#fn_420"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> So His Augustness the Deity-Producing-Wondrous-Ancestor&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_424"></A><A HREF="#fn_421"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> caused them to be taken and used as seeds.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

The student should consult Motowori's elaborate note on this passage in Vol. IX, pp. 1-5 of his Commentary. Tables of gifts are mentioned in Sect. XXXVII, Note 7 and Sect. XL, Note 13.</P>

<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_71"><font size="1" color="green">p. 71</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[<A HREF="errata.htm#14">SECT.</A> XVIII.&#8212;THE EIGHT-FORKED SERPENT.]</h2>  
<p>So, having been expelled, [His-Swift-impetuous-Male-Augustness] descended to a place [called] Tori-kami&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_425"></A><A HREF="#fn_422"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> at the head-waters of the River Hi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_426"></A><A HREF="#fn_423"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in the Land of Idzumo. At this time some chopsticks&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_427"></A><A HREF="#fn_424"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> came floating down the stream. So His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness, thinking that there must be people at the head-waters of the river, went up it in quest of them, when he came upon an old man and an old woman,&#8212;two of them,&#8212;who had a young girl between them,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_428"></A><A HREF="#fn_425"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and were weeping. Then he deigned to ask: "Who are ye?" So the old man replied, saying: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_429"></A><A HREF="#fn_426"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> am an Earthly Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_430"></A><A HREF="#fn_427"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> child of the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_431"></A><A HREF="#fn_428"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> I am called by the name of Foot-Stroking-Elder,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_432"></A><A HREF="#fn_429"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> my wife is called by the [61] name of Hand-Stroking Elder, and my daughter is called by the name of Wondrous-Inada-Princess."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_433"></A><A HREF="#fn_430"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Again he asked: What is the cause of your crying?" [The old man answered] saying: "I had originally eight young girls as daughters. But the eight-forked serpent of Koshi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_434"></A><A HREF="#fn_431"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> has come every year and devoured [one], and it is now its time to come, wherefore we weep." Then he asked him: "What is its form like?" [The old man] answered, saying: "Its eyes are like <i>akakagachi</i>,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_435"></A><A HREF="#fn_432"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> it has one body with eight heads and eight tails. Moreover on</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_72"><font size="1" color="green">p. 72</font></A></p>  
<p>its body grows moss, and also chamaecyparis&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_436"></A><A HREF="#fn_433"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and cryptomerias. Its length extends over eight valleys and eight hills, and if one look at its belly, it is all constantly [62] bloody and inflamed." (<small>What is called here <i>akakagachi</i> is the modern <i>hohodzuki</i>.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_437"></A><A HREF="#fn_434"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A></small>) Then His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness said to the old man: "If this be thy daughter, wilt thou offer her to me?" He replied, saying: "With reverence,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_438"></A><A HREF="#fn_435"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> but I know not thine august name." Then he replied, saying: "I am elder brother&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_439"></A><A HREF="#fn_436"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> to the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity. So I have now descended from Heaven." Then the Deities Foot-Stroker-Elder and Hand-Stroking-Elder said: "If that be so, with reverence will we offer [her to thee]." So His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness, at once taking and changing the young girl into a multitudinous and close-toothed comb which he stuck into his august hair-bunch, said to the Deities Foot-Stroking-Elder and Hand-Stroking-Elder: "Do you distill some eight-fold refined liquor.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_440"></A><A HREF="#fn_437"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> Also make a fence round about, in that fence make eight gates, at each gate tie [together] eight platforms,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_441"></A><A HREF="#fn_438"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> on each platform put a liquor-vat, and into each vat pour [63] the eight-fold refined liquor, and wait." So as they waited after having thus prepared everything in accordance with his bidding, the eight-forked serpent came truly as [the old man] had said, and immediately dipped a head into each vat, and drank the liquor. Thereupon it was intoxicated with drinking, and all [the heads] lay down and slept. Then His-Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness drew the ten-grasp sabre,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_442"></A><A HREF="#fn_439"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> that was augustly girded on him, and cut the serpent in pieces, so that the River Hi flowed on changed into a river of blood. So when he cut the middle tail, the edge of his august sword broke. Then, thinking it</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_73"><font size="1" color="green">p. 73</font></A></p>  
<p>strange, he thrust into and split [the flesh] with the point of his august sword and looked, and there was a great sword [within]. So he took this great sword, and, thinking it a strange thing, he respectfully informed the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_443"></A><A HREF="#fn_440"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> This is the Herb-Quelling Great Sword.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_444"></A><A HREF="#fn_441"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_74"><font size="1" color="green">p. 74</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_422"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_425">71:1</A> <a name="page_73"><font size="1" color="green">p. 73</font></A> Written with the characters <A NAME="img_07300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07300.jpg">, "bird's hairs," but these must surely be phonetic. In the "Chronicles" the same name is written <A NAME="img_07301"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07301.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_423"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_426">71:2</A> Or Hii, the chief river in Idzumo. The name is supposed by some to have been derived from the name of the god <i>Hi-hayabi</i> (see Section VIII, Note 6).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_424"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_427">71:3</A> Or in the Singular, "a chopstick."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_425"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_428">71:4</A> Literally "had placed a young girl between them," a similar construction to that in Section XIII, (Note 11).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_426"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_429">71:5</A> The humble character <A NAME="img_07302"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07302.jpg"> "servant" is used by the old man for the First Personal Pronoun.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_427"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_430">71:6</A> <A NAME="img_07303"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07303.jpg">. Being generally used antithetically to <A NAME="img_07304"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07304.jpg">, "Heavenly Deity," it seems better to translate the characters thus than by "Country "Deity" or "Deity of the Land." (See Section I, Note 11).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_428"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_431">71:7</A> <i>Oho-yama-tsu-mi-no-kami</i>, first mentioned in Sect. VI, (Note 17).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_429"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_432">71:8</A> <i>Ashi-nadzu-chi</i>, the wife's being <i>Te-nadzu-chi</i>. "One account" in the "Chronicles" gives <i>Ashi nadzu-te-nadzu</i> (<A NAME="img_07304"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07304.jpg">) as the name of the old father alone, while the mother is called <i>Inada-no-miya-nushi Susa-no-yatsu-mimi</i>. (<i>Inada-no-miya-nushi</i> signifies "Mistress of the Temple of Inada"; the signification of the second compound, which forms the name properly so called is not clear, but should probably be interpreted to mean "Impetuous-Eight-Ears," the word <i>susa</i>, "impetuous," containing an allusion to the name of her divine visitor, and "eight ears" being Honorific).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_430"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_433">71:9</A> <i>Kushi</i>-[<i>I</i>]<i>nada</i>-<i>hime</i>, <i>Inada</i> (<i>i.e.</i> <i>ina-da</i>, "rice-field") being the name of a place. <i>Kushi</i> signifies not only "wondrous" but "comb," and is indeed here written with the character for "comb" <A NAME="img_07305"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07305.jpg">, so that there is a play on the word in connection with the incident of her transformation into a comb which is mentioned immediately below, though most authorities agree in considering <A NAME="img_07306"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07306.jpg"> to be here used phonetically for <A NAME="img_07307"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07307.jpg">, which is the reading in the "Chronicles." Moribe, however, in his "<i>Idzu no Chi-waki</i>" suggests the etymology <i>Kushi-itadaki-hime</i> (<A NAME="img_07308"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07308.jpg">) <i>i.e.</i>, "Princess [used as] a comb [for] the head."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_431"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_434">71:10</A> <a name="page_74"><font size="1" color="green">p. 74</font></A> Derivation quite obscure. Motowori quotes an absurd etymology given in the "Japanese Words Classified and Explained," which identifies the name of <i>Koshi</i> with the Past Tense of the Verb <i>kuru</i>, "to come"! There is a district (<i>kohori</i>) named Koshi in the modern province of Echigo; but Koshi was down to historical times a somewhat vague designation of all the north-western provinces,&#8212;Echizen, Kaga, Noto, Etchi&#363;, and Echigo. A tradition preserved in the "Chronicles" tells us that it was meant to denote the Island of Yezo (or rather, perhaps, the land of the Yezo, <i>i.e.</i> the Ainos). The expression in the first Song in Sect. XXIV, and other similar ones in the early literature show that it was not looked upon as a part of Japan proper.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_432"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_435">71:11</A> See Note 13.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_433"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_436">72:12</A> A coniferous tree, the <i>Cham&aelig;cyparis obtusa</i>, in Japanese <i>hi-no-ki</i>. The cryptomeria is <i>Cryptomeria japonica</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_434"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_437">72:13</A> The winter-cherry, <i>Physalis Alkekengi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_435"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_438">72:14</A> For the word "reverence" here and a few lines further on. conf. Sect. IX, Note 4.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_436"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_439">72:15</A> He was her younger brother; but see Introduction, <A HREF="kj005.htm#page_xxxvii">p. xxxvii</A>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_437"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_440">72:16</A> In Japanese <i>sake</i>, and archaically <i>ki</i>, written with the character <A NAME="img_07400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07400.jpg"> and generally translated "rice-beer," but by Dr. Rein "rice-brandy" (<i>Reis-branntwein</i>). The modern <i>sake</i> resembles the Chinese <i>huang chiu</i> (<A NAME="img_07401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07401.jpg">). If we translated it by "rice-beer," we should of course have to render by "to brew" the Verb <i>kamu</i> or <i>kamosu</i> (<A NAME="img_07402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07402.jpg">) here rendered "to distill." It should be mentioned that Professor Atkinson who, like Dr. Rein, has studied the subject specially, uses the word "brewing;" but apparently no English term exactly represents the process which the liquor undergoes in the course of preparation. A curious question is suggested by the fact that the old Japanese word for "distilling" or "brewing" liquor is homonymous with the Verb "to chew," But there is not, beyond this isolated verbal resemblance, any documentary evidence in favour of the Japanese ever having practised a method of making liquor which still obtains in some of the South Sea Islands.&#8212;"One account" of the Chronicles of Japan makes <i>Susa-no-wo</i> say "Take <i>all the fruits</i>, and distill liquor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_438"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_441">72:17</A> The author doubtless intended, as Motowori suggests, to speak only of eight platforms,&#8212;one at each gate,&#8212;and not of sixty-four. But what he actually says is as in the translation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_439"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_442">72:18</A> See Section VIII, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_440"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_443">73:19</A> <a name="page_75"><font size="1" color="green">p. 75</font></A> The text is not quite clear, but the above gives the interpretation which the words most naturally lend themselves. Motowori, influenced by the parallel passage in the "Chronicles," which says explicitly that the sword itself was sent up to the Sun-Goddess, reads the passage thus: "thinking it a strange thing, he sent it up with a message to the Heaven-Shining-Great-August- Deity"; and Mr. Satow follows him in thus translating (see Note 4 to Ritual 8, Vol. IX, Pt. II, 198-200 of these "Transactions," where the whole of this legend is translated with one or two slight verbal differences from the version here given). In the opinion of the present writer, Hirata's arguments in favour of the view here taken are conclusive (see his "Sources of the Ancient Histories." Section LXXII, in the second part of Vol. III, pp. 66-67). That the sword afterwards appears at the temple of the Sun-Goddess in Ise (see end of Section LXXXII), by the high-priestess of which it is bestowed on the legendary hero Yamato-take, is not to the point in this connection, as it is not necessary that all the parts of a myth should be perfectly consistent.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_441"></A><A HREF="kj025.htm#fr_444">73:20</A> <i>Kusa-nagi no tachi</i>. For the applicability of this name see Sect. LXXXIII.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_75"><font size="1" color="green">p. 75</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XIX.&#8212;THE PALACE OF SUGA.]</h2>  
<p>So thereupon His Swift-Impetuous-Male-Augustness sought in the land of Idzumo for a place where he might build a palace. Then he arrived at a place [called] Suga,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_445"></A><A HREF="#fn_443"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and said: "On coming to this place my august heart is pure,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_446"></A><A HREF="#fn_442"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A>&#8212;and in that place he built a palace to dwell in. So that place is now called Suga.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_447"></A><A HREF="#fn_443"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> When this Great Deity first built&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_448"></A><A HREF="#fn_444"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> the palace of Suga, clouds rose up thence. Then he made an august song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_449"></A><A HREF="#fn_445"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> That song said:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_450"></A><A HREF="#fn_446"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Eight clouds arise. The eight-fold fence of Idzumo makes an eight-fold fence for the spouses to retire [within]. Oh! that eight-fold fence."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_451"></A><A HREF="#fn_447"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_76"><font size="1" color="green">p. 76</font></A></p>  
<p>[65] Then he called the Deity Foot-Stroking-Elder and said: "Thee do I appoint Headman&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_452"></A><A HREF="#fn_448"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> of my palace;" and moreover bestowed on him the name of Master-of-the-Temple-of-Inada-Eight-Eared-Deity-of-Suga.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_453"></A><A HREF="#fn_449"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_77"><font size="1" color="green">p. 77</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_442"></A><A HREF="kj026.htm#fr_446">75:1</A> <a name="page_76"><font size="1" color="green">p. 76</font></A> <i>I.e.,</i> "I feel refreshed." The Japanese term used is <i>suga-sugashi</i>, whence the origin ascribed to the name of the place Suga. But move probably the name gave rise to this detail of the legend.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_443"></A><A HREF="kj026.htm#fr_447">75:2</A> The real derivation of Suga is unknown, all the native commentators accepting the statement in the text, and Motowori supposing that up to the time of the Deity's arrival it had borne the name of Inada. We may perhaps conjecture some connection between <i>Suga</i> and <i>Susa-no-wo</i> ("Impetuous Male," see Motowori's Commentary, Vol. IX, p. 49), and it may be mentioned that the "Eight-Eared Deity of Suga" is also mentioned as the "Eight-Eared Deity of Susa."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_444"></A><A HREF="kj026.htm#fr_448">75:3</A> Or "began to build."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_445"></A><A HREF="kj026.htm#fr_449">75:4</A> "Ode" is another rendering of the Japanese term <i>uta</i>, which has been used by the present writer and by others. <i>Uta</i> being however connected with <i>utafu</i>, "to sing," it seems more consistent to translate it by the English word "song."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_446"></A><A HREF="kj026.htm#fr_450">75:5</A> Or perhaps rather "in that song he said."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_447"></A><A HREF="kj026.htm#fr_451">75:6</A> This difficult song has been rather differently rendered by Mr. Aston in the Second Appendix to his "Grammar of the Japanese Written Language" (2nd Edition), and again by Mr. Satow in the note to his translation of the Ritual already quoted. Mr. Aston (premising that he follows Motowori's interpretation) translates it thus:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Many clouds arise:<br> The clouds which come forth (are) a manifold fence:<br> For the husband and wife to retire within<br> They have formed a manifold fence:<br> Oh! that manifold fence!"</div></p>  
<p>Mr. Satow's translation is as follows:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Many clouds arise.<br> The manifold fence of the forth-issuing clouds<br> Makes a manifold fence<br> For the spouses to be within.<br> Oh! that manifold fence."</div></p>  
<p><a name="page_77"><font size="1" color="green">p. 77</font></A> In any case the meaning simply is that the multitudinous clouds rose up like a fence or screen behind which the newly-married deities might retire from public gaze, and Moribe suggests that the repetitions are an after-addition made to bring up to the usual number of thirty-one syllables what were originally but the three lines&#8212;</p>  
<p><i><div style="margin-left: 32px">Tachi-idzuru kumo mo<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Tsuma-gome ni<br> Yo-he-gahi tsukuru yo</i>!</div></p>  
<p><i>I.e.</i>&#8212;</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The uprising clouds even, to shut up<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the spouses, make an eight-fold fence."</div></p>  
<p>(See his discussion on this song in the "Idzu no Kotowaki Vol. I, pp. 1-3.)&#8212;The present writer has already stated in the Introduction (see <A HREF="kj006.htm#page_lx">p. lx</A>) his reasons for always rendering the native word for "eight" (<i>ya</i>) by "eight" instead of by "many" or "numerous," as is done by the two eminent scholars above quoted. With regard to the word <i>Idzumo</i> which they, in deference to the opinions of the native commentators, render by "clouds which come forth" or "forth-issuing clouds" (the Chinese characters <A NAME="img_07700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07700.jpg"> with which the word is written having that signification), the present writer cannot persuade himself that such a corruption as <i>idzumo</i> for <i>ide-kumo</i> either retained at the time of the composition of the song, or should now be credited with, the signification which this its supposed etymology assigns to it. The etymology moreover is far from being established, and in this, as in many other cases, the Chinese characters used to write the name of the province of Idzumo, may well have rested on nothing more than a vague similarity of sound, and probably no European scholar would endorse the opinion of the native commentators, to whom the "Records" are a sacred book, that the province of Idzumo received its name from this very poem. On the other hand, we need have no difficulty in conceding that the Pillow-Word <i>ya-kumo-tatsu</i>, by which Idzumo is preceded in poetical compositions, did probably here originate.&#8212;This song is in the "Chronicles" only quoted in a note, for which reason some authorities dispute its antiquity. In the note in question, we find the reading -<i>gome</i> (the "Records" have -<i>gomi</i>), the Transitive form instead of the Intransitive. If this were adopted, the translation would have to run thus: . . . . . "The eight-fold fence of Idzumo makes an eight-fold fence to shut up the spouse[s?] in;" and probably "spouse" should be understood in the Feminine to mean "wife."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_448"></A><A HREF="kj026.htm#fr_452">76:7</A> <a name="page_78"><font size="1" color="green">p. 78</font></A> <i>Obito</i>, written with the Chinese character <A NAME="img_07800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07800.jpg">, while the Japanese word is probably derived from <i>oho-bito</i>, "great man." When used, as it often is, as a "gentile name," the translator renders it by "Grandee."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_449"></A><A HREF="kj026.htm#fr_453">76:8</A> <i>Inada-no-miya-nushi Suga-no ya-tsui-mimi-no-kami</i>. It should be stated that Motowori, as usual, objects to the view that <i>mimi</i> signifies "ears" (its proper meaning) in this name. But he has no better explanation to offer, and the Chinese characters give us <i>ya-tsu mimi</i>, "eight ears." The author of the "<i>Tokiha-gusa</i>" ingeniously proposes to consider <i>ya-tsu mimi</i> as a corruption of <i>yatsuko mi&nbsp;mi</i> (<A NAME="img_07801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07801.jpg">) "servant august body," but this cannot be seriously entertained (Conf. Sect. XIII, Note 18).</P>
<p><HR>

<p><a name="page_78"><font size="1" color="green">p. 78</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XX.&#8212;THE AUGUST ANCESTORS OF THE DEITY-MASTER-OF-THE-GREAT LAND.]</h2>  
<p>Quare, quum incepit in thalamo [opus procreationis] cum Mir&acirc;-Her&acirc;-Inad&acirc;, procreavit Deum nomine Eight-Island Ruler.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_454"></A><A HREF="#fn_450"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> And again, having wedded the Divine-Princess-of-Great-Majesty,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_455"></A><A HREF="#fn_451"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> daughter of the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor, he begot children: the Great-Harvest Deity&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_456"></A><A HREF="#fn_452"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and the August-Spirit-of-Food.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_457"></A><A HREF="#fn_453"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> The elder brother the Deity Eight-Island-Ruler wedded Princess-Falling-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_458"></A><A HREF="#fn_454"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> daughter of the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor, and begot a child: the Deity Fuha-no-moji-Ku-nu-su-nu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_459"></A><A HREF="#fn_455"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> This Deity wedded Princess Hikaha,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_460"></A><A HREF="#fn_456"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> daughter of the Deity Okami,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_461"></A><A HREF="#fn_457"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and begot a child: Water-Spoilt-Blossom-of-Fuka-buchi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_462"></A><A HREF="#fn_458"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> This Deity [67] wedded the Deity Ame-no-tsudohe-chi-ne,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_463"></A><A HREF="#fn_459"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Great-Water-Master.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_464"></A><A HREF="#fn_460"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> This Deity wedded the Deity Grand-Ears&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_465"></A><A HREF="#fn_461"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> daughter of the Deity Funu-dzu-nu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_466"></A><A HREF="#fn_462"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Heavenly-Brandishing-Prince-Lord.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_467"></A><A HREF="#fn_463"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> This Deity wedded the Young-Princess-of-the-Small-Country,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_468"></A><A HREF="#fn_464"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> daughter of the Great-Deity-of-the-Small-Country,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_469"></A><A HREF="#fn_465"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> and begot a child: the</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

</p>

</p>  
<p>
</p>

</p>

<p><a name="page_79"><font size="1" color="green">p. 79</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_470"></A><A HREF="#fn_466"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> another name for whom is the Deity Great-Name-Possessor,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_471"></A><A HREF="#fn_467"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> and another name is the Deity-of-the-Reed-Plains,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_472"></A><A HREF="#fn_468"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> and another name is the Deity of Eight-Thousand-Spears,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_473"></A><A HREF="#fn_469"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> and another name is the Deity-Spirit-of-the-Living-Land.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_474"></A><A HREF="#fn_470"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> In all there were five names.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_475"></A><A HREF="#fn_471"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_450"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_454">78:1</A> <a name="page_79"><font size="1" color="green">p. 79</font></A> <i>Ya-shima-zhi-nu-mi</i>. Ya-shima means "eight islands." The syllables <i>zhi-nu-mi</i> are obscure, but the translator has little doubt "ruler" fairly represents their import. Motowori takes <i>zhi</i> to be an apocopated and <i>nigori&#8217;ed</i> form of <i>shiru</i>, "to rule," nu to be an apocopated form of <i>nushi</i>, "master," and <i>mi</i> to be an apocopated form of the Honorific termination <i>mimi</i>. Tanigaha Shisei considers <i>zhimu</i> to stand for <i>shidzumuru</i>, "to govern," which comes to the same thing so far as the sense is concerned.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_451"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_455">78:2</A> <i>Kamu-oho-ichi-hime</i>. The rendering of <i>Oho-ichi</i> as "Great Majesty" rests on a plausible conjecture of Hirata's, who proposes to, identify <i>ichi</i> with <i>idzu</i> (<A NAME="img_07900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07900.jpg">). Motowori thinks that <i>Oho-ichi</i> should be taken as the name of a place; but this seems less good.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_452"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_456">78:3</A> <i>Oho-toshi-no-kami</i>, written <A NAME="img_07901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07901.jpg">, the obvious rendering of which would be "great year." But the Japanese term <i>toshi</i> is believed to have originally signified, not "year" in the abstract, but that which was produced each year, viz., the harvest (conf. <i>toru</i>, "to take").</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_453"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_457">78:4</A> <i>Uka-no-mi-tama</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_454"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_458">78:5</A> <i>Ko-no-hana-chiru-hime</i>, so called, says Motowori, because she probably died young, as a blossom that falls from the tree. We might however perhaps take the Verb <i>chiru</i> in a Causative sense, and consider the name to signify "the Princess-Who-Causes-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees-to- Fall. A sister of this goddess appears in the pretty legend narrated in Sect. XXXVII under the parallel name of the Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees. See Note 3 to that Sect.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_455"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_459">78:6</A> <i>Fuha-no-moji-ku-nu-su-nu-no-kami</i>. The import of this name is quite uncertain. <i>Fuha</i> however seems to be the name of a place.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_456"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_460">78:7</A> "<i>Hi-kaha-mime</i>. <i>Hi-kaha</i> (lit. "sun-river") is supposed to stand for the name of a place in Musashi, which is however written "ice-river" (<A NAME="img_07902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07902.jpg"> and not <A NAME="img_07903"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/07903.jpg">), the old Japanese words for "ice" and "sun" being homonymous.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_457"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_461">78:8</A> <a name="page_80"><font size="1" color="green">p. 80</font></A> See Sect. VIII. (Note 9), where the name is given as <i>Kura okami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_458"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_462">78:9</A> <i>Fuka-buchi-no-midzu-yare-hana</i>. If Fuka-buchi were ascertained to be not, as is supposed, the name of a place, we should have to render it "deep pool," and the whole would mean in English "Water-Spoilt-Blossom-of-the-Deep-Pool."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_459"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_463">78:10</A> <i>Ame-no-tsudohe-chi-ne-no-kami</i>. In this name nothing is clear but the first three syllables, which signify "heavenly." But if Mabuchi's conjecture as to the meaning of the rest were accepted, we should have to translate the whole by "Heavenly-Assembling-Town-Lady."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_460"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_464">78:11</A> This is the meaning plausibly assigned by Motowori to the original <i>O-midzu-nu-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_461"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_465">78:12</A> <i>Fute-mimi-no-kami</i>, plausibly conjectured by Tominobu to stand for <i>Futo-mimi</i>, etc., which gives the sense here adopted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_462"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_466">78:13</A> <i>Funu-dzu-nu-no-kami</i>. Motowori believes Funu to be the name of a place, and interprets the name to signify "Master of Funu." But this seems highly uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_463"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_467">78:14</A> <i>Ame-no-fuyu-kinu-no-kami</i> (Motowori's reading) or <i>Ama-no</i>, etc. (Hirata's reading). The translation of the name follows Hirata's explanation, which is based on Motowori's, and according to which the characters <A NAME="img_08000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08000.jpg"> ("winter garments") in this text, and <A NAME="img_08001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08001.jpg"> read <i>Fuki-ne</i> in the "Chronicles," are merely phonetic, while the meaning is derived from a comparison of the sounds given by each. Though himself believing in the soundness of Hirata's conclusion, the translator must admit that it is not indisputable.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_464"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_468">78:15</A> <i>Sasu-kuni-waka-hime</i>, or <i>Sashi-kuni</i>, etc. The former reading, which Hirata's adopts, seems best. The meaning of <i>sasu</i>, here rendered "small," is open to doubt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_465"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_469">78:16</A> <i>Sasu-kuni-oho</i>-[<i>no</i>-]<i>kami</i>, or <i>Sashi</i>, etc. The syllable <i>no</i> in the Japanese reading seems to be a superfluous addition of the modern commentators.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_466"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_470">79:17</A> <i>Oho-kuni-nushi-ne-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_467"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_471">79:18</A> <i>Oho-na-muji-no-kami</i>, to which Tominobu proposes to give the sense of "Great Hole-Possessor," in connection with the story of the mouse-hole in which he took refuge from the fire lit by the Impetuous-Male-Deity (<i>Susa-no-wo</i>) for his destruction (see Sect. XXIII). But the interpretation followed in the translation is the most likely as well as the orthodox one, this Deity being entitled the possessor of a Great Name or of Great Names on account of his renown in Japanese mythic story.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_468"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_472">79:19</A> <a name="page_81"><font size="1" color="green">p. 81</font></A> <i>Ashi-hara-shiko-wo-no-kami</i>. The "reed-plains" are doubtless put by metonymy for Japan.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_469"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_473">79:20</A> <i>Yachi-hoko-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_470"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_474">79:21</A> <i>Utsushi-kuni-tama-no-kami</i>. The name must be understood to mean "Spirit of the Land of the Living," and to be antithetical to that of one of his fathers-in-law, the Impetuous Male-Deity (<i>Susa-no-wo</i>) who became the god of Hades.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_471"></A><A HREF="kj027.htm#fr_475">79:22</A> Or "he had five names."</P>

<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_81"><font size="1" color="green">p. 81</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXI.&#8212;THE WHITE HARE OF INABA.]</h2>  
<p>So this Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land had eighty Deities his brethren; but they all left the land to the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land. The reason for their leaving it was this: Each of these eighty Deities had in his heart the wish to marry the Princess of Yakami&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_476"></A><A HREF="#fn_472"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> in Inaba,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_477"></A><A HREF="#fn_473"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and they went together to Inaba, putting their bag on [the back of] the Deity Great-Name-Possessor, whom they took with them as an attendant. Hereupon. when they arrived at Cape Keta,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_478"></A><A HREF="#fn_474"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> [they found] a naked hare lying down. Then the eighty Deities spoke to the hare, saying: "What thou shouldest do is to bathe in the sea-water here, and lie on the slope of a high mountain exposed to the blowing of the wind." So the hare followed the instructions of the eighty Deities, and lay down. Then, as the sea-water dried, the skin of its body all split with the blowing of the wind, so that it lay weeping with pain. But the Deity Great-Name-Possessor, who came last of all, saw the hare, and said: "Why liest thou weeping?" The hare replied, saying: "I was in the Island of Oki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_479"></A><A HREF="#fn_475"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and wished to cross over to this land, but had no means of crossing over. For this reason [69] I deceived the crocodiles&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_480"></A><A HREF="#fn_476"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> of the sea, saying: 'Let you</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_82"><font size="1" color="green">p. 82</font></A></p>  
<p>and me compete, and compute the numbers of our [respective] tribes. So do you go and fetch every member of your tribe, and make them all lie in a row across from this island to Cape Keta. Then I will tread on them, and count them as I run across. Hereby shall we know whether it or my tribe is the larger.' Upon my speaking thus, they were deceived and lay down in a row, and I trod on them and counted them as I came across, and was just about to get on land, when I said: 'You have been deceived by me.' As soon as I had finished speaking, the crocodile who lay the last of all seized me and stripped off all my clothing. As I was weeping and lamenting for this reason, the eighty Deities who went by before [thee] commanded and exhorted me, saying: 'Bathe in the salt water, and lie down exposed to the wind.' So, on my doing as they had instructed me, my whole body was hurt." Thereupon the Deity Great-Name-Possessor instructed the hare, saying: "Go quickly now to the river-mouth, wash thy body with the fresh water, then take the pollen of the sedges [growing] at the river-mouth, spread it about, and roll about upon it, whereupon thy body will certainly be restored to its original state."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_481"></A><A HREF="#fn_477"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> So [the hare] did as it was instructed, and its body became as it had been originally. This was the White Hare of Inaba.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_482"></A><A HREF="#fn_478"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> It is now called the Hare Deity. So the hare said to the Deity Great-Name-Possessor: "These eighty Deities shall certainly not get the Princess of Yakami. Though thou bearest the bag, Thine Augustness shall obtain her."</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_472"></A><A HREF="kj028.htm#fr_476">81:1</A> <a name="page_82"><font size="1" color="green">p. 82</font></A> <i>Yakami-hime</i>. The etymology is uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_473"></A><A HREF="kj028.htm#fr_477">81:2</A> The name of a province not far from that of Idzumo. The word may possibly, as Motowori suggests, be derived from <i>ina-ba</i>, "rice-leaves."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_474"></A><A HREF="kj028.htm#fr_478">81:3</A> <a name="page_83"><font size="1" color="green">p. 83</font></A> <i>Kita-no-saki</i>. The etymology of the name seems uncertain. The meaning of the word <i>keta</i> is "the beams of a roof, the yards of a sail." But perhaps <i>Keta</i> and <i>keta</i> may be nothing more than homonyms of independent origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_475"></A><A HREF="kj028.htm#fr_479">81:4</A> Not far from the coast of Idzumo and of Inaba.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_476"></A><A HREF="kj028.htm#fr_480">81:5</A> See Translator's Introduction, <A HREF="kj004.htm#page_xxxiii">p. xxxiii</A>, Note 41.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_477"></A><A HREF="kj028.htm#fr_481">82:6</A> Literally "to its original skin"; that is to say that its skin would again be covered with fur.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_478"></A><A HREF="kj028.htm#fr_482">82:7</A> Motowori and Moribe agree in considering that the word "white" means "bare" in this place, and the latter in his Critique of the former's Commentary quotes examples which show that their view is probably correct.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_83"><font size="1" color="green">p. 83</font></A></p>  <h3 align="center" align="center">[SECT. XXII.&#8212;MOUNT TEMA.]</h3>  
<p>Thereupon the Princess of Yakami answered&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_483"></A><A HREF="#fn_479"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> the eighty Deities, saying: "I will not listen to your words. I mean to marry the Deity Great-Name-Possessor." So [70] the eighty Deities, being enraged, and wishing to slay the Deity Great-Name-Possessor, took counsel together, on arriving at the foot of Tema&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_484"></A><A HREF="#fn_480"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in the land of Hahaki, and said [to him]: "On this mountain there is a red boar. So when we drive it down, do thou wait and catch it. If thou do not wait and catch it, we will certainly slay thee." Having [thus] spoken, they took fire, and burnt a large stone like unto a boar, and rolled it down. Then, as [they] drove it down and [he] caught it,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_485"></A><A HREF="#fn_481"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> he got stuck to and burnt by the stone, and died. Thereupon Her Augustness his august parent&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_486"></A><A HREF="#fn_482"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> cried and lamented, and went up to Heaven, and entreated His Divine-Producing-Wondrous-Augustness,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_487"></A><A HREF="#fn_483"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> who at once sent Princess Cockle-Shell&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_488"></A><A HREF="#fn_484"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and Prince Clam&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_489"></A><A HREF="#fn_485"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> to bring him to life. Then Princess Cockle-Shell triturated and scorched&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_490"></A><A HREF="#fn_486"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> [her shell], and Princess Clam carried water and</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_84"><font size="1" color="green">p. 84</font></A></p>  
<p>smeared [him] as with mother's&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_491"></A><A HREF="#fn_487"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> milk, whereupon he became a beautiful young man, and wandered off. Hereupon the eighty Deities, seeing [this], again deceived him, [71] taking him with them into the mountains, where they cut down a large tree, inserted a wedge in the tree,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_492"></A><A HREF="#fn_488"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and made him stand in the middle, whereupon they took away the wedge and tortured him to death.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_493"></A><A HREF="#fn_489"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> Then on Her Augustness his august parent again seeking him with cries, she perceived him, and at once cleaving the tree, took him out and brought him to life, and said to him:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_494"></A><A HREF="#fn_490"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> "If thou remain here, thou wilt at last be destroyed by the eighty Deities." Then she sent him swiftly off to the august place of the Deity Great-House-Prince&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_495"></A><A HREF="#fn_491"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> in the land of Ki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_496"></A><A HREF="#fn_492"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> Then when the eighty Deities searched and pursued till they came up to him, and fixed their arrows [in their bows], he escaped by clipping under the fork of a tree, and disappeared.</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_479"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_483">83:1</A> <a name="page_84"><font size="1" color="green">p. 84</font></A> It must be understood that in the meantime they had arrived at her dwelling and begun to court her.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_480"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_484">83:2</A> Etymology unknown.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_481"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_485">83:3</A> The text is here concise to obscurity, but yet there ought not to be much doubt as to the author's intention.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_482"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_486">83:4</A> The text has the character <A NAME="img_08400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08400.jpg"> signifying properly "grand-parent," but frequently used in Archaic Japanese writings in the sense of "mother." It is then read <i>oya</i>, which the English word "parent" exactly represents.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_483"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_487">83:5</A> <i>Kami-musu-bi-no-mikoto</i>. See Sect. I, Note 6.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_484"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_488">83:6</A> <i>Kisa-gahi-hime</i>. The <i>kiga-gahi</i> here mentioned is the modern <i>aka-gahi</i>, a cockle, the <i>Arca inflata</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_485"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_489">83:7</A> <i>Umugi-hime</i>. The <i>umugi</i> here mentioned is the modern <i>hamagari</i>, a clam of the family <i>Mactrid&aelig;</i>, the <i>Cytherea Mereirix</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_486"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_490">83:8</A> The character used is <A NAME="img_08401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08401.jpg">, "collected," "gathered together." But the combined authority of Mabuchi, Motowori and Hirata obliges us either to consider it a copyist's error for <A NAME="img_08402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08402.jpg">, "scorched," or else to believe that in early time in Japan the two characters were used interchangeably.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_487"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_491">84:9</A> <a name="page_85"><font size="1" color="green">p. 85</font></A> Or "nurse's." The meaning is that a paste like milk was made of the triturated and calcined shell mixed with water. There is in this passage a play upon words which it is impossible to reproduce in English, the Japanese term for "triturating," <i>kisage</i> (which the author has taken care to write phonetically) resembling the name of Princess <i>Kisa-gahi</i> (Cockle-Shell), while <i>omo</i>, "mother" or "nurse," similarly recalls that of Princess <i>Umugi</i> (Clam). Motowori traces the names of the shell-fish in question to this exploit of the two goddesses. We shall be justified in applying an inverse interpretation to the legend.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_488"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_492">84:10</A> The original of this clause, <A NAME="img_08500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08500.jpg"> or according to another reading <A NAME="img_08501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08501.jpg">, etc. is a great crux to the native commentators, who can make sure neither of the exact sense nor of the Japanese reading of the first two characters, which seem to be ideographic for three others occurring immediately below, <A NAME="img_08502"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08502.jpg">, which are themselves of doubtful import. An elaborate discussion of the question will be found in Hirata's "Exposition of the Ancient Histories," Vol. XVII, pp. 25-27. The general sense at all events is that here given.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_489"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_493">84:11</A> The characters <A NAME="img_08503"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08503.jpg">, here rendered "tortured him to death," are by the modern commentators read <i>uchi-koroshiki</i>, which simply means killed [him]."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_490"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_494">84:12</A> Literally "to her child."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_491"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_495">84:13</A> <i>Oha-ya-biko-no-kami</i>. This Deity is identified with the Deity <i>I-dakeru</i> mentioned in the "Chronicle" as a son of <i>Susa-no-wo</i> (the "Impetuous-Male-Deity"), and as the introducer into the Island of Tsukushi in particular and into all the "Eight Great Islands" of Japan of the seeds of plants and trees. Motowori's note on this name in Vol. X, pp. 28-29, is worth consulting, though his idea of connecting the agricultural and arboricultural renown of the Deity bearing it with the name of the province of Ki is doubtless quite fanciful.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_492"></A><A HREF="kj029.htm#fr_496">84:14</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the land of tree" (<A NAME="img_08504"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08504.jpg">). Later the character <A NAME="img_08505"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08505.jpg"> was replaced by <A NAME="img_08506"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08506.jpg">, which in Sinico-Japanese has the same sound <i>ki</i>, while a second one, <A NAME="img_08507"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08507.jpg">, was added in order to conform to an edict of the Empress <i>Gem-miy&#333;</i> (A. D. 713) to the effect that all names of places were to be written with two Chinese characters, as was usual in China and Korea. The second character in this case simply carried on the <i>i</i> sound with which the first ends, so that the name became <i>Kii</i>.</P>

<p><a name="page_86"><font size="1" color="green">p. 86</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXIII.&#8212;THE NETHER-DISTANT-LAND.]</h2>  
<p>[The Deity Great-House-Prince spoke to him&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_497"></A><A HREF="#fn_493"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A>] saying: "Thou must set off to the Nether-Distant-Land where [72] dwells His Impetuous-Mate-Augustness. That Great Deity will certainly counsel thee." So on his obeying her command and arriving at the august place&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_498"></A><A HREF="#fn_494"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> of His Impetuous-Male-Augustness, the latter's daughter the Forward-Princess&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_499"></A><A HREF="#fn_495"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> came out and saw him, and they exchanged glances and were married, and [she] went in again, and told her father, saying: "A very beautiful Deity has come." Then the Great Deity went out and looked, and said: 'This is the Ugly-Male-Deity-of-the-Reed-Plain,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_500"></A><A HREF="#fn_496"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and at once calling him in, made him sleep in the snake-house. Hereupon his wife, Her Augustness the Forward-Princess, gave her husband a snake-scarf,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_501"></A><A HREF="#fn_497"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> saying: "When the snakes are about to bite thee, drive them away by waving this scarf thrice." So, on his doing as she had instructed, the snakes became quiet, so that he came forth after calm slumbers. Again on the night of the next day [the Impetuous-Male-Deity] put him into the centipede and wasp-house;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_502"></A><A HREF="#fn_498"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> but as she again gave him a centipede and wasp-scarf, and instructed him as before, he came forth calmly. Again [the Impetuous-Male-Deity] shot a whizzing barb&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_503"></A><A HREF="#fn_499"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> into the middle of a large moor, and sent him to fetch the arrow and, when he had entered the moor, at once set fire to the moor all round. Thereupon, while he [stood] knowing no place of exit, a mouse&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_504"></A><A HREF="#fn_500"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> came and said: "The inside is hollow-hollow; the outside is narrow-narrow."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_505"></A><A HREF="#fn_501"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Owing to its speaking thus, he trod on the place, where, upon he fell in and hid himself, during which time the</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_87"><font size="1" color="green">p. 87</font></A></p>  
<p>fire burnt past. Then the mouse brought out in its mouth and presented to him the whizzing barb. The feathers of the arrow were brought in their mouths by all the mouse's children. Hereupon his wife the Forward-Princess came bearing mourning-implements,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_506"></A><A HREF="#fn_502"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and crying. Her father the Great Deity, thinking that [the Deity Great-Name-Possessor] was already dead and done for, went out and stood on the moor, whereupon [the Deity Great-Name-Possessor] brought the arrow and presented it to him, upon which [the Great Deity], taking him into the house and calling him into an eight-foot spaced large room,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_507"></A><A HREF="#fn_503"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> made him take the lice off his head. So, on looking at the head [he saw that] there were many centipedes [there]. Thereupon, as his wife gave to her husband berries of the <i>muku</i> tree&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_508"></A><A HREF="#fn_504"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and red earth, he chewed the berries to pieces, and spat them out with the red earth which he held in his mouth, so that the Great Deity believed him to be chewing up and spitting out the centipedes, and, feeling fond [of him] in his heart, fell asleep. Then [the Deity Great-Name-Possessor], grasping the Great Deity's hair, tied it fast to the various rafters of the house, and, blocking up the floor of the house with a five hundred draught rock,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_509"></A><A HREF="#fn_505"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> and taking his wife the Forward Princess on his back, then carried off [74] the Great Deity's great life-sword&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_510"></A><A HREF="#fn_506"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> and life-bow-and-arrows,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_511"></A><A HREF="#fn_507"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> as also his heavenly speaking-lute,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_512"></A><A HREF="#fn_508"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> and ran out. But the heavenly speaking-lute brushed against a tree, and the earth resounded. So the Great Deity, who was sleeping, started at the sound, and pulled down the house. But while he was disentangling his hair which was tied to the rafters, [the Deity Great-Name-Possessor] fled a long way. So then, pursuing after him to the Even Pass</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_88"><font size="1" color="green">p. 88</font></A></p>  
<p>of Hades,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_513"></A><A HREF="#fn_509"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> and gazing on him from afar, he called out to the Deity Great-Name-Possessor, saying: "With the great life-sword and the life-bow-and-arrows which thou earnest, pursue thy half-brethren&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_514"></A><A HREF="#fn_510"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> till they crouch on the august slopes of the passes,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_515"></A><A HREF="#fn_511"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> and pursue them till they are swept into the reaches of the rivers, and do thou, wretch!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_516"></A><A HREF="#fn_512"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> become the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_517"></A><A HREF="#fn_513"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> and moreover, becoming the Deity Spirit-of-the-Living-Land, and making my daughter the Forward-Princess thy [75] consort,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_518"></A><A HREF="#fn_514"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> do thou make stout the temple-pillars at the foot of Mount Uka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_519"></A><A HREF="#fn_515"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> in the nethermost rock-bottom, and make high the cross-beams to the Plain-of-High-Heaven, and dwell [there], thou villain!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_520"></A><A HREF="#fn_516"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> So when, bearing the great sword and bow, he pursued and scattered the eighty Deities, he did pursue them till they crouched on the august slope of every pass,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_521"></A><A HREF="#fn_517"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> he did pursue them till they were swept into every river, and then he began to make the land.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_522"></A><A HREF="#fn_518"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> Quamobrem Hera Yamaki, secundum anterius pactum, [cum eo] in thalamo coivit. So he brought her with him; but, fearing his consort the Forward Princess, she stuck into the fork of a tree the child that she had borne, and went back.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_523"></A><A HREF="#fn_519"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> So the child was called by the name of the Tree-Fork-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_524"></A><A HREF="#fn_520"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> and another name was the Deity-of-August-Wells.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_525"></A><A HREF="#fn_521"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<p>

<p>

<p><a name="page_89"><font size="1" color="green">p. 89</font></A> <a name="page_90"><font size="1" color="green">p. 90</font></A></p>
