<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_493"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_497">86:1</A> <a name="page_88"><font size="1" color="green">p. 88</font></A> Literally, "to the child." The words placed in brackets, and which are not to be found in either of the early printed editions, are supplied in accordance with a suggestion of Moribe's contained in his Critique of Motowori's Commentary. Motowori himself had supplied the words "Her Augustness his august parent spoke to him," which seem less appropriate. It is true that one MS. is quoted by Motowori as favouring his view; but such authority is insufficient, and the mistake, moreover, peculiarly easy for a copyist to make (<i>mi oya</i> for <i>oho-ya</i>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_494"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_498">86:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Palace.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_495"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_499">86:3</A> <a name="page_89"><font size="1" color="green">p. 89</font></A> This is Motowori's view of the import of the original name <i>Suseri-bime</i>, which he connects with <i>susumu</i>, "to advance," "to press forward," and explains by reference to the bold, forward conduct of the young goddess.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_496"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_500">86:4</A> One of the alternative names of this Deity, who is mostly mentioned by one of his other four designations, for a list of which see sect. XX. (Notes 17 to 21).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_497"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_501">86:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "a scarf by waving which he might keep off the snakes." Similarly the "centipede and wasp-scarf" mentioned a little farther on must be understood to mean "a scarf to ward off centipedes and wasps with."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_498"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_502">86:6</A> The word <i>hachi</i>, translated "wasp," is a general name including other insects of the family of <i>Vespid&aelig;</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_499"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_503">86:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "arrow." The original expression is <i>nari-kabura</i> (<A NAME="img_08900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08900.jpg">), which has survived in the modern language under the modified form of <i>kabura-ya</i>, defined in Dr. Hepburn's Dictionary as "an arrow with a head shaped like a turnip, having a hole in it, which causes it to hum as it flies." It was used in China in the time of the Han dynasty.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_500"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_504">86:8</A> Or "rat."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_501"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_505">86:9</A> The translator cannot think of any better English equivalents for the child-like onomatopoeias <i>hora-hora</i> and <i>subu-subu</i> of the Japanese original.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_502"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_506">87:10</A> The edition of 1687 reads the two characters <A NAME="img_08901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08901.jpg"> (here translated "mourning implements,") <i>mo-gari no sonahe</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "preparations for the funeral." Such preparations are detailed in the latter part of Sect. XXXI.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_503"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_507">87:11</A> This is Mabuchi's interpretation, as quoted by Motowori, of the expression <i>ya-ta-ma no oho-muro-ya</i>. Motowori's own view is that <i>ya-ta</i> stands for <i>ya-tzu</i>, which give us in English "an eight-spaced large room." The character <A NAME="img_08902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08902.jpg">, "space" has been in later times used as a measure of length (six Japanese feet.) Altogether the precise meaning of the expression is not quite clear, but the general sense is a "large spacious room."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_504"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_508">87:12</A> <i>Aphananthe Aspera</i>, also sometimes called <i>Celtis Muku</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_505"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_509">87:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "a rock which it would require five hundred men to lift."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_506"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_510">87:14</A> <i>Iku-tachi</i> (<A NAME="img_08903"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08903.jpg">), supposed by Motowori to be "a sword having the virtue of conferring long life upon its possessor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_507"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_511">87:15</A> <i>Iku-yumi-ya</i> (<A NAME="img_08904"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08904.jpg">).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_508"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_512">87:16</A> <i>Ame no nori-goto</i> (<A NAME="img_08905"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/08905.jpg">), so called because, as will be seen Sect. XCVI, divine messages were conveyed through a person playing <a name="page_90"><font size="1" color="green">p. 90</font></A> on the lute. Hirata, in his "Exposition of the Ancient Histories." invents the reading <i>ame no nu-goto</i> (<A NAME="img_09000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09000.jpg">), "heavenly jewelled lute."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_509"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_513">88:17</A> See Sect. IX. (Note 16).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_510"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_514">88:18</A> They were not born of the same mother. The Chinese characters in the text (<A NAME="img_09001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09001.jpg">) imply, properly speaking, that the eighty brethren of the Great-Name-Possessor were the sons of concubines. But Motowori denies that such is the Japanese usage with regard to the characters in question.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_511"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_515">88:19</A> Or "hills."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_512"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_516">88:20</A> The word in the text is <i>ore</i>, an insulting equivalent Second Personal Pronoun. If we were translating into German, we might perhaps approximately represent its force by "<i>er</i>."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_513"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_517">88:21</A> Thus according to this legend, "Master-of-the-Great-Land" (<i>Oho-kuni-nushi</i>) was not the original name of the Deity commonly designated by it, and his sovereignty over the Land of the Living (whence the appropriateness of the second name in this context) was derived by investiture from the god of the Land of the Dead.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_514"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_518">88:22</A> The characters <A NAME="img_09002"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09002.jpg">, which are here used, designate specifically the chief or legitimate wife, as opposed to the lesser wives or concubines.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_515"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_519">88:23</A> <i>Uka-no-yama</i>. No satisfactory etymology of <i>Uka</i> is forthcoming.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_516"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_520">88:24</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Firmly planting in the rock the pillars forming the foundation of thy palace, and rearing its fabric to the skies, do thou rule therefrom the Land of the Living, thou powerful wretch, who hast so successfully braved me!"</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_517"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_521">88:25</A> Or "hill."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_518"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_522">88:26</A> This is taken to mean that he continued the act of creation which had been interrupted by the death of <i>Izanami</i> (the "Female-Who-Invites"). See Sect. IX, <A HREF="kj015.htm#page_35">p. 35</A>, where her husband Izanagi says to her: "The lands that I and thou made are not yet finished making." The words "<i>Kuni tsukuri</i>" (<A NAME="img_09003"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09003.jpg">), here used for "making the land," became a title for "Ruler-of-the-Land" and finally a "gentile name" (<i>kabane</i>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_519"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_523">88:27</A> <i>Q.d.</i>, to Inaba.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_520"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_524">88:28</A> <i>Ki-no-mata-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_521"></A><A HREF="kj030.htm#fr_525">88:29</A> <i>Mi-wi-no-kami</i>. He is supposed to have benefitted the country by digging wells in many places.</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_91"><font size="1" color="green">p. 91</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXIV.&#8212;THE WOOING OF THE DEITY-OF-EIGHT-THOUSAND-SPEARS.]</h2>  
<p>This Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_526"></A><A HREF="#fn_522"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> when he went forth&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_527"></A><A HREF="#fn_523"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> to woo the Princess of Nuna-kaha,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_528"></A><A HREF="#fn_524"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in the land of Koshi, on arriving at the house of the Princess of Nuna kaha sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"[I] His Augustness the Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears, [76] having been unable to find a spouse in the Land of the Eight islands, and having heard that in the far off Land of Koshi there is a wise maiden, having heard that there is a beauteous maiden, I am standing [here] to truly woo her, I am going backwards and forwards to woo her. Without having yet untied even the cord of my sword, without having yet untied even my veil, I push back the plank-door shut by the maiden; while I am standing [here], I pull it forward. While I am standing [here], the <i>nuye</i> sings upon the green mountain, and [the voice of] the true bird of the moor, the pheasant, resounds; the bird of the yard, the cock, crows. Oh! the pity that [the] birds should sing! Oh! these birds! Would that I could beat them till they were sick! Oh! swiftly-flying heaven-racing messenger, the tradition of the thing, too, this!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_529"></A><A HREF="#fn_525"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then the Princess of Nuna-kaha, without yet opening [77] the door, sang from the inside saying:&#8212;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_92"><font size="1" color="green">p. 92</font></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Thine Augustness the Deity-Of-Eight-Thousand-Spears! Being a maiden like a drooping plant, my heart is just a bird on a sand-bank by the shore; it will now indeed be a dotterel. Afterwards it will be a gentle bird; so as for thy life, do not deign to die. Oh! swiftly-flying heaven-racing messenger! the tradition of the thing, too, this!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_530"></A><A HREF="#fn_526"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p align="center">[78] [<i>Second Song of the Princess</i>.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_531"></A><A HREF="#fn_527"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A>]</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">When the sun shall hide behind the green mountains, in the night [black as] the true jewels of the moor will I come forth. Coming radiant with smiles like the morning sun, [thine] arms white as rope of paper-mulberry-bark shall softly pat [my] breast soft as the melting snow; and patting [each other] interlaced, stretching out and pillowing [ourselves] on [each other's] jewel-arms,&#8212; true jewel-arms,&#8212;and with outstretched legs, will we sleep. So speak not too lovingly, Thine Augustness the Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears! The tradition of the thing, too, this!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_532"></A><A HREF="#fn_528"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Quamobrem e&acirc; nocte non coierunt, sed sequentis diei nocte auguste coierunt.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_93"><font size="1" color="green">p. 93</font></A> <a name="page_94"><font size="1" color="green">p. 94</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_522"></A><A HREF="kj031.htm#fr_526">91:1</A> <a name="page_92"><font size="1" color="green">p. 92</font></A> In this Section, the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land is spoken of under this <i>alias</i>. See Sect. XX, Note 20).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_523"></A><A HREF="kj031.htm#fr_527">91:2</A> The characters <A NAME="img_09200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09200.jpg"> here, in accordance with the reading of the commentators, rendered by the words "went forth," as Honorific, being only properly applied to the progresses of a sovereign.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_524"></A><A HREF="kj031.htm#fr_528">91:3</A> <i>Kuna-kawa-hime</i>. <i>Nana-kaha</i> or <i>Nu-na-kaha</i> ("lagoon-river"), is supposed to be the name of a place in the province of Echigo.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_525"></A><A HREF="kj031.htm#fr_529">91:4</A> <a name="page_93"><font size="1" color="green">p. 93</font></A> The drift of this poem needs but little elucidation:&#8212;After giving his reasons for coming to woo the Princess of Nuna-kaha, the god declares that he is in such haste to penetrate to her chamber, that he does not even stay to ungird his sword or take off his veil, but tries to push or pull open the door at once. During these vain endeavours, the mountain. side begins to re-echo with the cries of the birds announcing the dawn, when lovers must slink away. Would that he could kill these unwelcome harbingers of day, and bring back the darkness!&#8212;The Land of the Eight Islands (<i>i.e.</i> Japan proper, beyond whose boundaries lay the barbarous northern country of Koshi) is in the original <i>Ya-shima-huni</i> (Conf. Sect. V, Note 27).&#8212;The <i>nuye</i> is a bird which must be fabulous if most of the accounts given of it are accepted. The "Commentary on the Lyric Dramas" tells us (with variations) that "it has the head of a monkey, the body of a racoon-faced dog, the tail of a serpent, and the hands (<i>sic</i>) and feet of a tiger," adding, as the reader will make no difficulty in allowing, that "it is a strange and peculiar creature." The <i>Wa-Kun Shiwori</i> says that "it is a bird much larger than a pigeon, and having a loud and mournful cry." It is likewise said to come out at night-time and retire during the day, for which reason doubtless Mabuchi likens it to the owl. A very ancient and curious Chinese book entitled the "Mountain and Sea Classic" (<A NAME="img_09300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09300.jpg">) the modern editions of which contain extremely droll illustrations of fabulous creatures, tells us of a bird called the "white <i>nuye</i>" (<A NAME="img_09301"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09301.jpg">) which is "like a pheasant, with markings on its head, white wings, and yellow feet, and whose flesh is a certain cure for the hiccough." The character <A NAME="img_09302"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09302.jpg"> and <A NAME="img_09303"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09303.jpg">, with which, as well as with <A NAME="img_09304"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09304.jpg"> the word <i>nuye</i> is variously written, seem to be unauthorized&#8212;The line here (following Motowori and Moribe's view) rendered "Would that I could beat them till they were sick!" will also bear the interpretation formerly proposed by Keichiyu, "Would that I could beat them till they left off!"&#8212;The last five lines, here rendered "Oh! swiftly flying heaven-racing messenger," etc., are extremely obscure. It is possible that <i>ishi tafu ya</i> (rendered "Oh! swiftly flying," in deference to Motowori's and Moribe's view) may be but a meaningless <i>refrain</i>. "Heaven racing messenger" is tolerably certain. Of the rest it is not easy to make sense. Motowori proposes to credit the five lines in question with the following general meaning: "May this song, like a messenger, "run down to future ages, preserving for them the tradition of this event!" Moribe, in his Critique of Motowori's Commentary, supposes the lines in question to be an addition made by the official singers, who in later <a name="page_94"><font size="1" color="green">p. 94</font></A> times sang these songs as an accompaniment to dances. Whatever their origin and proper signification, it is plain that they had come to be used as a <i>refrain</i>, from which the first two lines were sometimes omitted, as we see in some of the songs further on.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_526"></A><A HREF="kj031.htm#fr_530">92:5</A> The drift of the poem is this: "Being a tender maiden, my heart flutters like the birds on the sandy islets by the beach, and I cannot yet be thine. Yet do not die of despair; for I will soon comply with thy desires."&#8212;The word <i>nuye-kusa</i> (here rendered "drooping plant," in accordance with the views of the commentators) is a Pillow-Word of somewhat obscure derivation.&#8212;The word <i>chidori</i> (rendered "dotterel" throughout this translation) denotes in its modern acceptation, according to Messrs. Blakiston and Pryer, "any kind of sandpiper, plover or dotterel." Its proper and original signification is, however, greatly debated by the commentators, and some think that it is not the specific name of any kind of bird, but stands simply by apocope for <i>tachi-dori</i>, "rising bird," thus designating any kind of small bird that rises and flies along near the beach.&#8212;The word <i>na-dori</i> (here, in accordance with Moribe's view, rendered "gentle bird") is taken by Motowori to mean simply "gentle," "compliant." But both the construction and the context seem to impose on us the interpretation here given. Keichiyu, in his "<i>K&#333;gan-Sh&#333;</i>," interprets the whole passage differently; but in order to do so he, without sufficient authority, changes the readings of the text into <i>wa tori</i>, "my bird," and <i>na tori</i> "thy bird."&#8212;The refrain is the same as in the previous song.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_527"></A><A HREF="kj031.htm#fr_531">92:6</A> There is no break in the text; but the commentators rightly consider the following to be a separate poem.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_528"></A><A HREF="kj031.htm#fr_532">92:7</A> The import of this very plain-spoken poem needs no elucidation.&#8212;<i>Nubatama</i> (here rendered "true jewels of the moor") is the Pillow-Word for things black or related to darkness. The "true jewels of the moor" are supposed to be the jet-black berries of the <i>hiafugi</i> (pron. <i>hi&#333;gi</i>, <i>Ixia chinensis</i>). The whole etymology is, however, not absolutely certain.&#8212;Of which of the two lovers the words "coming radiant" with "smiles" are spoken, is not clear; but they probably refer to the male deity, as do the white arms, strange though such an expression may appear as applied to a man. The goddess represents herself and her lover as using each other's arms for pillows. The word "jewel-arms" means simply "beautiful arms."</P>
<p><HR>

<HTML>
<HEAD>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="../../css/marg.css">
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">
<META name="keywords" content="Kojiki Japan Shinto Mythology Legend Folklore Text Scripture Emperor Empress Chronology">
<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume I: Section XXV.&#8212;The Cup Pledge</TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="index.htm">Index</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj031.htm">Previous</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj033.htm">Next</A>&nbsp;
<HR><A HREF="http://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/B0028Y4SZY/internetsacredte">Buy this Book at Amazon.com</A></CENTER>
<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_95"><font size="1" color="green">p. 95</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXV.&#8212;THE CUP PLEDGE.]</h2>  
<p>[79] Again this Deity's Chief Empress,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_533"></A><A HREF="#fn_529"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Her Augustness the Forward-Princess, was very jealous. So the Deity her husband, being distressed, was about to go up from Idzumo to the Land of Yamato; and as he stood attired, with one august hand on the saddle of his august horse and one august foot in the august stirrup, he sang, saying:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"When I take and attire myself so carefully in my august garments black as the true jewels of the moor, and, like the birds of the offing, look at my breast,&#8212;though I raise my fins, [I say that] these are not good, and cast them off on the waves on the beach. When I take and attire myself so carefully in my august garments green as the kingfisher, and, like the birds of the oiling, look at my breast.&#8212;though I raise my fins, [I say that] these, too, are not good, and cast them off on the waves on the beach. When I take and attire myself so carefully in my raiment dyed in the sap of the dye-tree, the pounded madder sought in the mountain fields, and. like the birds of the offing. look at my breast,&#8212;though I raise my fins, [I say that] they are good. My dear young sister. Thine Augustness! Though thou say that thou wilt not weep,&#8212;if like the flocking birds, I flock and depart, if, like the led birds, I am led away and depart, thou wilt hang down thy head like <a name="page_96"><font size="1" color="green">p. 96</font></A> a single eulalia upon the mountain and thy weeping shall indeed rise as the mist of [80] the morning shower. Thine Augustness [my] spouse like the young herbs! The tradition of the thing, too, this!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_534"></A><A HREF="#fn_530"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then his Empress, taking a great august liquor-cup, and drawing near and offering it to him, sang, saying:&#8212;</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! Thine Augustness the Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears! [Thou], my [dear] Master-of-the-Great-Land indeed, being a man, probably hast on the various island-headlands [81] that thou seest, and on every beach headland that thou lookest on, a wife like the young herbs. But as for me alas! being a woman, I have no man except thee; I have no spouse except thee. Beneath the fluttering of the ornamented fence, beneath the softness of the warm coverlet, beneath the rustling of the cloth coverlet, [thine] arms white as rope of paper-mulberry bark softly patting [my] breast soft as the melting snow, and patting [each other] interlaced, stretching out and pillowing [our selves] on [each others arms],&#8212;true jewel arms, and with outstretched legs, will we sleep. Lift up the luxuriant august liquor!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_535"></A><A HREF="#fn_531"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>She having thus sung, they at once pledged [each other] by the cup with [their hands] on [each other's] necks,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_536"></A><A HREF="#fn_532"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and are at rest till the present time. These are called divine words.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_537"></A><A HREF="#fn_533"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_97"><font size="1" color="green">p. 97</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_529"></A><A HREF="kj032.htm#fr_533">95:1</A> <a name="page_97"><font size="1" color="green">p. 97</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, chief wife.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_530"></A><A HREF="kj032.htm#fr_534">96:2</A> The meaning of this poem is:&#8212;"I start for Yamato, there to search for a better wife, and I carefully array myself for the journey. Black,&#8212;the colour of mourning,&#8212;is not fair enough, and red is more beautiful than green; so it is on my red garments that my choice rests. And thou, jealous and imperious woman! for all that thou sayest that thou wilt not heed my going, thou wilt weep when I depart with my retainers as departs a flock of birds, and thou wilt bury thy head in thy hands, and thy tears shall be as the misty drops of the morning shower."&#8212;The words <i>hata tagi</i> (rendered in accordance with Motowori's view by "raise my fins") are supposed to signify "raise my sleeve." If the last syllable were found in any text written with a character not requiring the use of the <i>nigori</i> in the Japanese transcription, we should get the more satisfactory reading <i>ha tataki</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "beat my wings;" but the syllable in question does not seem to be anywhere so written;&#8212;The "madder" is in the original <i>akane</i>, here written (but doubtless only through the error of some copyist) <i>atane</i>. The words rendered "sought in the mountain fields" might also be translated "sown in the mountain fields," <i>magashi</i>, "sought," and <i>makishi</i>, "sowed" being thought to be convertible.&#8212;The words "my beloved" represent the Japanese <i>itokoya no</i>, whose meaning is obscure and much disputed.&#8212;The words "when I am led away" must be understood as if they were Active instead of Passive, signifying as they do "when I lead away my retinue of followers."&#8212;The eulalia (<i>Eulalia Japonica</i>) is a long king of grass very often alluded to in the later classical poetry.&#8212;The words "on the mountain" represent the Japanese words <i>yama-to no</i>, in accordance with Motowori's and Hirata's view of the meaning of the latter (<A NAME="img_09700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09700.jpg"> or <A NAME="img_09701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09701.jpg">). Th. <i>prim&aacute; facie</i> interpretation of "in the province of Yamato," which Keichiyu adopts, will not bear investigation.&#8212;It is not quite clear whether "the mist of the morning shower" means mist separate from the rain, or is simply a phrase for the rain-drops themselves. Motowori adopts the former opinion.&#8212;"Young herbs:" <i>waka-kusa</i>, is the Pillow-Word for "spouse,"&#8212;newly married youths and maidens being likened to the fresh-grown grass. The <i>refrain</i> is an abbreviated form of that found in the two previous poems.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_531"></A><A HREF="kj032.htm#fr_535">96:3</A> The import of this poem needs little explanation:&#8212;The goddess says to her husband, "Come back and live with me, and quaff this goblet as a sign of reconciliation; for though thou, as a man, mayest have a wife on every shore, I shall be left solitary if thou depart."&#8212;<a name="page_98"><font size="1" color="green">p. 98</font></A> The "ornamented fence" is supposed to mean "a curtain round the sleeping place."&#8212;The latter part to the poem (excepting the concluding phrase) is a repetition of lines that have already occurred in the last one of Sect. XXIV (note 7). The word <i>tate-matsurase</i> (here rendered "lift up") occasions some difficulty. It properly signifies "present to a superior;" but here it must be taken to mean "partake of," as the goddess is speaking to her spouse himself, unless indeed we suppose the final words of the song to be a command addressed to one of her attendants to present the cup to their common lord and master.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_532"></A><A HREF="kj032.htm#fr_536">96:4</A> This is the probable and generally accepted meaning of the original of this clause, which is written phonetically.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_533"></A><A HREF="kj032.htm#fr_537">96:5</A> Explained by Moribe to mean, with reference to the whole story, "conversation about divine events." Motowori proposes to supplement the character <A NAME="img_09800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09800.jpg">, "song," to the two (<A NAME="img_09801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/09801.jpg">) in the text, and to take the three together as designating the nature of the preceding songs, in accordance with the usage in other cases,&#8212;"Rustic Songs," "Courtier's Songs," etc. If this view were adopted, we should have to translate by "Divine Converse Songs."</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_98"><font size="1" color="green">p. 98</font></A> [82]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXVI.&#8212;THE DEITIES THE AUGUST DESCENDANTS OF THE DEITY MASTER-OF-THE-GREAT-LAND.]</h2>  
<p>So this Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land wedded Her Augustness Torrent-Mist-Princess, the Deity dwelling in the inner temple of Munakata.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_538"></A><A HREF="#fn_534"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and begot children: the Deity Aji-shiki-taka-hiko-ne,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_539"></A><A HREF="#fn_535"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> next his younger sister Her Augustness High-Princess,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_540"></A><A HREF="#fn_536"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> another name for whom is Her Augustness Princess Under-Shining.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_541"></A><A HREF="#fn_537"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> This Deity Aji-shiki-taka-hiko-ne is he who is now called the Great August Deity of Kamo.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_542"></A><A HREF="#fn_538"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Again the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land wedded Her Augustness Princess Divine-House-Shield&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_543"></A><A HREF="#fn_539"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Thing-Sign-Master.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_544"></A><A HREF="#fn_540"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Again he wedded the Deity Bird-Ears,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_545"></A><A HREF="#fn_541"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> daughter of the Deity Eight-Island-Possessor,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_546"></A><A HREF="#fn_542"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and begot</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_99"><font size="1" color="green">p. 99</font></A></p>  
<p>a child: the Deity Bird-Growing-Ears.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_547"></A><A HREF="#fn_543"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> This Deity wedded Hina-teri-nakata-bichi-wo-ikochini,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_548"></A><A HREF="#fn_544"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Land-Great-Wealth.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_549"></A><A HREF="#fn_545"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> This Deity wedded the Deity Ashi-nadaka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_550"></A><A HREF="#fn_546"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> another name for whom is Princess-Eight-Rivers-and-Inlets,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_551"></A><A HREF="#fn_547"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Swift-Awful-Brave-Sahaya-Land-Ruler.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_552"></A><A HREF="#fn_548"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> This Deity wedded Princess Luck-Spirit,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_553"></A><A HREF="#fn_549"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> daughter of the [84] Deity Heavenly-Awful-Master,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_554"></A><A HREF="#fn_550"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Awful-Master-Prince.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_555"></A><A HREF="#fn_551"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> This Deity wedded Princess Hina-rashi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_556"></A><A HREF="#fn_552"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> daughter of the Deity Okami,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_557"></A><A HREF="#fn_553"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Tahiri-kishi-marumi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_558"></A><A HREF="#fn_554"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> This Deity wedded the Deity Princess-Life-Spirit-Luck-Spirit,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_559"></A><A HREF="#fn_555"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> daughter of the Deity Waiting-to-See-the-Flowers-of-the-Holly,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_560"></A><A HREF="#fn_556"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Mira-na-mi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_561"></A><A HREF="#fn_557"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> This Deity wedded Princess Awo-numa-oshi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_562"></A><A HREF="#fn_558"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> daughter of the Master-of-Shiki-yama,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_563"></A><A HREF="#fn_559"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Nunoshi-tomi-tori-naru-mi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_564"></A><A HREF="#fn_560"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> This Deity wedded the Young-Day-Female-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_565"></A><A HREF="#fn_561"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Heavenly-Hibara-Great-Long-Wind-Wealth.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_566"></A><A HREF="#fn_562"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> This Deity wedded the Deity Toho-tsu-ma-chi-ne,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_567"></A><A HREF="#fn_563"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> daughter of the Deity Heavenly-Pass Boundary,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_568"></A><A HREF="#fn_564"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> and begot a child: the Deity Toho-tsu-yama-zaki-tarashi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_569"></A><A HREF="#fn_565"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">From the above-mentioned Deity Eight-Island-Ruler down to the Deity Toho-tsu-yama-zaki-tarashi are called the Deities of seventeen generations.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_570"></A><A HREF="#fn_566"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A></div></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_534"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_538">98:1</A> <a name="page_99"><font size="1" color="green">p. 99</font></A> See Sect. XIII, Note 15 and Sect. XIV. Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_535"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_539">98:2</A> <i>Aji-shiki taka-hiko-ne no-kami</i>. The meaning of the first two members of this compound name is altogether obscure. <i>Taka-hiko-ne</i> signifies "high-prince lord."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_536"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_540">98:3</A> <i>Taka-hime-no-mikoto</i>. <i>Taka-hime</i> is supposed by Hirata to be a mutilated form of <i>Taka-teru-hime</i>, "High-Shining-Princess," which would make the two names of this personage properly complementary.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_537"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_541">98:4</A> <a name="page_100"><font size="1" color="green">p. 100</font></A> <i>Shita-teru-hime-no-mikoto</i>. This goddess is popularly supposed to have been extremely beautiful, whence perhaps the name, which might be taken to imply that her beauty shone forth from under her garments as in the case of <i>So-towori-hime</i> (see Sect. CXXXVII, Note 9).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_538"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_542">98:5</A> Because there worshipped. The etymology of Kamo is not clear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_539"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_543">98:6</A> <i>Kamu-ya-tate-hime-no-mikoto</i>. The translation here follows the Chinese characters. Another proposal of Motowori's is to regard the syllables ya-tate as a corruption of <i>iya-taka-teri</i>, "more and more high shining," which would give us for the whole name in English "Divine-More-and-More-High-Shining-Princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_540"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_544">98:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the Deity who gave a sign of the thing he did." The Japanese original is <i>Koto-shire-nushi-no-kami</i>. The translation of the name here given follows Motowori's interpretation, which takes it to contain an allusion to the act by which its bearer symbolized his surrender of the sovereignty of the land to the descendant of the Sun-Goddess. Lengthened forms of the name are <i>Ya-he-koto-shiro-nushi-no-kami</i> ("the Deity Eight-Fold-Thing-Sign-Master") and <i>Tsumi-ba-ya-he-koto-shiro-nushi-no-kami</i>, the first three syllables of which latter are obscure. Both of the lengthened forms are supposed to contain a reference to the manifold "green branches" mentioned in the legend referred to,&#8212;that. viz., which forms the subject-matter of Sect. XXXII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_541"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_545">98:8</A> <i>Tori-mimi-no-kami</i>. Motowori suggests that tori, "bird," may be but the name of a place in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_542"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_546">98:9</A> <i>Ya-shima-muji-no-kami</i>. "Possessor" is the probable meaning of <i>muji</i>, regarded here and elsewhere as an alternative form of <i>mochi</i>. Motowori suggests that Yashima may be meant for the name of a district in Yamato, in which case both this god and his daughter would have been named from the places of their birth or residence, which are near each other in the same province.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_543"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_547">99:10</A> <i>Tori-nara-mi-no-kami</i>. The above interpretation, which is proposed by Motowori, seems more acceptable than "Bird-Sounding-Sea," which the Chinese characters yield. <i>Tori</i> "bird," if taken above to be the name of a place, must be likewise so considered here.&#8212;Motowori reasonably conjectures that a clause to the following effect is here omitted: "He wedded such and such a princess, daughter of such and such a Deity, and begot a child: the Deity <i>Take-mina-gata</i>" [<i>i.e.</i> probably Brave-August-Name-Firm] (See Sect. XXXII, Note 21). Hirata's text in his "Exposition of the Ancient Histories" is <A NAME="img_10000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10000.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_544"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_548">99:11</A> <a name="page_101"><font size="1" color="green">p. 101</font></A> The text is here evidently corrupt, and Motowori proposes to read either <i>Hina-teri-nukata-bichi-wo-no-kami no musume Iko-chi-ni-no-kami</i> which would give us in English "the Deity Ikochini, daughter of the male Deity Hina-teri-nukata-bichi," or else to take the whole as the father's name, and to suppose that the name of the daughter has been accidentally omitted. <i>Hina-teri</i> means "Rustic Illuminator," and the name resembles that of a deity mentioned in Sect. XIV, Note 6. <i>Nukata</i> and <i>Bichi</i> (or <i>Hiji</i>, reversing the position of the <i>nigori</i>) are supposed to be names of places. <i>Ikochini</i> is altogether obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_545"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_549">99:12</A> <i>Kuni-oshi-tomi-no-kami</i>, <i>oshi</i>, as in other instances, being considered a contraction of <i>ohoshi</i>, "great."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_546"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_550">99:13</A> <i>Ashi-nakada-no-kami</i>. It is not clear whether this is a personal name or, as Motowori supposes, the name of the place where the goddess resided. He quotes places named Ashidaka and Ashida; but this hardly seems satisfactory. In any case the name remains obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_547"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_551">99:14</A> <i>Ya-kaha-ye-hime</i>. The translation follows the meaning of the Chinese characters with which the name is written. It is, however, also open to us to consider <i>Yaka-ha-ye</i> as a corruption of <i>iya-ko-haye</i>, "more flourishing."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_548"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_552">99:15</A> <i>Haya-mika-no-take sahaya-ji-nu-mi-no-kami</i>. The syllables <i>sahaya</i> are obscure, and Motowori's proposal to consider them as the name of a place has only been followed in the translation for want of something more satisfactory.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_549"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_553">99:16</A> <i>Saki-tama-bime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_550"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_554">99:17</A> <i>Ame-no-mika-a-nushi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_551"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_555">99:18</A> <i>wika-nushi-hike-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_552"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_556">99:19</A> <i>Hina-rashi-bime</i>. Motowori takes Hina to be the name of a place, and <i>rashi</i>, to be an apocopated form of <i>tarashi</i> or some such word. But this is mere guess-work.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_553"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_557">99:20</A> <i>Okami-no-kami</i>. See Sect. VIII, Note 9.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_554"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_558">99:21</A> <i>Tahiri-kishi-marumi-no-kami</i>. The meaning of this name is quite obscure. Motowori throws out the suggestion that <i>Tahiri</i> may stand for <i>Tari-hiri</i> and <i>Kishi-marumi</i> for <i>Kizhima-tsu-mi</i>,&#8212;<i>Tarihi</i> and <i>Kizhiwa</i> being names of places, and <i>tsu-mi</i>, as usual, being credited with the signification of "possessor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_555"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_559">99:22</A> <i>Iku-tama-saki-tama-hime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_556"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_560">99:23</A> <i>Hihira-gi-no-sono-hana-madzu-mi-no-kami</i>. The interpretation of the name here given is conjectural as far as the words "waiting to see" (taken on Tominobu's authority to be the most likely meaning of <i>madzu-mi</i>) <a name="page_102"><font size="1" color="green">p. 102</font></A> are concerned. Motowori suggests that <i>hihira-gi-no</i> may be but a sort of Pillow-Word, and not part of the actual name at all, and the remaining characters corrupted. <i>Hihira-gi</i> rendered "holly," is properly the <i>Olea Aquifolia</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_557"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_561">99:24</A> <i>Miro-nami-no-kami</i>. Meaning obscure. <i>Miro</i> is supposed by Motowori to be the name of a place, and <i>na</i> and <i>mi</i> to be Honorific appellations.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_558"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_562">99:25</A> <i>Awo-numa-nu-oshi-hime</i>. Meaning obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_559"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_563">99:26</A> <i>Shiki-yama-nushi-no-kami</i>. <i>Shiki-yama</i> is supposed to be the name of a place in Echizen.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_560"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_564">99:27</A> <i>Nunoshi-tomi-tori-nara-mi-no-kami</i>. <i>Nunoshi</i> is supposed to be the name of a place, and identical with <i>Nunoshi</i>, which forms part of the mother's name. Motowori takes <i>tomi</i> to be an Honorific, and <i>Tori</i> (as previously in the case of the deities <i>Tori-mimi</i> and <i>Tori-naru-mi</i> (See Notes 8 and 10) to be the name of another place. The translator would prefer to take both words in their common signification, and (leaving <i>nunoshi</i> aside as incomprehensible) to render the rest of the name thus: "Wealth-Bird-Growing-Ears."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_561"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_565">99:28</A> <i>Waka-hiru-me-na-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_562"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_566">99:29</A> <i>Ame-no-hibara-oho-shi-na-domi-no-kami</i>. Motowori supposes Hibara to be the name of a place, a view which the translator has adopted for want of a better.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_563"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_567">99:30</A> <i>Toho-tsu-ma-chi-ne-no-kami</i>. Motowori supposes Tohotsu to be the name of a place, and the remaining syllables to be Honorific.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_564"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_568">99:31</A> There is no footnote 31&#8212;<i>JBH</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_565"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_569">99:32</A> <i>Toho-tsu-yama-zaki-tarashi-no-kami</i>. <i>Toho-tsu</i> (lit. "distant") and <i>yamazaki</i> ("mountain-cape") are both considered by Motowori to be names of places. Tarashi signifies "perfect" or "perfection." We might perhaps render the name thus: "Perfection-of-the-Distant-Mountain- Cape."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_566"></A><A HREF="kj033.htm#fr_570">99:33</A> <i>I.e.</i> "seventeen generations of Deities." But the construction is curious. Motowori points out that there is here an error in the computation, as the text enumerates but fifteen generations. The names of the gods and goddess mentioned in this section offer unusual difficulties Motowori says that it is with hesitation that he proposes many of his interpretations, and it is with still greater hesitation that the translator has accepted them.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_103"><font size="1" color="green">p. 103</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">SECT. XXVII.&#8212;THE LITTLE-PRINCE-THE-RENOWNED-DEITY.</h2>  
<p>So when the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land dwelt at the august cape of Miho&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_571"></A><A HREF="#fn_567"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> in Idzumo, there came riding on the crest&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_572"></A><A HREF="#fn_568"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> of the waves in a boat of heavenly <i>Kagami</i>&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_573"></A><A HREF="#fn_569"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> a Deity dressed in skins of geese&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_574"></A><A HREF="#fn_570"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> flayed with a complete [85] flaying, who, when asked his name, replied not; moreover the Deities who accompanied him, though asked, all said that they knew not. Then the toad&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_575"></A><A HREF="#fn_571"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> spoke, saying: "As for this, the Crumbling Prince&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_576"></A><A HREF="#fn_572"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> will surely know it." Thereupon [the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land] summoned and asked the Crumbling-Prince, who replied. saying: "This is the Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_577"></A><A HREF="#fn_573"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> the august child of the Deity-Producing-Wondrous-Deity."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_578"></A><A HREF="#fn_574"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> So on their then respectfully informing&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_579"></A><A HREF="#fn_575"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> His Augustness the Deity-Producing-Wondrous-August-Ancestor, he replied, saying: "This is truly my child. He among my children is the child who dipped between the fork of my hand.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_580"></A><A HREF="#fn_576"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> So do he and thou become [87] brethren, and make and consolidate this land."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_581"></A><A HREF="#fn_577"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> So from that time forward the two Deities the Great-Name-Possessor and the Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity made and consolidated this land conjointly. But afterwards the Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity crossed over to the Eternal Land.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_582"></A><A HREF="#fn_578"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> So [the Deity here] called the Crumbling Prince, who revealed the Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity, is what is now [called] the scarecrow in the mountain fields. This Deity, though his legs do not walk, is a Deity who knows everything in the Empire.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_583"></A><A HREF="#fn_579"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_567"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_571">103:1</A> <a name="page_103"><font size="1" color="green">p. 103</font></A> Not to be confounded with the better known Miho in Suruga. Derivation of the name seems uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_568"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_572">103:2</A> <a name="page_104"><font size="1" color="green">p. 104</font></A> The character used is <A NAME="img_10400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10400.jpg">, which properly denotes an ear of rice or other grain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_569"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_573">103:3</A> What plant the author intends by this name is not quite certain. The characters <A NAME="img_10401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10401.jpg"> and <A NAME="img_10402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10402.jpg"> are variously used to write it in the native work of reference, where also we learn that it probably corresponds to the plant known in different provinces of modern Japan as <i>chichi-gusa</i>, <i>tombo-no-chichi</i>, <i>kagarahi</i> and <i>gaga-imo</i>. We may best understand the <i>Ampelopsis serian&aelig;folia</i> to have been intended, as the plant is described as having a berry three or four inches long shaped like a towel-gourd, (<i>hechima</i>), so that, if scooped out, it would fairly resemble a boat in miniature.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_570"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_574">103:4</A> All the authorities are agreed in considering the character <A NAME="img_10403"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10403.jpg">, "goose," to be a copyist's error; but there is no agreement as to the character which should be substituted for it. Hirata reads <A NAME="img_10404"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10404.jpg">, "wren," changing the phonetic. "Wren" also is the reading in "One account" of the "Chronicles," and Moribe, commenting thereon in his "<i>Idzu no Chi-Waki</i>," thinks that "wren" must have been the bird originally intended by the framers of the tradition. Motowori, following a suggestion of the editor of 1687, prefers to consider the radical for "bird" to have been put by mistake for the radical for "insect," and reads <A NAME="img_10405"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10405.jpg"> which signifies "moth," especially the "silkworm moth." Motowori, however, proceeds to give to the character in question the Japanese reading of <i>hi mushi</i> (lit. "fire-insect," <i>i.e.</i> "ephemera"), which is not warranted. The proper Japanese reading is <i>hihiru</i>. The best would seem to be to adopt the reading <A NAME="img_10406"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10406.jpg"> "moth."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_571"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_575">103:5</A> The original word is <i>tani-guku</i>. Its derivation and the name of the species which it denoted are alike unknown. Indeed we might equally well translate by "frog."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_572"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_576">103:6</A> <i>Kuye-biko</i>. The interpretation of the name here adopted is Motowori's. Tominobu takes <i>Kuye</i> to be the name of a place, and the parsonage in question to have been the inventor of scarecrows, whence the tradition connected with his name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_573"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_577">103:7</A> <i>Sukuna-biko-na-no-kami</i>, or without the <i>nigori</i>, <i>Sukuna-hiko-na-no-kami</i>. The interpretation of the name here followed is that proposed by Motowori, but not followed by Hirata and Moribe, who prefer to consider it antithetical to that of <i>Oho-na-muji</i>, "the Great-name-Possess or."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_574"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_578">103:8</A> First mentioned in Sect. I, Note 6. Immediately below, his name is given in the lengthened form.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_575"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_579">103:9</A> Motowori (who, strange to say, is followed by Hirata,&#8212;conf. Sect. XVIII, Note 18) interprets the two characters <A NAME="img_10407"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10407.jpg"> (here in accordance <a name="page_105"><font size="1" color="green">p. 105</font></A> with general usage taken to signify "respectfully informed") as "informed and took up," thus making it appear that the diminutive deity was personally taken up to Heaven. Surely a recollection of the parallel passage in the "Chronicles," which says that "a messenger was sent up to inform the Heavenly Deities," should have preserved the commentators from thus offending against both grammar and common sense.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_576"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_580">103:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "slipped away between my fingers." In the legend as given in the "Chronicles," the father explains more particularly that the Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity had been a bad boy who ran away.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_577"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_581">103:11</A> For an explanation of this expression see Sect. XXIII. Note 26.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_578"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_582">103:12</A> <i>Toko-yo-no-kuai</i> (<A NAME="img_10500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10500.jpg">). Some kind of Paradise or Hades is meant, as is proved by innumerable references in the early literature of Japan: and we may suppose the idea to have been borrowed from the Chinese or through them from Buddhism, and to have been afterwards vaguely located in some distant country. In Sect. LXXIV we are told of the orange having been brought from the "Eternal Land" by Tajima-mori, who is said to have been of Korean extraction. Korea, which is to the west of Japan, and the Buddhist paradise in the west might well he confounded by tradition, though it is equally open to discussion whether Southern China or even the Loochoo Islands might not have been thus vaguely designated. In any case it was a distant place, imperfectly known, though specifically named. In the "Chronicles," Tajima-mori is made to say that it is "the retreat of Gods and Fairies, and not to be reached by common men."&#8212;Motowori's immense note on this word (see Vol. XXI, pp. 10-13 of his Commentary) is a specimen of the specious arguments by which he endeavours to ward off from the Early Japanese the imputation of ever having borrowed any ideas from their neighbours. He would have us believe that <i>Toko-yo</i> is derived from <i>soko yori</i>, "thence" (!) and that the name simply denotes foreign countries in general. This is on a par with the opinion emitted by Arawi Hakuseki in his "<i>Ko-shi Ts&#363;</i>," to the effect that the "Eternal Land" was simply a place in the province of Hitachi. The latter good old commentator apparently founded himself on no better reasons than his general rejection of supernatural or otherwise perplexing details, and the fact that one of the characters with which the name of the province in question written is <A NAME="img_10501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10501.jpg">, which also forms part of the name of <i>Toko-yo-no-kuni</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_579"></A><A HREF="kj034.htm#fr_583">103:13</A> Literally "everything beneath Heaven." "Beneath Heaven" (<A NAME="img_10502"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10502.jpg">), <i>i.e.</i> "all that is beneath the Heavens," is a common Chinese phrase for the Chinese Empire, which was in ancient days not unnaturally <a name="page_106"><font size="1" color="green">p. 106</font></A> supposed by its inhabitants to form the whole civilized world. The expression was borrowed by the Japanese to designate their own country, But its use by them had not the same plea of ignorance of other civilized lands, as they were acquainted with China and Korea, and had hence obtained nearly all the arts of life.</P>

<p><a name="page_106"><font size="1" color="green">p. 106</font></A> [88]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXVIII.&#8212;THE AUGUST-LUCK-SPIRIT-THE-AUGUST-WONDROUS-SPIRIT.]&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_584"></A><A HREF="#fn_580"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A></h2>  
<p>Thereupon the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land lamented himself, and said: "How shall I alone be able to make this land?&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_585"></A><A HREF="#fn_581"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Together with what Deity can I make this land?" At this time there came a Deity illuminating the sea. This Deity said: "If thou wilt lay me to rest&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_586"></A><A HREF="#fn_582"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> well, I can make it together with thee. If not, the land cannot be made." Then the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land said: "If that be so, what is the manner of reverently laying thee to rest?" He replied, saying: "Reverently worship me on Yamato's green fence, the eastern mountain's top."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_587"></A><A HREF="#fn_583"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> This is the Deity who dwells on the top of Mount Mimoro.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_588"></A><A HREF="#fn_584"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_580"></A><A HREF="kj035.htm#fr_584">106:1</A> <a name="page_106"><font size="1" color="green">p. 106</font></A> In the "Chronicles," this is given as the designation of the Deity who came over the sea, and Motowori therefore adopts it as the heading of this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_581"></A><A HREF="kj035.htm#fr_585">106:2</A> For an explanation of this expression see Sect. XXIII, Note 26.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_582"></A><A HREF="kj035.htm#fr_586">106:3</A> <i>I.e.</i> "if thou wilt build me a temple." The original might also be rendered "if thou wilt worship before me," or "at my shrine," of "if thou wilt establish a temple to me."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_583"></A><A HREF="kj035.htm#fr_587">106:4</A> <i>I.e.</i> on Mount Mimoro which stands as a protecting fence in the eastern part of the province of Yamato. <i>Awo-kaki-yama</i>, "green fence mountain," became a proper name used alternatively for Mount Mimoro (or, according to the later pronunciation, Mimuro). In like manner <i>Himukashi-yama</i> (in the later language <i>Higashi-yama</i>) "eastern mountain," has by some been considered to be a proper name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_584"></A><A HREF="kj035.htm#fr_588">106:5</A> <i>I.e.</i> "august house;" so called probably from the temple of the deity.</P>

<p><a name="page_107"><font size="1" color="green">p. 107</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXIX.&#8212;THE AUGUST CHILDREN OF THE GREAT-HARVEST-DEITY AND OF THE SWIFT-MOUNTAIN-DEITY.]</h2>  
<p>So the Great-Harvest-Deity wedded the Princess [of?] Inu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_589"></A><A HREF="#fn_585"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> daughter of the Divine-Life-Producing-Wondrous-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_590"></A><A HREF="#fn_586"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and begot children: the Deity August-Spirit-of-the-Great-Land;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_591"></A><A HREF="#fn_587"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> [89] next the Deity of Kara;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_592"></A><A HREF="#fn_588"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> next the Deity Sohori;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_593"></A><A HREF="#fn_589"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next the Deity White-Sun;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_594"></A><A HREF="#fn_590"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next the Sage-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_595"></A><A HREF="#fn_591"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> (Five Deities&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_596"></A><A HREF="#fn_592"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A>). Again he wedded the Refulgent-Princess,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_597"></A><A HREF="#fn_593"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and begot children: the Deity Great-Refulgent-Mountain-Dwelling-Grandee,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_598"></A><A HREF="#fn_594"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> next the August-Harvest-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_599"></A><A HREF="#fn_595"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> Again he wedded Princess Ame-shiru-karu-midzu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_600"></A><A HREF="#fn_596"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and begot children: the Deity Oki-tsu-hiko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_601"></A><A HREF="#fn_597"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> next Her Augustness Oki-tsu-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_602"></A><A HREF="#fn_598"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> another name for whom is [90] the Deity Great Furnace-Princess&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_603"></A><A HREF="#fn_599"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A>&#8212;this is the Deity of the Furnace&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_604"></A><A HREF="#fn_600"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> held in reverence by all people&#8212;next the Deity Great-Mountain-Integrator,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_605"></A><A HREF="#fn_601"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> another name for whom is the Deity-Great-Master-of-the-Mountain-End:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_606"></A><A HREF="#fn_602"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> this Deity dwells on Mount Hiye&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_607"></A><A HREF="#fn_603"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> in the land of Chika-tsu-Afumi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_608"></A><A HREF="#fn_604"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> and is likewise the Deity dwelling at Matsu-no-wo&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_609"></A><A HREF="#fn_605"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> in Kadzunu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_610"></A><A HREF="#fn_606"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> who uses the whizzing barb.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_611"></A><A HREF="#fn_607"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> Next the Deity-of-the-Fire-in-the-Yard;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_612"></A><A HREF="#fn_608"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> next the Deity Asahi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_613"></A><A HREF="#fn_609"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> next the Deity Hahigi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_614"></A><A HREF="#fn_610"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> next the Deity Refulgent-Mountain-Dwelling-Grandee;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_615"></A><A HREF="#fn_611"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> next the Deity [91] Swift-Mountain-Dwelling;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_616"></A><A HREF="#fn_612"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> next the High Deity-of-the-Fire-in-the-Yard;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_617"></A><A HREF="#fn_613"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> next the Great-Earth-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_618"></A><A HREF="#fn_614"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> another name for whom is the Deity August-Ancestor-of-Earth.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_619"></A><A HREF="#fn_615"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> (Nine Deities&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_620"></A><A HREF="#fn_616"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A>)</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">In the above paragraph the children of the Great-Harvest-Deity, from the Deity August-Spirit-of-the Great-Land down to the Great-Earth-Deity, are altogether sixteen Deities.</div></p>

<p>The Deity Swift-Mountain-Dwelling&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_621"></A><A HREF="#fn_617"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> wedded the Deity Princess-of-Great-Food,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_622"></A><A HREF="#fn_618"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> and begot children: the Deity Young-Mountain-Integrator;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_623"></A><A HREF="#fn_619"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A> next the Young-Harvest-Deity;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_624"></A><A HREF="#fn_620"><FONT SIZE="1">36</FONT></A> next his younger sister the Young-Rice-Transplanting-Female-Deity;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_625"></A><A HREF="#fn_621"><FONT SIZE="1">37</FONT></A> next the Water-Sprinkling-Deity;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_626"></A><A HREF="#fn_622"><FONT SIZE="1">38</FONT></A> next the Deity-of-the-High-Sun-of-Summer,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_627"></A><A HREF="#fn_623"><FONT SIZE="1">39</FONT></A> another name for whom is the Female-Deity-of-Summer;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_628"></A><A HREF="#fn_624"><FONT SIZE="1">40</FONT></A> next the Autumn-Princess;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_629"></A><A HREF="#fn_625"><FONT SIZE="1">41</FONT></A> next the Deity Stem-Harvest;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_630"></A><A HREF="#fn_626"><FONT SIZE="1">42</FONT></A> next the Deity Lord-Stem-Tree-Young-House-Rope.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_631"></A><A HREF="#fn_627"><FONT SIZE="1">43</FONT></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">In the above paragraph the children of the Deity Swift-Mountain-Dwelling, from the Deity Young-Mountain-Integrator down to the Deity Lord-Young-House-Rope,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_632"></A><A HREF="#fn_628"><FONT SIZE="1">44</FONT></A> are altogether eight Deities.</div></p>

<p><a name="page_109"><font size="1" color="green">p. 109</font></A> <a name="page_110"><font size="1" color="green">p. 110</font></A> <a name="page_111"><font size="1" color="green">p. 111</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_585"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_589">107:1</A> <a name="page_108"><font size="1" color="green">p. 108</font></A> <i>Inu-hime</i>. Motowori supposes <i>Inu</i> to be the name of a place. The word properly signifies "dog."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_586"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_590">107:2</A> <i>Kamu-iku-musu-bi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_587"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_591">107:3</A> <i>Oho-kuni-mi-tama-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_588"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_592">107:4</A> <i>Kara-no-kami</i>, <A NAME="img_10800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10800.jpg">. <i>Kara</i> signifies Korea and China, and the Deity thus named appears in the "Chronicle" under the name of <i>I-so-takeru</i> ("Fifty-fold-Valiant"), of whom it is related that he was taken over to Korea by his father <i>Susa-no-wo</i> (the "Impetuous-Male").</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_589"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_593">107:5</A> <i>Sohori-no-kami</i>. The etymology is not clear. Hirata derives the name from a Verb <i>soru</i>, "to ride," "to go in a boat," in connection with the story (mentioned in the preceding note) of I-so-takeru having been taken over to Korea. According to this view, <i>Sohori</i>, like <i>Kara-no-kami</i>, would be an alternative name of <i>I-so-takeru</i>. But the derivation is hazardous, to say the least.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_590"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_594">107:6</A> <i>Shira-hi-no-kami</i>. Motowori supposes <i>shira hi</i> (<A NAME="img_10801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10801.jpg">) to be a copyist's error for <i>makahi</i> (<A NAME="img_10802"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10802.jpg">). The latter, however, does not make satisfactory sense, and Tomonobu, proposes to invert the characters, thus: <A NAME="img_10803"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10803.jpg">, which means "sun-confronting." Motowori suggests that the word <A HREF="errata.htm#15">may</A>, after all, be but the name of a place.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_591"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_595">107:7</A> <i>Hizhiri-no-kami</i>, written with the characters <A NAME="img_10804"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10804.jpg">. The first of <A HREF="errata.htm#16">these</A> is defined as signifying him who is intuitively wise and good, <i>i.e.</i> <a name="page_109"><font size="1" color="green">p. 109</font></A> the perfect sage. But perhaps we should in Archaic Japanese take the term <i>hizhiri</i> in what is its probable native etymological sense, viz. "sun-governing" (<i>hizhiri</i>, <A NAME="img_10900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10900.jpg">), a title properly applied to the Japanese Emperors as descendants of the Sun-God, and of which the character <A NAME="img_10901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10901.jpg">, which is used of the Chinese Monarchs, is only an equivalent in so far as it, too, is employed as an Honorific title.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_592"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_596">107:8</A> Viz. from the August-Spirit-of-the-Great-Land to the Sage-Deity inclusive.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_593"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_597">107:9</A> <i>Kagaya-hime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_594"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_598">107:10</A> <i>Oho-kaga-yama-to-omi-no-kami</i>. The translation follows Hirata's interpretation, which nearly agrees with that proposed by Mabuchi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_595"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_599">107:11</A> <i>Mi-toshi-no-kami</i>. For the meaning of "harvest" attributed to the word <i>toshi</i> see Sect. XX, Note 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_596"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_600">107:12</A> <i>Ame-shiru-karu-midzu-hime</i>. The name might tentatively be translated thus: Heaven-Governing-Fresh-Princess-of Karu. Motowori suggests that <i>amerishiru</i> may be but a sort of Pillow-Word for the rest of the name. <i>Ama-tobu</i> is, however, the only Pillow-word for Karu found in the poems. After all, Karu may not here be the name of a place at all.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_597"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_601">107:13</A> <i>Oki-tsu-hiko-no-kami</i>. The translator ventures to think that the names of this deity and the next might simply be rendered (in accordance with the first character, <A NAME="img_10902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10902.jpg"> entering into their composing) "Inner Prince" and "Inner Princess" or "Prince of the Interior" and "Princess of the Interior." Motowori however suggests that <i>Okitsu</i> may be the name of a place, while Hirata derives the names from <i>oki-tsuchi</i>, "laid earth," finding therein a reference to the furnace (made of clay) mentioned immediately below.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_598"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_602">107:14</A> <i>Oki-tsu-hime-no-mikoto</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_599"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_603">107:15</A> <i>Oho-be-hime-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_600"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_604">107:16</A> <i>Kama-no-kami</i> (<A NAME="img_10903"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10903.jpg">). The "furnace" means the "kitchen." Neither Motowori nor Hirata informs us that the immense popularity of this Goddess, as well as her name, can clearly be traced to China.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_601"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_605">107:17</A> <i>Oho-yama-kuni-no-kami</i>. The meaning of <i>kuhi</i>, here (as in the case of <i>Tsumu-guhi</i> and <i>Iku-guhi</i> (see Sect. II, Note 4) rendered by the word "interior," is open to doubt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_602"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_606">107:18</A> <i>Yama-suwe-no-oko-mushi-no-kami</i>. Motowori supposes the word <i>suwe</i>, "end," to have the signification of "top."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_603"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_607">107:19</A> As it stands, the etymology of this name is not clear. In later times the mountain was called <i>Hiyei</i> (<A NAME="img_10904"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/10904.jpg">). But whether the, to outward appearance, native <i>Hiye</i> is but a corruption of this Chinese one, or <a name="page_110"><font size="1" color="green">p. 110</font></A> whether it be true that the latter (on this hypothesis bestowed on account of its likeness in sound to the native designation) was not used till the end of the eighth or beginning of the ninth century. as is commonly stated, is difficult to decide.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_604"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_608">107:20</A> <i>I.e.</i> "Close-Fresh-Sea." <i>Afumi</i> (modern pron. <i>Omi</i>, for <i>aha-umi</i>) alone signifies "fresh sea," i e. "lake." This province contains the large take commonly known as Lake Biha, (Biwa), but anciently simply called "the Fresh Sea," as being the lake par excellence of Japan. When one of the eastern provinces received, on account of a large lagoon or inlet which it contains, the name of <i>Toho-tsu-Afumi</i> (in modern pronunciation <i>T&#333;-t&#333;mi</i>), <i>i.e.</i> "Distant-Fresh-Sea," the epithet Close was prefixed to the name of the province nearer to the ancient centre of government.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_605"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_609">107:21</A> <i>I.e.</i> Pine-tree-Declivity.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_606"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_610">107:22</A> <i>I.e.</i> Pueraria-Moor.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_607"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_611">107:23</A> This passage (<A NAME="img_11000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/11000.jpg">) must be corrupt. Mabuchi proposes to insert the character <A NAME="img_11001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/11001.jpg"> before <A NAME="img_11002"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/11002.jpg">, and to understand the author to have meant to tell us that the deity was worshipped with arrows, that is to say, that arrows were offered at his shrine. Motowori's proposal to consider <A NAME="img_11003"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/11003.jpg"> as an error for <A NAME="img_11004"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/11004.jpg"> or <A NAME="img_11005"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/11005.jpg">, and to interpret the clause thus: "the Deity who was changed into an arrow" is also worthy of notice. But a further suggestion of his to read <A NAME="img_11006"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/11006.jpg"> for <A NAME="img_11007"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/11007.jpg"> and to interpret thus: "the Deity of the Red Arrow," seems best of all when taken in connection with the tradition, which he quotes from the "Topography of Yamashiro," to the effect that this god took the shape of a red arrow to gain access to his mistress <i>Tama-yori-hime</i>, such a transformation being one of the common-places of Japanese myth.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_608"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_612">107:24</A> <i>Niha-tsu-hi-no-kami</i>. The interpretation of this name here adopted is not Motowori's, who takes <i>hi</i> in the sense of "wondrous," but Hirata's. The latter-author makes it clear that this deity (for whom <i>Niha-taka-tsu-hi-no-kami</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "The High-Deity-of-the-Fire-in-the-Yard," is but a slightly amplified designation) was none other than the above-mentioned Deity of the Kitchen, and his name an inclusive one for the pair of deities <i>Oki-tsu-hiko</i> and <i>Oki-tsu-hime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_609"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_613">107:25</A> <i>Asuha-ho-kami</i>. The signification of this name is obscure, and Motowori's proposal to derive it from <i>ashi-niha</i>, "foot-place," because the god in question may be supposed to protect the place on which people stand, is not altogether convincing. In fact he himself only advances it with hesitation. It should be added, however, that Hirata stamps it with his special approval, as he does also Motowori's derivation of the following name, <i>Hahigi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_610"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_614">107:26</A> <a name="page_111"><font size="1" color="green">p. 111</font></A> <i>Hahi-gino-kami</i>. Obscure, but ingeniously derived by Motowori from <i>hachi-iri-gimi</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "entering prince," the deity in question being supposed to have been the special <A HREF="errata.htm#17">protector</A> of the entrances to houses, and to have thence received his name. Mr. Satow has translated it in the Rituals as "Entrance Limit."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_611"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_615">107:27</A> <i>Kaga-yama-to-omi-no-kami</i>. The name is almost identical with that in Note 10.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_612"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_616">107:28</A> <i>Ha-yama-to-no-kami</i>. The interpretation of the name is that proposed by Motowori, and which seems tolerably satisfactory.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_613"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_617">107:29</A> <i>Niha-taka-tsu-hi-no-kami</i>. See note 24.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_614"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_618">107:30</A> <i>Oho-tsuchi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_615"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_619">107:31</A> <i>Tsuchi-no-mi-oya-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_616"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_620">107:32</A> This number is obtained if (as is perhaps permissible from a Japanese point of view) we consider <i>Oki-tsu-hiko</i> and <i>Oki-tsu-hime</i> as forming a single deity. Otherwise there are ten. A similar remark applies to the number sixteen mentioned immediately below.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_617"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_621">108:33</A> See Note 28.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_618"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_622">108:34</A> See Sect. V, Note 8. The fact that this goddess is related to have been previously killed (see Sect. XVII) causes Motowori some embarrassment.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_619"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_623">108:35</A> <i>Waka-yama-kuhi-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_620"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_624">108:36</A> <i>Waka-toshi-no-kami</i>. Motowori proposes (considering this name in connection with the four that follow) to take <i>waka-toshi</i> in this place in the signification of the "the first sprouting" of the young rice. The five deities whose birth is here mentioned seem collectively to represent the natural succession of agricultural operations throughout the year.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_621"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_625">108:37</A> <i>Waka-sa-name-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_622"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_626">108:38</A> <i>Midzu-maki-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_623"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_627">108:39</A> <i>Natsu-taka-tsu-hi-no-kami</i>. Motowori's interpretation of <i>hi</i> as "wondrous" is perhaps as good as that here adopted, according to which it signifies "sun." His view would give us in English "the Summer-High-Wondrous-Deity."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_624"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_628">108:40</A> <i>Natsu-no-me-no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_625"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_629">108:41</A> <i>Aki-bime no-kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_626"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_630">108:42</A> <i>Kuku-toshi-no-kami</i>. The word <i>kuku</i>, "stem," seems to allude to the length of the well-grown rice.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_627"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_631">108:43</A> <a name="page_112"><font size="1" color="green">p. 112</font></A> <i>Kuku-ki-waka-muro-tsunane-no-kami</i>. Motowori supposes this god to have been the protector of houses, and interprets the name to denote the beams, and the ropes with which the beams were bound together. The word here read <i>tsuna</i>, "rope;" is written with the character, and might perhaps be rendered "pueraria." But as in early times the tendrils of such creeping plants formed the only substitute for rope, the two renderings come to have very nearly the same signification.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_628"></A><A HREF="kj036.htm#fr_632">108:44</A> The name is here abbreviated in the original to <i>Waka-muro-tsuna-ne-no-kami</i>.</P>

<p><a name="page_112"><font size="1" color="green">p. 112</font></A> [93]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXX.&#8212;THE AUGUST DELIBERATION FOR PACIFYING THE LAND.]</h2>  
<p>The Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity commanded, saying: "The Luxuriant-Reed-Plains-the-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears-of-a-Thousand-Autumns,&#8212;Of Long-Five-Hundred-Autumns&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_633"></A><A HREF="#fn_629"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> is the land which my august child His Augustness Truly-Conqueror-I-Conquer-Conquering-Swift-Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_634"></A><A HREF="#fn_630"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> shall govern." Having [thus] deigned to charge him, she sent him down from Heaven.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_635"></A><A HREF="#fn_631"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Hereupon His Augustness Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears, standing on the Floating Bridge of Heaven,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_636"></A><A HREF="#fn_632"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> said: "The Luxuriant-Reed-Plains-the-Land-of-Fresh-Rice-ears-of-a-Thousand-Autumns,&#8212;of Long-Five-Hundred-Autumns is painfully uproarious,&#8212;it is."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_637"></A><A HREF="#fn_633"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> With this announcement, he immediately re-ascended, and informed the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity. Then the High-August-Producing-Wondrous-Deity&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_638"></A><A HREF="#fn_634"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and the Heaven-Shining-Great-August-Deity commanded the eight hundred myriad Deities to assemble in a divine assembly in the bed of the Tranquil River of Heaven,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_639"></A><A HREF="#fn_635"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and caused the Deity Thought-Includer&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_640"></A><A HREF="#fn_636"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> to think [of a plan], and said:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_641"></A><A HREF="#fn_637"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> "This Central Land of Reed-Plains is the land with which we</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_113"><font size="1" color="green">p. 113</font></A></p>  
<p>have deigned to charge our august child as the land which he shall govern. So as he deems that violent and savage Earthly Deities&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_642"></A><A HREF="#fn_638"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> are numerous in this land, [69] which Deity shall we send to subdue them?" Then the Deity Thought-Includer and likewise the eight hundred myriad Deities took counsel and said: "The Deity Ame-no-ho-hi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_643"></A><A HREF="#fn_639"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> is the one that should be sent." So they sent the Deity Ame-no-ho-hi; but he at once curried favour with the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land, and for three years brought back no report.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_629"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_633">112:1</A> <a name="page_113"><font size="1" color="green">p. 113</font></A> <i>Toyo-ashi-hara-no-chi-aki-no-naga-i-ho-aki-no-midzu-ho-izo-kuni</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, freely rendered, "ever fruitful Japan with its reed-covered plains and its luxuriant rice-fields."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_630"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_634">112:2</A> See Sect. XIII, Note 18. Henceforward this tremendous name is mostly abbreviated to <i>Ame-no-oshi-ho-mimi</i> (probably signifying "Heavenly-Great-Great-Ears.")</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_631"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_635">112:3</A> So in the original. The sense, however, is rather "told him to descend from Heaven;" for he did not actually go further than the top of the "Floating Bridge," and never came down to earth.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_632"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_636">112:4</A> See Sect. III, Note 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_633"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_637">112:5</A> The words "it is" stand for <i>ari keri</i> in the original. <i>Conf</i>. Sect. X, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_634"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_638">112:6</A> <i>Taka-mi-musu-bi-no-kami</i>, first mentioned at the very commencement of the work. In this legend this god's name is constantly coupled with that of the Sun-Goddess, who alone, up to this point, had appeared as the ruler of Heaven.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_635"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_639">112:7</A> See Sect. XIII, Note 12.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_636"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_640">112:8</A> See Sect. XVI, Note 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_637"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_641">112:9</A> The meaning must be, as Motowori suggests, that the story was told first, and the Deity Thought-Includer asked for his advice after he had heard it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_638"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_642">113:10</A> See Sect. I, Note 11.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_639"></A><A HREF="kj037.htm#fr_643">113:11</A> See Sect. XIII, Note 19.</P>
