<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_766"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_770">139:1</A> <a name="page_139"><font size="1" color="green">p. 139</font></A> Etymology unknown.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_767"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_771">139:2</A> What species was denoted by this ancient name is not clear; but one of Motowori's suggestion, to the effect that it may have been identical with the modern <i>sarubo-yahi</i> (a shell of a family <i>Arcad&aelig;</i>, probably <i>Arca subcrenata</i>), the origin of whose name would thus be traced up to the mythological age, is at least ingenious.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_768"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_772">139:3</A> <a name="page_140"><font size="1" color="green">p. 140</font></A> <i>Soko-daku-mi-tama</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_769"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_773">139:4</A> <i>Tsubu-tatsu-mi-tama</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_770"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_774">139:5</A> <i>Aka-saku-mi-tama</i>. <i>Saku</i> might be translated by "opening," "forming," etc. It is the same word as that used to express the blossoming of a flower.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_771"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_775">139:6</A> The characters rendered "came back "are <A NAME="img_14000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14000.jpg">. Motowori and Hirata believe <A NAME="img_14001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14001.jpg"> to be put erroneously for <A NAME="img_14002"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14002.jpg">, which would give the sense of "arrived there," and would thus enable us to locate the episode of the fishes at Ise instead of in Hiuga, which would better suit the concluding clause of this Section narrating the participation of the Duchesses of Sara in the' first-fruits of the province of Shims. If the word Shima however here means, not the province of that name, but simply "islands" in general, there is nothing to be gained by the pro-posed emendation, which has moreover no sanction from any text; and it may be added that no notice is to be found in any history of the custom here said to have existed.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_772"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_776">139:7</A> <i>I.e.</i> all the fishes both great and small.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_773"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_777">139:8</A> Literally, "small string-sword," supposed to have been so called from its having been carried inside the garments, attached to the under-belt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_774"></A><A HREF="kj043.htm#fr_778">139:9</A> The smallest of the Japanese provinces, situated to the East of Ise. The name signifies "island," and it is possible that it ought here to be taken in that sense as a common noun.</P>

<p><a name="page_140"><font size="1" color="green">p. 140</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXXVII.&#8212;THE CURSE OF THE DEITY GREAT-MOUNTAIN-POSSESSOR.]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty met a beautiful person at the august cape of Kasasa, and asked her whose daughter she was. She replied, saying: "I am a daughter of the Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_779"></A><A HREF="#fn_775"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and my name is the Divine-Princess-of-Ata,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_780"></A><A HREF="#fn_776"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> another name by which I am called being Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_781"></A><A HREF="#fn_777"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Again he asked: "Hast thou</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_141"><font size="1" color="green">p. 141</font></A></p>  
<p>any brethren?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_782"></A><A HREF="#fn_778"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> She replied, saying: "There is my elder sister, Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_783"></A><A HREF="#fn_779"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Then he charged her, [saying]: "Ego sum cupidus coiendi tecum. Tibi quomodo videtur?" She replied, saying: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_784"></A><A HREF="#fn_780"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> am not able to say. My father the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor will say." So he sent a request [for her] to her father the Deity Great-Mountain-Possessor, who, greatly delighted, respectfully sent her off, joining to her&nbsp;her [116] elder sister Princess Long-as-the-Rocks, and causing merchandise to be carried on tables holding an hundred.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_785"></A><A HREF="#fn_781"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> So then, owing to the elder sister being very hideous, [His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty] was alarmed at the sight of her, and sent her back, only keeping the younger sister Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, whom he wedded for one night. Then the Deity-Great-Mountain-Possessor was covered with shame at Princess Long-as-the-Rocks being sent back, and sent a message [to His Augustness Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty], saying: "My reason for respectfully presenting both my daughters together was that, by sending Princess-Long-as-the-Rocks, the august offspring&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_786"></A><A HREF="#fn_782"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> of the Heavenly Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_787"></A><A HREF="#fn_783"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> though the snow&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_788"></A><A HREF="#fn_784"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> fall and the wind blow, might live eternally immovable like unto the enduring rocks, and again that by sending Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, [they] might live flourishingly like unto the flowering of the blossoms of the trees: to insure this,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_789"></A><A HREF="#fn_785"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> I offered&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_790"></A><A HREF="#fn_786"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> them. But owing to thy thus sending back&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_791"></A><A HREF="#fn_787"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> Princess Long-as-the-Rocks, and keeping only Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees, the august offspring of the Heavenly Deity shall be but as frail&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_792"></A><A HREF="#fn_788"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> as the flowers of the trees. So it is for this [117]</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_142"><font size="1" color="green">p. 142</font></A></p>  
<p>reason that down to the present day the august lives of Their Augustnesses the Heavenly Sovereigns&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_793"></A><A HREF="#fn_789"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> are not long.</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_775"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_779">140:1</A> <a name="page_142"><font size="1" color="green">p. 142</font></A> See Sect. VI. Note 17.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_776"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_780">140:2</A> <i>Kamu-ata-tsu-hime</i>. <i>Ata</i> is a place in Satsuma.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_777"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_781">140:3</A> Or "Tree." <i>Ka-no-hama-saku-ya-hime</i>. Perhaps (though there is no native authority for doing so) we might rather understand <i>saku</i> as a Causative in intention, though not in form, and render the name thus: "Princess-Causing-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees-to-Blossom." The tree alluded to is doubtless the cherry. This deity is now worshipped as the goddess of Mount Fuzhi (Fusiyama), and in common parlance the last member of the compound forming her name does not receive the <i>nigori</i>,&#8212;<i>hime</i> instead of <i>bime</i>. The syllable <i>ya</i> has no signification in this and similar names. It will be remembered that there was another sister named "Princess-Falling-like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees. (See Sect. XX, Note 5).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_778"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_782">141:4</A> Or perhaps, so written <A NAME="img_14200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14200.jpg">, the original expression were here better rendered by "sisters."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_779"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_783">141:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, as enduring as the rocks. The original name is <i>Iha-naga-hime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_780"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_784">141:6</A> The character used here and immediately below for the First Personal Pronoun is <A NAME="img_14201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14201.jpg"> "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_781"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_785">141:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, every kind of goods as a dowry for his daughters.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_782"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_786">141:8</A> The usual word child (<A NAME="img_14202"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14202.jpg">)is employed in the text; but it here almost certainly has, as Motowori suggests, a more extended meaning, and signifies the posterity of the Sun-Goddess or of Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty generally, <i>i.e.</i> the Emperors of Japan. The vaguer term "offspring "is therefore nearer to the author's intention.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_783"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_787">141:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, either of the Sun-Goddess or of Prince-Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, There is no difference in the sense, whichever of these two deities we take the speaker to refer to. The Sun-Goddess was his ancestress, and he was ancestor of the Japanese Emperors.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_784"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_788">141:10</A> Or "snow and rain," the reading being uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_785"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_789">141:11</A> Or "having sworn this," or "pledged [myself to the accomplishment of] this."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_786"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_790">141:12</A> The Chinese characters used are those properly denoting the presenting of tribute.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_787"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_791">141:13</A> Motowori (proposes an emendation in this passage of <A NAME="img_14203"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14203.jpg"> to <A NAME="img_14204"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14204.jpg"> which would not materially alter the sense.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_788"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_792">141:14</A> <a name="page_143"><font size="1" color="green">p. 143</font></A> The precise meaning of the syllables <i>a-ma-hi-no-mi</i>, here rendered by the words "but as frail "in accordance with Motowori's and Moribe's tentative interpretation, is extremely obscure. The parallel passage in the "Chronicles "is <A NAME="img_14300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14300.jpg">, <i>i.e.</i> "fading and falling like the flowers of the trees."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_789"></A><A HREF="kj044.htm#fr_793">142:15</A> The characters rendered "Heavenly Sovereign" are <A NAME="img_14301"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14301.jpg">, a common Japanese designation of the Emperor. It would, especially in the later volumes of this work where the expression is repeated on almost every page, be more convenient to translate by the single word "Emperor." But the commentators lay great stress on the high significance of the component portions of the title, which, they contend, was not borrowed from China, but was first used in Japan. It is first met with in Chinese history in the middle of the seventh century of our era, just early enough indeed for it to have been borrowed before the time of the compilation of these "Records." But as there was no difficulty in putting together the two component parts "Heavenly, Sovereign," it is possible that the contention of the Japanese commentators is correct. The ancient pure native term seems to have been <i>Sumera-mikoto</i>, for which Mr. Satow has proposed the rendering of "Sovereign Augustness."</P>

<p><a name="page_143"><font size="1" color="green">p. 143</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXXVIII.&#8212;THE AUGUST CHILD-BEARING OF PRINCESS-BLOSSOMING BRILLIANTLY-LIKE-THE-FLOWERS-OF-THE-TREES.]</h2>  
<p>So later on Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly-Like-the-Flowers-of-the-Trees waited on&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_794"></A><A HREF="#fn_790"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> [His Augustness Prince Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty, and said: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_795"></A><A HREF="#fn_791"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> am pregnant, and now the time for my delivery approaches. "It is not fit for me to be delivered of the august offspring of Heaven privately;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_796"></A><A HREF="#fn_792"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> so I tell thee." Then [His Augustness Prince Rice-ear-Ruddy-Plenty] said: "Princess-Blossoming-Brilliantly!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_797"></A><A HREF="#fn_793"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> what! pregnant after one night!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_798"></A><A HREF="#fn_794"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> It cannot be my child. It must surely be the child of an Earthly Deity."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_799"></A><A HREF="#fn_795"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> Then she replied, saying: "If the child with [118] which I am pregnant be the child of an Earthly Deity,</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_144"><font size="1" color="green">p. 144</font></A></p>  
<p>my delivery will not be fortunate. If it be the august child of the Heavenly Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_800"></A><A HREF="#fn_796"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> it will be fortunate;"&#8212;and thereupon she built a hall eight fathoms [long] without doors,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_801"></A><A HREF="#fn_797"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> went inside the hall and plastered up [the entrance] with earth; and when the time came for her delivery, she set fire to the hall and was delivered.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_802"></A><A HREF="#fn_798"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> So the name of the child that was born when the fire was burning most fiercely was His Augustness Fire-Shine&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_803"></A><A HREF="#fn_799"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> (<small>this is the ancestor of the Hayabito, Dukes of Ata</small>);&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_804"></A><A HREF="#fn_800"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> the name of the child born next was His Augustness Fire-Climax;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_805"></A><A HREF="#fn_801"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> the august&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_806"></A><A HREF="#fn_802"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> name of the child born next was His Augustness [119] Fire-Subside,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_807"></A><A HREF="#fn_803"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> another name for whom is His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_808"></A><A HREF="#fn_804"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> (<small>three Deities in all</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_809"></A><A HREF="#fn_805"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_790"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_794">143:1</A> <a name="page_144"><font size="1" color="green">p. 144</font></A> More literally "came to"; but the character which is employed implies that her visit was to a superior.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_791"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_795">143:2</A> Written with the character <A NAME="img_14400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/14400.jpg">, a "concubine" or "handmaid," a common self-depreciatory equivalent of the First Personal Pronoun in Chinese, when the speaker is a woman.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_792"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_796">143:3</A> <i>I.e.</i> "secretly," "without telling thee."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_793"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_797">143:4</A> In this one instance only is the name thus abbreviated. Motowori supposes it to be on account of the scorn implied in the god's words</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_794"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_798">143:5</A> Literally, "one sojourn."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_795"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_799">143:6</A> See Sect. I, Note 11. Here of course one of the gods of the same country-side is meant.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_796"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_800">144:7</A> <i>I.e.</i> "thy child and the Sun-Goddess descendant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_797"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_801">144:8</A> That is to say that it remained doorless after she had, as stated immediately below, plastered up the entrance.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_798"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_802">144:9</A> Viz. of child, not from the flames. There is no ambiguity in the Japanese expression.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_799"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_803">144:10</A> <i>Ho-deri-na-mikoto</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_800"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_804">144:11</A> <i>Hayabito-ata-no-kimi</i>. Ata is, as has been already stated in Note 2 to Sect. XXXVII, the name of a place in Satsuma. <i>Haya-bito</i> ("swift men," "bold men," literally, if we follow the Chinese characters "falcon men") was an ancient designation of the inhabitants of the south-western corner of Japan which was subsequently divided into the provinces <a name="page_145"><font size="1" color="green">p. 145</font></A> of Satsuma and Ohosumi, and came by metonymy to be used to denote the province of Satsuma itself, for which reason it remained as the Pillow-Word for the word Satsuma even after the exclusive use of this latter name had been established. In after times the <i>hayabito</i> (also contracted to <i>hayato</i> and <i>haito</i>) were chiefly known as forming the Infantry of the Imperial Guard, a curious choice of provincials for which mythological sanction was invoked. They are also said to have furnished the performers of a symbolic dance mentioned at the end of Sect. XLI (see Note 3 to that Sect.) In later Sections of this work, the translator has ventured to render <i>hayabito</i> by "man-at-arms."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_801"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_805">144:12</A> <i>Ho-suseri-no-mikoto</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_802"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_806">144:13</A> The Honorific is doubtless prefixed in this case and not in the others, because it was to this prince or deity that the Imperial House traced its descent. Motowori's <i>kana</i> reading, which prefixes Honorifics to all such names indifferently, obliterates this delicate distinction.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_803"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_807">144:14</A> <i>Ho-wori-no-mikoto</i>. The derivation of this name is less clear than that of his elder brothers. Motowori's proposal to consider it as a corruption of <i>ho-yohari</i>, "fire weakening," is however plausible; and as this triad of names is evidently intended to paint the stages in the progress of the conflagration, the import of the third must be something very like what Motowori suggests, even if his guess at the original form of the word be not quite correct. The names of all three brethren differ more or less in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles ".</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_804"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_808">144:15</A> <i>Ama-tsu-hi-daka-hiko-ho-ho-de-mi-no-mikoto</i>. The interpretation of the last four members of this compound name is extremely doubtful.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_805"></A><A HREF="kj045.htm#fr_809">144:16</A> The actual word in the text is not <i>kumi</i>, "deity," but its Auxiliary Numeral <i>hashira</i>.</P>

<p><a name="page_145"><font size="1" color="green">p. 145</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XXXIX.&#8212;THE AUGUST EXCHANGE OF LUCK.]</h2>  
<p>So His Augustness Fire-Shine was a prince who got his luck&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_810"></A><A HREF="#fn_806"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> on the sea, and caught things broad of fin and things narrow of fin. His Augustness Fire-Subside was a prince who got his luck on the mountains, and caught things rough of hair and things soft of hair. Then His Augustness Fire-Subside said to his elder brother His Augustness Fire-Shine: "Let us mutually exchange,</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_146"><font size="1" color="green">p. 146</font></A></p>  
<p>and use each other's luck." [Nevertheless], though he thrice made the request, [his elder brother] would not accede [to it]; but at last with difficulty the mutual exchange was obtained. Then His Augustness Fire-Subside, undertaking the sea-luck, angled for fish, but never got a single fish; and moreover he lost the fish-hook in the sea. Thereupon his elder brother His Augustness Fire-Shine asked him for the fish-hook, saying: "A mountain-luck is a luck of its own, and a sea-luck is a luck of its own. Let each of us now restore [to the other] his luck."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_811"></A><A HREF="#fn_807"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> To which the younger brother His Augustness Fire-Subside replied, saying: "As for thy fish-hook, I did not get a single fish by angling with it; and at last I lost it in the sea." But the elder brother required it of him [the more] urgently. So the younger brother, breaking his ten grasp sabre&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_812"></A><A HREF="#fn_808"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> that was augustly girded [120] on him, made [of the fragments] five hundred fish-hooks as compensation; but he would not take them. Again he made a thousand fish-hooks as compensation; but he would not receive them, saying: "I still want the real original fish-hook."</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_806"></A><A HREF="kj046.htm#fr_810">145:1</A> <a name="page_146"><font size="1" color="green">p. 146</font></A> For the archaic Japanese work <i>sachi</i>, here rendered "luck," there is no satisfactory English equivalent. Its original and most usual signification is "luck," "happiness; "then that which a man is lucky in or skilful at,&#8212;his "<i>forte</i>; "and finally that which he procures by his luck or skill and the implements which he uses in procuring it. The exchange negotiated below was doubtless that of the bow and arrows of one deity for the other deity's fish-hook.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_807"></A><A HREF="kj046.htm#fr_811">146:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Some men are naturally good hunters, and others naturally good fishermen. Let us therefore restore to each other the implements necessary to the successful following of our respective avocations."&#8212;The clause rendered "Let each of us now restore to the other his luck "is a little confused in the original; but the <i>kana</i> readings both old and new agree in interpreting it as has here been done.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_808"></A><A HREF="kj046.htm#fr_812">146:3</A> See Sect. VIII, Note 1.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_147"><font size="1" color="green">p. 147</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XL.&#8212;THE PALACE OF THE OCEAN-POSSESSOR.]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon, as the younger brother was weeping and lamenting by the sea-shore, the Deity Salt-Possessor&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_813"></A><A HREF="#fn_809"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> came and asked him, saying: "What is the cause of the Sky's-Sun-Height's&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_814"></A><A HREF="#fn_810"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> weeping and lamentation? "He replied, saying: "I had exchanged a fish-hook with my elder brother,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_815"></A><A HREF="#fn_811"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and have lost that fish-hook; and as he asks me for it, I have given him many fish-hooks as compensation; but he will not receive them, saying, 'I [121] still want the original fish-hook.' So I weep and lament for this." Then the Deity Salt-Possessor said: "I will give good counsel to Thine Augustness;"&#8212;and there-with built a stout little boat without interstices,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_816"></A><A HREF="#fn_812"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and set him in the boat, and instructed him, saying: "When I shall have pushed the boat off, go on for some time. There will be a savoury august road;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_817"></A><A HREF="#fn_813"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and if thou goest in the boat along that road, there will appear a palace built like fishes' scales,&#8212;which is the palace of the Deity, Ocean-Possessor.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_818"></A><A HREF="#fn_814"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> When thou reachest the august gate of that deity['s palace], there will be a multitudinous[-ly branching] cassia-tree&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_819"></A><A HREF="#fn_815"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> above the well at its side. So if thou sit on the top of that tree, the Sea-Deity's daughter will see thee, and counsel thee." So following [these] instructions, [His Augustness Fire-Subside] went a little [way], and everything happened as [the Deity Salt-Possessor] had said; and he forthwith climbed the cassia-tree, and sat [there]. Then when the hand-maidens of the Sea-Deity's daughter Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_820"></A><A HREF="#fn_816"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> bearing jewelled vessels, were about to draw water, there was a light in the well.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_821"></A><A HREF="#fn_817"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> On looking up, there was a beautiful young man. They thought it very strange. [122]</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_148"><font size="1" color="green">p. 148</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Then His Augustness Fire-Subside saw the handmaidens, and begged to be given some water. The handmaidens at once drew some water, put it into a jewelled vessel, and respectfully presented it to him. Then, without drinking the water, he loosened the jewel at his august neck, took it in his mouth, and spat it into the jewelled vessel. Thereupon the jewel adhered to the vessel, and the handmaidens could not separate the jewel [from the vessel]. So they took it with the jewel adhering to it, and presented it to Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess. Then, seeing the jewel, she asked her hand-maidens, saying: "Is there perhaps some one outside the gate?" They replied, saying: "There is some one sitting on the top of the cassia-tree above our well. It is a very beautiful young man. He is more illustrious even than our king. Lo, as he begged for water, we respectfully gave him water; but, without drinking the water, he spat this jewel into [the vessel]. As we were not able to separate this [from the other],&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_822"></A><A HREF="#fn_818"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> we have brought [the vessel] with [the jewel] in it to present to thee." Then Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, thinking it strange, went out to look, and was forthwith delighted at the sight. They exchanged glances, after which she spoke to her father, saying: "There is a beautiful person at our gate." Then the Sea-Deity him-self went out to look, and saying: "This person is the Sky's-Sun-Height, the august child of the Heaven's-Sun-Height,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_823"></A><A HREF="#fn_819"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> led him into the interior [of the palace], and spreading eight layers of rugs of sea-asses&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_824"></A><A HREF="#fn_820"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> skins, and spreading on the top other eight layers of silk rugs, and setting him on the top of them, arranged merchandise on tables holding an hundred,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_825"></A><A HREF="#fn_821"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> made an august banquet,</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_149"><font size="1" color="green">p. 149</font></A></p>  
<p>and forthwith gave him his daughter Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess in marriage. So he dwelt in that land for three years. Hereupon His Augustness Fire-Subside [123] thought of what had gone before,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_826"></A><A HREF="#fn_822"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> and heaved one&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_827"></A><A HREF="#fn_823"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> deep sigh. So Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess, hearing the sigh, informed her father, saying: "Though he has dwelt three years [with us], he had never sighed; but this night he heaved one deep sigh. What may be the cause of it?" The Great Deity her father asked his son-in-law saying: "This morning I heard my daughter speak, saying: 'Though he has dwelt three years [with us], he had never sighed; but this night he heaved one deep sigh.' What may the cause be? Moreover what was the cause of thy coming here?" Then [His Augustness Fire-Subside] told the Great Deity exactly how his elder brother had pressed him for the lost fish-hook. Thereupon the Sea-Deity summoned together all the fishes of the sea, great and small, and asked them, saying: "Is there perchance any fish that has taken this fish-hook?" So all the fishes replied: "Lately the <i>tahi</i>&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_828"></A><A HREF="#fn_824"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> has complained of something sticking in its throat&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_829"></A><A HREF="#fn_825"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> preventing it from eating; so it doubtless has taken [the hook]." On the throat of the <i>tahi</i> being thereupon examined, there was the fish-hook [in it]. Being forthwith taken, it was washed and respectfully presented to His Augustness Fire-Subside, whom the Deity Great-Ocean-Possessor then instructed, saying: "What thou shalt say when thou grantest this fish-hook to thine elder brother [is as follows]: 'This fish-hook is a big hook, an eager hook, a poor hook, a silly hook.'&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_830"></A><A HREF="#fn_826"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> Having [thus] spoken, bestow it with thy back hand.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_831"></A><A HREF="#fn_827"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> [124] Having done thus,&#8212;if thine elder brother make high</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_150"><font size="1" color="green">p. 150</font></A></p>  
<p>fields,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_832"></A><A HREF="#fn_828"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> do Thine Augustness make low fields; and if thine elder brother make low fields, do Thine Augustness make high fields. If thou do thus, thine elder brother will certainly be impoverished in the space of three years, owing to my ruling the water. If thine elder brother, incensed at thy doing thus, should attack thee, put forth the tide-flowing jewel&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_833"></A><A HREF="#fn_829"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> to drown him. If he express grief, put forth the tide-ebbing jewel to let him live. Thus shalt thou harass him." With these words, [the Sea-Deity] gave [to His Augustness Fire-Subside] the tide-flowing jewel and the tide-ebbing jewel,&#8212;two in all,&#8212;and forthwith summoned together all the crocodiles,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_834"></A><A HREF="#fn_830"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> and asked them, saying: "The Sky's-Sun-Height, august child of the Heaven's-Sun-Height, is now about to proceed out to the Upper-Land.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_835"></A><A HREF="#fn_831"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> Who will in how many days respectfully escort him, and bring back a report?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_836"></A><A HREF="#fn_832"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> So each according to the length of his body in fathoms spoke, fixing [a certain number of] days,&#8212;one of them, a crocodile one fathom [long], saying: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_837"></A><A HREF="#fn_833"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> will escort him, and come back in one day." So then [the Sea-Deity] [125] said to the crocodile one fathom [long]: "If that be so, do thou respectfully escort him. While crossing the middle of the sea, do not alarm him!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_838"></A><A HREF="#fn_834"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> Forthwith he seated him upon the crocodile's head, and saw him off. So [the crocodile] respectfully escorted him home in one day, as he had promised. When the crocodile was about to return, [His Augustness Fire-Subside] untied the stiletto&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_839"></A><A HREF="#fn_835"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> which was girded on him, and, setting it on the crocodile's neck,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_840"></A><A HREF="#fn_836"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> sent [the latter] back. So the crocodile one fathom [long] is now called the Deity Blade-Possessor.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_841"></A><A HREF="#fn_837"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_809"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_813">147:1</A> <a name="page_151"><font size="1" color="green">p. 151</font></A> <i>Shiho-tsuchi no kami</i>. The view of the meaning of this name which has here been taken is founded on the persistent use in all documents of the character <A NAME="img_15100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15100.jpg">, "salt," to write the first element of the compound, and of varying characters to write the syllables <i>tsu</i> and <i>chi</i>, an indication that the latter are to be taken phonetically and may therefore be interpreted to signify <i>tsu mochi</i>, "possessor of," as in numerous other instances. The fact that this god is known as the god of salt-manufacturers (see Tanigaha Shinsei's "Perpetual Commentary on the Chronicles of Japan" Vol. VII, p. 3) adds another reason for rejecting both Motowori's far-fetched derivation of the name for <i>Shiri-oho-tsu-mochi</i>, "Great Possessor of Knowledge," and his assertion that it denotes no <A HREF="errata.htm#22">individual</A> deity, but any one gifted with superior wisdom.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_810"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_814">147:2</A> <i>Sora-tsu-hi-daka</i>. It will be remembered that <i>Ama-tsu-hi-daka</i>, "Heaven's-Sun-Height," was the first part of Prince Fire-Subsides's alternative name (see Sect. XXXVIII, Note 15). The distinction between these two almost identical appellations would seem to be that the former is used of the Heir Apparent, the latter of the reigning sovereign. Both were therefore equally applicable to Prince Fire-Subside; and while that which he eventually bore is mentioned where his names are first given he is naturally spoken of in this place, when his father may be supposed to have been still living, by that variation of the name properly marking the Heir Apparent. These names, <i>Ama-tsu-hi-daka</i> and <i>Sora-tsu-hi-daka</i>, will be met with again below applied to other personages.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_811"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_815">147:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "I had received a fish-hook from my elder brother in exchange for a bow." The text is here concise to obscurity.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_812"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_816">147:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, as is supposed, a punt or tub made of strips of bamboo plaited so tightly that no water could find its way in between them.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_813"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_817">147:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, simply "a pleasant road." <i>Michi</i>, "a road" is properly a compound,&#8212;<i>mi-chi</i>, "august road,"&#8212;the single syllable <i>chi</i> being the most archaic Japanese word for "road." It is in this place written <A NAME="img_15101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15101.jpg">, showing that the etymology was not yet quite forgotten at the time of the compilation of these "Records." Generally, however, throughout the work we have <A NAME="img_15102"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15102.jpg"> or <A NAME="img_15103"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15103.jpg"> alone.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_814"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_818">147:6</A> See Sect. VI, Note 8, where the Adjective "Great" is prefixed to the name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_815"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_819">147:7</A> See Sect. XXXI, Note 10.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_816"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_820">147:8</A> <i>Toyo-tama-hime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_817"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_821">147:9</A> The character <A NAME="img_15104"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15104.jpg"> properly "light," "refulgence," is here taken by Motowori in the precisely opposite sense of "shadow" (the parallel <a name="page_152"><font size="1" color="green">p. 152</font></A> passage in the "Chronicles" having <A NAME="img_15200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15200.jpg"> "human shadow"), and his view is absolved from unreasonableness by the fact of the confusion between light and shade which has always existed in Japanese phraseology. Thus <i>hi-kage</i> may signify either "sunlight" or "a shadow cast by the sun." It is safest, however, to adhere to the Chinese characters employed by the author; and in this special instance we may well suppose him to have intended to say that a celestial light shone from the body of the god in question. Such an idea is not foreign to classical Japanese ways of thought and expression. See also Sect. XLVI, Note 9-10.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_818"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_822">148:10</A> Or, taking the character <A NAME="img_15201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15201.jpg"> as an initial Particle, "So, as we were not able to separate [one from the other]."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_819"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_823">148:11</A> See Note 2 to this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_820"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_824">148:12</A> This is a literal translation of the Chinese characters <A NAME="img_15202"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15202.jpg">, by which the Archaic word <i>michi</i>, here written phonetically, is elsewhere represented. Perhaps the sea-lion (<i>Otaria arsina</i>) or a species of seal may be intended.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_821"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_825">148:13</A> See Sect. XXXVII, Note 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_822"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_826">149:14</A> Literally, "thought of the first things."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_823"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_827">149:15</A> As the character for "one" is thrice repeated in this passage, Motowori is probably right in saying that it should be given its proper signification, and the translator therefore renders it by the Numeral "one" rather than by the Indefinite Article "a."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_824"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_828">149:16</A> Pronounced <i>tai</i> in modern parlance. Perhaps we should rather add <i>aka-dahi</i>, "red <i>tahi</i>," as in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles." Both these fishes belong to the family <i>Sparoidei</i>, the former being the <i>Pagrus cardinalis</i>, the latter probably the P. <i>major</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_825"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_829">149:17</A> Or, "of a fish-bone in its throat."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_826"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_830">149:18</A> Tanigaha Shisei, quoting from Urabe no Kaneyoshi, comments thus on the parallel passage in the "Chronicles," where the whole of this legend is given several times in slightly varying forms: "By big hook is meant one that will not serve its purpose [because too big]; eager signifies that which [endeavours to, but] cannot advance; silly means unintelligent; hence we have a hook which, not serving its purpose, will be of no use whatever, but rather a road to lead [him who possesses it] to poverty. Poor outwardly, and inwardly silly, he will be the most useless creature in the Empire." It should be noted, however, that Motowori interprets in the sense of "gloomy," and Moribe in the sense of "drowning," the phonetically written and obscure word obo, here rendered "great."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_827"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_831">149:19</A> <a name="page_153"><font size="1" color="green">p. 153</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, "with thy hand behind thy back." This is supposed by the commentators to have been a sort of charm by which evil was averted from the person of him who practised it, and they point out that Izanagi (the "Male-Who-Invites") brandished his sword behind him when he was pursued by the hosts of Hades (see Sect. IX, Note 15).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_828"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_832">150:20</A> By "high fields "and "low fields "are meant respective upland rice-fields where the rice is planted in the dry, and "paddy-fields" properly so called, where the rice perpetually stands in the water. Different varieties of rice are used for these different methods of culture.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_829"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_833">150:21</A> <i>Shiho mitsu tama</i>. The "tide-ebbing jewel "mentioned in the next sentence is in the Japanese <i>shiho hiru tama</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_830"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_834">150:22</A> See Introduction, <A HREF="kj004.htm#page_xxxiii">p. xxxiii</A>, Note 41.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_831"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_835">150:23</A> <i>Uha tsu kuni</i>, <A NAME="img_15300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15300.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_832"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_836">150:24</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Which of you will most speedily escort him home to the upper world, and bring back news of his safe arrival there?"</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_833"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_837">150:25</A> Written with the respectful <A NAME="img_15301"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15301.jpg">, "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_834"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_838">150:26</A> There is in, this sentence a character <A NAME="img_15302"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15302.jpg">, which is hard to explain if read <i>moshi</i>, "if," as usual in Japanese. Probably, however, it simply stands for <A NAME="img_15303"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15303.jpg"> "thou," and we might translate thus: "While thou art crossing," etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_835"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_839">150:27</A> See Sect. XXXVI, Note 8.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_836"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_840">150:28</A> <i>I.e.</i>, probably, tying it round the crocodile's neck.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_837"></A><A HREF="kj047.htm#fr_841">150:29</A> <i>Saki-mochi-no-kami</i>. "Blade "is the probable signification of <i>sahi</i> or <i>sabi</i>, though this particular proper name is written in the "Chronicles" with the Chinese character <A NAME="img_15304"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15304.jpg">, "hoe" or "mattock." Here the syllables <i>sa hi</i> are written phonetically.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_153"><font size="1" color="green">p. 153</font></A>[125]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XLI.&#8212;SUBMISSION OF HIS AUGUSTNESS FIRE-SHINE.]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon [His Augustness Fire-Subside] gave the fish-hook [to his elder brother], exactly according to the Sea-Deity's words of instruction. So thenceforward [the elder brother] became poorer, and poorer, and, with renewed savage intentions, came to attack him. When he was about to attack [His Augustness Fire-Subside, the latter] put forth the tide-flowing jewel to drown him; on</p>  
<p><a name="page_154"><font size="1" color="green">p. 154</font></A></p>  
<p>his expressing grief, he put forth the tide-ebbing jewel to save him. When he had thus been harassed, he bowed his head,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_842"></A><A HREF="#fn_838"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A> saying: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_843"></A><A HREF="#fn_839"><FONT SIZE="1">2a</FONT></A> henceforward will be Thine Augustness's guard by day and night, and respectfully serve thee." So down to the present day his various posturings when drowning are ceaselessly served up.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_844"></A><A HREF="#fn_840"><FONT SIZE="1">3a</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_838"></A><A HREF="kj048.htm#fr_842">154:1a</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "did humble obeisance by prostrating himself on the ground." The Old Printed Edition has <A NAME="img_15400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15400.jpg"> instead <A NAME="img_15401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15401.jpg">, and the <i>kana</i> gloss <i>kamugahemausu</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "reflected, and said": but this reading, though interesting, is less good.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_839"></A><A HREF="kj048.htm#fr_843">154:2a</A> Written with the humble character <A NAME="img_15402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15402.jpg">, "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_840"></A><A HREF="kj048.htm#fr_844">154:3a</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Prince Fire-Shine's descendants the <i>Hayabito</i> (see Sect. XXXVIII, Note 11) still constantly perform before the Court dances and posturings symbolical of the antics which their divine ancestor went through for the amusement of his younger brother, after the latter had saved him from drowning. "One account" in the "Chronicles" relates these antics at full, telling us that they represented the straits to which he was put as the waters gradually rose higher and higher; and we learn from other passages in the same work and in the "Chronicles of Japan Continued" that the <i>Hayabito</i> did really down to historical times combine the office of Court Jesters with that of Imperial Guardsmen.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p>[126]</p>  <h2 align="center">SECT. XLII.&#8212;THE PARTURITION-HOUSE OF CORMORANTS' FEATHERS]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon the Sea-Deity's daughter Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess herself waited on&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_845"></A><A HREF="#fn_841"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> [His Augustness Fire-Subside], and said: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_846"></A><A HREF="#fn_842"><FONT SIZE="1">2b</FONT></A> am already with child, and the time for my delivery now approaches. But me-thought that the august child of an Heavenly Deity&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_847"></A><A HREF="#fn_843"><FONT SIZE="1">3b</FONT></A> ought not to be born in the Sea-Plain.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_848"></A><A HREF="#fn_844"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So I have waited on thee here."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_849"></A><A HREF="#fn_845"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Then forthwith on the limit of the waves upon the sea-shore she built a parturition-hall,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_850"></A><A HREF="#fn_846"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> using</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_155"><font size="1" color="green">p. 155</font></A></p>  
<p>cormorants' feathers for thatch. Hereupon, before the thatch was completed,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_851"></A><A HREF="#fn_847"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> she was unable to restrain the urgency of her august womb. So she entered the parturition-hall. Then, when she was about to be delivered, she spoke to her husband&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_852"></A><A HREF="#fn_848"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> [saying]: "Whenever a foreigner is about to be delivered, she takes the shape of her native land to be delivered.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_853"></A><A HREF="#fn_849"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> So I now will take my native shape to be delivered. Pray look not upon [127] me!" Hereupon [His Augustness Fire-Subside], thinking these words strange, stealthily peeped at the very moment of delivery, when she turned into a crocodile&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_854"></A><A HREF="#fn_850"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> eight fathoms [long], and crawled and writhed about; and he forthwith, terrified at the sight, fled away. Then Her Augustness Luxuriant-Jewel-Princess knew that he had peeped; and she felt ashamed, and, straightway leaving the august child which she had borne, she said: 'I had wished always to come and go across the sea-path.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_855"></A><A HREF="#fn_851"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> But thy having peeped at my [real] shape [makes me] very shame-faced,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_856"></A><A HREF="#fn_852"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A>&#8212;and she forthwith closed the sea-boundary,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_857"></A><A HREF="#fn_853"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> and went down again.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_858"></A><A HREF="#fn_854"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> Therefore the name by which the august child whom she had borne was called was his Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_859"></A><A HREF="#fn_855"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> Nevertheless afterwards, although angry at his having wished to peep, she could not restrain her loving heart, and she entrusted to her younger sister Jewel-Good-Princess,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_860"></A><A HREF="#fn_856"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> on the occasion of her nursing the august child,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_861"></A><A HREF="#fn_857"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> a Song to be presented [to His [128] Augustness Fire-Subside]. The Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"As for red jewels, though even the string [they are strung on] shines, the aspect of [my] lord [who is] like unto white jewels is [more] illustrious."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_862"></A><A HREF="#fn_858"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_156"><font size="1" color="green">p. 156</font></A></p>  
<p>Then her husband replied by a Song, which said: </p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"As for my younger sister, whom I took to sleep [with me] on the island where light the wild-duck, the birds of the offing, I shall not forget her till the end of my life."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_863"></A><A HREF="#fn_859"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So His Augustness-Prince-Great-Rice-ears-Lord-Ears&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_864"></A><A HREF="#fn_860"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> dwelt in the palace of Takachiho for five hundred and eighty years&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_865"></A><A HREF="#fn_861"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> His august mausoleum&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_866"></A><A HREF="#fn_862"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> is likewise on the west of Mount Takachiho.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_157"><font size="1" color="green">p. 157</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_841"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_845">154:1b</A> <a name="page_156"><font size="1" color="green">p. 156</font></A> For "waited on "see Sect. XXXVIII, Note 1. The word "herself" (<A NAME="img_15600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15600.jpg"> <i>midzukara</i>) has no particular force or meaning in the Japanese original, where it is simply placed in imitation of the Chinese style.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_842"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_846">154:2b</A> See Sect. XXXVIII, Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_843"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_847">154:3b</A> Or "of <i>the</i> Heavenly Deity," <i>i.e.</i>, "thyself." But it seems better to understand the speaker to intimate that it would be unfitting for one who properly belonged to Heaven to be born in the sea, which was another country or kingdom.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_844"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_848">154:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, in the sea.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_845"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_849">154:5</A> Literally "come out and arrived."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_846"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_850">154:6</A> It has been noticed in the Introduction, <A HREF="kj004.htm#page_xxviii">p. xxviii</A>, that in early Japan a parturient woman was expected to build for herself a special hut in which to give birth to her child.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_847"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_851">155:7</A> Or, completely put on; literally, "thatched [so as] to meet."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_848"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_852">155:8</A> The text here has<A NAME="img_15601"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15601.jpg"> "prince," literally "sun-child," and so the older editors understood the expression. The translator, however, prefers Motowori's view, according to which the character <A NAME="img_15602"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15602.jpg"> should be supplied, and the whole read phonetically as <i>hikoi</i>, "husband," a word which occurs again a few lines further on.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_849"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_853">155:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, she assumes the shape proper to her in her native land.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_850"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_854">155:10</A> According to the parallel passage of the "Chronicles," she turned into a dragon. "One account "however agrees with our text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_851"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_855">155:11</A> The original of this passage is rather confused; but the interpretation here adopted from the Old Printed Edition is more natural than Motowori's according to which the Verbs are to be taken in a Causative sense, to the following effect: "I had always wished to let people come <a name="page_157"><font size="1" color="green">p. 157</font></A> and go across the sea-path.'' Probably it was only in order to make this clause fit in better with the following sentence, in which we are told that the crocodile-princess "closed the sea-boundary," and with the fact that there is at present no path leading to the Sea-God's palace, that Motowori was induced to sanction such a view of the grammar of this passage.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_852"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_856">155:12</A> This is Motowori's interpretation of the clause, he having emended <A NAME="img_15700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15700.jpg">, "action," "doing," which is found in the older editions, <A NAME="img_15701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15701.jpg">, "shame-faced." (The edition of 1687 mentions <A NAME="img_15702"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15702.jpg">, "strange," as an alternative reading). If we followed the older reading, we should have to translate thus: "Thy having peeped at my [real] shape is an outrageous action."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_853"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_857">155:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the boundary dividing the dominions of the Sea-God from the world of men.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_854"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_858">155:14</A> Viz., to the Sea-God's palace.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_855"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_859">155:15</A> <i>Ama-tsu-hi-daka-hiko-nagisa-take-u-gaya-fuki-ahesu no mikoto</i>. The older editors read <i>ahasezu</i> for <i>ahezu</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "causing to meet," instead of "meeting." Moribe, in his Critique on Motowori's Commentary, would have us believe that the name comes from <i>umi-ga kayohi fuki-ahezu</i> (<A NAME="img_15703"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15703.jpg">), <i>i.e.</i> "going and coming on sea and land and being unable to suckle"!</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_856"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_860">155:16</A> <i>Tama yori-bime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_857"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_861">155:17</A> <i>I.e.</i>, of Jewel-Good-Princess nursing the child, The mother did not return to the upper world, and so sent this poetic message by her sister, who had consented to act as the child's nurse.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_858"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_862">155:18</A> "The meaning of the Song," says Motowori, "is this: Although red jewels are so charming that the very string [whereon they are strung] doth shine, the august aspect of my lord, who is like unto white jewels, is still more lovely. Thus does she express her loving feeling."&#8212;Moribe supposed the "red jewels" (or "jewel" in the Singular) to be meant for the child, than whom her husband is yet dearer to her heart. The word <i>kimi</i>, here etymologically rendered "[my] lord," is commonly used in the sense of "thou," especially in poetry.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_859"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_863">156:19</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "I shall never forget thee who wast my wife in the realm of the Sea-God. The "birds of the <A HREF="errata.htm#23">offing</A>" are a description of the wild duck, used as a Pillow-Word for their name. In the same manner the whole phrase, "where light the wild-duck, the birds of the offing," may be taken simply as a "Preface" to the word "island." The Sea-God's dwelling is called an island because it is beyond the sea. The words <a name="page_158"><font size="1" color="green">p. 158</font></A> <i>yo no koto-goto ni</i>, here in deference to the views of the best commentators rendered by "till the end of my life," will also bear the interpretation of "night by night."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_860"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_864">156:20</A> The alternative name of the deity Fire-Subside.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_861"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_865">156:21</A> Probably the writer means us to understand that the total age reached by this deity was five hundred and eighty years. This is the first mention in these "Records "of anything approaching a date. The way in which it is recorded resembles that in which the chronicle of each Emperor's reign is brought to a close in the later volumes of the work.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_862"></A><A HREF="kj049.htm#fr_866">156:22</A> The character <A NAME="img_15800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/15800.jpg"> might also be rendered by the simple word "grave." But neither it nor its Japanese reading <i>misasaki</i> are ever used except honorifically of the Imperial tombs, and "mausoleum "seems therefore a more suitable English equivalent.</P>

<p><a name="page_158"><font size="1" color="green">p. 158</font></A> [129]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XLIII.&#8212;THE AUGUST CHILDREN OF HIS AUGUSTNESS CORMORANT-THATCH-MEETING-INCOMPLETELY]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Heaven's-Sun-Height-Prince-Wave-limit-Brave-Cormorant-Thatch-Meeting-Incompletely wedded his maternal aunt Her Augustness Jewel-Good-Princess, and begot august children named: His Augustness Five-Reaches;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_867"></A><A HREF="#fn_863"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> next His Augustness Boiled-Rice;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_868"></A><A HREF="#fn_864"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> next His Augustness August-Food-Master;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_869"></A><A HREF="#fn_865"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> next His Augustness Young-August-Food-Master,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_870"></A><A HREF="#fn_866"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> another name for whom is His Augustness Luxuriant-August-Food-Master,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_871"></A><A HREF="#fn_867"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and another name is His Augustness Divine-Yamato-Ihare-Prince.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_872"></A><A HREF="#fn_868"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> So His Augustness August-Food-Master, treading on the crest of the waves, crossed over to the Eternal Land.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_873"></A><A HREF="#fn_869"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> His Augustness Boiled-Rice went into the Sea-Plain, it being his deceased mother's&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_874"></A><A HREF="#fn_870"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> land.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_863"></A><A HREF="kj050.htm#fr_867">158:1</A> <a name="page_158"><font size="1" color="green">p. 158</font></A> <i>Itsu-se-no-mikoto</i>. The "reaches" are the reaches of a river: at least this seems the most natural view to take of the meaning of the name. Motowori and Moribe, however, consider it to be a corruption of <i>idzu-shine</i>, to which they assign the signification of "powerful rice." <a name="page_159"><font size="1" color="green">p. 159</font></A> Excepting for the fact of its bringing this name into harmony with the three that follow, and which all relate to food, there seems little to recommend so far-fetched a derivation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_864"></A><A HREF="kj050.htm#fr_868">158:2</A> <i>Inu-hi-na-mikoto</i>. If Motowori's <A HREF="errata.htm#24">derivation</A> of the name from <i>ina-ihi</i> is correct, it might be rendered with greater exactness "Rice-boiled-rice," ine denoting rice in the husk and ihi the same when boiled.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_865"></A><A HREF="kj050.htm#fr_869">158:3</A> <i>Mi-ke-nu-no-mikoto</i>. This name has been translated in accordance with Motowori's interpretation of the syllables that compose it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_866"></A><A HREF="kj050.htm#fr_870">158:4</A> <i>Waka-nu-ke-nu-no-mikoto</i>. <i>Conf</i>. preceding Note.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_867"></A><A HREF="kj050.htm#fr_871">158:5</A> Toyo-nu-ke-nu-no-mikoto. <i>Conf</i>. Note 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_868"></A><A HREF="kj050.htm#fr_872">158:6</A> <i>Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko-no-mikoto</i>. <i>Yamato</i> being the name of the province where this prince, the first Emperor of the so-called "human age," fixed his capital, it appropriately forms part of his name. For a discussion of the etymology of the word Yamato, see Sect. V, Note 26. <i>Ihare</i>, a word which is said to signify "assembling," is the name of a village in that province.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_869"></A><A HREF="kj050.htm#fr_873">158:7</A> See Sect. XXVII, Note 12.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_870"></A><A HREF="kj050.htm#fr_874">158:8</A> See Sect. XII, Note 8.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_159"><font size="1" color="green">p. 159</font></A> [130]</p>  <h1 align="center">VOL. II.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_875"></A><A HREF="#fn_871"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A></h1>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XLIV.&#8212;REIGN OF THE EMPEROR JIM-MU&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_876"></A><A HREF="#fn_872"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> (PART I.&#8212;HIS PROGRESS EASTWARD, AND DEATH OF HIS ELDER BROTHER)]</h2>  
<p>The two Deities His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_877"></A><A HREF="#fn_873"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and his elder brother His Augustness Itsu-se, dwelling in the palace of Takachiho.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_878"></A><A HREF="#fn_874"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> took counsel, saying: "By dwelling in what place shall we [most] quietly carry on the government of the Empire?&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_879"></A><A HREF="#fn_875"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> It were probably best to go east." Forthwith they left Himuka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_880"></A><A HREF="#fn_876"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> on their progress&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_881"></A><A HREF="#fn_877"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> to Tsukushi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_882"></A><A HREF="#fn_878"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> So when they arrived at Usa&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_883"></A><A HREF="#fn_879"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> in the Land of Toyo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_884"></A><A HREF="#fn_880"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> two of the natives, whose names were Usa-tsu-hiko and Usa-tsu-hime&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_885"></A><A HREF="#fn_881"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> built a</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_160"><font size="1" color="green">p. 160</font></A></p>  
<p>palace raised on one foot,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_886"></A><A HREF="#fn_882"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and offered them a great august banquet. Removing thence, they dwelt for one [131] year at the palace of Wokoda&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_887"></A><A HREF="#fn_883"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> in Tsukushi. Again making a progress up&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_888"></A><A HREF="#fn_884"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> from that land, they dwelt seven years at the palace of Takeri&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_889"></A><A HREF="#fn_885"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> in the land of Agi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_890"></A><A HREF="#fn_886"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> Again removing, and making a progress up from that land, they dwelt eight years at the palace of Takashima&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_891"></A><A HREF="#fn_887"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> in Kibi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_892"></A><A HREF="#fn_888"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> So when they made their progress up from that land, they met in the Hayasuhi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_893"></A><A HREF="#fn_889"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> Channel a person riding towards them on the carapace of a tortoise, and raising his wings&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_894"></A><A HREF="#fn_890"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> as he angled. Then they called to him to approach, and asked him, saying: "Who art thou?" He replied, saying: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_895"></A><A HREF="#fn_891"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> am an Earthly Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_896"></A><A HREF="#fn_892"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A>" Again they asked him, saying: "Knowest thou the sea-path?" He replied, saying: "I know it well." Again they asked him, saying: "Wilt thou follow and respectfully serve us?" He replied, saying: "I will respectfully serve you." So they pushed a pole&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_897"></A><A HREF="#fn_893"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> across to him, drew him into the august vessel, and forthwith conferred [132] on him the designation of Sawa-ne-tsu-hiko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_898"></A><A HREF="#fn_894"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> (<small>This is the ancestor of the Rulers of the land of Yamato.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_899"></A><A HREF="#fn_895"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> So when they went up from that land they passed the Namihaya&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_900"></A><A HREF="#fn_896"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> Crossing, and brought up at the haven of Shirakata.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_901"></A><A HREF="#fn_897"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> At this time Nagasune-biko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_902"></A><A HREF="#fn_898"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> of Tomi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_903"></A><A HREF="#fn_899"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> raised an army, and waited to go out to fight [against them]. Then they took the shields that had been put in the august vessel, and disembarked. So they called that place by the name of Tate-dzu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_904"></A><A HREF="#fn_900"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> It is what is now called the Tadetsu of Kusaka.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_905"></A><A HREF="#fn_901"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> Therefore when fighting with the Prince of Tomi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_906"></A><A HREF="#fn_902"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A> His Augustness Itsu-se was pierced in his august hand by the Prince of Tomi's hurtful arrow.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_907"></A><A HREF="#fn_903"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> So then he said: "It is not right for me, an august</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_161"><font size="1" color="green">p. 161</font></A></p>  
<p>child of the Sun-Deity, to fight facing the sun. It is for this reason that I am stricken by the wretched villain's&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_908"></A><A HREF="#fn_904"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> hurtful hand. I will henceforward turn round, and smite him with my back to the sun." Having [thus] decided, he, on making a progress round from the southern side, reached the sea of Chinu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_909"></A><A HREF="#fn_905"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A> and washed the blood on his august hand: so it is called the sea of Chinu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_910"></A><A HREF="#fn_906"><FONT SIZE="1">36</FONT></A> Making a progress round from thence, and arriving at the river-mouth of Wo&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_911"></A><A HREF="#fn_907"><FONT SIZE="1">37</FONT></A> in the land of Ki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_912"></A><A HREF="#fn_908"><FONT SIZE="1">38</FONT></A> he said: "Ah! that I should die stricken by the wretched villain's hand!" and expired&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_913"></A><A HREF="#fn_909"><FONT SIZE="1">39</FONT></A> as a valiant man.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_914"></A><A HREF="#fn_910"><FONT SIZE="1">40</FONT></A> So that river-mouth was called the river mouth of Wo.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_915"></A><A HREF="#fn_911"><FONT SIZE="1">41</FONT></A> The Mausoleum, too, is on Mount Kama&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_916"></A><A HREF="#fn_912"><FONT SIZE="1">42</FONT></A> in the land of Ki.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_871"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_875">159:1</A> <a name="page_161"><font size="1" color="green">p. 161</font></A> Literally, "Middle Volume," there being three in all. See Author's Preface, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_872"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_876">159:2</A> <i>Jim-mu</i> signifies "divine valour." It is the "canonical name" of the Emperor <i>Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko</i> (see Introduction, <A HREF="kj002.htm#page_xiv">p. xiv</A>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_873"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_877">159:3</A> In the preceding Section this name was rendered "Divine-Yamato-Ihare-Prince." But in the translation of Vols. II and III of this work, the Japanese proper names are not Englished, unless there be a special reason for so doing. (See Introduction, pp. <A HREF="kj003.htm#page_xviii">xviii</A> and <A HREF="kj003.htm#page_xix">xix</A>.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_874"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_878">159:4</A> See Sect. XXXIV, Note 5.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_875"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_879">159:5</A> See Sect. XXVII, Note 13.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_876"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_880">159:6</A> See Sect. X, Note 4.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_877"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_881">159:7</A> The Japanese expression here used is one which exclusively denotes an Imperial Progress, and not the movements of lesser people. It recurs perpetually in this and the following Volume.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_878"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_882">159:8</A> See Sect. V, Note 14.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_879"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_883">159:9</A> Etymology uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_880"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_884">159:10</A> See Sect. V, Note 17.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_881"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_885">159:11</A> <i>I.e.</i>, Prince of Usa and Princess of Usa.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_882"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_886">160:12</A> In the original, <A NAME="img_16100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16100.jpg">, read asks <i>hito-tsu agari no miya</i>. The parallel passage of the "Chronicles" has <A NAME="img_16101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16101.jpg"> which is directed to be read in the same manner. <A NAME="img_16102"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16102.jpg"> (<i>hashira</i>) however means, not "foot," but "pillar "; and the commentators understand both passages to allude <a name="page_162"><font size="1" color="green">p. 162</font></A> to a single pillar, which supported the weight of the entire building,&#8212;either as being in the middle of it, or (as Motowori opines) by standing in the water, the edifice, according to this view, being built on a river-bank overhanging the stream.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_883"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_887">160:13</A> This name signifies "hillock rice-field."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_884"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_888">160:14</A> <i>Q.d.</i> towards Yamato, the province where the capital was eventually fixed. In Japanese, as in English, people are said to go of to the capital and down to the country.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_885"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_889">160:15</A> Etymology uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_886"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_890">160:16</A> Etymology uncertain. This name is better known (without the <i>nigori</i> of the second syllable) as Aki. Aki is one of the provinces on the northern shore of the Inland Sea.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_887"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_891">160:17</A> This name signifies "high island."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_888"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_892">160:18</A> Etymology uncertain. Kibi is the name of a province.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_889"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_893">160:19</A> This name signifies "quick sucking."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_890"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_894">160:20</A> <i>I.e.</i>, as Motowori supposes, beckoning by waving his sleeve.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_891"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_895">160:21</A> The First Personal Pronoun is represented by the humble character <A NAME="img_16200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16200.jpg">, "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_892"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_896">160:22</A> See Sect. I, Note 11. Motowori wishes us here to understand this expression to mean "I am a Deity (<i>i.e.</i> a person) of the country-side." But there is no sufficient reason for departing from the precedent of rendering the characters <A NAME="img_16201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16201.jpg">, which are constantly used antithetically to <A NAME="img_16202"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16202.jpg">, by "Earthly Deity" (as opposed to "Heavenly Deity.") Motowori likewise proposes to append to this sentence the clause "and my name is Udzu-biko," which is found in the "Chronicles." The name may be taken to signify "precious prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_893"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_897">160:23</A> The characters <A NAME="img_16203"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16203.jpg"> are evidently, as Motowori says, meant to represent the Japanese word <i>sawo</i>, "pole," though they do not properly convey that meaning. Probably they are corrupt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_894"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_898">160:24</A> <i>I.e.</i>, if we suppress the syllable <i>ne</i>, which seems to be either Expletive or Honorific, the "prince of the pole."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_895"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_899">160:25</A> <i>Yamato no kuni no Miyadzuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_896"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_900">160:26</A> This is the reading of the name preferred by Mabuchi and Motowori; but the usual form <i>Naniha</i> seems to be at least as well supported by early documentary evidence. The "Chronicles" tell us that the place was called <i>Nani-haya</i> <A NAME="img_16204"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16204.jpg">, <i>i.e.</i> "wave swift," in allusion to the strong current which the Emperor Jim-mu here encountered; and at the present day it is still a dangerous place for navigation. The name properly denotes the water at the mouth of the River Yodo, on <a name="page_163"><font size="1" color="green">p. 163</font></A> which stands the modern town of Ohosaka (&#332;zaka), for whose name Naniha is still often used as a poetical synonym. <A NAME="img_16300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16300.jpg">, "wave flowers," and <A NAME="img_16301"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16301.jpg">, "dangerous waves," are alternative ways of writing it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_897"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_901">160:27</A> Motowori says that he cannot explain the etymology of this word; but "white sandbank" would seem a simple and obvious derivation. The Shirakata here mentioned is, according to Motowori, that situated in the province of Idzumo.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_898"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_902">160:28</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Prince of Nagasune. A plausible interpretation of <i>nagasune</i> would be "long-shank," which would give us Prince Long-Shank as the name of the worthy here mentioned; but the "Chronicles" states that Nagasune was properly the name of a place. The characters with which it is written, moreover, signify not exactly "long shank," but "long marrow," a designation which would have no evident personal applicability.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_899"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_903">160:29</A> A legend in the "Chronicles" connects the name of this place with the word <i>tobi</i>, "a kite," it being there related that a miraculous gold-coloured kite came and perched on the Emperor Jim-mu's bow, and helped him to the victory. Probably the legend grew out of the name of <i>Tobi</i>, which is obscure and may have had had nothing to do with a "kite "originally.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_900"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_904">160:30</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "shield-haven." But <i>conf</i>. next Note.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_901"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_905">160:31</A> The real etymology of <i>Tada-tsu</i> seems to be "knot-grass-haven," <A HREF="errata.htm#25">and</A> probably <i>Taka-tsu</i> (for <i>Takatsu</i>), which is mentioned in Sect. LXIX, Note 29, is but another form of the same name. Kusaka is a well-known name in the annals of early Japan. Its signification is obscure, and the characters (<A NAME="img_16302"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16302.jpg">), with which it is written, are particularly curious. There were two Kusaka, one in the province of Kahachi and the other in Idzumi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_902"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_906">160:32</A> Viz., <i>Nagasune-biko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_903"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_907">160:33</A> The wording of the original <A NAME="img_16303"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16303.jpg"> is very curious: Motowori reads it <i>Tomi-bike ga ita-ya wo ohashite</i>. Immediately below we have <A NAME="img_16304"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16304.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_904"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_908">161:34</A> The character is <A NAME="img_16305"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16305.jpg">, properly "slave."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_905"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_909">161:35</A> The most likely derivation of this name is from <i>chi-numa</i>, "eulalia lagoon," the fact that it will also bear the interpretation of "blood-lagoon "being probably but a coincidence of which the mythopoeic faculty took advantage.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_906"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_910">161:36</A> Here written with characters signifying "blood-lagoon."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_907"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_911">161:37</A> <a name="page_164"><font size="1" color="green">p. 164</font></A> The characters rendered "river-mouth "are <A NAME="img_16400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16400.jpg">, literally "water. gate; but here, as elsewhere, "river-mouth "seems to be the signification meant to be conveyed. Rivers in <A HREF="errata.htm#26">Japan</A>, even at the present day, do not bear one continuous name along their entire course, and there would be nothing unnatural in the fact of the water at the mouth of the river having a special designation. One of the significations of <i>wo</i> is "man," and the legendary etymology of the name given immediately below rests on the assumption that such is the meaning of wo in this place. Even Motowori, however, is not satisfied with it, and it is probably erroneous.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_908"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_912">161:38</A> See Sect. XXII, Note 14.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_909"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_913">161:39</A> The Chinese character <A NAME="img_16401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16401.jpg">, which is here used, is one that specially denotes the demise of an Emperor.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_910"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_914">161:40</A> Probably the sense meant to be conveyed is that he expired with a <A HREF="errata.htm#27">gesture</A> of anger and defiance.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_911"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_915">161:41</A> Here written <A NAME="img_16402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16402.jpg">, "man." Conf. Note 37.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_912"></A><A HREF="kj051.htm#fr_916">161:42</A> <i>Kama-yama</i>, <i>i.e.</i> furnace-mountain."</P>
