<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_164"><font size="1" color="green">p. 164</font></A> [134]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XLV.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART II.&#8212;THE CROSS-SWORD SENT DOWN FROM HEAVEN).]</h2>  
<p>So when His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko made a progress round from thence, and reached the village of Kumanu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_917"></A><A HREF="#fn_913"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> a large bear came out of the mountain,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_918"></A><A HREF="#fn_914"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and forthwith disappeared into it. Then His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko suddenly fainted away, and his august army likewise all fainted and fell prostrate. At this time Takakurazhi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_919"></A><A HREF="#fn_915"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> (<small>this is the name of a person</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_920"></A><A HREF="#fn_916"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> of Kumanu came bearing one cross-sword&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_921"></A><A HREF="#fn_917"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> to the place where the august-child of the Deity was lying prostrate, and presented it to him, upon which the august child of the Heavenly Deity forthwith rose up, and said: "How long I have slept!" So when he accepted the cross-sword, the savage Deities of the mountains of Kumanu all spontaneously fell cut down.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_922"></A><A HREF="#fn_918"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> Then the whole august</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_165"><font size="1" color="green">p. 165</font></A></p>  
<p>army, that had been bewildered and had fallen prostrate, awoke and rose up. So the august child of the Heavenly Deity asked him how he had got the cross-sword. Takakurazhi [135] replied, saying: "I was told in a dream that</p>  
<p>the two Deities the Heaven-Shining-Great-Deity&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_923"></A><A HREF="#fn_919"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and the High Integrating Deity&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_924"></A><A HREF="#fn_920"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> commanded and summoned the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_925"></A><A HREF="#fn_921"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and charged him [thus]: 'The Central Land of Reed-Plains&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_926"></A><A HREF="#fn_922"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> is painfully uproarious,&#8212;it is.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_927"></A><A HREF="#fn_923"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> Our august children must be ill at ease. As [therefore] the Central Land of Reed-Plains is a land which thou specially subduedst, thou the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity shalt descend [thither].' Then he replied, saying: 'I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_928"></A><A HREF="#fn_924"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> will not descend [myself], but I have the cross-sword wherewith I specially subdued the land. (<small>The name by which this sword is called is the Deity Thrust-Snap;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_929"></A><A HREF="#fn_925"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> another name by which it is called is the Deity Awful-Snap,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_930"></A><A HREF="#fn_926"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> and another name for it is the August-Snap-Spirit,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_931"></A><A HREF="#fn_927"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> This sword dwells in the temple of the Deity of Isonokami</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_932"></A><A HREF="#fn_928"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> The manner in which I will send this sword down will be to perforate the ridge of [the roof of] Takakurazhi's stone-house,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_933"></A><A HREF="#fn_929"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> and drop it through. (So the Brave-Awful-Possessing-Male-Deity instructed me, saying: 'I will perforate the ridge of [the roof of] thy store-house, and drop this sword through.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_934"></A><A HREF="#fn_930"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A>) So do thou, with the good eyes of [136] morning,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_935"></A><A HREF="#fn_931"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> take it and present it to the august child of the Heavenly Deity.' So, on my searching my store-house early next morning in accordance with the instructions of the dream, there really was a cross-sword there. So I just present this cross-sword to thee."</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_913"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_917">164:1</A> This name signifies "bear-moor." The name is now generally pronounced <i>Kumano</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_914"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_918">164:2</A> Motowori ingeniously conjectures the text of this passage <A NAME="img_16500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16500.jpg">, which makes no sense, to be a copyist's error for <A NAME="img_16501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16501.jpg">, which <a name="page_166"><font size="1" color="green">p. 166</font></A> gives the meaning rendered in the translation. The running hand form of <A NAME="img_16602"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16602.jpg"> might well be mistaken for that of the single character <A NAME="img_16603"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16603.jpg">. The editor of 1687 is less happy in his conjecture that the character intended may be <A NAME="img_16604"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16604.jpg">, "crocodile." This incident of the bear was thought important by the compiler for a mention of it to be inserted in his Preface. (See <A HREF="kj007.htm#page_5">p. 5</A>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_915"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_919">164:3</A> The signification of this name is not clear. Taking <i>zhi</i> as an apocopated <i>nigori&#8217;ed</i> form of the Postposition <i>shita</i>, we might suppose <i>taka-kura-zhi</i> to signify "under the high store house" in allusion to the legend which forms the subject of this section. There are, however, reasons for doubting this etymology. (See Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XVIII, p. 48). In the Preface we have simply <i>Takahura</i>, without the final syllable <i>zhi</i>; but the omission of <i>zhi</i> in that place is almost certainly to be accounted for on euphonic grounds.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_916"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_920">164:4</A> This note to the original is believed to be an interpolation,</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_917"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_921">164:5</A> <A NAME="img_16603"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16603.jpg">. Motowori avers that the character <A NAME="img_16604"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16604.jpg">, "cross," has no importance, and should be neglected in reading. But this assertion seems gratuitous in the face of, for instance, such a Chinese locution as <A NAME="img_16605"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16605.jpg">. We may be justified, perhaps, in paying no special heed to the Numeral "one" in this place, which Motowori neglects in his <i>kana</i> reading of the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_918"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_922">164:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, they fell down cut to pieces before they had even been cut at with this wonderful sword.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_919"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_923">165:7</A> The character <A NAME="img_16606"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16606.jpg">, "august," which should form the penultimate member of this compound name, is here omitted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_920"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_924">165:8</A> See Sect. I, Note 5.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_921"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_925">165:9</A> See Sect. VIII, Note 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_922"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_926">165:10</A> See Sect. IX, Note 18.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_923"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_927">165:11</A> Conf. Sect. X, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_924"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_928">165:12</A> The humble character <A NAME="img_16607"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16607.jpg">, "servant," is here used.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_925"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_929">165:13</A> <i>Sazhi-futsu no kami</i>. The translator follows Tanigaha Shisei in considering <i>sazhi</i> (Tanigaha Shisei in his "Perpetual Commentary" reads <i>sashi</i> without the <i>nigori</i>) to mean "thrust." For the rendering of <i>futsu</i> as "snap" in this and the two following names <i>conf</i>. Sect. VIII, Note 8. Moribe, however, in his "<i>Ikzu no Chi-waki</i>," asserts that <i>futsu</i> is but an alternative form of <i>futo</i>, "broad," "thick," or "vast," as shown by the existence of the phrase <i>ma-futsu no kagami</i>, "a true vast mirror."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_926"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_930">165:14</A> <i>Mika-futsu no kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_927"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_931">165:15</A> <i>Futsu no mi tame</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_928"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_932">165:16</A> <a name="page_167"><font size="1" color="green">p. 167</font></A> The name of this place, which is in the province of Yamato, seems to signify "above the rock." It is well known as the Pillow-Word for the syllables <i>furu</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_929"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_933">165:17</A> Properly what is known to Anglo-Orientals as a "godown."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_930"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_934">165:18</A> The sentence here placed between braces is proposed by Motowori to supplement an evident lacuna in the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_931"></A><A HREF="kj052.htm#fr_935">165:19</A> Or, "luckily with morning eyes." Motowori remarks that even in modern times, special joy is felt at a good discovery made in the morning.</P>

<p><a name="page_167"><font size="1" color="green">p. 167</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XLVI.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART III.&#8212;THE GIGANTIC CROW AND GODS WITH TAILS)]</h2>  
<p>"Then His&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_936"></A><A HREF="#fn_932"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Augustness the Great-High-Integrating-Deity again commanded and taught, saying: "August son of the Heavenly Deity! make no progress hence into the interior. The savage Deities are very numerous. I will now send from Heaven a crow eight feet [long].&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_937"></A><A HREF="#fn_933"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> So that crow eight feet [long] shall guide thee. Thou must make thy progress following after it as it goes." So on [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] making his progress following after the crow eight feet [long] in obedience to the Deity's instructions, he reached the lower course of the Yeshinu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_938"></A><A HREF="#fn_934"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> river, where there was a [137] person catching fish in a weir.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_939"></A><A HREF="#fn_935"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Then the august child of the Heavenly Deity asked, saying: "Who art thou?" He replied, saying: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_940"></A><A HREF="#fn_936"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> am an Earthly Deity&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_941"></A><A HREF="#fn_937"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and am called by the name of Nihe-motsu no Ko."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_942"></A><A HREF="#fn_938"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> (<small>This is the ancestor of the Cormorant-Keepers of Aha.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_943"></A><A HREF="#fn_939"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> On [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] making his progress thence, a person with a tail&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_944"></A><A HREF="#fn_940"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> came out of a well. The well shone. Then [His Augustness] asked: "Who art thou?" He</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_168"><font size="1" color="green">p. 168</font></A></p>  
<p>replied, saying: "I am an Earthly Deity, and my name is Wi-hika."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_945"></A><A HREF="#fn_941"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> This is the ancestor of the Headmen of Yeshinu).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_946"></A><A HREF="#fn_942"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> On his forthwith entering the mountains,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_947"></A><A HREF="#fn_943"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko again met a person with a tail. This person came forth pushing the cliffs apart. Then [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] asked: "Who art thou?" He replied, saying; "I am an Earthly Deity, and my name is Iha-oshi-waku no Ko. I heard [just] now that the august son of the Heavenly Deity was making his progress. So it is for that that I have come to meet thee." (<small>This is the ancestor of the Territorial [138] Owners of Yeshinu</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_948"></A><A HREF="#fn_944"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> Thence [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] penetrated over on foot to Uda.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_949"></A><A HREF="#fn_945"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> So they say: "The Ugachi of Uda."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_950"></A><A HREF="#fn_946"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_932"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_936">167:1</A> <a name="page_168"><font size="1" color="green">p. 168</font></A> The intention of the writer is here obscure, but he probably meant the following passage to form part of the dream, as is the case in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles." The inverted commas are therefore continued in the translation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_933"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_937">167:2</A> The characters <A NAME="img_16800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16800.jpg"> (<i>ya to-garasu</i>), with which the original of this expression is written, combined with the mention in the Preface of the "great crow," have determined the translator to adopt the interpretation favoured by Tanigaha Shisei, <A HREF="errata.htm#28">viz.</A>, a "crow eight feet [long]." Motowori understands the expression to mean "an eight-headed crow." For the arguments on both sides see the Perpetual Commentary on the Chronicles of Japan," Vol. VII, p. 16, and Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XVIII, pp. 60-62, and Vol. VIII, pp. 34-58. See also for the translation of a parallel passage Sect. XVI, Note 23.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_934"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_938">167:3</A> Better known by the classical and modern form of the name, <i>Yoshino</i>. It seems to signify "good moor." Yoshino, which is in the province of Yamato, has from the earliest times been renowned for the beauty of its cherry-blossoms, and also figures largely in the early and mediaeval history. Motowori points out geographical difficulties in the Imperial progress as here detailed. In the "Chronicles," the verisimilitudes of the journey are better observed.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_935"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_939">167:4</A> <a name="page_169"><font size="1" color="green">p. 169</font></A>The character <A NAME="img_16900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16900.jpg">, here rendered "weir" for want of a better word, is defined as signifying "a bamboo trap for catching fish."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_936"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_940">167:5</A> The First Personal Pronoun is here represented by the humble character <A NAME="img_16901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16901.jpg">, "servant." The other tailed deity mentioned immediately below uses the same expression.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_937"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_941">167:6</A> See Sect. I, Note 11, and Sect. XLIV, Note 22, for the considerations that make it better to translate thus than to render by "I am a Deity of the Land."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_938"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_942">167:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Offering-Bearing Child." Here and elsewhere the word <i>ko</i>, "child," as part of a proper name, should be understood as a kind of Honorific, employed probably in imitation of Chinese usage.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_939"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_943">167:8</A> <i>Ada</i> No <i>U-kaki</i>. This must be understood to be a "gentile name" (<i>kabane</i>). The etymology of Ada is uncertain. The practice of fishing with the help of cormorants, though now almost obsolete, seems to have been very common in Japan down to the Middle ages.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_940"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_944">167:9</A> Commenting on a similar passage a little further on, Motowori, naively remarks: "It appears that in very ancient times such persons were occasionally "to be met with." It should be added that they are also mentioned in Chinese literature.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_941"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_945">168:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Well-Shine."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_942"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_946">168:11</A> <i>Yeshinu no obito</i>. For Yeshinu see Note 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_943"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_947">168:12</A> <i>I.e.</i>, disappearing among the mountains.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_944"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_948">168:13</A> <i>Yeshinu no kuzu</i>. <i>Kuzu</i> is a contraction of <i>kuni-nushi</i> (properly <A NAME="img_16902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16902.jpg">, with which characters the name is found written at the commencement of Sect. CVIII, though elsewhere the semi-phonetic rendering <A NAME="img_16903"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16903.jpg"> or <A NAME="img_16904"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/16904.jpg"> is employed).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_945"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_949">168:14</A> <A HREF="errata.htm#29">Etymology</A> obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_946"></A><A HREF="kj053.htm#fr_950">168:15</A> <i>Uda no ugachi</i>. The meaning of the sentence is: "Hence the name of the Ugachi of Uda." <i>Ugachi</i> signifies "to penetrate." But the etymology seems a forced one, and Motowori is probably correct in identifying this "gentile name" with that of Ukashi, mentioned in the next sentence.</P>

<p><a name="page_169"><font size="1" color="green">p. 169</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XLVII.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (<A HREF="errata.htm#30">PART</A> IV.&#8212;THE UKASHI BRETHREN).]</h2>  
<p>So then there were in Uda two persons, Ukashi the Elder Brother and Ukashi the Younger Brother.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_951"></A><A HREF="#fn_947"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> So</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_170"><font size="1" color="green">p. 170</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] sent the crow eight feet [long] in advance to ask these persons, saying: "The august child of the Heavenly Deity has made a progress [hither]. Will ye respectfully serve him?" Hereupon Ukashi the Elder Brother waited for and shot at the messenger with a whizzing barb to make him turn back. So the place where the whizzing barb fell is called Kabura-zaki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_952"></A><A HREF="#fn_948"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Saying that he intended to wait for and smite [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko], he [tried to] collect an army. But being unable to collect an army he said deceitfully that he would respectfully serve [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko], and built a great palace,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_953"></A><A HREF="#fn_949"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and in that palace set a pitfall, and waited. Then Ukashi the Younger Brother came out to&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_954"></A><A HREF="#fn_950"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] beforehand, and made obeisance, saying: "Mine&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_955"></A><A HREF="#fn_951"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> elder brother Ukashi the Elder Brother has shot at and turned back the messenger [139] of the august child of the Heavenly Deity, and, intending to wait for and attack thee, has [tried to] collect an army; but, being unable to collect it, he has built a great palace, and set&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_956"></A><A HREF="#fn_952"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> a gin within it, intending to wait for and catch thee. So I have come out to inform [thee of this]." Then the two persons His Augustness Michi-no-Omi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_957"></A><A HREF="#fn_953"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> ancestor of the Ohotomo Chieftains,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_958"></A><A HREF="#fn_954"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and His Augustness Ohokume,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_959"></A><A HREF="#fn_955"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> ancestor of the Kume Lords,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_960"></A><A HREF="#fn_956"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> summoned Ukashi the Elder Brother and reviled him, saying: "Into the great palace which thou&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_961"></A><A HREF="#fn_957"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> hast built to respectfully serve [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko], be thou&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_962"></A><A HREF="#fn_958"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> the first to enter, and declare plainly the manner in which thou intendest respectfully to serve him; "&#8212;and forthwith grasping the hilts of their cross-swords, playing with their spears,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_963"></A><A HREF="#fn_959"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> and fixing arrows [in</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_171"><font size="1" color="green">p. 171</font></A></p>  
<p>their bows], they drove him in, whereupon he was caught in&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_964"></A><A HREF="#fn_960"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> the gin which he himself had set, and died. So they forthwith pulled him out, and cut him in pieces. So the place is called Uda-no-Chihara.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_965"></A><A HREF="#fn_961"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> Having done thus, [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] bestowed on his august army the whole of the great banquet presented [to him] by Ukashi the Younger Brother. At this time he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The woodcock, for which I laid a wood-cock-snare [140] and waited in the high castle of Uda, strikes not against it; but a valiant whale strikes against it. If the elder wife ask for fish, slice off a little like the berries of the stand soba; if the younger wife ask for fish, slice off a quantity like the berries of the vigorous <i>sasaki</i>."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_966"></A><A HREF="#fn_962"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Ugh!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_967"></A><A HREF="#fn_963"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> pfui! dolt! This is saying thou rascal. Ah! pfui! dolt! This is laughing [141] [him] to scorn."</div></p>  
<p>So Ukashi the Younger Brother (<small>he is the ancestor of the Water Directors of Uda</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_968"></A><A HREF="#fn_964"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_947"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_951">169:1</A> <a name="page_171"><font size="1" color="green">p. 171</font></A> <i>Ye-ukashi</i> and <i>Oto-ukashi</i>. <i>Ukashi</i>, as in the other compounds where it occurs, is probably in reality the name of a place. Its etymology is doubtful.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_948"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_952">170:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, Barb Point or Cape.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_949"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_953">170:3</A> Or, hall.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_950"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_954">170:4</A> The original has a respectful expression, which is elsewhere translated "waited on."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_951"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_955">170:5</A> The First Personal Pronoun is represented by the respectful character <A NAME="img_17100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/17100.jpg"> "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_952"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_956">170:6</A> Literally, "spread." This gin is supposed to have been of the kind whose top closes down after the man or animal has fallen into it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_953"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_957">170:7</A> <a name="page_172"><font size="1" color="green">p. 172</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Grandee of the Way." This gentile name is said in the "Chronicles "to have been bestowed on this worthy in consideration of the services as a guide to his master the Emperor on the occasion of the latter's progress eastward.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_954"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_958">170:8</A> See Sect. XXXIV, Note 12.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_955"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_959">170:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, perhaps "Great Round Eyes," supposed to be a descendant of His Augustness <i>Ama-tsu-kume</i> (see however Sect. XXXIV, Note 7 for a discussion of the etymology of <i>Kume</i>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_956"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_960">170:10</A> See Sect. XXXIV, Note 13.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_957"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_961">170:11</A> The expression <i>i ga</i>, here rendered "thou," is, as Motowori remarks, "extremely hard to understand," and its interpretation as an insulting form of the Second Personal Pronoun is merely tentative. Perhaps the text is corrupt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_958"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_962">170:12</A> The insulting Second Pronoun <i>ore</i> is here employed.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_959"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_963">170:13</A> Here again we have an expression written phonetically and of uncertain import. The translator has followed Motowori in tentatively rendering it according to the ideographic reading of the parallel passage of the "Chronicles."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_960"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_964">171:14</A> Literally "struck by."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_961"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_965">171:15</A> <i>I.e.</i>, Uda's Blood-Plain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_962"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_966">171:16</A> This Song is unusually difficult of comprehension: and the latest important commentator, Moribe, seems to show satisfactorily that all his predecessors, Motowori included, more or less misunderstood it. He had at least the advantage of coming after them, and the translator has followed his interpretation excepting with regard to <i>isukukashi</i>, the Pillow-Word for "whale," which is here rendered "valiant," in accordance with the traditional view of its signification. The <i>soba</i> tree is identified by Motowori with the <i>Kaname-mochi</i>, "<i>Photinia glabra</i>," <A HREF="errata.htm#31">This</A> <i>saka-ki</i>, taken together with its Prefix <i>ichi</i> (here rendered "vigorous") is supposed in this place to signify, not the usual <i>Cleyera japonica</i>, but another species popularly known as the <i>bishiya-gaki</i>, whose English or Latin name the translator has failed to ascertain. It has a large berry, whereas the soba has a small one. . . The following is the gist of Moribe's exposition of the general signification of the Song: "If for Ukashi's mean design to kill the Emperor in a gin there be sought a term of comparison in the whales and woodcock forming the Imperial banquet, then in lieu of the woodcock that he expected to catch in the trap that he set, that great whale, the Imperial host, has rushed up against it. Again if, as the fishermen's wives might do, your (<i>i.e.</i>, you soldiers') wives ask you <a name="page_173"><font size="1" color="green">p. 173</font></A> for fish, then let each of you give to his elder wife, of whom he must have grown weary, only a small and bony portion, and to his younger wife, who is doubtless his heart's favourite, a good fleshy piece. So jocular a guess at the "<i>penchants</i> of the young warriors excites their ardour, which they give vent to in the following shouts."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_963"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_967">171:17</A> Some of the Japanese originals of this string of Interjections are of uncertain import. The translator has been guided by Motowori's conjectures, with which Moribe mostly agrees. The exclamations are supposed not to form part of the actual Song, but to proceed from the mouths of the Imperial soldiers. The words rendered "this is saying thou rascal" (such is apparently their meaning) and those rendered "this is laughing [him] to scorn "seem to be glosses as old as the text, which had already been obscure in the eighth century. They are not written altogether phonetically.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_964"></A><A HREF="kj054.htm#fr_968">171:18</A> <i>Uda na Mohitori</i>. This tribe or guild of "water-directors" was entrusted with the charge of the water, the ice, and the gruel used in the Imperial household. In later times the word <i>Mohitori</i> was corrupted to <i>Mondo</i>.</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_173"><font size="1" color="green">p. 173</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XLVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART V.&#8212;THE EARTH-SPIDER OF THE CAVE OF OSAKA).]</h2>  
<p>When [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] made his progress, and reached the great cave of Osaka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_969"></A><A HREF="#fn_965"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> earth-spiders&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_970"></A><A HREF="#fn_966"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> with tails, [namely] eighty bravoes,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_971"></A><A HREF="#fn_967"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> were in the cave awaiting him. So then the august son of the Heavenly Deity commanded that a banquet be bestowed on the eighty bravoes. Thereupon he set eighty butlers, one for each of the eighty bravoes, and girded each of them with a sword, and instructed the butlers, saying: [142] "When ye hear me sing, cut [them down] simultaneously." So the Song by which he made clear to them to set about smiting the earth-spiders said:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Into the great cave <A HREF="errata.htm#33">of</A> Osaka people have entered in abundance, and are <a name="page_174"><font size="1" color="green">p. 174</font></A> [there]. Though people have entered in abundance, and are [there], the children of the augustly powerful warriors will smite and finish them with [their] mallet-headed [swords], [their] stone-mallet [swords]: the children of the augustly powerful warriors, with [their] mallet-headed [swords], [their] stone-mallet [swords], would now do well to smite."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_972"></A><A HREF="#fn_968"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Having thus sung, they drew their swords, and simultaneously smote them to death.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_965"></A><A HREF="kj055.htm#fr_969">173:1</A> <a name="page_174"><font size="1" color="green">p. 174</font></A> The etymology of this name is not clear, but readers will of course not confound it with that of the modern town of Ohosaka (Ozaka). The character rendered "cave," <A NAME="img_17400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/17400.jpg">, signifies simply "apartment;" but the traditional reading is <i>muro</i>, which means a cave or pit dug in the earth. That the latter is the idea which the author wishes to convey becomes clear by comparison with a greater number of passages in the older literature. For a more particular discussion of this subject see Mr. Milne's paper entitled "Notes on Stone Implements from Otaru and Hakodate," published in Vol. VIII, part I of these "Transactions," p. 76 <i>et seq.</i>, where a number of passages relative to the "earth-spiders" are likewise brought together.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_966"></A><A HREF="kj055.htm#fr_970">173:2</A> <i>Tsuchi-gumo</i>, generally written <A NAME="img_17401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/17401.jpg">, but here semi-phonetically <A NAME="img_17402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/17402.jpg">. There is little doubt that by this well-known name, which has given rise to much conjecture, a race of cave-dwelling savages or a class of cave-dwelling robbers is intended. Motowori supposes that their name had its origin in a comparison of their habits with those of the spider. But it were surely more rational to regard it as a corruption of <i>tsuchi-gomori</i>, "earth-hiders," a designation as obvious as it is appropriate. The "Chronicles" describe one tribe of them as "being short in stature, and having long arms and legs like pigmies." For a further discussion of the subject see Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XIX, pp. 30-31, the "Perpetual Commentary on the Chronicles of Japan," Vol. VIII, p. 35, the "<i>Tou-ya</i>," Vol. XX, <i>s.v.</i> <i>kumo</i> and the "Examination of Difficult Words," Vol. 1I, pp. 55 <i>et seq.</i></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_967"></A><A HREF="kj055.htm#fr_971">173:3</A> <a name="page_175"><font size="1" color="green">p. 175</font></A> The original term is <i>takeru</i> (<A NAME="img_17500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/17500.jpg">), which might also be rendered "bandit," or "robber <A HREF="errata.htm#32">chief</A>."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_968"></A><A HREF="kj055.htm#fr_972">174:4</A> The import of this poem is too clear to stand in need of explanation. The word <i>mitsumitsushi</i>, here rendered "augustly powerful" in accordance with Moribe's view, is understood by Motowori to mean "perfectly full," in allusion to the fully or perfectly round eyes of the deity Kume, to whose name he supposes there to be a reference. Mabuchi, on the other hand, explains the word to signify "young and flourishing." But Moribe's view both of this and of the import of <i>kume</i> as "warriors "seems so greatly preferable to any other, that the translator has not hesitated to follow him (<i>conf</i>. Sect. XXXIV, Note 7). The "<i>children</i> of the warriors" are of course the warriors themselves. With regard to the signification of the two kinds of swords here mentioned it has, however, been thought best to adhere to the usual view, and Note 10 to Sect. XXXIV should be referred to.</P>
<p><HR>

<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume II: Section XLIX.&#8212;Emperor Jim-mu (Part. VI.&#8212;The Prince of Tomi and the Shiki Brethren)</TITLE>

<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="index.htm">Index</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj055.htm">Previous</A>&nbsp;

<HR><A HREF="http://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/B0028Y4SZY/internetsacredte">Buy this Book at Amazon.com</A></CENTER>
<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_175"><font size="1" color="green">p. 175</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XLIX.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART. VI.&#8212;THE PRINCE OF TOMI AND THE SHIKI BRETHREN)]</h2>  
<p>After this, when about to smite the Prince of Tomi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_973"></A><A HREF="#fn_969"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> he sang, saying: [143]</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The children of the augustly powerful army will smite and finish the one stem of smelly chive in the millet-field,&#8212;the stem of its root, both its root and shoots."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_974"></A><A HREF="#fn_970"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again he sang:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The ginger, which the children of the augustly powerful army planted near the hedge, resounds in the mouth. I shall not forget it. I will smite and finish it."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_975"></A><A HREF="#fn_971"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_176"><font size="1" color="green">p. 176</font></A></p>  
<p>[144] Again he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Like the <i>turbinid&aelig;</i> creeping round the great rock in the sea of Ise [on which blows] the divine wind, [so] will we creep round, and smite and finish them."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_976"></A><A HREF="#fn_972"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again when he smote Shiki the Elder Brother and Shiki the Younger Brother,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_977"></A><A HREF="#fn_973"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> the august army was temporarily exhausted. Then he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"As we fight placing our shields in a row, going and watching from between the trees on Mount Inasa, oh! we are famished. Ye keepers of cormorants, the birds of the island, come now to our rescue!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_978"></A><A HREF="#fn_974"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_969"></A><A HREF="kj056.htm#fr_973">175:1</A> <a name="page_176"><font size="1" color="green">p. 176</font></A> See Sect. XLIV, Notes 28 <i>et seq</i>. The apparent want of sequence in this portion of the narrative is not noticed by Motowori. We might endeavour to, harmonize it by supposing that after having slain the "earth-spiders," etc., the Emperor Jim-mu turned round again to fight with the Prince of Tomi, who had harassed him in the earlier portion of his career as conqueror of Central Japan.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_970"></A><A HREF="kj056.htm#fr_974">175:2</A> The wild chive growing among the millet is of course the enemy, the Prince of Tomi and his host; and the gist of the Song is that the Imperial troops will smite and destroy them root and branch. The commentators suppose the simile to have been taken from the fields of millet which Jim-mu's troops planted for their subsistence during the long drawn out campaigns of early days.&#8212;The "stem of its root," <i>so ne ga moto</i>, is a curious expression, which is perhaps best accounted for by Moribe's supposition that we have here a pun on <i>Sune ga moto</i>, "Sune's house," Sune being a natural abbreviation of <i>Nagasune</i>, the name of the Prince of Tomi (see Sect. XLIV, Note 28).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_971"></A><A HREF="kj056.htm#fr_975">175:3</A> The sense of this Song is: "I shall not forget the bitterness of seeing my brother slain by Prince Nagasune's arrow (see the latter part of Sect. XLIV). The word hazhikami, here rendered ginger in accordance with Motowori's dictum, is taken by Moribe to signify the xanthoxylon. <a name="page_177"><font size="1" color="green">p. 177</font></A> "Resounding in the mouth" is a curious phrase here used to express bitterness.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_972"></A><A HREF="kj056.htm#fr_976">176:4</A> Motowori thus paraphrases this Song: "As the innumerable <i>turbinid&aelig;</i> [-shells] creep round the great rock, so will I with the myriads of the Imperial host encompass the Prince of Tomi on every side, that there may be no outlet whereby he can escape." The shell here mentioned is a kind of small conch. <i>Kama-kazo no</i>, lit, "of divine wind," is the Pillow-Word for Ise, and is of disputed derivation, as is the word Ise itself. The curious reader should refer to Fujihara no Hikomaro's "Inquiry into the Meaning of the Names of All the Provinces" <i>s.v.</i> for the legend to which the name of Ise and its Pillow-Word were anciently traced and other conjectures on the point, The "great rock" here mentioned is not otherwise known.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_973"></A><A HREF="kj056.htm#fr_977">176:5</A> <i>Ye-shiki</i> and <i>Otoshiki</i>. Shiki is the name of a district in the province of Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_974"></A><A HREF="kj056.htm#fr_978">176:6</A> This Song is a request for provisions made by the Emperor to some fishermen, who were working their cormorants along the mountain-streams. Moribe refers it to an incident, not in the war, but in the hunt, and interprets differently the word here, in accordance with its usual meaning and with older authority, rendered "as we fight." He attributes to it the sense of "as we put our shields together," and thinks that the poet may have compared to shields the trunks of the trees. According to this view, the Song should be viewed rather as a joke. It may be mentioned that there is good authority for considering the word <i>tata namete</i>, "placing shields in a row," as a Punning Preface or Pillow-Word for words commencing with <i>i</i> (<i>i</i> being the Root of <i>iru</i>, "to shoot"), so that Moribe's explanation need not involve any tautology. It seems however somewhat far-fetched.&#8212;The position of Mount Inasa is uncertain, and the name itself of obscure derivation.</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_177"><font size="1" color="green">p. 177</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. L.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART VII.&#8212;THE EMPIRE PACIFIED)]</h2>  
<p>So then His Augustness Nigi-hayabi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_979"></A><A HREF="#fn_975"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> waited on and said to the august child of the Heavenly Deity: "As I heard that [thou], the august child of the Heavenly Deity, hadst descended from Heaven, I have followed</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_178"><font size="1" color="green">p. 178</font></A></p>  
<p>down to wait on thee." Forthwith presenting to him the heavenly symbols,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_980"></A><A HREF="#fn_976"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> he respectfully served him. So His Augustness Nigi-hayabi wedded the Princess of Tomi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_981"></A><A HREF="#fn_977"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> [145] sister of the Prince of Tomi, and begot a child, His Augustness <i>Umashi-ma-ji</i>.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_982"></A><A HREF="#fn_978"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> (<small>He was the ancestor of the Chiefs of the Warrior-Clan,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_983"></A><A HREF="#fn_979"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> of the Grandees of Hodzumi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_984"></A><A HREF="#fn_980"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and of the Grandees of the Neck-Clan</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_985"></A><A HREF="#fn_981"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> So having thus subdued and pacified the savage Deities, and extirpated the unsubmissive people, [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] dwelt at the palace of Kashibara&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_986"></A><A HREF="#fn_982"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> near Unebi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_987"></A><A HREF="#fn_983"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_988"></A><A HREF="#fn_984"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_975"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_979">177:1</A> The component parts of this name, rendered according to the analogy of that in Sect. XXXIII, Note 5, may be interpreted to signify "Plenty-Swift." The genealogy of this god is not known.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_976"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_980">178:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the swords, quivers, bow, and arrows mentioned in Sect. XXXIII, as having been brought down from Heaven by the divine attendants of the Emperor Jim-mu's grandfather.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_977"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_981">178:3</A> <i>Tomi ya-bime</i>, The syllable <i>ya</i> is inexplicable, but perhaps merely an Expletive.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_978"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_982">178:4</A> The signification of this name is by no means clear; but, rendered according to the characters with which it is written in the "Chronicles," it would mean "Savoury-True-Hand."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_979"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_983">178:5</A> <i>Mononobe no murazhi</i>. This and the two following are of course "gentile names."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_980"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_984">178:6</A> <i>Hodzumi no omi</i>. Hodzumi, which is the name of a place, signifies "rice-ears piled up."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_981"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_985">178:7</A> <i>Une-be no omi</i>. The interpretation of this name is given according is Motowori, who explains that the members of this family,&#8212;in particular the female members,&#8212;waited at the Emperor's table, and wore veils over their necks when so employed. The name is commonly corrupted to <i>uneme</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_982"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_986">178:8</A> Better known as Kashihabara. The name signifies "oak-moor," or rather "a place planted with oaks." This is usually, though without sufficient foundation, reckoned the earliest of the historical capitals of Japan. It is in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_983"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_987">178:9</A> Unebi is the name of a hill in Yamato. The etymology of the word is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_984"></A><A HREF="kj057.htm#fr_988">178:10</A> <a name="page_179"><font size="1" color="green">p. 179</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, "ruled the Empire from his palace of Kashibara near Unebi. For the expression <A NAME="img_17900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/17900.jpg"> (literally "[all] beneath Heaven"), here rendered "Empire," see Sect. XXVII, Note 13.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_179"><font size="1" color="green">p. 179</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LI.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART. VIII.&#8212;HE WEDS <A HREF="errata.htm#34">I-SUKE-YORI-HIME</A>).]</h2>  
<p>So when he dwelt in Himuka, [His Augustness Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko] wedded&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_989"></A><A HREF="#fn_985"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Princess Ahira,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_990"></A><A HREF="#fn_986"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> younger sister of the Duke of Wobashi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_991"></A><A HREF="#fn_987"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in Ata,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_992"></A><A HREF="#fn_988"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and begot children: [146] there were two,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_993"></A><A HREF="#fn_989"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A>&#8212;His Augustness Tagishi-mimi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_994"></A><A HREF="#fn_990"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next His Augustness Kisu-mimi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_995"></A><A HREF="#fn_991"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> But when he sought for a beautiful maiden to make her his Chief Empress,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_996"></A><A HREF="#fn_992"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> His Augustness Oho-kume said: "There is here a beauteous maiden who is called the august child of a Deity. The reason why she is called the august child of a Deity is that the Princess Seya-datara,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_997"></A><A HREF="#fn_993"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> daughter of Mizokuhi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_998"></A><A HREF="#fn_994"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> of Mishima,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_999"></A><A HREF="#fn_995"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> was admired on account of her beauty by the Great-Master-of-Things the Deity of Miwa,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1000"></A><A HREF="#fn_996"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> qui, quum pulchra puella oletum fecit, in sagittam rubro [colore] fucatam se convertit, et ab inferiori parte cloacae [ad usum] faciendi oleti virginis privatas partes transfixit. Tunc pulchra virgo consternata est, et surrexit, et trepide fugit. Statim sagittam attulit, et juxta thalamum posuit. Subito [sagitta] formosus adolescens facta [147] est, qui cito pulchram puellam sibi in matrimonio junxit, et filiam procreavit nomine Hoto-tarara-i-susugi-hime;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1001"></A><A HREF="#fn_997"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> et est nomen alternativum Hime-tatara-i-suke-yori-hime.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1002"></A><A HREF="#fn_998"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> (<small>Id est posterior mutatio nominis, quoniam abhorruit facere mentionem privatarum partium</small>). So therefore she is called the august child of a Deity. Hereupon seven beauteous maidens were out playing on the moor of Takasazhi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1003"></A><A HREF="#fn_999"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> and I-suke-yori-hime&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1004"></A><A HREF="#fn_1000"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> was among them. His Augustness Ohokume,</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_180"><font size="1" color="green">p. 180</font></A></p>  
<p>seeing I-suke-yori-hime, spoke to the Heavenly Sovereign in a Song, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Seven maidens on the moor of Takasazhi in Yamato:&#8212;which shall be interlaced?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1005"></A><A HREF="#fn_1001"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then I-suke-yori-hime was standing first among the beauteous maidens. Forthwith the Heavenly Sovereign, having looked at the beauteous maidens, and knowing in his august heart&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1006"></A><A HREF="#fn_1002"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> that I-suke-yori-hime was standing in the very front, replied by a Song, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Even [after nought but] a fragment[ary glimpse], I will intertwine the lovely [one] standing in the very front.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1007"></A><A HREF="#fn_1003"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then His Augustness Ohokume informed I-suke-yori-hime [148] of the Heavenly Sovereign's decree, whereupon she, seeing the slit sharp eyes&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1008"></A><A HREF="#fn_1004"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> of His Augustness Ohokume, sang in her astonishment, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px"></p>  <table border="0">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="108">   
<p>"</p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="120">   
<p>?</p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="96">   
<p>?</p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="108">   
<p>"</p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="120">   
<p>?</p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="96">   
<p>?</p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" colspan="3" align="top" width="324">   
<p>"Wherefore   the slit sharp eye?&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1009"></A><A HREF="#fn_1005"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A></p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  
<p></div></p>  
<p>Then His Augustness Ohokume replied by a Song, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"My slit sharp eyes [are] in order to find the maiden immediately."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1010"></A><A HREF="#fn_1006"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So the maiden said that she would respectfully serve [the Heavenly Sovereign].&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1011"></A><A HREF="#fn_1007"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> Hereupon&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1012"></A><A HREF="#fn_1008"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> the house of Her Augustness&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1013"></A><A HREF="#fn_1009"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> I-suke-yori-hime was on [the back of] the River Sawi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1014"></A><A HREF="#fn_1010"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> The Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to the abode of I-suke-yori-hime, and augustly slept [149] [there] one night.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1015"></A><A HREF="#fn_1011"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> (<small>The reason why that river was called the River Sawi was that on the River's banks the mountain-lily-plant grew in abundance. So the name of the mountain-lily-plant was taken, and the designation</small></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_181"><font size="1" color="green">p. 181</font></A></p>  
<p><small>of River Sawi [bestowed]. The name by which the mountain-lily-plant was originally called was <i>sawi</i></small>). Afterwards, when I-suke-yori-hime came and entered into the palace, the Heavenly Sovereign sang augustly saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"In a damp hut on the reed-moor having spread layer upon layer of sedge mats, we two slept!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1016"></A><A HREF="#fn_1012"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>The names of the august children thus born were: His Augustness Hiko-ya-wi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1017"></A><A HREF="#fn_1013"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> next His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1018"></A><A HREF="#fn_1014"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> next His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1019"></A><A HREF="#fn_1015"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> (<small>Three Deities.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1020"></A><A HREF="#fn_1016"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_182"><font size="1" color="green">p. 182</font></A> <a name="page_183"><font size="1" color="green">p. 183</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_985"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_989">179:1</A> <a name="page_181"><font size="1" color="green">p. 181</font></A> Or, "<i>had</i> wedded"; for the episode here related must be supposed to have taken place <A HREF="errata.htm#35">before</A> Jim-mu and his army started eastward on their career of conquest.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_986"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_990">179:2</A> <i>Ahira-hime</i>. Ahira is supposed by Motowori to be the name of a place in Satsuma. Its etymology is quite obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_987"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_991">179:3</A> <i>Wobashi no kimi</i>. Wobashi is supposed by Motowori to be the name of a place in Satsuma. The characters with which it is generally written mean "small bridge."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_988"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_992">179:4</A> Ata is a place in Satsuma.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_989"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_993">179:5</A> Or, "there were two Deities." The character <A HREF="errata.htm#36">employed</A> is not that which itself actually signifies "deity," but is the Auxiliary <A HREF="errata.htm#37">Numeral</A> for divine beings.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_990"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_994">179:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, perhaps "rudder-ears."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_991"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_995">179:7</A> Motowori adduces good reasons for believing this name to be but a slightly altered form of the preceding one, and for holding that in the original form of the tradition there was but one child mentioned.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_992"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_996">179:8</A> See Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XX, pp. 10-15, for the reasons for thus interpreting the characters <A NAME="img_18100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/18100.jpg"> in the text. Elsewhere it has generally, for the sake of convenience, been simply rendered "Empress."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_993"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_997">179:9</A> <i>Seya-dotara-hime</i>. The signification of the name is obscure. Motowori supposes <i>Seya</i> to be a place and tatara (<i>nigori&#8217;ed</i> to <i>datara</i>) perhaps a plant written with the Chinese character <A NAME="img_18101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/18101.jpg">, said by Dr. Williams in his "Syllabic Dictionary" to be possibly a species of <i>Heteroiropa</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_994"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_998">179:10</A> It is uncertain whether this name should, or should not, be <a name="page_182"><font size="1" color="green">p. 182</font></A> regarded as properly that of a place. The meaning is equally obscure. The Chinese characters with which it is here written signify "ditch-eater," whereas those employed in the "Chronicles" signify "ditch-stake." Perhaps both transcriptions are simply phonetic.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_995"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_999">179:11</A> A district in the province of Tsu (Settsu). The name signifies "three islands."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_996"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1000">179:12</A> <i>Miwa-no-oho-mono-mushi-no-kami</i>. This god is supposed to be identical with Oho-kuni-nushi (the "Master of the Great Land," see end of Sect. XX and following Sects). The rigidly literal rendering of the name as here given would be "the Deity Great Master of Things of Miwa "; but the more intelligible version here given represents the Japanese author's meaning. For the traditional etymology of Miwa see the story related in Sect LXV.</p>  
<p>
<P><A NAME="fn_997"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1001">179:13</A> <i>Hoto</i> significat partes privatas. Verbi <i>tatara</i> sensum supra s.v. <i>Seya-datara-hime</i> pertractavimus. <i>I</i> est vox expletiva. <i>Susugi</i> sensus est "trepide fugiens." <i>Hime</i> indicat regiam puellam.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_998"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1002">179:14</A> <i>I.e.</i>, Princess Tatara-Startled-Good-Princess.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_999"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1003">179:15</A> Etymology obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1000"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1004">179:16</A> An abbreviated form of the princess's alternative name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1001"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1005">180:17</A> The meaning of this Song is: "To which of the seven maidens now disporting themselves on the moor of Takasazhi shall I convey the Emperor's command to come that he may make her his consort, and sleep with his arms intertwined in hers?"&#8212;Motowori, overlooking the difference between mart, which is the word in the text, and the <i>nigori</i>&#8217;ed form <i>magu</i> met with in some other passages, misinterprets the last clause thus: "Which shall be sought?" He makes the same mistake in his explanation of the next Song.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1002"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1006">180:18</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "having a presentiment."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1003"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1007">180:19</A> The translation of this Song follows Moribe's exegesis. Motowori interprets it thus; "Well, well! I will seek the lovely one standing in the very front." As here rendered, the little poem is quite clear,&#8212;simply a declaration on the Emperor's part that he will make the girl standing in front his wife.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1004"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1008">180:20</A> <i>Sakeru-to-me</i>, the original of the phrase here rendered "slit sharp eyes," is obscure and variously understood by the commentators. Moribe supposes the god to have worn a casque with a vizor, and the slit to have been made in the latter, and not actually in, or rather near, the eyes. It should however be observed that, though the Japanese word <i>saku</i> means "to slit," the Chinese character in the text properly signifies <a name="page_183"><font size="1" color="green">p. 183</font></A> "to tattoo (or brand) with ink," and is used with that meaning at the end of Sect. CXLIX, and elsewhere in the ancient books. The present writer, after comparing various passages in which the term occurs, thinks that we may understand a <A HREF="errata.htm#38">tattooing</A> of the outer corners of the eyes, which would give to the latter the appearance of being long and sharp, or, if the tattooing were very dark, of being actually slit.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1005"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1009">180:21</A> The first lines of this short poem are so hopelessly unintelligible that the commentators are not even agreed as to how the syllables composing them should be divided into words. For the straits to which Motowori and his predecessors were driven in their efforts to obtain some plausible signification, see his Commentary, Vol. XX, pp. 27-29, and for Moribe's totally divergent interpretation see "<i>Idzu no Koto-waki</i>," Vol. II, pp. 30-31. It is not worth while to quote here more such conjectures.&#8212;For the doubt attaching to the precise signification of the words rendered by "slit sharp eyes," see the preceding Note.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1006"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1010">180:22</A> The signification of his Song is as plain as that of the preceding one is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1007"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1011">180:23</A> <i>Q.d.</i>, as his wife.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1008"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1012">180:24</A> This initial expression is meaningless.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1009"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1013">180:25</A> Having become the Emperor's consort, this Honorific title is now prefixed for the first time to her name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1010"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1014">180:26</A> <i>Sawi-gaha</i>. <i>Sawi</i>, as we learn from the compiler's note below, was the name of a kind of lily.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1011"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1015">180:27</A> Literally, "one sojourn."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1012"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1016">181:28</A> The signification of this Song is: "Now indeed thou comest to share the majesty of the palace. But the beginning of our intimacy was on that night when I came to thy humble dwelling on the reed-grown moor where, when we slept together, we had to pile mat upon mat to keep out the damp."&#8212;The translator has followed Moribe's interpretation throughout. Motowori takes in the sense of "ugly" the word here rendered "damp," and all the previous commentators give a different explanation of the words <i>iya saya shikite</i>, here translated by "spreading layer upon layer." They take them to mean "spreading more land more <A HREF="errata.htm#39">cleanly</A>."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1013"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1017">181:29</A> This name may signify "prince eight-wells." But the interpretation of <i>ya wi</i> as "eight wells" in his and the following name is doubtful.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1014"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1018">181:30</A> This name may signify "divine-eight-wells-ears." But see preceding Note.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1015"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1019">181:31</A> <a name="page_184"><font size="1" color="green">p. 184</font></A> This name may signify "divine-lagoon-river-ears." But perhaps Nuna-kaha is the name of a place.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1016"></A><A HREF="kj058.htm#fr_1020">181:32</A> The character in the text is not actually "Deity," but <A NAME="img_18400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/18400.jpg"> <i>hashira</i>, the Auxiliary Numeral for Deities, which is constantly throughout these "Records" used in speaking of members of the Imperial family.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_184"><font size="1" color="green">p. 184</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LII.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART. IX&#8212;TROUBLES WHICH FOLLOWED HIS DECEASE).]</h2>  
<p>So when, after the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1021"></A><A HREF="#fn_1017"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> [150] the elder half-brother, His Augustness Tagishi-mimi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1022"></A><A HREF="#fn_1018"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> wedded&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1023"></A><A HREF="#fn_1019"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> the Empress I-suke-yori-hime, he plotted how he might slay his three younger brethren, pending which their august&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1024"></A><A HREF="#fn_1020"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> parent I-suke-yori-hime lamented, and made [the plot] known to her august children by a Song. The song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"From the River Sawi the clouds have risen across, and the leaves of the trees have rustled on Mount Unebi: the wind is about to blow."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1025"></A><A HREF="#fn_1021"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again she sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Ah! What rest on Mount Unebi as clouds in the day-time, will surely blow as wind at night-fall, [whence] the rustling of the leaves!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1026"></A><A HREF="#fn_1022"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>When hereupon her august children, hearing and knowing [of the danger], were alarmed and forthwith were about to slay Tagishi-mimi, His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi said to his elder brother His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi: "Thy dear Augustness, [do thou] take a weapon, and go in and slay Tagishi-mimi." So he took a weapon and went in, and was about to slay him. But his arms and legs trembled so, that he was</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_185"><font size="1" color="green">p. 185</font></A></p>  
<p>unable to slay him. So then the younger brother His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi begged [to be allowed] to take the weapon which his elder brother held, and [151] went in and slew Tagishi-mimi. So again, in praise of his august name, he was called His Augustness Take-nuna-kaha-mimi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1027"></A><A HREF="#fn_1023"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Then His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi resigned [in favour of] the younger brother His Augustness Take-nuha-kaha-mimi, saying: "I could not slay the foeman; but Thine Augustness was at once able to slay him. So, though I be the elder brother, it is not right that I should be the superior.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1028"></A><A HREF="#fn_1024"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> Wherefore do Thine Augustness be the superior, and rule [all] beneath the Heaven. I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1029"></A><A HREF="#fn_1025"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> will assist Thine Augustness, becoming a priest,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1030"></A><A HREF="#fn_1026"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and respectfully serving thee."</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1017"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1021">184:1</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Emperor Jim-mu. His decease is not otherwise specially mentioned; but a formula at the end of the Section, which is repeated <i>mutatis mutandis</i> in the case of each Emperor, tells us the number of years he lived or reigned, and the place of his sepulture. Throughout these "Records," much matter is often placed in the reign of a Monarch already deceased, and which, according to our ideas, would more naturally be narrated under the heading of his successor.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1018"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1022">184:2</A> Who was the deceased Emperor's son by Princess Ahira (see Sect. LI, Note 6,) and consequently step-son to the Empress and half-brother to her three sons.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1019"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1023">184:3</A> This is the meaning of the Chinese character in the text, Motowori tries to save the Empress-Dowager's reputation for conjugal fidelity by rendering it in his <i>kana</i> reading by a word signifying "raped."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1020"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1024">184:4</A> See Sect. XXII, Note 4.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1021"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1025">184:5</A> The import of this metaphorical poem, taken in its context, is too clear to need much comment. The rising off the clouds and the rustling of the leaves may be supposed to represent the murderer's preparations, and the blowing of the wind his actual onslaught.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1022"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1026">184:6</A> The meaning of this Song is: "The would-be murderer remains quiet during the day-time like the clouds hanging to the mountain-side; but at night he will I burst upon you like the storm-wind. Already I <a name="page_186"><font size="1" color="green">p. 186</font></A> hear the leaves begin to rustle; already he is gathering his men together."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1023"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1027">185:7</A> The word <i>take</i> prefixed to the name of this prince signifies "brave."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1024"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1028">185:8</A> <i>I.e.</i>, either "superior to thee," or as Motowori understands the phrase, "the superior of all," <i>scil</i>. the Emperor.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1025"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1029">185:9</A> Though the elder brother, he here uses the humble character <A NAME="img_18600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/18600.jpg"> "servant," to show his respect and deference.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1026"></A><A HREF="kj059.htm#fr_1030">185:10</A> Literally, "a person who shuns," <i>q.d.</i> who shuns all pollution, and avoids certain food at certain seasons. <i>Conf</i>. the gentile name <i>Imi-be</i> commented on in Sect. XXXIII, Note 32.</P>

<p><a name="page_186"><font size="1" color="green">p. 186</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LIII.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART X.&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>So His Augustness Hiko-ya-wi (<small>is the ancestor of the Chieftains of Mamuta,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1031"></A><A HREF="#fn_1027"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and of the Chieftains of Teshima.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1032"></A><A HREF="#fn_1028"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> His Augustness Kamu-ya-wi-mimi (<small>is the ancestor of the Grandees of Oho,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1033"></A><A HREF="#fn_1029"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> of the Chieftains of the Tribe of Chihisako,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1034"></A><A HREF="#fn_1030"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> of the chieftains of [152] the Tribe of Sahahi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1035"></A><A HREF="#fn_1031"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> of the Dukes <A HREF="errata.htm#40">of</A> Hi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1036"></A><A HREF="#fn_1032"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> of the Dukes of Ohokida,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1037"></A><A HREF="#fn_1033"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> of the Dukes of Aso,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1038"></A><A HREF="#fn_1034"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> of the Chieftains of the Granaries of Tsukushi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1039"></A><A HREF="#fn_1035"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> of the Grandees of the Sazaki Tribe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1040"></A><A HREF="#fn_1036"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Tribe of Sazaki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1041"></A><A HREF="#fn_1037"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> of the Rulers of Wo-Hatsuse,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1042"></A><A HREF="#fn_1038"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> of the Suzerains of Tsuke,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1043"></A><A HREF="#fn_1039"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the land of Iyo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1044"></A><A HREF="#fn_1040"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the land of Shinanu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1045"></A><A HREF="#fn_1041"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the land of Ihaki in Michinoku,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1046"></A><A HREF="#fn_1042"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the Land of Naka [153] in Hitachi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1047"></A><A HREF="#fn_1043"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> of the Rulers of the land of Nagasa,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1048"></A><A HREF="#fn_1044"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> of the Suzerains of Funaki in Ise,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1049"></A><A HREF="#fn_1045"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> of the Grandees of Niha in Wohari,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1050"></A><A HREF="#fn_1046"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> and of the Grandees of Shimada.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1051"></A><A HREF="#fn_1047"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1027"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1031">186:1</A> <a name="page_186"><font size="1" color="green">p. 186</font></A> <i>Mamuta no murazhi</i>. Mamuta is said to have been a place in the province of Kahachi. The etymology of the name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1028"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1032">186:2</A> <i>Teshima no murazhi</i>. Teshima is said to have been a place in the province of Tsu (Settsu). The name may signify "luxuriant island."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1029"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1033">186:3</A> <i>Oho no omi</i>. Oho is said to have been a place in the province of Yamato. The name is mostly written with characters signifying "vast" or "numerous."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1030"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1034">186:4</A> <i>Chihisako-be no murazhi</i>. Chihisako is said to have been a place in the province of Etchi&#363;. But the name of this family has also been traced to an incident mentioned in the "Newly Selected Catalogue of Family Names "as having occurred in the reign of the Emperor Y&#363;riyaku, <a name="page_187"><font size="1" color="green">p. 187</font></A>when, owing to a verbal error, a tax was collected in children instead of in cocoons. The monarch, amused at the mistake, is said to have granted to the tax-collector the "gentile name" of <i>Chihisako</i>, i.e., "Little Child."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1031"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1035">186:5</A> <i>Sakahi-be no muhazhi</i>. <i>Sakahi</i> signifies "boundary," and this "gentile name" is traced to the fact, mentioned in the "Newly Selected Catalogue of Family Names," that the founder of the family distinguished himself by setting up boundary-marks on the frontiers of different provinces in the reign of the Emperor In-giy&#333; (first half of the fifth century of the Christian era).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1032"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1036">186:6</A> <i>Hi no kimi</i>, Hi (<A NAME="img_18700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/18700.jpg">) is the name of a province (now two provinces) in the south-western island of Tsukushi. It is first mentioned in Sect. V, Note 17.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1033"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1037">186:7</A> <i>Ohokida no kimi</i>. Ohokida is the name of a district in the province of Toyo.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1034"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1038">186:8</A> <i>Aso no himi</i>. Aso is the name of a district in Higo, containing a celebrated volcano.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1035"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1039">186:9</A> <i>Tsukushi no miyake no murazhi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1036"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1040">186:10</A> <i>Sazaki-be no omi</i>. This name is connected by the compiler of the "Newly Selected Catalogue of Family Names" with that of the Emperor Nin-toku (Oho-sazaki no Mikoto), for which see Sect. CIV, Note 18.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1037"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1041">186:11</A> <i>Sazaki-be no miyatsuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1038"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1042">186:12</A> <i>Wo hatsuse no miyatsuko</i>. This name is connected with that of the Emperor Mu-retsu, whose name was Wo-Hatsuse no Waka-Sazaki.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1039"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1043">186:13</A> <i>Tsuke no atahe</i>. Tsuke is the name of a place in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1040"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1044">186:14</A> <i>Iyo no kuni no miyatsuko</i>. For the province of Iyo see Sect. V, Note 26.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1041"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1045">186:15</A> <i>Shinanu no kuni no miyatsuko</i>. For the province of Shinanu (Shinano) see Sect. XXXII, Note 26.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1042"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1046">186:16</A> <i>Michinoku no Ihaki no kuni no miyatsuko</i>. A popular derivation of Michinoku is from <i>michi no kuni</i>, "the country of the road;" but a more likely one, sanctioned by Motowori, is from <i>michi no oku</i>, "the furthest or more distant part of the road." (For the word "road," as here used, <i>conf</i>. Sect. LXV, Note 2.). It was for many centuries, and is still in poetry, a vague name for the entire north of Japan. <i>Ihaki</i>, sometimes considered a province, and at others only ranking as a district, formed its south-eastern portion along the Pacific sea-board. The name seems to signify "rock (or hard) castle."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1043"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1047">186:17</A> <a name="page_188"><font size="1" color="green">p. 188</font></A> <i>Hitachi no naka no huni no miyatzuko</i>. Hitachi is a province to the south of Ihaki. Motowori quotes more than one traditional derivation of its name, the best of which, taken from the old Topography of the province, is hita-michi, "plain road," referring to the level nature of that part of the country. Naka is the name of a district. The word signifies "middle," and may have arisen from the fact of the district bearing it being situated between two considerable rivers.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1044"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1048">186:18</A> <i>Nagasa no kuni no miyatsuko</i>. Nagasa is a district in that portion of the old province of Kadzusa which was in very early historical times cut off from the little province of Aha. The import of the name is not clear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1045"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1049">186:19</A> <i>Ise no Funaki no atahe</i>. For Ise see Sect. XLIX, Note 4. Of Funaki nothing is known. The characters with which the name is written signify "boat-tree."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1046"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1050">186:20</A> <i>Ohari no Niha no omi</i>. Wohari is one of the central provinces of Japan. The name is of uncertain origin. Niha is the name of a district, and is of uncertain origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1047"></A><A HREF="kj060.htm#fr_1051">186:21</A> <i>Shimada no omi</i>. Shimada is the name of a district in Wohari, and signifies "island rice-fields."</P></P>

<p><a name="page_188"><font size="1" color="green">p. 188</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LIV.&#8212;EMPEROR JIM-MU (PART XI.&#8212;HIS AGE AND PLACE OF BURIAL).</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi ruled the Empire. Altogether the august years of this Heavenly Sovereign Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko were one hundred and thirty-seven.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1052"></A><A HREF="#fn_1048"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> His august mausoleum is on the top of the Kashi Spur on the northern side of Mount Unebi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1053"></A><A HREF="#fn_1049"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1048"></A><A HREF="kj061.htm#fr_1052">188:1</A> <a name="page_188"><font size="1" color="green">p. 188</font></A> The author's confused style must not here mislead the student. It is after the decease of the Emperor Jim-mu (Kamu-yamato-ihare-biko), who attains to the age of a hundred and thirty-seven, that the Emperor Suwi-zei (Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi) begins to rule.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1049"></A><A HREF="kj061.htm#fr_1053">188:2</A> For <i>Unebi</i> see Sect. LI, Note 9. <i>Kashi</i> signifies "oak." The word rendered "spur "is <i>wo</i>.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_189"><font size="1" color="green">p. 189</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LV.&#8212;EMPEROR SUI-ZEI.]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Kamu-nuna-kaha-mimi dwelt at the palace of Takawoka in Kadzuraki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1054"></A><A HREF="#fn_1050"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded Kaha-mata-bime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1055"></A><A HREF="#fn_1051"><FONT SIZE="1">2a</FONT></A> ancestress of the Departmental Lords of Shiki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1056"></A><A HREF="#fn_1052"><FONT SIZE="1">3a</FONT></A> and begot [154] an august child: His Augustness Shiki-tsu-hiko-tama-demi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1057"></A><A HREF="#fn_1053"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> (one Deity), The Heavenly Sovereign's august years were forty-five. His august mausoleum is on the Mound of Tsukida.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1058"></A><A HREF="#fn_1054"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1050"></A><A HREF="kj062.htm#fr_1054">189:1a</A> <a name="page_189"><font size="1" color="green">p. 189</font></A> In the province of Yamato. <i>Taka-woka</i> signifies "high mound." <i>Kadzuraki</i> means "pueraria castle," a name accounted for by a legend in the "Chronicles," which relates how an earth-spider was caught in this place by means of a net made of pueraria tendrils. Kadzuraki was the name, not only of a town, but of a district.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1051"></A><A HREF="kj062.htm#fr_1055">189:2a</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Princess of Kahamata, a place in Kahachi. The name signifies "river-fork." For the omission in this and a few other places of the words "daughter of," etc., which might be expected instead of "ancestress," see Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXI, p. 4.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1052"></A><A HREF="kj062.htm#fr_1056">189:3a</A> <i>Shiki na agata-nushi</i>. Shiki is in Yamato. The signification of the name seems to be "stone castle."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1053"></A><A HREF="kj062.htm#fr_1057">189:4</A> <i>Shiki-tsu-hiko</i> signifies "Prince of Shiki." Motowori believes Tamade to be in like manner the name of a place, while he interprets mi as the common abbreviation of the Honorific (?) <i>mimi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1054"></A><A HREF="kj062.htm#fr_1058">189:5</A> A place in Yamato. Motowori derives the name from <i>tsuki</i> modern <i>toki</i>), the "ibis," and <i>ta</i>, "rice-field."</P>
