<p><a name="page_208"><font size="1" color="green">p. 208</font></A> <a name="page_209"><font size="1" color="green">p. 209</font></A> <a name="page_210"><font size="1" color="green">p. 210</font></A> <a name="page_211"><font size="1" color="green">p. 211</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1202"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1206">205:1</A> <a name="page_207"><font size="1" color="green">p. 207</font></A> For Kasuga see Sect. LVIII, Note 7. Izakaha is a place in Yamato. The signification of the name is uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1203"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1207">205:2</A> <i>Takanu-hime</i>. Takanu is the name of a district in Tango, and signifies "bamboo moor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1204"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1208">205:3</A> The signification of this name is quite obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1205"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1209">205:4</A> <i>Taniha no oho-agata-nushi</i>. <i>Taniha</i> (modern <i>Tamba</i>) is the name of a province (formerly including the province of Tango) in Central Japan. It is supposed to mean "the place of rice-fields," the rice offered at the shrine of the Sun-Goddess in Ise being brought thence.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1206"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1210">205:5</A> <a name="page_208"><font size="1" color="green">p. 208</font></A> <i>Hiko</i> signifies "prince." The other syllables of tie name are obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1207"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1211">205:6</A> See Sect. LXI, Note 8.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1208"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1212">205:7</A> <i>Biko</i> (<i>hiko</i>) signifies "prince." The other elements of this compound are obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1209"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1213">205:8</A> One is tempted to render this name by Princess of Mima. But there is no authority for regarding Mima either in this or in the preceding personal name as originally the name of a place.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1210"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1214">205:9</A> Motowori has no explanation to offer of the syllables Oke-tsu. <i>Hime</i> means "princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1211"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1215">205:10</A> <i>Hiko</i> means "prince "and <i>kuni</i> means "country.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1212"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1216">205:11</A> <i>Wani no omi</i>. <i>Wani</i> is a place in Yamato, and there is a pass or hill of that name (<i>Wani-zaka</i>). The only signification belonging to the word wani is "crocodile."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1213"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1217">205:12</A> <i>Hiko-imasu no miko</i>. Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1214"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1218">205:13</A> Or "the Princess of Washi "or "the Eagle Princess." In Japanese <i>Washihime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1215"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1219">205:14</A> <i>Kadzuraki</i> is the name of a district in Yamato, and Motowori believes Tarumi to be the name of a place in Settsu.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1216"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1220">205:15</A> <i>Take-toyo-hadzura-wake no miko</i>. The first two elements of the compound signify respectively "brave "and "luxuriant" while the last probably means "lord." The signification of <i>hadzura</i> is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1217"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1221">205:16</A> <i>Oho-tsutsuki-tari-ne no miko</i>. Tsutsuki being the name of a district in Yamashiro, the whole compound signifies "prince great sufficing lord of great Tsutsuki."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1218"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1222">205:17</A> <i>Sanugi-tari-ne no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "prince sufficing lord of Sanugi," (Sanuki,&#8212;see Sect. V, Note 6).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1219"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1223">205:18</A> <i>Yamashiro no Yena tsu Hime</i>. Yamashiro is the name of a province, and Yena that of a place in Settsu. The signification of the latter name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1220"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1224">205:19</A> Motowori believes <i>Karibata</i> to be the name of a place, and <i>tobe</i> (<i>to-me</i>) to signify "old woman," as in the name <i>Ishi-ko-ri-do-me</i>, which latter is however extremely obscure (see Sect. XVI, Note 12).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1221"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1225">205:20</A> <i>Oho-mata no miko</i>. The signification of this name and of the parallel name of the younger brother is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1222"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1226">205:21</A> <i>Wo-mata no miko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1223"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1227">205:22</A> <i>Shibumi no Sukune no miko</i>. Shibumi is probably the name of a place, there being a Shibumi in Ise.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1224"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1228">205:23</A> <i>Saho</i> is the name of a well-known place in Yamato, and <i>Kurami</i> <a name="page_209"><font size="1" color="green">p. 209</font></A> is supposed by Motowori to be the name of a place in Wakasa. <i>Oho</i> means "great," and <i>tome</i>, according to Motowori, means "old woman" or simply "female." <i>Conf</i>. Note 19.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1225"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1229">205:24</A> <i>Kasuga no Take-kuni-katsu-tome</i>. Motowori supposes this to be the name, not of the father, but the mother of the princess just mentioned. <i>Take</i> signifies "brave," and <i>kuni</i> "land." The meaning of <i>katsu</i> is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1226"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1230">205:25</A> <i>Saho-biko no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "Prince of Saho."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1227"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1231">205:26</A> <i>W&#333;-zaho no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "little (<i>q.d.</i> 'younger') prince of Saho."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1228"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1232">205:27</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the princess of Saho.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1229"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1233">205:28</A> It is uncertain whether we should understand this name to signify "princess Sahaji" or "the princess of Sahaji," but the latter seems the more probable.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1230"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1234">206:29</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Emperor Sui-nin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1231"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1235">206:30</A> <i>More-biko no miko</i>. <i>Muro-biko</i> signifies "Prince of Muro." Muro being a place in Yamato. It signifies "dwelling "and specially "cave."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1232"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1236">206:31</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "flourishing and good princess of Okinaga," the latter being the name of a place in Afumi (Omi). Its signification is not clear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1233"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1237">206:32</A> <i>Ame no Mikaga no kami</i>. The signification of Mikaga is obscure, as is also the connection between this deity and the deacons of Mikami.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1234"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1238">206:33</A> The signification of the name Mikami is obscure. The word rendered "deacon" is <i>hufuri</i>, the name of an inferior class of Shinto priests. See for a discussion of the etymology of the word, etc., Mr. Satow's remarks on p. 112 of Vol. VII of these Transactions. For Chika-tsu-Afumi see Sect. XXIX, Note 20.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1235"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1239">206:34</A> <i>Tanika no hiko Tatatsu-michi-no-ushi no miko</i>. The signification of <i>Tatatsu</i> is obscure, but we may accept it as the personal name of the worthy here mentioned. <i>Michi-no-ushi</i> means "master of the road," <i>i.e.</i> "lord of the province."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1236"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1240">206:35</A> <i>Midzuho no ma-waka no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "the True Young King of Midzuho," Midzuho being the name of a place in Afumi. It probably means "fresh young rice-ears."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1237"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1241">206:36</A> <i>Kamu-oho-ne no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, probably, "prince divine great lord."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1238"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1242">206:37</A> <i>Yatsuri-iri-biko no miko</i>. Yatsuri is the name of a village in Yamato, and is of uncertain origin. The signification of <i>iri</i> obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1239"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1243">206:38</A> <i>I-ho</i> signifies "five hundred "and <i>yori</i> probably signifies "good." The compound may therefore be taken to mean "manifoldly excellent princess of Midzuho."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1240"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1244">206:39</A> <a name="page_210"><font size="1" color="green">p. 210</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, probably "the Princess Miwi" (Miwi-dera in Afumi). <i>Mi-wi</i> signifies "three wells."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1241"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1245">206:40</A> This name is parallel to that which has been commented on in Note 9 to this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1242"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1246">206:41</A> <i>Yamashiro-no-oho-Tsutsuki no ma-waka no miko</i>. All the elements of this compound have already appeared in this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1243"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1247">206:42</A> <i>Hiko-osu no miko</i>. The signification of osu is obscure,</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1244"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1248">206:43</A> <i>Iri-ne no miko</i>. Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1245"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1249">206:44</A> <i>Ake-tatsu no miko</i>. See Sect. LXXII, Note 20.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1246"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1250">206:45</A> <i>Unakami no miko</i>. See Sect. LXXII, Note 19.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1247"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1251">206:46</A> <i>Ise no Homuji-be no kimi</i>. See the mention of the establishment of this Clan at the end of Sect. LXXII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1248"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1252">206:47</A> <i>Ise no Sana no miyatsuko</i>. The etymology of Sana is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1249"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1253">206:48</A> <i>Himeda no kimi</i>. Himeda is a place in Afumi. The signification of the name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1250"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1254">206:49</A> <i>Tagima no Magari no kimi</i>. Tagima is the name of a district in Yamato, and is of uncertain origin. Magari is the name of a place, and means "crook "or "bend."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1251"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1255">206:50</A> <i>Sasa no kimi</i>: Sasa is the name of a place in Iga, and is of uncertain signification.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1252"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1256">206:51</A> <i>Kusakabe no murazhi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1253"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1257">206:52</A> <i>Kahi no kuni no miyatsuko</i>. For Kahi see Sect. LXXXVI, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1254"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1258">206:53</A> <i>Kadzunu no wake</i>. Kadzunu is the name of a district in Yamashiro, and signifies "pueraria moor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1255"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1259">206:54</A> <i>Chika-tsu-Afumi no Kanu no wake</i>. Kanu is a village in Afumi. The name is written with characters signifying "mosquito moor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1256"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1260">206:55</A> <i>Wakasa no Mimi no wake</i>. Mimi is the name of a village, and is of uncertain signification.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1257"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1261">206:56</A> <i>Taniha no Kahakami no Masu no iratsume</i>. Masu is of uncertain. derivation. Kahakami is the name of a village, now comprised in the province of Tango. It signifies "river-land."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1258"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1262">206:57</A> <i>Hibasu-hime</i>. The signification of this name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1259"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1263">206:58</A> <i>Matonu-hime</i>. The signification of this name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1260"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1264">206:59</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the younger princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1261"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1265">206:60</A> This name, which is written <A NAME="img_21000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21000.jpg">, is curious, and Motowori has no suggestion to make touching its interpretation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1262"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1266">206:61</A> <i>Mikaha no Ho no wake</i>. Ho is the name of a district, and is of obscure derivation. Mikaha is the name of a maritime province. It <a name="page_211"><font size="1" color="green">p. 211</font></A> signifies "three rivers," with reference to two large rivers which flow through it and to another which forms the boundary between it and the province of Wohari.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1263"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1267">207:62</A> <i>Chika-tsu-Afumi no Yasu no atahe</i>. Yasu is the name of a district, and is of uncertain origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1264"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1268">207:63</A> <i>Minu no kuni no</i> [<i>miyatsuko</i>]. The word <i>miyatsuko</i>, which is not in the text, is supplied in Motowori's <i>kana</i> reading.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1265"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1269">207:64</A> <i>Motosu no kuni no miyatsuko</i>. Motosu is the name of a district in Mino, and seems to signify "original dwelling-place."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1266"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1270">207:65</A> <i>Nagahata-be no murazhi</i>. Nagahata is the name of a place in Hitachi, and seems to signify "long loom."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1267"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1271">207:66</A> <i>Mone no Ajisaha-bime</i>. This name is particularly obscure, and Mone probably corrupt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1268"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1272">207:67</A> <i>Kani-me-ikadzuchi no miko</i>. Motowori thinks that this name signifies "fierce like a crab's eye," with reference perhaps to some personal peculiarity of the prince who bore it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1269"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1273">207:68</A> <i>Takaki-hime</i>. This name is obscure and perhaps corrupt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1270"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1274">207:69</A> <i>Taniha no Tohotsu omi</i>. This name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1271"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1275">207:70</A> <i>Okinaga no sukune no miko</i>. For Okinaga see Note 31 to this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1272"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1276">207:71</A> <i>Kadzuraki no Takanuka-hime</i>. Takanuka is the name of a place in Yamato. It is written with characters. signifying "high brow."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1273"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1277">207:72</A> <i>Okinaga-tarashi-hime</i>. Okinaga is the name of a place (see Note 31). <i>Tarashi</i> is an honorific designation, signifying literally "sufficient," <i>i.e.</i>, "perfect," and is supposed by Motowori to have been bestowed after death on this princess, who was. the celebrated conqueror of Korea, and is better known to fame by her "canonical name" of Jing&#333; K&#333;g&#333;.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1274"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1278">207:73</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the princess of the sky."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1275"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1279">207:74</A> <i>Okinaga-hiko no miko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1276"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1280">207:75</A> <i>Kibi no Homuji no kimi</i>. Homuji is the name of a district in the modern province of Bingo, and may perhaps be of Chinese origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1277"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1281">207:76</A> <i>Harima no Aso no kimi</i>. Aso is the name of a place, and is of uncertain origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1278"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1282">207:77</A> <i>Kahamata no Ina-yori-bime</i>. Kahamata ("river-fork") is the name of a place in Kohachi. <i>Ina</i> signifies "rice," and <i>yori</i> probably signifies "good "in this and numerous other proper names.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1279"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1283">207:78</A> <i>Oho-tamu-saka no miko</i>. This name is obscure. Motowori thinks that <i>Tamu-saka</i> may be the name of a place, and signifying "winding ascent."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1280"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1284">207:79</A> <a name="page_212"><font size="1" color="green">p. 212</font></A> <i>Tajima no kuni no miyatsuko</i>. For <i>Tajima</i> see Sect. LXXIV, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1281"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1285">207:80</A> <i>Chi-mori no omi</i>. <i>Chi-mori</i> signifies "road-keeper," and perhaps we should translate this "gentile name," by "road-keeping grandees," and suppose that anciently they may have performed some functions in which the bestowal of it originated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1282"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1286">207:81</A> <i>Oshinumi-be no miyatsuko</i>. Oshinumi is the name of a district in Yamato, and is of uncertain import.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1283"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1287">207:82</A> <i>Mina-be no miyatsuko</i>. Perhaps we should rather translate thus, "the Rulers of Minabe," for the name is altogether obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1284"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1288">207:83</A> <i>Inaba no Oshinumi-be</i>. Motowori supposes a branch of this family, which was originally established in Yamato, to have removed to the province of Inaba.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1285"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1289">207:84</A> <i>Taniha no Takanu no wake</i>. Takanu is the name of a district in the modern province of Tango. It signifies "high moor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1286"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1290">207:85</A> <i>Yosami no obiko</i>. Yosami is the name of a place in Kahachi and is of uncertain origin, though the legends connect with the word and, "a net" (see Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXII, p. 81). It is chiefly known on account of its lake or pool, which is often mentioned in the early poetry. Abiko is a very rare "gentile name," which in the "Catalogue of Family Names "is written with the characters <A NAME="img_21200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21200.jpg">, but is derived by Motowori from <A NAME="img_21201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21201.jpg">, <i>i.e.</i>, "my grandchildren."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1287"></A><A HREF="kj069.htm#fr_1291">207:86</A> In Yamato. The name is of uncertain origin.</P>

<p><a name="page_212"><font size="1" color="green">p. 212</font></A> [173]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXIII.&#8212;EMPEROR S&#362;-JIN (PART I.&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Mima-ki-iri-biko-iniwe dwelt at the Palace of Midzu-gaki at Shiki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1292"></A><A HREF="#fn_1288"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded Tohotsu-no-ayu-me-me-kuhashi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1293"></A><A HREF="#fn_1289"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> daughter of Arakaha-to-be,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1294"></A><A HREF="#fn_1290"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Ruler of the land of Ki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1295"></A><A HREF="#fn_1291"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and begot august children: His Augustness Toyo-ki-iri-biko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1296"></A><A HREF="#fn_1292"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and next Her Augustness Toyo-suki-iri-bime&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1297"></A><A HREF="#fn_1293"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> (<small>two Deities</small>). Again, wedding the Great Princess of Ama,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1298"></A><A HREF="#fn_1294"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> ancestress of the Chiefs of Wohori,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1299"></A><A HREF="#fn_1295"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> he begot august children: His Augustness Oho-iri-ki;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1300"></A><A HREF="#fn_1296"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> next His Augustness</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_213"><font size="1" color="green">p. 213</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Ya-saka-no-iri-biko; next Her Augustness Nuna-ki-no-iri-bime; next Her Augustness Towochi-no-iri-bime&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1301"></A><A HREF="#fn_1297"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> (<small>four Deities</small>). Again, wedding Her Augustness Princess Mimatsu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1302"></A><A HREF="#fn_1298"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> daughter of His Augustness Oho-biko, he begot august children: His Augustness Ikume-iri-biko-isachi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1303"></A><A HREF="#fn_1299"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> next His Augustness Iza-no-ma-waka;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1304"></A><A HREF="#fn_1300"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> next Her Augustness Princess Kuni-kata;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1305"></A><A HREF="#fn_1301"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> next Her Augustness [159] Princess Chiji-tsuku-yamato;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1306"></A><A HREF="#fn_1302"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> next Her Augustness Princess Iga;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1307"></A><A HREF="#fn_1303"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> next His Augustness Yamato-Hiko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1308"></A><A HREF="#fn_1304"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> (<small>six Deities</small>). The august children of this Heavenly Sovereign [numbered] in all twelve Deities (<small>seven Kings and Queens</small>). So His Augustness Ikume-iri-biko-isachi [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire. The next, His Augustness Toyo-ki-iri-biko (<small>was the ancestor [of the Dukes] of Kami-tsu ke-nu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1309"></A><A HREF="#fn_1305"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> and the Dukes of Shimo-tsu-ke-nu)</small>.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1310"></A><A HREF="#fn_1306"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> The younger sister, Her Augustness Princess Toyo-Suki (<small>was high-priestess of&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1311"></A><A HREF="#fn_1307"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> the temple of the Great Deity of Ise.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1312"></A><A HREF="#fn_1308"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> The next brother, His Augustness Oho-iri-ki (<small>was ancestor of the Grandees of Noto</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1313"></A><A HREF="#fn_1309"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> The next, His Augustness Yamato-hiko,&#8212;(<small>in the time of this King a hedge of men was the first time set in the mausoleum</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1314"></A><A HREF="#fn_1310"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1288"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1292">212:1</A> <a name="page_213"><font size="1" color="green">p. 213</font></A> In Yamato. <i>Shiki</i> probably signifies "stone castle" (<i>ishi-ki</i>). <i>Midzugaki</i> signifies "fresh young hedge,"&#8212;an Honorific designation of the hedge round the Emperor's abode, which passed into a Proper Name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1289"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1293">212:2</A> According to Motowori's exegesis, this name is a rather remarkable instance of verbal usage, <i>ayu-me</i> ("trout-eyes") being not properly part of the name at all, but only a Pillow-Word for what follows, viz., <i>Me-kakushi-hime</i>, <i>i.e.</i> "Princess Beautiful Eyes." <i>Tohotsu</i> is the name of a place in the province of Ki, signifying "far harbour."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1290"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1294">212:3</A> <i>Arakaha</i> is the name of a place in Ki, and signifies "rough (<i>i.e.</i> impetuous and dangerous) river." The syllables <i>to-be</i> are of uncertain import.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1291"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1295">212:4</A> <i>Ki no kuni no miyatsuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1292"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1296">212:5</A> <i>Toyo</i> signifies "luxuriant" and <i>biko</i> (<i>hiko</i>) "prince." The other elements of the compound are obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1293"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1297">212:6</A> <a name="page_214"><font size="1" color="green">p. 214</font></A> <i>Bime</i> (<i>hime</i>) signifies "princess," and <i>suki</i> is identified by Motowori with Shiki, the name of the residence of the monarch whose daughter this princess was.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1294"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1298">212:7</A> <i>Oho-ama-hime</i>. Ama is the name of a district in Wohari, and probably signifies "fisherman."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1295"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1299">212:8</A> <i>Wohari no murazhi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1296"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1300">212:9</A> The signification of this and the two following names is uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1297"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1301">213:10</A> <i>Towochi</i> is the name of a district in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1298"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1302">213:11</A> <i>Mimatsu-hime</i>. Signification uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1299"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1303">213:12</A> Signification uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1300"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1304">213:13</A> The syllables <i>ma</i> and <i>waka</i>, literally "true and young" or "truly young "are honorific. <i>Iza</i> is of doubtful signification.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1301"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1305">213:14</A> <i>Kuni-kata-hime</i>. <i>Kuni</i> means "country," and <i>kata</i> here probably signifies "hard" or "firm."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1302"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1306">213:15</A> <i>Ohiji-tsuku-yamato-hime</i>. <i>Ohiji</i> probably means "a thousand," and <i>Yamato</i> is the name of a province. <i>Tsuku</i> is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1303"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1307">213:16</A> <i>Iga-hime</i>. <i>Iga</i> is the name of a district and of a province (see Sect. LVI, Note 9).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1304"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1308">213:17</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Yamato Prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1305"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1309">213:18</A> <i>Kami-tsu-ke-nu</i> [<i>no kimi</i>]. The character <A NAME="img_21400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21400.jpg"> (Dukes) is supplied by Motowori. This is the ancient form of the name now pronounced <i>K&#333;dzuke</i> (<i>conf</i>. <i>Shimo-tsu-ke-nu</i> corrupted to <i>Shimotsuke</i>). The author of the "Inquiry into the Meaning of the Names of All the Provinces" draws attention to the curious fact that, whereas the final syllable <i>nu</i> of the original word is dropped in speaking, it is the <i>ke</i> which is dropped in writing&#8212;the original form of the name, as written, being <A NAME="img_21401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21401.jpg">, whereas now only the first two of these three characters are used. Its signification is supposed to be "upper vegetation-moor," <i>ke</i> (<A NAME="img_21402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21402.jpg">) being regarded as the Archaic general term for trees and grasses, identical with <i>ke</i> that means "hairs," vegetation having struck the early speakers of the language as being similar to the hairs on the bodies of men and beasts.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1306"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1310">213:19</A> <i>Shimo-tsu-ke-nu no kimi</i>. <i>Shimo</i> means "lower." For the rest of the name see preceding Note. Both names are those of provinces in Eastern Japan.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1307"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1311">213:20</A> Or more literally, "worshipped and celebrated the festivals at," etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1308"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1312">213:21</A> <i>Viz</i>., of the Sun-Goddess (<i>Ama-terasu</i>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1309"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1313">213:22</A> <i>Noto no omi</i>. <i>Noto</i>, formerly a part of the province of Echizen, <a name="page_215"><font size="1" color="green">p. 215</font></A> is the name of the peninsula that juts out into the Sea of Japan on the western coast of the Main Island. The etymology of the name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1310"></A><A HREF="kj070.htm#fr_1314">213:23</A> The meaning of this imperfectly formed sentence is: On the occasion of "the interment of the next prince, His Augustness Yamato-hiko, the custom of setting a row of the deceased prince's retainers round his grave and burying them alive was first introduced." For a further notice of this custom see Sect. LXXV, Note 4. According to the "Chronicles," the "ancient" custom of burying retainers up to their necks in the neighbourhood of their lord's grave was abolished after this very same interment. Motowori endeavours to reconcile the two statements by supposing that the custom was really an old one, but that on the occasion here mentioned the number of victims was increased to an unprecedented degree, so that, as related in the "Chronicles," their cries, while their heads were being pulled to pieces by the crows and dogs, filled the Emperor with commiseration.</P>

<p><a name="page_215"><font size="1" color="green">p. 215</font></A> [175]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXIV.&#8212;EMPEROR S&#362;-JIN (PART II.&#8212;A PESTILENCE IS STAID BY OHO-TATA-NE-KO).]</h2>  
<p>In the reign of this Heavenly Sovereign a great pestilence arose, and the people died as if none were to be left.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1315"></A><A HREF="#fn_1311"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Then the Heavenly Sovereign grieved and lamented, and at night, while on his divine couch,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1316"></A><A HREF="#fn_1312"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> there appeared [to him] in an august dream the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1317"></A><A HREF="#fn_1313"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and said: "This is my august doing.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1318"></A><A HREF="#fn_1314"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So if thou wilt cause me to be worshipped&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1319"></A><A HREF="#fn_1315"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> by Oho-tata-ne-ko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1320"></A><A HREF="#fn_1316"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> the divine spirit shall not arise,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1321"></A><A HREF="#fn_1317"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and the land will be tranquillized." When, therefore, couriers&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1322"></A><A HREF="#fn_1318"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> were dispatched in every direction&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1323"></A><A HREF="#fn_1319"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> to search for the person [named] Oho-tata-ne-ko, he was discovered in the village of Minu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1324"></A><A HREF="#fn_1320"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> in Kafuchi, and was respectfully sent [to the Heavenly Sovereign].&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1325"></A><A HREF="#fn_1321"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> Then the Heavenly Sovereign deigned to ask: "Whose child art thou?" He replied, saying: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1326"></A><A HREF="#fn_1322"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> am Oho-tats-ne-ko, child of</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_216"><font size="1" color="green">p. 216</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> His Augustness Take-mika-dzu-chi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1327"></A><A HREF="#fn_1323"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> [who was] child of His Augustness Ihi-gata-sumi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1328"></A><A HREF="#fn_1324"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> [who was] child of His Augustness Kushi-mi-gata,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1329"></A><A HREF="#fn_1325"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> [who was] child of the Great Deity the Great-Master-of-Things by his wife Iku-tama-yori-bime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1330"></A><A HREF="#fn_1326"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> daughter of His Augustness Suwe-tsu-mimi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1331"></A><A HREF="#fn_1327"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> Hereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, being greatly rejoiced, commanded that the Empire should be tranquil, and the people flourish, and forthwith made His Augustness Oho-tata-ne-ko high priest&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1332"></A><A HREF="#fn_1328"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> to worship&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1333"></A><A HREF="#fn_1329"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> the Great Deity of Great Miwa&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1334"></A><A HREF="#fn_1330"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> on Mount Mimoro.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1335"></A><A HREF="#fn_1331"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> Again he ordered His Augustness Igaka-shiko-wo&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1336"></A><A HREF="#fn_1332"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> to make eighty heavenly platters, and reverently to establish the shrines of the Earthly Deities;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1337"></A><A HREF="#fn_1333"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> likewise to worship with a red-coloured shield and spear the Deity of Sumi-saka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1338"></A><A HREF="#fn_1334"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> at Uda, and with a black-coloured shield and spear the Deity of Oho-sake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1339"></A><A HREF="#fn_1335"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> likewise to present august offerings of cloth to all the Deities of the august declivities of the hills and to all the Deities of the reaches of the rivers, without neglecting any.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1340"></A><A HREF="#fn_1336"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A>&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1341"></A><A HREF="#fn_1337"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> In consequence of this the pestilential vapour ceased altogether, and the country was tranquillized.</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1311"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1315">215:1</A> <a name="page_216"><font size="1" color="green">p. 216</font></A> Literally, "about to be exhausted."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1312"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1316">215:2</A> This expression, which recurs at the commencement of Sect. CXLV, is difficult to explain. See Motowori's remarks in Vol. XXIII, pp. 24-25, and again in Vol. XL, pp. 14-15, of his Commentary.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1313"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1317">215:3</A> See Sect. LI, Note 12.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1314"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1318">215:4</A> Literally, "my august heart."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1315"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1319">215:5</A> Or, "cause my shrine to be worshipped at." The import of the god's words is that he wishes Oho-tata-ne-ko to be appointed chief priest of his temple. For the origin of this latter see the second half of Sect. XXXII (pp. <A HREF="kj034.htm#page_103">103</A>-105).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1316"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1320">215:6</A> Oho signifies "great," <i>Tata</i> (or <i>Tada</i>) is taken to be the name of a place, and the syllables <i>ne</i> and <i>ko</i> are regarded as Honorifics. The <a name="page_217"><font size="1" color="green">p. 217</font></A> whole name may therefore, though with some hesitation, be interpreted to mean "the Lord of the Great [Shrine of] Tata."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1317"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1321">215:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the divine anger shall no longer be kindled."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1318"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1322">215:8</A> Mounted couriers are almost certainly intended.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1319"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1323">215:9</A> Literally, "distributed to the four sides,"&#8212;"four sides" being a Chinese phrase for every direction.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1320"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1324">215:10</A> This name may signify either "three moors "or "august moor." The village of Minu must not be confounded with the province of Minu.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1321"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1325">215:11</A> The characters used are those which properly denote the presenting of tribute to the Monarch.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1322"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1326">215:12</A> Here and below the First Personal Pronoun is represented by the respectful character <A NAME="img_21700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21700.jpg">, "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1323"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1327">216:13</A> See Sect. VIII, Note 7, for the explanation of this name. But probably the deity here intended is another.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1324"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1328">216:14</A> The etymology and signification of 'this name are alike obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1325"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1329">216:15</A> Motowori interprets <i>kushi</i> in the sense of "wondrous," and <i>Migata</i> as the name of a place, which also occurs under the form of Higata.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1326"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1330">216:16</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "life-jewel-good-princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1327"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1331">216:17</A> The precise signification of this name is obscure. Motowori supposes <i>Suwe</i> to be the name of a place; <i>tsu</i> is the Genitive Particle, and <i>mimi</i> the Honorific of doubtful import, whose meaning has been discussed in Note 18 to Sect. XIII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1328"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1332">216:18</A> The exact meaning of the characters used to write the word <i>kayo-nushi</i> (modern <i>kamushi</i>), here rendered "high-priest," is "owner of the Deity." Though commonly used in modern parlance to denote any Shinto priest, it properly signifies only the chief priest in charge of a temple, whence the odd-sounding name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1329"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1333">216:19</A> Or, "conduct the worship at the shrine of."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1330"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1334">216:20</A> Viz., the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land. For the traditional etymology of Miwa see the legend in Sect. LXV.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1331"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1335">216:21</A> See Sect. XXVIII, Notes 4 and 5.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1332"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1336">216:22</A> Or, <i>Ikaga-shiko-wo</i>. The probable meaning of this name, pro-posed by Motowori, is (neglecting the initial letter <i>i</i> as expletive) "the refulgent ugly male."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1333"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1337">216:23</A> See Sect. I, Note 11 .</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1334"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1338">216:24</A> <i>Sumisaka</i> probably signifies "charcoal-hill." Uda, which has already been mentioned in Sect. XLVI, is in Yamato. This passage may equally well be rendered thus: "to present a red-coloured shield and <a name="page_218"><font size="1" color="green">p. 218</font></A> spear to the Deity of Sumisaka," and similarly in the following clause. The meaning comes nearly to the same.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1335"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1339">216:25</A> Literally, "great hill," or "great pass." It is at the boundary of the province of Yamato and Kahachi. Neither Motowori nor Tanigaha Shisei sanctions the view of the elder scholars, who fancied they saw in the distinction of red and black some mysterious import connected with the four cardinal points.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1336"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1340">216:26</A> In the Old Printed Edition the text of this passage differs slightly from that adopted by Motowori; but the meaning is exactly the same.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1337"></A><A HREF="kj071.htm#fr_1341">216:27</A> A large lacuna here occurs in the "Old Printed Edition," in which the four hundred and forty-five Chinese characters forming the original of the following part of the translation, from the words, "In consequence of this "down to the words immediately preceding "Methinks this is a sign" on p. 180 are missing. Both the editor of 1687 and Motowori are silent as to the manner in which they supplied the deficiency; but it may be presumed from their silence that the MS. authorities furnished them with what had accidentally been omitted from the printed text.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_218"><font size="1" color="green">p. 218</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXV.&#8212;EMPEROR S&#362;-JIN (PART III: STORY OF OHO-TATA-NE-KO'S BIRTH)]</h2>  
<p>The reason why this person called Oho-tata-ne-ko was known to be a Deity's child, was that the above-mentioned Iku-tama-yori-bime was regularly beautiful,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1342"></A><A HREF="#fn_1338"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> whereupon a [divine&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1343"></A><A HREF="#fn_1339"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A>] youth [who thought] the majesty of her appearance without comparison in the world,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1344"></A><A HREF="#fn_1340"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> came suddenly to her in the middle of the night, So, as they loved each other and lived in matrimony together, the maiden ere long was pregnant. Then the father and mother, astonished at their daughter being pregnant, asked her,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1345"></A><A HREF="#fn_1341"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> saying: "Thou art pregnant by thyself. How art thou with child without [having known] a man?" She replied, saying: I have naturally conceived through a beautiful young</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_219"><font size="1" color="green">p. 219</font></A></p>  
<p>man, whose name&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1346"></A><A HREF="#fn_1342"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> I know not, coming here every evening and staying with me." Therefore the father and mother, wishing to know the man, instructed their daughter, saying: "Sprinkle red earth in front of the couch,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1347"></A><A HREF="#fn_1343"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and pass a skein of hemp through a needle, and pierce [therewith] the skirt of his garment." So she did as they had instructed, and, on looking in the morning, the hemp that had been put in the needle went out through the hole of the door-hook,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1348"></A><A HREF="#fn_1344"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and all the hemp that remained was three twists&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1349"></A><A HREF="#fn_1345"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> only. Then forthwith, knowing how he had gone out by the hook-hole, they went on their quest following the thread, which, reaching Mount Miwa, stopped at the shrine of the Deity, So they knew [that Oho-tata-neko was] the child of the Deity [residing] there. So the place was called by the name of Miwa on account of the three twists of hemp that had remained. (<small>His Augustness Oho-tata-ne-ko, here referred to, was the ancestor of the Dukes of Miwa&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1350"></A><A HREF="#fn_1346"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and of the Dukes of Kamo.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1351"></A><A HREF="#fn_1347"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1338"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1342">218:1</A> It is not easy to render literally into English the force of the characters <A NAME="img_21900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21900.jpg">, containing this description of the maiden's beauty, and of <A NAME="img_21901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21901.jpg">, in the next clause. But it is hoped that at least the translation represents them better than do Motowori's readings <i>kaho yokariki</i> and <i>kaho sugata</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1339"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1343">218:2</A> This word, which is not in most texts, was supplied by the editor of 1687, and is adopted by Motowori on apparently satisfactory grounds.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1340"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1344">218:3</A> Literally, "in the time."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1341"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1345">218:4</A> The text places the word "daughter "here, instead of in the preceding clause. For the sake of clearness, the translator has taken the liberty of transposing it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1342"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1346">219:5</A> The Chinese characters are i, <i>i.e.</i>, "surname and personal (what we should call 'Christian') name." But Motowori's simple reading <A NAME="img_21902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/21902.jpg"> "name," approves itself as probably near to the author's intention.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1343"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1347">219:6</A> Motowori indulges in several conjectures as to the meaning of <a name="page_220"><font size="1" color="green">p. 220</font></A> this detail, which, it will be seen, is not referred to in the sequel, and is therefore pointless.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1344"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1348">219:7</A> The same Japanese word <i>kagi</i>, which is used as the equivalent of the Chinese character <A NAME="img_22000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22000.jpg">, "hook," came in latter times to denote a key.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1345"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1349">219:8</A> "Three threads "are in Japanese <i>mi wa</i>, whence the etymology of the name of Miwa given below in the text. The real derivation is altogether doubtful. The shrine of Miwa was in very early times regarded with such extraordinary reverence, that the term <i>Oho-gami</i>, "Great Deity," unless otherwise qualified, was commonly understood to refer to the god of Miwa.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1346"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1350">219:9</A> <i>Miwa no kimi</i>, written simply <A NAME="img_22001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22001.jpg"> (literally, "Divine Dukes,") another sign of the estimation in which the shrine of Miwa was held.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1347"></A><A HREF="kj072.htm#fr_1351">219:10</A> <i>Kama no kimi</i>.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_220"><font size="1" color="green">p. 220</font></A> [179]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXVI.&#8212;EMPEROR S&#362;-JIN (PART IV.&#8212;WAR WITH KING TAKE-HANI-YASU).]</h2>  
<p>Again in this august reign His Augustness Oho-biko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1352"></A><A HREF="#fn_1348"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> was sent to the circuit of Koshi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1353"></A><A HREF="#fn_1349"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and his son, His Augustness Take-nuna-kaha-wake,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1354"></A><A HREF="#fn_1350"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> was sent to the twelve circuits to the eastward to quiet the unsubmissive people. Again Hiko-imasu was sent to the land of Taniha&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1355"></A><A HREF="#fn_1351"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> to slay Kugamimi-no-mikasa&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1356"></A><A HREF="#fn_1352"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> (<small>this is the name of a person</small>). So when His Augustness Oho-biko was going away to the land of Koshi, a young girl wearing a loin-skirt&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1357"></A><A HREF="#fn_1353"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> stood on the Pass of Hera&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1358"></A><A HREF="#fn_1354"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> in Yamashiro, and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">[180] "Now then! Oh Prince Mima-ki-iri! Oh Prince Mi-ma-ki-iri! Ignorant that they, to steal and slay one's life, cross backwards and forwards by the back-door, cross backwards and forwards by the front door and spy,&#8212;Oh, Prince Mima-ki-iri!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1359"></A><A HREF="#fn_1355"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_221"><font size="1" color="green">p. 221</font></A></p>  
<p>Hereupon His Augustness Oho-kiko, thinking it strange, turned his horse back, and asked the young girl, saying: "These words that thou speakest, what are they?" The young girl replied, saying: "I said nothing; I was only singing a song,"&#8212;and thereupon she suddenly vanished, none could see whither. So his Augustness Oho-biko returned up again [to the capital] and made a report [of the matter] to the Heavenly Sovereign, who replied and charged him [saying]: "Methinks this is a sign that my half-brother, King Take-hani-yasu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1360"></A><A HREF="#fn_1356"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> who dwells in the land of Yamashiro, is planning some foul plot.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1361"></A><A HREF="#fn_1357"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> [Do thou,] uncle, raise an army, and go [after him]." When he forthwith sent him off, joining to him his Augustness Hiko-kuni-buku,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1362"></A><A HREF="#fn_1358"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> ancestor of the Grandees of Wani,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1363"></A><A HREF="#fn_1359"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> they set sacred jars on the Pass of Wani,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1364"></A><A HREF="#fn_1360"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> and went away. Thereupon, when they reached the River Wakara&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1365"></A><A HREF="#fn_1361"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> [181] in Yamashiro, King Take-hani-yasu, who had raised an army, was waiting to intercept [their passage], and [the two hosts] stood confronting and challenging each other with the river between them.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1366"></A><A HREF="#fn_1362"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> So the place was called by the name of Idomi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1367"></A><A HREF="#fn_1363"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A>&#8212;what is now called Idzumi. Then His Augustness Hiko-kuni-buku spoke, begging the other side&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1368"></A><A HREF="#fn_1364"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> to let fly the first arrow.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1369"></A><A HREF="#fn_1365"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> Then King Take-hani-yasu shot, but could not strike. Thereupon, on his Augustness Kuni-buku shooting an arrow, it forthwith struck King Take-hani-yasu dead. So the whole army was routed, and fled in confusion. Then the [Imperial troops pursued] after the fugitive army as far as the ferry of Kusuba, when harassed by the pursuit, exterunt [hostium] excrementa, quae bracis adhaeserunt. Quare isti loco impositum est nomen Kusobakama. In pr&#339;senti nominatur Kusu-ba.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1370"></A><A HREF="#fn_1366"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> Again, on</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_222"><font size="1" color="green">p. 222</font></A></p>  
<p>being intercepted in their flight and cut down, [their bodies] floated like cormorants in the river. So the river was called by the name of U-kaha.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1371"></A><A HREF="#fn_1367"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> Again, because the warriors were cut to pieces, the place was called by the name of Hafuri-sono.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1372"></A><A HREF="#fn_1368"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> Having thus finished [the work of] pacification, they went up [to the capital] to make their report [to the Heavenly Sovereign].</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_223"><font size="1" color="green">p. 223</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1348"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1352">220:1</A> <a name="page_222"><font size="1" color="green">p. 222</font></A> See Sect. LXI, Note 5.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1349"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1353">220:2</A> Literally, "to the Lord of Koshi," <i>i.e.</i>, "to the land of Koshi;" which provinces are intended by the "twelve circuits to the eastward "mentioned immediately below is uncertain; but Motowori hazards the guess that we should understand Ise (including Iga and Shima), Wohari, Mikaha, Tohotafumi (pron. T&#333;t&#333;mi), Suruga, Kahi, Idzu, Sagami Musashi, Fusa (the modern Kadzusa, Shimofusa, and Aha), Hitachi, and Michinoku (a vague name for the north-eastern portions of the Main Island of the whole east and north-east of the country. He likewise supposes the use of the word "road" for circuit or province to have had its origin in the "road" along which the Imperial officers despatched to the outlying provinces had to travel to reach their post, and remarks very pertinently in another passage of his commentary that the term "road "denotes a province more especially from the point of view of its subjugation or government. His explanation is, however, rendered untenable by the fact that the division of the country into such "roads" or "circuits" was an idea evidently borrowed from the neighbouring peninsula of Korea. At first, as in this passage, somewhat vaguely used in the sense of province," it settled down into the designation of "a set of adjacent provinces." Thus the T&#333;-kai-d&#333;, or "Eastern Maritime Circuit," includes fifteen provinces, the Hoku-roku-d&#333; or "Northern Land Circuit," includes seven provinces, and so on. Cont. Sect. LXII, Note 20.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1350"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1354">220:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "brave-lagoon-river-youth."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1351"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1355">220:4</A> See Sect. LXII, Note 4.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1352"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1356">220:5</A> Motowori is unable to help us to any understanding of this name.&#8212;or names,&#8212;for he suggests that the character <A NAME="img_22200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22200.jpg">, <i>no</i>, may be an error for <A NAME="img_22201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22201.jpg"> <i>mata</i> ("also"), and that two individuals may be intended. The note in the original telling us that "this is the name of a person" might equally well be translated in the Plural,&#8212;" these are the names of persons."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1353"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1357">220:6</A> <a name="page_223"><font size="1" color="green">p. 223</font></A> The nature of this garment is not known. One would suppose, from the way it is mentioned in the text, that there was perhaps some-thing contrary to custom in its use by a young girl. The parallel passage in the "Chronicles" does not mention it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1354"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1358">220:7</A> Or, "Hill of Hera, "&#8212;<i>Hera-zaka</i>. The "Chronicles" write this name with the characters <A NAME="img_22300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22300.jpg"> <i>Hira-zaka</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "Even Pass" or "Hill."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1355"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1359">220:8</A> The meaning of this poem, which must be considered as one pro-longed exclamation, is: "Oh my sovereign! Oh my sovereign! Heedless or ignorant of "the plots hatched against thy life near the very precincts of thy palace, thou "sendest away thy soldiers to fight in distant parts. Oh my sovereign!"&#8212;It will be remembered that Prince Mima-ki-ri was the (abbreviated) native name of the reigning monarch, commonly known to posterity by his "canonical name" of S&#363;jin. The word rendered "life" is literally "thread" and the Impersonal Pronoun "one's" used in the translation, must be understood to refer to the Emperor.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1356"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1360">221:9</A> See Sect. LXI, Notes 12 and 10.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1357"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1361">221:10</A> Literally, "foul heart."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1358"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1362">221:11</A> <i>I.e.</i>, probably. "prince land-pacifier." The first element of the compound is sometimes omitted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1359"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1363">221:12</A> <i>Wani no omi</i>. Wani ("crocodile") 13 the name of a place in the province of Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1360"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1364">221:13</A> <i>Wani-zaka</i>. For the setting of jars <i>conf</i>. Sect LX, Note 20.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1361"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1365">221:14</A> <i>Wakara gaha</i>. It is what is now called the Idzumi-gaha. Of Wakara we have nothing but an altogether untenable etymology given in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1362"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1366">221:15</A> More literally, "each having put the river in the middle, and mutually challenging."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1363"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1367">221:16</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "challenging." The more likely etymology of <i>Idzumi</i>, which is written with the character <A NAME="img_22301"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22301.jpg">, is "source "or "spring."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1364"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1368">221:17</A> The original has the very curious expressions <A NAME="img_22302"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22302.jpg">, literally," people of the side-building," which was a great crux to the early editors, Motowori is probably right in interpreting it in the sense of "the other side," <i>i.e.</i>, "the enemy."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1365"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1369">221:18</A> <A NAME="img_22303"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22303.jpg">; literally "the arrow to be shunned, or avoided,"&#8212;but rather, in accordance with Archaic Japanese parlance, "the sacred arrow." Motowori says: "At the commencement of a battle it was the custom for each side to let fly an "initial arrow." Being the commencement of <a name="page_224"><font size="1" color="green">p. 224</font></A> the affair, the arrow was considered "specially important and was shot off reverently with prayers to the Gods,&#8212;" whence its name."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1366"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1370">221:19</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "excrements [f&#339;dat&aelig;] brac&aelig;." But it is not at all probable that this is the correct etymology of the name. The stream is a small one in the eastern part of the province of Kahachi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1367"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1371">222:20</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "cormorant-river."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1368"></A><A HREF="kj073.htm#fr_1372">222:21</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the garden of cutting-to-pieces."</P>

<p><a name="page_224"><font size="1" color="green">p. 224</font></A> [182]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXVII.&#8212;EMPEROR S&#362;-JIN (PART V.&#8212;PEACE RESTORED AND TRIBUTE LEVIED).]</h2>  
<p>So His Augustness Oho-biko went away to Koshi in accordance with the previous [Imperial] commands. Then Take-nuna-kaha-wake, who had been sent round by the east, and his father Oho-biko met together in Ahidzu. So the place was called by the name of Ahidzu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1373"></A><A HREF="#fn_1369"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Wherefore, each of them, having settled the government of the land to which he had been sent, made his report [to the Heavenly Sovereign]. Then the Empire was at peace and the people prosperous. Thereupon tribute on the arrow-notches of the men and tribute on the finger-tips of the women was first levied.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1374"></A><A HREF="#fn_1370"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> So in praise of this august reign they said: "The Heavenly Sovereign Mimaki, who ruled the first land."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1375"></A><A HREF="#fn_1371"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Again, in this reign the Pool of Yosami&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1376"></A><A HREF="#fn_1372"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> was made; moreover the Pool of Sakawori at Karu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1377"></A><A HREF="#fn_1373"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> was made.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1369"></A><A HREF="kj074.htm#fr_1373">224:1</A> A district forming the southern part of the modern province of Ihashiro in north-eastern Japan. The derivation here given, from <i>ahi-dzu</i> "meeting port," seems fanciful.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1370"></A><A HREF="kj074.htm#fr_1374">224:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, taxes levied on the produce of the chase, by which the men gained their livelihood, and on the domestic handwork of the women.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1371"></A><A HREF="kj074.htm#fr_1375">224:3</A> <a name="page_225"><font size="1" color="green">p. 225</font></A> Motowori has a not particularly satisfactory note, in which he endeavours to explain this obscure phrase. The word "first" should evidently qualify the Verb "ruled," and not the Substantive "land," and the applicability of the saying to a sovereign, of whom it is not recorded that he initiated anything save the taxes, is not apparent. The author of the "Chronicles" observes the verisimilitudes better by applying a synonymous designation to the first "Earthly Emperor" Jim-mu.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1372"></A><A HREF="kj074.htm#fr_1376">224:4</A> See Sect. LXII, Note 85.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1373"></A><A HREF="kj074.htm#fr_1377">224:5</A> Reference to the parallel passage of the "Chronicles" shows that probably a couple of words are here omitted from the text, which should read "the Pool of Karu and the Pool of Sakawori" (<i>Karu no ike, Sakawori no ike</i>). Karu is the celebrated ancient capital mentioned in Sect. LVII, Note 1, Sakawori is quite unknown except from this notice of it, and the derivation of the name is uncertain.</P>

<p><a name="page_225"><font size="1" color="green">p. 225</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR S&#362;-JIN (PART VI.&#8212;HIS AGE AND PLACE OF BURIAL).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign's august years were one hundred and sixty-eight. His august mausoleum is on the mound at the corner of the Yamanobe road.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1378"></A><A HREF="#fn_1374"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1374"></A><A HREF="kj075.htm#fr_1378">225:1a</A> This place, where the Emperor Kei-ko is likewise said to have been interred, was in the province of Yamato, and the road mentioned is supposed by Motowori to have been the highway from Hatsuse into the province of Yamashiro. The word Yamanobe signifies "in the neighbourhood of the mountain" (<i>yama no he</i>).</P>

<p>[183]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXIX.&#8212;EMPEROR SUI-NIN (PART I.&#8212;GENEALOGIES)]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Ikume-iri-biko-isachi dwelt at the palace of Tama-kaki in Shiki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1379"></A><A HREF="#fn_1375"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded Her Augustness the</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_226"><font size="1" color="green">p. 226</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Princess Sahaji,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1380"></A><A HREF="#fn_1376"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> younger sister of His Augustness Saho-biko, and begot an august child: His Augustness Homo-tsu-wake&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1381"></A><A HREF="#fn_1377"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again, wedding Her Augustness the Princess Hibasu, daughter of King Tatsu-michi-no-ushi, Prince of Taniha, he begot august children: His Augustness Ini-shiki-no-iri-biko;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1382"></A><A HREF="#fn_1378"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> next His Augustness Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1383"></A><A HREF="#fn_1379"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next His Augustness Oho-naka-tsu-hiko;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1384"></A><A HREF="#fn_1380"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next His Augustness Yamato-hime;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1385"></A><A HREF="#fn_1381"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> next His Augustness Waka-ki-iri-biko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1386"></A><A HREF="#fn_1382"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> (<small>five Deities</small>). Again, wedding Her Augustness Nubata-no-iri-bika,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1387"></A><A HREF="#fn_1383"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> younger sister of Her Augustness Princess Hibasu, he begot august children: His Augustness Nu-tarashi-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1388"></A><A HREF="#fn_1384"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> next His Augustness Iga-tarashi-hiko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1389"></A><A HREF="#fn_1385"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> (<small>two Deities</small>). Again, wedding Her Augustness Azami-no-iri-bime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1390"></A><A HREF="#fn_1386"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> younger [184] sister of His Augustness Nubata-no-iri-bime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1391"></A><A HREF="#fn_1387"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> he begot august children: His Augustness Ikobaya-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1392"></A><A HREF="#fn_1388"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> next Her Augustness the Princess of Azami&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1393"></A><A HREF="#fn_1389"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> (two Deities). Again, wedding Her Augustness Kagu-ya-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1394"></A><A HREF="#fn_1390"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> daughter of King Oho-tsutsuki-tari-ne, he begot an august child: King Wozabe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1395"></A><A HREF="#fn_1391"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again, wedding Karibata-tobe daughter of Fuchi Ohokuni in Yamashiro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1396"></A><A HREF="#fn_1392"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> he begot august children: King Ochi-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1397"></A><A HREF="#fn_1393"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> next King Ika-tarashi-hiko;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1398"></A><A HREF="#fn_1394"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> next King Itoshi-wake.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1399"></A><A HREF="#fn_1395"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> Again, wedding Oto-karibata-tobe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1400"></A><A HREF="#fn_1396"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> daughter of Fuchi of Otokuni, he begot august children: King Iha-tsuku-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1401"></A><A HREF="#fn_1397"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> next Her Augustness Iha-tsuku-bime, another name for whom was Her Augustness Futaji-no-iri-bime&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1402"></A><A HREF="#fn_1398"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> (<small>two Deities</small>). The august children of this Heavenly Sovereign [numbered] altogether sixteen (thirteen Kings and three Queens). So His Augustness Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire. (<small>His august stature was ten feet&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1403"></A><A HREF="#fn_1399"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> [185] two inches: the length of his august shank was four feet one inch</small>),</p>

HREF="#fn_1400"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> again he made the pool of Sayama,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1405"></A><A HREF="#fn_1401"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> again he made the pool of Takatsu at Kusaka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1406"></A><A HREF="#fn_1402"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> Again he dwelt at the palace of Kahakami at Totori,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1407"></A><A HREF="#fn_1403"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> and caused a thousand cross-swords&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1408"></A><A HREF="#fn_1404"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> to be made, and presented them to the temple of the Deity of Iso-no-kami.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1409"></A><A HREF="#fn_1405"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> Forthwith he dwelt at that palace,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1410"></A><A HREF="#fn_1406"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A> and established the Kahakami Tribe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1411"></A><A HREF="#fn_1407"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> The next, His Augustness Oho-naka-tsu-hiko, (<small>was the ancestor of the Lords of Yamanobe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1412"></A><A HREF="#fn_1408"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> of the Saki. kusa,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1413"></A><A HREF="#fn_1409"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A> of the Lords of SIZE="1">39</FONT></A> of the Lords of Koromo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1418"></A><A HREF="#fn_1414"><FONT SIZE="1">40</FONT></A> of the Lords of Takasuka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1419"></A><A HREF="#fn_1415"><FONT HREF="#fn_1417"><FONT SIZE="1">43</FONT></A> The next, Her Augustness Yamato-hime, (<small>was the high-priestess of &nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1422"></A><A HREF="#fn_1418"><FONT SIZE="1">44</FONT></A> the temple of the Great Deity of Ise</small>). The next, King Ikobaya-wake (<small>was the ancestor of the Lords Anahobe at Saho</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1423"></A><A HREF="#fn_1419"><FONT SIZE="1">45</FONT></A> The next, Her Augustness the Princess of Azami (<small>was married to King Inase-biko</small>). The next, King Ochi-wake (was the ancestor of the Mountain Dukes of Wotsuki&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1424"></A><A HREF="#fn_1420"><FONT SIZE="1">46</FONT></A> and of the Duke of Koromo in Mikaha</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1425"></A><A HREF="#fn_1421"><FONT SIZE="1">47</FONT></A> The next, King Ika-tarashi-hiko (<small>was the ancestor of the Mountain Dukes Kasuga,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1426"></A><A HREF="#fn_1422"><FONT SIZE="1">48</FONT></A> of the Dukes of Ike in Koshi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1427"></A><A HREF="#fn_1423"><FONT SIZE="1">49</FONT></A> and of the Dukes of Kasugahe</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1428"></A><A HREF="#fn_1424"><FONT SIZE="1">50</FONT></A> The next, King Itoshi-wake (<small>owing to his having no children, made the Itoshi Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1429"></A><A HREF="#fn_1425"><FONT SIZE="1">51</FONT></A> his proxy</small>). The next, King Iha-tsuku-wake, (was the ancestor of the Dukes of Haguchi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1430"></A><A HREF="#fn_1426"><FONT SIZE="1">52</FONT></A> and of the Dukes of Miwo).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1431"></A><A HREF="#fn_1427"><FONT SIZE="1">53</FONT></A> The next, Her Augustness Futaji-no-Iri-hime (<small>became the empress of His Augustness Yamato-take</small>).</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1375"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1379">225:1b</A> <a name="page_227"><font size="1" color="green">p. 227</font></A> For Shiki see Sect. LXIII, Note 1. <i>Tama-kaki</i> signifies "jewel (<i>i.e.</i>, beautiful) hedge."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1376"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1380">226:2</A> This name and the next have already been met with in Sect. LXI, as have those of Princess Hibasu, King Tatasu-mechi, King Oho-tsutsuki-ne, Princess Kari-bata-tobe, and King Inase-biko.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1377"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1381">226:3</A> See Sect. LXXI, Note 8.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1378"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1382">226:4</A> The signification of this name is not clear, but Motowori identifies Shiki with the place of the same name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1379"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1383">226:5</A> <a name="page_228"><font size="1" color="green">p. 228</font></A> This name seems to be a string of Honorifics <A HREF="errata.htm#44">signifying</A> "great perfect prince ruling lord."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1380"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1384">226:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "great middle prince," he being third of five children.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1381"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1385">226:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Yamato princess." She is a very celebrated personage in Japanese legendary story,&#8212;high priestess of Ise and aunt of the hero Yamato-take. A miraculous tale is related of her birth, and she is supposed to have lived several hundreds of years.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1382"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1386">226:8</A> The signification of this name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1383"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1387">226:9</A> The signification of this name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1384"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1388">226:10</A> Motowori's conjectural interpretation of this name is "jewel-perfect-lord."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1385"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1389">226:11</A> The signification of <i>iga</i> is obscure. The other two elements of the compound signify "perfect prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1386"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1390">226:12</A> Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1387"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1391">226:13</A> Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1388"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1392">226:14</A> Signification obscure. The "Chronicles "read this name <i>Ike-baya</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1389"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1393">226:15</A> <i>Azami-tsu-him</i>e, Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1390"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1394">226:16</A> <i>i.e.</i>, probably "the refulgent princess," the syllable <i>ya</i> being void of signification as in <i>Ka-no-Nana-saku-ya-hime</i> (see Sect. XXXVII, Note 3). This name is celebrated as that of the heroine of the fairy-tale entitled "Tale of a Bamboo-Cutter." though there is no reason for identifying the two personages.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1391"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1395">226:17</A> This name is obscure, and Motowori suspects it of being corrupt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1392"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1396">226:18</A> <i>Yamashiro no ohokunino fuchi</i>. Yamashiro is the name of a province, and Ohokuni ("great land" that of a village, while Fuchi is a personal name written with a character signifying "deep pool."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1393"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1397">226:19</A> <i>Ochiwake no miko</i>. Motowori derives <i>ochi</i> from <i>oho</i>, "great, and <i>chi</i>, supposed to be an Honorific, while <i>wake</i> is taken to mean "lord." After all, the signification of the name remains obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1394"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1398">226:20</A> <i>Ika-tarashi-hiko no miko</i>. The name probably signifies "severe (or dignified) perfect prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1395"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1399">226:21</A> This name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1396"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1400">226:22</A> <i>I.e.</i>, Karibata-tobe, the younger sister.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1397"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1401">226:23</A> This name and the next are obscure. The first of the two is not in the older editions, but Motowori supplies what appears to be a lacuna in the text by adding the five characters <A NAME="img_22800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/22800.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1398"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1402">226:24</A> Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1399"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1403">226:25</A> The actual word "feet "is not in the original, but an equivalent Chinese measure is used.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1400"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1404">227:26</A> <a name="page_229"><font size="1" color="green">p. 229</font></A> <i>Chinu no ike</i>. The "Sea of Chinu" in the province of Idzumi, which is the same as the "Pool" here mentioned, has been mentioned in Sect. XLIV, Note 36.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1401"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1405">227:27</A> <i>Sayama no ike</i>, in the province of Kahachi. The name probably signifies a "gorge" or "defile."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1402"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1406">227:28</A> See above Sect. XLIV, Note 31.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1403"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1407">227:29</A> <i>Totori</i> (lit. "bird-catching") was in the province of Idzumi, and the name is said to have been derived from the place having been one of those through which Ohotaka of Yamanobe passed when pursuing the bird whose sight was to make Prince Homachi-wake obtain the power of speech. (See the story as given at the beginning of the next Section). The name of Kaha-kami ("head-waters of the river"), as we learn by comparison with the parallel <A HREF="errata.htm#45">passage</A> of the "Chronicles," is to be traced to the River Udo, near whose head waters the palace in question is said to have been situated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1404"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1408">227:30</A> See Sect. XLV, Note 5.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1405"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1409">227:31</A> See Sect. XLV, Note 16.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1406"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1410">227:32</A> Or, "in that temple."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1407"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1411">227:33</A> <i>Kahakami-be</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1408"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1412">227:34</A> <i>Yamanobe no wake</i>. Yamanobe (or Yamabe) is the name of a district in Yamato and signifies "mountain-slope."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1409"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1413">227:35</A> <i>Sakikusa no wake</i>. Of Sakikusa nothing is known. The word means "lily."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1410"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1414">227:36</A> <i>Inaki no wake</i>. Which Inaki is meant is not known, there being several places of that name in Japan. The name is connected with the word <i>ine</i>, "rice."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1411"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1415">227:37</A> <i>Ada no wake</i>. Of Ada nothing is known.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1412"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1416">227:38</A> <i>Wohari no kuni no Minu no wake</i>. Minu is the name of a village, and signifies "three moors."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1413"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1417">227:39</A> <i>Kibi no Ihanashi no wake</i>. Ihanashi is the name of a district, forming part of the modern province of Bizen, and seems to signify "rockless."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1414"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1418">227:40</A> <i>Koromo no wake</i>. Motowori supposes this name to be corrupt. Koromo is the name of a village in Mikaha.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1415"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1419">227:41</A><i> Takasuka no wake</i>. Nothing is known either of the place or of the family.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1416"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1420">227:42</A> <i>Asuka no kimi</i>. It is not known where was this Asuka, which must not be confounded with the famous Asuka mentioned in Sect. CXXXIII, Note 11.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1417"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1421">227:43</A> <a name="page_230"><font size="1" color="green">p. 230</font></A> <i>Mure no wake</i>. There are several places called Mure. The signification of the name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1418"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1422">227:44</A> Or more literally, "worshipped and celebrated the festivals at," etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1419"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1423">227:45</A> <i>Saho no Anahobe-wake</i>. The name Anahobe is derived from Anahobe, the name of the Emperor Yu-riyaku, and <i>be</i> "a tribe," it being related in the "Chronicles" that the tribe which was established as his "name-proxy" was so called.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1420"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1424">227:46</A> <i>Wotsuki no yama no kimi</i>. Wotsuki is the name of a place in Afumi (Omi). The family name must be interpreted to signify that they were wardens of the mountain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1421"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1425">227:47</A> <i>Mikaha no Koromo no kimi</i>. <i>Conf</i>. the name in Note 40, with which this is probably identical. Motowori suspects an error in the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1422"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1426">227:48</A> <i>Kazuga no yama no kimi</i>. <i>Conf</i>. the name in Note 46.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1423"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1427">227:49</A> <i>Koshi no ike no kimi</i>. Nothing is known of the place or of the family; Koshi may or may not be the northern province of that name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1424"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1428">227:50</A> <i>Kasugabe no kimi</i>. There were two places of the name of Kasugabe (<i>i.e.</i> "Kasuga Clan," so called perhaps after a family that had resided there). It is not known which is here alluded to.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1425"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1429">227:51</A> <i>Itoshi-be</i>. The name, which is thus restored by Motowori, is variously mutilated in the older editions. This is the first mention of adoption, lit. in Japanese "child-proxy making." The custom is perpetually referred to in the later portion of these "Records."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1426"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1430">227:52</A> <i>Haguhi no kimi</i>. Haguhi is the name of a district in Noto. The derivation is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1427"></A><A HREF="kj076.htm#fr_1431">227:53</A> <i>Miwo no kimi</i>. Miwo is the name of a place in Afumi. It probably means "three mountain-folds."</P>
<p><HR>
