<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_230"><font size="1" color="green">p. 230</font></A> [187]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXX. EMPEROR SUI-NIN (PART II. CONSPIRACY OF KING SAHO-BIKO AND THE EMPRESS SAHO-BIME).]</h2>  
<p>When this Heavenly Sovereign made Saho-bime his Empress, Her Augustness Saho-bime's elder brother, King Saho-biko, asked his younger sister, saying: "Which is dearer [to thee], thine elder brother or thy</p>  
<p><a name="page_231"><font size="1" color="green">p. 231</font></A></p>  
<p>husband?" She replied, saying "Mine elder brother is dearer." Then King Saho-biko conspired, saying: "If I be truly the dearer to thee, let me and thee rule the empire," and forthwith he made an eight times tempered stiletto,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1432"></A><A HREF="#fn_1428"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and handed it to his younger sister, saying: "Slay the Heavenly Sovereign in his sleep with this small knife." So the Heavenly Sovereign, not knowing of this conspiracy, was augustly sleeping, with the Empress&#8217; august knees as his pillow. Then the Empress tried to cut his august throat with the stiletto; but though she lifted it thrice, she could not cut the throat for an irrepressible feeling of sadness, and she wept tears, which fell overflowing&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1433"></A><A HREF="#fn_1429"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> onto [the Heavenly Sovereign's] august face. Straightway the Heavenly Sovereign started up, and asked the Empress, saying: "I have had a strange dream: A violent shower came from the direction of Saho and suddenly wetted my face; again a small damask-coloured snake coiled itself round my neck. Of what may such a dream be the omen?" Then the Empress, thinking it improper to dispute,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1434"></A><A HREF="#fn_1430"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> forthwith informed the Heavenly Sovereign, saying: "Mine elder brother King Saho-biko asked me,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1435"></A><A HREF="#fn_1431"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> saying: 'Which is dearer [to thee], thy husband or thine elder brother?' So, as I was embarrassed by [this] direct question, I replied, saying: 'Oh! mine elder brother is the dearer.' Then he charged&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1436"></A><A HREF="#fn_1432"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> me, saying: 'I and thou will together rule the [188] Empire; so the Heavenly Sovereign must be slain;'&#8212;and so saying, he made an eight times tempered stiletto, and handed it to me. Therefore I wanted to cut thine august throat; but though I thrice lifted [the weapon], a feeling of regret suddenly arose, so that I could not cut thy throat, and the tears that I wept fell and wetted</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_232"><font size="1" color="green">p. 232</font></A></p>  
<p>thine august face. [The dream] was surely the omen of this." Then the Heavenly Sovereign said: "How nearly have I been destroyed! "and forthwith he raised an army to smite King Saho-biko, whereupon the King made a rice-castle&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1437"></A><A HREF="#fn_1433"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> to await the fray. At this time Her Augustness Saho-bime, unable to forget her elder brother, fled out through the back-gate [of the palace], and came into the rice-castle.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1428"></A><A HREF="kj077.htm#fr_1432">231:1</A> For stiletto see above, Sect. XXXVI, Note 8. The curious word ya-shio-wori (<A NAME="img_23200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/23200.jpg">) in the text seems to have the sense of "eight times tempered," <i>i.e.</i>, tempered over and over again, which Motowori assigns to it. The same expression is used in Sect. XVIII (Note 16) to denote the refining of rice-liquor.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1429"></A><A HREF="kj077.htm#fr_1433">231:2</A> This word "overflowing" is more appropriately placed in the version of the story given in the "Chronicles," where the author makes her tears first fill her sleeve (a common Japanese figure of speech), and thence "overflow "on to the sleeping Monarch's face.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1430"></A><A HREF="kj077.htm#fr_1434">231:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, seeing that it would be vain in deny the truth.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1431"></A><A HREF="kj077.htm#fr_1435">231:4</A> The First Personal Pronoun is written with the self-depreciatory character <A NAME="img_23201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/23201.jpg">, "concubine."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1432"></A><A HREF="kj077.htm#fr_1436">231:5</A> Or "enticed."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1433"></A><A HREF="kj077.htm#fr_1437">232:6</A> This expression, which is repeated elsewhere, is one which has given rise to a considerable amount of discussion. The "Chronicles" tell us expressly that "rice [stalks] were piled up to make a castle,"&#8212;an assertion which, as Motowori remarks, is simply incredible. He therefore adopts Mabuchi's suggestion that a castle <i>like</i> a rice-castle is what is intended,&#8212;"rice-castle" being taken "to mean rice-store" or "granary," such granaries having probably been stoutly built in order to protect them from thieves. The historian of the Tang dynasty quoted in the "Exposition of the Foreign Notices of Japan" says that the Japanese had no castles, but only palisades of timber. The latter might well however have been called castles by the Japanese, though they <A HREF="errata.htm#46">would</A> not have been accounted such by the Chinese, who already built theirs of stone.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_233"><font size="1" color="green">p. 233</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXI.&#8212;EMPEROR SUI-NIN (PART III.&#8212;BIRTH OF PRINCE HOMU-CHI-WAKE AND DEATH OF THE CONSPIRATORS)]</h2>  
<p>At this time the Empress&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1438"></A><A HREF="#fn_1434"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> was pregnant. Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign could not restrain [his pity for] the Empress, who was pregnant and whom he had loved for now three years. So he turned his army aside, and did not hasten the attack. During this delay, the august child that she had conceived was born. So having put out the august child and set it outside the rice-castle. she caused [these words( to be said to the Heavenly Sovereign: "If this august child be considered to be [189] the Heavenly Sovereign's august child, let him&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1439"></A><A HREF="#fn_1435"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> deign to undertake it." Hereupon the Heavenly Sovereign said:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1440"></A><A HREF="#fn_1436"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> "Although detesting the elder brother, I yet cannot repress my love for the Empress," and forthwith planned to secure the Empress. Wherefore, choosing from among his warriors a band of the strongest and deftest, he charged [them, saying]: "When ye take the august child, likewise abduct the queen its mother. Whether by the hair or by the hands, or wherever ye may best lay hold of her, clutch her and drag her out." Then the Empress, knowing his intention beforehand, shaved off all her hair and covered her head with her hair, and likewise made her jewel-string rotten and wound it thrice round her arm, and moreover made her august garments rotten by means of rice-liquor and put on the garments as if they were whole. Having made these preparations, she took the august child in her arms and pushed it outside the castle. Then the strong men, taking the august child, forthwith clutched at the august parent. Then, on their clutching her august hair, the august hair</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_234"><font size="1" color="green">p. 234</font></A></p>  
<p>fell off of itself; on their clutching her august arms, the jewel-string likewise snapped; on their clutching her august garments, the august garments at once tore. Therefore they obtained the august child, but did not get the august parent. So the warriors came back [to the Sovereign], and reported, saying: "On account of her august hair falling off of itself, of her august garments easily tearing, and moreover of the jewel-string which was wound round her august hand at once snapping, we have not got the august parent; but we have obtained the august child." Then the Heavenly Sovereign, sorry and angry, hated the people who made the jewels, [190] and deprived them all of their lands.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1441"></A><A HREF="#fn_1437"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So the proverb says: "Landless jewels-makers."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1442"></A><A HREF="#fn_1438"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Again did the Heavenly Sovereign cause&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1443"></A><A HREF="#fn_1439"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> the Empress to be told, saying: "A child's name must be given by the mother; by what august name shall this child be called?" Then she replied, saying: "As he was born now at the time of the castle being burnt with fire and in the midst of the fire, it were proper to call him by the august name of Prince&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1444"></A><A HREF="#fn_1440"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Homu-chi-wake."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1445"></A><A HREF="#fn_1441"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> And again he caused her to be asked: "How shall he be reared?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1446"></A><A HREF="#fn_1442"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> She replied, saying: "He must be reared by taking an august mother&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1447"></A><A HREF="#fn_1443"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and fixing on old bathing-women and young bathing-women."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1448"></A><A HREF="#fn_1444"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> So he was respectfully reared in accordance with the Empress's instructions. Again he asked the Empress, saying: "Who shall loosen the fresh small pendant&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1449"></A><A HREF="#fn_1445"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> which thou elitist make fast?" She replied, [191] saying: "It were proper that Ye-hime and Oto-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1450"></A><A HREF="#fn_1446"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> daughters of King Tatasu-michi-no-ushi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1451"></A><A HREF="#fn_1447"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> prince of Taniha, should serve thee, for these two queens are of unsullied parentage."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1452"></A><A HREF="#fn_1448"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> So at last [the Heavenly Sovereign] slew King Saho-biko, and his younger sister followed him.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1453"></A><A HREF="#fn_1449"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_235"><font size="1" color="green">p. 235</font></A> <a name="page_236"><font size="1" color="green">p. 236</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1434"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1438">233:1</A> <a name="page_235"><font size="1" color="green">p. 235</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, Her Augustness Saho-bime, who was the subject of the preceding sentence.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1435"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1439">233:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Sovereign. The import of this passage is, according to Motowori, that the Empress imagined that her own conduct might perhaps influence the Emperor to refuse to give the child' she bore him its proper rank,&#8212;not from doubts as to its legitimacy, but as having a rebel mother. By "undertaking "the child is of course meant undertaking the care and education of it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1436"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1440">233:3</A> Motowori supposes the Chinese character rendered "said" to be an error, and prefers to consider this clause as containing not the words, but the thought of the Monarch. It would certainly be more convenient to adopt this view, if it were sanctioned by any text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1437"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1441">234:4</A> Or, as Motowori prefers to read, "deprived them of all their <A HREF="errata.htm#47">lands</A>."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1438"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1442">234:5</A> There is nowhere else any reference to this saying. Motowori supposes it to point to those who, hoping for reward, get punishment instead, these jewellers having doubtless rotted the, string on which the beads were strung by special desire of the Empress, whereas they ended by getting nothing but confiscation for their pains.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1439"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1443">234:6</A> Motowori (following Mabuchi) is evidently correct in supposing the character <A NAME="img_23500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/23500.jpg"> in this place, and again a little further on, to be a copyist's error for <A NAME="img_23501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/23501.jpg">, "caused," and the translator has rendered it accordingly,</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1440"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1444">234:7</A> "Prince "is here written <A NAME="img_23502"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/23502.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1441"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1445">234:8</A> This name may also be read <i>Ho-muchi-wake</i>, and is in the "Chronicles" given as <i>Ho-muchi-wake</i> while it appears as <i>Homuchi-wake</i> at the commencement of Sect. LXIX. The first two elements apparently signify "fire-possessing;" while <i>wake</i> is the frequently recurring Honorific signifying either "lord "or "young and flourishing."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1442"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1446">234:9</A> Lit., "his days be reverently prolonged." The same expression is repeated thrice below.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1443"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1447">234:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, foster-mother.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1444"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1448">234:11</A> The characters <A NAME="img_23503"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/23503.jpg"> used in the original of this passage would, if they stood alone, be of difficult interpretation. But a comparison with the passage in "One account" of "Chronicles," which relates the nursing of <A HREF="errata.htm#48">Fuki-ahezu-no-mikoto</A>, the father of the first "Earthly Emperor "Jim-mu, leaves no doubt that the author intended to speak of bathing-women attached to the service of the Imperial infant.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1445"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1449">234:12</A> The words <i>midzu no wo-himo</i>, literally rendered "fresh small pendant," call for some explanation. <i>Midzu</i>, which includes in a single <a name="page_236"><font size="1" color="green">p. 236</font></A> term the ideas of youth, freshness, and beauty, is here used as an Honorific. The "small pendant "is interpreted by Mabuchi and Motowori to signify the "inner, girdle" which held together the under-garment of either sex. The old literature of Japan teems with allusions to the custom of lovers or spouses making fast each other's inner girdle, which might not be untied till they met again, and the poets perpetually make a lover ask some such question as "When I am far from thee, who shall loosen my girdle?" The translator cannot refrain from here quoting, for the benefit of the lover of Japanese verse (though he will not attempt to translate them), the two most graceful of the many stanzas from the "Collection of a Myriad Leaves" brought together by Motowori to illustrate this passage:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">Wagimoko ga<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Yuhiteshi himo wo<br> Tokame ye mo:<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Toyeba tayu to mo<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Tada ni afu made ni,<br> Unabara wo<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Tohoku watarite<br> Toshi-fu to-mo<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Ko-ra ga musuberu<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Himo toku na yume.</div></p>  
<p>Tanigaha Shisei also appropriately quotes the following:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">Futari shite<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Musubiski himo wo<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Hitori shite<br> Ware ha toki-mizhi<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Tada ni afu made ha.</div></p>  
<p>a literal rendering of which would run thus: "I will not, till we meet face to face, loosen alone the girdle which we two tied together."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1446"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1450">234:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the "Elder Princess and the Younger Princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1447"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1451">234:14</A> Motowori is probably right in explaining <i>tatasu</i> as the Honorific Causative of <i>tatsu</i>, "to stand" and <i>michi no ushi</i> as <i>michi-nushi</i> or <i>kuni-nushi</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "owner of the province," "ruler."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1448"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1452">234:15</A> Lit., "are pure subjects."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1449"></A><A HREF="kj078.htm#fr_1453">234:16</A> <i>I.e.</i>, was slain with him.</P>

<p><a name="page_237"><font size="1" color="green">p. 237</font></A> [192]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXII.&#8212;EMPEROR SUI-NIN (PART IV.&#8212;THE DUMB PRINCE HOMU-CHI-WAKE).]</h2>  
<p>So the way they led about and amused the august child was by making a two-forked boat&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1454"></A><A HREF="#fn_1450"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> out of a two-forked cryptomeria from Ahidzu in Wohari,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1455"></A><A HREF="#fn_1451"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> bringing it up and floating it on the Pool of Ichishi and on the Pool of Karu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1456"></A><A HREF="#fn_1452"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in Yamato, [thus] leading about and amusing the august child. Nevertheless the august child spoke never a word, though his eight-grasp beard reached to the pit of his stomach.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1457"></A><A HREF="#fn_1453"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1458"></A><A HREF="#fn_1454"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> it was on hearing the cry of a high-flying swan&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1459"></A><A HREF="#fn_1455"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> that he made his first utterance.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1460"></A><A HREF="#fn_1456"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Then [the Heavenly Sovereign] sent Yamanobe-no-Ohotaka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1461"></A><A HREF="#fn_1457"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> (<small>this is a name of a person</small>) to catch the bird. So this person, pursuing the swan, arrived in the Land of Harima from the Land of Ki, and again in his pursuit crossed over to the Land of Inaba, then reaching the Land of Taniba and the Land of Tajima; [thence] pursuing round [193] to the eastward, he reached the Land of Afumi. and thereupon crossed over into the Land of Minu; and, passing along by the Land of Wohari, pursued it into the Land of Shinanu, and at length, reaching in his pursuit the Land of Koshi, spread a net in the Estuary of Wanami,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1462"></A><A HREF="#fn_1458"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and, having caught the bird, brought it up [to the capital] and presented it [to the Sovereign]. So that estuary is called the Estuary of Wanami. It had been thought that, on seeing the bird again, he would speak; but he did not speak, as had been thought.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1463"></A><A HREF="#fn_1459"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> Hereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, deigning to be grieved, augustly fell asleep, when, in an august dream, he was instructed, saying: "If thou wilt build my temple like unto thine august abode, the august child shall surely speak." When he had been thus instructed, [the Heavenly</p>

Then [it was discovered that] the curse was the august doing of the Great Deity of Idzumo.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1465"></A><A HREF="#fn_1461"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> So when about to send the august child to worship [at] that Great Deity's temple, [he made divination to discover&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1466"></A><A HREF="#fn_1462"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A>] by whom it were well to have him attended. Then the lot fell on King Ake-tatsu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1467"></A><A HREF="#fn_1463"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> So he [194] made King Ake-tatsu swear,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1468"></A><A HREF="#fn_1464"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> saying: "If there is truly to be an answer&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1469"></A><A HREF="#fn_1465"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> to our adoration of this Great Deity, may the heron dwelling on the tree by the Pool of Sagisu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1470"></A><A HREF="#fn_1466"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> here fall [through my] oath." When he thus spoke, the heron that had been sworn by fell to the ground dead. Again on his commanding it to come to life] in answer to his] oath, it then came to life again.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1471"></A><A HREF="#fn_1467"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> Moreover he caused to wither by an oath and again brought to life again by an oath a broad-foliaged bear-oak on Cape Amakashi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1472"></A><A HREF="#fn_1468"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> Then [the Heavenly Sovereign] granted to Prince Ake-tatsu the name of Prince Yamato-oyu-shiki-tomi-tomi-toyo-asakura-ake-tatsu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1473"></A><A HREF="#fn_1469"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> So when the august child was sent off with the two Princes, Prince Ake-tatsu and Prince Una-kami,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1474"></A><A HREF="#fn_1470"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> as his attendants, it was divined&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1475"></A><A HREF="#fn_1471"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> that [if they went out] by the Nara gate,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1476"></A><A HREF="#fn_1472"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> [195] they would meet a lame person and a blind person;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1477"></A><A HREF="#fn_1473"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> [if they went out] by the Ohosaka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1478"></A><A HREF="#fn_1474"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> gate, they would likewise meet a lame person and a blind person, and that only the Ki gate,&#8212;a side gate,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1479"></A><A HREF="#fn_1475"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A>&#8212;would be the lucky gate; and when they started off, they established the Homuji clan&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1480"></A><A HREF="#fn_1476"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> in every place they arrived at. So when they had reached Idzumo and had finished worshipping the Great Deity, and were returning up [to the capital], they made in the middle of the River Hi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1481"></A><A HREF="#fn_1477"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> a black plaited bridge and respectfully offered a temporary palace [for the august</p>

<p>child] to dwell in.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1482"></A><A HREF="#fn_1478"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> Then when the ancestor of the rulers of the Land of Idzumo, whose name was Kihisa-tsu-mi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1483"></A><A HREF="#fn_1479"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> [196] having made an imitation green-leafed mountain,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1484"></A><A HREF="#fn_1480"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> placed [it] in the lower reach of the river, and was about to present the great august food the august child&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1485"></A><A HREF="#fn_1481"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A> spoke, saying: "What here resembles a green-leafed mountain in the lower [reach of the] river; looks like a mountain, but is not a mountain. Is it perchance the great court&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1486"></A><A HREF="#fn_1482"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> of the deacons&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1487"></A><A HREF="#fn_1483"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> who holds in reverence the Great Deity Ugly-Male-of-the-Reed-Plains&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1488"></A><A HREF="#fn_1484"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A> that dwells in the temple of So at Ihakuma in Idzumo?&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1489"></A><A HREF="#fn_1485"><FONT SIZE="1">36</FONT></A> [Thus] he deigned to ask. Then the Kings, who had been sent in august attendance [on him], hearing with joy and seeing with delight,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1490"></A><A HREF="#fn_1486"><FONT SIZE="1">37</FONT></A> set the august child to dwell in the palace of Nagaho at Ajimasa,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1491"></A><A HREF="#fn_1487"><FONT SIZE="1">38</FONT></A> and despatched a courier [to inform the Heavenly Sovereign]. Then the august child wedded [197] Princess Hinaga&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1492"></A><A HREF="#fn_1488"><FONT SIZE="1">39</FONT></A> for one night. So, on looking privately at the beautiful maiden, [he found her] to be a serpent, at the sight of which he fled away alarmed. Then Princess Hinaga was vexed, and, illuminating the sea-plain,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1493"></A><A HREF="#fn_1489"><FONT SIZE="1">40</FONT></A> pursued after them in a ship; and they, more and more alarmed at the sight, pulled the august vessel across the mountain-folds,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1494"></A><A HREF="#fn_1490"><FONT SIZE="1">41</FONT></A> and went fleeing up [to the capital]. Thereupon they made a report, saying: "We have come up [to the capital] because thy great and august child has become able to speak through worship-ping the Great Deity." So the Heavenly Sovereign, delighted, forthwith sent King Unakami back to build the Deity's temple. Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, on account of this august child, established the Totori Clan, the Torikahi Clan, the Homuji Clan, the Ohoyuwe and the Wakayuwe.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1495"></A><A HREF="#fn_1491"><FONT SIZE="1">42</FONT></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1450"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1454">237:1</A> <a name="page_240"><font size="1" color="green">p. 240</font></A> From a comparison with a passage in the "Chronicles," where the same expression occurs, one is led to suppose that the craft here mentioned was a sort of double boat, in each half of which passengers could sit.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1451"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1455">237:2</A> Nothing is known of any place called Ahidzu in the province of Wohari.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1452"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1456">237:3</A> Karu has been mentioned in Sect. LVII, Note 1. The Pool of Ihare.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1453"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1457">237:4</A> Lit., "in front of his heart." This phrase descriptive of a long beard has already occurred at the commencement of Sect. XII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1454"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1458">237:5</A> Motowori reasonably supposes the character <A NAME="img_24000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24000.jpg"> in this sentence to be a copyist's error for the emphatic <A NAME="img_24001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24001.jpg">, and the translation has been made accordingly.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1455"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1459">237:6</A> The original has the character <A NAME="img_24002"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24002.jpg">, which is now applied to a small species of swan (<i>Cignus minor</i>, Pallas; <i>Cygnus Bewickii</i>, Yarrell). But it is uncertain what bird is intended by the author.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1456"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1460">237:7</A> A more or less inarticulate utterance is probably meant; but the expression in the original is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1457"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1461">237:8</A> Motowori supposes the Note in the original to refer only to the word Ohotaka, while he takes Yamamobe to be the name of a place (already mentioned in Sect. LXVIII, Note 1). The surname of Ohotaka, signifying "great hawk," was, according to the same commentator, giver to the worthy here mentioned in consequence of the incident related in the text. As the bird was not a hawk, this does not seem very convincing, and Motowori's apparent idea that the man was likened to a hawk because he pursued the other bird as a hawk would do, is extremely far-fetched. It is moreover doubtful whether the name should not be read <i>Oho-washi</i> (this is Mabuchi's reading), "great." The "Chronicles "give an altogether different name, viz., <i>Ame-no-yukata-tana</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1458"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1462">237:9</A> No such place is now known. The name may be interpreted to mean "snare-net "in allusion to this story, as stated in the next sentence of the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1459"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1463">237:10</A> The various texts and printed editions all differ slightly in their reading of this passage, and from some it might be gathered that the prince did indeed speak as it had been thought that he would do, u t could not speak freely. The translation follows Motowori's emended text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1460"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1464">238:11</A> Literally, "heart."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1461"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1465">238:12</A> <i>I.e.</i>, <i>Oho-kuni-nushi</i> (the Master of the Great Land), the aboriginal monarch of Idzumo, the descendant of the Sun Goddess, whose <a name="page_241"><font size="1" color="green">p. 241</font></A> abdication of the .sovereignty of Japan in favour of the descendant of the Sun Goddess forms the subject-matter of Sect. XXXII. The word <i>tatari</i>, here written with the Chinese character <A NAME="img_24100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24100.jpg"> and rendered "curse," signifies properly the vengeance of a spirit, <i>i.e.</i>, either of a deity or of the ghost of a dead man. The word translated "doing "is literally "heart."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1462"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1466">238:13</A> That some such words must be supplied is evident, and the translator has followed Mabuchi and Motowori in supplying them.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1463"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1467">238:14</A> Lit., "King Ake-tatsu at the divination."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1464"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1468">238:15</A> Remember that the original word <i>ukehi</i> combines the meanings of our words "wager," "oath," "pledge," "curse," etc.,&#8212;being in fact a general name for all words to which any mysterious importance attaches.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1465"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1469">238:16</A> Lit., a "sign," a "proof."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1466"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1470">238:17</A> <i>Sagisu no ike</i>, a pool in Yamato. <i>Sagi-su</i>, signifies "heron's nest."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1467"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1471">238:18</A> The reading of the characters <A NAME="img_24101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24101.jpg"> (rendered "then") in this passage has been a crux to all the editors. Fortunately they make no difference to the sense.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1468"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1472">238:19</A> <i>Amakashi no saki</i>, Perhaps "Amakashi Point "would be a better rendering if, as Motowori supposes, an inland place in the province of Yamato is meant. It might be the point or extremity of a hill or bluff. <i>Ame-kashi</i> signifies literally "sweet oak." The "broad-foliaged bear-oak" mentioned immediately above is supposed by Motowori to be the usual evergreen oak, and not any special kind. The epithet "broad-foliaged" is not, as he remarks, specially appropriate, and he moreover supposes the word <i>kuma</i>, "bear," to be a corruption of <i>kumi</i> or <i>kumori</i>, words which would refer to the thick luxuriance of the foliage. The dictionaries do not help us much to a decision on the point.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1469"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1473">238:20</A> The component parts of this tremendous name, which is happily abbreviated to Ake-tatsu in the subsequent portions of the text, are somewhat obscure, especially the word <i>oyu</i>, whose reading rests only on a conjecture of Motowori's, who emends the evidently erroneous character <A NAME="img_24102"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24102.jpg"> to <A NAME="img_24103"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24103.jpg"> (<i>oyu</i>,) "old." <i>Toyo</i>, "luxuriant," is an Honorific, <i>ake</i> and <i>tatsu</i> signify respectively "dawn" and "rise," while the rest seem to be names of places of which this Prince may be supposed to have been the possessor.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1470"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1474">238:21</A> Or, the Prince of Unakami, as Unakami is the name of a place Kadzusa.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1471"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1475">238:22</A> <i>I.e.</i>, shown by divination.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1472"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1476">238:23</A> <a name="page_242"><font size="1" color="green">p. 242</font></A> Nara in Yamato, which is here mentioned for the first time, was the capital, of Japan from A.D. 710 to 784, and has always been famous in Japanese history and literature. The name is derived by the author of the "Chronicles "from the verb <i>narasu</i>, "to cause to resound," the hosts of the Emperor Su-jin having, it is said, caused the earth to resound with their trampling when they went out to do battle with Haniyasu. A more probable derivation is from <i>nara</i>, the name of a kind of deciduous oak, the <i>Quercus glandulifera</i>. The word rendered "gate" should possibly be taken simply in the sense of "exit "or "approach.'</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1473"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1477">238:24</A> Or, "lame <A HREF="errata.htm#49">people</A> and blind people," a peculiarly unlucky omen for travellers, to whom, as Motowori remarks, sound feet and good eye-sight are indispensable to carry them on their way.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1474"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1478">238:25</A> See Sect. LXIV, Note 25.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1475"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1479">238:26</A> In the text the word "gate "is here, by a copyist's error written "moon." When the author says that the Ki gate, <i>i.e.</i>, gate or exit leading to the province of Ki, as a "side-gate," he means that it was; not the one by which travellers would naturally have left the town:&#8212;the province of Ki, indeed, is to the South of Yamato where the capital was, whereas the province of Idzumo, whither they were bound, was to the north-west. This road into Ki over Matsuchi-yama is one famous in the classical poetry of Japan.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1476"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1480">238:27</A> <i>Homuji-be</i>. The meaning of the clause is that they granted the surname of Homuji to persons in every important locality through which they passed on their journey.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1477"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1481">238:28</A> See Sect. XVIII, Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1478"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1482">239:29</A> The signification of this passage is: "They built as a temporary abode for the prince a house in the River Hi (whether with its foundations actually in the water or on an island is left undetermined), connecting it with the main land by a bridge made of branches of trees twisted together and with their bark left on them" (this is here the import of the word "black"). Such bridges have been met with by the translator in the remote northern province of Deha, where the country people call them <i>shiba-bashi</i> (or, rather, in their patois <i>suba-bashi</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "twig-bridge"). The traveller is so likely to fall through interstices into the stream below, that it is not to be wondered at that they should now be confined to the rudest localities.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1479"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1483">239:30</A> Motowori supposes <i>Kihisa</i> to be the name of a place, and <i>tsu-mi</i> to stand as usual for <i>tsu mochi</i>, "possessor," according to which view the name would mean "lord" or "possessor of Kihisa.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1480"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1484">239:31</A> <a name="page_243"><font size="1" color="green">p. 243</font></A> No book of reference with which the translator is acquainted throws any light on this curious expression, and there is no parallel passage in the "Chronicles" to look for help.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1481"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1485">239:32</A> Viz., to the Prince ("the august child"). The preparations which <i>Kihisa-tsu-mi</i> is here said to have made are supposed by Motowori to have been prompted by a desire to add beauty to the feast. But the whole passage is very obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1482"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1486">239:33</A> Viz., the court in front of, or the approach to, the shrine, which would naturally be planted with the sacred tree, the <i>saka-ki</i> (<i>Cleyera japonica</i>), and thus justly the prince's comparison to it of the artificial grove at which he was looking.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1483"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1487">239:34</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the priest attached to the worship of, etc. For "deacon" see Note 33 to Sect. LXII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1484"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1488">239:35</A> <i>Ashihara-shiko-wo</i>, one of the many names of the Deity <i>Oho-kuni-nushi</i> ("Master of the Great Land," see Sect. XX, Note 19). the Deity whom the Prince and his followers had just been worshipping.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1485"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1489">239:36</A> These names cannot now be identified, and are of uncertain etymology. Ikakuma seems, however, to mean "curve in the rock." One would have expected in this place, instead of these unknown names, to find a reference to the main temple of the Deity, which was styled <i>Kidzuki no oho-yashiro</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the great shrine of Kidzuki."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1486"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1490">239:37</A> Some such words as "the changed and more intelligent appearance of the Prince, and his attainment of the power of speech "must be mentally supplied in order to bring out the sense which the author intends to convey.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1487"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1491">239:38</A> These names cannot be identified. Nagaho signifies "long-rice-ear," while <i>ajimasa</i> in modern usage is the name of a palm (the <i>Levistona Sinensis</i>); but Motowori supposes that it formerly designated the palmetto or some cognate tree.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1488"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1492">239:39</A> <i>Hi-naga-hime</i>. The signification of the name is obscure, but it would seem most natural to suppose it connected with the River Hi which figures in the Idzumo cycle of legends. A proposal of Motowori's to read <i>Koye-naga</i> instead of the traditional <i>Hi-naga</i> seems scarcely to be meant in earnest. If accepted, it would give us the meaning of "fat and long princess," with reference to the story of her being a serpent.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1489"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1493">239:40</A> It will be remembered that the Province of Idzumo is a maritime one, and that the fugitives might be supposed to reach the sea-shore in their flight. It is true that this is exactly the reverse of the direction which they would be obliged to take in travelling up to the capital, which was in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1490"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1494">239:41</A> <i>I.e.</i>, <a name="page_244"><font size="1" color="green">p. 244</font></A> the depressions or valleys separating one mountain from another.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1491"></A><A HREF="kj079.htm#fr_1495">239:42</A> In the original <i>Totori-be</i>, <i>Torikahi-be</i>, <i>Homuji-be</i>, <i>Oho-yuwe</i> and <i>Waka-yuwe</i>. All these "gentile names" have a meaning connecting them either really or apparently with the story above related,&#8212;<i>to-tori</i> signifying "bird-catcher" and <i>tohi-kahi</i> "bird-feeder," while the name of the <i>Homuji</i> Clan is of course derived from that of the Prince (Homuchi or Homuji), and <i>Oho-yuwe</i> and <i>Waka-yuwe</i> signify respectively "elder bather "and "younger bather."</P>
<p><HR>
<CENTER>

<p><a name="page_244"><font size="1" color="green">p. 244</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXIII. EMPEROR SUI-NIN (PART. V.&#8212;HIS LATER WIVES.)]</h2>  
<p>Again, in accordance with the Emperor's words, he summoned Her Augustness Princess Hibasu, next Her Augustness Princess Oto, next Her Augustness Princess Utakori, next Her Augustness Princess Matonu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1496"></A><A HREF="#fn_1492"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> daughters of Prince Michi-no-ushi&#8212;four Deities in all. Now he [198] kept the two Deities Her Augustness Princess Hibasu and Her Augustness Princess Oto; but as for the two Deities the younger queens, he sent them back to their native place on account of their extreme hideousness. Thereupon Princess Matonu said with mortification: "When it is known in the neighbouring villages that, among sisters of the same family, we have been sent back on account of our ugliness, it will be extremely mortifying;" and, on reaching Sagaraka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1497"></A><A HREF="#fn_1493"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in the Land of Yamashiro, she tried to kill herself&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1498"></A><A HREF="#fn_1494"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> by hanging herself from a branch of a tree. So that place was called by the name of Sagariki. It is now called Sagaraka. Again, on reaching Otokuni,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1499"></A><A HREF="#fn_1495"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> she at last killed herself by jumping&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1500"></A><A HREF="#fn_1496"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> into a deep pool. So that place was called by the name of Ochikuni. It is now called Otokuni.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1492"></A><A HREF="kj080.htm#fr_1496">244:1</A> <a name="page_245"><font size="1" color="green">p. 245</font></A> <i>Hibasu-hime</i>, <i>Oto-hime</i>, <i>Utakori-hime</i> and <i>Matonu-hime</i>. The first two of these names have already appeared above, where the etymology of Hibasu was said to be doubtful, while <i>Oto</i> signifies "younger sister." <i>Matonu</i> has likewise already appeared, and is of uncertain derivation. Motowori supposes this last name to be in this place but an alias for <i>Utakori</i>, which he explains in the sense of "sad heart" with reference to the story of this princess as here told. In any case there is confusion in the legend, for in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles" five princesses are mentioned, whereas at the end of Sect. LXXI of these "Records" the Empress is made to speak of only two. The father's name has been already there explained.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1493"></A><A HREF="kj080.htm#fr_1497">244:2</A> The real derivation of this name is obscure. The ancient (perhaps here and elsewhere suppositious ancient) form <i>Sagari-ki</i> signifies "hanging-tree." Saga-raka is written <A NAME="img_24500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24500.jpg">, a good example of the free manner in which some Chinese characters were anciently used for phonetic purposes. <i>San-raku</i>, <i>Sa-raku</i> or <i>Sa-gara</i> would be the only readings possible in the modern tongue.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1494"></A><A HREF="kj080.htm#fr_1498">244:3</A> Literally, "wished to die." Motowori supposes that her design was frustrated by her attendants.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1495"></A><A HREF="kj080.htm#fr_1499">244:4</A> Written with characters signifying "younger country," but here supposed by the author to be derived from <i>ochi-kuni</i>, "falling country," in connection with this legend.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1496"></A><A HREF="kj080.htm#fr_1500">244:5</A> Lit. "died by falling."</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_245"><font size="1" color="green">p. 245</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXIV.&#8212;EMPEROR SUI-NIN (PART VI.&#8212;TAJI-MORI BRINGS BACK THE ORANGE FROM THE ETERNAL LAND.)]</h2>  
<p>Again the Heavenly Sovereign sent Tajima-mori,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1501"></A><A HREF="#fn_1497"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> ancestor of the Chiefs of Miyake,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1502"></A><A HREF="#fn_1498"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> to the Eternal Land&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1503"></A><A HREF="#fn_1499"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> to fetch the fruit of the everlasting&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1504"></A><A HREF="#fn_1500"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> fragrant tree. So Tajima-mori at last reached that country, plucked the fruit of the tree, and brought of clubmoss eight and of spears eight; but meanwhile the Heavenly Sovereign had died. Then Tajima-mori set apart of clubmoss four and</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_246"><font size="1" color="green">p. 246</font></A></p>  
<p>of spears four, which he presented to the Great Empress,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1505"></A><A HREF="#fn_1501"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and set up of clubmoss four and of spears four as an offering at the door of the Heavenly Sovereign's august mausoleum,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1506"></A><A HREF="#fn_1502"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and, raising on high the fruit of the tree, wailed and wept, saying: "Bringing the fruit of the ever-lasting fragrant tree from the Eternal Land, I have come to serve thee;" and at last he wailed and wept himself to death. This fruit of the everlasting fragrant tree is what is now called the orange.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1507"></A><A HREF="#fn_1503"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1497"></A><A HREF="kj081.htm#fr_1501">245:1</A> <a name="page_246"><font size="1" color="green">p. 246</font></A> The meaning of this name, which is written phonetically both here and in the "Chronicles," has, given rise to differences of opinion, some deriving it from the name of the province of Tajima (itself of obscure origin) and from the word <i>mori</i> "keeper," while others think it comes from <i>tachibana</i>, the Japanese word for orange, with reference to the story here told. The supporters of the former view, on the other hand, derive the <i>tachibana</i> from <i>Tajima-mori</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1498"></A><A HREF="kj081.htm#fr_1502">245:2</A> <i>Miyake no murazhi</i>. Whether <i>miyake</i> is simply the name of a place or whether it should be taken in the sense of "granary," is uncertain. If the latter view be adopted, it would be natural to suppose that this family had originally furnished the superintendents of the Imperial Granaries. In any case it traced its origin to a Korean source (see the "Catalogue of Family Names," and the genealogies in Sect. CXV).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1499"></A><A HREF="kj081.htm#fr_1503">245:3</A> See Sect. XXV.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1500"></A><A HREF="kj081.htm#fr_1504">245:4</A> Written in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles "with characters signifying literally "timeless." The whole of this circumlocution for the orange has indeed to be interpreted by the help of the "Chronicles." it being here written phonetically and offering some difficulties as it stands.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1501"></A><A HREF="kj081.htm#fr_1505">246:5</A> This corrupt and obscure passage seems to be well restored by Motowori, whose explanation of it is likewise as convincing as it is ingenious. The expression "clubmoss-oranges "signifies oranges as they grow on the branch surrounded by leaves, while "spear-oranges "are the same divested of leaves, and hanging to the bate twig. Thus the words clubmoss "and "spear "come to be used as "Auxiliary Numerals "for oranges plucked in these two different manners.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1502"></A><A HREF="kj081.htm#fr_1506">246:6</A> Viz., says Motowori, Princess Hibasu, who however, according to the account in the "Chronicles," was already dead at this time.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1503"></A><A HREF="kj081.htm#fr_1507">246:7</A> <a name="page_247"><font size="1" color="green">p. 247</font></A> The word <i>tachibana</i> (written <A NAME="img_24700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24700.jpg">) in the text should probably be taken as a specific and not as a general term. In modern usage it designates the <i>Citrus japonica</i>. But it is a matter of dispute whether the application of the term has not altered since ancient times, and whether we should not understand by it one of the other kinds of orange now to be found in Japan,&#8212;perhaps the <i>Citrus nobilis</i>.</P>

<p><a name="page_247"><font size="1" color="green">p. 247</font></A> [200]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXV.&#8212;EMPEROR SUI-NIN (PART VII.&#8212;HIS DEATH AND THAT OF THE EMPRESS HIBASU.)]</h2>  
<p>This Heavenly Sovereign's august years were one hundred and fifty-three. His august mausoleum is in the middle of the moor of Mitachi at Sugahara.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1508"></A><A HREF="#fn_1504"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Again in the time of the Great Empress Her Augustness Princess Hibasu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1509"></A><A HREF="#fn_1505"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> the Stone-Coffin-Makers&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1510"></A><A HREF="#fn_1506"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> were established, and also the Earthenware-Masters' Clan&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1511"></A><A HREF="#fn_1507"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> was established. This Empress was buried in the mausoleum of Terama near Saki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1512"></A><A HREF="#fn_1508"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1504"></A><A HREF="kj082.htm#fr_1508">247:1</A> Both the locality and the etymology of <i>Mitachi</i> are obscure. <i>Sugahara</i> ("sedge-moor") is known to be in the province of Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1505"></A><A HREF="kj082.htm#fr_1509">247:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, at the time of the burial of the great Empress, etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1506"></A><A HREF="kj082.htm#fr_1510">247:3</A> The character <A NAME="img_24701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24701.jpg">, ("to pray") in the text is indubitably a copyist's error for "<A NAME="img_24702"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/24702.jpg">, coffin." These stone coffins are described by Mr. Henry von Siebold in his "Note on Japanese Archaeology" p.5. It must be understood that, from being the name of an office, Stone-Coffin-Maker (<i>Ishi-ki-tsukuri</i>) became a "gentile name."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1507"></A><A HREF="kj082.htm#fr_1511">247:4</A> <i>Hanishi-be</i>. The meaning of this expression becomes clear by reference to the parallel passage of the "Chronicles," which it may be worth while to quote at length from Mr. Satow's translation in pp. 229-330 of Vol. VIII, Pt. III, of these Transactions: "In the autumn of 32nd year, on the <i>tsuchi no to u</i> day of the moon, which rose on the <i>ki no ye inu</i> day, the empress Hi ba su hime no Mikoto (in another source called Hi-ba-su ne no Mikoto) died, and they were several days going to bury her. The Mikado commanded all his high officers, saying: "We knew <a name="page_248"><font size="1" color="green">p. 248</font></A> before that the practice of following the dead is not good. In the case of the present burying what shall be done? Thereupon Nomi no Sukune advanced and said: "It is not good to bury living men standing at the sepulchre of a prince, and this cannot be handed down to posterity. I pray leave now to propose a convenient plan. and to lay this before the sovereign." And he sent messengers to summon up a hundred of the clay-workers' tribe of the country of Izumo, and he himself directed the men of the clay-workers' tribe in taking clay and forming shapes of men, horses and various things, and presented them to the Mikado, saying: 'From now and henceforward let it be the law for posterity to exchange things of clay for living men, and set them up at sepulchres.' Thereupon the Mikado rejoiced, and commanded Nomi no Sukune, saying: 'Thy expedient plan has truly pleased Our heart; and the things of clay were for the first time set up at the tomb of Hi-ba-su hime no Mikoto. Wherefore these things were <i>haniwa</i> (a circle of clay). Then he seat down an order, saying: 'From now and henceforward, be sure to sit up these things of clay at sepulchres, and let not men be slain.' Mikado bountifully praised Nomi no Sukune, bestowed on him a kneading-place, and appointed him to the charge of the clay-workers' tribe."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1508"></A><A HREF="kj082.htm#fr_1512">247:5</A> In the province of Yamato. In the old poetry there are many plays or, this word <i>Saki</i>, which is homonymous with the Verb "to blossom." But whether that be its real derivation, it were hard to say. <i>Terama</i> appears to signify "Buddhist temple-space," an etymology which is embarrassing to the Shinto commentators who, accepting every word of our text as authentic history, are hard-driven to explain how Buddhist temples could have existed in Japan before the date assigned for the introduction of Buddhism.</P>

===== kj083.html (via web.archive.org snapshot 20190320062420 of sacred-texts.com) =====
<HTML>
<HEAD>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="../../css/marg.css">
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">
<META name="keywords" content="Kojiki Japan Shinto Mythology Legend Folklore Text Scripture Emperor Empress Chronology">
<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume II: Section LXXVI.&#8212;Empress Kei-ko (Part I,&#8212;Genealogies)</TITLE>
</HEAD>

<p><a name="page_248"><font size="1" color="green">p. 248</font></A> [201]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXVI.&#8212;EMPRESS KEI-KO (PART I,&#8212;GENEALOGIES)]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake dwelt in the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1513"></A><A HREF="#fn_1509"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded the Elder Lady of Inabi in Harima,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1514"></A><A HREF="#fn_1510"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> daughter of Waka-take, Prince of Kibi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1515"></A><A HREF="#fn_1511"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> ancestor of the Grandees of Kibi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1516"></A><A HREF="#fn_1512"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and begot</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_249"><font size="1" color="green">p. 249</font></A></p>  
<p>august children: King Kushi-tsunu-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1517"></A><A HREF="#fn_1513"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next His Augustness Ohousu;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1518"></A><A HREF="#fn_1514"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next His Augustness Wo-usu, another name for whom is His Augustness Yamato wo-guna;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1519"></A><A HREF="#fn_1515"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> next His Augustness Yamato-ne-ko;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1520"></A><A HREF="#fn_1516"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> next King Kamu-kushi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1521"></A><A HREF="#fn_1517"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Again wedding Her Augustness Princess Yasaka-no-iri,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1522"></A><A HREF="#fn_1518"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> [202] daughter of His Augustness Prince Yasaka-no-iri, he begot august children: His Augustness Prince Waka-rarashi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1523"></A><A HREF="#fn_1519"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> next His Augustness Prince Iho-ki-no-iri;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1524"></A><A HREF="#fn_1520"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> next His Augustness Oshi-no-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1525"></A><A HREF="#fn_1521"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> next Her Augustness Princess Iho-ki-no-iri.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1526"></A><A HREF="#fn_1522"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> Children by another concubine were: King Toyo-to-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1527"></A><A HREF="#fn_1523"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> next the Lady Nunoshiro.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1528"></A><A HREF="#fn_1524"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> Children by another concubine were: the Lady Nunaki;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1529"></A><A HREF="#fn_1525"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> next Her Augustness Princess Kago-yori;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1530"></A><A HREF="#fn_1526"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> next King Prince Waka-ki-no-iri;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1531"></A><A HREF="#fn_1527"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> next King the Elder Prince of Kibi-no-ye;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1532"></A><A HREF="#fn_1528"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> next Her Augustness Princess Takaki;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1533"></A><A HREF="#fn_1529"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> next Her Augustness Princess Oto.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1534"></A><A HREF="#fn_1530"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> Again wedding Princess Mi-hakashi of Himuku,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1535"></A><A HREF="#fn_1531"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> he begot an august child: King Toyo-kuni-wake.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1536"></A><A HREF="#fn_1532"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> Again wedding the Younger Lady of Inabi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1537"></A><A HREF="#fn_1533"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> younger sister of the Elder Lady of Inabi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1538"></A><A HREF="#fn_1534"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> he begot august children: King Ma-waka; next King Hiko-hito-no-oho-ye.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1539"></A><A HREF="#fn_1535"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> Again wedding Princess [203] Ka-guro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1540"></A><A HREF="#fn_1536"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> daughter of King Princess Sume-iro-oho-naka-tsu-hiko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1541"></A><A HREF="#fn_1537"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> great-grand-child of His Augustness Yamato-take,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1542"></A><A HREF="#fn_1538"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> he begot an august child: King Oho-ye.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1543"></A><A HREF="#fn_1539"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> The august children of this Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko numbered in all twenty-one kings and queens&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1544"></A><A HREF="#fn_1540"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A> of whom there is a register, and fifty-nine kings and queens of whom there is no record,&#8212;eighty kings and queens altogether, out of whom His Augustness Waka-tarashi-hiko and also His Augustness Yamato-take, and also His Augustness Prince I-ho-ki-no-iri,&#8212;these three Kings,&#8212;bore the name of Heirs Apparent.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1545"></A><A HREF="#fn_1541"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> The seventy-seven</p>

<p><a name="page_250"><font size="1" color="green">p. 250</font></A></p>  
<p>kings and queens beside these&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1546"></A><A HREF="#fn_1542"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> were all granted Rulerships in the various lands, or else [posts as] Lords, Territorial Lords or Departmental Chiefs.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1547"></A><A HREF="#fn_1543"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A> So His Augustness Waka-tarashi-hiko [was he who afterward] ruled the Empire. His Augustness Wo-usu subdued the savage deities and likewise the unsubmissive people in the East [204] and West. The next, King Kushi-tsunu-wake (<small>was the ancestor of the chiefs of Mamuta</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1548"></A><A HREF="#fn_1544"><FONT SIZE="1">36</FONT></A> The next, His Augustness Oho-Usu, (<small>was the ancestor of the Dukes of Mori,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1549"></A><A HREF="#fn_1545"><FONT SIZE="1">37</FONT></A> of the Dukes of Ohota&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1550"></A><A HREF="#fn_1546"><FONT SIZE="1">38</FONT></A> and of the Dukes of Shimada.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1551"></A><A HREF="#fn_1547"><FONT SIZE="1">39</FONT></A> The next, King Kamukushi, (<small>was the ancestor of the Sakabe Abiko in the Land of Ki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1552"></A><A HREF="#fn_1548"><FONT SIZE="1">40</FONT></A> and of the Sakabe of Uda</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1553"></A><A HREF="#fn_1549"><FONT SIZE="1">41</FONT></A> The next, King Toyo-kuni-wake (<small>was the ancestor of the Rulers of the Land of Himuka.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1554"></A><A HREF="#fn_1550"><FONT SIZE="1">42</FONT></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1509"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1513">248:1</A> <a name="page_250"><font size="1" color="green">p. 250</font></A> In the province of Yamato. The etymology of <i>Makimuku</i> is obscure. <i>Hishiro</i> is tentatively derived by Motowori from <i>hi</i>, the <i>Chamaecyparis obtusa</i> (a kind of conifer), and <i>shiro</i>, "an enclosure."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1510"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1514">248:2</A> <i>Harima no inabi no oho-iratsume</i>. Inabi is also known under the alternative form of <i>Inami</i>: etymology uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1511"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1515">248:3</A> <i>Waka-take Kibi tsu biko</i>, <i>Waka-take</i> signifies "young brave."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1512"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1516">248:4</A> <i>Kibi no omi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1513"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1517">249:5</A> <i>Kushi</i> signifies "wondrous," and wake either "young," or "lord." The meaning of <i>tsunu</i> is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1514"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1518">249:6</A> The names of this prince and the next signify respectively "great-foot-pestle" and "little foot-pestle," the origin of the bestowal of which singular designations is thus related in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles:" "The Imperial child Oho-usu and His Augustness Wo-usu were born together the same day as twins. The Heavenly Sovereign, astonished, informed the foot-pestle. So the two Kings were called Great Foot-pestle and <A HREF="errata.htm#50">Little</A> Foot-pestle." What the import of this passage may be is, however, a mystery both to Tanigaha Shisei and to Motowori.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1515"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1519">249:7</A> Motowori supposes <i>wo-guna</i> to have been an archaic word for "boy," "me-guna" signifying "girl." <i>Yamato wo-guna</i> would thus signify <i>the</i> boy of Japan." a not inappropriate designation for this prince, who under his later name of Yamato-take (Japan Brave," <i>i.e.</i> <i>the</i> brave man of Japan") has remained as the chief legendary type of the martial prowess of his native land.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1516"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1520">249:8</A> <a name="page_251"><font size="1" color="green">p. 251</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>. Yamato Prince.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1517"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1521">249:9</A> <i>Komu-kushi no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "divine wondrous."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1518"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1522">249:10</A> <i>Yamasaka no iri-bime no mikoto</i>. The signification of this name and of the next (<i>Ya-saka no iri-biko no mikoto</i>) is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1519"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1523">249:11</A> <i>Waka-tarashi-hiko no mikoto</i>, i.e., "young and perfect prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1520"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1524">249:12</A> <i>I-ho-ki no iri-biko no mikoto</i>. Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1521"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1525">249:13</A> Or, <i>Oshi-wake</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, perhaps "Great Lord."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1522"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1526">249:14</A> <i>I-ho-ki no iri-bime no mikoto</i>. Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1523"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1527">249:15</A> <i>Toyo-to-wake no mikoto</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, perhaps "luxuriant swift prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1524"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1528">249:16</A> <i>Nunoshiro no iratsumo</i>. Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1525"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1529">249:17</A> <i>Nunaki no iratsume</i>. Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1526"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1530">249:18</A> <i>Kago yori-hime no mikoto</i>. <i>Yori ime</i> probably means "good princess." The sense of <i>kago</i> is very doubtful, for it may either be the name of a place, or else identical with the Verb <i>kagayaku</i> "to shine," or with <i>kago</i>, "a stag."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1527"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1531">249:19</A> <i>Waka-ki no iri-biko no mikoto</i>. The signification of this name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1528"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1532">249:20</A> <i>Kibi no ye-hike no mikoto</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1529"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1533">249:21</A> <i>Takaki-hime no mikoto</i>. The meaning of <i>takaki</i> in this place is not certain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1530"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1534">249:22</A> <i>Oto-hime no mikoto</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the younger princes."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1531"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1535">249:23</A> <i>Himuka no Mi-hakashi-bime</i>. <i>Mi-hakashi</i> signifies "august sabre." See Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXVI, p. 11, for a gloss on this curious name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1532"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1536">249:24</A> <i>Toyo-kuni-wake no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, perhaps "lord of the luxuriant land," or else "lord of the land of Toyo," the Emperor Kei-k&#333; having, according to the account in the "Chronicles," spent some years fighting in South-Western Japan, where the province of Toyo is situated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1533"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1537">249:25</A> <i>Inabi no waki-iratsume</i>. See Note 2 to this Section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1534"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1538">249:26</A> <i>Ma-waka no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "truly young prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1535"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1539">249:27</A> <i>Hiko-hito no oho-ye no miko</i>. <i>Hiko</i> signifies "prince," <i>hito</i> is "person" (or here, according to Motowori, "headman"), and <i>oho ye</i> is "great elder brother."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1536"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1540">249:28</A> <i>Ka-guro-hime</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, probably "the black-haired princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1537"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1541">249:29</A> <i>Sume-iro-oho-naka-tsu-biko-no-mikoto</i>. The signification of this name is not clear. Motowori identifies <i>sume</i> with the like-sounding Verb signifying "to be supreme." <i>Oha-naka-tsu-hiko</i> may signify "great middle prince," referring to the comparative ages of this prince and his brethren.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1538"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1542">249:30</A> <a name="page_252"><font size="1" color="green">p. 252</font></A> There is here an evident error in the genealogy, as it would make the emperor marry his own great-great-grand daughter! A guess of the editor of 1687 that for Yamato-take we should read Waka-take (a son of the Emperor K&#333;-rei) is approved by Motowori, and may be adopted as probably correct,&#8212;<i>i.e.</i> (what is but little likely) if this portion of the "Records" should eventually be proved to be historically trustworthy. The question is discussed by Motowori in Vol. XXVI, pp. 12-14. of his Commentary.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1539"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1543">249:31</A> <i>Oho-ye no miko</i>. This name would, as Motowori remarks, appear to have erroneously crept in here through the influence of the name mentioned in Note 27, the whole account of this union with Princess Ka-guro being corrupt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1540"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1544">249:32</A> The Japanese term (<A NAME="img_25200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25200.jpg"> <i>miko</i>) includes both males and females.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1541"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1545">249:33</A> <A NAME="img_25201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25201.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1542"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1546">250:34</A> As above remarked, the Japanese term includes both males and females, and moreover some of the female children are specially mentioned. The difficulty as to how females could have been appointed to the offices here mentioned is not solved by Motowori, whose note on this passage is evasive.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1543"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1547">250:35</A> The four names of offices (also used as "gentile names") here mentioned are in the original Japanese <i>Kuni no Miyatsuko</i>, <i>Wake</i>, <i>Inaki</i>, and <i>Agata-mushi</i>. (See Introduction, <A HREF="kj002.htm#page_xvi">p. xvi</A>.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1544"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1548">250:36</A> <i>Mamuta no murazhi</i>. (See Sect. LIII, Note 1.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1545"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1549">250:37</A> <i>Mori no kimi</i>. <i>Mori</i> seems to be the name of a place (perhaps in Mino); but nothing is known of this family.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1546"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1550">250:38</A> <i>Ohota no kimi</i>. <i>Ohota</i> is the name of a place in Mino, and signifies "great rice-field."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1547"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1551">250:39</A> <i>Shimada no kimi</i>. <i>Shimada</i> is perhaps the name of a place in Wohari. It signifies "island rice-fields."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1548"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1552">250:40</A> <i>Ki no kuni no sakabe no abiko</i>. For also see Sect. LXXII, Note 85. <i>Sakabe</i> seems to signify "liquor tribe," this family and the next having been entrusted with the management of the Imperial feasts.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1549"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1553">250:41</A> <i>Uda no sakabe</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, the "Liquor Tribe of Uda." (in Yamato).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1550"></A><A HREF="kj083.htm#fr_1554">250:42</A> <i>Himuka no kuni no miyatsuko</i>.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_253"><font size="1" color="green">p. 253</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXVII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART II.&#8212;THE MAIDENS YE-HIME AND OTO-HIME).]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, to assure himself of what he had heard of the beauty of the two maidens Ye-hime and Oto-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1555"></A><A HREF="#fn_1551"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> daughters of King Kamu-ohone,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1556"></A><A HREF="#fn_1552"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> ancestor of the Rulers of the Land of Minu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1557"></A><A HREF="#fn_1553"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> sent his august child, His Augustness Oho-usu, to summon them up [to the Capital]. So His Augustness Oho-usu who had been sent, instead of summoning them up, forthwith wedded both the maidens himself, and then sought other women, to whom he falsely gave the maidens' names, and sent them up [to his father]. Hereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, knowing them to be other women, frequently subjected them to his long glances;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1558"></A><A HREF="#fn_1554"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> but, never wedding them, caused them to sorrow. So the child that His Augustness Oho-usu begot on wedding Ye-hime, [205] was King Oshi-kuro-no-ye-hiko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1559"></A><A HREF="#fn_1555"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> (<small>he was the ancestor of the Lords of Unesu in Minu.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1560"></A><A HREF="#fn_1556"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> Again, the child that he begot on wedding Oto-hime, was King Oshi-kuro-no-oto-hiko (he was the ancestor of the Dukes of Mugetsu.)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1561"></A><A HREF="#fn_1557"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1551"></A><A HREF="kj084.htm#fr_1555">253:1</A> <a name="page_253"><font size="1" color="green">p. 253</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, the elder princess and the younger princess.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1552"></A><A HREF="kj084.htm#fr_1556">253:2</A> See Sect. LXII, Note 36.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1553"></A><A HREF="kj084.htm#fr_1557">253:3</A> <i>Minu no kuni no miyatsuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1554"></A><A HREF="kj084.htm#fr_1558">253:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "gazed at them intently." The Classical word <i>nagamuru</i>, "to gaze," is properly a compound of <i>naga</i>, "long," and <i>miru</i>, "to see."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1555"></A><A HREF="kj084.htm#fr_1559">253:5</A> The meaning of the syllables <i>oshi</i> in this name and the companion one (<i>Oshi-kuro no oto hiko</i>) immediately below is probably "great;" <i>kuro</i> is obscure; <i>ye-hiko</i> signifies "elder prince" and <i>oto-hiko</i> "younger prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1556"></A><A HREF="kj084.htm#fr_1560">253:6</A> <i>Mimi no Unesu no wake</i>. Of Unesu nothing is known.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1557"></A><A HREF="kj084.htm#fr_1561">253:7</A> <i>Mugetsu no kimi</i>. Mugetsu or Muge was in the province of Mini (Mino).</P>

<p><a name="page_254"><font size="1" color="green">p. 254</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART III. VARIOUS DEEDS.)]</h2>  
<p>In this august reign the Labourers' Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1562"></A><A HREF="#fn_1558"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A> was established; again, the port of Aha in the East was established; again, the Great Butlers' Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1563"></A><A HREF="#fn_1559"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> was established; again, the granaries of Yamato were established; again, the Pool of Sakate was made, and bamboos planted on the bank.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1564"></A><A HREF="#fn_1560"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1558"></A><A HREF="kj085.htm#fr_1562">254:1a</A> <a name="page_254"><font size="1" color="green">p. 254</font></A> Such is the reasonable explanation of the original term <i>tabe</i> (<A NAME="img_25400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25400.jpg">) given by Motowori. It seems to have become a "gentile-name."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1559"></A><A HREF="kj085.htm#fr_1563">254:2</A> <i>Kashikade no oho-tomo-be</i>. This "gentile name" originally denoted one who was butler, steward, or cook, in the Emperor's household. The tradition of its origin is preserved in the "Chronicles."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1560"></A><A HREF="kj085.htm#fr_1564">254:3</A> Motowori supposes that the mention both in his history and in the "Chronicles of Japan" of the planting of bamboos on the banks of this pool or lake should be attributed to the rarity of such a proceeding in ancient times.</P>

LXXIX.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART IV.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE SLAYS HIS ELDER BROTHER).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign said to His Augustness Wo-usu: "Why does not thine elder brother come forth to the morning and evening great august repasts?&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1565"></A><A HREF="#fn_1561"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> Be thou the one to take the trouble to teach him [his duty]." Thus he commanded; but for five days after, still [the prince] came not forth. Then the Heavenly Sovereign deigned to ask His Augustness Wo-usu [saying]: "Why is thine elder brother so long of coming? Hast thou perchance not yet taught him [his duty]?" He replied, [206] saying: "I have been at that trouble." Again [the Heavenly Sovereign] said "How didst thou take the</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_255"><font size="1" color="green">p. 255</font></A></p>  
<p>trouble?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1566"></A><A HREF="#fn_1562"><FONT SIZE="1">2a</FONT></A> He replied, saying: "In the early morning when he went into the privy, I grasped hold of him and crushed him, and, pulling off his limbs,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1567"></A><A HREF="#fn_1563"><FONT SIZE="1">3a</FONT></A> wrapped them in matting and flung them away."</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1561"></A><A HREF="kj086.htm#fr_1565">254:1b</A> Viz., to attend on his Imperial father.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1562"></A><A HREF="kj086.htm#fr_1566">255:2a</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "How didst thou do it?"</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1563"></A><A HREF="kj086.htm#fr_1567">255:3a</A> Literally, "branches."</P>

<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXX. EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART V.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE SLAYS THE KUMASO BRAVOES).]</h2>  
<p>Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, alarmed at the valour and ferocity of his august child's disposition, commanded him, saying: "In the West there are two Kumaso bravoes,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1568"></A><A HREF="#fn_1564"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A>&#8212;unsubmissive and disrespectful men. So take&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1569"></A><A HREF="#fn_1565"><FONT SIZE="1">2b</FONT></A> them,"&#8212;and [with this command] he sent him off. It happened that at this time his august hair was bound at the brow.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1570"></A><A HREF="#fn_1566"><FONT SIZE="1">3b</FONT></A> Then His Augustness Wo-usu was granted by his aunt Her Augustness Yamato-hime&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1571"></A><A HREF="#fn_1567"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> her august [upper] garment and august skirt; and, with a sabre hidden in his august bosom, he went forth.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1572"></A><A HREF="#fn_1568"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> So, on reaching the house of the Kumaso bravoes, he saw that near the house there was a three-fold belt of warriors, who had made a cave&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1573"></A><A HREF="#fn_1569"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> to dwell in. Hereupon they, noisily discussing a rejoicing for the august cave,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1574"></A><A HREF="#fn_1570"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> were getting food ready. So [Prince Wo-usu sauntered about the neighbourhood, waiting for the day of the [207] rejoicing. Then when the day of the rejoicing came, having combed down after the manner of girls his august hair which was bound up,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1575"></A><A HREF="#fn_1571"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and having put on his aunt's august [upper] garment and august skirt, he looked quite</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_256"><font size="1" color="green">p. 256</font></A></p>  
<p>like a young girl, and, standing amidst the women,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1576"></A><A HREF="#fn_1572"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> went inside the cave. Then the elder brother and the younger brother, the two Kumaso bravoes, delighted at the sight of the maiden, set her between them, and rejoiced exuberantly. So, when [the feast was] at its height, [His Augustness Wo-usu], drawing the sabre from his bosom, and catching Kumaso&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1577"></A><A HREF="#fn_1573"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> by the collar of his garment, thrust the sabre through his chest, whereupon, alarmed at the sight, the younger bravo ran out. But pursuing after and reaching him at the bottom of the steps&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1578"></A><A HREF="#fn_1574"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> of the cave, and catching him by the back,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1579"></A><A HREF="#fn_1575"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> [Prince Wo-usu] thrust the sabre through his buttock. Then the Kumaso bravo spoke, saying: "Do not move the sword; I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1580"></A><A HREF="#fn_1576"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> have something to say." Then [His Augustness Wo-usu], respited him for a moment, holding him down [as he lay] prostrate. Hereupon [the bravo] said: "Who is Thine Augustness?" Then he said: "I am the august child of Oho-tarashi-hiko-oshiro-wake, the Heavenly Sovereign who, dwelling in the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku, rules the Land of the Eight Great Islands; and my name is King Yamato-wo-guna. Hearing that you two [fellows&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1581"></A><A HREF="#fn_1577"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A>], the Kumaso bravoes, were unsubmissive and disrespectful, [the Heavenly Sovereign] sent me with the command to take and slay you." Then the Kumaso bravo said: "That must [208] be true. There are no persons in the West so brave and strong as we two.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1582"></A><A HREF="#fn_1578"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> Yet in the Land of Great Yamato there is a man braver than we two,&#8212;there is.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1583"></A><A HREF="#fn_1579"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> Therefore will I offer thee an august name. From this time forward it is right that thou be praised as the August Child Yamato-take."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1584"></A><A HREF="#fn_1580"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> As soon as he had finished saying this, [the Prince] ripped him up&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1585"></A><A HREF="#fn_1581"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> like a ripe</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_257"><font size="1" color="green">p. 257</font></A></p>  
<p>melon,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1586"></A><A HREF="#fn_1582"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> and slew him.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1587"></A><A HREF="#fn_1583"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> So thenceforward he was praised by being called by the august name of&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1588"></A><A HREF="#fn_1584"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> his Augustness Yamato-take. When he returned up [to the capital] after doing this, he subdued and pacified every one of the Deities of the mountains and of the Deities of the rivers and likewise of the Deities of Anado,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1589"></A><A HREF="#fn_1585"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> and then went up to [the capital].</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>
