<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1564"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1568">255:1</A> <a name="page_257"><font size="1" color="green">p. 257</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, presumably "bravoes at Kumaso; "but it is to be remarked that in this and like compounds with <i>takeru</i> ("bravo") the Japanese language uses no Postposition. For Kumaso see Sect. V, Note 17.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1565"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1569">255:2b</A> Motowori seems right in interpreting "take" here and elsewhere in the sense of "slay." But "take "is in the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1566"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1570">255:3b</A> <i>I.e.</i>, caught up from the brow and tied together on the crown of the head. This being the way in which the hair of boys was dressed, the author thus intimates that His Augustness was still a youth.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1567"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1571">255:4</A> Who was high-priestess of the temple of the Great Deity of Ise, as mentioned in Sect. LXIX (Note 44).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1568"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1572">255:5</A> The characters used for these last two words are those properly restricted to the mention of an Imperial progress, but Yamato-take is constantly spoken of as if he had actually sat on the throne.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1569"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1573">255:6</A> The character used is <A NAME="img_25700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25700.jpg">, which simply means apartment; but see Sect. XLVIII, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1570"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1574">255:7</A> Motowori reads "<i>New</i> cave," but the word "August" is in the text. At the same time we see that this feast was intended as a house-warming. <i>Conf</i>. the commencement of Sect. CLXIV.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1571"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1575">255:8</A> The parallel passage of the "Chronicles" puts the same meaning into plainer words. It says: "undid his hair, and made it appear like a girl's."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1572"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1576">256:9</A> Or, according to the old reading, "mixing with the concubines."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1573"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1577">256:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the elder bravo of Kumaso.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1574"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1578">256:11</A> The word rendered "steps" is of doubtful interpretation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1575"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1579">256:12</A> Or perhaps "the skin of his back" or "the (beast's?) skin on his back." But Motowori is probably right in supposing the character <A NAME="img_25701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25701.jpg">, "skin" to be an error for <A NAME="img_25702"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25702.jpg">, "with," to be construed with the word "sabre." (In the English idiom this Particle falls away.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1576"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1580">256:13</A> Written with the humble character <A NAME="img_25703"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25703.jpg">, "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1577"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1581">256:14</A> <a name="page_258"><font size="1" color="green">p. 258</font></A> The contemptuous Second Personal Pronoun <i>ore</i> is used here and in the next clause.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1578"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1582">256:15</A> There is Motowori's authority for thus understanding the bravo's words. Taken still more literally, they would seem to imply that there were no brave and strong men in the West <i>excepting</i> himself and his brother.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1579"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1583">256:16</A> The words "there is" are an attempt at rendering the termination keri of the original. See X, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1580"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1584">256:17</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "Yamato-Brave," <i>q.d.</i>, "the Bravest in Yamato." It is by this name that the hero is commonly spoken of. Remember that "august child "signifies prince.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1581"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1585">256:18</A> <A NAME="img_25800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25800.jpg">, "broke," in the text is, as the commentators observe, an evident error for <A NAME="img_25801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25801.jpg">, "ripped."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1582"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1586">257:19</A> Or specifically, the "musk melon."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1583"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1587">257:20</A> The translator has followed Motowori's restoration of this passage, in which, by the transposition of the characters <A NAME="img_25802"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25802.jpg"> and <A NAME="img_25803"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25803.jpg">, the end of this sentence and the beginning of the next were mixed together in the older editions.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1584"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1588">257:21</A> Lit., "[they] praised the august name, calling him," etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1585"></A><A HREF="kj087.htm#fr_1589">257:22</A> Or, "of the Ana passage" (lit. door), the modern Strait of Shimonoseki. The word <i>ana</i> signifies "hole," and there is a tradition (which Motowori quotes in his note on this name in Vol. XXVII, pp. 26-29 of his Commentary) to the effect that formerly the Main bland and the island of Kiushiu were continuous at this point, there being only a sort of natural tunnel, through which junks could pass.</P>

<p><a name="page_258"><font size="1" color="green">p. 258</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXI.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART VI.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE SLAYS THE IDZUMO BRAVO).</h2>  
<p>Forthwith entering the Land of Idzumo, and wishing to slay the Idzumo bravo, he on arriving, forthwith bound [himself to him in] friendship. So, having secretly [209] made [the wood of] an oak [-trees&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1590"></A><A HREF="#fn_1586"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A>] into a false sword and augustly girded it, he went with the bravo to bathe the River Hi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1591"></A><A HREF="#fn_1587"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Then, His Augustness Yamato-take</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_259"><font size="1" color="green">p. 259</font></A></p>  
<p>getting out of the river first, and taking and girding on the sword that the Idzumo bravo had taken off and laid down, said: "Let us exchange swords!" So afterwards the Idzumo bravo, getting out of the river, girded on His Augustness Yamato-take's false sword. Hereupon His Augustness Yamato-take, suggested, saying: "Come on! let us cross&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1592"></A><A HREF="#fn_1588"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> swords." Then on drawing his sword, the Idzumo bravo could not draw the false sword. Forthwith His Augustness Yamato-take drew his sword and slew the Idzumo bravo. Then he sang augustly, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Alas that the sword girded on the Idzumo bravo, and wound round with many a creeper, should have had no true blade!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1593"></A><A HREF="#fn_1589"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So having thus extirpated the [bravoes] and made [the land] orderly, he went up [to the capital], and made his report [to the Heavenly Sovereign].</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1586"></A><A HREF="kj088.htm#fr_1590">258:1</A> The species mentioned (<i>ichihi</i>) is the <i>Quercus gilva</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1587"></A><A HREF="kj088.htm#fr_1591">258:2</A> See Sect. XVIII, Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1588"></A><A HREF="kj088.htm#fr_1592">259:3</A> Lit., "let us join swords." The word "suggested" (<A NAME="img_25900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25900.jpg">) in this sentence is an emendation of Motowori's, the text having <A NAME="img_25901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25901.jpg">, "slandered." The older printed editions, while retaining the character <A NAME="img_25902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/25902.jpg">, read it <i>azamukite</i>, "deceived."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1589"></A><A HREF="kj088.htm#fr_1593">259:4</A> In its position in the present text, this Song must be taken as an ironical lament of the Prince for the dead bravo. In the "Chronicle" the time and the heroes of the episode, and the singers of the Song are all different, and in that context the lament sounds like a genuine one. The reader will remember what was said in the Introduction as to the use of creepers for string. That mentioned in the text is supposed to be the <i>Cocculus thunbergi</i>.</P>

<p><a name="page_260"><font size="1" color="green">p. 260</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART VII.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE IS SENT TO SUBDUE THE EAST, AND VISITS HIS AUNT AT ISE).]</h2>  
<p>Then the Heavenly Sovereign again urged a command on His Augustness Yamato-take, saying: "Subdue and pacify the savage Deities and likewise the unsubmissive people of the twelve roads of the East;"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1594"></A><A HREF="#fn_1590"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and when he sent him off, joining to him Prince Mi-suki-tomo-mimi-take,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1595"></A><A HREF="#fn_1591"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> ancestor of the Grandees of Kibi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1596"></A><A HREF="#fn_1592"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> he bestowed on [210] him a holly-wood&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1597"></A><A HREF="#fn_1593"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> spear eight fathoms [long]. So when he had received the [Imperial] command and started off, he went into the temple of the Great August Deity of Ise, and worshipped the Deity's court,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1598"></A><A HREF="#fn_1594"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> forthwith speaking to his aunt, Her Augustness Yamato-hime, saying: "It must surely be that the Heavenly Sovereign thinks&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1599"></A><A HREF="#fn_1595"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> I may die quickly; for after sending me to smite the wicked people of the West, I am no sooner come up again [to the capital] than, without bestowing on me an army, he now sends me off afresh to pacify the wicked people of the twelve circuits of the East. Consequently I think that he certainly thinks I shall die quickly." When he departed with lamentations and tears, Her Augustness Yamato-hime bestowed on him the "Herb-Quelling-Sabre,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1600"></A><A HREF="#fn_1596"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and likewise bestowed on him an august bag,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1601"></A><A HREF="#fn_1597"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and said: "If there should be an emergency, open the mouth of the bag."</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1590"></A><A HREF="kj089.htm#fr_1594">260:1</A> <a name="page_260"><font size="1" color="green">p. 260</font></A> See Sect. LXVI. Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1591"></A><A HREF="kj089.htm#fr_1595">260:2</A> <i>Mi-suki-tomo-mini-take-hiko</i>. <i>Mi</i> is an <A HREF="errata.htm#51">Honorific</A>, <i>mimi</i> probably signifies "ears," and <i>take</i> means "bravo." The words <i>suki</i> and <i>tomo</i> are obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1592"></A><A HREF="kj089.htm#fr_1596">260:3</A> <i>Kibi na omi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1593"></A><A HREF="kj089.htm#fr_1597">260:4</A> Properly the <i>Olea aquifolium</i>, which resembles holly. Motowori <a name="page_261"><font size="1" color="green">p. 261</font></A> supposes that an entirely wooden spear or stick is here meant to be spoken of, and not the weapon with a metal point which is commonly understood by the word "spear" (<i>hoko</i>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1594"></A><A HREF="kj089.htm#fr_1598">260:5</A> Perhaps we should write "august court," for the characters <A NAME="img_26100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/26100.jpg"> in the text are evidently intended for the homonymous <A NAME="img_26101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/26101.jpg">. The court in front of the Deity's temple is what is here alluded to, and it would perhaps be a not unpardonable departure from the text to insert the Preposition "at," or "in," and translate thus: "worshipped in the Deity's court."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1595"></A><A HREF="kj089.htm#fr_1599">260:6</A> Here and below, the word "thinks," may be understood to mean "wishes."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1596"></A><A HREF="kj089.htm#fr_1600">260:7</A> <i>Kusa-nagi no tsurugi</i>. The discovery of this sword by the deity Susa-no wo ("Impetuous Male") inside one of the tails of the eight-headed serpent which he had slain, is narrated at the end of Sect. XVIII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1597"></A><A HREF="kj089.htm#fr_1601">260:8</A> The use of the contents of this bag will be seen in the next Section.</P>

<p><a name="page_261"><font size="1" color="green">p. 261</font></A> [211]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXIII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART VIII.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE SLAYS THE RULERS OF SAGAMU.)]</h2>  
<p>So reaching the Land of Wohari, he went into the house of Princess Miyadzu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1602"></A><A HREF="#fn_1598"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> ancestress of the Rulers of Wohari,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1603"></A><A HREF="#fn_1599"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and forthwith thought to wed her; but thinking again that he would wed her when he should return up [toward the capital], and having plighted his troth, he went [on] into the Eastern Lands, and subdued and pacified all the savage Deities and unsubmissive people of the mountains and rivers. So then, when he reached the Land of Sagamu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1604"></A><A HREF="#fn_1600"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> the Ruler of the land lied, saying: "In the middle of this moor is a great lagoon, and the Deity that dwells in the middle of the lagoon is a very violent Deity." Hereupon [Yamato-take] entered the moor to see the Deity. Then the Ruler of the land set fire to the moor. So, knowing that he had been</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_262"><font size="1" color="green">p. 262</font></A></p>  
<p>deceived, he opened the mouth of the bag which his aunt, Her Augustness Yamato-hime had bestowed on him, and saw that inside of it there was a fire-striker.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1605"></A><A HREF="#fn_1601"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Hereupon he first mowed away the herbage with his august sword, took the fire-striker and struck out fire, and, kindling a counter-fire, burnt [the herbage] and drove back [the other fire], and returned forth, and killed and destroyed all the Rulers&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1606"></A><A HREF="#fn_1602"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> of that Land, and forthwith set fire to and burnt them. So [that place] is now called Yakidzu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1607"></A><A HREF="#fn_1603"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1598"></A><A HREF="kj090.htm#fr_1602">261:1</A> <a name="page_262"><font size="1" color="green">p. 262</font></A> Miyazu-hime (in the "Chronicles "and in the printed editions of these "Records "previous to Motowori's written Miyasu-hime without the <i>nigori</i>). Neither Motowori nor Tanigaha Shisei makes any suggestion as to the signification of this name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1599"></A><A HREF="kj090.htm#fr_1603">261:2</A> <i>Wohari no miyatsuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1600"></A><A HREF="kj090.htm#fr_1604">261:3</A> In the present time <i>Sagami</i>. No authority great or small has given a satisfactory etymology of this name, though numerous and elaborate attempts have been made to explain it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1601"></A><A HREF="kj090.htm#fr_1605">262:4</A> In the original <i>hi-uchi</i> (<A NAME="img_26200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/26200.jpg">). Mr. Satow, who has given a translation of this passage in a note to his third paper on the "Rituals "to be found in Vol. IX, Pt. II. p. 202 of these "Transaction," renders this word by "steel." The present writer prefers not to prejudge the question as to whether the fire-striker "intended by the author was a steel, or a wooden fire-drill. Motowori would seem to have held the latter view, as in his gloss on this passage he refers to the previous passage near the end of Sect. XXXII, where the fire-drill is <A HREF="errata.htm#52">explicitly</A> mentioned. He also quotes an ancient one in which "a fire-striker of metal "is specially referred to, so that it would seem that all fire-strikers were not of that material.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1602"></A><A HREF="kj090.htm#fr_1606">262:5</A> Remember that this word "Ruler" (Miyatsuko) had the acceptation of a "gentile name "as well as of the name of an office, so that we may understand the author to mean that Yamato-take destroyed the whole Ruling Family of Sagami. Parallel passage of the "Chronicles'' has "he burnt all that rebel band, and destroyed them."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1603"></A><A HREF="kj090.htm#fr_1607">262:6</A> The words rendered "that place" are supplied by Motowori, their omission being evidently a copyist's error. <i>Yaki-dzu</i> signifies "the port of burning."</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_263"><font size="1" color="green">p. 263</font></A> [212]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXIV.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART IX.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE'S EMPRESS STILLS THE WAVES.)</h2>  
<p>When he thence penetrated on, and crossed the sea of Hashiri-midzu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1608"></A><A HREF="#fn_1604"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> the Deity of that crossing raised the waves, tossing the ship so that it could not proceed across. Then [Yamato-take's] Empress,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1609"></A><A HREF="#fn_1605"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> whose name was Her Augustness Princess Oto-tachibana&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1610"></A><A HREF="#fn_1606"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> said: "I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1611"></A><A HREF="#fn_1607"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> will enter the sea instead of the august child.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1612"></A><A HREF="#fn_1608"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> The august child must complete the service&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1613"></A><A HREF="#fn_1609"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> on which he has been sent, and take back a report [to the Heavenly Sovereign]." When she was about to enter the sea, she spread eight thicknesses of sedge rugs,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1614"></A><A HREF="#fn_1610"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> eight thicknesses of skin rugs and eight thicknesses of silk rugs on the top of the waves, and sat down on the top [of them] Thereupon the violent waves at once went down, and the august ship was able to proceed. Then the. Empress sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Ah! thou [whom I] enquired of, standing in the midst of the flames of the fire burning on the little moor of Sagamu, where the true peak pierces!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1615"></A><A HREF="#fn_1611"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So seven days afterwards the Empress's august comb [213] drifted onto the sea-beach,&#8212;Which comb was forthwith taken and placed in an august mausoleum which was made.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1604"></A><A HREF="kj091.htm#fr_1608">263:1</A> <a name="page_263"><font size="1" color="green">p. 263</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, "running water."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1605"></A><A HREF="kj091.htm#fr_1609">263:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, his consort. Conf. Sect. <A HREF="errata.htm#53">???</A>, Note 5.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1606"></A><A HREF="kj091.htm#fr_1610">263:3</A> <i>Oto-tachibana-hime no mikoto</i>. (See Sect. XCII, Note 3.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1607"></A><A HREF="kj091.htm#fr_1611">263:4</A> Written with the humble character <A NAME="img_26300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/26300.jpg">, literally "concubine."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1608"></A><A HREF="kj091.htm#fr_1612">263:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, instead of thee, the Prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1609"></A><A HREF="kj091.htm#fr_1613">263:6</A> More literally, "finish the government."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1610"></A><A HREF="kj091.htm#fr_1614">263:7</A> Or "mats." But the same word is used as that which must be translated "rugs" immediately below.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1611"></A><A HREF="kj091.htm#fr_1615">263:8</A> <a name="page_264"><font size="1" color="green">p. 264</font></A> This Song gives much trouble to the commentators, whose remarks (to be found in Motowori's "Commentary." Vol. XXVII, pp. 67-9, and Moribe's "<i>Idzu no Koto-Waki</i>" Vol. III, pp, 6-9,) should be consulted by the student desirous of forming an opinion of his own. The general purport of the poem is of course to allude to Yamato-take's adventure on the burning moor, and at the same time to the love which bound him and his consort together; almost each individual line offers matter for doubt. Thus it is not certain whether the Verb <i>tohishi</i>, here rendered "enquired of" (<i>i.e.</i>, attended upon by the Empress). should not rather be given the word "thou" as subject, in which case the signification would be "thou who enquiredst of [<i>i.e.</i>, wooedst]." The word used for "thou;" is the Honorific equivalent of that Pronoun signifying literally "prince." Moribe disputes the propriety of considering Sagamu in this place as the name of a province, and the word <i>sanesashi</i>, here translated "where the true peak pierces" (Mt. Fuji being by some supposed to be thus alluded to) is of very doubtful interpretation. Motowori tells us that the final Particles <i>ha mo</i>, rendered by the initial Interjection "Oh," should here be understood as an exclamation more forcible than that which usually belongs to him. Finally Moribe points out that the Song does not suit the context in which it is found, and has probably been erroneously inserted here instead of in an earlier portion of the text.</P>

<p><a name="page_264"><font size="1" color="green">p. 264</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXV.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART X.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE SLAYS THE DEITY OF THE ASHIGARA PASS.)]</h2>  
<p>When, having thence penetrated on and subdued all the savage Yemishi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1616"></A><A HREF="#fn_1612"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and likewise pacified all the savage Deities of the mountains and rivers, he was returning up [to the capital], he, on reaching the foot of the Ashigara Pass,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1617"></A><A HREF="#fn_1613"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> was eating his august provisions, when the Deity of the pass, transformed into a white deer, came and stood [before him]. Then forthwith, on his waiting&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1618"></A><A HREF="#fn_1614"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and striking [the deer] with a scrap of wild chive,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1619"></A><A HREF="#fn_1615"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> [the deer] was hit in the eye and struck dead. So, mounting to</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_265"><font size="1" color="green">p. 265</font></A></p>  
<p>the top of the pass, he sighed three times and spoke, saying: "<i>Adzuma ha ya!</i>"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1620"></A><A HREF="#fn_1616"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> So that land is called by the name of Adzuma.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1612"></A><A HREF="kj092.htm#fr_1616">264:1</A> This is the traditional ancient reading of what is according to the modern pronunciation <i>Yezo</i>, while the Chinese characters <A NAME="img_26500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/26500.jpg">, with which the name is written, signify "Prawn Barbarians," in allusion (if Motowori may be trusted) to the long beards which make their fades resemble a prawn's head. The hairy barbarians known to English readers as <i>Ainos</i>, and whose name of <i>Yezo</i> is applied by the Japanese to the northernmost large island of the Japanese Archipelago, which is still chiefly tenanted by them, are almost certainly here referred to. In ancient times they inhabited a great part of the Main Island of Japan. The translator may add that the genuiness of the so-called ancient reading "<i>Yemishi</i>" appears to him doubtful. The name known to the people themselves, and which apparently can be traced as far as Kamschatka, is <i>Yezo</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1613"></A><A HREF="kj092.htm#fr_1617">264:2</A> <i>Ashigara-zaka</i>, one of the passes from Sagami into Suruga leading towards Mount Fuji.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1614"></A><A HREF="kj092.htm#fr_1618">264:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, lying in ambush.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1615"></A><A HREF="kj092.htm#fr_1619">264:4</A> <i>Nira</i>, the <i>Allium odorum</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1616"></A><A HREF="kj092.htm#fr_1620">265:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "my wife! "<i>Adzuma</i> is still used as a poetical designation of Eastern Japan. The translator doubts the correctness of the derivation of it given in the text, although it is universally accepted and certainly fits in well with the graceful legend by which it is here accounted for.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p>[214]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXVI.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART XI.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE DWELLS IN THE PALACE OF SAKAWORI.)]</h2>  
<p>When, forthwith crossing over from that land out into Kahi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1621"></A><A HREF="#fn_1617"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> he dwelt in the palace of Sakawori,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1622"></A><A HREF="#fn_1618"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"How many nights have I slept since passing Nihibari and Tsukuha?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1623"></A><A HREF="#fn_1619"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_266"><font size="1" color="green">p. 266</font></A></p>  
<p>Then the old man, who was the lighter of the august fire,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1624"></A><A HREF="#fn_1620"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> completed the august Song, and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! having put the days in a row, there are of nights nine nights, and of days ten days!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1625"></A><A HREF="#fn_1621"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Therefore [Yamato-take] praised the old man, and forthwith bestowed [on him] the Rulership of the Eastern Land[s].&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1626"></A><A HREF="#fn_1622"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1617"></A><A HREF="kj093.htm#fr_1621">265:1</A> <a name="page_266"><font size="1" color="green">p. 266</font></A> This name is identified by the native etymology with an homonymous Substantive signifying "a place between mountains."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1618"></A><A HREF="kj093.htm#fr_1622">265:2</A> The etymology of this name is uncertain. But the most likely opinion is that it signifies "a zigzag road down a pass."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1619"></A><A HREF="kj093.htm#fr_1623">265:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, since leaving the province of Hitachi, of which Tsukuha (in modern parlance <i>Tsukuba</i>, with the last syllable <i>nigori</i>&#8217;ed) and Nihibari (modern <i>Nihiharu</i>) are two districts. In the later poetry <i>Nibari no</i> is often used as a Pillow-Word for the name of Mount Tsukuba. The etymology of both names is uncertain, but "newly tilled "seems to be the most probable etymology of the first of the two.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1620"></A><A HREF="kj093.htm#fr_1624">266:4</A> Not necessarily a fire kindled for the sake of obtaining warmth, but fire in general, including, as Motowori suggests, torches and fires lit to drive away mosquitoes. There are frequent mentions in the classical literature of this latter sort of fire, which may indeed still be met with in some districts where mosquito-nets are not yet in common use.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1621"></A><A HREF="kj093.htm#fr_1625">266:5</A> The meaning is: "On counting up, I find that we have been ten days and nine nights."&#8212;Previous to Motowori the expression <i>ka-ga nabette</i>, "having put in a row (<i>i.e.</i> counted) the days" was curiously misunderstood, and subjected to various far-fetched interpretations. There can however be no doubt but that Motowori is right.&#8212;The reason why the old man is said to have "completed "the Prince's song is that the former taken alone is of incomplete rhythm.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1622"></A><A HREF="kj093.htm#fr_1626">266:6</A> Or, as Motowori would prefer to <A HREF="errata.htm#54">consider</A> it, "the Rulership of an Eastern Land," viz., one out of the twelve Eastern provinces.</P>

<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">

<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_267"><font size="1" color="green">p. 267</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXVII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART XII.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE WOOES PRINCESS MIYAZU).]</h2>  
<p>Having crossed over from that land into the land of Shinanu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1627"></A><A HREF="#fn_1623"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and subdued the Deity of the Shinanu pass,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1628"></A><A HREF="#fn_1624"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> he came back to the land of Wohari, and went to dwell in the house of Princess Miyazu, to whom he had before plighted his troth. Hereupon, when presenting to him the great august food, Princess Miyazu lifted up a great liquor-cup and presented it to him. Tunc Her&aelig; Miyazu veli or&aelig; adh&aelig;serunt menstrua. Quare [Augustus Yamato-take] ilia menstrua vidit, et auguste cecinit, dicens:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Ego volui reclinare [caput] in fragili, molli brachiolo [tuo, quod est simile] vallo impingenti acut&aelig; falci in Monte Kagu in c&#339;lo formato quasi cucurbita;&#8212;ego desideravi dormire [tecum]. Sed in or&acirc; veli quod induis luna surrexit."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1629"></A><A HREF="#fn_1625"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Tunc Her&aelig; Miyazu augusto cantui respondit, dicens: [216]</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Alt&egrave; resplendentis solis auguste puer! Placid&egrave; administrationem faciens mi magne domine! Renovatis annis venientibus et effluentibus, renovat&aelig; lun&aelig; eunt veniendo patienter expecto, luna su&agrave;pte surgit in or&acirc; veli quod ego induo!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1630"></A><A HREF="#fn_1626"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Quare tune [ille] coivit [cum ill&acirc;], after which, placing in Princess Miyazu's house his august sword "the Grass-Quelling Sabre," he went forth&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1631"></A><A HREF="#fn_1627"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> to take the Deity of [Mount] Ibuki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1632"></A><A HREF="#fn_1628"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_268"><font size="1" color="green">p. 268</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1623"></A><A HREF="kj094.htm#fr_1627">267:1</A> <a name="page_267"><font size="1" color="green">p. 267</font></A> See Sect. XXXIII, Note 26.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1624"></A><A HREF="kj094.htm#fr_1628">267:2</A> <i>Shinanu no saka</i>, a pass between the provinces of Shinano and Mino which is no longer used.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1625"></A><A HREF="kj094.htm#fr_1629">267:3</A> <a name="page_268"><font size="1" color="green">p. 268</font></A> Even taken apart from its immediate context, the import of this Song is plain, notwithstanding Moribe's efforts to explain away its indelicacy. The details of the first part, however, require some comment in order to make them comprehensible to the European reader, the words in question being these which might in English be rendered "thy fragile, slender, delicate arm [which resembles] a post striking against the sharp sickle on Mount Kagu of the gourd-shaped heaven." In Japanese they run thus:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px"><i>Hisa-kata no</i><br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Ame no Kagu-yamo</i><br> <i>To-kama ni</i><br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Sa-wataru kuhi:&#8212;</i><br> <i>Hiha-boso</i><br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Ta-waya-gahina wo</i> etc.</div></p>  
<p>It will he remarked that the first four lines form a "Punning Preface "to the fifth. Such Punning Prefaces have not necessarily any logical connection with what follows, as has been explained by the present writer in a paper "On the Use of Pillow Words and Plays upon Words in Japanese Poetry," to be found in Vol. V, Pt. I, pp. 79 <i>et seq.</i> of these "Transactions." In this particular case, however, there is sufficient continuity of sense to warrant the continuous translation above given. The word "post," though such a use of it is very curious, must be <A HREF="errata.htm#55">understood</A> to denote not a dead, but a living trunk, or rather the stem of some delicate plant or grass which falls beneath the sickle of the mower on Mount Kagu in Heaven, or, as it may better be understood, on the Heavenly Mount Kagu [in Yamato]. "Gourd-shaped "is the translation of <i>hisa-kata no</i> or <i>hisa-gata no</i>, the Pillow-Word for "heaven." Its meaning is disputed, but Mabuchi in his "Dictionary of Pillow-Words" and Motowori agree in giving to it the sense here adopted (see the above-mentioned paper "On the Use of Pillow-Words, etc.," p. 81).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1626"></A><A HREF="kj094.htm#fr_1630">267:4</A> The total sense of this Song is quite plain.&#8212;In the first lines of it the Prince is addressed as if he were the reigning sovereign. The words <i>placid&egrave; administrationem faciens</i> represent the Japanese <i>yasumishishi</i>, the Pillow-Word for <i>wa ga oho-kimi</i>, "my great lord." Elsewhere the English rendering "who tranquilly carries on the government" has been adopted. The word <i>aratama no</i>, rendered by the Adjective <i>renovatis</i>, is the Pillow-Word for "sun," "moon" and "year," and is of not quite certain import. The interpretation here adopted has, however, for it the weight of probability and of native authority, Mabuchi in his "Dictionary of Pillow-Words "deriving it from the Verb <i>aratamaru</i>, "to be renewed."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1627"></A><A HREF="kj094.htm#fr_1631">267:5</A> <a name="page_269"><font size="1" color="green">p. 269</font></A> The characters in the text might also be rendered "he made a progress," as they are those only properly applied to the movements of a reigning sovereign. Here and elsewhere, they are used in speaking of Yamato-take. (Conf. Sect. LXXX, Note 5.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1628"></A><A HREF="kj094.htm#fr_1632">267:6</A> On the frontier of Afumi (Omi) and Mince Ibuki seems to signify "blowing," in allusion, it is said, to the pestilential breath or influence of the god by whom the place was tenanted. The word rendered "Mount "is supplied by the editor of 1687.</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_269"><font size="1" color="green">p. 269</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART XIII.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE MEETS THE DEITY OF MOUNT IBUKI).]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon he said: "As for the Deity of this mountain, I will simply take him empty-handed."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1633"></A><A HREF="#fn_1629"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A>&#8212;and was ascending the mountain, when there met him on the mountain-side a white boar whose size was like unto that of a bull.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1634"></A><A HREF="#fn_1630"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Then he lifted up words,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1635"></A><A HREF="#fn_1631"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and said: "This creature that is transformed into a white boar must be a messenger from the Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1636"></A><A HREF="#fn_1632"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Though I slay it not now, I will slay it when I return,"&#8212;and [so saying.] ascended. Thereupon the Deity caused heavy ice-rain&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1637"></A><A HREF="#fn_1633"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> to fall, striking and perplexing His Augustness Yamato-take. (<small>This creature transformed into a white boar was not a messenger from the Deity,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1638"></A><A HREF="#fn_1634"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> but the very Deity in person. Owing to the lifting up of words, he appeared and misled [Yamato-take.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1639"></A><A HREF="#fn_1634"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A>])</small> So when, on descending back, he reached the fresh spring of Tama-kuro-be&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1640"></A><A HREF="#fn_1635"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and rested there, his august heart awoke somewhat.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1641"></A><A HREF="#fn_1636"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> So that fresh spring is called by the name of the fresh spring of Wi-same.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1629"></A><A HREF="kj095.htm#fr_1633">269:1</A> <a name="page_269"><font size="1" color="green">p. 269</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, without weapons, and specially without the magic sword which he had left behind in Princess Miyazu's house.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1630"></A><A HREF="kj095.htm#fr_1634">269:2</A> Or "ox," or "cow," the original word not distinguishing between the sexes.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1631"></A><A HREF="kj095.htm#fr_1635">269:3</A> <a name="page_270"><font size="1" color="green">p. 270</font></A> The Japanese expression <i>kota-age shite</i>, here rendered "lifted up. words," very frequently has the signification of "lifting up a prayer" to some superhuman being. In this passage, however, it conveys no more than its proper etymological meaning.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1632"></A><A HREF="kj095.htm#fr_1636">269:4</A> Viz., the god of Mount Ibuki.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1633"></A><A HREF="kj095.htm#fr_1637">269:5</A> Perhaps "hail" may be intended by this expression, and so Motowori decides. But this interpretation of the term seems to agree well with the Song in Sect. CXLII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1634"></A><A HREF="kj095.htm#fr_1639">269:6</A> The commentators disagree as to whether this note should or should not be considered to form part of the original text. Motowori so considers it. He however, in the opinion of the translator, is not happy in his alteration of the <i>kana</i> reading given by the editor of 1687, which latter has accordingly been followed in the English version.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1635"></A><A HREF="kj095.htm#fr_1640">269:7</A> The literal meaning of this name is "jewel-store-tribe;" but complete uncertainty attaches both to the etymology of the word and to the position of the place. The first printed edition has <i>Tama-kuhi-be</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1636"></A><A HREF="kj095.htm#fr_1641">269:8</A> He had been misled and dazed, but now came to himself again. Thence, according to the etymology of our author, the name of <i>Wi-same</i>, which signifies "dwelling (resting) and awaking," given to the spring.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_270"><font size="1" color="green">p. 270</font></A></p>  
<p align="center"><font size="-1" color="green">The title was omitted from the printed version I was working from. I have interpolated what I believe to be a plausible title&#8212;JBH</font></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. LXXXIX. EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART XIV.&#8212;THE DEATH OF YAMATO-TAKE).]</h2>  
<p>When he departed thence and reached the moor of [218] Tagi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1642"></A><A HREF="#fn_1637"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> he said: "Whereas my heart always felt like flying through the sky, my legs are now unable to walk. They have become rudder-shaped."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1643"></A><A HREF="#fn_1638"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> So that place was called by the name of Tagi. Owing to his being very weary with progressing a little further beyond that place, he leant upon an august staff to walk a little. So that place is called by the name of the Tsuwetsuki pass.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1644"></A><A HREF="#fn_1639"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> On arriving at the single pine-tree on Cape Wotsu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1645"></A><A HREF="#fn_1640"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> an august sword, which he had forgotten at that place before when augustly eating,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1646"></A><A HREF="#fn_1641"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> was still [there] not lost. Then he augustly sang, saying:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_271"><font size="1" color="green">p. 271</font></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"O mine elder brother, the single pine-tree that art on Cape Wotsu which directly faces Mohari! If thou, single pine-tree! wert a person, I would gird [my] sword [upon thee], I would clothe thee with [my] garments,&#8212;O mine elder brother, the single pine-tree!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1647"></A><A HREF="#fn_1642"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>When he departed thence and reached the village of Mihe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1648"></A><A HREF="#fn_1643"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> he again said: "My legs are like three-fold crooks,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1649"></A><A HREF="#fn_1644"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and very weary." So that place was called by [219] the name of Mihe. When he departed thence and reached the moor of Nobe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1650"></A><A HREF="#fn_1645"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> he, regretting&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1651"></A><A HREF="#fn_1646"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> [his native] land,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1652"></A><A HREF="#fn_1647"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"As for Yamato, the most secluded of lands&#8212;Yamato, retired behind Mount Awogaki encompassing it with its folds is delightful!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1653"></A><A HREF="#fn_1648"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Let those whose life may be complete stick [in their hair] as a head-dress the leaves of the bear-oak from Mount Heguri,&#8212;those children!"</div></p>  
<p>This song is a Land-Regretting Song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1654"></A><A HREF="#fn_1649"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> Again he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"How sweet! ah! from the direction of home clouds are rising and coming!"</div></p>  
<p>This is an Incomplete Song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1655"></A><A HREF="#fn_1650"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> At this time, his august sickness was very urgent. Then, he sang augustly, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The sabre-sword which I placed at the maiden's bed-side, alas! that sword!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1656"></A><A HREF="#fn_1651"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>As soon as he had finished singing, he died, Then a courier was despatched [to the Heavenly Sovereign.]</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_272"><font size="1" color="green">p. 272</font></A> <a name="page_273"><font size="1" color="green">p. 273</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1637"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1642">270:1</A> <a name="page_272"><font size="1" color="green">p. 272</font></A> <i>Tagi-nu</i>. We might, following the Chinese characters, translate thus; "and arrived on the Moor of Tagi." But the character <A NAME="img_27200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/27200.jpg"> has in this context scarcely any meaning. The real etymology of <i>Tagi</i> (in classical and modern parlance <i>taki</i> without the <i>nigori</i>) is "rapid "or "waterfall," the cascade formed by the river Vo-ro in Mino being alluded to. The derivation in the next sentence of the text from <i>tagishi</i> supposed to mean "a rudder "is a mere fancy.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1638"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1643">270:2</A> The word here fended "rudder" is <i>tagishi</i>, which is written phonetically and does not occur elsewhere, except in a few Proper Names of doubtful import. There is however some probability in favour of the meaning assigned to it by the native commentators.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1639"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1644">270:3</A> <i>Tzuwe-tsuki-zaka</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the pass of leaning on a staff." It is in the province of Ise between Yokaichi and Ishi-yakushi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1640"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1645">270:4</A> <i>Wotsu-no-saki</i>, in the province of Ise. The name probably signifies "&deg; harbour of the mountain declivity."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1641"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1646">270:5</A> The former portion of the text tells us nothing either of the meal or of the sword here mentioned.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1642"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1647">271:6</A> This quaintly simple and apparently very ancient poem needs no elucidation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1643"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1648">271:7</A> In Ise. <i>Mihe</i> signifies "three fold."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1644"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1649">271:8</A> This is the literal rendering of the text. Motowori thinks, however, that we should understand that there were various swellings on his legs, such as would be produced if the limb were tightly tied round with cord in three places.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1645"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1650">271:9</A> <i>Nobo-un</i> in the province of Ise. The name seems to signify "the moor of mounting."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1646"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1651">271:10</A> The Chinese character here used signifies simply "thinking of;" but in such a context its common Japanese interpretation is "loving "or "regretting," and so Motowori means us to understand it when he reads <i>shinukashite</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1647"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1652">271:11</A> Viz., Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1648"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1653">271:12</A> This Song and the two following form but one in the pages of the "Chronicles," where they appear with several verbal differences, and are attributed, not to the Prince, but to his father the Emperor. Moribe decides that in the latter particular the text of these "Records" gives the preferable account, but that the "Chronicles" are right in making the three Songs one continuous poem. The expression "this Song is a Land-Regretting Song" strongly supports this view; for, though we might also render in the Plural "these Songs are, etc.," such a translation would be less natural, as in similar cases the numeral is used, thus <a name="page_273"><font size="1" color="green">p. 273</font></A> "these <i>two</i> Songs are, etc." The expression "this is an Incomplete Song "points as <A HREF="errata.htm#56">decidedly</A> to some mutilation of the original document, from which the compiler of the "Records" copied this passage. Taking then the three Songs as one, the entire drift is that of a paean on Yamato, the poet's native land, which he could not hope ever to see again:&#8212;Commencing by praising its still seclusion as it lies there behind its barrier of protecting mountains, he goes on to mention the rural pleasures enjoyed by those who, wandering over the hill-sides, deck their hair with garlands of leaves and flowers. For himself indeed these delights are no more; "but," says he, "do you, ye children full of health and happiness, pursue your innocent enjoyment!" In conclusion he. lovingly apostrophises the clouds which, rising up from the south-west, are, as it were, messengers from home. The word <i>mahoroha</i>, rendered "secluded," is a great crux to the commentators, and Motowori's "Examination of the Synonyms of Japan," pp. 17-18. and Moribe's "<i>Idzu no Koto Waki</i>," Vol. III, p. 31, should be consulted by the student desirous of forming his own opinion on the point. Another apparent difficulty is the word <i>gomoreru</i>, whose position in the sentence Motowori seems to have misunderstood. By following Moribe, and taking it as a compound with the word <i>Awogaki-yama</i> into <i>Awogaki yama-gomoreru</i> the difficulty vanishes, and we are likewise relieved from the necessity of supposing anything so highly improbable as that the Verb <i>komoreru</i> when not compounded, should have commenced with a <i>nigori</i>&#8217;ed syllable. "Complete "signifies "healthy." Mount Heguri is preceded in the original by <i>tatamikomo</i> (Moribe reads <i>tatamigomo</i> with the <i>nigori</i>) a Pillow-Word whose import is disputed. In any case, being a punning one, it cannot be translated. For the "bear-oak" see Sect. LXXII, Note 19. Moribe labours, but without success, to prove that "come," the last word of the translation, signifies "go," and imagines that the prince is expressing his envy of the clouds which are rising and going off in the direction of the home which he will never revisit.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1649"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1654">271:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, a Song of loving regret for his native land.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1650"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1655">271:14</A> "Incomplete Song" <A HREF="errata.htm#57">must</A> be understood as the designation of a poem of a certain number of lines, viz, three, and was probably given by comparison with the greater length of poetical compositions in general.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1651"></A><A HREF="kj096.htm#fr_1656">271:15</A> This poem is an exclamation of distress at the thought of the sword which he had left with his mistress Princess Miyazu and which, if he had had it with him, would doubtless have preserved him from the evil influences of the god of Mount Ibuki, which were the beginning of <a name="page_274"><font size="1" color="green">p. 274</font></A> his end.&#8212;" Sabre-sword" (<A HREF="errata.htm#58"><i>tsurugi</i></A> <i>no tachi</i>) is a curious expression, which Moribe thinks means "double-edged sword."</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_274"><font size="1" color="green">p. 274</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XC.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART XV.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE TURNS INTO A WHITE BIRD)]</h2>  
<p>Thereupon [his] Empresses&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1657"></A><A HREF="#fn_1652"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and likewise [his] august [221] children, who dwelt in Yamato, all went down&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1658"></A><A HREF="#fn_1653"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and built an august mausoleum, and, forthwith crawling hither and thither in the rice-fields encompassing [the mausoleum]. sobbed out a Song, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The <i>Dioscorea quinqueloba</i> crawling hither and thither among the rice-stubble, among the rice-stubble in the rice-fields encompassing [the mausoleum] . . ."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1659"></A><A HREF="#fn_1654"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Thereupon [the dead prince], turning into a white dotterel&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1660"></A><A HREF="#fn_1655"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> eight fathoms [long], and soaring up to Heaven, flew off towards the shore. Then the Empress and likewise the august children, though they tore their feet treading on the stubble of the bamboo-grass, forgot the pain, and pursued him with lamentations. At that time they sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Our loins are impeded in the plain [over-grown with] short bamboo-grass. We are not going through the sky, but oh! we are on foot."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1661"></A><A HREF="#fn_1656"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[222] Again when they entered the salt sea,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1662"></A><A HREF="#fn_1657"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and suffered as they went, they sang, saying.</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"As we go through the sea, our loins are impeded,&#8212;tottering in the sea like herbs growing in a great river-bed."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1663"></A><A HREF="#fn_1658"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_275"><font size="1" color="green">p. 275</font></A></p>  
<p>Again when [the bird] flew and perched on the sea-side, they sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The dotterel of the beach goes not on the beach, but follows the seaside."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1664"></A><A HREF="#fn_1659"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>These four Songs were all sung at [Yamato-take's] august interment. So to the present day these Songs are sung at the great interment of a Heavenly Sovereign. So [the bird] flew off from that country,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1665"></A><A HREF="#fn_1660"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and stopped at Shiki in the land of Kafuchi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1666"></A><A HREF="#fn_1661"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> So they made an august mausoleum there, and laid [Yamato-take] to rest.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1667"></A><A HREF="#fn_1662"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> <A HREF="errata.htm#59">Forthwith</A> that august mausoleum was called by the [223] name of the "August-Mausoleum of the White-Bird."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1668"></A><A HREF="#fn_1663"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> Nevertheless the bird soared up thence to heaven again, and flew away.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_276"><font size="1" color="green">p. 276</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1652"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1657">274:1</A> <i>I.e.</i>, wives. It will be remembered that the historian habitually mentions Yamato-take as if he had been Emperor.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1653"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1658">274:2</A> <i>Q.d.</i>, to the land of Ise.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1654"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1659">274:3</A> The drift of the Song is a comparison of the; helpless wanderings of the mourners in the neighbourhood of the tomb to the convolutions of the <i>Dioscorea quinqueloba</i> (a creeping plant) growing among the rice in the adjacent fields. But there are evidently some lines omitted. If we were to adopt the elegant verses conjecturally supplied by Moribe, the entire translation would run thus: "The <i>Dioscorea quinqueloba</i> crawl hither and thither among the rice-stubble, among the rice-stubble in the rice-fields encompassing [the mausoleum]; but though like it, we crawl hither and thither, and weep and speak to thee, thou answerest not a word."&#8212;Moribe supposes this poem to be the Empress's composition, and the following three to have proceeded from the children.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1655"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1660">274:4</A> As usual when the word chidori (defined as "any kind of dotterel, plover or sandpiper") is used, it is doubtful what bird is really intended. At the end of this Section we are told that the Mausoleum was called the Mausoleum of the White Bird (<A NAME="img_27500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/27500.jpg">)." Specifically, however, these characters are used with their Sinico-Japanese pronunciation of <i>haku-cho</i> as the name of the swan. But as swans are nowhere else mentioned in these "Records "and as moreover their habits are not <a name="page_276"><font size="1" color="green">p. 276</font></A> such as to accord with the legend here narrated, it will perhaps be safer to retain "dotterel "in the translation. "Heron "also has been suggested.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1656"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1661">274:5</A> The signification of this Song is: "It is easy enough for thee, thou bird-spirit! to fly through the air. But remember that we are on foot, and that our feet are getting torn by the short stubble of the bamboo-grass (<i>Bambusa shino</i>)."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1657"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1662">274:6</A> When the bird flew over the sea, they too waded after it through the waves.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1658"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1663">274:7</A> The signification of the Song is: "As we pursue thee through the sea, we sink in the waves up to our middles, and totter like the water-plants against "which strikes the current of a great river."&#8212;The word <i>uwe-gusa</i>, lit. "herbs planted," is curious; but it simply means "herbs growing," as in the translation (<i>conf</i>. our word "plant"). The latter part of the poem is in the original highly elliptical.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1659"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1664">275:8</A> The point of the Song seems to rest on a delicate distinction between the words <i>hama</i>, "beach "and <i>iso</i>, "seaside," which does not obtain in the later Japanese language any more than it does in English. Both <i>hama</i> and <i>iso</i>, "beach" and "seaside," denote the boundary-line between sea and land; but we must suppose with the commentators that while the former was used with special reference to the land, the latter considered the idea (so to speak) from the point of view of the sea. The import of the song is therefore to upbraid the bird for flying over the waves instead of flying along the adjacent shore.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1660"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1665">275:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, says Motowori, from Ise.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1661"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1666">275:10</A> Not to be confounded with the Shiki in Yamato, which is written with different phonetic character.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1662"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1667">275:11</A> The Verb used in the original is <i>shizumeru</i>, "to repress," "to quiet," "to lay," "to establish," hence "to build a temple to a god," "to worship." The grammatical vagueness of the Japanese language helps in all this passage to preserve the connection of ideas in a manner which it is difficult to render in an English translation. Using no pronouns, it does not require to specialise in each instance whether it is the bird that is meant, or Yamato-take, but the two are confounded together in language as they were in thought.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1663"></A><A HREF="kj097.htm#fr_1668">275:12</A> <i>Shira-tori no misasaki</i>. According to the parallel passage of the "Chronicles," it was not only this tomb in Kafuchi, but the previously mentioned tomb at Nobonu, and also another in Yamato, which were severally known by this designation.</P>

<p><a name="page_277"><font size="1" color="green">p. 277</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCI.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART XVI.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE'S BUTLER).]</h2>  
<p>During all the time that this [Prince] His Augustness Yamato-take went about pacifying countries, Nana-tsuka-hagi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1669"></A><A HREF="#fn_1664"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A> ancestor of the Suzerains of Kuna,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1670"></A><A HREF="#fn_1665"><FONT SIZE="1">2a</FONT></A> always followed and respectfully served him as butler.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1664"></A><A HREF="kj098.htm#fr_1669">277:1a</A> The name signifies "seven-grasp shins," implying that the worthy here mentioned was so big and strong as to have shins seven hand-breadths in length. For the use of the word "grasp "as a measure of length, see Sect. VIII, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1665"></A><A HREF="kj098.htm#fr_1670">277:2a</A> This family has already been mentioned at the end of Sect. XXXIV, as descended from Ama-tsu-kume no Mikoto, one of the companions of the Emperor Jim-mu's grandfather on the occasion of his descent from Heaven. But see Note 7 to that Sect. for the probable mistake with regard to the origin of the name.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART XVII.&#8212;YAMATO-TAKE'S DESCENDANTS).]</h2>  
<p>This [Prince] His Augustness Yamato-take wedded Her Augustness Princess Futaji-no-iri,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1671"></A><A HREF="#fn_1666"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> daughter of the Heavenly Sovereign Ikume, and begot an august child: His Augustness Tarashi-naka-tsu-hiko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1672"></A><A HREF="#fn_1667"><FONT SIZE="1">2b</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again, wedding Her Augustness Princess Oto-tachibana&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1673"></A><A HREF="#fn_1668"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> who [afterwards] entered the sea,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1674"></A><A HREF="#fn_1669"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> he begot an august child: King Waka-take&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1675"></A><A HREF="#fn_1670"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again, wedding Princess [224] Futaji,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1676"></A><A HREF="#fn_1671"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> daughter of Oho-tamu-wake,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1677"></A><A HREF="#fn_1672"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> ancestor of the Rulers of the Land of Yasu in Chika-tsu-Afumi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1678"></A><A HREF="#fn_1673"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> he begot an august child: King Ine-yori-wake&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1679"></A><A HREF="#fn_1674"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again, wedding Princess Oho-kibi-take,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1680"></A><A HREF="#fn_1675"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> younger sister of Take-hiko [ancestor of the] Grandees of Kiki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1681"></A><A HREF="#fn_1676"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> he begot an</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<p>

<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_278"><font size="1" color="green">p. 278</font></A></p>  
<p>august child: King Take-kahiko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1682"></A><A HREF="#fn_1677"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again, wedding Princess Kukuma-mori of Yamashiro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1683"></A><A HREF="#fn_1678"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> he begot an august child, King Ashi-kagami-wake&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1684"></A><A HREF="#fn_1679"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). A child by another wife was King Okinaga-ta-wake.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1685"></A><A HREF="#fn_1680"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> Al-together the entire [number] of the august children of His Augustness Yamato-take was six Deities. So His Augustness Tarashi-naka-tsu-hiko [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire. The next, King Ine-yori-wake (<small>was the ancestor of the Dukes of Inukami&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1686"></A><A HREF="#fn_1681"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> and of the Dukes of Takebe</small>.)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1687"></A><A HREF="#fn_1682"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> [225] The next, King Take-kahiko (<small>was the ancestor of the Dukes of Aya in Sanugi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1688"></A><A HREF="#fn_1683"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> the Dukes of Wake in Iyo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1689"></A><A HREF="#fn_1684"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> the Lords of Towo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1690"></A><A HREF="#fn_1685"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> the Headmen of Masa&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1691"></A><A HREF="#fn_1686"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> and the Lords of Miyaji.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1692"></A><A HREF="#fn_1687"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> King Ashi-kagami-wake (<small>was the ancestor of the Lords of Kamakura,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1693"></A><A HREF="#fn_1688"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> the Dukes of Wodzu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1694"></A><A HREF="#fn_1689"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> the Lords of Ihashiro&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1695"></A><A HREF="#fn_1690"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A> and the Lords of Fukita.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1696"></A><A HREF="#fn_1691"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> The child of the next, King Okinaga-ta-wake was King Kuhi-mata-naga-hiko.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1697"></A><A HREF="#fn_1692"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> This King's children were: Her Augustness Princess Ihinu-ma-guro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1698"></A><A HREF="#fn_1693"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> next Okinaga-ma-waka-naka-tsu-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1699"></A><A HREF="#fn_1694"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> next Oto-hime&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1700"></A><A HREF="#fn_1695"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> (<small>three Deities</small>). So the above mentioned King Waka-take wedded Princess Ihinu-ma-guro, [226] and begot King Sume-iro-oho-naka-tsu-hiko.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1701"></A><A HREF="#fn_1696"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> This King wedded Princess Shibanu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1702"></A><A HREF="#fn_1697"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A> daughter of Shibanu-iri-ki&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1703"></A><A HREF="#fn_1698"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> of Afumi, and begot a child, Her Augustness Princess Kaguro.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1704"></A><A HREF="#fn_1699"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> So the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-tarashi-hiko wedded this [lady] Her Augustness Princess Kaguro, and begot King Oho-ye&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1705"></A><A HREF="#fn_1700"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). This King wedded his younger half-sister Queen Shiro-kane,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1706"></A><A HREF="#fn_1701"><FONT SIZE="1">36</FONT></A> and begot children: King Oho-na-gata,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1707"></A><A HREF="#fn_1702"><FONT SIZE="1">37</FONT></A> and next Her Augustness Oho-naka-tsu-hime&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1708"></A><A HREF="#fn_1703"><FONT SIZE="1">38</FONT></A> (<small>two Deities</small>). So this [Lady] Her Augustness Oho-naka-tsu-hime was the august mother&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1709"></A><A HREF="#fn_1704"><FONT SIZE="1">39</FONT></A> of King Kagosaka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1710"></A><A HREF="#fn_1705"><FONT SIZE="1">40</FONT></A> and King Oshikuma.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1711"></A><A HREF="#fn_1706"><FONT SIZE="1">41</FONT></A></p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1666"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1671">277:1b</A> <a name="page_278"><font size="1" color="green">p. 278</font></A> For this name see Sect. LXIX, Note 24.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1667"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1672">277:2b</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the perfect middle prince," a name which is justified by <a name="page_279"><font size="1" color="green">p. 279</font></A> the genealogy as given in the "Chronicles," where he is mentioned as the second of three sons borne by this princess.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1668"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1673">277:3</A> <i>Oto-tachibana-hime no mikoto</i>. <i>Oto</i> signifies "younger [sister]," and <i>Oto-tachibana</i> is the name of the orange.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1669"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1674">277:4</A> See the story in Sect. LXXXIV.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1670"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1675">277:5</A> <i>Waka-tate no miko</i>. This name signifies "young brave."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1671"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1676">277:6</A> <i>Futaji-hime</i>. Signification obscure. Futaji may be the name of a place.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1672"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1677">277:7</A> If <i>Tamu</i> is, as Motowori surmises, the name of a place, this personal name signifies "Great Lord of Tamu."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1673"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1678">277:8</A> <i>Chika-tsu-Afumi no Yasu no kuni no miyatsuko</i>. For <i>Yasu</i> see Sect. LXII, Note 62.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1674"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1679">277:9</A> <i>Ine-yori-wake no miko</i>. This name probably signifies "rice-good-lord."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1675"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1680">277:10</A> <i>Oho-kibi-take-hime</i>. <i>Oho</i> signifies "great." For the other two elements of the compound see next Note.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1676"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1681">277:11</A> The text has <i>Kibi no omi Take-hiko</i>, as if this worthy had been himself the "Grandee of Kibi." Motowori however compares the commencement of Sect. LXXXII (Notes 2 and 3), and supplies the words "ancestor of." <i>Kibi</i> is of course the province of that name (the modern, Bizen, Bitchi&#363;, and Bingo), and <i>take</i> signifies "brave."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1677"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1682">278:12</A> <i>Take-kahiko no miko</i>. <i>Take</i> signifies "brave," <i>kahiko</i> is either "egg "or "cocoon," or else perhaps a corruption of some other word.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1678"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1683">278:13</A> <i>Yamashiro no Kukuma mori-hime</i>. This name is obscure. Motowori identifies Kukuma with a place called <i>Kurihuma</i>, and <i>mori</i> is probably the Verb "to guard."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1679"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1684">278:14</A> <i>Ashi-kagami-wake no miko</i>. This name is written with characters signifying "foot-mirror-[lord]."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1680"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1685">278:15</A> <i>Okinaga-ta-wake no miko</i>. This name is obscure. Motowori believes Okinaga to be the name of a place in Afumi, but has no explanation to offer of <i>ta</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1681"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1686">278:16</A> <i>Inukami no kimi</i>. Inukami is the name of a district in Afumi, Its signification is not clear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1682"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1687">278:17</A> <i>Takebi no kimi</i>. <i>Takebe</i> became the name of a place in Idzumo, but it originally signified "brave tribe," the family having, as in so many other cases, given its name to the place of its residence, instead of being called after the latter. See the origin of the name, given in Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXIV, pp. 35-36.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1683"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1688">278:18</A> <i>Sanugi no Aya no kimi</i>. For <i>Sanugi</i> see Sect. V, Note 6. <i>Aya</i> is a district in the province; the name is of doubtful origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1684"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1689">278:19</A> <a name="page_280"><font size="1" color="green">p. 280</font></A> <i>Iyo no wake no kani</i>. For <i>Iyo</i> see Sect. V, Note 4. (The text here has <i>Ise</i> for Iyo, and the word <i>wake</i> is missing, but Motowori's emendation may be accepted). <i>Wake</i> is the name of a district in Iyo.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1685"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1690">278:20</A> <i>Towo no wake</i>. Of <i>Towo</i> nothing is known.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1686"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1691">278:21</A> <i>Masa no obito</i>. Of <i>Masa</i> nothing is known.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1687"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1692">278:22</A> <i>Miyagi</i> (<A NAME="img_28000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28000.jpg">) <i>no wake</i>. This is Motowori's ingenious emendation of the characters in the text, <A NAME="img_28001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28001.jpg">, out of which it is impossible to make a <A HREF="errata.htm#60">family</A> name. <i>Miyagi</i> is the name of a place in the province of Mikaha, and signifies "temple road."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1688"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1693">278:23</A> <i>Kamakura no wake</i>. Kamakura is the name of a district in the province of Sagami, which became famous during the Middle Ages as the site of an immense town,&#8212;the capital of the Sh&#333;gun, and the centre of the feudalism which then ruled Japan. The import of the name (literally "sickle-store") is not clear, though it has been fancifully explained by native etymologists.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1689"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1694">278:24</A> <i>Wodzu no kimi</i>. The words <i>no kimi</i> are supplied by Motowori, this name and the next being in the text run into one. Wodzu seems to be the name of a place in Afumi, and signifies "little mart."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1690"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1695">278:25</A> <i>Ihashiro no wake</i>. Motowori says that this Ihashiro is not the province of that name, but a place in Kishiu. The meaning of the name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1691"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1696">278:26</A> <i>Fukita no wake</i>. This is but Motowori's conjectural restoration (founded on a statement in the "Chronicles of Old Matters of Former Ages") of the name as given in the text, <A NAME="img_28002"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28002.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1692"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1697">278:27</A> <i>Kuhimata-naga-hiko no miko</i>. <i>Kuhimata</i> (modern <i>Kumata</i>) is the name of a place in Settsu. The signification is obscure. <i>Naga-hiko</i> means "long prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1693"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1698">278:28</A> <i>Ihinu-ma-guro-hime</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "quite black princess of Ihinu," the blackness being doubtless predicated of her hair. <i>Ihinu</i> is the name of a district in Ise, and is written with characters signifying "boiled-rice-moor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1694"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1699">278:29</A> For <i>Okinaga</i> see Note 15. <i>Ma-waka</i> means "truly young." <i>Naka-tsu-hime</i> means "middle princess," referring to her being the second of three.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1695"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1700">278:30</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "younger princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1696"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1701">278:31</A> See Sect. LXXVI, Note 29.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1697"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1702">278:32</A> <i>Shibanu-hime</i>. This name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1698"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1703">278:33</A> <i>Shibunu iri-ko</i>. This name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1699"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1704">278:34</A> <i>Ka-gara hime</i>, see Sect. LXXVI, Note 28.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1700"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1705">278:35</A> <a name="page_281"><font size="1" color="green">p. 281</font></A> For the confusion in this portion of the genealogy see Sect. LXXVI, Note 30.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1701"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1706">278:36</A> <i>Shiro-kane no miko</i>. <i>Shiro-kane</i> means "silver," but Motowori suspects corruption in the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1702"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1707">278:37</A> <i>Oho-nagata no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "great prince of Nagata," the latter being the name of a place in Settsu, signifying "long rice-field."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1703"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1708">278:38</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "great middle princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1704"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1709">278:39</A> Literally, "ancestress."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1705"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1710">278:40</A> Or, "the King of Kagosaka," for it is' uncertain whether Kagosaka should or should not be regarded as the name of a place. The etymology of the name may be <i>kago</i>, "a stag" and <i>saka</i>, "an ascent." The original form of the name and title is <i>Kagosaka no miko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1706"></A><A HREF="kj099.htm#fr_1711">278:41</A> Or, "the King of Oshikuma," <i>Oshikuma no miko</i>. <i>Oshikuma</i> is a word of doubtful etymology.</P>

<p><a name="page_281"><font size="1" color="green">p. 281</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCIII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-K&#332; (PART XVIII. HIS AGE AND PLACE OF BURIAL).]</h2>  
<p>This Heavenly Sovereign's august years were one hundred and thirty-seven, and his august mausoleum is above the Yamanobe road.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1712"></A><A HREF="#fn_1707"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A></p>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCIV.&#8212;EMPEROR SEI-MU.]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign Wata-tarashi-hiko dwelt at the palace of Taka-anaho at Shiga&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1713"></A><A HREF="#fn_1708"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> in Chika-tsu-Afumi and ruled the empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded [227] the Lady Oho-takara,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1714"></A><A HREF="#fn_1709"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> daughter of Take-oshiyama-tari-ne,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1715"></A><A HREF="#fn_1710"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> ancestor of the Grandees of Hodzumi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1716"></A><A HREF="#fn_1711"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and begot an august child: King Wata-nuke&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1717"></A><A HREF="#fn_1712"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> (one Deity). So [the</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_282"><font size="1" color="green">p. 282</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Heavenly Sovereign] raised the Noble Take-uchi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1718"></A><A HREF="#fn_1713"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> [to the office of] Prince Minister,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1719"></A><A HREF="#fn_1714"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> deigned to settle the Rulers of the Great Countries and Small Countries,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1720"></A><A HREF="#fn_1715"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and likewise deigned to settle the boundaries of the various countries, as also the Department Lords of the Great Departments and Small Departments.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1721"></A><A HREF="#fn_1716"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> The Heavenly Sovereign's august years were ninety-five, and his august mausoleum is at Tatanami near Saki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1722"></A><A HREF="#fn_1717"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1708"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1713">281:1b</A> <i>Shiga no Taka-anaho</i>. <i>Shiga</i> is the name of a well known district, and is of uncertain, signification, as is also <i>Taka-anaho</i>. For <i>Chika-tsu-Afumi</i> see Sect. XXIX, Note 20.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1709"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1714">281:2</A> <i>Oto-takara no iratsume</i>. <i>Oto</i> signifies "younger [sister]," and <i>takara</i> is "treasure."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1710"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1715">281:3</A> <i>Oshiyama</i> is the name of a place in Ise, <i>take</i> signifies "brave" and <i>tari</i> and <i>ne</i> are Honorifics of frequent occurrence.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1711"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1716">281:4</A> <i>Hodzumi no omi</i>. See Sect. LXI, Note 4.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1712"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1717">281:5</A> <i>Waka-nuke no miko</i>. This name is of doubtful signification, and Motowori suspects that it is corrupt, and that the true reading would be <i>Waka-take</i>, "young-brave."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1713"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1718">282:6</A> See Sect. LXI, Note 25.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1714"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1719">282:7</A> <A NAME="img_28200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28200.jpg">. Motowori tries to prove that in the earliest times this official title was simply an Honorific surname formed by prefixing the Adjective <A NAME="img_28201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28201.jpg"> "great" to <A NAME="img_28202"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28202.jpg">, a surname read "Omi" (the character signifies properly "attendant," "subject.") Probably like other "gentile names" it combined both characters, and had a tendency to become hereditary.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1715"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1720">282:8</A> <i>Oho-kuni wo-kuni no kuni no miyatsuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1716"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1721">282:9</A> <i>Oho-agata wo-agata no agata nushi</i> (<A NAME="img_28203"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28203.jpg">). Their duties are supposed to have consisted in supervising the government farms.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1717"></A><A HREF="kj101.htm#fr_1722">282:10</A> For <i>Saki</i> see Sect. LXXV, Note 5. <i>Tatanami</i> may perhaps signify "putting shields in a row."</P>
