<p><a name="page_283"><font size="1" color="green">p. 283</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCV.&#8212;EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART I.&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign Tarashi-naka-tsu-hiko dwelt at the palace of Toyora at Anado,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1723"></A><A HREF="#fn_1718"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and likewise at the palace of Kashihi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1724"></A><A HREF="#fn_1719"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in Tsukushi, and ruled the Empire. [328] This Heavenly Sovereign wedded Her Augustness Oho-naka-tsu-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1725"></A><A HREF="#fn_1720"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> daughter of King Oho-ye, and begot august children: King Kagosaka and King Oshikuma (two Deities). Again he wedded Her Augustness Princess Okinaga-tarashi. This Empress&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1726"></A><A HREF="#fn_1721"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> gave birth to august children: His Augustness Homu-ya-wake,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1727"></A><A HREF="#fn_1722"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and next His Augustness Oho-tomo-wake,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1728"></A><A HREF="#fn_1723"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> another name for whom was His Augustness Homuda-wake.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1729"></A><A HREF="#fn_1724"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> The reason why this Heir Apparent&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1730"></A><A HREF="#fn_1725"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> was given the august name of His Augustness Oho-tomo-wake was that when first&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1731"></A><A HREF="#fn_1726"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> born, he had on his august arm [a protuberance of] flesh resembling an elbow-pad,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1732"></A><A HREF="#fn_1727"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> whence the august name bestowed on him. By this it was known while he was in the womb that he would rule countries.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1733"></A><A HREF="#fn_1728"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> In this august reign the granaries of Ahaji were established.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1718"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1723">283:1</A> <a name="page_283"><font size="1" color="green">p. 283</font></A> For <i>Anado</i> see Sect. LXXX (Note 22). <i>Toyora</i> (for <i>Toyo-ura</i>) signifies "fertile shore."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1719"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1724">283:2</A> This name seems to be derived from that of the evergreen oak. It will be noticed that both these capitals are in the South-Western Island of Kiushiu, whereas, from Jim-mu downwards, the capitals of all the Emperors previously mentioned are either in Yamato or in one of the adjacent central provinces.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1720"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1725">283:3</A> For this and the three following names see Sect. XCII, and for <i>Okinaga tarashi</i> Sect. LXII, Note 72.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1721"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1726">283:4</A> Written <A NAME="img_28300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28300.jpg">. It is she who is celebrated in Japanese history under the name of Jin-g&#333; K&#333;g&#333;, and in the "Chronicles" her reign is counted separately. In these "Records," however, the period of her rule is forming part of the reign of her son O-jin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1722"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1727">283:5</A> The signification of this name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1723"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1728">283:6</A> <a name="page_284"><font size="1" color="green">p. 284</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, "great <A HREF="errata.htm#61">elbow-pad</A> lord," <i>tomo</i> signifying "elbow pad." The next sentence of the text gives the traditional origin of this curious name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1724"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1729">283:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, lord of Homuda. <i>Homuda</i> is supposed by Motowori and Moribe to be the name of a place, they (apparently with reason) rejecting as a late addition a note to the "Chronicles," which states that <i>homuda</i> was synonymous with <i>tomo</i> "elbow-pad."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1725"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1730">283:8</A> For "heir apparent "see Sect. XXXIII, Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1726"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1731">283:9</A> This word, says Motowori, is redundant.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1727"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1732">283:10</A> For the use of elbow-pads in war see Sect XIII, Note 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1728"></A><A HREF="kj102.htm#fr_1733">283:11</A> The word rendered "rule" (<i>shiru</i>, <A NAME="img_28400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28400.jpg">) is supplied by the editor of 1687. Motowori supplies the evident lacuna in the text by the word "establish" (<i>sadamaru</i> <A NAME="img_28401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28401.jpg">); but this seems less good. Motowori's reasons for taking the word <i>kuni</i> ("country") in the Plural are, however, convincing,&#8212;the three countries into which Korea was anciently divided, and which are appropriately designated by the title of <i>San Kan</i> (<A NAME="img_28402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28402.jpg">), being evidently designated by the expression in the text, as may be seen both by reference to the parallel passage in the "Chronicles," and also by considering that in this manner that warlike implement the elbow-pad, with the semblance of which the young Emperor was born, obtains its proper significance. This Emperor (for it is he who is known as &#332;-jin Ten-n&#333;) is sometimes designated by the name of the "Emperor in the Womb" (<A NAME="img_28403"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28403.jpg">).</P>

<p><a name="page_284"><font size="1" color="green">p. 284</font></A> [229]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCVI. EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART II.&#8212;THE POSSESSION OF KOREA DIVINELY PROMISED).]</h2>  
<p>This Empress, Her Augustness Princess Okinaga-tarashi, was at that time,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1734"></A><A HREF="#fn_1729"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> divinely possessed. So when the Heavenly Sovereign, dwelling at the palace of Kashihi in Tsukushi, was about to smite the Land of Kumaso,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1735"></A><A HREF="#fn_1730"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> the Heavenly Sovereign played on his august lute, and the Prime <A HREF="errata.htm#62">Minster</A> the Noble Take-uchi, being in the pure court,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1736"></A><A HREF="#fn_1731"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> requested the divine orders. Hereupon the Empress, divinely possessed, charged him with this instruction and counsel: "There is a land to the Westward,</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_285"><font size="1" color="green">p. 285</font></A></p>  
<p>and in that land is abundance of various treasures dazzling to the eye, from gold and silver downwards.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1737"></A><A HREF="#fn_1732"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> I will now bestow this land upon thee." Then the Heavenly Sovereign replied, saying: "If one ascend to a high place and look Westward, no country is to be seen. There is only the great sea;" and saying,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1738"></A><A HREF="#fn_1733"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> "They are lying Deities,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1739"></A><A HREF="#fn_1734"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> he pushed away his august lute, did not play on it, and sat silent. Then the Deities were very angry, and said: "Altogether as for this empire, it is not a land over which thou oughtest to rule. Do thou go to the one road!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1740"></A><A HREF="#fn_1735"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Hereupon the Prince Minister the Noble Take-uchi said; "[I am filled with] awe, my Heavenly Sovereign!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1741"></A><A HREF="#fn_1736"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> Continue playing thy great [230] august lute." Then he slowly drew his august lute to him, and languidly played on it. So almost immediately the sound of the august lute became inaudible. On their forthwith lifting a light and looking, [the Heavenly Sovereign] was dead.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1729"></A><A HREF="kj103.htm#fr_1734">284:1</A> At what time, we are not told.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1730"></A><A HREF="kj103.htm#fr_1735">284:2</A> See Sect. V, Note 17.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1731"></A><A HREF="kj103.htm#fr_1736">284:3</A> This is Motowori's interpretation of the obscure original word <i>sa-niha</i>, which is written phonetically. He supposes it to have <A HREF="errata.htm#63">been</A> so called as being a place used for enquiring the will of the gods, and therefore kept clean and held in reverence. "Place" would perhaps represent the Japanese word <i>niha</i> as well as "court," though "court" has been its usual acceptation in later times.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1732"></A><A HREF="kj103.htm#fr_1737">285:4</A> Literally, "making gold and silver the origin."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1733"></A><A HREF="kj103.htm#fr_1738">285:5</A> Motowori tells us to understand "saying "in the sense of "thinking."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1734"></A><A HREF="kj103.htm#fr_1739">285:6</A> As already frequently remarked, the Japanese mind does not occupy itself much with the distinction (to us all-important) of Singular and Plural. The reason why the translator renders the word <i>kami</i> by the Plural "Deities" throughout this passage is because we learn later on that four divine personages were intended by the author.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1735"></A><A HREF="kj103.htm#fr_1740">285:7</A> <a name="page_286"><font size="1" color="green">p. 286</font></A> With the commentators we must accept this as an alternative name of Hades, without being able satisfactorily to explain it. The expression "eighty road-windings" (<i>yaso kumado</i>) in Sect. XXXII (Note 27) may be compared with this one.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1736"></A><A HREF="kj103.htm#fr_1741">285:8</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "I tremble Sire, for the consequences of thine impiety."</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_286"><font size="1" color="green">p. 286</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCVII.&#8212;EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART III. PREPARATIONS FOR THE CONQUEST OF KOREA).]</h2>  
<p>Then, astonished and alarmed, they set him in a mortuary palace,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1742"></A><A HREF="#fn_1737"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and again taking the country's great offerings,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1743"></A><A HREF="#fn_1738"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> seeking out all sorts of crimes, such as flaying alive and flaying backwards,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1744"></A><A HREF="#fn_1739"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> breaking down the divisions of rice-fields, filling up ditches, evacuating excrements and urine, marriages between superiors and inferiors,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1745"></A><A HREF="#fn_1740"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> marriages with horses, marriages with cattle, marriages with fowls, and marriages with dogs, and having made a great purification of the land,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1746"></A><A HREF="#fn_1741"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> the Noble Takeuchi again stood in the pure court and requested the Deities' commands. Thereupon the manner of their instruction and counsel was exactly the same as on the former day: "Altogether this land is a land to be ruled over by the august child in Thine <A HREF="errata.htm#64">Augustness's</A> august womb."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1747"></A><A HREF="#fn_1742"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> Then the Noble Take-uchi said, "[I am filled with] awe, my Great Deities] The august child in this Deity's [231] womb,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1748"></A><A HREF="#fn_1743"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> what [sort of] child may it be?" [The Deities] replied, saying: "It is a male child." Then [the Noble Take-uchi] requested more particularly, [saying]: "I wish to know the august names of the Great Deities whose words have now thus instructed us." Forthwith [the Deities] replied, saying: "It is the august doing&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1749"></A><A HREF="#fn_1744"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> of</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_287"><font size="1" color="green">p. 287</font></A></p>  
<p>the Great-August-Heaven-Shining-Deity, likewise it is the three great Deities Bottom-Possessing-Male, Middle-Possessing Male and Surface-Possessing-Male.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1750"></A><A HREF="#fn_1745"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> (<small>At this time the august names of these three great Deities were revealed.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1751"></A><A HREF="#fn_1746"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></small>) If now thou truly thinkest to seek that land, thou must, after presenting the offerings&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1752"></A><A HREF="#fn_1747"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> to every one of the Heavenly Deities and Earthly Deities,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1753"></A><A HREF="#fn_1748"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and likewise of the Deities of the mountains and also of all the Deities of the river and of the sea, and setting our august spirits&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1754"></A><A HREF="#fn_1749"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> on the top of thy vessel, put into gourds&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1755"></A><A HREF="#fn_1750"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> the ashes of the <i>podocarpus macrophylla</i> tree,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1756"></A><A HREF="#fn_1751"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> and likewise make a quantity of chopsticks and also of leaf platters,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1757"></A><A HREF="#fn_1752"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> and must scatter [232] them all on the waves of the great sea, that thou mayest cross over." So when [she] punctually fulfilled these instructions, equipped an army, marshalled [her vessels, and crossed over, the fishes of the sea-plain, both great and small, all bore the august vessels&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1758"></A><A HREF="#fn_1753"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> across their backs, and a strong favourable wind arose, and the august vessel followed the billows.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1737"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1742">286:1</A> <a name="page_287"><font size="1" color="green">p. 287</font></A> A temporary resting-place for the corpse before interment. (See Sect. XXXI, Note 20.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1738"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1743">286:2</A> Or, if, with Motowori, we take country in the Plural, "the great offerings of the countries," <i>i.e.</i>, of the various countries or provinces of Japan or of Kiushiu. These "offerings" (<i>nusa</i>) are the same as those mentioned in Sect. XVI (Notes 24 and 25) under the names <i>nigi-te</i> and <i>mitegura</i>. They consisted of cloth, for which in later times paper has been substituted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1739"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1744">286:3</A> There are different views as to the exact bearing of this curious expression. <i>Conf</i>. Sect. XV, Note 10.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1740"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1745">286:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, incest between parents and children.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1741"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1746">286:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, a general purification.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1742"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1747">286:6</A> The Deities now speak to, as well as through, the Empress. Before the quotation marks announcing their words we must understand some such clause as and they added this divine charge." It would <a name="page_288"><font size="1" color="green">p. 288</font></A> also be possible to translate the whole passage thus: "Thereupon the manner of their instruction and counsel. was '[Things] being exactly as on the former day, altogether this land,'" etc., etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1743"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1748">286:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, in the Empress's womb. Motowori supposes that she is thus spoken of as a Deity on account of her being at that moment divinely possessed.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1744"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1749">286:8</A> Literally, "heart."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1745"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1750">287:9</A> <i>Soko-dzu-tsu-no-wo</i>, <i>Naka-dzu-tsu-no wo</i>, and <i>Uha-dzu-tsu-no-wo</i> three of the deities born at the time of the purification of Izanagi (the "Male-Who-Invites") on his return from Hades, and known collectively as the Deities of the Inlet of Sumi. (See Sect. X, Notes 18 and 22). The grammar of this sentence is, as Motowori remarks, not lucid. One would expect the author to say that it was "the august doing" of all the four deities mentioned.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1746"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1751">287:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, says Motowori, they then first informed Take-uchi who they were. Up in that time, it had not been known by what Deities the Empress was possessed. Mabuchi, however, rejected this gloss as a later additions.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1747"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1752">287:11</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the sacred offerings of white and blue cloth.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1748"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1753">287:12</A> Here <A HREF="errata.htm#65">written with</A> the Chinese locution <A NAME="img_28800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28800.jpg">, by some rendered "the Spirit of Heaven and Earth." <i>Conf</i>. Sect. I. Note II.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1749"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1754">287:13</A> Here, as before, the Singular would be at least as natural an interpretation as the Plural. The three ocean-deities are supposed to be specially referred to, and in that case, the three being easily conceived as one (like the deified peaches mentioned in Sect. IX, Note 19) owing to the want of discrimination in Japanese between Singular and Plural, we might retain the Singular in English. Altogether the Sun-goddess seems out of place in this passage, and it would be satisfactory to have some authority for expunging from it the mention of her name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1750"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1755">287:14</A> Or, "into a gourd."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1751"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1756">287:15</A> In the original <i>maki</i> (<A NAME="img_28801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28801.jpg">). In modern <i>ma-ki</i> signifies the <i>P. macrophylla</i>, as in the translation. It is however uncertain whether that or the <i>Cham&aelig;cyparis obtusa</i> (both being conifers), or simply any "true" (<i>i.e.</i>, good) tree is here intended by the author.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1752"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1757">287:16</A> <i>I.e.</i>, broad shallow platters made of the oak-tree, and used for placing food on.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1753"></A><A HREF="kj104.htm#fr_1758">287:17</A> Viz., that in which the Empress herself took passage.</P>

<p><a name="page_289"><font size="1" color="green">p. 289</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART IV.&#8212;THE EMPRESS JIN-G&#332; CONQUERS KOREA)]</h2>  
<p>So the wave&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1759"></A><A HREF="#fn_1754"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> of the august vessel pushed up onto the land of Shiragi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1760"></A><A HREF="#fn_1755"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> reaching to the middle of the country. Thereupon the chieftain&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1761"></A><A HREF="#fn_1756"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> of the country, alarmed and trembling. petitioned&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1762"></A><A HREF="#fn_1757"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> [the Empress], saying: "From this time forward obedient to the Heavenly Sovereign's commands, I will feed his august horses and will marshal vessels every year, nor ever let the vessels' keels&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1763"></A><A HREF="#fn_1758"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> dry or their poles and oars dry, and will respectfully serve him without drawing back while heaven and earth shall last."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1764"></A><A HREF="#fn_1759"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> So therefore the Land of <A HREF="errata.htm#66">Shiragi</A>&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1765"></A><A HREF="#fn_1760"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> was constituted the feeder of the august horses, and the Land of Kudara [133] was constituted the crossing store.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1766"></A><A HREF="#fn_1761"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> Then the Empress stuck her august staff on the gate of the chieftain of Shiragi, and having made the Rough August Spirits&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1767"></A><A HREF="#fn_1762"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> of the Great Deities of the Inlet of Sumi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1768"></A><A HREF="#fn_1763"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> the guardian Deities of the land, she laid them to rest,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1769"></A><A HREF="#fn_1764"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> and crossed back. So while this business&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1770"></A><A HREF="#fn_1765"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> was yet unconcluded, [the child] with which she was pregnant was about to be born. Forthwith, in order to restrain her august womb, she took a stone and wound it round the waist of her august skirt,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1771"></A><A HREF="#fn_1766"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> and the august child was born after she had crossed [back] to the Land of Tsukushi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1772"></A><A HREF="#fn_1767"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> So the name by which the place was called where the [234] august child was born was Umi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1773"></A><A HREF="#fn_1768"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> Again the stone which she wound round her august skirt is at the village of Ito&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1774"></A><A HREF="#fn_1769"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> in the Land of Tsukushi.</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1754"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1759">289:1</A> <a name="page_289"><font size="1" color="green">p. 289</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the wave on which the august vessel was riding."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1755"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1760">289:2</A> In Sinico-Japanese <i>Shin ra</i> (<A NAME="img_28900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/28900.jpg">), one of the three states into which Korea was anciently divided, the other two being known in pure <a name="page_290"><font size="1" color="green">p. 290</font></A> Japanese as <i>Kudara</i> and <i>Koma</i> (in Sinico-Japanese <i>Hiyaku-sai</i> <A NAME="img_29000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29000.jpg"> and K&#333;rai <A NAME="img_29001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29001.jpg">). <i>Shiragi</i> is evidently a mere corruption of the Sinico-Japanese form, which closely resembles the native Korean <i>Shin-la</i>. The origin of the pure Japanese forms of the other two names is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1756"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1761">289:3</A> The editions previous to Motowori's have "King" (<A NAME="img_29002"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29002.jpg"> instead of <A NAME="img_29003"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29003.jpg">); but as the latter character is used in all parallel passages of this work, we must attribute the occurrence of the former in this single place to a copyist's error, and accuse the author rather than his commentator of the ill-natured degradation of the Korean King into a mere chieftain (more literally a "master").</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1757"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1762">289:4</A> The character <A NAME="img_29004"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29004.jpg">, which is here used, is that employed in speaking of a subject's addressing his sovereign.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1758"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1763">289:5</A> Literally "bellies."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1759"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1764">289:6</A> Literally, "with heaven and earth."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1760"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1765">289:7</A> See Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1761"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1766">289:8</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the sea-store." The author means to say that from the Land of Kudara tribute was to be paid with the regularity implied by the King's asseveration to the effect that the keels, poles, and oars of the [tribute-bearing] vessels should never remain dry.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1762"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1767">289:9</A> <i>Ara-mi-tama</i>, the antithetical term to which is <i>Nigi-mi-tama</i>, '' Gentle August Spirit." We also find <i>Saki-mi-tama</i> and <i>Kushi-mi-tama</i>, which signify respectively "August Luck-Spirit "and "Wondrous August Spirit." In this passage it must be understood that the spirits which floated above the Imperial junk to protect it were the "Gentle August Spirits," while the "Rough August Spirits" presided at the Empress's feats of arms and kept the enemy in subjection. Motowori warns us not to fall into the mistake of supposing that the Rough and Gentle Spirits of a god were separate individualities, they being only, according to him, various manifestations of the same individuality. The student is advised to consult his beautifully written note on the subject of these spirits in Vol. XXX, pp. 72-76 of his Commentary.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1763"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1768">289:10</A> See Sect. X Note 22.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1764"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1769">289:11</A> Literally "established and worshipped." Motowori says that this mention of their being laid to rest is made with an implied reference to the journey on which the deities in question had accompanied the Imperial army. He also tries to prove that this laying to rest of the deities must have occurred after the return of the Empress to Japan, as it is not possible to suppose that the gods could find a home in a foreign land (!). But the wording of the text is against him</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1765"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1770">289:12</A> <a name="page_291"><font size="1" color="green">p. 291</font></A> Literally "government"</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1766"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1771">289:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, as Motowori suggests, "she wrapped the stone up, and tied it into the waist of her skirt in something resembling a sash."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1767"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1772">289:14</A> In South-Western Japan.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1768"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1773">289:15</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "bearing." The word, however, also signifies "sea." According to the "Chronicles" the original name of the village was Kada.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1769"></A><A HREF="kj105.htm#fr_1774">289:16</A> This word signifies "thread," and would therefore, one might think, find a more appropriate place in I the legend next narrated, where the "threads "of the Empress's garment are specially mentioned.</P>

<p><a name="page_291"><font size="1" color="green">p. 291</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. XCIX.&#8212;EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART V.&#8212;THE EMPRESS JIN-G&#332; FISHES IN TSUKUSHI).]</h2>  
<p>Again when, having reached the village of Tamashima&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1775"></A><A HREF="#fn_1770"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> in the Department of Matsura&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1776"></A><A HREF="#fn_1771"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in Tsukushi, she partook of an august meal on the bank of the river, it being then the first decade of the fourth moon, she then sat on a shoal&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1777"></A><A HREF="#fn_1772"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in the middle of the river, picked out threads from her august skirt, used grains of rice as bait, and hooked the trout&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1778"></A><A HREF="#fn_1773"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> in the river. (<small>The name by which the river is called is the Wo-gaha;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1779"></A><A HREF="#fn_1774"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> again the name by which the shoal is called is Kachi-do-hime.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1780"></A><A HREF="#fn_1775"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></small>) So down to the present time it is an uninterrupted [custom] for women in the first decade of the fourth moon to pick out threads from their skirts, use grains as bait, and hook trout.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1770"></A><A HREF="kj106.htm#fr_1775">291:1</A> <a name="page_291"><font size="1" color="green">p. 291</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>. "jewel-island."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1771"></A><A HREF="kj106.htm#fr_1776">291:2</A> <i>Matsura-gata</i>. The "Chronicles" give an absurd derivation of Matsura from the Adjective <i>medzurashi</i>, "astonishing," which the Empress is supposed to have ejaculated on finding a trout hooked to her line! The obvious etymology is <i>matsu-ura</i>, "pine-beach."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1772"></A><A HREF="kj106.htm#fr_1777">291:3</A> The character in the original is <A NAME="img_29100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29100.jpg"> (for <A NAME="img_29101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29101.jpg">), in Japanese <i>iso</i>, which may or may not be connected with the word <i>ishi</i>, "stone." In any case Motowori is not justified in saying that it must be understood to mean <a name="page_292"><font size="1" color="green">p. 292</font></A> "stone "in this place, as <i>iso</i> means rather a sandy than a stony place, rising above the water level.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1773"></A><A HREF="kj106.htm#fr_1778">291:4</A> In Japanese <i>ayu</i>, a small species of the salmon family (<i>Plecoglossus altivelis</i>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1774"></A><A HREF="kj106.htm#fr_1779">291:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "little river."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1775"></A><A HREF="kj106.htm#fr_1780">291:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "princess of the gate of victory." But though the words lend themselves to this interpretation, it can hardly be supposed that such is their real etymology, and indeed the editor of 1687 draws attention in a Note to the difficulty of accepting the statement in the text.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_292"><font size="1" color="green">p. 292</font></A> [235]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. C.&#8212;EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART VI.&#8212;THE EMPRESS JIN-G&#332; SUBDUES YAMATO).]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon, when Her Augustness Princess Okinaga-tarashi was returning up to Yamato, she, owing to doubts concerning the disposition&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1781"></A><A HREF="#fn_1776"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> of the people, prepared a mourning-vessel,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1782"></A><A HREF="#fn_1777"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> set the august child in that mourning-vessel, and let a report ooze out that the august child was already dead. While she went up thus, King Kagosaka and King Oshikuma,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1783"></A><A HREF="#fn_1778"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> having heard [of the circumstance], thought to waylay&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1784"></A><A HREF="#fn_1779"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> her, went forth to the moor of Toga,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1785"></A><A HREF="#fn_1780"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and hunted for an omen. Then King Kagosaka climbed up an oak-tree,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1786"></A><A HREF="#fn_1781"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and then&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1787"></A><A HREF="#fn_1782"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> a large and angry boar came forth, dug up the oak-tree, and forthwith devoured King Kagosaka. His younger brother, King Oshikuma, undaunted by this circumstance, raised an army and lay in wait [for the Empress], to close with the mourning-vessel as being an empty&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1788"></A><A HREF="#fn_1783"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> vessel. Then an army was landed from the mourning-vessel,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1789"></A><A HREF="#fn_1784"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and joined in combat [with the opposing forces]. At this time King Oshikuma made the Noble Isahi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1790"></A><A HREF="#fn_1785"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> ancestor of [236] the Kishi Clan of Naniha,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1791"></A><A HREF="#fn_1786"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> his generalissimo;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1792"></A><A HREF="#fn_1787"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and on</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_293"><font size="1" color="green">p. 293</font></A></p>  
<p>the august side of the Heir Apparent His Augustness Naniha-ne-ko-take-furu-kuma,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1793"></A><A HREF="#fn_1788"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> ancestor of the Grandees of Wani,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1794"></A><A HREF="#fn_1789"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> was made generalissimo. So when [the Empress's troops] had driven [King Oshikuma's troops] as far as Yamashiro, [the latter] turned and made a stand, and both [sides] fought together without retreating. Then His Augustness Take-furu-kuma planned, and caused it to be said that, as Her Augustness Okinaga-tarashi was already dead, there was no need for further fighting,&#8212;forthwith snapping his bowstrings and feigning submission. Therefore King Oshikuma's generalissimo, believing the falsehood, unbent his bows and put away his arms. Then [the Empress's troops] picked out of their topknots some prepared bowstrings (<small>one name [of the bowstrings] was <i>usa-yu-dzuru</i>;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1795"></A><A HREF="#fn_1790"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A></small>) stretched [their bows] again, and pursued and smote [the enemy]. So [these] fled away to Afusaka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1796"></A><A HREF="#fn_1791"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> rallied, and fought again. Then [the Empress's troops] pursued on, and defeated them, and cut to pieces that army at Sasanami.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1797"></A><A HREF="#fn_1792"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> Thereupon King Oshikuma, together with the Noble Isahi, being pursued and pressed, got on board a vessel and floated on the sea, and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Come on, my lord! rather than be stricken [237] by Furu-kuma's hurtful hand, I will plunge like the grebe into the Sea of Afumi,&#8212;I will!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1798"></A><A HREF="#fn_1793"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Forthwith they plunged into the sea, and died together.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1776"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1781">292:1</A> <a name="page_293"><font size="1" color="green">p. 293</font></A> Literally, "the hearts."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1777"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1782">292:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, a boat or junk containing a coffin. We might also (adopting the interpretation given by the older editors to the character in this passage) translate by "specially prepared a mourning-vessel."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1778"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1783">292:3</A> These two princes, who are first mentioned at the end of Sect. <a name="page_294"><font size="1" color="green">p. 294</font></A> XCII (Notes 40 and 41), were. according to the story, elder sons of the late monarch Chi&#363;-ai, and therefore step-sons of the Empress Jing&#333; and half-brothers to the young Emperor &#332;-jin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1779"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1784">292:4</A> Literally, "wait for and catch." This "catch" is always taken by Motowori to mean "slay."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1780"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1785">292:5</A> <i>Taga-nu</i>. It was in the province of Settsu. The etymology of the name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1781"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1786">292:6</A> The species mentioned in the text the <i>Quercus serrata</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1782"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1787">292:7</A> Motowori's conjecture that the character <A NAME="img_29400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29400.jpg">, "then," is a copyist's error for <A NAME="img_29401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29401.jpg">, "saw "or "looked," seems hardly called for, and the translator has therefore not departed from the traditional reading.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1783"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1788">292:8</A> <i>I.e.</i>, defenceless, not filled with troops.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1784"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1789">292:9</A> Which of course was in reality no mourning-vessel, but full of the soldiers who had just returned from conquering Korea.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1785"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1790">292:10</A> <i>Isahi no Sakune</i>. <i>Isahi</i> or <i>Isachi</i> is supposed to mean "leading elder."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1786"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1791">292:11</A> <i>Naniha no Kishi be</i>. Naniha is the old name of the sea and river-shore on which I now stands the town of Ohosaka. The name Kishi is said by Motowori to be properly a Korean official designation (<A NAME="img_29402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29402.jpg">), but it is one whose origin is to be sought in China.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1787"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1792">292:12</A> <A NAME="img_29403"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29403.jpg">, <i>Sh&#333;gun</i>. This is the earliest mention of this office, which, passing from the military to the political sphere, played such a great part in the mediaeval and modern history of Japan.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1788"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1793">293:13</A> The signification of all the elements of this compound name is not clear, but it is partly Honorific and descriptive of the bravery of its bearer.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1789"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1794">293:14</A> <i>Wani no omi</i> (see Sect. LXII, Note 11).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1790"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1795">293:15</A> The text is here somewhat obscure, and the note in small print is of doubtful authenticity. If we retain it, we must understand it to mean that <i>usa-yu-dzuru</i>, a term whose derivation is by no means clear, was an alternative name of the <i>make dzuru</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "prepared bowstrings," such as they had brought <A HREF="errata.htm#67">with</A> them concealed in their top-knots.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1791"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1796">293:16</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the pass [or hill] of meeting." It was on the boundaries of the provinces of Yamashiro and Afumi. The modern pronunciation is <i>Osaka</i> (not to be confounded with the like-sounding name of a well-known town in Central Japan).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1792"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1797">293:17</A> <i>I.e.</i>, in Afumi. Mabuchi, in his "Dictionary of Pillow-Words," explains this name to mean "bamboo-grass bending." Motowori, following the <i>Shim-puku-ji</i> MS., alters the character <A NAME="img_29404"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29404.jpg"> before the word <i>Sasanami</i> to <A NAME="img_29405"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29405.jpg">, but without sufficient warrant.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1793"></A><A HREF="kj107.htm#fr_1798">293:18</A> <a name="page_295"><font size="1" color="green">p. 295</font></A> The meaning of the poem is. "Rather than fall beneath the attacks of the enemy, let us drown ourselves in the Sea of Afumi'' (Lake Biwa).&#8212;For the expression "stricken by a hurtful hand "see Sect. XLIV, Note 33.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_295"><font size="1" color="green">p. 295</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CI.&#8212;EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART VIII.&#8212;THE HEIR APPARENT EXCHANGES NAMES WITH THE GREAT DEITY IZASA-WAKE).]</h2>  
<p>So when His Augustness the Noble Take-uchi, taking with him the Heir Apparent for the purpose of purification,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1799"></A><A HREF="#fn_1794"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> passed through the lands of Afumi and Wakasa,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1800"></A><A HREF="#fn_1795"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> he built a temporary palace at Tsunuga&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1801"></A><A HREF="#fn_1796"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> at the mouth of the Road of Koshi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1802"></A><A HREF="#fn_1797"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> [for the Heir Apparent] to dwell in. Then His Augustness the Great Deity Izasa-wake,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1803"></A><A HREF="#fn_1798"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> who dwelt in that place, appeared at night in a dream,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1804"></A><A HREF="#fn_1799"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and said: "I wish to exchange my name for the august name of the august child." Then [the dreamer of the dream] prayed, saying: "[I] am filled with awe!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1805"></A><A HREF="#fn_1800"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> The name shall be respectfully exchanged according to thy command." Again the Deity charged [him, saying]: "To-morrow morning [the Heir Apparent] must go out on the beach; I will present my [thank] offering for the name [given me] in exchange." So when [the Heir Apparent] went out in the morning to the beach, the [238] whole shore was lined with broken-nosed dolphin-fishes.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1806"></A><A HREF="#fn_1801"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> Thereupon the august child caused the Deity to be addressed, saying: "Thou bestowest on me fish of thine august food."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1807"></A><A HREF="#fn_1802"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> So again his august name was <A HREF="errata.htm#68">honoured</A> by his being called the Great Deity of August Food.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1808"></A><A HREF="#fn_1803"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A>" So he is now styled the Food-Wondrous-Great-Deity.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1809"></A><A HREF="#fn_1804"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_296"><font size="1" color="green">p. 296</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Again the blood from the noses of the dolphin-fishes stank. So the strand was called by the name of Chiura.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1810"></A><A HREF="#fn_1805"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> it is now styled Tsunuga.</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1794"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1799">295:1</A> Viz., by water, as described in Sect. X.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1795"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1800">295:2</A> Etymology obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1796"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1801">295:3</A> The marvellous etymology of this name which the author seems to adopt will be found at the end of the Section (Note 12). The compiler of the "Chronicles "is probably nearer the truth when he derives it from <i>tsunu-ga</i>, "horned stag."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1797"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1802">295:4</A> For the meaning of this curious expression see Sect. LX, Note 20.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1798"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1803">295:5</A> The commentators give no explanation of this one of the three names of the deity in question. It would appear to be made up of a word expressive of solicitation and of a portion of the Heir Apparent 's name, thus signifying perhaps "Come on, Wake, [give me thy name] "with reference to the legend here narrated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1799"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1804">295:6</A> To which of the two personages of the legend is not clear. Motowori, however, prefers to suppose that it was to Take-uchi, as, if the prince himself were intended, the word "dream "would probably receive the Honorific <A NAME="img_29600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/29600.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1800"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1805">295:7</A> Or, "I reverence [thy commands]."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1801"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1806">295:8</A> Motowori supposes that they were caught by being speared in the nose.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1802"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1807">295:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "fish that would naturally have formed part of thine august food," is less good to translate by "fish for <i>mine</i> august food." As usual, the original Japanese text has no Personal Pronouns to guide the reader; but, though Emperors are sometimes made to use the Honorific in speaking of themselves, this is not the custom in the case of princes' and &#332;-jin is supposed to have not yet assumed the Imperial dignity.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1803"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1808">295:10</A> <i>Mi-ke-tsu-oho-kami</i>. Motowori mentions several Deities of this name, who were, according to him, separate beings.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1804"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1809">295:11</A> <i>Kehi no oho-kami</i>. The meaning of the syllable <i>hi</i>, rendered by "wondrous "in accordance with Motowori's suggestion, is not certain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1805"></A><A HREF="kj108.htm#fr_1810">296:12</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the strand of blood." From <i>chi-ura</i> Motowori is obliged to derive Tsunuga as well as he can in order not to throw discredit on the implied assertion of the author: that the latter is but a mispronunciation of the former. The true derivation of Tsunuga is probably from <i>tsunuga</i> "horned stag," as already stated in Note 3.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_297"><font size="1" color="green">p. 297</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CII.&#8212;EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART VIII.&#8212;THE EMPRESS JIN-G&#332; PRESENTS LIQUOR TO THE HEIR APPARENT).]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon, when the [Heir Apparent] returned up [to the Capital], his august parent, Her Augustness Princess Okinaga-tarashi. distilled some waiting-liquor,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1811"></A><A HREF="#fn_1806"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and presented it to him. Then his august parent sang augustly, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"This august liquor is not my august liquor;&#8212;oh! it is august liquor respectfully brought as a divine congratulation, a repeated congratulation, a bountiful congratulation, a reiterated congratulation by the Small August Deity, who dwells eternally, [239] firmly standing. Partake not shallowly! Go on! go on!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1812"></A><A HREF="#fn_1807"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Having thus sung, she presented to him the great august liquor. Then His Augustness the Noble Takeuchi replied for the august child and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Whatever person distilled this august liquor must surely have distilled it singing the while with that drum on the mortar,&#8212;must surely have distilled it dancing the while, for this august liquor, august liquor, to be ever more and more joyful. Go on! go on!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1813"></A><A HREF="#fn_1808"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>These are Drinking Songs.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1814"></A><A HREF="#fn_1809"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1806"></A><A HREF="kj109.htm#fr_1811">297:1</A> <a name="page_297"><font size="1" color="green">p. 297</font></A> <i>Machi-sake</i>. This expression, which recurs in the poems of the "Collection of a Myriad Leaves," signifies liquor distilled for an absent friend by those who are awaiting his return.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1807"></A><A HREF="kj109.htm#fr_1812">297:2</A> The General signification of the Song is: "Think not that this liquor was made by me. &#8217;Tis a present from the small August Deity (<i>Suku-na-biko-no</i>), who dwells forever in unshaken power and who sends <a name="page_298"><font size="1" color="green">p. 298</font></A> it to thee with endless congratulation. Come on! come on! drink deeply!"&#8212;Some of the expressions in this Song are a subject of debate among the commentators. Excepting the clause "partake not shallowly," in which the translator has adopted the opinion of the author of the "Explanation of the Songs in the Chronicles of Japan," Moribe's interpretation has been followed throughout. The latter critic would identify <i>asazu</i> ("not slowly") with <i>amasazu</i> ("without leaving anything"). But there seems no warrant for supposing such an elision of the syllable <i>sa</i>. The use of the expression <i>karuhoshi</i> and <i>motohoshi</i> to express reiteration is worthy of notice. It will be remembered that the Deity mentioned was the microscopic personage who came riding over the waves to share the sovereignty of Idzumo with the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land (see Sect. XXVII).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1808"></A><A HREF="kj109.htm#fr_1813">297:3</A> This Song signifies; "Such a joyful feast must surely have been preceded by a joyful distilling of the liquor for it. Continue to drink, oh Prince!"&#8212;The commentators disagree on the subject of one or two of the words of this Song, in which the translator has followed Motowori's interpretation throughout. The words "that drum" are the chief difficulty. Motowori supposes that drums, being originally unknown in Japan, were first seen by the Japanese on the occasion of the conquest of Korea in this very reign, and he thinks that the drum would be placed by the side of the mortar during the pounding of the rice out of which the liquor was to be made. "That drum" means the drum belonging to the pounder of the rice. The original words <i>so no</i>, "that," might also be rendered by "his."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1809"></A><A HREF="kj109.htm#fr_1814">297:4</A> Literally, "liquor-rejoicing songs."</P>

<p><a name="page_298"><font size="1" color="green">p. 298</font></A> [240]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CIII.&#8212;EMPEROR CHI&#362;-AI (PART IX.&#8212;HIS DEATH AND THAT OF THE EMPRESS JIN-G&#332;).]</h2>  
<p>Altogether the august years of this Heavenly Sovereign Tarashi-naka-tsu-hiko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1815"></A><A HREF="#fn_1810"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> were fifty-two. His august mausoleum is at Nagaye,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1816"></A><A HREF="#fn_1811"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> near Wega,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1817"></A><A HREF="#fn_1812"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in Kafuchi. (<small>The Empress died at the august age of one hundred. She was buried in the mausoleum of Tatanami in Saki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1818"></A><A HREF="#fn_1813"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></small>)</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1810"></A><A HREF="kj110.htm#fr_1815">298:1</A> <a name="page_298"><font size="1" color="green">p. 298</font></A> The Emperor Chi&#363;-ai. The author of these "Records "not recognizing, <a name="page_299"><font size="1" color="green">p. 299</font></A> as does the author of the "Chronicles," the time during which the Empress Jin-g&#333; held sway as a separate reign, Chi&#363;-ai is by fiction supposed to have reigned down to the moment his posthumous son &#332;-jin mounted the throne after the conquest of Korea and of Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1811"></A><A HREF="kj110.htm#fr_1816">298:2</A> <i>I.e.</i> "long branch," or perhaps "long inlet.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1812"></A><A HREF="kj110.htm#fr_1817">298:3</A> Etymology obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1813"></A><A HREF="kj110.htm#fr_1818">298:4</A> Mabuchi and Motowori seem right in supposing the sentence in small type to be an addition to the text, copied from the "Chronicles." But as all the MSS. and printed editions previous to Motowori's contain it, it has been retained in the translation.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_299"><font size="1" color="green">p. 299</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CIV.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1819"></A><A HREF="#fn_1814"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> (PART 1.&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Homuda-wake dwelt at the palace of Akira at Karushima,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1820"></A><A HREF="#fn_1815"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded three&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1821"></A><A HREF="#fn_1816"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> queens, daughters of King Homuda-no-Ma-waka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1822"></A><A HREF="#fn_1817"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> the name of one of whom was Her Augustness Princess Takagi-no-iri;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1823"></A><A HREF="#fn_1818"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> of the next, Her Augustness Naka-tsu-hime;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1824"></A><A HREF="#fn_1819"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and of the next, Her Augustness Oto-hime.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1825"></A><A HREF="#fn_1820"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> (<small>The father of these Queens, King Homuda-no-ma-Waka, was the son of His Augustness Prince Iho-ki-noiri,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1826"></A><A HREF="#fn_1821"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> by his [241] wife Shiritsuki-tome,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1827"></A><A HREF="#fn_1822"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> daughter of the Noble Take-inada,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1828"></A><A HREF="#fn_1823"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> ancestor of the Chiefs of Wohari.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1829"></A><A HREF="#fn_1824"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> So the august children of Her Augustness Princess Takagi-no-iri were: His Augustness Nakuta-no-oho-waka-tsu-hiko;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1830"></A><A HREF="#fn_1825"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> next His Augustness Oho-yama-mori;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1831"></A><A HREF="#fn_1826"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> next His Augustness Iza-no-ma-waka;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1832"></A><A HREF="#fn_1827"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> next his younger sister the Lady of Ohohara;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1833"></A><A HREF="#fn_1828"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> next the Lady of Komuku.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1834"></A><A HREF="#fn_1829"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> (<small>Five Deities</small>). The august children of Her Augustness Naka-tsu-hime were: the Lady of Arata in Ki;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1835"></A><A HREF="#fn_1830"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> next His Augustness Oho-sazaki;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1836"></A><A HREF="#fn_1831"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> next His Augustness Netori.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1837"></A><A HREF="#fn_1832"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A> (Three Deities). The august [242] children of Her Augustness Oto-hime were: the Lady Abe;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1838"></A><A HREF="#fn_1833"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> next the Lady of Mihara in Ahaji;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1839"></A><A HREF="#fn_1834"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> next</p>  
<p>

<p><a name="page_300"><font size="1" color="green">p. 300</font></A></p>  
<p>the Lady of Unu in Ki;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1840"></A><A HREF="#fn_1835"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> next the Lady of Minu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1841"></A><A HREF="#fn_1836"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A> (<small>five Deities</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1842"></A><A HREF="#fn_1837"><FONT SIZE="1">24</FONT></A> Again he wedded the Princess Miya-nushi-ya-kaha-ye,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1843"></A><A HREF="#fn_1838"><FONT SIZE="1">25</FONT></A>daughter of the Grandee Wani-no-Hifure, and begot august children: Uji-no-waki-iratsuko;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1844"></A><A HREF="#fn_1839"><FONT SIZE="1">26</FONT></A> next his younger sister Yata-no-waki-iratsume;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1845"></A><A HREF="#fn_1840"><FONT SIZE="1">27</FONT></A> next Queen Medori.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1846"></A><A HREF="#fn_1841"><FONT SIZE="1">28</FONT></A> (<small>Three <A HREF="errata.htm#73">Deities</A></small>). Again he wedded Wo-nabe-no-iratsume,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1847"></A><A HREF="#fn_1842"><FONT SIZE="1">29</FONT></A> younger sister of Yakaha-ye-hime, and begot an august child: Uji-no-iratsume.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1848"></A><A HREF="#fn_1843"><FONT SIZE="1">30</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again he wedded Okinaga-ma-waka-naka-tsu-hima,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1849"></A><A HREF="#fn_1844"><FONT SIZE="1">31</FONT></A> daughter of King Kuhimata-naga-hiko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1850"></A><A HREF="#fn_1845"><FONT SIZE="1">32</FONT></A> and begot an august child: King Waka-nuke-futa-mata&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1851"></A><A HREF="#fn_1846"><FONT SIZE="1">33</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again he wedded the Princess of Itowi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1852"></A><A HREF="#fn_1847"><FONT SIZE="1">34</FONT></A> daughter of Shima-tari-ne,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1853"></A><A HREF="#fn_1848"><FONT SIZE="1">35</FONT></A> ancestor [243] of the Agricultural Chiefs of Sakurawi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1854"></A><A HREF="#fn_1849"><FONT SIZE="1">36</FONT></A> and begot an august child; His Augustness Hayabusa-wake&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1855"></A><A HREF="#fn_1850"><FONT SIZE="1">37</FONT></A> (<small>one Deity</small>). Again, he wedded Naga-hime of Idzumi in Himuka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1856"></A><A HREF="#fn_1851"><FONT SIZE="1">38</FONT></A> and begot august children: King Oho-haye,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1857"></A><A HREF="#fn_1852"><FONT SIZE="1">39</FONT></A> next King Wo-haye;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1858"></A><A HREF="#fn_1853"><FONT SIZE="1">40</FONT></A> next Hata-bi-no-waki-iratsume&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1859"></A><A HREF="#fn_1854"><FONT SIZE="1">41</FONT></A> (<small>three Deities</small>). Again he wedded Princess Ka-guro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1860"></A><A HREF="#fn_1855"><FONT SIZE="1">42</FONT></A> and begot august children: Kaha-rada-no-iratsume;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1861"></A><A HREF="#fn_1856"><FONT SIZE="1">43</FONT></A> next, Tama-no-iratsume,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1862"></A><A HREF="#fn_1857"><FONT SIZE="1">44</FONT></A> next, Osaka-no-oho-naka-tsu-hime;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1863"></A><A HREF="#fn_1858"><FONT SIZE="1">45</FONT></A> next, Toho-hi-no-iratsume;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1864"></A><A HREF="#fn_1859"><FONT SIZE="1">46</FONT></A> next, King Kataji&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1865"></A><A HREF="#fn_1860"><FONT SIZE="1">47</FONT></A> (<small>five Deities</small>). Again, he wedded Nu-iro-me of Kadzuraki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1866"></A><A HREF="#fn_1861"><FONT SIZE="1">48</FONT></A> and begot an august [244] child: King Iza-no-ma-waka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1867"></A><A HREF="#fn_1862"><FONT SIZE="1">49</FONT></A> (one Deity). The august children of this Heavenly Sovereign [numbered] altogether twenty-six (<small>eleven Kings and fifteen Queens</small>). Of these His Augustness Oho-sazaki [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire.</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1814"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1819">299:1</A> Son of the Emperor Chi&#363;-ai and the Empress Jin-g&#333;.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1815"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1820">299:2</A> In Yamato. <i>Akira</i> Signifies "brilliant." <A HREF="errata.htm#69"><i>Karushima</i></A> seems to mean "the neighbourhood of Karu, Karu being the often mentioned place of that name in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1816"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1821">299:3</A> The Auxiliary Numeral for deities is here used.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1817"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1822">299:4</A> <a name="page_301"><font size="1" color="green">p. 301</font></A> <i>Homuda-no-ma-waka no miko</i>. <i>Homuda</i> has already been met with as the came of a place in Kahachi. <i>Ma-waka</i> signifies "truly young." The name might therefore be rendered "truly young king of Homuda."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1818"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1823">299:5</A> <i>Takagi no iri-bime no mikoto</i>. Motowori identifies this princess with the Takaki-hime of Sect. LXXVI, Note 21.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1819"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1824">299:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "middle princess," she being the second of three sisters.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1820"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1825">299:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "younger princess," she being the youngest of the sisters.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1821"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1826">299:8</A> <i>I-ho-ki-no-iri-biko no mikoto</i>. See Sect. LXXVI, Note 12.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1822"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1827">299:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, probably "old woman of Shiritsuki." But it is not certain that Shiritsuki is the name of a place.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1823"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1828">299:10</A> <i>Take-inada no sukune</i>. In the "Chronicles of Old Matters of Former Ages" the name is written <i>Take-ina-dane</i>, and it may therefore mean "brave-rice-seed."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1824"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1829">299:11</A> <i>Wohari no murazhi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1825"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1830">299:12</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "great middle Prince of Nukata," the latter being the name of a place in Yamato. It is of uncertain signification.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1826"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1831">299:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "great mountain-warden." For the appropriateness of this name conf. Sect. CV.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1827"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1832">299:14</A> The same name has appeared in Sect. LXIII, Note 13.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1828"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1833">299:15</A> <i>Ohohara no iratsume</i>. <A HREF="errata.htm#70">Ohohara</A> is the name of a place in Yamato It signifies "great moor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1829"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1834">299:16</A> <i>Komuku no iratsume</i>. This name is written <A NAME="img_30100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/30100.jpg"> and its reading as <i>Komuku</i> is somewhat <A HREF="errata.htm#71">hypothetical</A>. It is the name of a place in Kahachi, and probably signifies "an overflowing pool of water."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1830"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1835">299:17</A> <i>Ki no Arata no iratsume</i>. <i>Ki</i> is the <A HREF="errata.htm#72">province</A> of that name, and Arata is a place in it. The latter name probably means "uncultivated fields."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1831"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1836">299:18</A> This name signifies "Great Wren," and is thus accounted for by the author of the "Chronicles": "On the day when the Emperor [this Prince became the Emperor Nin-toku] was born, an owl flew into the parturition-hall. Next morning early, the Heavenly Sovereign Homuda [<i>i.e.</i>, the Emperor &#332;-jin] sent for the Prime Minister, the Noble Takeuchi, and asked him whereof this might be a sign. The Prime Minister replied, saying: 'It is a good omen. Moreover yesterday, when thy servant's wife was delivered of a child, a wren flew into the parturition-house, likewise a strange thing.' Then the Heavenly Sovereign said: 'It is a portent from heaven that my child and thine should be born on the same day, and both be attended by a good omen. So let the names of the birds be taken,' and each used for the name of the other [<i>i.e.</i>, <a name="page_302"><font size="1" color="green">p. 302</font></A> the name of the owl for him into whose parturition-house the wren flew, and <i>vice-vers&acirc;</i>], as a covenant for the future.' So the wren's name was bestowed on the Heir Apparent, who was called Great-Wren Prince, and the owl's name was give Ito the Prime Minister's child. who was called the Noble Owl."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1832"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1837">299:19</A> This name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1833"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1838">299:20</A> <i>Abe no iratsume</i>. Abe is the name of several places in different provinces, and is of obscure derivation and import.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1834"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1839">299:21</A> <i>Ahaji no Mikara no iratsume</i>. The text properly has <i>Ayuchi</i>, but Motowori emends this to <i>Ahaji</i> on the authority of the "Chronicles."' Mihara is the name of a district in the island of Ahaji, and probably signifies "three moors."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1835"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1840">300:22</A> <i>Ki no Unu</i> <A HREF="errata.htm#74"><i>no</i></A> <i>iratsume</i>. <i>Ki</i> is the province of that name, and <i>Unu</i> a place in it. The latter name is of uncertain import.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1836"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1841">300:23</A> <i>Minu no iratsume</i>. <i>Minu</i> (<i>Mino</i>) is the province of that name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1837"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1842">300:24</A> "Five" must here be a mistake for "four."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1838"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1843">300:25</A> For this name and the next see Sect. CVI, Notes 5 and 4.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1839"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1844">300:26</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the young lord of Uji." Uji is the name of a district in Yamashiro, famous in classical and modern times for its tea. The etymology is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1840"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1845">300:27</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the young lady of Yata." Yata is the name of a place in Yamato. The etymology is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1841"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1846">300:28</A> <i>Medori no</i> miko. <i>Medori</i> signifies "hen-bird:" but the reason for the application of so strange a name to this princess, whose fortunes are related at some length in Sect. CXXVI and CXXVII, does not appear. A similar remark applies to the next name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1842"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1847">300:29</A> <i>I.e.</i>, probably "the lady of the little kettle."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1843"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1848">300:30</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the young lady of Uji."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1844"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1849">300:31</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the truly young middle princess of Okinaga."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1845"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1850">300:32</A> See Sect. XCII, Note 27.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1846"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1851">300:33</A> <i>Waka-muke-futa-mata no miko</i>. This name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1847"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1852">300:34</A> <i>Itowi-hime</i>. Itowi is the name of a place in Yamato, and is of uncertain origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1848"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1853">300:35</A> <i>Shima</i> is probably the name of a place, while <i>tari</i> and <i>ne</i> are the frequently recurring Honorifics rendered respectively "perfect" and "lord "in former parts of this translation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1849"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1854">300:36</A> <i>Sakurawi no ta-be no murazhi</i>. <i>Ta-be</i>, rendered "agricultural," is literally "rice-field tribe." <i>Sakurawi</i> ("cherry well") is the name of a place in Kahachi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1850"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1855">300:37</A> <i>I.e.</i>, falcon-lord.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1851"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1856">300:38</A> <a name="page_303"><font size="1" color="green">p. 303</font></A> <i>Himuka no Idzumi no Naga-hime</i>. Himuka is the name of a province, and Idzumi that of a district now comprised within .the limits of Satsuma. <i>Nagahime</i>, literally "long princess," probably signifies "elder princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1852"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1857">300:39</A> <i>Oho-haye no miko</i>. Signification obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1853"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1858">300:40</A> <i>Wo-haye no miko</i>. Signification obscure. The antithesis of the Adjectives <i>oho</i> and <i>wo</i> ("great" and "small") shows however that the names partly served to distinguish the elder from the younger brother.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1854"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1859">300:41</A> <i>Waki-iratsume</i> is "younger lady." <i>Hata-bi</i> is incomprehensible.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1855"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1860">300:42</A> See Sect. LXXVI, Note 28.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1856"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1861">300:43</A> <i>I.e.</i>, probably "the lady of Kaharada." The latter name (literally "rice-field on the border of a river") is often met with.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1857"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1862">300:44</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the jewel lady."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1858"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1863">300:45</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the great middle lady of Osaka," the latter being the name of a place in Yamato (see Sect. XLVIII, Note 1).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1859"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1864">300:46</A> Motowori identifies this name with that <i>Koto-fushi no iratsume</i> in Sect. CXVII, <i>q.v.</i>, and thinks that both this and the preceding name have only crept into this Section by mistake.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1860"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1865">300:47</A> <i>Kataji no miko</i>, Signification obscure,</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1861"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1866">300:48</A> <i>Kadzuraki no Nu-iro-me</i>. All the elements of this name have already been met with several times.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1862"></A><A HREF="kj111.htm#fr_1867">300:49</A> This child has already appeared early in this Section, and the name is here doubtless only repeated through some copyist's error.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_303"><font size="1" color="green">p. 303</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CV.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART II.&#8212;HE DIVIDES THE INHERITANCE BETWEEN HIS THREE SONS)]</h2>  
<p>Hereupon the Heavenly Sovereign asked His Augustness Oho-yama-mori and His Augustness Oho-sazaki, saying: "Which think ye the dearer, an elder child or a younger child?" (<small>The reason why the Heavenly Sovereign propounded this question was because it was his intention&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1868"></A><A HREF="#fn_1863"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> to make Uji-no-waki-iratsuko rule the Empire</small>). Then His Augustness Oho-yama-mori said: "The elder child is the dearer." Next His Augustness Oho-sazaki, knowing the august</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_304"><font size="1" color="green">p. 304</font></A></p>  
<p>feeling which made the Heavenly Sovereign deign to ask [the question], said: "The elder child, having already become a man, gives no trouble; but the younger child, not being yet a man, is the dearer." Then the Heavenly Sovereign said: "My lord Sazaki's words agree with my thoughts," and forthwith ordained the division [of the inheritance] thus: His Augustness Oho-yama-mori to administer the government of the mountains and the sea,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1869"></A><A HREF="#fn_1864"><FONT SIZE="1">2a</FONT></A> His Augustness Oho-sazaki to take and deign to report on the government of the realm,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1870"></A><A HREF="#fn_1865"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and Uji-no waki-iratsuko to rule the succession of Heaven's sun.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1871"></A><A HREF="#fn_1866"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So His Augustness Oho-sazaki was not disobedient to the Heavenly Sovereign's commands.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1872"></A><A HREF="#fn_1867"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1863"></A><A HREF="kj112.htm#fr_1868">303:1</A> <a name="page_304"><font size="1" color="green">p. 304</font></A> Literally, "heart."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1864"></A><A HREF="kj112.htm#fr_1869">304:2a</A> <i>I.e.</i>, Motowori thinks, to have control over the guilds of foresters and fishermen.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1865"></A><A HREF="kj112.htm#fr_1870">304:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, to act as regent or minister.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1866"></A><A HREF="kj112.htm#fr_1871">304:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, to inherit the empire.&#8212;It will be remembered that the Japanese Emperors claim to descend from the Sun-Goddess.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1867"></A><A HREF="kj112.htm#fr_1872">304:5</A> This statement refers proleptically to the contrary course which was taken by the elder Oho-yama-mori.</P>

<HEAD>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="../../css/marg.css">
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">

<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="index.htm">Index</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj112.htm">Previous</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj114.htm">Next</A>&nbsp;
<HR><A HREF="http://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/B0028Y4SZY/internetsacredte">Buy this Book at Amazon.com</A></CENTER>
<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">SECT. CVI.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART III.&#8212;HE WOOES PRINCESS MIYA-NUSHI-YA-KAHA-YE).]</h2>  
<p>One day&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1873"></A><A HREF="#fn_1868"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> the Heavenly Sovereign, when he had crossed over into the land of Afumi, augustly stood on the moor of Uji, gazed on the moor of Kadzu, and sang, saying: [245]</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"As I look on the Moor of Kadzu in Chiba. both the hundred thousand-fold abundant house-places are visible, and the land's acme is visible."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1874"></A><A HREF="#fn_1869"><FONT SIZE="1">2b</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_305"><font size="1" color="green">p. 305</font></A></p>  
<p>So when he reached the village of Kohara,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1875"></A><A HREF="#fn_1870"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> a beautiful maiden met him at a fork in the road, Then the Heavenly Sovereign asked the maiden, saying: "Whose child art thou?" She replied, saying: "I am the daughter of the Grandee Wani-no-Hifure,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1876"></A><A HREF="#fn_1871"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and my name is Princess Miya-nushi-ya-kaha-ye."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1877"></A><A HREF="#fn_1872"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> The Heavenly Sovereign forthwith said to the maiden: "When I return on my progress to-morrow, I will enter into thy house." So Princess Ya-kaha-ye told her father all that [had happened]. Thereupon her father replied, saying: "Ah! it was the Heavenly Sovereign! [His commands are] to be respected. My child, respectfully serve him!"&#8212;and so saying he grandly decorated the house, and awaited [the Heaven ly Sovereign's return], whereupon he came in on the next day.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1878"></A><A HREF="#fn_1873"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> So when [the father] served [the Heavenly Sovereign] a great august feast, he made his daughter Her Augustness&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1879"></A><A HREF="#fn_1874"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Princess Ya-kaha take the great august [246] liquor-cup and present it. Thereupon, while taking the great liquor-cup, the Heavenly Sovereign augustly sang, saying:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh this crab! whence this crab? [It is] a crab from far-distant Tsunuga. Whither&nbsp; reaches its sideward motion? [It has] come towards Ichiji-shima and Mi-shima. It must be because, plunging and breathless like the grebe, I went without stopping along the up and down road by the wavelets, that the maiden I met on the Kohata road has a back oh! like a small shield, a row of teeth like acorns. Oh! the earth of the Wani pass at Ichihiwi! Owing to the skin of the first earth being ruddy, to the last <a name="page_306"><font size="1" color="green">p. 306</font></A> earth being of a reddish black, she, without exposing to the actual sun that makes one bend one's head the middle earth like three chestnuts, draws thickly down her drawn eye-brows;&#8212;the women I met, the child I saw and wanted in this way, the child I saw and wanted in that way, oh! she is opposite to me at the height of the feast! oh! she is at my side!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1880"></A><A HREF="#fn_1875"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[247] Ita auguste coivit [cum ill&acirc;], et procreavit filium Uji-no-waki-iratsuko.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_307"><font size="1" color="green">p. 307</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1868"></A><A HREF="kj113.htm#fr_1873">304:1</A> Literally, "one time."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1869"></A><A HREF="kj113.htm#fr_1874">304:2b</A> According to Moribe, whose interpretation has been followed throughout, this Song signifies: "As I gaze across from Uji to the Moor of Toba, I see the numerous and prosperous homesteads of the people, I see the most fertile portion of the country."&#8212;On this view Chiba is identified with Toba, the name of a district; and the word <i>ho</i>, rendered "acme," is taken to mean the best, highest, most showy part of anything. For Motowori's opinion, which is that of the older commentators as well, that <i>chi-ba</i> is a Pillow-Word, there is much to be said, and if we followed it, we should have to render the first two lines thus: "As I look on the thousand-leafed pueraria-moor," etc. (<i>kadzu</i> signifying "pueraria.") Motowori's explanation of <i>momo-chi-dare</i> (here rendered by "hundred thousand-fold abundant") as referring to the soot of the peasant's roofs, and of <i>ho</i> as signifying "a plain surrounded by mountains "seems much less good than Moribe's interpretation of those difficult expressions.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1870"></A><A HREF="kj113.htm#fr_1875">305:3</A> In the district of Uji in the province of Yamashiro. The characters with which the name is written signify "tree-flag."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1871"></A><A HREF="kj113.htm#fr_1876">305:4</A> <i>Wani no Hifure no omi</i>. For <i>Wani no omi</i> see Sect. LXII, Note 11. The meaning of <i>Hifure</i> is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1872"></A><A HREF="kj113.htm#fr_1877">305:5</A> <i>Miya-nushi ya-kata-hime</i>. <i>Miya-nushi</i> is "priestess," or more literally "temple-guardian." For the rest of the name see Sect. XXVI, Note 14, though the personages are of course meant to be different.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1873"></A><A HREF="kj113.htm#fr_1878">305:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, that day having passed by, the Emperor came on the next day according to his promise.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1874"></A><A HREF="kj113.htm#fr_1879">305:7</A> Motowori supposes with apparent reason that the character <A NAME="img_30600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/30600.jpg">, <a name="page_307"><font size="1" color="green">p. 307</font></A> "Augustness," has only crept into the text through the attraction of the following character <A NAME="img_30700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/30700.jpg">, "made," which it resembles in appearance.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1875"></A><A HREF="kj113.htm#fr_1880">306:8</A> It must be understood that in this Song the Imperial singer commences by referring to what doubtless formed part of the feast,&#8212;a crab,&#8212;and thence passes on by an imperceptible transition to allude to his own adventure with the maiden. As the crab when alive walked sideways, so was the Emperor zigzagging up and down the road that lines the shore of Lake Biwa, pursuing his breathless course like that of the busy grebe that perpetually plunges into the water, when the maiden met him near Kohata. Beautiful indeed was she: her back straight as a shield, her teeth like a row of acorns, and the artificial eye-brows painted a dark colour on her forehead drawn low down in a perfect crescent-shape. She had been careful in selecting the clay to make the paint, rejecting the upper layer of earth, for that was of too bright a red, rejecting likewise the lower layer, for that was too dark, but taking the middle, which was of the correct blue tint, and drying it, not in the fierce, but in a mildly tempered, sun-light. And now this maiden, for whom his heart had been panting and turning this way and that ever since the previous day, is actually seated opposite to him, nay! at his very side, and he is feasting in her sweet company.&#8212;Tsunuga is the name of a place in the province of Echizen. "Far-distant" is an imperfect attempt at rendering the force of the Pillow-Word <i>momo-dzutafu</i>, which implies that the traveller must pass through a hundred other places before reaching his destination. "Whither reaches its sideward motion?" signifies "whither is it going with its sideward motion? "Ichiji-shima and Mishima are places of which nothing is known, so that the allusion to them is obscure. At this point Motowori's interpretation diverges from that of Moribe, which has been followed throughout. <i>Sasanami</i>, here rendered "wavelets," is taken by him, as by the older commentators, as the name of a place, and the description of the maiden's teeth is misunderstood to signify that she had a beak filled with a row of teeth like the water-caltrop! Motowori also would here divide the Song in two, a proceeding for which there is not sufficient warrant. On other minor points, too, his decisions do not seem so happy as Moribe's. The view of both commentators will be found at length in Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXXII, pp. 33.51, and in Moribe's "<i>Idzu no Kato-Waki</i>," <i>in loco</i>. Three chestnuts" (<i>mitsu-guri no</i>) is a common Pillow-Word for <i>naka</i>, "middle," founded on the fact, real or supposed, that one burr always contains three nuts, whereof one of course is in the middle, between the other two.</P>
<p><HR>
