<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_308"><font size="1" color="green">p. 308</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CVII.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART IV.&#8212;HE GRANTS PRINCESS KAMINAGA TO HIS SON OHO-SAZAKI).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign, hearing of the beauty of Princess Kaminaga,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1881"></A><A HREF="#fn_1876"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> daughter of the Duke of Muragata&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1882"></A><A HREF="#fn_1877"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in the land of Himuka, and thinking to employ her&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1883"></A><A HREF="#fn_1878"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> sent down for her,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1884"></A><A HREF="#fn_1879"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> whereupon the Heir Apparent&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1885"></A><A HREF="#fn_1880"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> His Augustness Oho-sazaki, having seen the maiden land at [248] the port of Naniha, and being charmed with the grace of her appearance, forthwith directed the Prince Minister the Noble Taka-uchi, to intercede for him in the august presence of the Heavenly Sovereign, and make [the latter] grant to him Princess Kami-naga, whom he had sent down for. Then on the Prime Minister the Noble Take-uchi requesting the great commands,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1886"></A><A HREF="#fn_1881"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> the Heavenly Sovereign forthwith granted Princess Kami-naga to his august child. The way he granted her was this:&#8212;the Heavenly Sovereign, on a day when he partook of a copious feast,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1887"></A><A HREF="#fn_1882"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> gave Princess Kami-naga the great august liquor oak-[leaf&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1888"></A><A HREF="#fn_1883"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A>] to present to the Heir Apparent. Then he augustly sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Come on, children! oh! the fragrant flowering orange-tree on my way as I go to pluck the wild garlic,&#8212;to pluck the garlic,&#8212;has its uppermost branches withered by birds perching on them, and its lowest branches withered through people plucking from them. But the budding fruit on the middle branch, like three chestnuts,&#8212;the ruddy maiden, oh! if thou lead her off with thee, it will be good, oh!'&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1889"></A><A HREF="#fn_1884"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>[249] Again he augustly sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Driving the dyke-piles into Lake Yosami <a name="page_309"><font size="1" color="green">p. 309</font></A> where the water collects, my heart (ignorant of the pricking of the stumps of the water-caltrop, ignorant of the creeping of the roots of the <i>Brasenia peltata</i>), being more and more laughable, is now indeed repentant."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1890"></A><A HREF="#fn_1885"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Having thus sung, he bestowed [her on the Heir Apparent]. So after having been granted the maiden, the Heir Apparent sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! the maiden of Kohada in the back of the road! though I heard of her like the thunder, we mutually intertwine [our arms] as pillows."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1891"></A><A HREF="#fn_1886"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again he sang saying":</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"I think lovingly ah! of how the maiden [250] of Kohada in the back of the road sleeps [with me] without disputing"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1892"></A><A HREF="#fn_1887"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_310"><font size="1" color="green">p. 310</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1876"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1881">308:1</A> <i>Kami-naga-hime</i>. The name signifies "the long-haired princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1877"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1882">308:2</A> <i>Murakata no kami</i>. <i>Murakata</i> seems to signify "many towns."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1878"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1883">308:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, wed her.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1879"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1884">308:4</A> Literally, "summoned her up." The same phrase occurs immediately below.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1880"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1885">308:5</A> <A NAME="img_30900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/30900.jpg">. Mabuchi thinks that <A NAME="img_30901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/30901.jpg">, "august child," should be substituted for the reading in the text. But Motowori insists that the title translated Heir Apparent was anciently borne by all the sons of an Emperor, and that consequently no emendation is called for.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1881"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1886">308:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Emperor's orders.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1882"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1887">308:7</A> The native term translated "copious feast" is <i>toyo no akari</i>, variously written with the characters <A NAME="img_30902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/30902.jpg">, <A NAME="img_30903"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/30903.jpg">, <A NAME="img_30904"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/30904.jpg">, etc., etc. It literally signifies "copious brightness," in allusion to the ruddy glow which wine gives to the faces of the revellers, and henceforward perpetually recurs in this history. In later times it specifically denoted the festival of, the tasting of the first rice, but anciently its meaning was not thus limited. Motowori's note on the subject, in Vol. XXXII, pp. 57-59 of his Commentary, may be consulted with advantage.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1883"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1888">308:8</A> <i>I.e.</i>, an oak-leaf which was used as a cup to sip out of. Leaf-platters <a name="page_310"><font size="1" color="green">p. 310</font></A> for food have already been mentioned. Motowori says that the word <i>kashika</i> (properly the name of a deciduous oak, the <i>Quercus dentata</i>) was employed to denote any kind of leaf thus used.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1884"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1889">308:9</A> The whole gist of this Song is contained in the last three lines. "The ruddy maiden, oh if thou lead her off with thee, it will be good,"&#8212;<i>i.e.</i> "thou and the maiden, will form a fitting couple." All that goes before is what is technically called a "Preface," though its bearing is so clear as to admit of translation, and even in English to form an appropriate introduction to the Song:&#8212;It is not the stinking garlic, but the fragrant orange that the singer has met by the way, and it is the choicest young fruit in the very middle of the tree that forms a suitable comparison for the lovely young girl.&#8212;With the favourite allusion to upper, middle, and lower the reader is already familiar, and the Pillow-Word "three chestnuts" was explained in the note on the <A HREF="errata.htm#75">preceding</A> Song (Sect. CVI, Note 8).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1885"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1890">309:10</A> The gist of the Song is: "I knew not that thou, my son, hadst conceived a secret passion for the maiden; but I am now conscious of my own mistake, and my foolish old heart is ashamed of itself." With this explanation the elaborate comparison between the state of the monarch's mind and the condition of the peasant driving piles for the foundation of a dyke, and having his feet either lacerated by the stumps of the water-caltrop, or made slimy by brushing against the roots of the <i>Brasenia peltata</i> at the bottom of the water, becomes intelligible and appropriate.&#8212;The word <i>kuri</i>, rendered "roots," perplexed Motowori, who suggests that it may be but a second name of the <i>Brasenia</i>, appended to the first; but Moribe's suggestion that it is to be identified with <i>kori</i>, and taken in the signification of "roots" though not quite convincing, is at least more plausible. The text of this Song is corrupt in these "Records" and has to be corrected by a comparison with that of the "Chronicles." Moribe goes into an amusing ecstasy over the picture of ancient manners which it presents, and lauds the simplicity of days when a father and son could so peacefully woo the same maiden without mutual concealment or disastrous consequences!</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1886"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1891">309:11</A> The meaning of this Song is: "At first I heard of the maiden of Kohada in the furthest parts of Himuka as one hears the distant thunder; but now she is mine, and we sleep locked in each other's arms."&#8212;This Kohada in Himuka must not be confounded with the Kohata in Yamashiro mentioned in the preceding Section. The "back of the road" means the remotest portion (conf. Sect. LX, Note 20). The thunder must be understood to refer to a very faint and distant <a name="page_311"><font size="1" color="green">p. 311</font></A> sound: the Prince had first heard of the maiden vaguely, but now she is his and has been his for some time; for this Song must be supposed to have been composed after the occasion of the feast with the story of which it is here connected.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1887"></A><A HREF="kj114.htm#fr_1892">309:12</A> The meaning of this Song is: "I love this maiden of Kohada in Himuka, who disputed not my desire and my father's grant, but willingly became my wife."&#8212;It is hard to render into English the force of the string of Particles <i>wo shi zo mo</i> in the penultimate line.</P>
<p><HR>

<p><a name="page_311"><font size="1" color="green">p. 311</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART V.&#8212;SONGS OF THE TERRITORIAL OWNERS OF YESHINU).]</h2>  
<p>Again, the Territorial Owners of Yeshinu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1893"></A><A HREF="#fn_1888"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> seeing the august sword which was girded on His Augustness Oho sazaki, sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Sharp is the beginning, freezing is the end of the sword girded on Oho-sazaki, Oho, sazaki, the solar august child of Homuda,&#8212;[it is] chilly, chilly like the trees beneath the trunks of the winter trees."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1894"></A><A HREF="#fn_1889"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again, having made a cross-mortar&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1895"></A><A HREF="#fn_1890"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> at Kashifu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1896"></A><A HREF="#fn_1891"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> in [251] Yeshinu, and having in that cross-mortar distilled&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1897"></A><A HREF="#fn_1892"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> some great august liquor, they, when they presented the great august liquor [to the Heavenly Sovereign], sang as follows, drumming with their mouths:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"We have made a side-mortar at Kashinofu, and in the side-mortar we have distilled some great august liquor, which do thou sweetly partake of, oh our lord!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1898"></A><A HREF="#fn_1893"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>This Song is one which it is the custom to chant down to the present day when, from time to time, the Territorial Owners present a great feast [to the Sovereign].</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1888"></A><A HREF="kj115.htm#fr_1893">311:1</A> <a name="page_312"><font size="1" color="green">p. 312</font></A> Yeshinu is the modern Yoshino, in the province of Yamato (see Sect. XLVI, Note 3). For the title of <i>kudzu</i> see Sect. XLVI, Note 13, where it also occurs in connection with Yeshinu.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1889"></A><A HREF="kj115.htm#fr_1894">311:2</A> According to Moribe, whose interpretation seems best to the translator. the signification of this difficult poem is: "The sword worn by Prince Oho-sazaki, son of the Emperor Homuda (O-jin) is double-edged at its upper part, and like glistening ice towards its point;&#8212;oh! &#8217;tis like the icicles on the plants that cluster about the trunks of the dead trees in winter!" Almost every line, however (excepting those giving the name and title of the Prince), is a subject of controversy, and the "<i>G&#333;-Gan Sh&#333;</i>" <i>in loco</i> and Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXXIII, pp. 2-5, should be consulted for Keichi&#363;'s, Mabuchi's and Motowori's views on the disputed point.&#8212;The expression "solar august child" signifies "sun-descended prince," in allusion to the supposed descent of the Japanese monarchs from the Sun-Goddess.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1890"></A><A HREF="kj115.htm#fr_1895">311:3</A> <i>Yoko-usu</i> or <i>yokusu</i> (<A NAME="img_31200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31200.jpg">). It is not plain what sort of mortar the author intended to designate by this term. Motowori supposes it to mean a broad flat mortar in contradistinction to a high and narrow one. <A HREF="errata.htm#76">Keichi&#363;'s</A> view, which he quotes, to the effect that it was a mortar that had been carved out of the, block against the grain of the wood, seems an equally good guess, where all is guess-work.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1891"></A><A HREF="kj115.htm#fr_1896">311:4</A> In the Song this same name is read <i>Kashinofu</i>; but the commentators tell us that the Genitive Particle <i>no</i> ("of") is simply inserted for the sake of rhythm, and it is not unlikely that they are right. The name seems to signify "[a place where] oak-trees grow."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1892"></A><A HREF="kj115.htm#fr_1897">311:5</A> See Sect. XVIII, Note 16. The character <A NAME="img_31201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31201.jpg">, rendered by "distil" or "brew," according to the view which one may take of the resulting liquor, would seem to be here used in the sense of "to pound."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1893"></A><A HREF="kj115.htm#fr_1898">311:6</A> In this simple Song the Territorial Owners of Yoshino beg the Monarch to deign to partake of the sake which they have made.</P>

<p><a name="page_312"><font size="1" color="green">p. 312</font></A><b></b></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CIX.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART VI.&#8212;VARIOUS DEEDS)]</h2>  
<p>In this august reign were graciously established the Fisher Tribe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1899"></A><A HREF="#fn_1894"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> the Mountain Tribe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1900"></A><A HREF="#fn_1895"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> the Mountain Warden Tribe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1901"></A><A HREF="#fn_1896"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and the Ise Tribe.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1902"></A><A HREF="#fn_1897"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Again the Pool of Tsurugi was made. Again there came over [to Japan] some</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_313"><font size="1" color="green">p. 313</font></A></p>  
<p>people from Shiragi. Therefore His Augustness the Noble Take-uchi, having taken them with him and set them to labour on pools and embankments, made the Pool of Kudara.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1903"></A><A HREF="#fn_1898"><FONT SIZE="1">5a</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1894"></A><A HREF="kj116.htm#fr_1899">312:1</A> <a name="page_313"><font size="1" color="green">p. 313</font></A> <i>Ama-be</i> (written <A NAME="img_31300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31300.jpg"> and read <i>Una-be</i> in the Old Printed Edition and in the edition of 1687, and perhaps better rendered "Sea-Tribe.") The name of this guild or clan does not seem to have remained, like the two mentioned together with it, as a "gentile name."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1895"></A><A HREF="kj116.htm#fr_1900">312:2</A> <i>Yama-be</i>. Motowori thinks that this word has crept into the text erroneously through the influence of that next mentioned, as the functions of the tribes or guilds thus separately named were identical The differentiation may have taken place after the terms had come to be used as "gentile names."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1896"></A><A HREF="kj116.htm#fr_1901">312:3</A> <i>Yama-moribe</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1897"></A><A HREF="kj116.htm#fr_1902">312:4</A> <i>Ise-be</i>. Nothing is known of this tribe or guild.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1898"></A><A HREF="kj116.htm#fr_1903">313:5a</A> Doubtless so named after the Korean labourers employed upon it,&#8212;Kudara and Shiragi, as different parts of the same peninsula, being confounded in thought.</P>

<p>[252]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CX.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART VIII.&#8212;TRIBUTE FROM KOREA).]</h2>  
<p>Again King Sh&#333;-ko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1904"></A><A HREF="#fn_1899"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> the Chieftain of the land of Kudara, sent as tribute by Achi-kishi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1905"></A><A HREF="#fn_1900"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> one stallion and one mare. (<small>This Achi-kishi was the ancestor of the Achiki Scribes.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1906"></A><A HREF="#fn_1901"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></small>) Again he sent as tribute a cross-sword,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1907"></A><A HREF="#fn_1902"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and likewise a large mirror. Again he was graciously bidden&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1908"></A><A HREF="#fn_1903"><FONT SIZE="1">5b</FONT></A> to send as tribute a wise man, if there were any such in the land of Kudara. Therefore receiving the [Imperial] commands, he sent as tribute a man named Wani-kishi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1909"></A><A HREF="#fn_1904"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and likewise by this man he sent as tribute the Confucian Analects&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1910"></A><A HREF="#fn_1905"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> in ten volumes and the Thousand Character Essay&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1911"></A><A HREF="#fn_1906"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> in one volume,&#8212;altogether eleven volumes.</p>

<p><a name="page_315"><font size="1" color="green">p. 315</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXI.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART VIII.&#8212;THE EMPEROR INTOXICATED).]</h2>  
<p>Again there came over [to Japan] the ancestor of the Hada Rulers,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1916"></A><A HREF="#fn_1911"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> the ancestor of the Aya Suzerains,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1917"></A><A HREF="#fn_1912"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and likewise a man who knew how to distil liquor, and whose name was Nim-pan,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1918"></A><A HREF="#fn_1913"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> while another name for him was Susukori.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1919"></A><A HREF="#fn_1914"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So this [man] Susukori distilled some great august liquor, and presented it to the Heavenly Sovereign, who, excited with the great august liquor that had been presented to him augustly sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"I have become intoxicated with the august liquor distilled by Susukori. I have become intoxicated with the soothing liquor, with the smiling liquor."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1920"></A><A HREF="#fn_1915"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>On his walking out singing thus, he hit with his [254] august staff a large stone in the middle of the Ohosaka&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1921"></A><A HREF="#fn_1916"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> road, upon which the stone ran away. So the proverb says: "Hard stones get out of a drunkard's way."</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1911"></A><A HREF="kj118.htm#fr_1916">315:1</A> <a name="page_315"><font size="1" color="green">p. 315</font></A> <i>Hada na miyatsuko</i>, <A NAME="img_31500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31500.jpg">, a "gentile name." <i>Hada</i> is the native Japanese word used as the equivalent of the Chinese name <A NAME="img_31501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31501.jpg">, <i>Ch&#8217;in</i>. Its origin is uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1912"></A><A HREF="kj118.htm#fr_1917">315:2</A> <i>Aya no ataha</i> <A NAME="img_31502"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31502.jpg">, a "gentile name." The use of Aya to represent the Chinese name <A NAME="img_31503"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31503.jpg">, <i>Han</i>, is as difficult to account for as is that of Hada mentioned in the preceding Note.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1913"></A><A HREF="kj118.htm#fr_1918">315:3</A> <A NAME="img_31504"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31504.jpg">. Another and more Japanese-like reading, <i>Niho</i>, is invented by Motowori; but the older editors read <i>Nim-pan</i> according to the usual Sinico-Japanese sound of the characters. The modern Korean reading would be In-pon.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1914"></A><A HREF="kj118.htm#fr_1919">315:4</A> Written phonetically <A NAME="img_31505"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31505.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1915"></A><A HREF="kj118.htm#fr_1920">315:5</A> Thus translated, this Song is too clear to need any explanation. The lines, however, which are rendered by "with the soothing liquor, with the smiling liquor."&#8212;in Japanese <i>koto nagu shi we-guzhi-ni</i>,&#8212;are in reality extremely obscure, and Moribe understands them to signify, "Oh! <a name="page_316"><font size="1" color="green">p. 316</font></A> how difficult it is for me to speak! Oh! how ill at ease I am!" In order to do so he has, however, to change and add to the text; and the translator, though not sure of being in the right path, has preferred to follow Motowori, whose interpretation, without requiring any such extreme measures, yet gives a very plausible sense.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1916"></A><A HREF="kj118.htm#fr_1921">315:6</A> See Sect. LXIV, Note 25.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_316"><font size="1" color="green">p. 316</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXII.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART IX.&#8212;TROUBLES WHICH FOLLOWED HIS DECEASE)]</h2>  
<p>So after the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign, His Augustness Ohosazaki, in conformity with the Heavenly Sovereign's commands, ceded the Empire to Uji-no-waki-iratsuko. Thereupon His Augustness Ohoyama-mori, disobeying the Heavenly Sovereign's commands, and anxious in spite thereof to obtain the Empire, had the design to slay the Prince&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1922"></A><A HREF="#fn_1917"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> his younger brother, secretly raised an army, and prepared to attack him. Then His Augustness Oho-sazaki, hearing that his elder brother had prepared an army, forthwith despatched a messenger to apprise Uji-no-waki-iratsuko. So, startled at the news, [the latter] set troops in ambush by the river-bank, and likewise, after having drawn a fence of curtains and raised a tent on the top of the hill, placed there publicly on a throne&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1923"></A><A HREF="#fn_1918"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> one of his retainers to pretend that he was the King,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1924"></A><A HREF="#fn_1919"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> the manner in which all the officials&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1925"></A><A HREF="#fn_1920"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> reverentially went and came being just like that [usual] in the King's presence. And moreover, preparing for the time [255] when the King his elder brother&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1926"></A><A HREF="#fn_1921"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> should cross the river, he arranged and decorated a boat and oars, and moreover&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1927"></A><A HREF="#fn_1922"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> ground [in a mortar] the root of the <i>Kadzura japonica</i>, and having taken the slime of its juice, rubbed</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_317"><font size="1" color="green">p. 317</font></A></p>  
<p>therewith the grating&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1928"></A><A HREF="#fn_1923"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> inside the boat, so as to make any who should tread on it fall down, and then himself&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1929"></A><A HREF="#fn_1924"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> put on a cloth coat and trowsers, and having assumed the appearance of a common fellow, stood in the boat holding the oar. Hereupon, when the King his elder brother, having hid his troops in ambush and put on armour beneath his clothes, reached the river-bank and was about to get into the boat, he gazed at the grandly decorated place [on the hill], thought the King his younger brother was sitting on the throne, being altogether ignorant [of the fact] that he was standing in the boat holding the oar, and forthwith asked the fellow who was holding the oar, saying: "It has been reported to me that on this mountain there is a large and angry boar. I wish to take that boar. Shall I peradventure get that boar? "Then the fellow holding the oar replied, saying: "Thou canst not." Again he asked, saying: "For what reason?" [The boat-man] answered, saying: "He is not to be got, however often and in however many places he be chased. Wherefore I say that thou canst not [catch him either]. "When they had crossed as far as the middle of the river, [Prince Uji-no-waki-iratsuko] caused the boat to be tilted over, and [his elder brother] to fall into the water.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1930"></A><A HREF="#fn_1925"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Then forthwith he rose to the surface, and floated down with the current. Forthwith, as he floated, he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Whoever is swiftest among the boatmen of the Uji ferry will come to me."'&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1931"></A><A HREF="#fn_1926"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Thereupon the troops that had been hidden on the [256] river-bank rose up simultaneously on this side and on that side, and fixing their arrows [in their bows], let him go floating down. So he sank on reaching Kawara</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_318"><font size="1" color="green">p. 318</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Point.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1932"></A><A HREF="#fn_1927"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> So on their searching with hooks&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1933"></A><A HREF="#fn_1928"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> the place where he had sunk, [the hooks] struck on the armour inside his clothes, and made a rattling sound.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1934"></A><A HREF="#fn_1929"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> So the place was called by the name of Kawara Point. Then when they hooked up&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1935"></A><A HREF="#fn_1930"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> his bones, the younger King, sang saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"<i>Catalpa</i> bow, <i>Evonymus</i> standing by the ferry-bank of Uji! My heart had thought to cut [you], my heart had thought to take [you]; but at the base methought of the lord, at the extremity methought of the younger sister; grievously methought of this, sorrowfully methought of, that; and I came [back] without cutting it,&#8212;the <i>Catalpa</i> bow, the <i>Evonymus</i>."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1936"></A><A HREF="#fn_1931"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[257] So the bones of His Augustness Oho-yama-mori were buried on the Nara&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1937"></A><A HREF="#fn_1932"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> mountain. His Augustness Oho-yama-mori (<small>was the ancestor of the Dukes of Hijikata,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1938"></A><A HREF="#fn_1933"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> the Dukes of Heki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1939"></A><A HREF="#fn_1934"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> and the Dukes of Harihara.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1940"></A><A HREF="#fn_1935"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A></small>)</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_319"><font size="1" color="green">p. 319</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1917"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1922">316:1</A> <a name="page_318"><font size="1" color="green">p. 318</font></A> <A NAME="img_31800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31800.jpg">. This is the only passage in the work where this expression occurs. <i>Uji-no-waki-iratsuko</i> is the personage thus designated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1918"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1923">316:2</A> The same expression has been in Sect. XXXI (near Note 16) rendered "couch." The characters in the original are <A NAME="img_31801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31801.jpg"> or <A NAME="img_31802"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31802.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1919"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1924">316:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, <i>Uji-na-maki-iratsuko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1920"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1925">316:4</A> The Chinese phrase <A NAME="img_31803"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31803.jpg">, "the hundred officials," is here used.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1921"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1926">316:5</A> <i>Q.d.</i>, his Augustness Oho-yama-mori.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1922"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1927">316:6</A> The text has the character <A NAME="img_31804"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31804.jpg">, which, in combination with the preceding words "oars" gives the sense of "oarsman," "boatman." But Motowori reasonably suggests that it is an error for <A NAME="img_31805"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31805.jpg">, the grass hand forms of the two characters closely resembling each other, and <A NAME="img_31805"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31805.jpg"> making much better sense; for who would talk of "decorating an oarsman"?</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1923"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1928">317:7</A> A bamboo grating.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1924"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1929">317:8</A> Literally "that king's son."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1925"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1930">317:9</A> It must be understood that Uji-no-waki-iratsuko and his men. <a name="page_319"><font size="1" color="green">p. 319</font></A> having planned to act thus, were on their guard, and did not fall into the water as did Oho-yama-mori, who was taken unawares.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1926"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1931">317:10</A> This is Motowori's view of the meaning of the Song, which he interprets as a request for help to some friendly boatman. Moribe adopts quite a different view, and thinks that the drowning prince is rather giving vent to sentiments of pride and defiance. He says (speaking in the Prince's name): "It is not that I have been capsized out of the boat into the river. but that I am swimming off after a pole which has fallen into the water. If there be any strong and willing fellows among my partizans, let them swim after me." It must be explained that the word rendered "boatmen" in the translation is literally "pole-takers" (or, according to Moribe's view, "to take a pole.") Motowori's interpretation seems to do less violence to the wording of the original, and Moribe's has not even the merit of accounting for the use of the Future <i>komu</i> where the Imperative <i>kone</i> would be what we should naturally expect.&#8212;<i>Uji</i> is preceded by the, in this context, untranslatable Pillow-Word <i>chihayaburu</i> (see "Dictionary of Pillow-Words," <i>s.v.</i>).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1927"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1932">318:11</A> <i>Kawara no saki</i>. The author, in the next sentence, derives this name from the rattling sound made by the books as they struck on the armour. But there seems a great deal to be said in favour of Arawi Hakuseki's view that <i>kawara</i> is an old word itself signifying "armour."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1928"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1933">318:12</A> The word <i>kagi</i> here used occurs elsewhere to denote the hooks employed for fastening doors, and in later times took the specific meaning of "key."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1929"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1934">318:13</A> Literally, "sounded <i>kawara</i>."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1930"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1935">318:14</A> The text has the characters <A NAME="img_31900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31900.jpg">. But Motowori says that <A NAME="img_31901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31901.jpg"> stands for <A NAME="img_31902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/31902.jpg">, and that we must interpret the passage to mean that they scratched [about to find] and take out [his corpse].</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1931"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1936">318:15</A> The signification of this Song is: "I came here meaning to kill thee as I might cut down and kill that <i>Catalpa</i> tree, that <i>Evonymus</i>, growing on the river-bank. But the thought of our father and of thy sister (or wife) touched me with pity, and I return without having drawn my bow at thee."&#8212;Uji is preceded by the untranslatable Pillow-Word <i>chihayahito</i> (see Dictionary of Pillow-Words" s.v.;&#8212;Motowori reads it <i>chihaya-hito</i> without the <i>nigori</i>).&#8212;The words <i>adzusa-yumi ma-yumi</i>, here respectively rendered "<i>Catalpa</i> bow "and "<i>Evonymus</i>," are difficult, and the doubt as to whether we should understand the prince to be speaking simply of the trees, or to intend likewise to allude to his bow which was made of the wood of one of those trees, is probably not to be settled, as the <A HREF="errata.htm#78">words</A> in question have always oscillated between the two <a name="page_320"><font size="1" color="green">p. 320</font></A> meanings, and here evidently contain a double allusion. Motowori thinks that the first of the two forms only a sort of Pillow-Word for the second.&#8212;The word rendered "bank," in accordance with Moribe's suggestion, is literally "reach."&#8212;No special importance must be attached to the expressions "base" (or "main part") and "extremity," though they may doubtless be thought to allude to the father and sister, the recollection of whom softened the victorious younger brother's heart. The word <i>iranakeku</i>, rendered "grievously," is of not quite certain interpretation.&#8212;It must be understood that though, by overturning the boat, Uji-no-waki-iratsuko did constructively cause Oho-yama-mori's death, he did not actually shoot at and slay him when in the water, but followed down the river-side lamenting over what had happened.&#8212;This Song is singled out by Moribe for special praise.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1932"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1937">318:16</A> See Sect. LXXII, Note 23.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1933"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1938">318:17</A> Tohotafumi (T&#333;t&#333;mi). In the original <i>Hijikata no kimi</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1934"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1939">318:18</A> <i>Heki na kimi</i>. Of Heki nothing is known,</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1935"></A><A HREF="kj119.htm#fr_1940">318:19</A> <i>Harihara no kimi</i>. In Tohotafumi. <i>Harihara</i> signifies "alder plantation."</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_320"><font size="1" color="green">p. 320</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXIII.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART X.&#8212;PRINCES OHO-SAZAKI AND UJI-NO-WAKI-IRATSUKO CEDE THE EMPIRE TO EACH OTHER)]</h2>  
<p>Thereupon while the two Deities&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1941"></A><A HREF="#fn_1936"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> His Augustness Oho-sazaki and Uji-no-waki-iratsuko were, each of them, ceding the Empire to the other,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1942"></A><A HREF="#fn_1937"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> a fisherman&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1943"></A><A HREF="#fn_1938"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> came with a great feast as tribute.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1944"></A><A HREF="#fn_1939"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So they each resigned it to the other. So the elder brother refused it, and caused [258] it to be offered to the younger brother, and the younger brother refused it, and caused it to be offered to the elder brother, during which mutual cedings many days elapsed. As such mutual ceding took place not [only] once or twice, the fisherman wept from the fatigue of going backwards and forwards. So the proverb says:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_321"><font size="1" color="green">p. 321</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> "Ah! the fisherman weeps on account of his own things."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1945"></A><A HREF="#fn_1940"><FONT SIZE="1">5a</FONT></A> Meanwhile Uji-no-waki-iratsuko died early.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1946"></A><A HREF="#fn_1941"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> So His Augustness Oho-sazaki did rule the Empire.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1936"></A><A HREF="kj120.htm#fr_1941">320:1</A> It is not actually the word <i>kami</i>, "deity," that is here used in the original, but <i>hashira</i>, which is the Auxiliary Numeral for Deities.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1937"></A><A HREF="kj120.htm#fr_1942">320:2</A> Neither being willing to accept the Imperial dignity.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1938"></A><A HREF="kj120.htm#fr_1943">320:3</A> Or, "some fishermen," and similarly in the Plural throughout.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1939"></A><A HREF="kj120.htm#fr_1944">320:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, came to present fish to His Majesty.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1940"></A><A HREF="kj120.htm#fr_1945">321:5a</A> Motowori is probably right in saying that the point of this proverb lies in the consideration that, whereas people in general weep for that which they have not, this fisherman wept on account of the trouble which was caused to him by the fish which he had.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1941"></A><A HREF="kj120.htm#fr_1946">321:6</A> Or, "died first," The use in this place of the character <A NAME="img_32100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32100.jpg">, properly confined to the meaning of the "death of an Emperor," is remarkable. See Motowori's observations on the point in Vol. XXXIII, pp. 78-80.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXIV.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART XI.&#8212;AMA-NO-HI-BOKO CROSSES OVER TO JAPAN)]</h2>  
<p>Moreover of old there had been [a man] called by the name of Ama-no-hi-boko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1947"></A><A HREF="#fn_1942"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> child of the ruler of the land of Shiragi. This person crossed over here [to Japan]. The reason of his crossing over here was [this]: In the land of Shiragi there was a certain lagoon,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1948"></A><A HREF="#fn_1943"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> called by the name of the Agu Lagoon.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1949"></A><A HREF="#fn_1944"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> On the bank of this lagoon&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1950"></A><A HREF="#fn_1945"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> a certain poor girl was [taking her] midday sleep. Tunc solis radii, coelesti arcui similes, in privatas partes impegerunt. Again there was a certain poor man, [259] who, thinking this occurrence&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1951"></A><A HREF="#fn_1946"><FONT SIZE="1">5b</FONT></A> strange, constantly watched the woman's behaviour. So the woman, having conceived from the time of that midday sleep, gave birth to</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_322"><font size="1" color="green">p. 322</font></A></p>  
<p>a red jewel. Then the poor man who had watched her begged [to be allowed] to take the jewel, and kept it constantly wrapped up by his side.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1952"></A><A HREF="#fn_1947"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> This person, having planted a rice-field in a valley,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1953"></A><A HREF="#fn_1948"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> had loaded a cow&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1954"></A><A HREF="#fn_1949"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> with food for the labourers, and was getting into the middle of the valley, when he met the ruler's son, Ama-no-hi-boko, who thereupon asked him, saying: "Why enterest thou the valley with a load of food upon a cow? Thou wilt surely kill this cow and eat her." Forthwith he seized the man and was about to put him into prison, when the man replied, saying: "I was not going to kill the cow. I was simply taking food to the people in the fields." But still [the ruler's child] would not let him go. 'Then he undid the jewel [which hung] at his side, and [therewith] bribed [the ruler's child]. So [the latter] let the poor man go, brought the jewel [home], and placed it beside his couch. Forthwith it was trans-formed into a beautiful maiden, whom he straightway wedded, and made his chief wife. Then the maiden perpetually prepared all sorts of dainties with which she constantly fed her husband. So the ruler's child [grew] proud in his heart, and reviled his wife. But the woman said: "I am not a woman who ought to be the wife of such as thou. I will go to the land of my ancestors;"&#8212;and forthwith she secretly embarked in a boat, and fled away across here [to Japan], and landed&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1955"></A><A HREF="#fn_1950"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> at Naniha.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1956"></A><A HREF="#fn_1951"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> (<small>This is the deity called Princess Akaru,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1957"></A><A HREF="#fn_1952"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> who dwells in the shrine of Hime-goso&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1958"></A><A HREF="#fn_1953"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> at Naniha.</small>) Thereupon Ame-no-hi-boko, hearing [260] of his wife's flight, forthwith pursued her across hither, and was about to arrive at Naniha, when the Deity of the passage&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1959"></A><A HREF="#fn_1954"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> prevented his entrance. So he went back again, and landed in the country of Tajima.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1960"></A><A HREF="#fn_1955"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<p>

<p><a name="page_323"><font size="1" color="green">p. 323</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXV.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART XII.&#8212;DESCENDANTS OF AMA-NO-HI-BOKO, AND TREASURES BROUGHT BY HIM.)]</h2>  
<p>Forthwith staying in that country, he wedded Saki-tsu-mi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1961"></A><A HREF="#fn_1956"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> daughter of Tajima-no-matawo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1962"></A><A HREF="#fn_1957"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and begot a child: Tajima-morosuku.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1963"></A><A HREF="#fn_1958"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> The latter's child was Tajima-hi-ne.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1964"></A><A HREF="#fn_1959"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> The latter's child was Tajima-hinaraki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1965"></A><A HREF="#fn_1960"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> The</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_324"><font size="1" color="green">p. 324</font></A></p>  
<p>latter's children were Tajima-mori,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1966"></A><A HREF="#fn_1961"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next Tajima-hitaka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1967"></A><A HREF="#fn_1962"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> next Kiyo-hiko&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1968"></A><A HREF="#fn_1963"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> (<small>three Deities</small>).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1969"></A><A HREF="#fn_1964"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> This Kiyo-hiko wedded Tagima-no-mehi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1970"></A><A HREF="#fn_1965"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and begot children: Suga-no-morowo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1971"></A><A HREF="#fn_1966"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> next his younger sister Suga-kama-yura-domi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1972"></A><A HREF="#fn_1967"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> So the above mentioned Tajima-hitaka wedded his niece Yura-domi, and begot a child: Her Augustness Princess Takanuka of Kadzuraki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1973"></A><A HREF="#fn_1968"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> (<small>This was the august parent&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1974"></A><A HREF="#fn_1969"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> of Her Augustness Princess Okinaga-tarashi.</small>) So the things which Ama-no-hi-boko brought over here, and which were called the "precious treasures,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1975"></A><A HREF="#fn_1970"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> were: two strings of pearls:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1976"></A><A HREF="#fn_1971"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> likewise a wave-shaking scarf, a wave-cutting scarf, a wind-shaking scarf, and a wind-cutting scarf;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1977"></A><A HREF="#fn_1972"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> likewise a mirror of the offing and a mirror of the shore,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1978"></A><A HREF="#fn_1973"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A>&#8212;eight articles in all. (<small>These are the Eight Great Deities of Idzushi.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1979"></A><A HREF="#fn_1974"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1956"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1961">323:1</A> <a name="page_324"><font size="1" color="green">p. 324</font></A> This name may mean "lucky ears," or "possessor of luck;" but it is obscure, and is moreover in the ''Chronicles" (where it is given as the name, not of the daughter, but of the father) read <i>Mahe-tsu-mi</i>,&#8212;a reading which, will not bear either of these interpretations.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1957"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1962">323:2</A> Matawo seems to signify "complete (<i>i.e.</i>, healthy or vigorous) male." Observe that the word Tajima enters into the designations of most of his descendants.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1958"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1963">323:3</A> In the "Chronicles" <i>Morosuke</i>, and elsewhere <i>Morosugi</i>. The etymology of these names is obscure except that of the last-mentioned, which signifies "many cryptomerias."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1959"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1964">323:4</A> <i>Hi-ne</i> may perhaps signify "wondrous lord."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1960"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1965">323:5</A> The meaning of this name is obscure, but that of <i>Hina-rashi-hime</i> in Sect. XXVI (Note 19) may be compared.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1961"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1966">324:6</A> See Sect. LXXIV, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1962"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1967">324:7</A> <i>Hi-taka</i> may <A HREF="errata.htm#79">signify</A> either "sun-height" or "wondrous height."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1963"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1968">324:8</A> This name signifies "pure prince."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1964"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1969">324:9</A> As usual, it is not the actual word Deity that is used, but the Auxiliary Numeral for Deities.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1965"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1970">324:10</A> <i>Tagima</i> is the name of a place, not to be confounded with the province of Tajima. The signification of <i>mehi</i> is quite obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1966"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1971">324:11</A> <i>Suga</i> may either be the name of place in Tajima, as proposed<a name="page_325"><font size="1" color="green">p. 325</font></A> by Motowori, or identical with the Suga of Sect. XIX. The meaning of Morowo is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1967"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1972">324:12</A> The signification of this name is obscure. But Suga, Kama, and Yura are apparently the names of places.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1968"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1973">324:13</A> <i>Kadzuraki no Taka-nuka-hime</i>. Kadzuraki is the name of a department, and Takanuka that of a place in that department, in the province of Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1969"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1974">324:14</A> Literally, "ancestress." But see Sect. XXII, Note 4. It will be remembered that <i>Okinaga-tarashi-hime</i> was the Empress Jin-go.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1970"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1975">324:15</A> Literally, "treasures of jewels."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1971"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1976">324:16</A> Or, "beads."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1972"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1977">324:17</A> <i>I.e.</i>, a scarf to raise the waves and a scarf to still the waves, a scarf to raise the wind and a scarf to still the wind. <i>Conf</i>. the magic scarfs mentioned hear the beginning of Sect. XXIII, by waving which the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land (<i>Oho-kuni-nushi</i>) kept off the snakes, the wasps and the centipedes.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1973"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1978">324:18</A> This seems to be the signification of the original terms <i>oki tsu kagami</i> and <i>hi tsu kagami</i>, but we are not hereby helped to a very clear understanding of the nature of the articles which the author <A HREF="errata.htm#80">meant</A> to describe. The parallel passage of the "Chronicles" tells us of a "sun, mirror." Indeed it enumerates the "eight precious treasures" in a manner that diverges a great deal from the account given in these "Records."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1974"></A><A HREF="kj122.htm#fr_1979">324:19</A> Or, the "Eight-fold Great Deity." As has already frequently been remarked, the distinction which we so rigorously draw between Singular and Plural does not occupy the Japanese mind, and "eight "and "eight-fold" are taken to mean much the same thing, In the following sentence we find these eight deities (or this eight-fold deity) spoken of in such a manner as to necessitate the use of the Singular Number in the translation. Motowori supposes that they (or he) took the form of a young man (as in several other legends) to become the father of the Goddess mentioned in the text. . . . <i>Idzushi</i> seems to signify "wonderful stone."</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_326"><font size="1" color="green">p. 326</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXVI.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART XIII.&#8212;THE YOUTH-OF-THE-GLOW-ON-THE-AUTUMN-MOUNTAINS AND THE YOUTH-OF-THE-HAZE-ON-THE-SPRING-MOUNTAINS).]</h2>  
<p>So this Deity had a daughter whose name was the Deity Maiden-of-Idzushi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1980"></A><A HREF="#fn_1975"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> So eighty Deities wished to [262] obtain this Maiden-of-Idzushi in marriage, but none of them could do so.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1981"></A><A HREF="#fn_1976"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Hereupon there were two Deities, brothers, of whom the elder was called the Youth-of-the-Glow-on-the-Autumn-Mountains,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1982"></A><A HREF="#fn_1977"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and the younger was named the Youth-of-the-Haze-on-the-Spring-Mountains.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1983"></A><A HREF="#fn_1978"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So the elder brother said to the younger brother: "Though I beg for&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1984"></A><A HREF="#fn_1979"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> the Maiden of Idzushi, I cannot obtain her in marriage. Wilt thou [be able] to obtain her?" He answered, saying: "I will easily obtain her." Then the elder brother said: "If thou shalt obtain this maiden, I will take off my upper and lower garments, and distil liquor in a jar of my own height,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1985"></A><A HREF="#fn_1980"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and prepare all the things of the mountains and of the rivers&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1986"></A><A HREF="#fn_1981"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> [and give them to thee] in payment of the wager." Then the younger brother told his mother everything that the elder brother had said. Forthwith the mother, having taken wistaria-fibre, wove and sewed in the space of a single night an upper garment and trowsers, and also socks and boots, and likewise made a bow and arrows, and clothed him in this upper garment, trowsers, [263] etc., made him take the bow and arrows, and sent him to the maiden's house, where both his apparel and the bow and arrows all turned into wistaria-blossoms. Thereupon the Youth-of-the-Haze-on-the-Spring-Mountains hung up the bow and arrows in the maiden's privy. Then, when the Maiden-of-Idzushi, thinking the blossoms strange, brought them [home, the Youth-of-the-Haze-on-the-Spring-Mountains]</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_327"><font size="1" color="green">p. 327</font></A></p>  
<p>followed behind the maiden into the house, and forthwith wedded her. So she gave birth to a child.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1987"></A><A HREF="#fn_1982"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> Then he spoke to his elder brother, saying: "I have obtained the Mayden-of-Idzushi." Thereupon the elder brother, vexed that the younger brother should have wedded her, did not pay the things he had wagered. Then when [the younger brother] complained to his mother, his august parent replied, saying: "During my august life the Deities indeed are to be well imitated; moreover it must be because he imitates mortal men&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1988"></A><A HREF="#fn_1983"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> that he does not pay those things." Forthwith, in her anger with her elder child, she took a jointed bamboo&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1989"></A><A HREF="#fn_1984"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> from an island in the River Idzushi, and made a coarse basket with eight holes,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1990"></A><A HREF="#fn_1985"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> and took stones from the river, and mixing them with brine, wrapped them in the leaves of the bamboo&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1991"></A><A HREF="#fn_1986"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and caused this curse to be spoken:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1992"></A><A HREF="#fn_1987"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> "Like unto the becoming green of these bamboo-leaves, [do thou] become green and wither! [264] Again, like unto the flowing and ebbing of this brine&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1993"></A><A HREF="#fn_1988"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> [do thou] flow and ebb! Again, like unto the sinking of these stones, [do thou] sink and be prostrate! "Having caused this curse to be spoken, she placed [the basket] over the smoke.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1994"></A><A HREF="#fn_1989"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> Therefore the elder brother dried up, withered, sickened, and lay prostrate&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1995"></A><A HREF="#fn_1990"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> for the space of eight years. So on the elder brother entreating his august parent with lamentations and fears, she forthwith caused the curse to be reversed.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1996"></A><A HREF="#fn_1991"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> Thereupon his body became sound&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1997"></A><A HREF="#fn_1992"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> as it had been before. (This is the origin of the term "a divine wager payment.")&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1998"></A><A HREF="#fn_1993"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_328"><font size="1" color="green">p. 328</font></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1975"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1980">326:1</A> <a name="page_327"><font size="1" color="green">p. 327</font></A> <i>Idzushi-wotome no kami</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1976"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1981">326:2</A> Literally "eighty Deities wished to obtain this Maiden of Idzushi, but none could wed (her)." But the sense is that given in the translation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1977"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1982">326:3</A> <a name="page_328"><font size="1" color="green">p. 328</font></A> <i>Ahi yama no shita-bi-wotoko</i>. The explanation of the name is that given by Motowori (following Mabuchi), who sees in it a reference to the ruddy brilliance of the leaves, which is so marked a feature of the Japanese woods in autumn. The Chinese characters used have, indeed, the signification of the lower ice of the autumn mountains; but "lower ice "may well be simply phonetic in this case.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1978"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1983">326:4</A> <i>Haru-yamu no kasumi-wotoko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1979"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1984">326:5</A> In Japanese <i>kohedomo</i>, written with the characters <A NAME="img_32800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32800.jpg">. Perhaps Motowori is right in supposing this Verb to have been originally identical with <i>kofuru</i>, "to love" (<A NAME="img_32801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32801.jpg">) whose corresponding form is <i>kofuredomo</i>. If so, the author may have meant to make his hero say, "though I love the maiden, etc." But it is better to be guided by the characters, and to suppose that he referred to the request made to her mother to grant her to him.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1980"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1985">326:6</A> Literally, "compute the height of my person and distil liquor in a jar."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1981"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1986">326:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, all the valuable produce of the chase and of the fisheries, such as are perpetually mentioned in the Shinto "Rituals" as being presented to the gods, Thus in the "Service of the Goddess of Food" (see Mr. Satow's translation in Vol. VII, Pt. IV, p. 414 of these "Transactions,") we read that the worshipper offered: "as to things which dwell in the mountains&#8212;things soft of hair and things rough of hair; as to things which grow in the great-field-plain sweet herbs and bitter herbs; as to things which dwell in the blue-sea-plain&#8212;things wide of fin and things narrow of fin, down to weeds of the offing and weeds of the shore."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1982"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1987">327:8</A> Literally, "one child."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1983"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1988">327:9</A> The Japanese original of the words here unavoidably rendered by "mortal men" in order to mark the antithesis to the word "Deities, has been more literally translated by "living people" in an earlier passage of the work (see Sect. IX, Note 17). The signification of the entire sentence is: "During my lifetime, thy brother should be careful to imitate the upright conduct of the gods. For if, instead of doing so, he be dishonest and untruthful as are the sons of men, it will be at his own peril."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1984"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1989">327:10</A> Or, according to the more usual reading, "a one-jointed bamboo;" but in either case the meaning is obscure. Motowori, who adopts the reading that has been followed in the translation, suggests that the expression may simply be a periphrasis for the bamboo in general.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1985"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1990">327:11</A> <A NAME="img_32802"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32802.jpg">. Motowori remarks that the word "eight" in this <a name="page_329"><font size="1" color="green">p. 329</font></A> place (where, to indicate a considerable number we should rather expect "eighty") is curious, and he surmises that <A NAME="img_32900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32900.jpg"> may be an error for <A NAME="img_32901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32901.jpg">, "large." The word "coarse" itself is sufficient to show that the apertures left in the plaiting of the basket were large.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1986"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1991">327:12</A> <i>Scil</i>. of which the basket was woven.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1987"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1992">327:13</A> <i>Scil</i>. by her younger son.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1988"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1993">327:14</A> In this case, as Motowori remarks, it is the sea-water that is intended to be spoken of, whereas the allusion in the previous sentence is to hard salt. But the Japanese language uses the same word for both, and the same Chinese character is here also used in both contexts. For this curse <i>conf</i>. Sect. XL (Note 18 <i>et. seq.</i>) and Sect. XLI.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1989"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1994">327:15</A> <i>Scil</i>. of the furnace (kitchen) in the younger brother's house, as Motowori suggests.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1990"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1995">327:16</A> The text has the character <A NAME="img_32902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32902.jpg">, which signifies "to wither" or "dry up" (spoken of trees). But the translator agrees with Motowori in considering it to be in all probability an error for <A NAME="img_32903"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32903.jpg">, "to be prostrate; and in any case it could not here be rendered by either of the verbs "dry up" or "wither "without introducing into the English version a tautology which does not exist in the Japanese original.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1991"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1996">327:17</A> Such seems to be the meaning of the obscure original <i>sono tokohi-do wo kahesashimeki</i> (<A NAME="img_32904"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32904.jpg">), Motowori would understand it in a rather more specialized sense to signify that "she caused the implement of the curse (<i>i.e.</i>, the basket) to be taken away,"</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1992"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1997">327:18</A> Literally, "was pacified."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1993"></A><A HREF="kj123.htm#fr_1998">327:19</A> Or, if we take <A NAME="img_32905"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32905.jpg"> in the text as equivalent to <A NAME="img_32906"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/32906.jpg">, "this is the origin of "divine water-payments."</P>

<p><a name="page_329"><font size="1" color="green">p. 329</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXVII.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART XVI.&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>Again this Heavenly Sovereign Homuda's&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_1999"></A><A HREF="#fn_1994"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> august child King Wake-nuke-futa-mata wedded his mother's younger sister Momo-shiki-iro-be,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2000"></A><A HREF="#fn_1995"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> another name for whom was Her Augustness Oto-hime-ma-wake-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2001"></A><A HREF="#fn_1996"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and begot children: Oho-iratsuko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2002"></A><A HREF="#fn_1997"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> another name for whom [265] was King Ohohodo;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2003"></A><A HREF="#fn_1998"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next her Augustness Osaka-no-oho-naka-tsu-hime:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2004"></A><A HREF="#fn_1999"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_330"><font size="1" color="green">p. 330</font></A></p>  
<p>next Tawi-no-naka-tsu-hime;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2005"></A><A HREF="#fn_2000"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> next Tamiya-no-naka-tsu-hime;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2006"></A><A HREF="#fn_2001"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> next Fujihara-no-koto-fushi-no-ira-tsume;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2007"></A><A HREF="#fn_2002"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> next Queen Torime;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2008"></A><A HREF="#fn_2003"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> next King Sane.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2009"></A><A HREF="#fn_2004"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> (<small>Seven Kings (and Queens).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2010"></A><A HREF="#fn_2005"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A></small>) <small>So King Oho-hodo (was the ancestor of the Dukes of Mikuni,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2011"></A><A HREF="#fn_2006"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> the Dukes of Hata,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2012"></A><A HREF="#fn_2007"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> the Dukes of Okinaga,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2013"></A><A HREF="#fn_2008"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> the Dukes of Sakahito of Sakata,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2014"></A><A HREF="#fn_2009"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> the Dukes of Yamaji,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2015"></A><A HREF="#fn_2010"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> the Dukes of [266] Meta in Tsukushi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2016"></A><A HREF="#fn_2011"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A> and the Dukes of Fuse.)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2017"></A><A HREF="#fn_2012"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A></small> Again King Netori wedded his younger half-sister the Lady Mihara, and begot children: King Naka-tsu-hiko;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2018"></A><A HREF="#fn_2013"><FONT SIZE="1">20</FONT></A> next King Iwa-shiha&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2019"></A><A HREF="#fn_2014"><FONT SIZE="1">21</FONT></A> (<small>Two Kings.</small>) Again the child of King Kata-shiha&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2020"></A><A HREF="#fn_2015"><FONT SIZE="1">22</FONT></A> was King Kuni.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2021"></A><A HREF="#fn_2016"><FONT SIZE="1">23</FONT></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_1994"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_1999">329:1</A> <a name="page_330"><font size="1" color="green">p. 330</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, the Emperor &#332;-jin's.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1995"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2000">329:2</A> The import of this compound is not clear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1996"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2001">329:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the&nbsp; younger princess, the truly young princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1997"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2002">329:4</A> <i>i.e.</i>, "the great lord."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1998"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2003">329:5</A> <i>Oho-hodo no miko</i>. The signification of <i>Oho-hodo</i> is obscure. Motowori surmises it to have been originally the name of a place.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_1999"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2004">329:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the great middle princess of Osaka. Osaka is the name of a place in Yamato. The word "middle "should by the analogy of other such genealogies indicate the fact that this princess was the fourth child out of seven. Here however she is mentioned second, and the same designation is applied to the two next daughters. There is evidently some confusion in the tradition.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2000"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2005">330:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the middle princess of Tawi,"&#8212;a place in Kahachi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2001"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2006">330:8</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the middle princess of Tamiya.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2002"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2007">330:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the lady Koto-fushi of Fuji-hara." But the meaning of Kato fushi is obscure, and Motowori surmises it to be an alternative or corrupt form of <i>Sotohoshi</i>. (For the celebrated princess of the latter name see Sect. CXXXVII, Note 9.) Fujihara is the name of a place in Yamato, and signifies "wistaria-moor."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2003"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2008">330:10</A> <i>Torime no miko</i>. This name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2004"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2009">330:11</A> <i>Sane no miko</i>. Motowori believes <i>sane</i> to stand erroneously for <i>sami</i>; but both forms are obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2005"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2010">330:12</A> The Japanese word includes both genders.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2006"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2011">330:13</A> <a name="page_331"><font size="1" color="green">p. 331</font></A> <i>Mikuni no kimi</i>. <i>Mikuni</i> is the name of a well-known place in the province of Echizen. It signifies "three countries."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2007"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2012">330:14</A> <i>Hata no kimi</i>. There are several places called Hata, and it is not known which of them is here intended. The signification of the name is also uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2008"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2013">330:15</A> <i>Okinaga no kimi</i>. See Sect. LXII, Note 31.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2009"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2014">330:16</A> <i>Sakata no Saka-bito no kimi</i>. This is Motowori's restoration of an apparently corrupt text. Sakata and Sakabito are both taken to be names of places, the first of a district in Afumi, the second of a place in Settsu. Sakabito (<A NAME="img_33100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33100.jpg">) seems a very curious compound for the name of a place. Moreover the double title is unusual, and it may be thought that the word "Dukes" has fallen out of the text, and that in reality two families were intended to be spoken of.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2010"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2015">330:17</A> <i>Yamaji no kimi</i>. <i>Yamaji</i> ("mountain road") is supposed by Motowori to be the name of a place,&#8212;perhaps in the province of Higo.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2011"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2016">330:18</A> <i>Tsukushi no Meta no kimi</i>. Tsukushi is the old name of the whole of the South-Western island of the Japanese archipelago and Meta the name of a place in the province of Hizen in that island. The etymology of Meta is uncertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2012"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2017">330:19</A> <i>Fuse no kimi</i>. Fuse is the name of uncertain import found in several provinces. It is not known which is meant to be here designated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2013"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2018">330:20</A> <i>Naka-tsu-hiko no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the middle prince," a designation which would lead one to expect to find mention of an elder brother.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2014"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2019">330:21</A> <i>Iwashima no miko</i>. Iwashima seems to be the name of a place, but the signification of <i>Iha</i> (not to be confounded with <i>iha</i> "stone" or "rock") is altogether obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2015"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2020">330:22</A> <i>Katashiha no miko</i>. This prince has not been mentioned in the previous genealogies, which is curious. Katashiha is the name of a place in Chikuzen, and signifies "hard rock."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2016"></A><A HREF="kj124.htm#fr_2021">330:23</A> <i>Kunu no miko</i>. <i>Kunu</i> is altogether obscure.</P>

<p><a name="page_332"><font size="1" color="green">p. 332</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR &#332;-JIN (PART XV.&#8212;HIS AGE AND PLACE OF BURIAL).]</h2>  
<p>The august years of this Heavenly Sovereign Homuda were altogether one hundred and thirty. His august mausoleum is on the mound of Mofusu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2022"></A><A HREF="#fn_2017"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> at Wega in Kafuchi.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2017"></A><A HREF="kj125.htm#fr_2022">332:1</A> <a name="page_332"><font size="1" color="green">p. 332</font></A> Or, as Motowori reads it, <i>Mofushi</i>. The etymology is uncertain. <i>Wega</i> has already appeared in Sect. CIII (Note 3). The Old Printed Edition and some Manuscripts have at the conclusion of this volume the following note: <A NAME="img_33200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33200.jpg">, "It is the mausoleum of Mozu." But Mozu is in the province of Idzumi, and all the later editions discard this note as an interpolation.</P>

<HEAD>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="../../css/marg.css">
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">
<META name="keywords" content="Kojiki Japan Shinto Mythology Legend Folklore Text Scripture Emperor Empress Chronology">
<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume III: Section CXIX.&#8212;Emperor Nin-toku (Part I.&#8212;Genealogies)</TITLE>
</HEAD>

<p><a name="page_333"><font size="1" color="green">p. 333</font></A>[267]</p>  <h1 align="center">VOL. III.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2023"></A><A HREF="#fn_2018"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A></h1>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXIX.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART I.&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Oho-sazaki dwelt in the palace of Takatsu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2024"></A><A HREF="#fn_2019"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> at Naniha, and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded (<small>the Empress&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2025"></A><A HREF="#fn_2020"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></small>) Her Augustness Iha-no-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2026"></A><A HREF="#fn_2021"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> daughter of Kadzuraki-no-sotsu-biko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2027"></A><A HREF="#fn_2022"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and begot august children: His Augustness Ohoye-no-izaho-wake;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2028"></A><A HREF="#fn_2023"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next the Middle King of the Inlet of Sumi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2029"></A><A HREF="#fn_2024"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> next His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake of Tajihi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2030"></A><A HREF="#fn_2025"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> next His Augustness the Noble Wo-asadzuma-no-waku-go&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2031"></A><A HREF="#fn_2026"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> (<small>four Deities.</small>) Again he wedded Princess Kami-naga, daughter of the Duke of Muragata in Himuka, as mentioned above,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2032"></A><A HREF="#fn_2027"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and begot august children: Hatabi-no-oho-iratsuko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2033"></A><A HREF="#fn_2028"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> another [268] name for whom was the King of Great Kusaka;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2034"></A><A HREF="#fn_2029"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> next Hatabi-no-waki-iratsume,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2035"></A><A HREF="#fn_2030"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> another name for whom was Her Augustness Princess Nagahi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2036"></A><A HREF="#fn_2031"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> and another name was Her Augustness Waka-kusaka-be&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2037"></A><A HREF="#fn_2032"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A>(<small>Two Deities.</small>) Again he wedded his younger half-sister Yata-no-waki-iratsume&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2038"></A><A HREF="#fn_2033"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> Again he wedded his younger half-sister Uji-no-waki-iratsume. These two Deities had no august children. Altogether the august children of this Heavenly Sovereign Oho-sakaki [numbered] in all six Deities, (<small>Five Kings and one Queen</small>). So His Augustness Izaho-wake [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire. Next His Augustness Tajihi-no midzu-ha-wake likewise ruled the Empire. Next His Augustness the Noble Oh-asadzuma-no-waku-go likewise ruled the Empire.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2039"></A><A HREF="#fn_2034"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2018"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2023">333:1</A> <a name="page_333"><font size="1" color="green">p. 333</font></A> Literally, "lower volume"(there being three in all). See Author's Preface, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2019"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2024">333:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "high port."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2020"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2025">333:3</A> <a name="page_334"><font size="1" color="green">p. 334</font></A> Motowori surmises that the reason why the characters <A HREF="errata.htm#81">signifying</A> "Empress" are in all the text here written in small characters is on account of this personage not having been of Imperial birth.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2021"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2026">333:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the rock princess." Motowori supposes the name to be indicative of prosperity and long life.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2022"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2027">333:5</A> See Sect. LXI, Note 55,</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2023"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2028">333:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the elder brother lord Izaho," the latter name being of uncertain import.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2024"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2029">333:7</A> <i>Sumi-no ye-no-naka-tsu-miko</i>. Both the phrase "middle king" and the Inlet of Sumi have been already commented on.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2025"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2030">333:8</A> <i>Tajihi no midzu-ha-wake</i>. Tajihi is the name of a place in Kahachi. The traditional origin of its application to this will be found in Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXXV, p. 6. <i>Midzu-ha-wake</i> probably means "the lord with the beautiful teeth."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2026"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2031">333:9</A> <i>Wo-asadzuma-no-waku-go no sukune</i>. Asadzuma is the name of a place in Yamato, and <i>wo</i> (though written <A NAME="img_33400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33400.jpg">) seems to be the slightly Honorific Prefix <i>wo</i> (<A NAME="img_33401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33401.jpg">) whose proper signification is "small" <i>Waku-go</i> means "younger child."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2027"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2032">333:10</A> See Sect. CVII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2028"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2033">333:11</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the great lord of Hatabi." <i>Hatabi</i> is altogether obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2029"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2034">333:12</A> <i>Oha-kusaka no miko</i>. For <i>Kusaka</i> see Sect. CI, Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2030"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2035">333:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the young lady of Hatabi." Conf. Note 1 I.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2031"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2036">333:14</A> <i>Nagahi-hime</i>. This name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2032"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2037">333:15</A> <i>Kusaka-be</i> is an alternative form of <i>Kusaka</i>. The compound therefore signifies "young princess of Kusaka."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2033"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2038">333:16</A> This name and the following have already appeared in the genealogies of the preceding reign (Sect. CIV.)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2034"></A><A HREF="kj126.htm#fr_2039">333:17</A> These were the Emperors Ri-chiu, Han-zei, and In-giyo.</P>

<p><a name="page_334"><font size="1" color="green">p. 334</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXX: EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART II.&#8212;VARIOUS DEEDS).]</h2>  
<p>In the august reign of this Heavenly Sovereign the Kadzuraki Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2040"></A><A HREF="#fn_2035"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> was established as the august proxy of the Empress, Her Augustness Iha-no-hime. Again the Mibu</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_335"><font size="1" color="green">p. 335</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2041"></A><A HREF="#fn_2036"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> was established as the august proxy of the Heir Apparent, His Augustness Izaho-wake. Again the Tajihi Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2042"></A><A HREF="#fn_2037"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> was established as the august proxy of His Augustness Midzuna-wake. Again the Oho-kusaka Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2043"></A><A HREF="#fn_2038"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> was [269] established as the august proxy of King Oho-kusaka, and the Waka-kusaka Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2044"></A><A HREF="#fn_2039"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> was established as the august proxy of King Waga-kusake-be. Again people from Hada were set to labour, and the embankment at Mamuta&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2045"></A><A HREF="#fn_2040"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and also the granaries of Manuta were made. Again the Pool of Wani&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2046"></A><A HREF="#fn_2041"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and the Pool of Yosemi were made. Again the Naniha Channel&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2047"></A><A HREF="#fn_2042"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> was dug, and [the waters of the rivers] led to the sea. Again the Wobashi Channel&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2048"></A><A HREF="#fn_2043"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> was dug. Again the port of the inlet of Sumi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2049"></A><A HREF="#fn_2044"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> was established.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>
