<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2035"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2040">334:1</A> <a name="page_335"><font size="1" color="green">p. 335</font></A> <i>Kadzuraki be</i>. For Kadzuraki see Sect. LV, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2036"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2041">335:2</A> <i>Mibu-be</i>. Motowori quotes approvingly a derivation of the "gentile name" of Mibu from <i>Bi-fuku-mon</i> (<A NAME="img_33500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33500.jpg">), the name of a gate which the first bearer of the name is related to have constructed. Taking into account the letter-changes which occurred in older times in the passage of words from Chinese into Japanese, the etymology is plausible enough.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2037"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2042">335:3</A> <i>Tajihi-be</i>. Tajihi is the name of a place in Kahachi, and is of uncertain origin.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2038"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2043">335:4</A> <i>Oho-kusaka-be</i>. This tribe of course took its name simply from that of Prince Oho-kusaka.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2039"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2044">335:5</A> <i>Waka-kusaka-be</i>. A similar observation to that in the last applies to this name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2040"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2045">335:6</A> See Sect. LIII, Note I.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2041"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2046">335:7</A> <i>Wani no ike</i>, in the province of Kahachi. <i>Wani</i> signifies "crocodile," and it was also the name of the Korean personage mentioned in Sect. CX (Note 6). But the reason why the Pool here spoken of was so called does net appear. The Pool of Yosami has already been mentioned in Sect. LXII (Note 85). Motowori supposes that it must have dried up during the interim.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2042"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2047">335:8</A> <i>Naniha no hori-ye</i>. Motowori tells us that the regularization of <a name="page_336"><font size="1" color="green">p. 336</font></A> the channels of the Yodo and Yamato Rivers, whose mouths nearly meet at this point with various intersecting branches, is what is here intended to be referred to.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2043"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2048">335:9</A> <i>Wobashi no ye</i>. <i>Wo-bashi</i> ("little bridge") is the name of a village in the province of Settsu.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2044"></A><A HREF="kj127.htm#fr_2049">335:10</A> <i>Suminoye no tsu</i>. Close of Naniha; it is the modern <i>Sumiyoshi</i>. Conf. Sect. X, Note 22.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_336"><font size="1" color="green">p. 336</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXI.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU [PART III.&#8212;HE REMITS THE TAXES)]</h2>  
<p>Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, ascending a lofty mountain and looking on the land all round, spoke, saying: "In the whole land there rises no smoke; the land is all poverty-stricken. So I remit&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2050"></A><A HREF="#fn_2045"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> all people's taxes and [forced labour] from now till three years [hence.]" Therefore the great palace became dilapidated, and the rain leaked in everywhere; but no repairs were made. The rain that leaked in was caught in troughs,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2051"></A><A HREF="#fn_2046"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and [the inmates] removed from [its reach] to places where there was no leakage. When later [the Heavenly Sovereign]] looked on all the land, the smoke was abundant in the land. So finding the people rich, he now exacted taxes and forced labour. Therefore the peasantry&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2052"></A><A HREF="#fn_2047"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> prospered, and did not suffer from forced labour. So in praise of that august reign, it was called the reign of the Emperor-Sage.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2053"></A><A HREF="#fn_2048"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2045"></A><A HREF="kj128.htm#fr_2050">336:1</A> Motowori's reading of this Verb in the Imperative Mood (as if containing an order addressed by the monarch to his ministers) seems less natural than the order reading in the Indicative, which accordingly the translator has followed.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2046"></A><A HREF="kj128.htm#fr_2051">336:2</A> There is uncertainty as to the exact character in the original. <a name="page_337"><font size="1" color="green">p. 337</font></A> But the older editions read it as the Japanese word <i>hako</i>, "boxes." while Motowori prefers <i>hi</i>, "tubes." "Troughs "seems to conciliate both views, and to be also appropriate to the use mentioned in the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2047"></A><A HREF="kj128.htm#fr_2052">336:3</A> Or simply, "the people." But the expression <A NAME="img_33700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33700.jpg"> is generally used in Japanese of the peasantry only.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2048"></A><A HREF="kj128.htm#fr_2053">336:4</A> <A NAME="img_33701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33701.jpg">; If, following most texts, we omitted the final character <A NAME="img_33702"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33702.jpg">, "reign," the English translation would be "in praise of that august reign, (the Heavenly Sovereign) was called the Emperor-Sage."</P>

<CENTER>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_337"><font size="1" color="green">p. 337</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. <A HREF="errata.htm#82">CXXII</A>.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART IV.&#8212;HE LOVES PRINCESS KURO).]</h2>  
<p>His Empress, Her Augustness Iha-no-hime, was exceedingly jealous. So the concubines employed by the Heavenly Sovereign could not even peep inside the palace; and if anything happened,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2054"></A><A HREF="#fn_2049"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> [the Empress] stamped with jealousy. Then the Heavenly Sovereign, hearing of the regular beauty of Princess Kuro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2055"></A><A HREF="#fn_2050"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> daughter of the Suzerain of Ama in Kibi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2056"></A><A HREF="#fn_2051"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and having sent for her, employed her. But she, afraid of the Empress's jealousy, fled down to her native land, The Heavenly [271] Sovereign, gazing from an upper story upon Princess Kuro's departure by boat upon the sea, sang saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"In the offing there are rows of small boats. My wife Masadzuko of Kurozaki goes down towards her [native] land."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2057"></A><A HREF="#fn_2052"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So the Empress was very angry on hearing this august Song, and sent people to the great strand&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2058"></A><A HREF="#fn_2053"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> to drive Princess Kuro ashore, and chase her away on foot.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2059"></A><A HREF="#fn_2054"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, for love of Princess Kuro, deceived the Empress, saying that he wanted to see the Island of Ahaji.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2060"></A><A HREF="#fn_2055"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> And when he made his progress</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_338"><font size="1" color="green">p. 338</font></A></p>  
<p>and was in the Island of Ahaji, he, gazing afar, sang saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"When, having departed from the point of wave-beaten Naniha, I look at the country,&#8212;the Island of Aha, the Is-land of Onogoro, and also the Island of Ajimasa are visible. The Island of Saketsu is visible."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2061"></A><A HREF="#fn_2056"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Forthwith passing on from that island, he made a progress to the land of Kibi. Then Her Augustness Princess Kuro- made him grandly reside at a place among the mountain-fields,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2062"></A><A HREF="#fn_2057"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> and presented to him great august food, When for this [purpose] she plucked cabbage in that place to boil into great august soup, the Heavenly Sovereign went to the place where the maiden was plucking the cabbage, and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! how delightful it is to pluck with a person of Kibi the cabbage sown in the mountain fields!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2063"></A><A HREF="#fn_2058"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>When the Heavenly Sovereign made his progress up,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2064"></A><A HREF="#fn_2059"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></p>  
<p>Princess Kuro presented an august&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2065"></A><A HREF="#fn_2060"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> Song saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Even though the west wind blow up towards Yamato, and the clouds part, and we be separated, shall I forget [thee]?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2066"></A><A HREF="#fn_2061"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[273] Again she sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Whose spouse is it that goes towards Yamato? Whose spouse is it that creeps from beneath like hidden water?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2067"></A><A HREF="#fn_2062"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_339"><font size="1" color="green">p. 339</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2049"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2054">337:1</A> Motowori shows by collating various passages in other ancient works that this is the probable signification of the curious expression in <a name="page_339"><font size="1" color="green">p. 339</font></A> the original, <i>kotodateba</i> (<A NAME="img_33900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33900.jpg"> for <A NAME="img_33901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/33901.jpg">). The reference of course is to the occurrence of anything noteworthy among the concubines, such as the birth of a son, etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2050"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2055">337:2</A> <i>Kuro-hime</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "black princess" probably meaning "black-haired princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2051"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2056">337:3</A> <i>Kibi no Ama no atahe</i>. Of this family nothing is known. <i>Ama</i> signifies "fisherman." <i>Kibi</i> is the name of a province.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2052"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2057">337:4</A> Thus interpreted (according to Moribe), the general sense of the Song is quite clear. The word <i>Masadzuko</i>, considered by Moribe to be one of the names of Princess Kuro, is however not so understood by Motowori, who is inclined to see in it rather an Honorific description of her. <i>Kurozaki</i> likewise (<i>i.e.</i>, "black cape," the word <i>kuro</i> seemingly containing an allusion to the name of the Princess) is but the best of many emendations of the name as it stands in the text, viz., <i>Furozaya</i>. See Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXXV. p. 33, for all the possible emendations proposed by him or his predecessors.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2053"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2058">337:5</A> <i>Scil</i>, of the neighbourhood of Naniha. Or possible <i>Oho-ura</i> ("Great Strand") should be taken as the name of a place, though Motowori does not suggest such a view.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2054"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2059">337:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, to make her perform the journey on foot.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2055"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2060">337:7</A> See Sect. V, Note 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2056"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2061">338:8</A> Moribe, commenting on the import of this Song, says: Though the alleged reason was a tour of inspection, it was truly out of love for Princess Kuro that the Monarch had undertaken the journey. When her vessel could no longer be descried, he could still alas! see the islands that remained behind,&#8212;the Island of Aha and the Island of Ajimasa; he could still, alas! see the Islands of Onogoro and Saketsu. Alas for him left alone, parted from his love! Though he spoke not openly, those around him understood the under-current of his "words."&#8212;"Wave-beaten "is the accepted interpretation of <i>oshiteru ya</i> (or <i>oshiteru</i>), the Pillow-Word for Naniha. For the Islands of Aha and Onogoro see respectively Sect. IV, Note 5 and Sect. iii, Note 5. Of the Islands of Ajimasa and Saketsu nothing is known. <i>Ajimasa</i> is the name of a species of palm, the <i>Livistona sinensis</i>, and Motowori supposes that one of the islands in that neighbourhood may anciently have received its name from the palm-trees growing on it. Palms of any kind are, however, not very common in Japan, and seem only to grow when specially cultivated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2057"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2062">338:9</A> Motowori thinks we should in this place understand the word <i>yamagata</i> (for <i>yama-agata</i>) as the name of a place. But in the Song <a name="page_340"><font size="1" color="green">p. 340</font></A> which immediately follows, it must certainly be taken in its etymological sense of "mountain-fields," and it seems therefore quite inconsistent to translate it differently here. Moreover it is allowed that no such place as Yamagata in Kibi is anywhere made mention of.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2058"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2063">338:10</A> The import of this Song is perfectly clear, "the person of Kibi "being of course the Imperial poet's lady-love.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2059"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2064">338:11</A> <i>I.e.</i>, was about to start back to the capital, which was in the province of Settsu.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2060"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2065">338:12</A> This Honorific seems so out of place (seeing that it is not applied to the Emperor's own Songs given in this Section), that it is supposed by the commentators to be an erroneous addition to the text.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2061"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2066">338:13</A> We might also translate thus: "Even though we be separated, as the clouds that part owing to the west wind blowing up towards Yamato, etc.;"&#8212;for the initial lines of the poem which contain the allusion to the wind and to the clouds are simply a Preface, and their import may therefore at will be either considered separately, or else made continuous with that of the rest of the poem.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2062"></A><A HREF="kj129.htm#fr_2067">338:14</A> The meaning of this Song l is: "Whose spouse is it that returns to Yamato? Whose spouse is it that comes thus secretly to make love to me, like a stream flowing underground?"&#8212;The allusion contained in the twice repeated words "whose spouse "is of course to the Empress. The poetess, full of tenderness or the Emperor, regrets for his sake, as well as for her own, that he should be the husband of so jealous' a wife. "Hidden water is the accepted interpretation of the Pillow-Word <i>kontoridzu no</i>, which is with apparent reason supposed to be a contraction of <i>komori-midzu no</i>.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_340"><font size="1" color="green">p. 340</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXIII. EMPEROR NIN-TOKU PART V.&#8212;THE EMPRESS RETIRES TO YAMASHIRO).]</h2>  
<p>After this time the Empress made a progress to the land of Ki in order to pluck aralia-leaves for a copious feast;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2068"></A><A HREF="#fn_2063"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and in the mean while the Heavenly Sovereign wedded Yata-no-waki-iratsume. Hereupon, when the Empress was returning in her august vessel loaded full</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_341"><font size="1" color="green">p. 341</font></A></p>  
<p>of aralia-leaves, a coolie from Kozhima&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2069"></A><A HREF="#fn_2064"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in the land of Kibi, who was in the service of the Superintendent of the Water-Directors,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2070"></A><A HREF="#fn_2065"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> being on his way off to his own country, met at the great passage&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2071"></A><A HREF="#fn_2066"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> of Naniha the vessel of a lady of the train&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2072"></A><A HREF="#fn_2067"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> who had got behind, and forthwith told her, saying: "The Heavenly Sovereign has [274] recently&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2073"></A><A HREF="#fn_2068"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> wedded Yata-no-waki-iratsume, and plays with her day and night. It must probably be because the Empress has not heard of this thing, that she quietly makes progress for pleasure." Then the lady of the train, having heard this narrative, forthwith pursued and reached the august vessel, and reported everything exactly as the coolie had told it. Hereupon the Empress, greatly vexed and angry, threw away into the sea all the aralia-leaves which she had put on board the august vessel. So the place,[where she did so] is called by the name of Cape Mitsu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2074"></A><A HREF="#fn_2069"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Forthwith without entering the palace, but taking her august vessel [from it]&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2075"></A><A HREF="#fn_2070"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and ascending the channel&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2076"></A><A HREF="#fn_2071"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> against the current, she made a progress up into Yamashiro by the river;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2077"></A><A HREF="#fn_2072"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> At this time she sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! the river of Yamashiro where the seedlings grow in succession! As I ascend, ascend the river, oh! on the bank of the river [there] stands growing a <i>sashibu!</i>&#8212;a <i>sashibu</i>-tree; below it stands growing a broad-foliaged five hundred[-fold branching] true camellia-tree; oh! he who is brilliant like its blossoms, widely powerful like its foliage, is the great lord."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2078"></A><A HREF="#fn_2073"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Forthwith going round by Yamashiro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2079"></A><A HREF="#fn_2074"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and arriving at [275] the entrance of the <A HREF="errata.htm#83">Nara</A> Mountain,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2080"></A><A HREF="#fn_2075"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> she sang, saying:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_342"><font size="1" color="green">p. 342</font></A></p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! the river of Yamashiro where the seedlings grow in succession! As I ascend, ascend to Miya, I pass Nara, I pass Yamato with its shield of mountains; and the country I fain would see is Takamiya in Kadzuraki, the neighbourhood of my home."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2081"></A><A HREF="#fn_2076"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[276] Having sung thus, she returned and entered for some time into the house of a person from Kara&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2082"></A><A HREF="#fn_2077"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> named Nurinomi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2083"></A><A HREF="#fn_2078"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A> at Tsutsuki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2084"></A><A HREF="#fn_2079"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_343"><font size="1" color="green">p. 343</font></A></p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2063"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2068">340:1</A> See Sect. CVII, Note 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2064"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2069">341:2</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "small island." It is first mentioned in Sect V (Note 29).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2065"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2070">341:3</A> See Sect. XLVII, Note 18.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2066"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2071">341:4</A> <i>Oho watari</i>. The mouth of the River Yedo is meant to be designated by this name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2067"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2072">341:5</A> The original, expression <i>kuru-bito-me</i> (<A NAME="img_34200"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/34200.jpg">) is obscure, being met with nowhere else in Japanese literature. Motowori conjectures that the function exercised by this lady. was one connected with the Emperor's privy purse.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2068"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2073">341:6</A> The text has the character <A NAME="img_34201"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/34201.jpg">, "all," which make no sense; and Motowori (following Mabuchi) reasonably emends it to <A NAME="img_34202"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/34202.jpg">, "recently," "just now."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2069"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2074">341:7</A> <i>Mitsu no saki</i>. <i>Mitsu</i>, signifying "three," is supposed by the author to refer to the three-cornered leaves of the aralia (the name of the latter being <i>mitsuna gashiha</i>); but a more likely opinion is that which would have us take <i>mitzu</i> as two words, in the sense of "august harbour." In the parallel passage of the "Chronicles," we are told that the place was called <i>Kashiha no watari</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "Oak passage."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2070"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2075">341:8</A> <i>I.e.</i>, going on up the river without stopping at Naniha where the palace was.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2071"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2076">341:9</A> Jr., ,the artificial bed of the river mentioned in Sect. CXX, Note, 8.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2072"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2077">341:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the river Yodo.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2073"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2078">341:11</A> The meaning of this Song is: "As I make my way up the river by boat, I see a <i>sashibu</i> (the name of a tree which cannot now be identified), below which,&#8212;that is to say nearer to the water,&#8212;there grows a <a name="page_343"><font size="1" color="green">p. 343</font></A> camellia-tree, wide-spreading and full of blossoms. Ah! how the sight of the sturdy brilliant beauty of this camellia-tree brings back my lord and master to my mind!"&#8212;It must be remembered that in Japan the camellia-trees grow to a size far superior to that reached by their representatives in Europe. <i>Tsuginefu</i>, rendered according to the view taken by Motowori and Moribe by the phrase "where the seedlings grow in succession," is the Pillow-Word for Yamashiro, and its import is disputed. The interpretation here adopted considers it to refer to the regular succession of young trees planted on a mountain's side when a tract of older timber has been cut down. Mabuchi, in his "Dictionary of Pillow-Words," sees in it, on the contrary, a reference to the rising of peak upon peak in a mountainous district (<i>tsugi-ne fu</i>&#8212;<A NAME="img_34300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/34300.jpg">). Both interpretations rest on the connection between this term and <i>yama</i>, the first half of the name of the province of Yamashiro, which it qualifies. "Five <A HREF="errata.htm#84">hundred</A>[-fold-branching]"and "true" are ornamental epithets applied by the poetess to the camellia-tree. Moribe would take the syllable <i>ma</i>, "true," in the sense of <i>ha</i>, "leaf but this seems less good.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2074"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2079">341:12</A> For the straight road from Naniha in Settsu-to Nara in Yamato would have taken her through the province of Kafuchi. and not through Yamashiro.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2075"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2080">341:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the pass or hill leading from the district of Sagara in Yamashiro to Nara in Yamato. For Nara see Sect. LXXII, Note 23.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2076"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2081">342:14</A> This Song expresses the Empress's desire to return to her parental house at Takamiya in the district of Kadzuraki,&#8212;a desire which, however, her restless frame of mind did not allow her to fulfil.&#8212;The Pillow-Word for Yamashiro, which here recurs, has already been discussed in Note 11. There are two other Pillow-Words in this Song,&#8212;<i>awoniyoshi</i>, which is prefixed to Nara, and <i>wo-date</i> (or <i>wo-date-yama</i> according to the old reading, or <i>wo-date tatsu</i> according to another reading), which is prefixed to Yamato. The former of these is so obscure that, rather than attempt to render it into English, the translator prefers to refer the student to the remarks of the various commentators,&#8212;Mabuchi <i>s.v.</i> in his "Dictionary of Pillow-Words," Motowori in his Commentary, Vol. XXXVI, pp. 22-24, and Moribe <i>in loco</i>. <i>Wodate</i> [-<i>yama</i>] seems to refer undoubtedly to the circle of mountains that guard the approach to the province of Yamato, and it has been rendered accordingly. The great difficulty of the Song lies in the line rendered "ascend to Miya," and the commentators from Keichi&#363; downwards make all sorts of efforts to explain it. Moribe's view, according to which the word should be regarded <a name="page_344"><font size="1" color="green">p. 344</font></A> as a familiar abbreviation of Takamiya, naturally used by one whose native place it was, seems the most acceptable. Motowori takes the line to signify: "When I ascend past the palace [of Naniha]."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2077"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2082">342:15</A> <A NAME="img_34400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/34400.jpg">, <i>i.e.</i>, Korea.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2078"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2083">342:16</A> For <i>Nuri no omi</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the Grandee of Nuri." Nuri is probably a corrupt form of some Korean name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2079"></A><A HREF="kj130.htm#fr_2084">342:17</A> Or Tsudzuki, in Yamashiro. Etymology obscure.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_344"><font size="1" color="green">p. 344</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXIV.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART VI.&#8212;HE FOLLOWS THE EMPRESS INTO YAMASHIRO).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign, having heard that the Empress had made a progress up by Yamashiro, made a person,&#8212;a retainer called by the name of Toriyama,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2085"></A><A HREF="#fn_2080"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A>&#8212;give an august Song,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2086"></A><A HREF="#fn_2081"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> which said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Reach [her] in Yamashiro, Toriyama! Reach [her]! reach [her]! Ah! wilt thou reach and meet my beloved spouse?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2087"></A><A HREF="#fn_2082"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again he continued by despatching Kuchiko, Grandee of Wani,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2088"></A><A HREF="#fn_2083"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and sang, saying: [277]</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Wilt thou be without thinking even of the Heart that is in the moor of Ohowiko, the moor of Ohowiko, that is by Takaki at Mimoro?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2089"></A><A HREF="#fn_2084"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"If indeed I had pillowed [my head] on the white arm like the whiteness of the roots, the great roots, that were beaten with wooden hoes by the women of Yamashiro where the seedlings grow in succession, [then] mightest thou say, 'I know [thee] not'."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2090"></A><A HREF="#fn_2085"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_345"><font size="1" color="green">p. 345</font></A></p>  
<p>So when the Grandee of Kuchiko was repeating this [278] august Song [to the Empress,] it was raining heavily. Then upon his, without avoiding the rain, coming and prostrating himself at the front door of the palace,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2091"></A><A HREF="#fn_2086"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> she on the contrary went out at the back door; and on his coming and prostrating himself at the back door of the palace, she on the contrary went out at the front door. Then, as he crept backwards and forwards on his knees in the middle of the court, the streams of water&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2092"></A><A HREF="#fn_2087"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> reached to his loins. Owing to the grandee being clad in a garment dyed&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2093"></A><A HREF="#fn_2088"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> green and with a red cord, the streams of water brushed against the red cord, and the green all changed to red colour. Now the Grandee of Kuchiko's younger sister Princess Kuchi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2094"></A><A HREF="#fn_2089"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> was in the service of the Empress.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2095"></A><A HREF="#fn_2090"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> So Princess Kuchi sang saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! how tearful is my lord-elder brother, saying things in the palace of Tsutsuki in Yamashiro!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2096"></A><A HREF="#fn_2091"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then when the Empress asked the reason,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2097"></A><A HREF="#fn_2092"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> she replied, saying: "He is my brother the Grandee of Kuchiko." Thereupon the Grandee of Kuchiko and also his younger sister Princess Kuchi and likewise Nurinomi [all] three took counsel [together,] and sent to report to the Heavenly [279] Sovereign, saying: "The reason of the Empress's progress is that there are [some] insects reared by Nurinomi,&#8212;strange insects changing in three ways,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2098"></A><A HREF="#fn_2093"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> once becoming creeping insects, once becoming cocoons,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2099"></A><A HREF="#fn_2094"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> and once becoming flying birds&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2100"></A><A HREF="#fn_2095"><FONT SIZE="1">16</FONT></A>&#8212;and it is only to go and look at them that she has entered into [Nurinomi's house.] She has no strange intentions."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2101"></A><A HREF="#fn_2096"><FONT SIZE="1">17</FONT></A> When they had thus reported, the Heavenly Sovereign said: "That being so, I want to go and see [these insects,] as</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_346"><font size="1" color="green">p. 346</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> I think [they must be] strange; [and with these words] he made a progress up from the great palace. When he entered into Nurinomi's house, Nurinomi, had already presented to the Empress the three-fold insects reared by him. Then the Heavenly Sovereign augustly stood at the door of the palace where the Empress-dwelt, and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Pure as the great roots that were beaten with their wooden hoes by the women of Yamashiro where the seedings grow in succession:&#8212;it is because thou spokest tumultuously that I come in here [with my retainers numerous] as the more and more flourishing trees that I look across at."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2102"></A><A HREF="#fn_2097"><FONT SIZE="1">18</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[280] These six Songs by the Heavenly Sovereign and by the Empress are Changing Songs which are Quiet Songs.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2103"></A><A HREF="#fn_2098"><FONT SIZE="1">19</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_347"><font size="1" color="green">p. 347</font></A> <a name="page_348"><font size="1" color="green">p. 348</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2080"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2085">344:1</A> <a name="page_346"><font size="1" color="green">p. 346</font></A> This name signifies "bird-mountain." The commentators presume that it contains an allusion to the fact of its bearer being an Imperial courier.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2081"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2086">344:2</A> This is the actual sense conveyed by the original <A NAME="img_34600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/34600.jpg">, and we naturally infer that Toriyama was made the bearer to the Empress of the following Song. The Song itself, however, is addressed not to her, but to Toriyama on his departure. On the other hand, the two poems which follow are evidently for the Empress, and it is impossible to suppose that the first messenger was not likewise intended to convey to her some poetic missive. All that we can do is to render the text as it stands, and to suppose it corrupt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2082"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2087">344:3</A> The meaning of this Song is: "O Toriyama! pursue her into Yamashiro! I tremble at the thought of the possibility of thy not finding her."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2083"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2088">344:4</A> <i>Wani no omi Kuchiko</i> (further on he is mentioned as <i>Kuchiko no omi</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the Grandee (of) Kuchiko.") <i>Kuchi-ko</i> may be interpreted <a name="page_347"><font size="1" color="green">p. 347</font></A> to mean "mouth child" and Moribe thinks that this personage was so called on account of the verbal messages of which he was made the bearer. The translator would prefer to consider <i>ko</i> as an abbreviation of <i>hiko</i>, "prince," especially as the sister's name is <i>Kuchi-hime</i>, where the word hime must mean "princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2084"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2089">344:5</A> This Song is so obscure that Motowori and Moribe differ completely as to its interpretation. The translator has followed Moribe, though by no means persuaded that the latter has hit on the proper signification. According to this view, the Emperor makes a pun on the word "heart," which is supposed to have been the name of a pool situated on the moor of Ohowiko near Takaki at Mimoro,&#8212;all names of places with which the Empress was familiar,&#8212;and reproaches her for having no thought of his heart which beats so lovingly for her. Motowori, on the other hand, thinks that the poem proper consists only of its last two lines (in the English translation they necessarily I come first): "Wilt thou be without thinking even of the heart?"&#8212;and that all the rest is a "Preface "to the Pillow-Word <i>kimo-mukafu</i> by which the word <i>kokoro</i>, "heart," is preceded. As for <i>oho-wi-ko</i> and <i>takaki</i>, they are taken, not as names of places, but as common Nouns. According to this view of the structure of the Song, it ceases (with the exception of its last two lines) to have any rational signification, and it is needless to attempt to translate it for the English reader. Persons familiar with Japanese are therefore referred to Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXXVI, pp. 34-36.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2085"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2090">344:6</A> The meaning of this Song is: "If thou and I had not so long been spouses, then indeed mightest thou break with me, and declare that thou knowest me not. But how canst thou so far forget our wedded life as to desert me now?"-"The "great root," <i>oho-ne</i>, is the modern <i>dai-kon</i> (Raphanus sativus), a kind of radish which is a favourite vegetable with the Japanese and is distinguished by its brilliantly white appearance. "Beaten" here signifies "dug up." The use of the Past Tense is curious. <i>Ko-guha</i>, here in accordance with Motowori's view rendered "wooden hoes," is interpreted by Moribe to mean "little hoes." "Where the seedlings grow in succession "is the English rendering of <i>tsugi-ne fu</i>, the Pillow-Word for Yamashiro (see Sect. CXXIII Note 11).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2086"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2091">345:7</A> The Empress was lodging with a private individual, but her presence warrants the application of the term "palace "to his house.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2087"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2092">345:8</A> It was raining too hard for the water to stop on the surface in the shape of puddles, so it streamed off in little rivulets.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2088"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2093">345:9</A> Literally, "rubbed." See Introduction <A HREF="kj004.htm#page_xxx">p. xxx</A>. Instead of "'green," <a name="page_348"><font size="1" color="green">p. 348</font></A> we might equally well translate by "blue." The garment intended must be the upper garment or coat.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2089"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2094">345:10</A> <i>Kuchi-hime</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2090"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2095">345:11</A> Literally, "respectfully served the Empress."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2091"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2096">345:12</A> The meaning of these lines, which can only be called poetry because they are in metre, is plain: in them the speaker draws the Empress's attention to the pitiful condition of the messenger who is doing his best to deliver to her the Emperor's message. Probably the reading in our text has been corrupted; for that in the "Chronicles," which may be translated thus; "Oh! how tearful am I when I see my lord elder brother," etc. is much preferable.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2092"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2097">345:13</A> <i>Scil</i>. of her attendant thus taking the messenger's part.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2093"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2098">345:14</A> Literally, "colours."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2094"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2099">345:15</A> This is Motowori's conjectural restoration of the reading of this word, which in all the texts is hopelessly corrupt.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2095"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2100">345:16</A> According to another reading, "flying insects."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2096"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2101">345:17</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "she is not meditating any evil conduct."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2097"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2102">346:18</A> The Song consists of two divisions, the first of which is but a Preface for the second, the pivot being formed by the word <i>sawa-sawa-ni</i>, which has the meaning of "pure" "cool," or "refreshing," with reference to what precedes it, and the meaning of "tumultuously" (<i>sawasawa ni</i>&#8212;<i>sawagaskiku</i>) when taken together with what follows. The difficulties which present themselves in the first division have all been explained in Note 11 to the last <A HREF="errata.htm#85">and</A> Note 6 to the present Section. The general sense of the second division is plain enough; but the precise application of the comparison to the "more and more flourishing tree" is obscure. Motowori's view has been adopted by the translator, and the words in brackets supplemented accordingly. Moribe prefers to consider that the reference is to the repeated visits first of the Emperor's messengers and afterwards of the Emperor himself The words "look across at" must be explained by supposing that the trees were in the neighbourhood of Nurinomi's house; they were shoots springing up from roots that had been cut down close to the ground.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2098"></A><A HREF="kj131.htm#fr_2103">346:19</A> The commentators thus explain these obscure expressions: "A Quiet Song is one which is sung to a tranquil tune. A Changing Song is one temporarily sung while the tone (mode?) is changing." The six Songs in question must be supposed to have combined both characteristics.</P>

<p><a name="page_349"><font size="1" color="green">p. 349</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXV.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART VIII.&#8212;HE LOVES YATA-NO-WAKI-IRATSUME).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign, loving Yata-no-waki-iratsume, deigned to send her an august Song. That Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Will the one sedge-stem of Yata, having no children, wither as it stands? Poor sedge-moor! Sedge-moor indeed is what I may <i>say</i>&#8212;poor pure girl!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2104"></A><A HREF="#fn_2099"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then Yata-no-waki-iratsume replied in a Song, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Even though the one sedge stem of Yata be alone, if the Great Lord say it is right even though it be alone [it is right.]"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2105"></A><A HREF="#fn_2100"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So the Yata Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2106"></A><A HREF="#fn_2101"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> was established as the august proxy of Yata-no-waki-iratsume.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2099"></A><A HREF="kj132.htm#fr_2104">349:1</A> In this Song the Emperor condoles with his mistress on her childlessness: "Will the single sedge on the moor of Yata die without leaving any offspring? Sedge, indeed! Yes, sedge is the term I use for my metaphor, but what is in my thoughts is the girl I love."&#8212;There is in the original a <i>jeu-de-mots</i>, not capable of translation into English, between <i>suge</i> or <i>suga</i>, "sedge, and <i>sugashi</i> pure."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2100"></A><A HREF="kj132.htm#fr_2105">349:2</A> The girl replies: "Even though I be childless. I care not if my lord cares not."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2101"></A><A HREF="kj132.htm#fr_2106">349:3</A> <i>Yata-be</i>.</P>

<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="index.htm">Index</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj132.htm">Previous</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj134.htm">Next</A>&nbsp;
<HR><A HREF="http://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/B0028Y4SZY/internetsacredte">Buy this Book at Amazon.com</A></CENTER>
<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXVI.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART VIII.&#8212;DEATH OF KING HAYABUSA-WAKE AND QUEEN MEDORI).]</h2>  
<p>Again the Heavenly Sovereign begged for his younger half-sister Queen Medori, using as middle-man his younger brother King Haya-busa-wake. Then Queen Medori [281] spoke to King Hayabusa-wake, saying: "Owing to the</p>  
<p><a name="page_350"><font size="1" color="green">p. 350</font></A></p>  
<p>violence of the Empress, [the Heavenly Sovereign] has not deigned to take Yata-no-waki-iratsume [into the Palace.] So I will not respectfully serve him. I will become the wife of Thine Augustness." Forthwith they wedded each other, wherefore King Hayabusa-wake made no report [to the Heavenly Sovereign.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2107"></A><A HREF="#fn_2102"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A>] Then the Heavenly Sovereign, going straight to the place where Queen Medori dwelt, stood on the door-sill of the palace. Hereupon, Queen Medori being at her loom, was weaving garments. Then the Heavenly Sovereign sang saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! for whom may be the garments that my Great Lady Medori weaves?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2108"></A><A HREF="#fn_2103"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Queen Medori replied in a Song saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"For an august veil for the high-going Falcon-Lord."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2109"></A><A HREF="#fn_2104"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So the Heavenly Sovereign, perceiving her feelings, returned into the palace. At this time&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2110"></A><A HREF="#fn_2105"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> when her husband King Hayabusa-wake came, his wife Queen Medori sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The lark flies to heaven. Oh! high-going Falcon-Lord, catch the wren."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2111"></A><A HREF="#fn_2106"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[282] The Heavenly Sovereign, hearing this Song,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2112"></A><A HREF="#fn_2107"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> forthwith raised an army, wishing to slay King Hayabusa and Queen Medori, who then fled away together, and ascended Mount Kurahashi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2113"></A><A HREF="#fn_2108"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Thereupon King Hayabusa-wake sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Owing to the steepness of ladder-like Mount Kurahashi, being unable to clamber [up] the rocks, oh! she takes my hand!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2114"></A><A HREF="#fn_2109"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>Again he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Though ladder-like Mount Kurahashi be <a name="page_351"><font size="1" color="green">p. 351</font></A> steep, it is not steep when I ascend it with my younger sister."</div></p>  
<p>So when they fled thence, and reached Soni in Uda,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2115"></A><A HREF="#fn_2110"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> the Imperials&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2116"></A><A HREF="#fn_2111"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> army pursued, overtook, and slew them.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2102"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2107">350:1</A> <a name="page_351"><font size="1" color="green">p. 351</font></A> <i>Scil</i>. of the success of his mediation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2103"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2108">350:2</A> Or, "for whom is the loom [employed], with which my Great Lady Medori weaves?"&#8212;The word <i>hata</i> in Archaic Japanese signifies both "garment" and the instrument which is used to weave a garment, <i>i.e.</i> a "loom" (<A NAME="img_35100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35100.jpg"> and <A NAME="img_35101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35101.jpg">). In later times the second meaning has prevailed to the exclusion of the first.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2104"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2109">350:3</A> There is here a play on the name of the Queen's paramour Hayabusa-wake, which signifies "Falcon-Lord" as in the translation&#8212;The parallel passage of the "Chronicles" gives these two Songs as a single one which is put into the mouth of Queen Medori's handmaidens,&#8212;is a more acceptable version of the incident.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2105"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2110">350:4</A> Motowori suspects that there is here an error in the text, which should, according to him, read: "After this."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2106"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2111">350:5</A> The gist of this Song is an instigation to murder the Emperor (whose name was <i>Oho-sazaki</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "Great Wren." Conf. Sect. CIV, Note 18), addressed to the singer's husband (whose name was <i>Hayabusa-wake</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "Falcon Lord"). But the allusion to the lake remains obscure. Keichi&#363; suggests that it is simply mentioned as a term of comparison for the falcon's power of flight, while Motowori opines that the meaning rather is: "The lark flies so high up to heaven that it would be hard to catch it; but the wren is an easy prey."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2107"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2112">350:6</A> Viz., as may be supposed, repeated by some fourth person.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2108"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2113">350:7</A> <i>Kurahashi-yama</i>, in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2109"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2114">350:8</A> The Song, like the next, is too clear to stand in need of explanation. "Ladder-like" is an attempt to render the force of the Pillow-Word <i>hashi-tate</i>. See Mabuchi's "Dictionary of Pillow-Words," s.v., for the exact force attributed to it by Mabuchi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2110"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2115">351:9</A> For Uda see Sect. XLVI, Note, 14. The etymology of Soni is equally obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2111"></A><A HREF="kj133.htm#fr_2116">351:10</A> The character <A NAME="img_35102"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35102.jpg">, though read by the commentators with the usual Japanese Honorific <i>mi</i>, "august," has here its proper Chinese signification of "Imperial."</P>

<p><a name="page_352"><font size="1" color="green">p. 352</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXVII.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART VIII.&#8212;QUEEN MEDORI'S ARMLET).]</h2>  
<p>Chief Ohotate of Yamabe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2117"></A><A HREF="#fn_2112"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> who was the generalissimo of that army, took the jewelled armlet which was wound round Queen Medori's august arm, and gave it to his own wife. After this time, when a copious feast&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2118"></A><A HREF="#fn_2113"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> was to be held, the women of the various families all went to court. Then the wife of Chief Ohotate came with that Queen's jewelled armlet wound round her own arm. [283] Thereupon the Empress, Her Augustness Iha-no-hime, herself took the oak-leaves&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2119"></A><A HREF="#fn_2114"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> [full] of great august liquor and graciously gave them to the women of the various families. Then the Empress, recognizing the jewelled armlet, gave [the wearer] no oak-leaf[-full] of great august liquor, but forthwith sent her away;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2120"></A><A HREF="#fn_2115"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and sending. for the husband, Chief Ohotate, said: "Owing to that King and Queen's impropriety, [the Emperor] deigned to send them away. This was nothing strange. And a slave such as thou despoils of the jewelled armlet that was wound round her august arm the body of his lady [that was still] warm, and gives it to his own wife!"&#8212;and forthwith he was condemned to death.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2121"></A><A HREF="#fn_2116"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2112"></A><A HREF="kj134.htm#fr_2117">352:1</A> <a name="page_352"><font size="1" color="green">p. 352</font></A> <i>Yamabe no Ohotate no murazhi</i>. The "gentile name" was <i>Yamabe no murazhi</i>, and the personal name <i>Ohotate</i>, though the confused wording of this passage does not make it appear so. <i>Yama-be</i> signifies mountain (<i>i.e.</i>, hunters') tribe. <i>Oho-tate</i> is "big shield."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2113"></A><A HREF="kj134.htm#fr_2118">352:2</A> See Sect. CVII, Note 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2114"></A><A HREF="kj134.htm#fr_2119">352:3</A> Or, perhaps rather "aralia-leaves" (Con/. Sect. CXXIII).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2115"></A><A HREF="kj134.htm#fr_2120">352:4</A> Or, "had her dragged away."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2116"></A><A HREF="kj134.htm#fr_2121">352:5</A> Literally, "was granted the punishment of death," or "(the Emperor) deigned to condemn him to death.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_353"><font size="1" color="green">p. 353</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART IX.&#8212;A WILD-GOOSE LAYS AN EGG).]</h2>  
<p>Another time, the Heavenly Sovereign, when about to hold a copious feast,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2122"></A><A HREF="#fn_2117"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> made a progress to the Island of Hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2123"></A><A HREF="#fn_2118"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> just when a wild-goose had laid an egg on that island. Then, sending for His Augustness the Noble Takeuchi, he asked him in a Song about the laying of an egg by a wild goose. This Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Court Noble of Uchi! thou indeed art a long-lived person. Hast thou [ever] heard of a wild-goose laying an egg in the land of Yamato?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2124"></A><A HREF="#fn_2119"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Hereupon the Noble Take-uchi spoke in a song, saying: [284]</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"August Child of the high-shining Sun, it is indeed natural that thou shouldest deign to ask, it is indeed right that thou shouldest ask. I indeed am a long-lived person, [but] have not yet heard of a wild goose laying an egg in the land of Yamato."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2125"></A><A HREF="#fn_2120"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Having thus spoken, he was granted the august&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2126"></A><A HREF="#fn_2121"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> lute and sang saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh thou prince! the wild goose must have laid the egg because thou wilt at last rule."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2127"></A><A HREF="#fn_2122"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>This is a Congratulatory Incomplete Song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2128"></A><A HREF="#fn_2123"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_354"><font size="1" color="green">p. 354</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2117"></A><A HREF="kj135.htm#fr_2122">353:1</A> <a name="page_353"><font size="1" color="green">p. 353</font></A> See Sect. CVII, 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2118"></A><A HREF="kj135.htm#fr_2123">353:2</A> <i>Hime-shima</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "Princess Island." The name is supposed to be connected with that of the goddess of Himegoso mentioned near the end of Sect. CXIV, and first occurs in Sect. V (Note 33).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2119"></A><A HREF="kj135.htm#fr_2124">353:3</A> The wild-goose goes far north at the approach of spring, and the translator is informed by Capt. Blakiston that the latter has not known <a name="page_354"><font size="1" color="green">p. 354</font></A> of any breeding even on the island of Yezo. The Emperor was therefore naturally astonished at so strange an occurrence as that of a wild-goose laying an egg in Yamato, and asks the Noble Take-uchi whether he had ever heard of the like of it before, Take-uchi being at that time more than two hundred years old (!) according to the chronology of the "Chronicles," and therefore the oldest and most experienced man in the Empire.&#8212;"Court Noble" represents the Japanese word <i>Aso</i> (for <i>Asomi</i>, believed by Motowori and Moribe to be derived from <i>a se omi</i> <A NAME="img_35400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35400.jpg">, lit, "my elder brother minister" but used simply as a title), The words Uchi and Yamato are preceded in the original by their respective Pillow-Words <i>tamaki-haru</i> and <i>soramitsu</i>, whose force it is impossible to render in English, and whose origin indeed is obscure. The words rendered "laying an egg "are literally "giving birth to a child."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2120"></A><A HREF="kj135.htm#fr_2125">353:4</A> This Song is too clear to need explanation. As in the preceding one, Yamato is accompanied by the Pillow-Word <i>sora-mitsu</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2121"></A><A HREF="kj135.htm#fr_2126">353:5</A> Or, "Imperial."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2122"></A><A HREF="kj135.htm#fr_2127">353:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, say Motowori and Moribe, who refer this episode to a time previous to Nin-toku's accession, "The wild-goose has laid an egg in token of the future accession to the throne." The translator prefers the view expressed by Keichi&#363; in his <i>K&#333;-Gan Sh&#333;</i>, and adopted in the "<A HREF="errata.htm#86">Explanation</A> of the Songs in the Chronicles of Japan," that the words <i>tsuki na</i> "at last," must here be taken in the sense of "long," and the Song interpreted to mean "The wild-goose lays an egg as an omen that thy reign will be a long one." This view is supported by the story in the "Chronicles," which places the Song in the Emperor's fiftieth year and gives him thirty-six years of subsequent existence, thus making the prophecy amply fulfil itself, as one would expect that it should do in the pages of such a work. According to the other view, the text of the "Chronicles" calls for emendation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2123"></A><A HREF="kj135.htm#fr_2128">353:7</A> <i>Hogi-uta no kata-uta</i>. For "Incomplete Song" see Sect. LXXXIX, Note 14.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_355"><font size="1" color="green">p. 355</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXIX:&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART X.&#8212;A VESSEL IS MADE INTO A LUTE)]</h2>  
<p>In this august reign there was a tall tree on the west of the river Tsuki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2129"></A><A HREF="#fn_2124"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> The shadow of this tree, on its being struck by the morning sun, reached to the Island of Ahaji:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2130"></A><A HREF="#fn_2125"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and on its being struck by the evening sun, it crossed Mount Takayasu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2131"></A><A HREF="#fn_2126"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> So the tree was cut down and made into a vessel, and a very swift-going vessel it was. At the time, this vessel was called by the name of Karanu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2132"></A><A HREF="#fn_2127"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> So with this vessel the water of the Island of Ahaji was drawn morning and evening, and presented as the great august water.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2133"></A><A HREF="#fn_2128"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> The broken [pieces] of this vessel were used [as fuel] to burn salt and the pieces of wood that remained over from the burning were made into a lute, whose sound re-echoed seven miles&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2134"></A><A HREF="#fn_2129"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> [off]. So [some one&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2135"></A><A HREF="#fn_2130"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A>] sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Karanu was burnt [as fuel] for salt; the remainder was made into a lute; oh! when struck, it sounds like the wet plants standing rocked on the reefs in the middle of the harbour, the harbour of Yura."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2136"></A><A HREF="#fn_2131"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>This is a Changing Song which is a Quiet song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2137"></A><A HREF="#fn_2132"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> [285]</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2124"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2129">355:1</A> <a name="page_355"><font size="1" color="green">p. 355</font></A> This is Moribe's reading (given without any comment) of the original characters <A NAME="img_35500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35500.jpg">. Motowori pronounces them corrupt; but, having no emendation to propose, simply leaves them without any <i>kana</i> reading.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2125"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2130">355:2</A> See Sect. V, Note 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2126"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2131">355:3</A> <i>Takayasu no yama</i>, in the province of Kahachi. The characters with which the name is written signify "high and easy."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2127"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2132">355:4</A> The significance of this name, written <A NAME="img_35501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35501.jpg">, remains obscure notwithstanding the efforts of the commentators to explain it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2128"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2133">355:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, this vessel was used to bring over every morning and evening <a name="page_356"><font size="1" color="green">p. 356</font></A> the water for the Imperial household, which was drawn on the Island of Ahaji.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2129"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2134">355:6</A> <A NAME="img_35600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35600.jpg">, the Chinese <i>li</i> Japanese <i>ri</i>. The length of the <i>ri</i> has varied greatly at different times and in different parts of the country. The modern standard Japanese <i>ri</i> is equivalent to about 2.44 English statute miles: but Motowori supposes the <i>ri</i> of the epoch mentioned in our text to have been less than one-seventh of that distance.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2130"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2135">355:7</A> In the "Chronicles" this story is placed in the reign of the Emperor &#332;-jin, and the Song is attributed to that monarch.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2131"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2136">355:8</A> In this Song the sound of the twanging of the lute that had been made from the remnant of the boat Karanu is compared to the rustling of the plants standing half out of water on the reefs in the harbour of Yura.&#8212;The compound word <i>kaki-hiku</i>, rendered by "struck," signifies literally "scratched and struck," the lute being struck with the nail. The onomatopoetic word <i>saya-saya</i>, of which "sound" is but a colourless equivalent, represents both the delightful ring of the lute and the rustling of the sea-plants. What plants are intended by the expression "wet plants" (<i>nadzu no ki</i>) is a point that has been much disputed. Moribe even thinks that the term is meant for the name of a particular species of (apparently) coral now found in the island of Hachijo. Yura is in the Island of Ahaji.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2132"></A><A HREF="kj136.htm#fr_2137">355:9</A> See Sect. CXXIV, Note 19.</P>

<p><a name="page_356"><font size="1" color="green">p. 356</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXX.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-TOKU (PART XI.&#8212;HIS AGE AND PLACE OF BURIAL).]</h2>  
<p>The august years of this Heavenly Sovereign were eighty-three. His august mausoleum is on the Ear-Moor of Mozu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2138"></A><A HREF="#fn_2133"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2133"></A><A HREF="kj137.htm#fr_2138">356:1</A> <a name="page_356"><font size="1" color="green">p. 356</font></A> <i>Mozu no mimi-hara</i>. The origin of this singular name is thus explained in the "Chronicle" (Emperor Nin-toku, 67th year, Winter, 10th Moon): "(The Emperor made a progress to the moor of Ishidzu in Kafuchi to fix the site of his mausoleum. On the day when the construction of his mausoleum was begun, a deer suddenly ran out from the middle of the moor, rushed into the midst of the coolies, fell down, and <a name="page_357"><font size="1" color="green">p. 357</font></A> died. The suddenness of its death causing astonishment, its wound was looked for, whereupon a shrike came out of its ear, and flew away. So on looking into the ear, it was found to be all eaten away. So that is the reason why the place is called <i>Mozu no mimi-hare</i> (the 'Shrike's Ear-Moor.')"</P>

<p><a name="page_357"><font size="1" color="green">p. 357</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXXI.&#8212;EMPEROR RI-CHIU (PART I.&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Iza-ho-wake dwelt in the palace of Wakasakura at Ihare,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2139"></A><A HREF="#fn_2134"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded Her Augustness Princess Kuro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2140"></A><A HREF="#fn_2135"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> daughter of the Noble of Ashida,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2141"></A><A HREF="#fn_2136"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> child of So-tsu-biko [287] of Kadzuraki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2142"></A><A HREF="#fn_2137"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and begot august children: King Oshiha of Ichinobe;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2143"></A><A HREF="#fn_2138"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next King Mima:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2144"></A><A HREF="#fn_2139"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next his younger sister Awomi-no-iratsume,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2145"></A><A HREF="#fn_2140"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> another name for whom was Ichi-toyo-no-iratsume.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2146"></A><A HREF="#fn_2141"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2134"></A><A HREF="kj138.htm#fr_2139">357:1</A> <a name="page_357"><font size="1" color="green">p. 357</font></A> For <i>Ihare</i> see Sect. XLIII, Note 26. <i>Waka-sakura</i> signifies "young cherry-tree." The origin of the name is traced, rightly or wrongly, to an incident mentioned in the "Chronicles" under the reign of this Emperor, 3rd year.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2135"></A><A HREF="kj138.htm#fr_2140">357:2</A> <i>Kuro-hime</i> <i>i.e.</i>, "black princess." The same name occurs several times, and has reference to the black hair of the person so designated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2136"></A><A HREF="kj138.htm#fr_2141">357:3</A> <i>Ashida no sukune</i>. <i>Ashida</i> signifies "reed-moor." It is the name of a place in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2137"></A><A HREF="kj138.htm#fr_2142">357:4</A> <i>Kadzuraki no So-tsu-biko</i>. For this name, which is here abbreviated, see Sect. LXI, Note 55.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2138"></A><A HREF="kj138.htm#fr_2143">357:5</A> <i>Ichinobe no Oshiha no miko</i>. Ichinobe is in the province of Yamashiro, and the name seems to mean "near the market." The name of Oshiha refers to the "uneven teeth" of this personage which are mentioned in Sect. CLXVII (near Note 5).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2139"></A><A HREF="kj138.htm#fr_2144">357:6</A> <i>Mima no miko</i>. The signification of this name is quite obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2140"></A><A HREF="kj138.htm#fr_2145">357:7</A> <i>Awomi no iratsume</i>. <i>Awomi</i> is supposed by Motowori to be the name of a place.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2141"></A><A HREF="kj138.htm#fr_2146">357:8</A> <i>Ihitoyo no iratsume</i>. <i>Ihitoyo</i> is supposed by Motowori to be the name of a bird, perhaps a kind of owl.</P>
<p><HR>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_358"><font size="1" color="green">p. 358</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXXII.&#8212;EMPEROR RI-CHIU (PART II.&#8212;HE IS TAKEN TO ISO-NO-KAMI).]</h2>  
<p>Originally, when dwelling at the palace of Naniha, [the Heavenly Sovereign] on holding a copious feast when at the great tasting,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2147"></A><A HREF="#fn_2142"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> was intoxicated with the great august liquor, and fell greatly and augustly asleep. Then his younger brother, King Sumi-no-ye-naka-tsu, wishing to take the Heavenly Sovereign, set fire to the great palace. Thereupon the Suzerain of Achi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2148"></A><A HREF="#fn_2143"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> ancestor of the Suzerains of Aya&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2149"></A><A HREF="#fn_2144"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> in Yamato, having taken him away by stealth, set him on an august horse, and caused him to make a progress into Yamato. So [the Heavenly Sovereign] awoke on reaching the moor of Tajihi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2150"></A><A HREF="#fn_2145"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and said: "What place is this?" Then the Suzerain of Achi said: "King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu set fire to the great palace; so I am fleeing with thee into Yamato." Then the Sovereign sang, saying: [257]</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Had I known that I should sleep on the Moor of Tajihi, oh! I would have brought my dividing matting, had I known that I should sleep!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2151"></A><A HREF="#fn_2146"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>On reaching the Pass of Hanifu&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2152"></A><A HREF="#fn_2147"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> and gazing at the palace of Naniha, the fire was still bright. Then the Heavenly Sovereign sang again, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The group of houses sparklingly burning, as I stand and look from the Pass of Hanifu, is in the direction of the house of my spouse."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2153"></A><A HREF="#fn_2148"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So when they reached the entrance of the Ohosaka mountain,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2154"></A><A HREF="#fn_2149"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> they met one woman. This woman said: "A number of men bearing weapons are barring [the</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_359"><font size="1" color="green">p. 359</font></A></p>  
<p>way across] the mountain. Thou shouldst cross it going round by way of Tagima.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2155"></A><A HREF="#fn_2150"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Then the Heavenly Sovereign sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! on asking the way of the maiden we met at Ohosaka, she tells not [the] direct [way], but tells of the Tagima way."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2156"></A><A HREF="#fn_2151"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So making his progress up, he dwelt in the temple of [289] the Deity of Isonokami.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2157"></A><A HREF="#fn_2152"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2142"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2147">358:1</A> <a name="page_359"><font size="1" color="green">p. 359</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, on the occasion of his performing the religious ceremony of tasting the first rice of the season.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2143"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2148">358:2</A> <i>Achi no atahe</i>, supposed to be of Korean origin, and to be a descendant of <A NAME="img_35900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35900.jpg">, great grandson of the Chinese Emperor <A NAME="img_35901"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35901.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2144"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2149">358:3</A> <i>Aya no atahe</i>. This family was of continental origin, <i>Aya</i> being the Japanese reading of the character <A NAME="img_35902"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/35902.jpg">; see Sect. CXI, Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2145"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2150">358:4</A> <i>Tajihi no nu</i>, in the provinces of Kahachi. The signification of the name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2146"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2151">358:5</A> This Song expresses the Monarch's regret at not having brought his mats with him.&#8212;From the expression used in the text (<i>tatsu-gomo</i>), the, commentators suppose that such mats were used as a sort of screen to avert draughts. One proposal is to consider <i>tatsu</i> as the Verb <i>tatsuru</i>, "to set up," because these mats must have been "set up" round the room. But it agrees better with grammatical usage to take it in its other sense of "cutting," or "dividing," and to suppose that the mats were so called because they "cut off" the draught from the person sitting behind them.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2147"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2152">358:6</A> Or "Hill of Hanifu," <i>Hanifu-zaka</i>, in the province of Kahachi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2148"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2153">358:7</A> The meaning of this Song is perfectly clear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2149"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2154">358:8</A> See Sect. LXIV, Note 25. The word rendered "entrance&nbsp; here and below in the same context is literally "mouth."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2150"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2155">359:9</A> See Sect. LXII, Note 49.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2151"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2156">359:10</A> Moribe thus paraphrases this Song: "If the maiden whom I met at Ohosaka and whom I sought direction of had been a common mortal, she would have simply told me the shortest road. But now I see why it was that she bid me go round by way of Tagima: it was to preserve me from danger. Ah! she must have been a Goddess."&#8212;The <a name="page_360"><font size="1" color="green">p. 360</font></A> words <i>tada ni</i> generally have the sense of "directly," "immediately," and are indeed here so understood by Motowori. Moribe's interpretation, which has been followed by the translator, does but little violence to the text, and suits the general meaning better.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2152"></A><A HREF="kj139.htm#fr_2157">359:11</A> See Sect. XLV, Note 16.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_360"><font size="1" color="green">p. 360</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXXIII.&#8212;EMPEROR.&#8212;RI-CHIU (PART III.&#8212;HIS REBELLIOUS BROTHER AND THE LATTER'S RETAINER SOBAKARI ARE SLAIN)]</h2>  
<p>Thereupon his younger brother His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake came, <A HREF="errata.htm#87">and</A> sent [to ask for] an audience.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2158"></A><A HREF="#fn_2153"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Then the Heavenly Sovereign caused him to be told [these words]: As I am in doubt whether perhaps Thine Augustness may [not] be of like mind&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2159"></A><A HREF="#fn_2154"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> with King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, I will not meet and speak with thee." [His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake] replied, saying: "I have no evil intent. I am not of like mind with King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu." [The Heavenly Sovereign] again caused him to be told [these words]: "If that be so, [do thou] now return down, and slay King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, and come up [again hither]. At that time I will surely meet and speak with thee." So he forthwith returned down to Naniha, and deceived [a man] named Sobakari,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2160"></A><A HREF="#fn_2155"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> a man-at-arms&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2161"></A><A HREF="#fn_2156"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> in the personal service of&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2162"></A><A HREF="#fn_2157"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> King Sumi-no-ye-no-naka-tsu, saying: "If thou wilt obey my words, I shall become Heavenly Sovereign, and will make thee prime Minister, to rule the Empire.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2163"></A><A HREF="#fn_2158"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> How [would this be]?" Sobakari replied, saying "" [I [290] will do] according to thy command." Then plenteously endowing that man-at-arms, he said: "If that be so,</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_361"><font size="1" color="green">p. 361</font></A></p>  
<p>slay the King." Thereupon Sobakari watched for the time when his King went into the privy, and thrust him to death with a spear. So when [His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake] was making his progress to Yamato taking Sobakari with him, he, on reaching the entrance of the Ohosaka mountain, thought [thus]: "Although Sobakari deserves very well of me, he has truly&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2164"></A><A HREF="#fn_2159"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> slain his lord. This is unrighteous. Nevertheless if I reward not his deed, I may be called untruthful; and if I quite carry out my promise, his intentions are on the contrary to be feared. So, though recompensing his deed, I will destroy his actual person." Therefore he said to Sobakari: "I will halt here to-day and bestow on thee the rank of Prime Minister, and to-morrow will [continue my] progress up." So a halt was made at the entrance to the mountain, a temporary palace forthwith built, a copious feast&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2165"></A><A HREF="#fn_2160"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> suddenly held, the rank of Prime Minister forthwith bestowed on the man-at-arms, and all the officials&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2166"></A><A HREF="#fn_2161"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> made to do obeisance [to him]. The man-at-arms, delighted, thought that he had accomplished his design. Then [His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake] said to the man-at-arms: "To-day I will drink liquor from the same cup as the Prime Minister." And when they drank together, a bowls large [enough] to hide the face was filled with the liquor presented.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2167"></A><A HREF="#fn_2162"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> Hereupon the King's child drank first, and the man-at-arms drank afterwards. So when the man-at-arms was drinking, the great cup covered his face. Then [His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake] drew forth a sabre which he had laid under the matting, and cut off the head of the man-at-arms. Forthwith on the morrow he made his progress up. So the place was called by the name of Chika-tsu-Asuka.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2168"></A><A HREF="#fn_2163"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_362"><font size="1" color="green">p. 362</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span>  [291] Going up and reaching Yamato, he said: "I will halt here to-day and, having purified myself, will go forth to-morrow and worship at the temple of the Deity."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2169"></A><A HREF="#fn_2164"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> So that place is called by the name of Toho-tsu-Asuka.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2170"></A><A HREF="#fn_2165"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> So going forth to the temple of the Deity of Iso-no-kami&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2171"></A><A HREF="#fn_2166"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A>, he sent to report to the Heavenly Sovereign that he had come up to serve him after accomplishing the work [with which he had been entrusted].&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2172"></A><A HREF="#fn_2167"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A> So [the Heavenly Sovereign] sent for, and met, and spoke with him.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<p><a name="page_363"><font size="1" color="green">p. 363</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXXIV.&#8212;EMPEROR RI-CHIU (PART IV.&#8212;VARIOUS DEEDS).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign thereupon first appointed the Suzerain of Achi to the office of Treasurer,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2173"></A><A HREF="#fn_2168"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and likewise bestowed on him domains.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2174"></A><A HREF="#fn_2169"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Again in this august reign the name of Waka-sakura Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2175"></A><A HREF="#fn_2170"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> was granted to the Grandees of the Waka-sakura Tribe.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2176"></A><A HREF="#fn_2171"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Again the gentile name&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2177"></A><A HREF="#fn_2172"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> of Dukes of Himeda&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2178"></A><A HREF="#fn_2173"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> was granted to the Dukes of Himeda. Again the Ihare Clan&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2179"></A><A HREF="#fn_2174"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> was established.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2168"></A><A HREF="kj141.htm#fr_2173">363:1</A> <a name="page_363"><font size="1" color="green">p. 363</font></A> In Japanese the same word is used for a "store-house" and for the "treasury." But the appointment here mentioned would seem really to correspond to what we should call Lord of the Treasury or Minister of Finance. The characters in the original are <A NAME="img_36302"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36302.jpg">.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2169"></A><A HREF="kj141.htm#fr_2174">363:2</A> Literally, "ration grounds."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2170"></A><A HREF="kj141.htm#fr_2175">363:3</A> <i>Waka-sakura-be</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2171"></A><A HREF="kj141.htm#fr_2176">363:4</A> <i>Waka-sakura-be no omi</i>. Conf. Sect. CXXXI, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2172"></A><A HREF="kj141.htm#fr_2177">363:5</A> All the editors agree in here reading as <i>kabane</i> ("gentile name," see Sect. XIV, Note 5) the character <A NAME="img_36303"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36303.jpg">, which signifies properly "family name."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2173"></A><A HREF="kj141.htm#fr_2178">363:6</A> <i>Himeda no kimi</i>. Nothing is known of this family.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2174"></A><A HREF="kj141.htm#fr_2179">363:7</A> <i>Ihare-be</i>. For Ihare see Sect. XLIII, Note 6. It will be remembered that the Emperor of whose reign the present Section forms part held his court at Ihare.</P>
