<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXXV.&#8212;EMPEROR HAN-ZEI.]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Midzu-ha-wake dwelt in the palace of Shibakaki at Tajihi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2181"></A><A HREF="#fn_2176"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. The length of this Heavenly sovereign's august person was nine feet two inches and a half.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2182"></A><A HREF="#fn_2177"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> The length of his august teeth was one inch, and their breadth two lines, and the upper and lower [row] corresponded exactly, [like jewels strung together]. The Heavenly Sovereign wedded the Lady of Tsunu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2183"></A><A HREF="#fn_2178"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> daughter of Kogoto, Grandee of Wani,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2184"></A><A HREF="#fn_2179"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> and begot august children: the Lady of Kahi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2185"></A><A HREF="#fn_2180"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next the Lady of Tsubura&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2186"></A><A HREF="#fn_2181"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> (<small>two Deities</small>). Again he wedded Oto-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2187"></A><A HREF="#fn_2182"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> daughter of the same Grandee, and begot august children: King Takara;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2188"></A><A HREF="#fn_2183"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> next the Lady of Takabe.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2189"></A><A HREF="#fn_2184"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A>&#8212;-altogether four Kings [and Queens].&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2190"></A><A HREF="#fn_2185"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> The Heavenly Sovereign's august years were sixty. His august mausoleum is on the Moor of Mozu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2191"></A><A HREF="#fn_2186"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2176"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2181">364:1</A> <a name="page_364"><font size="1" color="green">p. 364</font></A> For Tajihi see Sect. CXXXII, Note 4. <i>Shiba-kaki</i> (or <i>Shiba-gaki</i>) signifies "a fence of brushwood."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2177"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2182">364:2</A> As to the ancient Japanese measures we have no accurate information, and the English equivalents used in this passage correspond but approximately to the modern Japanese standards. The character rendered "line" is <A NAME="img_36400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36400.jpg">, which denotes the tenth part of a <A NAME="img_36401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36401.jpg"> or "inch." Motowori remarks that the dimensions of the teeth are not anything extraordinary <a name="page_365"><font size="1" color="green">p. 365</font></A> judged by the present standard, and suppose that anciently the measures of length must have been smaller than at present.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2178"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2183">364:3</A> <i>Tsunu no iratsume</i>. The signification of this name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2179"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2184">364:4</A> <i>Wani no kogoto no omi</i>. The meaning of Kogoto is obscure, Wani has already often appeared.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2180"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2185">364:5</A> <i>Kahi no iratsume</i>. Kahi is the name of a province, but it cannot be said for certain that it is from it that this Princess derived her name.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2181"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2186">364:6</A> <i>Tsubura no iratsume</i>. The meaning of <i>Tsubura</i> is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2182"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2187">364:7</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the younger princess."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2183"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2188">364:8</A> <i>Takara no miko</i>. <i>Takara</i> signifies "treasure."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2184"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2189">364:9</A> <i>Takabe no iratsume</i>. <i>Takabe</i> seems to be the name of a place unless it be considered to be connected with the word <i>taka</i>, "hawk."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2185"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2190">364:10</A> Remember that the single character <A NAME="img_36500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36500.jpg"> includes both sexes.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2186"></A><A HREF="kj143.htm#fr_2191">364:11</A> See Sect. CXXX. Note 1.</P>

<p><a name="page_365"><font size="1" color="green">p. 365</font></A> [293]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXXVII.&#8212;EMPEROR IN-GIY&#332;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2192"></A><A HREF="#fn_2187"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> (PART I&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Wo-asa-dzu-ma-waku-go-no-sukune dwelt in the Palace of Toho-tsu-Asuka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2193"></A><A HREF="#fn_2188"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign wedded Her Augustness Osaka-no-oho-naka-tsu-hime,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2194"></A><A HREF="#fn_2189"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> younger sister of King Oho-hodo, and begot august children: King Karu of Kinashi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2195"></A><A HREF="#fn_2190"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> next Nagata-no-oho-iratsume;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2196"></A><A HREF="#fn_2191"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> next King Kurohiko of Sakahi;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2197"></A><A HREF="#fn_2192"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> next His Augustness Anaho;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2198"></A><A HREF="#fn_2193"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> next Karu-no-oho-iratsume&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2199"></A><A HREF="#fn_2194"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> another name for whom is Sotohoshi-no-iratsume.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2200"></A><A HREF="#fn_2195"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> (<small>the reason for her being given the august name of Queen So-tohoshi was that the refulgence of her person passed through her garments</small>); next King Shiro-biko of Yatsuri;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2201"></A><A HREF="#fn_2196"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> next His Augustness [294] Oho-hatsuse:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2202"></A><A HREF="#fn_2197"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> (<small>nine Deities</small>). Altogether the Heavenly Sovereign's august children [numbered] nine Deities&#8212;(<small>five Kings and four Queens</small>). Of these nine Kings and</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_366"><font size="1" color="green">p. 366</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Queens, His Augustness Anaho&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2203"></A><A HREF="#fn_2198"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire. Next his Augustness Oho-hatsuse&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2204"></A><A HREF="#fn_2199"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> ruled the Empire.</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2187"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2192">365:1</A> <a name="page_366"><font size="1" color="green">p. 366</font></A> Also pronounced <i>In-kiyo</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2188"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2193">365:2</A> See Sect. CXXXIII, Note 13.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2189"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2194">365:3</A> This name and the next have already appeared in Sect. CXVII.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2190"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2195">365:4</A> <i>Kinashi no Karu no miko</i>. Karu is properly the name of a place in Yamato which has already often appeared in the text. It is uncertain whether <i>kinashi</i> is likewise the name of a place or of a particular kind of pear; but Motowori inclines to the former view.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2191"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2196">365:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the great lord of Negate." There are many places of this name (lit. "long rice-field"), and it is not known which is here intended.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2192"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2197">365:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the black prince of Sakahi." The latter word signifies "frontier." It is not known where Sakahi is, neither is the reason for the name of "black prince" applied to this personage known (<i>Conf</i>. the "white prince" mentioned a little further on).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2193"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2198">365:7</A> Or, "of Anaho," for Anaho is properly the name of a place in Yamato. Its import is not clear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2194"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2199">365:8</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the great lady of Karu."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2195"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2200">365:9</A> Written <A NAME="img_36600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36600.jpg">, <i>i.e.</i>, "the garment-passing lady." <i>So-tohoshi</i> is Motowori's reading of the characters, the usual reading being <i>So-tohori</i> (the Intransitive instead of the Transitive form of the Verb). He likewise identifies Koto-fushi (see Sect. CXVII, Note 9) with this celebrated princess, who is commonly worshipped as Goddess of Poetry. There is much confusion in the traditions concerning her, and Motowori's notes on the subject in Vol. XXXIV, pp. 53-54 and in Vol. XXXIX of his Commentary, p. 3, should be consulted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2196"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2201">365:10</A> <i>Yatsuri no shiro-bike no miko</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "the white prince of Yatsuri." Yatsuri is the name of a place in Yamato. It is written with characters signifying "eight melons."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2197"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2202">365:11</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "great Hatsuse," so called from Hatsuse, a celebrated place in Yamato, which has already been mentioned.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2198"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2203">366:12</A> <i>I.e.</i> "the great lady of Tachibana," the latter being the name of a place in Yamato. The word signifies "orange."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2199"></A><A HREF="kj144.htm#fr_2204">366:13</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "the lady of Sakami," the latter being apparently the name of a place either in Harima or in Wohari. Its derivation is not clear.</P>

<p><a name="page_367"><font size="1" color="green">p. 367</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXXVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR IN-GIY&#332; (PART II.&#8212;HIS SICKNESS IS CURED BY A KOREAN PHYSICIAN).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign, when first about to rule the succession of Heaven's Sun,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2205"></A><A HREF="#fn_2200"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A> declined, saying: "I have a long sickness; I cannot rule the sun's succession." Nevertheless, as from the Empress downwards all the magnates strongly urged him, he forthwith ruled the Empire. At this time the ruler of Shiragi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2206"></A><A HREF="#fn_2201"><FONT SIZE="1">2a</FONT></A> dutifully sent eighty-one vessels with august tribute. Then the chief envoy&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2207"></A><A HREF="#fn_2202"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> sent with the august tribute, whose name was Komu-ha-chimu-kamu-ki-mu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2208"></A><A HREF="#fn_2203"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> was a man deeply versed in the medical art. So he cured the Heavenly Sovereign's august sickness.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2200"></A><A HREF="kj145.htm#fr_2205">367:1a</A> <a name="page_367"><font size="1" color="green">p. 367</font></A> For this expression see Sect. XXXIII, Note 27. The story of the refusal of this monarch to accept the crown which was offered to him by the magnates of the nation is told at considerable length in the parallel passage of the "Chronicles." According to the same authority he belonged to a collateral branch of the Imperial family, and was therefore not in the regular line of succession.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2201"></A><A HREF="kj145.htm#fr_2206">367:2a</A> See Sect. XCVIII. Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2202"></A><A HREF="kj145.htm#fr_2207">367:3</A> Literally, "great messenger."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2203"></A><A HREF="kj145.htm#fr_2208">367:4</A> <A NAME="img_36700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36700.jpg"> Motowori decides that <A NAME="img_36701"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36701.jpg"> is the surname, <A NAME="img_36702"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36702.jpg"> an official title, <A NAME="img_36703"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36703.jpg"> an official designation of the kinsmen of the Korean King, and <A NAME="img_36704"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36704.jpg"> the personal name.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXXXIX.&#8212;EMPEROR IN-GIY&#332; (PART III. HE RECTIFIES THE PEOPLE'S NAMES).]</h2>  
<p>Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, lamenting the transgressions in the surnames and gentile names of the people of all the surnames and names in the Empire&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2209"></A><A HREF="#fn_2204"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> placed jars [for trial by] hot water&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2210"></A><A HREF="#fn_2205"><FONT SIZE="1">2b</FONT></A> at the Wondrous</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_368"><font size="1" color="green">p. 368</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Cape of Eighty Evils in Words at Amakashi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2211"></A><A HREF="#fn_2206"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and deigned to establish the surnames and gentile names of the eighty heads of companies.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2212"></A><A HREF="#fn_2207"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Again the Karu Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2213"></A><A HREF="#fn_2208"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> was established as the august proxy of King Karu of Ki-nashi; the Osaka Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2214"></A><A HREF="#fn_2209"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> was established as the Empress's august proxy; and the Kaha Tribe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2215"></A><A HREF="#fn_2210"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> was established as the august proxy of the Empress's younger sister Ta-wi no Naka-tsu-hime.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2216"></A><A HREF="#fn_2211"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2204"></A><A HREF="kj146.htm#fr_2209">367:1b</A> <a name="page_368"><font size="1" color="green">p. 368</font></A> The original is; <A NAME="img_36800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36800.jpg">, which Motowori reads <i>ame no shita no uji-uji na-na no hito domo no uji kabane</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2205"></A><A HREF="kj146.htm#fr_2210">367:2b</A> We learn from the "Chronicles" that he whose hand was injured in the process of dipping it into the jar of boiling water was pronounced a deceiver, while those who stood the trial unhurt were considered to be telling the truth.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2206"></A><A HREF="kj146.htm#fr_2211">368:3</A> <i>Amakashi no koio-yo-maga-tsu-hi no saki</i>. Motowori truly observes that this does not sound like an actual geographical name, but was rather, it may be supposed, a new designation given to Cape Amakashi (see Sect. LXXII, Note 10) on account of the incident here mentioned. The name reminds us of that of one of the deities born from the purification of the person of the creator Izanagi after his return from Hades (see X, Note 14).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2207"></A><A HREF="kj146.htm#fr_2212">368:4</A> <i>Ya-sotomo-no-wo</i>. See Sect. XXXIII, Note 19.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2208"></A><A HREF="kj146.htm#fr_2213">368:5</A> <i>Karu-be</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2209"></A><A HREF="kj146.htm#fr_2214">368:6</A> <i>Osaka-be</i>, so called after the Empress's native place (See Sect. CXXXVII, Note 3, and Sect. CXVII, Note 6). The reading of <i>Osaka-be</i> is given in all the editions to the characters in the text, <A NAME="img_36801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36801.jpg">, where we should expect <A NAME="img_36802"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/36802.jpg">. Motowori's explanation of the reason why the name was thus written will be found in Vol. XXXIX, p. 19, of his Commentary.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2210"></A><A HREF="kj146.htm#fr_2215">368:7</A> <i>Kaha-be</i>. Motowori supposes that there is here some corruption of the text, as no connection can be discovered between the name of this Tribe and that of the Princess whose proxy the tribe became.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2211"></A><A HREF="kj146.htm#fr_2216">368:8</A> See Sect. CXVII, Note 7.</P>

<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p>[296]</p>  <h2 align="center">[<A HREF="errata.htm#88">SECT</A>. CXLI.&#8212;EMPEROR IN-GIY&#332; (PART V.&#8212;PRINCE KARU LOVES HIS SISTER PRINCESS SO-TOHOSHI)]</h2>  
<p>After the decease of the Heavenly Sovereign, it was settled that King Karu of Ki-nashi should rule the Sun's succession.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2218"></A><A HREF="#fn_2213"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> But in the interval before his accession, he debauched his younger sister the Great Lady of Karu, and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Making rice-fields on the mountain, making hidden conduits run on account of the mountain's height:&#8212;to-day indeed [my] body easily touches the younger sister whom I wooed with a hidden wooing, the spouse for whom I wept with a hidden weeping."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2219"></A><A HREF="#fn_2214"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>This is a Hind-Lifting Song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2220"></A><A HREF="#fn_2215"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Again he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The rattle-rattle of the hail against the bamboo-grass:&#8212;After I shall have certainly slept, what though I be plotted against by people! When I shall have slept delightfully, if there is the disorder of the cut <i>Hydropyrum latifolium</i>, let there be disorder,&#8212;when I shall have slept a good [297] sleep!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2221"></A><A HREF="#fn_2216"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>This is a Rustic Lifting Song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2222"></A><A HREF="#fn_2217"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_370"><font size="1" color="green">p. 370</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2213"></A><A HREF="kj148.htm#fr_2218">369:1b</A> <a name="page_370"><font size="1" color="green">p. 370</font></A> See Sect. XXXII. Note 27. The wording of this sentence would make it appear that it was only <i>after</i> the Emperor In-giyo's death that King Karu was chosen to succeed him. But probably King Karu had been appointed Heir Apparent (<A NAME="img_37000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/37000.jpg">) during his Father's life time, as is indeed expressly stated in the "Chronicles," and is implied in later passages of this work; and what our author meant to say was: "It was settled that King Karu should rule the "Empire after the former Sovereign's decease." etc.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2214"></A><A HREF="kj148.htm#fr_2219">369:2</A> The meaning of the Song is: "The sister, the mistress, whom I wooed with such difficulty, is now easily mine."&#8212;The first phrase, down to "mountain's height," is but a "Preface "to the poem properly so called, serving to introduce by a <i>jeu-de-mots</i> the word <i>shita-dohi</i>, which means not only "hidden conduit," but "hidden wooing." At the same time the implied <A HREF="errata.htm#89">comparison</A> of the poet's secret love of one so difficult to obtain as his own sister, to the course of the water in hidden conduits which is carried up the mountain's side to irrigate a field perched in a spot almost inaccessible, is by no means devoid of aptness. The word "mountain" (<i>yama</i>) is in the original preceded by the Pillow-Word <i>ashihiki</i> (or <i>askiki</i>) <i>no</i>, whose signification is obscure and much disputed.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2215"></A><A HREF="kj148.htm#fr_2220">369:3</A> <i>Shirage-uta</i> (written phonetically). The interpretation of the term here adopted is that which has the sanction of Motowori and Moribe. They explain it to signify that the voice rose gradually toward the latter part of the Song.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2216"></A><A HREF="kj148.htm#fr_2221">369:4</A> As in the case of the preceding Song, the first phrase is but a Preface, which plays on the coincidence in sound between the words <i>tashi-dashi</i>, "rattling," and <i>tashika</i>, "certainly," <i>i.e.</i> "undisturbedly." The signification of the Song proper is: "If I shall but have gratified my passion, what care I however men may plot against me? If I can but press my beloved to my bosom, let all things go to rack and ruin, like the Hydropyrum latifolium, a grass which, when cut, falls into disorder!"&#8212;Of the sentiment of the Song, the less said the better; but viewed simply from a literary point of view, it is certainly one of the most fascinating little productions of the early Japanese muse, and the literal rendering of it into English does it woful injustice. Moribe rightly rejects Motowori's proposal to divide the poem in two after the words <i>hito hakayu to mo</i>, "plotted against by people." <i>Kari-komo no</i>, "of the <i>Hydropyrum latifolium</i>," is a Pillow-Word.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2217"></A><A HREF="kj148.htm#fr_2222">369:5</A> <i>Hinaburi no ageuta</i>. The commentators have nothing more precise to tell us concerning the expression "Lifting-Song "than that "it refers to the lifting of the voice in singing."</P>

<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_371"><font size="1" color="green">p. 371</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXLII.&#8212;EMPEROR IN-GIY&#332; (PART VI.&#8212;WAR BETWEEN PRINCE KARU AND PRINCE ANAHO).]</h2>  
<p>Therefore all the officials&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2223"></A><A HREF="#fn_2218"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and likewise the people of the Empire turned against the Heir Apparent Karu, and towards the August Child Anaho. Then the Heir Apparent Karu, being alarmed, fled into the house of the Grandee the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2224"></A><A HREF="#fn_2219"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and made a provision of implements of war. (<small>The arrows made at this [298] time&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2225"></A><A HREF="#fn_2220"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> were provided with copper arrow-insides:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2226"></A><A HREF="#fn_2221"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> so those arrows are called by the name of Karu arrows.</small>) Prince Anaho likewise made implements of war. (<small>The arrows made by this Prince were just the arrows of the present time:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2227"></A><A HREF="#fn_2222"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> they are called Anaho arrows.</small>) Thereupon Anaho raised an army, and beleaguered the house of the noble Oho-make Wo-mahe. Then, when he reached the gate, heavy ice-rain&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2228"></A><A HREF="#fn_2223"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> was falling. So he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Come thus under cover of the metal gate of the Noble Oho-mahe Wo-mahe! We will stand till the rain stops."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2229"></A><A HREF="#fn_2224"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then the Noble Oho-mahe came singing, lifting his hands, striking his knees, dancing, and waving his arms. The Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The courtiers are tumultuous, [saying] that the small bell of the garter of the courtiers has fallen off. Country-people, too, beware!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2230"></A><A HREF="#fn_2225"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>This Song is of a Courtier's Style.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2231"></A><A HREF="#fn_2226"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Singing thus, he [299] came near and said: "August Child of our Heavenly Sovereign! Come not with arms against the King thine elder brother. If thou shouldst come against him with arms, people will surely laugh. I&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2232"></A><A HREF="#fn_2227"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> will secure him and</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_372"><font size="1" color="green">p. 372</font></A></p>  
<p>present him to thee."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2233"></A><A HREF="#fn_2228"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> The Prince Anaho disbanded his troops and went away. So the Noble Oho-make Wo-mahe secured Prince Karu, and led him forth, and presented him [to Prince Anaho]. The captive Prince sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Maiden of heaven-soaring Karu! if thou cry violently, people will know. Cry quietly like the doves on Mount Hasa."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2234"></A><A HREF="#fn_2229"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again he sang:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Maiden of heaven-soaring Karu! Come and sleep, and [then] pass on, oh maiden of Karu!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2235"></A><A HREF="#fn_2230"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_373"><font size="1" color="green">p. 373</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2218"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2223">371:1</A> <a name="page_372"><font size="1" color="green">p. 372</font></A> See Sect. CXII, Note 4.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2219"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2224">371:2</A> <i>Oho-mahe Wo-make sukune no omi</i> (according to the old reading <i>Oho-saki Wo-saki</i>, etc. Motowori considers this double name to denote two brothers, the words <i>oho</i> and <i>wo</i> ("great "and "small") naturally lending themselves to the interpretation of "elder" and "younger." Moribe, on the contrary, thinks that there was but one, and is supported both by the authority of the "Chronicles of Japan" and by the fact that, except in the "Chronicles of Old Matters of Former Ages." which is believed to be a forgery, no second brother is anywhere mentioned. He explains the use of the double name in the prose text as having crept in through the influence of the text of the following Song (see Note 7 below). This seems to the translator the better view.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2220"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2225">371:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "on this occasion."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2221"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2226">371:4</A> There is here an evident corruption of the text, and Motowori aptly conjectures that arrow-heads, or, as they are called in Japanese, arrow-points, are intended. He adds that up till then arrow-heads had always been made of iron.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2222"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2227">371:5</A> The author's style is here rather at fault; for he apparently wishes to say that the arrows employed by Prince Anaho were those which had been used in ancient times and were still the most universally employed&#8212;that, in fact, they were the usual style of arrow in contradistinction to those of Prince Karu's invention.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2223"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2228">371:6</A> See Sect, LXXXVIII, Note 5.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2224"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2229">371:7</A> <a name="page_373"><font size="1" color="green">p. 373</font></A> The prince, in this Song, bids his troops follow his example, and take refuge from the rain under cover of the gate of Oho-mahe's house. Such, at least, is the actual sense of the words used; but Motowori sees in them nothing less than a slightly veiled exhortation to his followers to attack the castle, while Moribe, on the other hand, thinks they were meant to convey to Oho-mahe a hint of his presence, and enable the beleaguered prince, for whom (as being his elder brother) Prince Anaho retained a great affection and respect, to devise some method of escape. This seems extremely far-fetched.&#8212;The word "metal" probably refers only to the fastenings of the gate, and not to its whole structure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2225"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2230">371:8</A> The exact purport and application of this Song is disputed, but this much seems clear: that the composer of it seeks to quiet both the besieging army (out of politeness called courtiers), and the peasants who had joined the fray, by making light of the whole occurrence, which he compares to so trivial an accident as the falling of a bell from a man's "garter" or "leggings." The custom of ornamenting this article of dress with a smell bell is, however, not mentioned elsewhere. The word <i>yume</i>, which concludes the Song and is here rendered "beware," is identified by Motowori and Moribe with the Imperative of the Verb <i>iwu</i> "to avoid," "to shun," "not to do."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2226"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2231">371:9</A> <i>Miya-hito-buri</i>. This is one of the cases which lend support to Motowori's view that the names of the so called styles of Songs are derived from their initial words.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2227"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2232">371:10</A> Written with the humble character <A NAME="img_37300"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/37300.jpg">, "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2228"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2233">372:11</A> The word used in the text, here and also in the next sentence, is that which properly denotes the presenting of tribute.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2229"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2234">372:12</A> Another reading gives this sense:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"As, if the maiden of heaven-soaring Karu cried violently, people would know, she cries quietly like the doves on Mount Hasa."</div></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> According to this reading, the poet simply explains the reason of the undemonstrativeness of his mistress's grief; according to that in the text, he implores her not to weep too passionately.&#8212;<i>Amadamu</i> or <i>amadamu ya</i>, "heaven-soaring, "is the Pillow-Word for Karu, applied to it punningly on account of its similarity in sound to the word <i>kari</i>, "a wild. goose," which well deserves the epithet "heaven-soaring." Of Mount Hasa nothing is known.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2230"></A><A HREF="kj149.htm#fr_2235">372:13</A> <a name="page_374"><font size="1" color="green">p. 374</font></A> Rendered thus according to Moribe's exegesis, which quite approves itself to the translator's mind, this Song signifies: "Oh! maiden of Karu! come and sleep with me but once, before my impending banishment renders it hard for us to meet again." Motowori chooses to interpret <i>nete</i> as a crasis of <i>nayete</i>, "bending." and sees in the Song an invitation to the maiden to come quietly so as not to attract observation.&#8212;The final word, translated "maiden," is <i>wotome-domo</i>, properly a Plural, but here used in a Singular sense, as <i>watakuski-domo</i>, "I" (properly "we"), so constantly is in the modern Colloquial Dialect. For the Pillow-Word "heaven-soaring "see preceding Note.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_374"><font size="1" color="green">p. 374</font></A> [300]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXLIII.&#8212;EMPEROR IN-GIY&#332; (PART VII.&#8212;DEATH OF PRINCE KARU AND PRINCESS SO-TOHOSHI).]</h2>  
<p>So Prince Karu was banished to the hot waters of Iyo.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2236"></A><A HREF="#fn_2231"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Again when about to be banished, he sang saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The heaven-soaring birds, too, are indeed messengers. When thou hearest the voice of the crane, ask my name."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2237"></A><A HREF="#fn_2232"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>These three songs are of a Heaven-Soaring style.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2238"></A><A HREF="#fn_2233"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Again he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"If they banish the Great Lord to an island, he will indeed make the remaining return voyage. Beware of my mat! Mat indeed in words,&#8212;beware of my spouse!&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2239"></A><A HREF="#fn_2234"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[301] This Song is of a Partly Lowered Rustic style.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2240"></A><A HREF="#fn_2235"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Queen So-tohoshi presented a Song [to him]. That Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Let not thy feet tread on the oyster-shells of the shore of Ahine with its summer herbs! Pass there [after] having made clear!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2241"></A><A HREF="#fn_2236"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_375"><font size="1" color="green">p. 375</font></A></p>  
<p>So when afterwards again, being unable to restrain her love, she went after him, she sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Thy going has become long past. I will go, oh! to meet thee. Wait! I can not wait." (<small>What is here called <i>yama-tadzu</i> is [what is] now [known by the name of] <i>tatsuge</i>.</small>)&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2242"></A><A HREF="#fn_2237"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So when in her pursuit she reached [the place where Prince Karu was, he, who had been] pensively waiting, sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Alas! beloved spouse, who settledst the [302] whereabouts of our grave, setting up flags in the great vale, setting up flags in the little vale of Hatsuse the hidden castle! Alas! beloved spouse, whom I see after [our many troubles], prostrate like a <i>tsuki</i> bow, standing like an <i>adzusa</i> bow!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2243"></A><A HREF="#fn_2238"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Driving sacred piles in the upper reach, driving true piles in the lower reach of the river of secluded Hatsuse, and hanging on 303 the sacrificial piles a mirror, bunging on the true piles true jewels:&#8212;if they said that the younger sister whom I love like a true jewel, that the spouse whom I love like a mirror were [there], I would go home, I would long for my country."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2244"></A><A HREF="#fn_2239"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Having thus sung, they forthwith killed themselves together.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2245"></A><A HREF="#fn_2240"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> So these two songs are Reading Songs.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2246"></A><A HREF="#fn_2241"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_376"><font size="1" color="green">p. 376</font></A> <a name="page_377"><font size="1" color="green">p. 377</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2231"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2236">374:1</A> <a name="page_375"><font size="1" color="green">p. 375</font></A> For Iyo see Sect. V, Note 4. Its hot springs are often mentioned in early documents. Motowori identifies them with a place now called D&#333;-go (<A NAME="img_37500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/37500.jpg">).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2232"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2237">374:2</A> The meaning of this Song is: "I go where perchance no messengers will reach me. But thou must ask tidings of me from the birds."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2233"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2238">374:3</A> <a name="page_376"><font size="1" color="green">p. 376</font></A> <i>Ama-da-buri</i>. The title seems to be derived from the initial Pillow-Word of these three Songs.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2234"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2239">374:4</A> The meaning of this Song seems to the translator to be: "Even if they dare to banish me now, I shall some day return again. Respect my mat during my absence. Mat, indeed! It is my wife that must be respected." The commentators consider the concluding words to be a command addressed to the wife, and interpret the phrase to mean, "My spouse, beware! "But surely this makes less good sense, and moreover fails to suit the exactly parallel passage in the first Song of Sect. CXXV. By the words "Great Lord" the princely poet denotes himself,&#8212;perhaps with a touch of anger at the indignity to which he is subjected. The difficult expression <i>funa-amari</i> is here, in accordance with Moribe's view rendered by the words "remaining voyage," <i>i.e.</i>, "the voyage homeward," which is that part of a voyage that may be said to remain over for an outward-bound vessel when she has reached her destination. Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XXXIX, pp. 50-51, should be consulted for older views of the meaning of the term. The expression "beware of my mat" reminds us that in early days the entire floor of a Japanese room was not matted according to the modern custom, but that each individual had his own mat on which to sit and sleep. Great care was always taken not to defile another's mat, <i>Conf</i>, an elegy from the "Collection of a Myriad Leaves "translated by the <A HREF="errata.htm#90">present</A> writer in his "Classical Poetry of the Japanese," p. 79.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2235"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2240">374:5</A> <i>Hina-buri no kata-oroshi</i>. Like most of the names of styles of Songs, this one is extremely obscure. The commentators suppose that one part was sung in a lower voice than the rest. But they are merely guessing.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2236"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2241">374:6</A> The actual words of the Song signify: "Lacerate not thy feet by walking on the unseen oyster-shells of the shore of Ahine that is covered with the summer herbs; but walk there after dawn." (This is Keichi&#363;'s interpretation of the word <i>akashite</i>, "having made clear," and is the best in the present writer's opinion; the latter commentators see in it a recommendation to the exiled prince to clear the grass away on either side.) The word <i>Ahine</i> calls, however, for special explanation in order that the full import of the poem may be brought out. It properly signifies "sleeping together" or "lying on each other," and is therefore applicable either to the two spouses or to the summer grass. Indeed it is doubtful if it be the name of any real place at all. The word <i>natsu-kusa</i> may also be taken simply as a Pillow-Word for <i>Ahine</i>.&#8212;The total gist of the Song is in any case a warning from the maiden to her lover to guard himself against the perils of the journey.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2237"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2242">375:7</A> <a name="page_377"><font size="1" color="green">p. 377</font></A> The meaning of this Song is: "It is too long since thy departure. I can wait no longer, but will go and meet thee."&#8212;The Verb "to meet" (<i>mukahe</i>) is in the original preceded by the Pillow-Word <i>yama-tadzu</i>, which forms the subject of the note appended to the poem by the compiler. The commentators are not agreed as to the precise nature of the instrument intended; but it seems to have been some kind of axe. The cause of its use as a Pillow-Word for "meeting "is equally disputed. It only occurs written phonetically. The term <i>tatsu-ge</i>, by which it is explained in the text, is there written <A NAME="img_37700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/37700.jpg">, which does not help us much towards understanding what is meant to be designated.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2238"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2243">375:8</A> So obscure is this Song in the original, that Motowori confesses himself unable to make any sense of it. The translator has adopted Mortise's interpretation, according to which the gist of it is this: "Alas! my dear wife, who wast so willing to be for ever united to me that thou didst even fix on the spot in the funereal vale of Hatsuse where we should one day be buried together! Alas for thee, whom at last I now see again "&#8212;In order to arrive at this meaning, Moribe is obliged to prove more less satisfactorily that the thrice repeated word <i>wo</i> signifies "vale "or "mountain-fold "the first two times that it occurs, and "grave" the third, and that <i>komoriku no hatsuse</i>, usually interpreted as secluded "Hatsuse," means "the hidden castle," the "final place," <i>i.e.</i>, "the tomb, It is also necessary to suppose, without authority, that the flags mentioned by the poet are meant for funeral flags, and that the words "prostrate like a <i>tsuki</i> bow," etc., which, according to the laws of Japanese construction, precede instead of following the phrase "alas! beloved spouse," etc., are but a Preface for the latter.&#8212;It will be seen that the foundation on which Moribe's interpretation rests is slight, and that Motowori was scarcely to be blamed for pronouncing the Song incomprehensible. At the same time the translator has thought it better, by following Moribe, to give <i>some</i> translation of it than to leave the passage blank. With this warning, the student may search for other possible meanings if he pleases.&#8212;Hatsuse is a still existent and celebrated place among the mountains of Yamato. The etymology of the name, unless we accept Moribe's mentioned above, is obscure. It is now usually pronounced <i>Hase</i>. The <i>tsuki</i> is said to be almost indistinguishable from the <i>keyaki</i> tree (<i>Zelkowa keaki</i>). The <i>adzusa</i> seems to be the <i>Catalpa kaempferi</i>, but some believe it to be the cherry tree.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2239"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2244">375:9</A> The first half of this Song down to the words "hanging on the true piles true jewels" is a Preface for what follows. The signification <a name="page_378"><font size="1" color="green">p. 378</font></A> of the rest is: "If my dearly loved sister-wife were still at Hatsuse in Yamato, I would fly to her either in thought or deed; but now that she has followed me into exile, the land of exile is good enough:"&#8212;Moribe, while allowing the first half of the Song to be a Preface for the rest, contends that it also should be credited with a signification bearing on the subject-matter of the main part of the Song. He supposes, namely, the religious ceremony, whatever it was, of driving piles into the bed or bank of the river and of decorating them with beads and a mirror, to have been one really performed by Princess So-tohoshi to compass her lover's, return. In the translator's opinion, it is more elegant and more in accordance with Archaic usage to consider the Preface as having no special significance or connection (otherwise than verbal) with the rest of the poem. The word <i>i-kuhi</i> or <i>i-guhi</i>, rendered "sacred piles," occasions some difficulty; for it is not certain whether Motowori is right in giving to the initial syllable <i>i</i> the meaning of "sacred." It may be simply what has been termed an "Ornamental Prefix," devoid of meaning. Motowori however points out that this usage of it is restricted to Verbs, and does not occur with Substantives. <i>Komoriku no</i>, the Pillow-Word for Hatsuse, is rendered by "secluded" in accordance with Mabuchi's usually accepted derivation from <i>komori-kuni</i>, "retired land." Moribe, notwithstanding what he has said in his exegesis of the preceding poem (Note 8), is willing to allow that, though perhaps not its original, this was its common, meaning even in ancient times.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2240"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2245">375:10</A> <i>I.e.</i>, committed suicide together.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2241"></A><A HREF="kj150.htm#fr_2246">375:11</A> This expression is interpreted to mean that these Songs were recited in monotone, as one would read a book or tell a tale.</P>

<p><a name="page_378"><font size="1" color="green">p. 378</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXLIV.&#8212;EMPEROR AN-K&#332; (PART I.&#8212;HE SLAYS KING OHO-KUSAKA).]</h2>  
<p>The august child&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2247"></A><A HREF="#fn_2242"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Anaho dwelt at the palace of Anaho at Isonokami,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2248"></A><A HREF="#fn_2243"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. The Heavenly Sovereign sent the Grandee of Ne,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2249"></A><A HREF="#fn_2244"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> ancestor of the Grandees of Sakamoto, to the residence of King Oho-kusaka, on behalf of his younger brother Prince Oho-hatsuse to command thus: "I wish Thine Augustness's younger sister</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_379"><font size="1" color="green">p. 379</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Queen Waka-kusaka to wed Prince Oho-hatsuse. So do thou present her."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2250"></A><A HREF="#fn_2245"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Then King Oho-kusaka did obeisance four times, and said: "Owing to a supposition that there might be some such Great Commands, I have kept her always indoor.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2251"></A><A HREF="#fn_2246"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> With reverence&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2252"></A><A HREF="#fn_2247"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> will I respectfully offer her according to the Great Commands." Nevertheless, thinking it disrespectful [merely] to send a message,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2253"></A><A HREF="#fn_2248"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> he forthwith, as a ceremonial gift&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2254"></A><A HREF="#fn_2249"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> from his younger sister, made [the Grandee of Ne] take a pushwood jewel head-dress&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2255"></A><A HREF="#fn_2250"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> to present [to the Heavenly Sovereign]. The Grandee of Ne forthwith stole the jewel headdress meant as a ceremonial gift, and slandered King Oho-kusaka, saying: "King Oho-kusaka would not receive the Imperial Commands, but said: "An soror mea fiet ejusdem stirpis [viri] inferior storea?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2256"></A><A HREF="#fn_2251"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> and, grasping the hilt of his cross-sword,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2257"></A><A HREF="#fn_2252"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A> was angry." So the Heavenly Sovereign, having in his great anger slain King Oho-kusaka, took that King's chief wife Nagata-no-oho-iratsume,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2258"></A><A HREF="#fn_2253"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A> and made her Empress.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<P><A NAME="fn_2250"></A><A HREF="kj151.htm#fr_2255">379:9</A> <a name="page_380"><font size="1" color="green">p. 380</font></A> The original term <i>oshi-ki no tam-akadzura</i> is extremely obscure. <P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_380"><font size="1" color="green">p. 380</font></A>[305]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXLV.&#8212;EMPEROR AN-K&#332; (PART II.&#8212;HE IS SLAIN BY KING MA-YOWA).]</h2>  
<p>After this, the Heavenly Sovereign, being on [his] divine couch,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2259"></A><A HREF="#fn_2254"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> was sleeping at midday. Then he spoke to his Empress, saying: "Is there anything on thy mind?" She replied, saying: "Being the object of the Heavenly Sovereign's generous favour, what, can there be on my mind?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2260"></A><A HREF="#fn_2255"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Hereupon the Empress's former child,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2261"></A><A HREF="#fn_2256"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> King Ma-yowa, who was seven years old that year, happened to be just then playing outside the apartment.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2262"></A><A HREF="#fn_2257"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Then the Heavenly Sovereign, not Knowing that the young King was playing outside the apartment, spoke to the Empress, saying: "I have constantly something upon my mind, namely [the fear] that thy child King Ma-yowa, when he comes to man's estate, may, on learning that I slew the King his father, requite me with a foul heart."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2263"></A><A HREF="#fn_2258"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Thereupon King Ma-yowa, who had been playing outside</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_381"><font size="1" color="green">p. 381</font></A></p>  
<p>the apartment, and whose ear had caught these words, forthwith watched for the Heavenly Sovereign to be augustly asleep, and, taking the great sword [that lay] by his side,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2264"></A><A HREF="#fn_2259"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> forthwith struck off the Heavenly Sovereign's head, and fled into the house of the Grandee Tsubura.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2265"></A><A HREF="#fn_2260"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> The Heavenly Sovereign's august years were fifty-six, His august <A HREF="errata.htm#92">masoleum</A> is on the mound of Fushimi at Sugahara.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2266"></A><A HREF="#fn_2261"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2254"></A><A HREF="kj152.htm#fr_2259">380:1</A> <i>Conf</i>. Sect. LXIV, Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2255"></A><A HREF="kj152.htm#fr_2260">380:2</A> Literally, "Hast thou anything to think about? "The same construction is used in the next sentence.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2256"></A><A HREF="kj152.htm#fr_2261">380:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, her son by her former husband King Oho-kusaka.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2257"></A><A HREF="kj152.htm#fr_2262">380:4</A> Literally, "below the palace." The same expression recurs further on. The parallel passage in the "Chronicles" has "below the upper storey," <i>i.e.</i>, in the court or garden of a two-storeyed house. With the small proportions assumed by Japanese architecture, conversation could well be overheard under these conditions.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2258"></A><A HREF="kj152.htm#fr_2263">380:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "take vengeance upon me."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2259"></A><A HREF="kj152.htm#fr_2264">381:6</A> <i>Scil</i>. by the Emperor's side.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2260"></A><A HREF="kj152.htm#fr_2265">381:7</A> <i>Tsubura omi</i>. The etymology of Tsubura is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2261"></A><A HREF="kj152.htm#fr_2266">381:8</A> For Sugahara see Sect. LXXV, Note I. The Fushimi here mentioned, which is in Yamato, must not be confounded with the better known Fushimi in Yamashiro. The popular etymology of this name (and it is to be found in many books) traces it to <i>Fushi mi</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "lying three," in connection with the story of a man who "lay on the mound for three years." Probably <i>fuse-midzu</i>, "water laid on," a name perhaps given on account of an aqueduct or of water-pipes, was the original designation, which has been corrupted.</P>

<p><a name="page_382"><font size="1" color="green">p. 382</font></A> [306]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXLVI.&#8212;EMPEROR AN-K&#332; (PART III.&#8212;PRINCE OHO HATSUSE SLAYS PRINCES KURO-BIKO AND SHIRO-BIRO).]</h2>  
<p>Then Prince Oho-hatsuse,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2267"></A><A HREF="#fn_2262"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> who at that time was a lad, was forthwith grieved and furious on hearing of this event, and went forthwith to his elder brother King Kurobiko,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2268"></A><A HREF="#fn_2263"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> and said: "They have slain&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2269"></A><A HREF="#fn_2264"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> the Heavenly Sovereign. What shall be done?" But King Kurobiko was not startled, and was of unconcerned heart.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2270"></A><A HREF="#fn_2265"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> There upon King Oho-hatsuse reviled his elder brother, saying: "For one thing it being the Heavenly Sovereign, for another thing it being thy brother, how is thy heart without concern?&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2271"></A><A HREF="#fn_2266"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> What! not startled, but unconcerned on hearing that they have slain thine elder brother!"&#8212;and forthwith he clutched him by the collar; dragged him out, drew his sword, and slew him. Again, going to his elder brother King Shiro-biko, he told him the circumstances as before. The unconcernedness again was like [that shown by] King Kuro-biko. [So King Oho-hatsuse,] having forthwith clutched him by the collar, pulled him along, and dug a pit on reaching Woharida,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2272"></A><A HREF="#fn_2267"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> buried him as he stood,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2273"></A><A HREF="#fn_2268"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> so that by the time he had been buried up to the loins, both his eyes burst out, and he died.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2274"></A><A HREF="#fn_2269"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<P><A NAME="fn_2263"></A><A HREF="kj153.htm#fr_2268">382:2</A> See Sect. CXXXVII, Note 6.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_383"><font size="1" color="green">p. 383</font></A> [269]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXLVII.&#8212;EMPEROR <A HREF="errata.htm#95">AN-K&#332;</A> (PART IV.&#8212;DEATH OF PRINCE MA-YOWA AND OF THE GRANDEE TSUBURA).]</h2>  
<p>Again he raised an army and beleaguered the house of the Grandee Tsubura. Then [the other side also] raised an army to resist the attack,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2275"></A><A HREF="#fn_2270"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and the arrows that were shot forth were like unto the falling down of the [ears of the] reeds.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2276"></A><A HREF="#fn_2271"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Thereupon King Oho-hatsuse, using his spear as a staff, peeped in,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2277"></A><A HREF="#fn_2272"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and said: "Is perchance the maiden, with whom I spoke, in this house?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2278"></A><A HREF="#fn_2273"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> Then the Grandee Tsubura, hearing these commands,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2279"></A><A HREF="#fn_2274"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> came forth himself, and having taken off the weapons with which he was girded, did obeisance eight times, and said: "The maiden Princess Kara, whom anon thou deignedst to woo, is at thy service. Again in addition I will present to thee five granaries. (<small>What are called the five granaries are now the gardeners of the five villages of Kadzuraki:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2280"></A><A HREF="#fn_2275"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></small>) Meanwhile the reason why she does not come out to meet thee in person is that from of old down to the present time grandees and chiefs have been known to hide in the palaces of Kings, but Kings have not yet been known to hide in the houses of grandees.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2281"></A><A HREF="#fn_2276"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Therefore I think that, though a vile slave of a grandees&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2282"></A><A HREF="#fn_2277"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> exerting his utmost <A HREF="errata.htm#96">strength</A> in the fight can scarcely conquer, yet must he die rather than desert a Prince who, trusting in him, has entered into his house."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2283"></A><A HREF="#fn_2278"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> Having thus</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_384"><font size="1" color="green">p. 384</font></A></p>  
<p>spoken, he again took his weapons and went in again to <A HREF="errata.htm#97">fight</A>. Then, their strength being exhausted and their arrows finished, he said to the Prince: "My&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2284"></A><A HREF="#fn_2279"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A> hands are wounded, and our arrows likewise are finished. We cannot now fight. What shall be done? "The Prince [266] replied, saying: "If that be so, there is nothing more to do. [Do thou] now slay me. "So [the Grandee Tsubura] thrust the Prince to death with his sword, and forthwith killed himself by cutting off his own head.</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2270"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2275">383:1</A> <a name="page_384"><font size="1" color="green">p. 384</font></A> Literally, "to wait and fight."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2271"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2276">383:2</A> The character <A NAME="img_38400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38400.jpg">, "to come" (here in accordance with English idiom rendered by "down") is supposed to be an error. One conjectural emendation of it, viz., <A NAME="img_38401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38401.jpg">, would suggest the "plentiful" falling of the flowers of the reeds.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2272"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2277">383:3</A> <i>I.e.</i>, he lifted himself on tiptoe by leaning on his spear, so as to be able to peep in.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2273"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2278">383:4</A> The maiden thus suddenly introduced into the story is Tsubura's daughter Kara, whom it must be supposed that the Prince had previously been wooing.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2274"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2279">383:5</A> Or rather, "Imperial words." The application of the characters <A NAME="img_38402"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38402.jpg"> to the words of one who was not yet actually Emperor is curious.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2275"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2280">383:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, the places where the five granaries originally were are now the five villages inhabited by the men who cultivate the Imperial gardens. For Kadzuraki see Sect. LV, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2276"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2281">383:7</A> Or we may, following Motowori's proposal, take the character <A NAME="img_38403"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38403.jpg"> in this clause in its slightly different acceptation of "subject," which better suits the sense. The partly phonetic wording of the next sentence <A NAME="img_38404"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38404.jpg"> shows how the writer was perplexed by the double use of the term.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2277"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2282">383:8</A> <i>Q.d.</i>. in comparison with a prince of the Imperial family, even a grandee was but a vile slave.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2278"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2283">383:9</A> The character <A NAME="img_38405"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38405.jpg"> in the original of this passage <A NAME="img_38406"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38406.jpg"> is corrupt. But the sense remains clear, and it is scarcely worth while looking about for a probable emendation. Motowori has no satisfactory proposal to make.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2279"></A><A HREF="kj154.htm#fr_2284">384:10</A> The humble character <A NAME="img_38407"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38407.jpg">, "servant" here used for the First <a name="page_385"><font size="1" color="green">p. 385</font></A> Personal pronoun. The expression <A NAME="img_38500"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38500.jpg">, here literally rendered "my hands are all wounded," is very curious. Motowori reads it <i>ita-te ohinu</i>, <i>i.e.</i>, "I have received (or suffered from) hurtful hands," and compares two somewhat similar expressions found in Sect. XLIV (see Note 33 to that Sect). The translator may however point out that the similarity is much more apparent in Motowori's <i>kana</i> reading than it is in the Chinese text itself. May not the sense of the present passage rather be: "All our men are wounded?" for the word <i>te</i> (<A NAME="img_38501"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38501.jpg">) "hand," is frequently used in Japanese,&#8212;in compounds at least,&#8212;in the sense of "man," somewhat as it is in English naval, mining, and other technical parlance.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_385"><font size="1" color="green">p. 385</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXLVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR AN-K&#332; (PART V:&#8212;PRINCE OHO-HATSUSE SLAYS PRINCE OSHIHA).]</h2>  
<p>After this Karu-fukuro,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2285"></A><A HREF="#fn_2280"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> ancestor of the Dukes of Yama of Sasaki in Afumi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2286"></A><A HREF="#fn_2281"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> said [to King Oho-hatsuse]: "At Kuta&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2287"></A><A HREF="#fn_2282"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> [and?] on the moor of Kaya at Wata in Afumi, boars and deer are abundant. Their legs as they stand are like a moor [covered] with <i>wogi</i>;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2288"></A><A HREF="#fn_2283"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> the horns they point up are like withered trees." At this <A HREF="errata.htm#98">time</A> [King Oho-hatsuse], taking with him King Ichi-no-be-no-oshiha, made a progress to Afumi, and on reaching this moor, each of them built a separate temporary palace to lodge in. Then next morning, before the sun had risen, King Oshiha with a tranquil heart rode along on his august horse, and, reaching and standing beside King Oho-hatsuse's temporary Palace, said to King Oho-hatsuse's attendants: "Is he not awake yet? He must [309] be told quickly [that I am come]. It is already day-light.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2289"></A><A HREF="#fn_2284"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> He must come to the hunting-ground,"&#8212;and forthwith urging his horse, he went forth. Then the people who served the august person of King Oho-hatsuse</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_386"><font size="1" color="green">p. 386</font></A></p>  
<p>said: "As [King Oshiha] is a violent-spoken&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2290"></A><A HREF="#fn_2285"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> Prince, thou shouldst be on thy guard, and likewise it were well to arm thine august person." Forthwith he put on armour underneath his clothes, took and girded on him his bow and arrows, rode off on horseback, and in a sudden interval setting his horse by the side [of the other King's], took out an arrow, shot King Oshiha down, forthwith moreover cut his body [to pieces], put [them] into a horse's manger, and buried them level with the earth.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2280"></A><A HREF="kj155.htm#fr_2285">385:1</A> <a name="page_386"><font size="1" color="green">p. 386</font></A> This name has the curious signification of "Korean (or Chinese) bag."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2281"></A><A HREF="kj155.htm#fr_2286">385:2</A> <i>Afumi no Sasaki no yama no kiwi</i>. <i>Conf</i>. Sect. LXIX, Note 46.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2282"></A><A HREF="kj155.htm#fr_2287">385:3</A> This and the following names are altogether obscure, neither is it evident whether two places are meant, or only one. The present passage reads as if two were intended, but a little further down the author seems to be speaking of but one.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2283"></A><A HREF="kj155.htm#fr_2288">385:4</A> The <i>Hedysarum esculentum</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2284"></A><A HREF="kj155.htm#fr_2289">385:5</A> Literally "the night has already finished dawning."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2285"></A><A HREF="kj155.htm#fr_2290">386:6</A> Motowori endeavours, not every successfully, to explain the use of this epithet by Prince Oho-Hatsuse's attendants. As the sequel shows, the violence was all on the other side.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CXLIX.&#8212;EMPEROR AN-K&#332; (PART VI.&#8212;FLIGHT OF PRINCES OHOKE AND WOKE)].</h2>  
<p>Hereupon King Ichi-no-be's children&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2291"></A><A HREF="#fn_2286"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> King Ohoke and King Woke (two Deities), having heard of this affray, fled away. So when they reached Karibawi&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2292"></A><A HREF="#fn_2287"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> in Yamashiro and were eating their august provisions, an old man with a tattooed face came and seized the provisions. Then the two Kings said: "We do not grudge the provisions. But</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_387"><font size="1" color="green">p. 387</font></A></p>  
<p>who art thou? "He replied, saying: "I am a boar-herd in Yamashiro." So they fled across the River Kusuba,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2293"></A><A HREF="#fn_2288"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> reached the land of Harima,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2294"></A><A HREF="#fn_2289"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> entered the house of a native of that country named Shizhimu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2295"></A><A HREF="#fn_2290"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> hid their persons, and worked as grooms and cow-herds.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2286"></A><A HREF="kj156.htm#fr_2291">386:1</A> <a name="page_387"><font size="1" color="green">p. 387</font></A> Literally "prince" (<A NAME="img_38700"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38700.jpg">). Their names apparently signify "big basket" and "little basket."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2287"></A><A HREF="kj156.htm#fr_2292">386:2</A> Known in later times as Kaniha and Kabawi. The name signifies (if the characters with which it is written may be relied on) "the well where the leaves were cut."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2288"></A><A HREF="kj156.htm#fr_2293">387:3</A> See Sect. LXVI. Note 19.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2289"></A><A HREF="kj156.htm#fr_2294">387:4</A> See Sect. LX, Note 19.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2290"></A><A HREF="kj156.htm#fr_2295">387:5</A> Or Shizhimi. Properly the name of a village, it is here used as the name of a man. The etymology is obscure.</P>

<p>[310]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CL.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU, (I.&#8212;GENEALOGIES).]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Oho-hatsuse-no-waka-take dwelt in the palace of Asakura at Hatsuse,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2296"></A><A HREF="#fn_2291"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. The Heavenly Sovereign wedded Queen Wake-kusaka-be, younger sister of King Oho-kusaka (<small>no children</small>). Again he wedded Princess Karu, daughter of the Grandee Tsubura, and begot august children: His Augustness Shiraka; next his younger sister Her Augustness Princess Waka-tarashi (<small>two Deities</small>).</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2291"></A><A HREF="kj157.htm#fr_2296">387:1</A> <a name="page_387"><font size="1" color="green">p. 387</font></A> For Hatsuse see Sect. CXLIII, Note 8. Several Asakuras are named in the pages of these "Records." That here named is in Yamato. The name seems to mean "morning store-house."</P>

<p><a name="page_388"><font size="1" color="green">p. 388</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLI.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART II.&#8212;VARIOUS DEEDS).]</h2>  
<p>So the Shiraka Clan&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2297"></A><A HREF="#fn_2292"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> was established as the august proxy of Prince Shiraka. Again the Hatsuse-Clan-Retainers&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2298"></A><A HREF="#fn_2293"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> were established. At this time there came over people from Kure. Again the Kahase Retainers&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2299"></A><A HREF="#fn_2294"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> were established. These people from Kure&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2300"></A><A HREF="#fn_2295"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> were lodged&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2301"></A><A HREF="#fn_2296"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> at Kure-hara. So the place was called by the name of Kure-hara.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2302"></A><A HREF="#fn_2297"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2292"></A><A HREF="kj158.htm#fr_2297">388:1</A> <a name="page_388"><font size="1" color="green">p. 388</font></A> <i>Shiraka-be</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2293"></A><A HREF="kj158.htm#fr_2298">388:2</A> <i>Hatuse-be no tomire</i>. This clan was called after the reigning Emperor. Remember that the word "Retainers" is here a "gentile name."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2294"></A><A HREF="kj158.htm#fr_2299">388:3</A> <i>Kahase no toneri</i>. <i>Kaha-se</i> signifies "river-reach," and the "Chronicles," under date of the eleventh year of this reign, tell a story of the appearance of a white cormorant, to commemorate which this family was established. Cormorants, it will be remembered, were used for catching fish in rivers; hence the appropriateness of the name bestowed on the family in question.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2295"></A><A HREF="kj158.htm#fr_2300">388:4</A> The name given by the early Japanese to Wu (<A NAME="img_38800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38800.jpg">), an ancient state in Eastern China to the South of the Yang-tzo River. In Japanese it however, like other names of portions of China, often denotes the whole of that country in a somewhat vague manner. The derivation the word <i>Kura</i> is obscure. The most acceptable proposition is that which would see in it corruption of the original Chinese term <i>Wu</i>, of which <i>Go</i> is the Sinico-Japanese pronunciation. But what of the second syllable <i>re</i>?</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2296"></A><A HREF="kj158.htm#fr_2301">388:5</A> The phrase <A NAME="img_38801"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38801.jpg"> is in this place used for "lodged."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2297"></A><A HREF="kj158.htm#fr_2302">388:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, Kure Moor. It is in Yamato. According to the "Chronicles," the former name of the place had been <i>Himokuma-nu</i>.</P>

<p><a name="page_389"><font size="1" color="green">p. 389</font></A> [311]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT CLII.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART III.&#8212;THE ROOF OF THE HOUSE OF THE GREAT DEPARTMENTAL LORD OF SHIKI).]</h2>  
<p>In the beginning, when the Empress&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2303"></A><A HREF="#fn_2298"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> dwelt at Kusaka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2304"></A><A HREF="#fn_2299"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> [the Heavenly Sovereign] made a progress in Kafuchi by way of the Tadagoye&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2305"></A><A HREF="#fn_2300"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> road at Kusaka. Then, on climbing to the top of the mountain and gazing on the interior of the country, [he perceived that] there was a house built with a raised roof-frame.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2306"></A><A HREF="#fn_2301"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> The Heavenly Sovereign sent to ask [concerning] that house, saying: "Whose roof with a raised frame is that?" The answer was: "It is the house of the great Departmental Lord of Shiki."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2307"></A><A HREF="#fn_2302"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Then the Heavenly Sovereign said: "What! a slave builds his own house in imitation of the august abode of the Heavenly Sovereign!" . . . . and forthwith he sent men to burn the house [down], when the Great Departmental Lord, with trembling and dread, bowed his head,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2308"></A><A HREF="#fn_2303"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> saying: "Being a slave, I like a slave did not understand, and have built overmuch. I am in great dread."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2309"></A><A HREF="#fn_2304"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> So the thing that he presented as an august offering [in token] of his entreaty was a white dog [312] clothed in cloth&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2310"></A><A HREF="#fn_2305"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> and with a bell hung [round its neck]; and he made a kinsman of his own, named Koshihaki,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2311"></A><A HREF="#fn_2306"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> lead it by a string and present it [to the Heavenly Sovereign]. So the Heavenly Sovereign ordered them to desist from burning [the house].</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2298"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2303">389:1</A> <a name="page_389"><font size="1" color="green">p. 389</font></A> <i>I.e.</i>, <i>Waka-kusaka-be</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2299"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2304">389:2</A> See Sect. XLIV, Note 31. The Kusaka here mentioned is that in Kafuchi.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2300"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2305">389:3</A> From <i>tada</i>, "straight "and <i>koyuru</i> "to cross," this being a short cut over the mountains.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2301"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2306">389:4</A> The original of this clause is <A NAME="img_38900"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/38900.jpg">, which is read <i>katsuwo wo agete ya wo tsukureru ihe ari</i>. The <i>katsuwo</i> (properly <a name="page_390"><font size="1" color="green">p. 390</font></A> <i>katsuwo-gi</i> <A NAME="img_39000"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/39000.jpg">) is the name of the uppermost portion of the roof in modern Shinto temples, and apparently in ancient times also in houses that were not devoted to religious purposes. The difficulty is not with the sense, but with the derivation of the word <i>katsuwo-gi</i>. Following the characters with which it is here and elsewhere written, Motowori sees in it a reference to the shape of the blocks of wood resembling "dried bonitoes," which is the modern signification of <i>katsuwo</i>. But Moribe, in his "Examination of Difficult Words," proposes a derivation which approves itself more to the present writer's mind, viz., <i>kadzuku wo-gi</i> (<A NAME="img_39001"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/39001.jpg">), "small timbers atop" (see "Examination of Difficult Words," <i>s.v.</i>). Motowori's Commentary, Vol. XLI, pp. 11-14, should be consulted for a discussion of the whole question of the use of these frames in ancient times, and for the special force to be attributed to the word "raised" (<A NAME="img_39002"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/39002.jpg">) in this passage.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2302"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2307">389:5</A> <i>Shiki no oho-agata-nushi</i>. For Shiki see Sect. LXIII, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2303"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2308">389:6</A> <i>i.e.</i>, did humble obeisance by prostrating himself on the ground.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2304"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2309">389:7</A> Or, according to the older reading, "This <i>i.e.</i>, thy command) [is to be received with] awe."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2305"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2310">389:8</A> Or, "tied with [a string of] cloth." The translation follows Motowori's interpretation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2306"></A><A HREF="kj159.htm#fr_2311">389:9</A> The name signifies "loin-girded," <i>i.e.</i>, as may be presumed, "wearing a sword."</P>

<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_390"><font size="1" color="green">p. 390</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLIII.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART IV.&#8212;HE WOOES PRINCESS WAKA-KUSAKA-BE).]</h2>  
<p>Forthwith making a progress to the residence of Queen Wakakusaka-be the Heavenly Sovereign sent the dog as a message, saying: "This thing is a strange thing which I got to day on the road. So it is a thing to woo with,"&#8212;and so saying, sent it in as a present. Thereupon Queen Waka-kusaka-be sent to say to the Heavenly Sovereign: "It is very alarming that thou shouldst make a progress with thy back to the sun.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2312"></A><A HREF="#fn_2307"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> So I will come up straight [to the capital], and respectfully</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_391"><font size="1" color="green">p. 391</font></A></p>  
<p>serve thee."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2313"></A><A HREF="#fn_2308"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> When therefore he returned up and dwelt in the palace, he went and stood on the ascent&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2314"></A><A HREF="#fn_2309"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> of that mountain, and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><small>"In the hollow between the nearer and the further mountain, this Mount Kusakabe and Mount Heguri, [is] growing the flourishing broad-leafed boar-oak; at the base grow intertwining bamboos; on the top grow luxuriant bamboos:&#8212;we sleep not [now] intertwined like the intertwining bamboos, we sleep not certainly like the luxuriant bamboos: [but] oh! my beloved [313] spouse, with whom [I] shall afterwards sleep intertwined!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2315"></A><A HREF="#fn_2310"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></small></p>  
<p>And he forthwith sent back a messenger with this Song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2316"></A><A HREF="#fn_2311"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2307"></A><A HREF="kj160.htm#fr_2312">390:1</A> <a name="page_391"><font size="1" color="green">p. 391</font></A> For he had come from Yamato in the East to Kafuchi in the West.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2308"></A><A HREF="kj160.htm#fr_2313">391:2</A> The meaning is: "Thy Majesty must not come to woo me here, as the direction is unlucky. But I will myself come up straightway to the palace to be "thine Empress."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2309"></A><A HREF="kj160.htm#fr_2314">391:3</A> The ascent or way up here mentioned is, says Motowori, the Tadagoye Road, and the mountain is Mount Kusaka. See Sect. CLII, Notes 2 and 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2310"></A><A HREF="kj160.htm#fr_2315">391:4</A> In this Song the Emperor consoles himself for the delay in his union with Princess Waka-kusaka-be by reflecting that after all she will soon be his.&#8212;The first half of the poem down to the colon and dash is a Preface to the rest. Most of the difficult words occurring in it have been explained in previous notes; for the "broad-leafed bear-oak "see Sect. LXXII, Note, 19; for <i>tatami-komo</i>, the Pillow-Word by which Heguri is preceded in the Japanese text, see Sect. LXXXIX, Note 12. <i>Kusaka-be</i> is curious, for whereas it properly signifies Kusaka-Tribe,&#8212;this tribe or family being called after the place where they resided,&#8212;the place itself came to be renamed after them when the fact of the posterior origin of the family designation had been forgotten. The reason (or the <a name="page_392"><font size="1" color="green">p. 392</font></A> mention in the Preface of the oak-tree, which is not referred to in the main text of the poem, is difficult to ascertain. Moribe thinks, however that it is on account of the luxuriance of its foliage which, as if it were a Preface within the Preface, paves the way for the mention of the thick-growing bamboos. The punning connection between <i>tashinu-dake</i>, "luxuriant bamboos," and <i>tashi ni ha wi-nezu</i>, "we sleep not certainly," is necessarily obliterated in the English translation. "Certainly" must be taken in the sense of "undisturbedly."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2311"></A><A HREF="kj160.htm#fr_2316">391:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, as may be conjectured, a messenger dispatched to him by his mistress. It seems best to suppose the author to represent the Emperor as not having actually gone to her house at all, but as having only communicated with her by messenger.</P>
<p><HR>

<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="../../css/marg.css">

<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume III: Section CLIV.&#8212;Emperor Y&#363;-riyaku (Part V.&#8212;Story of the Woman Akawi-ko)</TITLE>

<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
