<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_392"><font size="1" color="green">p. 392</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLIV.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART V.&#8212;STORY OF THE WOMAN AKAWI-KO).]</h2>  
<p>Again once when the Heavenly Sovereign going out for amusement, reached the River Miwa,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2317"></A><A HREF="#fn_2312"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> there was a girl, whose aspect was very beautiful, washing clothes by the river-side. The Heavenly Sovereign asked the girl, [saying]: "Whose child art thou?" She replied, saying: "My name is Akawi-ko of the Hiketa Tribe."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2318"></A><A HREF="#fn_2313"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Then he caused her to be told, saying: "Do not thou [314] marry a husband. I will send for thee, "&#8212;and [with these words] he <A HREF="errata.htm#99">returned</A> to the palace. So eighty years had already passed while she reverently awaited the Heavenly Sovereign's commands. Thereupon Akawi-ko thought: "As, while looking for the [Imperial] commands, I have already passed many years, and as my face and form are lean and withered, there is no longer any hope. Nevertheless, if I do not show [the Heavenly Sovereign] how truly I have waited, my disappointment will be unbearable;"&#8212;and [so saying] she caused merchandise</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_393"><font size="1" color="green">p. 393</font></A></p>  
<p>to be carried on tables holding an hundred,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2319"></A><A HREF="#fn_2314"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and came forth and presented [these gifts as] tribute. Thereat the Heavenly Sovereign, who had quite forgotten what he had formerly commanded, asked Akawi-ko, saying: "What old woman art thou, and why art thou come hither?" Then Akawiko replied, saying: "Having in such and such a month of such and such a year received the Heavenly Sovereign's commands, I have been reverently awaiting the great command until this day, and eighty years have past by. Now my appearance is quite decrepit, and there is no longer any hope. Nevertheless I have come forth in order to show and declare my faithfulness." Thereupon the Heavenly Sovereign was greatly startled [and exclaimed]: "I had quite forgotten the former circumstance; and thou meanwhile, ever faithfully awaiting my commands, hast vainly let pass by the years of thy prime. This is very pitiful." In his heart he wished to marry her, but shrank from her extreme age, and could not make the marriage; but he conferred on her an august Song. That Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"How awful is the sacred oak-tree, the oak-tree of the august dwelling! Maiden of the oak-plain!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2320"></A><A HREF="#fn_2315"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Again he sang, saying: [315]</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The younger chestnut orchard plain of Hiketa:&#8212;o si dormivissem cum ili&acirc; in juvent&acirc;! Oh! how old she has become!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2321"></A><A HREF="#fn_2316"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then the tears that Akawi-ko wept quite drenched the red-dyed sleeve that she had on.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2322"></A><A HREF="#fn_2317"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> In reply to the great august Song, she sang, saying:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Left over from the piling up of the jewel-wall piled up round the august dwelling,<a name="page_394"><font size="1" color="green">p. 394</font></A>&#8212;to whom shall the person of the Deity's temple go?"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2323"></A><A HREF="#fn_2318"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[316] Again she sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! how enviable is she who is in her bloom like the flowering lotus,&#8212;the lotus of the inlet, of the inlet of Kusaka!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2324"></A><A HREF="#fn_2319"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then the old woman was sent back plentifully endowed. So these four <A HREF="errata.htm#102">Songs</A> are Quiet Songs.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2325"></A><A HREF="#fn_2320"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2312"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2317">392:1</A> <i>Miwa gawa</i>. It is the stream which flows past Hatsuse. For Miwa see Sect. LXV, Note 8.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2313"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2318">392:2</A> <i>Hiketa-bo no Akawi-ko</i>. <i>Hiketa</i> is in Yamato. The etymology of the word is obscure. <i>Akawi-ko</i> signifies "red boar child;" but the appropriateness of the name to the woman in the story is not made to appear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2314"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2319">393:3</A> See Sect. XXXVII, Note 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2315"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2320">393:4</A> Moribe says that, in this Song, the forgetful <A HREF="errata.htm#100">Monarch</A> calls to mind the majestic and awful appearance of the sacred tree in the temple-grounds, and is moved by this religious thought to repent of his neglectful treatment as her who had so patiently waited for him through so many years. Motowori, on the contrary, sees in the words nothing more than a comparison of the old woman to some sacred tree of immemorial age, and the aversion felt by the monarch to an union with her.&#8212;The oak mentioned (the Kashi, <i>Quercus myrsin&aelig;folia</i>) is an evergreen species. Both Motowori and Moribe consider that <i>mimoro</i> in the original Japanese of this Song should be taken, not as a proper name (see Sect. XXVIII, Notes 3 and 5), but simply as signifying "a sacred dwelling." As Miwa is mentioned in the earlier part of the story, it might seem more natural to regard <i>mimoro</i> as likewise being a Proper Name. But the word mimoro itself signifying "sacred spot," the difference between the two views does not amount to much, and it is best to follow native authority. "Oak-plain" (<i>kashi-hara</i>) means "a place planted with oak-trees." The first sentence of the Song must be looked on as a sort of preface to the second.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2316"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2321">393:5</A> The first words of this Song down to the colon and dash are a Preface to the Song proper, whose meaning stands in need of no explanation,&#8212;Moribe surmises that the word <i>kuri</i>, "chestnut," was formerly <a name="page_395"><font size="1" color="green">p. 395</font></A> a general name for all sorts of fruits, somewhat like our <A HREF="errata.htm#101">English</A> word "berry."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2317"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2322">393:6</A> The drenching of the sleeve with tears is a common figure in Japanese poetry.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2318"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2323">394:7</A> Or we might (following Moribe) render thus: "Left over from the guarding of the jewel-grove guard at the august dwelling," etc. The wording of his Song is far from clear. While Motowori sees in it a reference to the construction of a wall round the ground of a temple, the overplus of the materials for which sacred wall could not, it may be presumed, be applied to any profane purpose, Moribe disputes the propriety of such an interpretation of the word <i>kaki</i> which, according to him, denotes the grove planted in temple-grounds, temples never having been surrounded by walls such as Motowori assumes the existence of, nor even by "hedges" or "fences," which is the more usual acceptation of the term. He thinks, therefore, that the superficial signification of the actual words of the Song is that the priest, who has all his life been in the service of one particular shrine, cannot desert it for the adoration of some other deity. The underlying deeper significance of the little poem is in either case the same: Akawi-ko had, during her long waiting of eighty years, remained true to her first love, the Emperor. For every reason it had been impossible for her ever to give her affections to another, and she had now come up to the capital to demonstrate to him who had forgotten her the unchangeable nature of her feelings.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2319"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2324">394:8</A> This pretty little poem is too clear to need any comment. Moribe supposes that some lotuses brought from Kusaka may have been among the presents made by Akawi-ko to the Emperor. In the original Japanese the reference to the lotuses comes first, as a sort of preface to the rest of the poem. The laws of English construction necessitate its being put last in the translation.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2320"></A><A HREF="kj161.htm#fr_2325">394:9</A> See Sect. CXXIV, Note 19.</P>

<p><a name="page_395"><font size="1" color="green">p. 395</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLV.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART VI.&#8212;HE MAKES A PROGRESS TO YESHINU).]</h2>  
<p>When the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to the palace of Yeshinu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2326"></A><A HREF="#fn_2321"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> there was on the bank of the Yeshinu</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_396"><font size="1" color="green">p. 396</font></A></p>  
<p>river a girl of beautiful appearance. So having wedded this girl, he returned to the Palace. Afterwards, when he again made a progress to Yeshinu, he halted where he had met the girl, and in that place raised a great august throne,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2327"></A><A HREF="#fn_2322"><FONT SIZE="1">2a</FONT></A> seated himself on that august throne, played on his august lute, and made the maiden dance. Then he composed an august Song on account of the maiden's good dancing. That Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! that the maiden dancing to the lute-playing, of the august hand of the Deity seated on the throne might continue for ever!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2328"></A><A HREF="#fn_2323"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2321"></A><A HREF="kj162.htm#fr_2326">395:1</A> See Sect. XLVI, Note 3.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2322"></A><A HREF="kj162.htm#fr_2327">396:2a</A> See Sect. CXII, Note 2.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2323"></A><A HREF="kj162.htm#fr_2328">396:3</A> This Song presents no difficulties. In it the Emperor speaks of himself as a Deity, and is enthusiastically praised by the commentator Moribe for so doing.</P>

<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p>[317]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLVI.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART VII.&#8212;THE HORSE-FLY AND THE DRAGON-FLY).]</h2>  
<p>When forthwith he made a progress to the Moor of Akidzu,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2329"></A><A HREF="#fn_2324"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and augustly hunted, the Heavenly Sovereign sat on an august throne. Then a horse-fly bit his august arm, and forthwith a dragon-fly came and ate up&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2330"></A><A HREF="#fn_2325"><FONT SIZE="1">2b</FONT></A> the horse-fly, and flew [away]. Thereupon he composed an august Song. That Song said:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Who is it tells in the great presence that game is lying on the peak of Womuro at Mi-yeshinu? Our Great Lord, who tranquilly carries on the government, being <a name="page_397"><font size="1" color="green">p. 397</font></A> seated on the throne to await the game, a horse-fly alights on and stings the fleshy part of his arm fully clad in a sleeve of white stuff, and a dragon-fly quickly eats up that horse-fly. That it might properly bear its name, the land of Yamato was called the Island of the Dragon-Fly."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2331"></A><A HREF="#fn_2326"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So from that time that moor was called by the name [318] of Akidzu-nu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2332"></A><A HREF="#fn_2327"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2324"></A><A HREF="kj163.htm#fr_2329">396:1</A> <a name="page_397"><font size="1" color="green">p. 397</font></A> <i>Akidzu-nu</i>. See Note 4 to this section.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2325"></A><A HREF="kj163.htm#fr_2330">396:2b</A> Or, "bit."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2326"></A><A HREF="kj163.htm#fr_2331">397:3</A> The signification of the greater portion of this Song is clear enough, and is sufficiently explained by the context. The word "who" however admits of two interpretations, Motowori taking it to signify some one," whereas Moribe, keeping the literal meaning of "who?" sees in it an angry exclamation of the monarch's at having been brought out to the hunt under exaggerated promises of game. Womuro means "little cave," but is here a proper name. <i>Mi-yeshinu</i> is a form of the word Yoshino which is frequently met with in poetry, the syllable mi being probably, as Mabuchi tells us in his "Commentary on the Collection of a Myriad Leaves," equivalent to <i>ma</i>, and therefore simply an '"Ornamental Prefix." The phrase "tranquilly carries on the government" represents the Japanese <i>yasumishishi</i>, the Pillow-Word for <i>wa go oho-kimi</i>, "our Great Lord," which latter phrase descriptive of the Sovereign is here put into the Sovereign's own mouth. "Of white stuff, <i>shiro-tahe no</i>, is another Pillow-Word. The only real difficulty in this Song meets us is the interpretation of its concluding sentence. The meaning apparently intended to be conveyed is that it was in order to prove itself worthy of its name that the dragon-fly performed the loyal deed which forms the subject of the tale. But it so, the author forgets that it was not the dragon-fly that was called after Japan, but Japan that was called after the dragon-fly (<i>Akidzushima</i>, "Dragon-fly-Island," from <i>akidzu</i>, "dragon-fly"). What should be the point of the whole poem therefore fails of application. The name "Island of the Dragon-Fly" has already appeared in Sect. V (Note 26).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2327"></A><A HREF="kj163.htm#fr_2332">397:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, Dragon-Fly Moor. See Motowori's remarks in his "Examination of the Synonyms for Japan," p. 26.</P>

<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">

<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume III: Section CLVII.&#8212;Emperor Yu-riyaku (Part VII.&#8212;Adventure with a Wild Boar)</TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="index.htm">Index</A>&nbsp;

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_398"><font size="1" color="green">p. 398</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLVII.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART VII.&#8212;ADVENTURE WITH A WILD BOAR).]</h2>  
<p>Again once the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress up to the summit of Mount Kadzuraki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2333"></A><A HREF="#fn_2328"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> Then a large [wild] boar ran out. When the Heavenly Sovereign forthwith shot the boar with a whizzing barb,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2334"></A><A HREF="#fn_2329"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> the boar, furious, came towards him roaring.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2335"></A><A HREF="#fn_2330"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> So the Heavenly Sovereign, alarmed at the roaring, climbed up to the top of an alder. Then he sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The branch of the alder-tree on the opportune mound which I climbed in my flight on account of the terribleness of the roaring of the boar, of the wounded boar, which our great lord who tranquilly carries on the government had been pleased to shoot!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2336"></A><A HREF="#fn_2331"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2328"></A><A HREF="kj164.htm#fr_2333">398:1</A> <a name="page_398"><font size="1" color="green">p. 398</font></A> See Sect. LV, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2329"></A><A HREF="kj164.htm#fr_2334">398:2</A> See Sect. XXIII, Note, 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2330"></A><A HREF="kj164.htm#fr_2335">398:3</A> This is the sense attributed by the commentators to the obscure word <i>utaki</i>, which seems to be only found written phonetically.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2331"></A><A HREF="kj164.htm#fr_2336">398:4</A> Our author cannot be right in attributing this Song to the Emperor, and we need not hesitate to accept the different version of the story given in the parallel passage of the "Chronicle," where the Monarch, as might be expected from all the other details that have been preserved concerning him, bravely faces the boar, while it is one of his attendants who runs away and climbs a tree to be out of danger, and afterwards composes these lines. This Song is a good instance of what Mr. Aston (in his "Grammar of the Japanese Written Language," 2nd Edit., p. 194) has said concerning some of the short poems of a later date: "These sentences are not statements of fact; they merely picture to the mind a state of things without making any assertion respecting it." Here we, as it were, simply see the frightened courtier sitting breathless and terrified amid the branches of the alder, and the whole verse has but the meaning of an exclamation. The term <i>ari-wo</i> rendered "opportune mound." is the only word in the text which raises any difficulties <a name="page_399"><font size="1" color="green">p. 399</font></A> of interpretation. Moribe's exegesis has here been followed. According to the older view it signifies "barren mound." For the words "our great lord who tranquilly carries on the government" see Sect CLVI, Note 3.</P>
<p><HR>
<CENTER>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_399"><font size="1" color="green">p. 399</font></A> [319]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART IX.&#8212;REVELATION OF THE GREAT DEITY OF KADZURAKI, LORD OF ONE WORD).]</h2>  
<p>Again once, when the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress up Mount Kadzuraki, the various officials&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2337"></A><A HREF="#fn_2332"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> were all clothed in green-stained garments with red cords that had been granted to them. At that time there were people ascending the mountain on the opposite mountain acclivity quite similar to the order of the Heavenly Monarch's retinue. Again the style of the habiliments and likewise the people were similar and not distinguishable.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2338"></A><A HREF="#fn_2333"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Then the Heavenly Sovereign gazed, and sent to ask, saying: "There being no other King in Yamato excepting myself, what person goeth thus?" The style of the reply again was like unto the commands of a Heavenly Sovereign. Hereupon the Heavenly Sovereign, being very angry, fixed his arrow [in his bow], and the various officials all fixed their arrows [in their bows]. Then those people also all fixed their arrows [in their bows]. So the Heavenly Sovereign again sent to ask, saying: "Then tell thy name. Then let each of us tell his name, and [then] let fly his arrow." Thereupon [the other] replied, saying: "As I was the first to be asked, I will be the first to tell my name. I am the Deity who dispels with a word the evil and with a word the good,&#8212;the Great Deity of Kadzuraki, Lord of One</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_400"><font size="1" color="green">p. 400</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> [320] Word."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2339"></A><A HREF="#fn_2334"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> The Heavenly Sovereign hereupon trembled, and said: "I reverence [thee], my Great Deity. I understood not that thy great person would be revealed;"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2340"></A><A HREF="#fn_2335"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A>&#8212;and having thus spoken, he, beginning by his great august sword and likewise bow and arrows, took off the garments which the hundred officials had on, and worshipfully presented them [to the Great Deity].&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2341"></A><A HREF="#fn_2336"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> Then the Great Deity, Lord of One Word, clapping his hands,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2342"></A><A HREF="#fn_2337"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> accepted the offering. So when the Heavenly Sovereign made his progress back, the Great Deity came down the mountain,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2343"></A><A HREF="#fn_2338"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and respectfully escorted him to the entrance&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2344"></A><A HREF="#fn_2339"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> of the Hatsuse mountain. So it was at that time the Great Deity Lord of One Word was revealed.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<p><a name="page_401"><font size="1" color="green">p. 401</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT CLIX.&#8212;EMPEROR <A HREF="errata.htm#104">Y&#362;-RIYAKU</A> (PART X.&#8212;THE MOUND OF THE METAL SPADE).]</h2>  
<p>Again when the Heavenly Sovereign made a progress to Kasuga to wed Princess Wodo,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2345"></A><A HREF="#fn_2340"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A> daughter of the Grandee Satsuki of Wani,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2346"></A><A HREF="#fn_2341"><FONT SIZE="1">2a</FONT></A> a maiden met him by the way, and forthwith seeing the Imperial progress, ran and hid on the side of a mound. So he composed an august Song. That august Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! the mound where the maiden is hiding! Oh for five hundred metal spades! then might [we] dig her out!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2347"></A><A HREF="#fn_2342"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So that mound was called by the name of the Mound [321] of the Metal Spade.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2348"></A><A HREF="#fn_2343"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2340"></A><A HREF="kj166.htm#fr_2345">401:1a</A> <i>Wodo-hime</i>. The signification of this name is obscure.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2341"></A><A HREF="kj166.htm#fr_2346">401:2a</A> <i>Wani no Satsuki no omi</i>. For <i>Wani</i> see Sect. LXII, Note 11. <i>Satsuki</i> is the old Japanese name of the fifth moon.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2342"></A><A HREF="kj166.htm#fr_2347">401:3</A> Moribe thus paraphrases this Song: "The Monarch had met a girl carrying a spade in her hand, and as she was beautiful, wished to address her; but she ran off and hid on the hill-side, leaving her spade behind her. His words express a desire for five hundred spades like hers, with which to break down the hill-side and dig her out. . . . It is in joke that he talks of the maiden who was on the <i>other side</i> of the hill as being <i>inside</i> it." That in ancient times all digging implements were not made of metal will be seen by reference to Sect. CXXIV, Note 9.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2343"></A><A HREF="kj166.htm#fr_2348">401:4</A> <i>Kanasuki no woko</i>.</P>

<HTML>
<HEAD>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="../../css/marg.css">
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">
<META name="keywords" content="Kojiki Japan Shinto Mythology Legend Folklore Text Scripture Emperor Empress Chronology">
<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume III: Section CLX.&#8212;Emperor Y&#363;-riyaku (Part XI.&#8212;The Leaf in the Cup)</TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="index.htm">Index</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj166.htm">Previous</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj168.htm">Next</A>&nbsp;
<HR><A HREF="http://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/B0028Y4SZY/internetsacredte">Buy this Book at Amazon.com</A></CENTER>
<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLX.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART XI.&#8212;THE LEAF IN THE CUP).]</h2>  
<p>Again when the Heavenly Sovereign made a copious feast under a hundred-branching <i>tsuki</i>-tree&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2349"></A><A HREF="#fn_2344"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> at Hatsuse, a female attendant from Mihe&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2350"></A><A HREF="#fn_2345"><FONT SIZE="1">2b</FONT></A> in the land of Ise lifted</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_402"><font size="1" color="green">p. 402</font></A></p>  
<p>up the great august cup, and presented it to him. Then from the hundred-branching <i>tsuki</i>-tree there fell a leaf and floated in the great august cup. The female attendant, not knowing that the fallen leaf was floating in the cup, did not desist from presenting&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2351"></A><A HREF="#fn_2346"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> the great august liquor to the Heavenly Sovereign, who, perceiving the leaf floating in the cup, knocked the female attendant down, put his sword to her neck, and was about to cut off her head, when the female attendant spoke to the Heavenly Sovereign, saying: "Slay me not! There is something that I must say to thee:" and forthwith she sang, saying:</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"The palace of Hishiro at Makimuku is a palace where shines the morning sun, a palace where glistens the evening sun, a palace plentifully rooted as the root of the bamboo, a palace with spreading roots like the roots of the trees, a palace pestled with oh! eight hundred [loads of] earth, As for the branches of the hundred-fold flourishing <i>tsuki</i>-tree growing by the house of new licking at the august gate [made of] [322] <i>cham&aelig;cyparis</i> [wood], the uppermost branch has the sky above it, the middle branch has the east above it, the lowest branch has the country above it. A leaf from the tip of the uppermost branch falls against the middle branch; a leaf from the tip of the middle branch falls against the lowest branch; a leaf from the tip of the lowest branch, falling into the oil floating in the fresh jewelled goblet which the maid <a name="page_403"><font size="1" color="green">p. 403</font></A> of Mihe is lifting up, all [goes] curdle-curdle. Ah! this is very awful, August Child of the High-Shining Sun! The tradition of the thing, too this!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2352"></A><A HREF="#fn_2347"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>So on her presenting this Song, her crime was [323] pardoned. Then the Empress sang. Her Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Present the luxuriant august liquor to the august child of the high-shining sun, who is broad like the leaves, who is brilliant like the blossoms of the broad-foliaged five hundred[-fold branching] true camellia-tree that stands growing by the house of new licking in this high metropolis of Yamato, on this high-timbered mound of the metropolis The tradition of this thing, too this!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2353"></A><A HREF="#fn_2348"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Forthwith the Heavenly Sovereign sang, saying: [324]</p>  
<p>"The people of the great palace, having put on scarfs like the quail-birds having put their tails together like wagtails' and congregated together like the yard-sparrows, may perhaps to-day be truly steeped in liquor,&#8212;the people of the palace of the high-shining sun. The tradition of the thing, too, this."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2354"></A><A HREF="#fn_2349"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>These three Songs are Songs of Heavenly Words.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2355"></A><A HREF="#fn_2350"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> [325] So at this copious feast this female attendant from Mihe was praised and plentifully endowed.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_404"><font size="1" color="green">p. 404</font></A> <a name="page_405"><font size="1" color="green">p. 405</font></A> <a name="page_406"><font size="1" color="green">p. 406</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2344"></A><A HREF="kj167.htm#fr_2349">401:1b</A> <a name="page_403"><font size="1" color="green">p. 403</font></A> Said to be scarcely distinguishable from the <i>keyaki</i> (<i>Zelkowa keaki</i>)</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2345"></A><A HREF="kj167.htm#fr_2350">401:2b</A> See Sect. LXXXIX, Note 7.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2346"></A><A HREF="kj167.htm#fr_2351">402:3</A> Literally "still presented."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2347"></A><A HREF="kj167.htm#fr_2352">403:4</A> <a name="page_404"><font size="1" color="green">p. 404</font></A> To understand the allusion at the beginning of this Song to the palace of Hishiro at Makimuku, which had been the residence of the Emperor Kei-k&#333; (See Sect. LXXVI, Note 1), it must be known that in the account of the reign of that monarch as given in the "Chronicles" there is a story which, like that in the text, turns on carelessness in dealing with a goblet,&#8212;carelessness which Kei-k&#333; graciously pardoned. Moreover the scene of the incident here related was in the immediate neighbourhood of the old palace of Hishiro. There was therefore a double reason for referring to that place; and the under-current of insinuation is, that as Kei-k&#333; in the olden time forgave the courtiers who forgot his goblet, will not the present Sovereign forgive the maid of Mihe for letting a leaf fall into his? The poetess, after describing the splendour and solidity of the Imperial abode, passes on to a mention of the luxuriant and many-branching <i>tsuki</i>-tree growing near "the house of new licking," <i>i.e.</i>, the sacred hall where the Sovereign performed each year the ceremony of tasting the first-fruits of the harvest. The "gate" may either be taken in its literal acceptation, or else regarded as used by metonymy for the palace itself. The description of that which the middle and lowest branches "have above them" is somewhat obscure, and perhaps the words should not be too strictly pressed for a perfectly rational meaning, their chief use being as metrical parallelisms. The supposition of the commentators is however that the poetess, in speaking of this immense tree, meant to say that the middle branch (or branches) spread eastward, and the lowest branches westward. Next we are told of the fall of the fatal leaf into the oil, <i>i.e.</i>, into the liquor, contained in the Imperial goblet; and the poetess, before acknowledging the awfulness of her misdemeanour, skilfully brings in an allusion to the Japanese account of the creation, when the drops that fell from the spear used by the creator and creatrix Izanagi and Izanami to make the brine "go curdle-curdle" did very good work indeed; for they were piled up and became the first-formed island for the Japanese archipelago (see Sect. III): for drops to fall down, or for leaves to fall into drops (of wine), must therefore surely be a good omen rather than a crime. Conformably with the hesitating nature of her allusion, the maiden leaves it quite uncertain what is conceived of as "going curdle-curdle" in the present instance. In fact, neither must the thought be pressed too far, nor the sentence searched too rigorously from a grammatical point of view. Such intentional vagueness is one of the specific characteristics of a great deal of the poetry of Japan. The words "the tradition of the thing, <a name="page_405"><font size="1" color="green">p. 405</font></A> too, this!", which conclude the poem, are obscure in another and more usual sense; but, having been already treated of in Note 4 to Sect. XXIV, they need not detain us here. They do not affect the sense of the rest of the poem. Two points more remain to be noticed: one is that the word <i>Mihe</i> and <i>hi no mi hado</i> ("august gate of <A HREF="errata.htm#105">cham&aelig;cyparis</A>") are respectively preceded by the Pillow-Words <i>ariginu no</i>, whose signification is disputed, and <i>makisaku</i>, which signifies "splitting true trees;" the other, that the original of the word "glistens" near the commencement of the poem only has that sense if, following <A HREF="errata.htm#106">Moribe</A>, we identify <i>hi-gakeru</i> with <i>hi-kagayakeru</i>. As it stands, the word <i>kakeru</i> lends itself more naturally to the interpretation of "sets." But the logical difficulty of accepting the phrase "where the sun sets" in such a context, where on the contrary some phrase of good omen is alone appropriate, seems greater than the philological difficulty of deriving <i>hi-gakeru</i> by a process of contraction from <i>hi-kagayakeru</i>. The designation of the Emperor or Heir Apparent by the title of "august child of the high-shining sun" has been met with before, and needs no explanation when the solar ancestry claimed by the Japanese monarchs is called to mind.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2348"></A><A HREF="kj167.htm#fr_2353">403:5</A> The gist of this Song, which must be supposed to be addressed to the female attendant, is simply: "Present the goblet full of liquor to the Emperor."&#8212;In accordance with the rules of Japanese construction the Imperative "present," which is the chief Verb of the sentence, comes last, and is preceded by the comparison of the Monarch to the leaves and flowers of the camellia-tree, while the comparatively unimportant words describing the position of the tree come at the beginning. Thus in a literal English translation the climax is necessarily spoilt through the reversal of the order of the words. The "broad-leafed camellia "has already appeared in Sect. CXXIII, Note 11, the "house of new licking" has been explained in the note immediately preceding the present one, and the incomprehensible concluding exclamation has been discussed in Sect. XXIV, Note 4. The "high metropolis "of Yamato is of course the then capital. There is however some doubt whether the word take-chi, which is here thus rendered, should not rather be considered as a proper name. The expression <i>ko-dakaru</i>, rendered "high-timbered." is also doubtful. Motowori interprets it simply as "slightly high." Moribe seems right in explaining the word <i>tsukasa</i> to mean "a mound."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2349"></A><A HREF="kj167.htm#fr_2354">403:6</A> This Song is here out of place, and is supposed by Motowori to have been composed, not by the Emperor, but by some court-lady who was absent from the feast. The meaning simply is: "Ah yes," &#8217;tis to-day that the court ladies are "drinking their fill of rice-liquor[.&#8212;and <a name="page_406"><font size="1" color="green">p. 406</font></A> would that I were with them)!"&#8212;The picture here presented of the manners of the court is not attractive; but the comparison of the ladies' appearance with that of various birds is quaint. The commentators tell us that <A HREF="errata.htm#107">the</A> appropriateness of the use of the word "scarfs" as applied to the quail lies in the peculiar plumage of that bird, which makes it look as if it had a scarf on. "Having put their tails together" means "standing with their trains in a row." The epithet "yard "applied to the sparrows paints the habits of that bird. The words "great palace" are in the original preceded by the Pillow-Word <i>momoshiki no</i>, whose signification is disputed. After lines</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px"><i>Kefu mo ka mo</i><br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Saka-mi-dzuku-rashi</i>.</div></p>  
<p>rendered "may perhaps to day be truly steeped in liquor," Moribe would like to consider the lines</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">Asu ma koma<br> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Saka-mi-dzuku-rashi</i>,</div></p>  
<p><i>i.e.</i>, "may perhaps to-morrow be truly steeped in liquor" to have been accidentally omitted. There is no doubt but that their insertion would add to the effect of the poem from the point of view of style.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2350"></A><A HREF="kj167.htm#fr_2355">403:7</A> <A NAME="img_40600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/40600.jpg">, read <i>ama-koto-uta</i>. This expression is altogether obscure, and the commentators differ in their interpretations of it. Mabuchi, following the characters, sees in them an allusion to the words "august child of the high-shining sun" which recurs in each of the three Songs thus bracketed together. Motowori thinks that <i>ama-koto</i> should be regarded as standing for <i>amari-goto</i> (<A NAME="img_40601"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/40601.jpg">) "surplus words," in allusion to the meaningless <i>refrain</i> with which the Songs in question terminate. Other Songs, however, which end in the same manner, are not thus designated. Moribe's exegesis, though founded on Motowori's is preferable to it. Accepting <i>ama-koto</i> as a contraction of <i>amari-goto</i>, he would take the second half of the compound in the sense of "things," not "words" (<A NAME="img_40602"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/40602.jpg"> not <A NAME="img_40603"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/40603.jpg">), and regard the whole as signifying that the Songs were composed or sung after the conclusion of the actual feast. Against this view must be set the fact that the Chinese characters lend it no support. The translator, has, as usual when in doubt, preferred to adhere to the sense given by the characters.</P>
<p><HR>

<HEAD>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="../../css/marg.css">
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_407"><font size="1" color="green">p. 407</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXI.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU (PART XII.&#8212;SONGS BY THE EMPEROR AND PRINCESS WODO).]</h2>  
<p>On the day of this copious feast the Heavenly Sovereign, when Princess Wodo of Kasuga&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2356"></A><A HREF="#fn_2351"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> presented to him the great august liquor, sang again, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! the grandee's daughter holding the excellent flagon! [If] thou hold the excellent flagon, hold it firmly! Hold it quite firmly, more and more firmly, child holding the excellent flagon."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2357"></A><A HREF="#fn_2352"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>This is a Cup Song.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2358"></A><A HREF="#fn_2353"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Then Princess Wodo presented [326] a Song. That Song said:</p>  
<p>"Would that I were [thou,] the lower board of the arm-rest whereon our great lord who tranquilly carries on the government stands leaning at morn, stands leaning at eve! Oh! mine elder brother!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2359"></A><A HREF="#fn_2354"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A></p>  
<p>This is a Quiet Song.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2351"></A><A HREF="kj168.htm#fr_2356">407:1</A> <i>Kasuga no Wodo-hime</i>. See Sect. CLIX. Note I.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2352"></A><A HREF="kj168.htm#fr_2357">407:2</A> This Song is simply a reiterated, and playful injunction to the maiden to hold firmly the flagon containing the intoxicating liquor; and Motowori is, as Moribe remarks, putting more into the words than they are really meant to convey, when he says that they imply <i>praise</i> on the Monarch's part,&#8212;The English words "grandee's daughter" represent the Japanese <i>omi no omina</i>, a somewhat remarkable expression, which is interpreted by Motowori to signify "attendant maiden." The translator prefers the view propounded in Moribe's comment on this Song, and has therefore adopted it. The expression is in the original preceded by the untranslatable Pillow-Word <i>minasossoku</i> (Moribe reads the last syllable with the <i>nigori</i>,&#8212;<i>gu</i>), The word rendered "excellent flagon" is <i>ho-dari</i>, the first element of the compound being explained by the commentators in the sense of "excellent," <i>i.e.</i>, "big," while the second is the same as the modern word <i>taru</i>, "a cask." In ancient times, however, the signification of <i>tari</i> or <i>taru</i> was that of a vessel to pour liquor from, not <a name="page_408"><font size="1" color="green">p. 408</font></A> to store liquor in,&#8212;<i>i.e.</i>, a flagon, not a cask. The words "quite firmly, more and more firmly" represent the Japanese <i>shita-gataku ya-gataku</i> according to Moribe's exegesis. Motowori's interpretation of them in the sense of "[take the] bottom firmly and the top firmly" is less acceptable.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2353"></A><A HREF="kj168.htm#fr_2358">407:3</A> Thus does the editor of 1687, who is followed by Moribe, understand the original expression <i>uki-uta</i>. Motowori's interpretation, "Floating Song," seems less good.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2354"></A><A HREF="kj168.htm#fr_2359">407:4</A> So enamoured is the maiden of the Sovereign that she <A HREF="errata.htm#108">would</A> fain be even the board of the arm-rest on which he leans.&#8212;The expression "lower board "is misleading, for it refers simply to the self-evident fact that the board forming the top of the little low table used as an arm-rest by one squatting on his mat is below the arm, as whose support it serves. The words "stands leaning" must probably be understood to signify "sits" or "squats leaning." The expression "our great lord who tranquilly carries on the government" is a frequently recurring periphrasis for the word "Emperor," and has been explained in Sect. LXXXVII, Note 4. The words "at morn" and "at eve" are literally in the original "at morning doors" and "at evening doors," the reference being to the fact that the doors of a house are respectively opened and closed in the early morning and at nightfall. The exclamation "Oh! mine elder brother" is addressed to the board of the arm-rest. <i>Conf</i>. the first Song in Sect LXXXIX, where Yamato-take apostrophizes a pine-tree in the same terms.</P>

<p><a name="page_409"><font size="1" color="green">p. 409</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXIII.&#8212;EMPEROR SEI-NEI (PART I.&#8212;SEARCH FOR A SUCCESSOR TO HIM).]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Shiraka-no-oho-yamato-ne-ko dwelt at the palace of Mikakuri at Ihare,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2361"></A><A HREF="#fn_2356"><FONT SIZE="1">1a</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire. This Heavenly Sovereign had no Empress, and likewise no august children. So the Shiraka-Clan&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2362"></A><A HREF="#fn_2357"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> was established as his august proxy. So after the Heavenly Sovereign's decease, there was no King to rule the Empire. Thereupon, on enquiry [being made] for a King who should rule the sun's succession, Oshinumi-no-iratsume,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2363"></A><A HREF="#fn_2358"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> another name for whom was Princess Ihi-toyo, younger sister of Prince Ichinobe-oshiha-wake,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2364"></A><A HREF="#fn_2359"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> [was found to be] residing at the palace of Tsunusashi at Takaki in Oshinumi in Kadzuraki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2365"></A><A HREF="#fn_2360"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2356"></A><A HREF="kj170.htm#fr_2361">409:1a</A> For Ihare see Sect. XLIII, Note 26. <i>Mika-kuri</i> signifies "jar-chestnut."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2357"></A><A HREF="kj170.htm#fr_2362">409:2</A> <i>Shiraka-be</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2358"></A><A HREF="kj170.htm#fr_2363">409:3</A> In Sect. CXXXI (Note 7) this name appears as <i>Awomi-no-iratsume</i>. Both <i>Awomi</i> and <i>Oshinumi</i> are supposed to be names of places. The latter is the name of a district in Yamato. Its etymology is obscure. For <i>Ihi-toyo</i> see Sect. CXXXI, Note 8.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2359"></A><A HREF="kj170.htm#fr_2364">409:4</A> See Sect. CXXXI (Note 5), where however the title of <i>wake</i> ("Lord") is omitted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2360"></A><A HREF="kj170.htm#fr_2365">409:5</A> For <i>Kadzuraki</i> see Sect. LV, Note 1, and for Oshinumi see Note 3 to the present Sect. <i>Takaki</i> seems to signify "high castle," while <i>Tsunusashi</i> is obscure. (See Motowori's remarks on these two names in Vol. XLIII, p. 3 of his Commentary.)</P>

<HTML>
<HEAD>
<link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="../../css/marg.css">
<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">
<META name="description" content="The Kojiki, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], full text etext at sacred-texts.com">
<META name="keywords" content="Kojiki Japan Shinto Mythology Legend Folklore Text Scripture Emperor Empress Chronology">
<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume III: Section CLXIV.&#8212;Emperor Sei-nei (Part II.&#8212;Princes Ohoke and Woke are Discovered)</TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="index.htm">Index</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj170.htm">Previous</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj172.htm">Next</A>&nbsp;
<HR><A HREF="http://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/B0028Y4SZY/internetsacredte">Buy this Book at Amazon.com</A></CENTER>
<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXIV.&#8212;EMPEROR SEI-NEI (PART II.&#8212;PRINCES OHOKE AND WOKE ARE DISCOVERED).]</h2>  
<p>Then Wodate, Chief of the Mountain Clan&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2366"></A><A HREF="#fn_2361"><FONT SIZE="1">1b</FONT></A> when appointed governor of the land of Harima, arrived just at</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_410"><font size="1" color="green">p. 410</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> [328] [the time of] a rejoicing for the new cave of an inhabitant called Shizhimu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2367"></A><A HREF="#fn_2362"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Hereupon, when the feasting and the drinking were at their height, they all danced in turn. So two young children&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2368"></A><A HREF="#fn_2363"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> [employed] to light the fire sat beside the furnace.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2369"></A><A HREF="#fn_2364"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> These young children were made to dance. Then one of the young children said: "Do thou the elder brother dance first." The elder brother likewise said: "Do thou the younger brother dance first." When they thus yielded to each other, the people who were met together laughed at their manner of yielding to each other.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2370"></A><A HREF="#fn_2365"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> So at last the elder brother danced, [and when he had] finished, the younger when about to dance chanted, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"On the bamboos on the mountain-slopes, behind which are hidden as soon as they appear my warrior-mate's sword, on whose hilt red earth was daubed, for whose cord red cloth was cut, and his red flags that were set up!:&#8212;Beggarly descendants of King Ichinobe-no-oshiha, august child of the Heavenly Sovereign Izaho-wake, who ruled the Empire as it were cutting the [bamboos'] roots and bending down their extremities, and like playing on an eight-stringed lute!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2371"></A><A HREF="#fn_2366"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>[329] Then forthwith Chief Wodate, starting at the sound [of these words], and rolling off his couch,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2372"></A><A HREF="#fn_2367"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> drove away the people of the cave; and having set the two&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2373"></A><A HREF="#fn_2368"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> princes [one] on his left knee and [the other] on <A HREF="errata.htm#109">his</A> right and wept and lamented, he collected the people together, and having built a temporary palace, and set [the two princes]</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_411"><font size="1" color="green">p. 411</font></A></p>  
<p>to dwell in that temporary palace, he sent a courier up [to the capital]. Thereupon their aunt, Queen Ihi-toyo, delighted to hear [the news], made them come up to the palace.</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2361"></A><A HREF="kj171.htm#fr_2366">409:1b</A> <i>Yama-be no murazhiwodate</i>. <i>Yama-be</i> has already appeared. <i>Wo-date</i> signifies "small shield."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2362"></A><A HREF="kj171.htm#fr_2367">410:2</A> For this name see Sect. CXLIX, Note 5. A similar festival at the inauguration of a new cave is mentioned in Sect. LXXX.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2363"></A><A HREF="kj171.htm#fr_2368">410:3</A> Motowori's vain attempts to reconcile the dates with this statement of Princes Ohoke and Woke being "young children "at this time, after an interval of two reigns since the death of their father, will be found in Vol. XLIII, pp. 10-11, of his Commentary.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2364"></A><A HREF="kj171.htm#fr_2369">410:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, as the commentators <A HREF="errata.htm#110">suppose</A>, a place or vessel holding a light with which to kindle other lights for the feast. The word can scarcely here have its common signification of a "kitchen-range."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2365"></A><A HREF="kj171.htm#fr_2370">410:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, at the fact of their being so courteous to each other.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2366"></A><A HREF="kj171.htm#fr_2371">410:6</A> This so-called "chant,"&#8212;it is not a Song, because not in metre, and is accordingly not transcribed syllabically,&#8212;is at first sight so difficult as to seem to defy translation, and to make the student apply to the whole of his interpretation Motowori's closing remark on his exegesis of one of phrases contained in it,&#8212;"this is mere guess-work, and the text demands further consideration." A little inspection shows, however, that the drift of the words is by no means so inscrutable as its partly ideographic and partly phonetic transcription makes it appear. The first part down to the colon and dash is a "Preface" to the second, the "Pivot" joining the two parts in the original Japanese being the word "bamboos." The laws of English construction unfortunately do not admit of the force of the <A HREF="errata.htm#111">original</A>, which entirely depends on the position of the words, being rendered into our language. The appropriateness of the Preface to the body of the chant rests on the consideration that the bright articles mentioned in it, viz., the sword painted and decorated with red streamers (or perhaps tied on with a red sash) and also the red banners are easily <i>hidden</i> behind the thick leaves of a bamboo-grove, just as the Imperial origin of the two young Princes was hidden beneath the vile office which they filled in Shizhimu's household. The clause "cutting the [bamboos'] roots and bending down their extremities" forms the chief difficulty. Indeed the word "roots" is supplied by Motowori, and his interpretation of the phrase is merely tentative. We may, <a name="page_412"><font size="1" color="green">p. 412</font></A> however, until some better explanation is offered, see in it a reference to the energetic manner in which the Empire was ruled by the young princes grandfather, the Emperor Izaho-wake (i-chi&#363;), or else perhaps by their father Ichinobe-no-Oshiha. This latter view is preferred by Motowori, though according to the history Ichinobe-no-oshiha never actually ascended the throne. The position of the Verb "ruled" in the Japanese text permits of either interpretation. The comparison of the government of the Empire to playing on a lute is poetical and appropriate. It <A HREF="errata.htm#112">should</A> be noticed that in the Japanese text the construction of the sentence forming the main body of the chant is the reverse of what it is made to appear to be in the translation. The words "beggarly descendants," by which, as a climax, the singer reveals his own and his brother's illustrious descent, therefore come last of all and produce on Wodate the startling effect which we read of in the next sentence.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2367"></A><A HREF="kj171.htm#fr_2372">410:7</A> Or, "seat." In ancient times each person in a room sat on a special mat, and it is that small mat which is here meant.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2368"></A><A HREF="kj171.htm#fr_2373">410:8</A> The Numeral is accompanied by the Auxiliary <i>hashira</i>, properly used for gods and goddesses.</P>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  
<p><a name="page_412"><font size="1" color="green">p. 412</font></A> [330]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXV.&#8212;EMPEROR SEI-NEI (<A HREF="errata.htm#113">PART III</A>.&#8212;THE GRANDEE SHIBI).&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2374"></A><A HREF="#fn_2369"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A>]</h2>  
<p>So when the government of the Empire was about to be assumed,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2375"></A><A HREF="#fn_2370"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> the Grandee Shibi,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2376"></A><A HREF="#fn_2371"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> ancestor of the Grandees of Heguri&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2377"></A><A HREF="#fn_2372"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> mixed in the Songs, and took the hand of the beautiful person whom His Augustness Woke was about to wed. This maiden was a daughter of one of the Headmen of Uda,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2378"></A><A HREF="#fn_2373"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and her name was Ofuwo.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2379"></A><A HREF="#fn_2374"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> Then His Augustness Woke likewise mixed in the Song-Hedge.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2380"></A><A HREF="#fn_2375"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> Thereupon the Grandee Shibi sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">(iv) "The further fin of the roof of the great palace is bent down at the corner."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2381"></A><A HREF="#fn_2376"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>When he had thus sung, and requested the conclusion</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_413"><font size="1" color="green">p. 413</font></A></p>  
<p>of the Song, His Augustness Woke sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">(v) "It is on account of the great carpenter's [331] awkwardness that it is bent down at the corner."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2382"></A><A HREF="#fn_2377"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then the Grandee Shibi sang again, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">(viii)"The great lord, on account of the magnanimity of his heart, does not enter and stand in the eight-fold hedge of branches of the child of a grandee."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2383"></A><A HREF="#fn_2378"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Hereupon the Prince sang again, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">(i) "Looking on the breakers of the briny current, I see my spouse standing by the fin of the tunny that comes sporting."</div></p>  
<p>Then the Grandee Shibi, getting more and more angry sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">(ix) "[Though] the eight-fold hedge of branches of the Prince the Great Lord be made fast at eight places, be made fast all round, &#8217;tis a hedge that shall be cut, &#8217;tis a hedge that shall be burnt."&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2384"></A><A HREF="#fn_2379"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Then the Prince again sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">(ii) "Oh fisherman that spearest the tunny, the great fish! He being [there], thou must be sad at heart, tunny-spearing fisherman!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2385"></A><A HREF="#fn_2380"><FONT SIZE="1">12</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Having thus sung, the feast was concluded at dawn, [332] and they all retired. Next morning the two Deities,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2386"></A><A HREF="#fn_2381"><FONT SIZE="1">13</FONT></A> His Augustness Ohoke and His Augustness Woke, took counsel, saying: "All the people of the Court go to Court in the morning, and assemble at Shibi 's gate at noon. So&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2387"></A><A HREF="#fn_2382"><FONT SIZE="1">14</FONT></A> Shibi must surely now be sleeping, and,</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_414"><font size="1" color="green">p. 414</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> [333] moreover there will be nobody at the gate. So unless it be now, it were hard to plot against him,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2388"></A><A HREF="#fn_2383"><FONT SIZE="1">15</FONT></A>&#8212;and forthwith they at once raised an army, and beleaguered the house of the Grandee Shibi, and slew him.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_415"><font size="1" color="green">p. 415</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2369"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2374">412:1</A> <a name="page_414"><font size="1" color="green">p. 414</font></A> The student should compare the version of the story in this Sect. with that give in the "Chronicles of Japan," where it is placed some years later at the commencement of the reign of the Emperor Mu-retsu, and not only do many of the details disagree, but the arrangement and number of the Songs is different. It is impossible to make a consistent whole out of the story as here given; so, while noticing the linguistic peculiarities of each of the Songs in the order in which they appear in the present text, the translator has thought it advisable, following Moribe, to give in Note 12 a consistent scheme of interpretation for the whole. The small Roman numbers placed in brackets at the commencement of each Song indicate its place in the text as restored by Moribe.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2370"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2375">412:2</A> By one or other of the two Princes Ohoke and Woke. "Each," we are afterwards told, "ceded the Empire to the other," and it therefore remained for some time uncertain which was to be the Sovereign.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2371"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2376">412:3</A> <i>Shibi no omi</i>. In some of the Songs that follow there is a play on the identity of this name with that of the tunny-fish (<i>shibi</i>). But whether that be really the derivation it is difficult to ascertain.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2372"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2377">412:4</A> <i>Heguri no omi</i>. Conf. Sect. LXI, Note 45.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2373"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2378">412:5</A> <i>Uda no obito-ra</i>. <i>Uda</i> is the name of a place in Yamato.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2374"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2379">412:6</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "big fish." But see the remark on this name in Note 12.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2375"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2380">412:7</A> <i>Uta-gaki</i>. The derivation of this curious expression is disputed; but the meaning seems to be "strophic" or "choric song," or "a place where singing in which more than one takes part is going on."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2376"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2381">412:8</A> In this Song the "further fin" (<i>woto tsu hata-de</i>, explained by the characters <A NAME="img_41400"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/41400.jpg"> or <A NAME="img_41401"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/41401.jpg"> is supposed to signify a pent-roof, or the eaves of the roof, or else an out-house connected by a slanting roof with the main building. The "great palace" is the palace of Prince Woke.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2377"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2382">413:9</A> The "great carpenter" is the carpenter employed to build the roof above-mentioned.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2378"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2383">413:10</A> The "eight-fold hedge of branches" is simply a "hedge," and the "child of a grandee" the Grandee Shibi himself.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2379"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2384">413:11</A> <a name="page_415"><font size="1" color="green">p. 415</font></A> The words "made fast" refer to the tying of the fence at certain places to give it strength. If we accepted Moribe's emendation of the final Verb <i>yakemu</i>, "burn," to <i>yaremu</i>, we should have to translate the last clause thus: "&#8217;tis a fence that shall be broken."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2380"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2385">413:12</A> "The great fish" (<i>ofuwo yo shi</i>) is the Pillow-Word for <i>shibi</i>, "tunny." The word "he" (which might also be rendered "<i>it</i>,"&#8212;the original being (<i>so</i>) must be taken to refer both to the fish itself and to the Grandee Shibi (<i>i.e.</i>, the grandee Tunny), who bore its name.&#8212;Following Moribe's acceptable restoration of the original story, which is founded on a comparison of the text of these "Records" with that of the "Chronicles of Japan," we find that in the first Song of the series the young Prince half jokingly remarks on the fact of the Grandee Shibi appearing in public with the damsel who was to have been his (the Prince's) bride. Shibi's name, which, as already stated, signifies "tunny," furnishes the occasion for the marine metaphors borrowed from the current and the breakers. Shibi's answer (Song II,&#8212;in the "Records" wrongly ascribed to the prince), takes up the same strain, but in a more <A HREF="errata.htm#114">daunting</A> tone: the prince is likened to a fisherman who would fain make a futile attempt to spear the great tunny, and his (the tunny's, <i>i.e.</i>, the Grandee Shibi's) presence must indeed be pain and grief to him. In a third Song. which is given in the "Chronicles," but not in the "Records," the prince retorts that he relies on his good sword to win the girl for him in the end, and in Song IV the Grandee jeers at the dilapidated condition of his palace, and by implication at the sorry state of his fortunes,&#8212;a taunt to which the prince replies in Song V by saying that if the palace is dilapidated, and the Empire in disorder, the fault belongs to none other than to the Grandee <A HREF="errata.htm#115">himself</A>. Songs VI and VII, which are not found in the "Records," only serve to continue the growing war of words, which in Song VII (in the "<A HREF="errata.htm#116">Records</A>" wrongly attributed to the Grandee) comes to a climax by the prince exclaiming that if he does not force his way into the Grandee's mansion to seize his lady-love, it is only on account of the magnanimity of his disposition. To this the Grandee replies in Song IX (in the "Records" erroneously attributed to the prince) by a sort of <i>tu quoque</i>, vowing that he will cut and burn his way into the prince's palace. This is not the end of the dispute in the pages of the "Chronicles," but it is all that need detain the reader of the "Records." It should, however, be mentioned that in the "Chronicles" the name of the girl is <i>Kage-hime</i>: <i>Ofuwo</i> "Big Fish," which is here given, would seem to be nothing more <a name="page_416"><font size="1" color="green">p. 416</font></A> than a nickname, which perhaps arose from the incidents of this metrics war of words.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2381"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2386">413:13</A> The word used in the original is <i>hashira</i>, the Auxiliary Numeral for Deities. It recurs at the commencement of the next Section, where however it is not convenient to translate it.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2382"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2387">413:14</A> The original here has the character <A NAME="img_41600"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/41600.jpg">, "again'' or "moreover." But this must be, as Motowori points <A HREF="errata.htm#117">to</A> a copyist's error, Almost immediately below the same character recurs where it is equally out of place. The translator has followed Motowori in rendering it the first time by "so," and the second by "surely."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2383"></A><A HREF="kj172.htm#fr_2388">414:15</A> <i>I.e.</i>, There is no time like the present for plotting against him.</P>

<p><a name="page_416"><font size="1" color="green">p. 416</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXVI.&#8212;EMPEROR SEI-NEI (PART IV.&#8212;PRINCE OHOKE CEDES THE EMPIRE TO PRINCE WOKE).]</h2>  
<p>Then each of the two Princes ceded the Empire to the other, and His Augustness Ohoke [finally] ceded it to the younger brother His <A HREF="errata.htm#118">Augustness</A> Woke, saying: "Had not Thine Augustness revealed our names when we dwelt in the house of Shizhimu in Harima, we should never have arrived at being the lords of the Empire. This is quite owing to Thine Augustness's deed. So, though I be the elder brother, do Thine Augustness rule the Empire first,"&#8212;and [with these words] he urgently ceded [his claim]. So, being unable to refuse, His Augustness Woke ruled the Empire first.</p>

<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume III: Section CLXVII.&#8212;Emperor Ken-z&#333; (Part I.&#8212;The Old Woman Oki-Me)</TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="index.htm">Index</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj173.htm">Previous</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="kj175.htm">Next</A>&nbsp;
<HR><A HREF="http://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ASIN/B0028Y4SZY/internetsacredte">Buy this Book at Amazon.com</A></CENTER>
<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXVII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEN-Z&#332; (PART I.&#8212;THE OLD WOMAN OKI-ME).]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Woke-no-ihasu-wake dwelt at the palace of Chika-tsu-Asuka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2389"></A><A HREF="#fn_2384"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and ruled the Empire for</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_417"><font size="1" color="green">p. 417</font></A></p>  
<p>eight years. The Heavenly Sovereign wedded the Queen of Naniha,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2390"></A><A HREF="#fn_2385"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> daughter of the King of Ihaki.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2391"></A><A HREF="#fn_2386"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> He had no children. At the time when this Heavenly Sovereign was searching for the august bones of the King his father, King Ichinobe,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2392"></A><A HREF="#fn_2387"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> there came out from the land of Afumi [to the palace] a poor old woman, who said: "The place where the prince's august bones are buried is specially well known to me,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2393"></A><A HREF="#fn_2388"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> and moreover [his skeleton] can be known by his august teeth." (<small>His august teeth were teeth uneven like a lily.</small>) Then people were set&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2394"></A><A HREF="#fn_2389"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A> to dig the [334] ground and search for the august bones; and the bones having been forthwith obtained, an august mausoleum was made on the mountain east of the Moor of Kaya,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2395"></A><A HREF="#fn_2390"><FONT SIZE="1">7</FONT></A> and they were interred, and the children of Kara-fukuro&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2396"></A><A HREF="#fn_2391"><FONT SIZE="1">8</FONT></A> were made to guard the august mausoleum. Afterwards the august bones were brought up [to the Capital]. So having returned up [to the Capital, the Heavenly Sovereign] sent for the old woman, praised her for having, without forgetting, kept the place in mind, and conferred upon her the name of the Old Woman Oki-me:&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2397"></A><A HREF="#fn_2392"><FONT SIZE="1">9</FONT></A> thus did he send for her into the palace, and deign to treat her with deep and wide kindness. So he built a house for the old woman to dwell in dose to the palace, and always sent for her every day. So he hung a bell by the door of the great hall, and always rang it when he wished to call the old woman. So he composed an august Song. That Song said:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Oh! the far-distant bell tinkles when she has past the moor with its low eulalias and the little valley. Oh! Oki-me must be coming!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2398"></A><A HREF="#fn_2393"><FONT SIZE="1">10</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>Hereupon the old woman said: "I am very aged, [335]</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_418"><font size="1" color="green">p. 418</font></A></p>  
<p>and would fain depart to my native land." So when the Heavenly Sovereign let her depart according to her request, he saw her off and sang, saying:</p>  
<p><div style="margin-left: 32px">"Ah Okime! Okime from Afumi! from to-morrow [onwards] wilt [thou] be hidden behind the deep mountains, and alas! not seen!"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2399"></A><A HREF="#fn_2394"><FONT SIZE="1">11</FONT></A></div></p>  
<p>&nbsp;</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_418"><font size="1" color="green">p. 418</font></A></p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2384"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2389">416:1</A> <a name="page_418"><font size="1" color="green">p. 418</font></A> See Sect. CXXXIII, Note 11.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2385"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2390">417:2</A> <i>Naniha no miko</i>. For <i>Naniha</i> see Sect. XLIV, Note 26</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2386"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2391">417:3</A> <i>Ihaki no miko</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2387"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2392">417:4</A> Who had been treacherously slain by the Emperor Y&#363;-riyaku (see Sect. CXLVIII).</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2388"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2393">417:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, says Motowori, "it is known to me, and to none besides."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2389"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2394">417:6</A> The character used is <A NAME="img_41800"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/41800.jpg">, which is more applicable to the raising of troops than to the setting to work of peasants. It seems however here to be used in the latter sense; or perhaps we should consider it to mean that people were got together.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2390"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2395">417:7</A> See Sect. CXLVIII, Note 3. Possibly the "mountain east" should be a Proper Name,&#8212;Eastern Mountain,&#8212;but it is not taken as such by Motowori.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2391"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2396">417:8</A> See Sect. CXLVIII, Note 1.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2392"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2397">417:9</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "keeping an eye." <i>q.d.</i>, on the place of burial of the Emperor's father. Grammar would lead us to expect the order of the words forming the name to be reversed thus, <i>Mo-oki</i>; but see Motowori's remarks in Vol. XLIII, p. 56.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2393"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2398">417:10</A> This Song is not comprehensible except by reference to the text of the "Chronicles," whose author gives a somewhat varying version of the story. He tells us that, as a support to the infirm old lady, the Emperor had a string or rope stretched as a sort of hand-rest along the way she was obliged to pass in order to reach the Imperial apartments, and that at the end of the rope was a bell whose tinkling notified the Emperor of her approach. The conjectural exclamation which <A HREF="errata.htm#119">closes</A> the little poem has therefore an obvious sense, which would be wanting if the bell were at the other end, as in the version here given; for the Emperor would not give expression to surprise at her approach, if he had himself just rung for her to come.&#8212;"Far-distant" is an imperfect attempt to represent the Pillow-Word <i>momo-dzutafu</i>, which here alludes to the stages <a name="page_419"><font size="1" color="green">p. 419</font></A> along which the old woman may be supposed to be travelling. The valley and the moor overgrown with short grass form an allusion to the way,&#8212;long and arduous for her,&#8212;which Oki-me had to traverse to reach the Imperial. apartments, and they contain possibly a further allusion to her <A HREF="errata.htm#120">original</A> journey to the capital.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2394"></A><A HREF="kj174.htm#fr_2399">417:11</A> The meaning of this Song is quite clear.&#8212;The second time the name Oki-me occurs, it might, instead of being as here taken as an exclamation, be made the subject of the sentence, thus: "Oki-me from Afumi will by to-morrow, etc." The words "wilt [thou]," which represent <i>ka</i> of the original Japanese may be taken either as an exclamation properly so-called, or as a sort of rhetorical interrogation whose force is simply exclamatory. The meaning comes to the same in either case, and is literally rendered by the same English words; but according to the latter view, we should have to replace the point of exclamation by a point of interrogation.</P>

<p><a name="page_419"><font size="1" color="green">p. 419</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEN-Z&#332; (PART II.&#8212;HE SLAYS THE BOAR-HERD).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign searched for the old boar-herd who had seized his august provisions at the time when he first met with adversity and was fleeing;&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2400"></A><A HREF="#fn_2395"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> and, having sought him out, sent for him up [to the Capital], beheaded him in the bed&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2401"></A><A HREF="#fn_2396"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> of the River Asuka,&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2402"></A><A HREF="#fn_2397"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> and cut the knee-tendons of all his kindred. Wherefore down to the present time his descendants, on the day when&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2403"></A><A HREF="#fn_2398"><FONT SIZE="1">4</FONT></A> they [285] come up to Yamato, always limp of their own accord. So the man's abode had been well seen and divined.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2404"></A><A HREF="#fn_2399"><FONT SIZE="1">5</FONT></A> So the place was named Shimesu.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2405"></A><A HREF="#fn_2400"><FONT SIZE="1">6</FONT></A></p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2395"></A><A HREF="kj175.htm#fr_2400">419:1</A> <a name="page_419"><font size="1" color="green">p. 419</font></A> See Sect. CXLIX.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2396"></A><A HREF="kj175.htm#fr_2401">419:2</A> Motowori would have us understand the text to mean "in the neighbourhood of the river." There is, however, no difficulty in accepting the author's statement literally, as any one who is acquainted with the broad, stony beds of Japanese rivers will readily admit.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2397"></A><A HREF="kj175.htm#fr_2402">419:3</A> <a name="page_420"><font size="1" color="green">p. 420</font></A> <i>Asuki-gaka</i>. For Asuka see Sect. CXXXIII. Note 11.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2398"></A><A HREF="kj175.htm#fr_2403">419:4</A> <i>I.e.</i>, probably "whenever."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2399"></A><A HREF="kj175.htm#fr_2404">419:5</A> <i>I.e.</i>, "discovered by augury," or else simply "found and pointed out,"&#8212;by whom does not appear.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2400"></A><A HREF="kj175.htm#fr_2405">419:6</A> The real etymology of this name is obscure, but the author's intention is to connect it with the "dividing "or "pointing out" mentioned in the preceding sentence, which is given phonetically as [<i>mi</i>] <i>shimeki</i>.</P>

<p><a name="page_420"><font size="1" color="green">p. 420</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXIX.&#8212;EMPEROR KEN-Z&#332; (PART III.&#8212;THE EMPEROR Y&#362;-RIYAKU'S MAUSOLEUM IS DISFIGURED).]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign, deeply hating the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-hatsuse, who had slain the King his father, wished to be revenged on his spirit.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2406"></A><A HREF="#fn_2401"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> So when wishing to destroy the august mausoleum of the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-hatsuse, he [was about to] send people [to execute this design], his elder brother, His Augustness Ohoke, addressed' him, saying: "To demolish this august mausoleum thou shouldst not send other people. None but myself shall go, and I will demolish it according to the Heavenly Sovereign's august heart.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2407"></A><A HREF="#fn_2402"><FONT SIZE="1">2</FONT></A> Then the Heavenly Sovereign commanded: "Make thy progress, then, according to thy decree,"&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2408"></A><A HREF="#fn_2403"><FONT SIZE="1">3</FONT></A> Wherefore His Augustness Ohoke, having proceeded down himself, slightly excavated the side of the august mausoleum, and returned up [to the capital], and reported that he had dug up and demolished it. Then the Heavenly Sovereign, astonished at the quickness of his return up, asked how he had demolished it. He replied, saying: "I slightly excavated the earth at the side of the august mausoleum." The Heavenly Sovereign said: "Wishing to be revenged on the enemy, of the King our father, I had counted on.</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p>
</p>  
<p><a name="page_421"><font size="1" color="green">p. 421</font></A></p>  
<p>the complete demolition of the mausoleum, Why hast thou [only] slightly excavated it? "He replied, saying: [337] "The reason why I did so was that the wish to be revenged on the spirit of the foe of the King our father is truly just. Nevertheless the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-hatsuse, though he were our father's foe, was still our uncle, and moreover was an Heavenly Sovereign who ruled the Empire. So if we now, simply from the consideration of his having been our father's enemy, were completely to demolish the mausoleum of an Heavenly Sovereign who ruled the Empire, after-generations would surely revile us. Meanwhile the wrongs of the King our father must not be unrevenged. So I slightly excavated the side of the mausoleum. This insult will quite suffice as a token to future ages." On his thus addressing him, the Heavenly Sovereign said: 'This also is very just, Be it as thou sayest."</p>  
<HR>
<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2401"></A><A HREF="kj176.htm#fr_2406">420:1</A> <A NAME="img_42100"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/42100.jpg">, read <i>ni tama</i> or <i>tamashihi</i>. We might also translate it by the word "ghost."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2402"></A><A HREF="kj176.htm#fr_2407">420:2</A> The respectful character <A NAME="img_42101"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/42101.jpg"> is used for this word, and again below we have the First Personal Pronoun represented by <A NAME="img_42102"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/42102.jpg">, "servant."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2403"></A><A HREF="kj176.htm#fr_2408">420:3</A> This sentence ends in the original with the characters <A NAME="img_42103"></A>
<IMG SRC="img/42103.jpg">, which it is not necessary to render into English. They imply that the speaker will come back, and report on what he has done.</P>
