CLXXI.&#8212;EMPEROR NIN-KEN.]&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2411"></A><A HREF="#fn_2406"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A></h2>  
<p>His Augustness Ohoke dwelt at the palace of Hirataka at Isono-kami, and ruled the Empire. The Heavenly Sovereign wedded Kasuga-no-oho-iratsume, the august daughter of the Heavenly Sovereign Oho-hatsuse-no-waka-take, and begot august children: Takaki-no-iratsume; next Takara-no-iratsume; next Kasubi-no-iratsume; next Tashiraka-no-iratsume; next His Grandeur Wo-hatsuse-no-waka-sazaki; next Prince Ma-waka. The child born to him by his next wife Naka-no-waku-go-no-iratsume, daughter of the Grandee <A HREF="errata.htm#121">Hitsuma (?)</A> of [338] Wani, was: Kasuga-no-yamada-no-iratsume. The august children of this Heavenly Monarch numbered seven altogether. Of these His Augustness Wo-hatsuse-no-waka-sazaki [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire.</p>

<p>His Grandeur Wo-hatsuse-no-waka-sazaki dwelt in the palace of Namiki at Hatsuse, and ruled the Empire for eight years. This Heavenly Monarch had no august children. So the Wo-hatsuse Tribe was established as</p>  
<p><a name="page_423"><font size="1" color="green">p. 423</font></A></p>  
<p>his august proxy. His august mausoleum is on the mound of Ihatsuki at Karawoka. On the death of this Heavenly Monarch there was no prince to inherit the Empire, So His Augustness Ohodo, the fifth descendant of the Heavenly Monarch Homuda, was sent for down to the land of Afumi, and married to her Augustness Tashiraka, and presented with the Empire.</p>

<HEAD>

<META HTTP-EQUIV="Content-Type" CONTENT="text/html; charset=UTF-8">

<TITLE>The Kojiki: Volume III: Section CLXXIII.&#8212;Emperor Kei-tai</TITLE>
</HEAD>
<BODY>
<CENTER>
<A HREF="../../cdshop/index.htm"><IMG SRC="../../cdshop/cdinfo.jpg" BORDER="0"></A><BR>
<A HREF="../../index.htm">Sacred Texts</A>&nbsp;
<A HREF="../index.htm">Shinto</A>&nbsp;

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXXIII.&#8212;EMPEROR KEI-TAI.]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Ohodo dwelt in the Palace of Tamaho at Ihare, and ruled the Empire. The (<small>two</small>) august children born to this Heavenly Monarch by Waka-hime, ancestress of the Dukes of Miwo, were: Oho-iratsuko, next Idzumo-no-iratsume. The (<small>two</small>) august children born to him by his next wife, Meko-no-iratsume, sister of the Chieftain Ofushi, ancestor of the Chieftains of Wohari, were: His Augustness Hiro-kuni-oshi-taka-kana-hi; next His Augustness Take-wo-hiro-kuni-oshi-tate. The (<small>one</small>) august child born to him by his next wife (<small>the Great Empress</small>) Her Augustness Tashiraka, the august daughter of the Heavenly Monarch Ohoke, was: His Augustness Ame-kuni-oshi-haruki-hiro-niha. The (<small>one</small>) august child born to him by his next wife Wo-kumi-no-iratsume, daughter of Prince Okinaga-no-mate, was: Sasage-no-iratsume. The three august children born to him by his next wife Kuro-hime, daughter of Prince Sakata-no-oho-mata, were: Kamu-saki-no-iratsume; next Mamuta-no-iratsume; next Uma-tsuta-no-iratsume. The (<small>three</small>) august children born to him by his next wife Seki-hime, daughter of Womochi Grandee of Mamuta were: Mamuta-no-oho-iratsume; next Shira-saka-no-iku-hi-no-iratsume; next Wo-nu-no-iratsume, another name for whom is Naga-me-hime. The (<small>four</small>) children born to him by his [339]</p>  
<p><a name="page_424"><font size="1" color="green">p. 424</font></A></p>  
<p>next wife Yamato-hime, younger sister of Katabu Duke of Miwo, were: <A HREF="errata.htm#123">Oho-iratsume (?)</A>; next Prince Maroko; next Prince Mimi; next Aka-hime-no-iratsume. The (<small>three</small>) children born to him by his next wife Abe-no-haye-hime, were: Waka-ya-no-iratsume; next Tsubura-no-iratsume; next Prince Adzu. The august children of this Heavenly Monarch numbered nineteen in all (seven Kings and twelve Queens). Of these His Augustness Ame-kuni-oshi-haruki-hiro-niha [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire; next His Augustness Hiro-kuni-oshi-take-kana-hi ruled the Empire; the next, Queen Sasage, presided at the temple of the Deity of Ise. In this august reign Ihawi, Lord of Tsukushi, was disobedient to the Imperial Decrees, and was exceedingly disrespectful. Soy the Great Chieftain Mononobe-no-arakawi and the Chieftain Ohotomo-no-kanamura were both sent to slay Ihawi.&nbsp;<A NAME="fr_2412"></A><A HREF="#fn_2407"><FONT SIZE="1">1</FONT></A> The august years of this Heavenly Monarch were forty-three. His august mausoleum is at Awi in Mishima.</p>  
<p>
</p>

<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXXV.&#8212;EMPEROR SEN-KUWA.]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Take-wo-hiro-kuni-oshi-tate dwelt in the Palace of Ihorinu at Hinokuma, and ruled the Empire.</p>  
<p><a name="page_425"><font size="1" color="green">p. 425</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> The august children born to this Heavenly Sovereign by his wife Her Augustness Tachi-bana-no-naka-tsu-hime, the august daughter of the Heavenly Sovereign Ohoke, were: Her Augustness Ishi-hime; next Her Augustness Wo-ishi-hime; next King Kura-no-waka-ye. The august children born to him by his next wife, Kafuchi-no-waku-go-hime, were: King Honoho; next King Weha. The august children of this Heavenly [340] Sovereign numbered altogether five (<small>three Kings and two Queens</small>). So King Honoho (<small>was the ancestor of the Dukes Shihida.</small>) Prince Weha (<small>was the ancestor of the Dukes of Wina and of the Dukes of Tajihi.</small>)</p>  
<p><HR>

<HR>
<P ALIGN="CENTER"><FONT SIZE="-1" COLOR="GREEN"><A HREF="index.htm"><IMG SRC="img/tease.jpg"></A><BR><I>The Kojiki</I>, translated by Basil Hall Chamberlain, [1919], at sacred-texts.com</FONT></P><HR></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXXVI.&#8212;EMPEROR KIM-MEI.]</h2>  
<p>The Heavenly Sovereign Ame-kuni-oshi-haruki-hiro-niha dwelt in the Great Palace of Shikishima, and ruled the Empire. The (<small>three</small>) august children born to this Heavenly Sovereign by his wife, Her Augustness Ishi-hime, the august daughter of the Heavenly Sovereign Hi-no-kuma, were: King Yata; next His Augustness Nu-na-kura-tama-shiki; next King Kasanuhi. The (<small>one</small>) august child born to him by his next wife Her Augustness Wo-ishi-hime, younger sister [of the first one], was: King Kami. The (<small>three</small>) august children born to him by his next wife Nukako-no-iratsume, daughter of the Grandee Hitsuma of Kasuga, were: Kasuga-no-yamada-no-iratsume; next King Maroko; next King Soga-no-kura. The (<small>thirteen</small>) children born to him by his next wife Kitashi-hime, daughter of the Prime Minister the Noble Inawe of Soga were: His Augustness Tachibana-no-toyo-hi; next his younger sister Queen Ihakumo; next King Atori; next</p>  
<p><a name="page_426"><font size="1" color="green">p. 426</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> Her Augustness Toyo-mike-kashiki-ya-hime; next King Mata-maroko; next King Oho-yake; next King Imigako; next King [of?] Yamashiro; next his younger sister Queen Oho-tomo; next King Sakurawi-no-yumi-hari; next King Manu; next King Tachibana-moto-no-waku-go; next King Tone. The five august children born to him by his next wife Wo-ye-hime, aunt of Her Augustness Kitashi-hime, were: King Umaki; next King Kadzuraki; next King Hashi-bito-no-ana-ho-be; next King Saki-kusa-be-no-ana-ho-be, another name for whom was Sume-irodo; next His Augustness Hatsuse-be-no-waka-sazaki. Altogether the august children of this Heavenly Sovereign numbered twenty-five Kings and Queens. Of these His Augustness Nu-na-kura-futo-tama-shiki [was he who afterwards] ruled the Empire. Next His Augustness Tachibana-no-toyo-hi ruled the Empire. Next Her Augustness Toyo-mike-hashiki-ya-hime ruled the Empire. Next His Augustness Hatsusebe-no-waka-sazaki ruled the Empire. In all there were four Kings and Queens that ruled the Empire.</p>

<p>[341]</p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXXVII.&#8212;EMPEROR BI-DATSU.]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki dwelt in the Palace of Wosada, and ruled the Empire for fourteen years. The (<small>eight</small>) children born to this Heavenly Sovereign by his wife, his half-sister Her Augustness Toyo-mike-kashiki-ya-hime, were: King Shidzu-kahi, another name for whom was Kahi-dako; next King Takeda, another name for whom was King Wo-kahi; next King Woharita; next King Umori; next King Wohari; next</p>  
<p><a name="page_427"><font size="1" color="green">p. 427</font></A></p>  
<p><span class="contnote"><FONT SIZE=-2 COLOR=GREEN>[paragraph continues]</FONT></span> King Tame; next King Sakurawi-no-yumi-hari. The (<small>two</small>) august children born to him by his next wife Wo-kuma ko-no-iratsume, daughter of the Headman Ohoka of Ise, were: Her Augustness Futo-hime; next Queen Takara, another name for whom was Queen Nukade-hime. The (<small>three</small>) august children born to him by his next wife Her Augustness Hiro-hime, daughter of King Okinaga-no-made, were: King Osako-no-hiko-hito, another name for whom was King Maroko; next King Saka-nobori; next King Uji. The (<small>four</small>) august children born to him by his next wife Omina-ko-no-iratsume, daughter of Kasuga-no-naka-tsu-waku-go, were: King Naniha; next King Kuhada; next King Kasuga; next King Oho-mata. Of the august children of this Heavenly Monarch,&#8212;seventeen Kings and Queens altogether,&#8212;King Hiko-hito begot by his wife his half-sister Queen Tamura, another name for whom was Her Augustness Nukade-hime, (<small>three</small>) august children, namely: the Heavenly Sovereign that ruled the Empire from the Palace of Wokamoto; next King Nakatsu; next King Tara. The (<small>two</small>) august children born to him by his next wife, Queen Ohomata, younger sister of King Aya, were: King Chinu; next his younger sister Queen Kuhada. The (<small>two</small>) august children born to him by his next wife his half-sister Princess Yumi-hari, were: King Yamashiro; next Queen Kasanuhi,&#8212;altogether seven Kings and Queens, The august mausoleum [of the Heavenly Sovereign Nuna-kura-futo-tama-shiki] is at Shinaga in Kafuchi.</p>

<p><a name="page_428"><font size="1" color="green">p. 428</font></A></p>  <h2 align="center">[SECT. CLXXVIII.&#8212;EMPEROR Y&#332;MEI.]</h2>  
<p>His Augustness Tachibana-no-toyo-hi dwelt in the Palace of Ikenobe, and ruled the Empire for three years. The one august child born to this Heavenly Sovereign by his wife Oho-gitashi-hime, daughter of the Prime Minister the noble name, was: King Tame. The (<small>four</small>) [342] august children born to him by his next wife, his half-sister Princess Hashi-bito-no-anaho-be, were: His Augustness Uhe-no-miya-no-uma-ya-dono-toyo-to-mimi; next King Kume; next King We-kuri; next King Mamuta. The august children born to him by his next wife Ihime-no-ko, daughter of Tagima-no-kura-bito-hiro, were: King Tagima; next his younger sister Sugashiroko-no-iratsume. The august mausoleum of this Heavenly Sovereign, which had been by the borders of Lake Ihare, was afterwards removed to the middle sepulchre of Shinaga.</p>

<H3 ALIGN="CENTER">Footnotes</H3>
<P><A NAME="fn_2408"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2413">A1:1</A> There are few various readings of the text of these poems. Where any occur, the translator has been guided by the decisions of Motowori and Moribe. Occasionally these two authorities differ as to the division of the words into lines, and Moribe in particular does not hesitate to propose such emendations as seem to him necessary. The translator has in almost all cases adhered to the traditional text, but gives in foot-notes such emendations as appear worthy of notice. Moribe's division of the lines being in almost every case preferable to Motowori's, it has however here been generally adopted.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2409"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2414">A3:2</A> Motowori reads <i>Magishi&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Atane tsuki</i> as two lines.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2410"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2415">A3:3</A> Motowori reads <i>Sagiri&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;ni Tatamu zo</i> as two lines.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2411"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2416">A4:4</A> Motowori reads <i>Mitani&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Futa watarasu</i> as two lines.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2412"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2417">A5:5</A> Motowori reads <i>Uda no Taka-ki ni</i> as two lines.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2413"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2418">A5:6</A> Moribe emends <i>haru</i> to <i>hari</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2414"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2419">A5:7</A> Motowori divides these lines thus: <i>Tachi-soba no mi no&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nakeku we</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2415"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2420">A9:8</A> Motowori reads <i>gomoreru</i> as a line by itself, and similarly <i>uruhashi</i> as a line by itself.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2416"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2421">A9:9</A> Moribe restores the reading of the first line of this poem to <i>Naduzki-ta no</i>, and both he and Motowori suggest conjectural concluding lines to supplement the evidently incomplete text. Moribe's are very elegant:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Shi ga tsura no</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>I-hahi motohori</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Motohorite</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Ne-naki tohedomo</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" colspan="2" align="top" width="615">   
<p align="center"><i>Koto mo   norasanu</i></p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2417"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2422">A10:10</A> Moribe reads <i>Umi-ga ha isahofu</i> as one line. It is difficult, on any method of division, to find rhythm in this Song.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2418"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2423">A11:11</A> Motowori strangely makes <i>Mi ki no</i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Aya ni</i> into two lines. The syllable <i>ki</i> in the last line of the Song is supplied by Moribe.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2419"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2424">A11:12</A> Motowori divides these lines thus: <i>Han ami ha shi</i>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Hishi nasu</i>. He also proposes here to divide the poem in two.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2420"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2425">A12:13</A> Motowori divides these lines thus: <i>Mayo-gaki ko ni</i>.&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<i>Kaki tare</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2421"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2426">A12:14</A> The defective text of this line is restored by the help of the parallel passage in the "Chronicles."</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2422"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2427">A13:15</A> Moribe proposes to emend the second half of this poem to</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Koto nagushi we</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Kokoro-gushi we</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" colspan="2" align="top" width="615">   
<p align="center"><i>Ware wehi ni   keri</i>.</p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2423"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2428">A14:16</A> Near the commencement of this Song Motowori divides the lines thus:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Watari-ze ni</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Tateru</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Adzusa-yumi</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Mo yumi</i></p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p>and again at the end:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>I-kirazu zo kuru</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Adzusa-yumi</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" colspan="2" align="top" width="615">   
<p align="center"><i>Ma-yumi.</i></p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2424"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2429">A14:17</A> See Sect. CXXII, Note, 4 for this doubtful word.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2425"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2430">A15:18</A> Motowori divides this line in two, thus:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Habiro</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Yutsuma-tsubaki</i>.</p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2426"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2431">A16:19</A> Instead of these concluding long lines Motowori divides thus:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Wa ga mikahoshi</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Kumi ha</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Kadzuraki</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="307">   
<p><i>Taka-miya</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" colspan="2" align="top" width="615">   
<p align="center"><i>Wagihe no atari</i>.</p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2427"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2432">A16:20</A> Motowori reads the words <i>Hara ni aru</i> as a separate line.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2428"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2433">A20:21</A> Moribe, following the reading in the "Chronicles," omits the Postposition <i>no</i> after <i>Karu</i>; and Motowori reads <i>hato no</i> as a line by itself.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2429"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2434">A21:22</A> To the word <i>ashi</i> Moribe would prefix the Honorific <i>mi</i> which he finds in an old MS. The metre would gain by this emendation of the line.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2430"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2435">A21:23</A> This is Moribe's emendation of usual reading <i>ka</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2431"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2436">A22:24</A> Motowori divides <i>Ari to ihaba koso ni</i> into two lines after the Particle <i>to</i>, and Moribe omits the Particle <i>ni</i> after <i>koso</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2432"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2437">A23:25</A> It seems less good to divide thus with Motowori:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Tare zo oho-mahe ni</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Mawosu</i>,</p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p>or thus with Mabuchi:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Tare zo</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Oho-maye ni mawosu</i>.</p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2433"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2438">A24:26</A> Motowori divides the lines of this Song thus:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Yasumishishi</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Wa ga oho-kimi no</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Asobashishi</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Shishi no</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Yami-shishi no</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Utaki kashikomi</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Wa ga nike</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Noborishi</i></p>   </td>  </tr>  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Ari-wo no</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Hari no hi no yeda.</i></p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2434"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2439">A25:27</A> Motowori divides this line in two, thus:</p>  <div align="center">  <table border="0" width="75%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Mina koworo</i></p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="295">   
<p><i>Koworo ni</i></p>   </td>  </tr> </table>  </div>  
<p></P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2435"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2440">A25:28</A> Motowori divides this line in two after the word <i>ha-biro</i>.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2436"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2441">A27:29</A> Moribe's proposal to emend <i>yakemu</i> to <i>yaremu</i> would be acceptable if it were supported by the authority of any texts.</P>
<P><A NAME="fn_2437"></A><A HREF="kj188.htm#fr_2442">A27:30</A> Motowori's edition and most other texts have <i>shibi</i> as the final word, But Moribe's emendation to <i>ama</i> is necessary to the sense, and has at least the authority of one MS. to support it.</P>

<p><a name="page_A28"><font size="1" color="green">p. A28</font></A> [368]</p>  <h2 align="center">APPENDIX II.</h2>  
<p align="center">THE HITHERTO ACCEPTED CHRONOLOGY OF THE EARLY JAPANESE SOVEREIGNS MENTIONED IN THE "RECORDS OF ANCIENT MATTERS" ("<i>KO-JI-KI</i>") AND IN THE "CHRONICLES OF JAPAN" ("<i>NI-HONGI</i>" ).</p>  
<p>[This "Accepted Chronology "is contained in the first three columns of figures, whereof the first two, giving the corresponding dates according to the European reckoning are transcribed from some Comparative Chronological Tables by Mr. Ernest Satow, printed for private distribution in 1874. The ages of the monarchs in the third column are from "The Digest of the Imperial Pedigree," a work published by the Imperial Japanese Government is 1877, and therefore carrying with it the weight of authority. It might perhaps be too much to say that even its decisions are universally bowed to by the native <i>literati</i>, but the differences between various writers are all slight, and excepting on points that affect only a very few years, the chronology contained in the first three columns may justly be styled the "Accepted Chronology" both as far as natives and as far as foreigners are concerned. It will be seen that it is founded in the main on the statements contained in the "Chronicles of Japan," though sometimes differing therefrom as well as from the "Records." The fourth column contains the ages of the monarchs according to the "Records" and the fifth their ages according to the "Chronicles." The portion printed in italics, and including a little over a thousand years, is that which has been shown in Section V of the Translator's Introduction to be undeserving of credence.</p>  <table border="1" width="100%">  <tr>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="136">   
<p>&nbsp;</p>   </td>   <td valign="top" align="top" width="136">
